## Foundations & techniques

### Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)

**Added: 2026-11-22** (deepened to full Level-2/3/4 standard: 2026-11-27)

**What it is / why it matters.** The founding idea of modern high-performance CPU design: let hardware reorder instructions at run time so independent work fills the execution units instead of stalling behind a slow operation. Developed by Robert Tomasulo at IBM and first implemented in the floating-point unit of the IBM System/360 Model 91 (paper published January 1967), it is the direct ancestor of the scheduler in every out-of-order core shipping today — from Pentium Pro to Apple Silicon.

**Building blocks.** Six named pieces, and the connections between them are the design:
- **Floating-point operation stack (FLOS)** — an 8-entry in-order queue between the instruction unit and the floating-point execution unit. The instruction unit maps every FP instruction into pseudo-register-to-register form and hands it to FLOS; FLOS decode sends each instruction to a free reservation station.
- **Reservation stations ×5** — three add stations (A1–A3) and two multiply/divide stations (M/D1–M/D2), numbered 8–12 as tags. Each station holds one waiting instruction — its operation, its operand values or the tags of the producers that will supply them, and a busy bit. A station, not a central hazard unit, decides when its instruction can run: the moment all its operands are present.
- **Register renaming — tags on 4 FP registers** — System/360 has just four floating-point registers, and Tomasulo renames them in hardware: each register carries a tag naming the reservation station that will produce its next value, plus a busy bit. Two instructions writing the same register take different tags, so WAR and WAW hazards dissolve.
- **Common data bus (CDB)** — one shared broadcast bus fed by both execution units and read by every consumer: all five reservation stations, the four FP registers and the three store data buffers. A completing unit puts its result and its tag on the bus; every station waiting on that tag ingates the value in the same cycle.
- **FP add unit + multiply/divide unit** — two pipelined functional units that run concurrently: an adder and a multiply/divide unit, with planning latencies of 2 cycles for add, 6 for multiply and 18 for divide (the paper notes achieved times of 3, 12 and 2 for the same three operations in the same order). Multiply is pipelined; divide is iterative and not pipelined.
- **Load buffers (6 FLB) + store data buffers (3 SDB)** — the instruction unit maps all of storage into six floating-point buffers for load operands and three store data buffers for store data, so FLOS sees only pseudo-register-to-register operations. Tomasulo's own note: the fetch and store buffers can be considered specialized one-operand reservation stations.

**The piece that makes it special:** the tag and the bus, together. Renaming turns every register name into a tag — the number of the reservation station that will produce the value — and the CDB turns every result into a broadcast that all waiting stations hear in the same cycle. Neither half works alone: tags without the bus would still need a writeback stage to poll, and a bus without tags could not tell consumers which result is theirs. The pair dissolves false dependencies and collapses the producer-to-register-file-to-consumer round trip into a single broadcast — the two ideas every out-of-order scheduler since is built on.

**The architecture.** The Model 91 splits execution into separate fixed-point and floating-point areas, and the floating-point area has two pipelined functional units that can run concurrently: an adder and a multiply/divide unit. Around them Tomasulo built three mechanisms:

- **Reservation stations.** Each functional unit gets several input buffers (three on the adder, two on the multiply/divide unit) that each hold one waiting instruction plus its operands. An instruction is issued in order from the floating-point operation stack (FLOS) into a free reservation station even while the unit is busy, so issue never stalls on a busy unit — the station waits for its operands instead.
- **Register renaming by tags.** The machine's four architectural floating-point registers are renamed in hardware. When an instruction issues, each source operand is either copied from the register file (if ready) or replaced by the *tag* — the reservation-station number — of the instruction that will produce it. This eliminates false dependencies (WAR and WAW hazards): two instructions writing the same register no longer serialize, because only the last writer's result ever reaches the register file.
- **The common data bus (CDB).** All results travel on one broadcast bus from the functional units to every reservation station and to the register file. A waiting station watches the bus for its tag, captures the value the moment it appears, and can start executing without ever touching the register file. One bus, one broadcast, every consumer served at once.
- **Issue–execute–writeback lifecycle.** Issue is in order (from FLOS into a reservation station); execution starts whenever a station's operands are all ready, in any order; results are written back on the CDB. Loads and stores are kept in program order relative to each other, and no instruction may begin execution until earlier branches have resolved.

**Key numbers.** IBM System/360 Model 91, announced 1964, first shipped October 1967 to NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; Tomasulo's paper, "An Efficient Algorithm for Exploiting Multiple Arithmetic Units," IBM Journal of R&D, January 1967. Five reservation stations in the floating-point unit (3 add, 2 multiply/divide). Planning latencies: floating-point add 2 cycles, multiply 6 cycles, divide 18 cycles (achieved 3, 12 and 2). 60 ns machine cycle; only 30 ns of it needed for all CDB functions. Issue window roughly 14 instructions deep — nearly three times the CDC 6600 scoreboard's window of about 5. About 15 Model 91s were built (sources disagree: 10–20 are all cited).

**Signature ideas.**
1. **Hardware register renaming** — the tag system that made out-of-order execution safe, now universal in every superscalar core.
2. **Reservation stations** — distributed, per-unit waiting buffers replacing a single central hazard unit; the direct ancestor of the modern scheduler / issue queue.
3. **The common data bus** — result broadcast with tag matching, so a producer's value reaches all consumers in one cycle; the ancestor of today's bypass/forwarding networks.
4. **Dynamic scheduling without compiler help** — the hardware "looks ahead" about eight instructions and optimizes locally, so ordinary compiled code gets the speedup.

**Limits & tradeoffs.** The CDB is a single broadcast resource: only one result per cycle, so it becomes a bottleneck as functional units multiply — modern cores use multiple broadcast buses and clustered bypass networks instead. The original design had no speculation and no precise-exception machinery; out-of-order completion meant imprecise interrupts, so the machine shipped a non-overlapped mode that ran at Model 75 speed for debugging. It covered floating-point only; integer out-of-order execution came later. And it was built from discrete transistor logic (SLT modules), so the five reservation stations and the tag comparators were expensive in board area and power — the idea had to wait for VLSI to become cheap.

**Lineage.** Descended from the CDC 6600 scoreboard (1964), which centralized hazard detection; Tomasulo distributed the control into the reservation stations and added renaming. Revived and generalized in the 1990s: MIPS R10000, HP PA-8000, PowerPC 604/620, DEC Alpha 21264, Intel Pentium Pro (P6, launched 1 November 1995). Tomasulo received the Eckert–Mauchly Award in 1997 for the algorithm. Every modern out-of-order core — Zen, Apple Firestorm/Avalanche, Cortex-X, Golden Cove — is a Tomasulo machine with a reorder buffer, multiple CDBs, and speculation added on top.

**One-line summary.** Tomasulo's algorithm taught hardware to rename registers, wait in reservation stations, and broadcast results on a common bus — the three ideas that let processors execute instructions out of order, and the foundation of every high-performance CPU since.

#### Inside the signature block: The reservation station — where instructions wait for data

**Inside it.** Five stations do all the waiting. The three add stations (A1, A2, A3) feed the pipelined adder; the two multiply/divide stations (M/D1, M/D2) feed the multiply/divide unit. Each station is a small named slot holding one instruction: the operation, a sink tag naming the register it will write, source operand slots that hold either a 64-bit value or the 4-bit tag of the producer that will supply it, and a busy bit. Issue is in order — FLOS decode places each instruction in a free station for its unit, renaming its sources to values or tags as it goes — but execution is dataflow: a station fires its instruction the cycle its operands are all present, whatever the program order says. The stations are numbered 8–12 as tags (adders 10–12, multiply/dividers 8–9), and those numbers are the whole renaming scheme: a tag is a station number. Around the stations sit the supporting buffers the paper treats as the same idea: six floating-point load buffers (FLB) and three store data buffers (SDB), which Tomasulo calls specialized one-operand reservation stations, and the 8-entry FLOS queue that feeds issue.

**Trace — one unit of work.**
1. **Decode and rename.** FLOS decode takes the next FP instruction, maps it to pseudo-register-to-register form (R1 is always one of the four FP registers), and looks up each source: a ready value is copied from the register file, an in-flight value is replaced by its producer's tag.
2. **Take a station.** The instruction is placed in a free reservation station for its unit — A1–A3 for an add, M/D1–M/D2 for a multiply or divide. The station's sink tag is recorded against the destination register, so later readers wait on this station, not on the register name.
3. **Wait, watching the CDB.** The station compares its sink and source tags against every CDB broadcast. When a matching tag appears, the station ingates the 64-bit value in the same cycle and marks that operand ready. The functional unit is untouched while the station waits.
4. **Fire when ready.** The cycle the last operand lands, the station releases the operation to its unit — an add takes 2 cycles, a multiply 6 planned (3 achieved), a divide 18 planned (12 achieved). Independent instructions in other stations fire in parallel, in any order.
5. **Broadcast and free.** The unit puts its result and its tag on the CDB; every waiting station and the register file capture it at once, and the station clears its busy bit for the next instruction. Issue never waited on execution — only on a free station.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the in-order stall: a slow divide no longer freezes the machine — independent adds and multiplies flow around it, which is why the paper's PDE loop runs 11 cycles with the CDB against 17 without. Creates two new ceilings: the window is only as deep as the hardware — 8 FLOS entries plus 5 stations, roughly 14 instructions in flight counting the ones in the units — and a station held by one stalled instruction is a station no other instruction can use, so a long-latency operation at the head of the queue still throttles issue. The direct motivation for the far larger windows — hundreds of entries — in every successor.

**Governing numbers.** 5 reservation stations (3 add, 2 multiply/divide); 8-entry FLOS; 6 floating-point load buffers; 3 store data buffers; 4 architectural FP registers; 17 four-bit tag registers; station tags numbered 8–12; planning latencies add 2 / multiply 6 / divide 18 cycles (achieved 3 / 12 / 2).

**Primary source.** Tomasulo, "An Efficient Algorithm for Exploiting Multiple Arithmetic Units", IBM J. Res. Dev. 11(1):25–33, Jan 1967 (esp. Fig. 2, Fig. 4 and the worked loop, pp. 25–33); Anderson, Earle, Goldschmidt & Powers, "The IBM System/360 Model 91: Floating-Point Execution Unit", IBM J. Res. Dev. 11(1):34–53, Jan 1967.

#### Inside the signature block: The common data bus — one broadcast, every consumer

**Inside it.** The CDB is a single shared bus, 64 bits of data plus a 4-bit tag, fed by both execution units and read by every consumer in the floating-point area: all five reservation stations, the four FP registers and the three store data buffers. It exists to collapse a round trip: without it, a result would have to be written to the register file and read back before a dependent instruction could use it, and the paper's loop shows that costs 6 cycles per iteration (17 vs 11). With it, the producer puts result and tag on the bus and every consumer that needs it takes it in the same cycle — the register file becomes one consumer among several, not the only operand source. The bus runs on the machine's 60 ns cycle, and the paper notes only 30 ns of that interval is needed for all CDB functions — the bus is not the timing bottleneck at this scale. Units request the bus when a result is ready (the paper's worked timing shows an adder requesting the CDB mid-execution), and the bus carries one result per cycle: that single-result limit is the whole arbitration problem, and the paper is explicit that the CDB can function with any number of accumulators and any number of execution units — the mechanism scales, the bandwidth does not.

**Trace — one unit of work.**
1. **A unit finishes.** An adder or the multiply/divide unit completes an operation — say an add that took 2 cycles — and requests the CDB.
2. **Result and tag go on the bus.** The unit drives its 64-bit result and its 4-bit station tag onto the bus. The 30 ns of CDB function fits inside the 60 ns cycle, so the broadcast costs no extra cycle.
3. **Every consumer compares at once.** Each active reservation station compares its sink and source tags to the CDB tag; the register file and the store data buffers do the same. A match ingates the data in the same cycle — no polling, no writeback stage, no second trip.
4. **Dependents fire next cycle.** A station whose last operand just landed releases its operation to its unit, and the chain continues: the bus is the dataflow graph executing in hardware, one broadcast at a time.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the writeback serialization: results reach consumers the cycle they are produced instead of queuing through the register file, worth about one-third on the paper's PDE loop. Creates the bottleneck that defines every later scheduler: one result per cycle on one bus, so as functional units multiply the bus saturates and the machine must add more buses, clustered bypass networks and banked register files — the exact direction P6, Alpha and every modern core took. The paper already concedes the point: the CDB can function with any number of accumulators and any number of execution units, but one bus still carries one result at a time.

**Governing numbers.** One CDB; 64-bit data + 4-bit tag; 60 ns machine cycle, 30 ns of it for CDB functions; one result per cycle; 17-cycle loop without CDB vs 11 with (about one-third faster); 5 reservation stations + 4 FP registers + 3 store data buffers all listening.

**Primary source.** Tomasulo, "An Efficient Algorithm for Exploiting Multiple Arithmetic Units", IBM J. Res. Dev. 11(1):25–33, Jan 1967 (CDB definition, p. 25; worked loop, pp. 32–33); Anderson, Earle, Goldschmidt & Powers, "The IBM System/360 Model 91: Floating-Point Execution Unit", IBM J. Res. Dev. 11(1):34–53, Jan 1967.

#### Down to the primitives: The reservation station — where instructions wait for data

Decomposed in issue order — an instruction is decoded and renamed in FLOS, takes a reservation station, waits on its tags, fires when ready, and frees the station on broadcast. The 1967 papers publish the station counts, the FLOS depth, the buffer counts, the four FP registers and the 17 four-bit tag registers, but nothing below that contract: no comparator organisation, no mux tree structure, no FLOS entry width, no gate-level detail. Where a number below is computed from published geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **Reservation-station array (operand storage)** — Five stations, each holding one instruction: the operation, a sink tag, two 64-bit operand slots (value or 4-bit tag) and a busy bit. The array is five entries deep and two operands wide; the 64-bit operand width is the paper's double-precision throughout, and the 4-bit tag width is the paper's 17 four-bit tag registers. The array's read/write port counts and its cell form are not published.
- **Tag registers (17 × 4-bit)** — One 4-bit tag register per FP register (4), per source and sink register of each of the five reservation stations (10), and per store data buffer (3) — 17 tag registers in total, four bits each, exactly as the paper counts them in Fig. 4. The tags are the station numbers 8–12 for the five stations. The register implementation (latch vs flip-flop) is not published.
- **Tag comparators (CAM-style match)** — Each active reservation station compares its sink and source tags against the tag broadcast on the CDB, and ingates the data on a match. That is up to ten 4-bit equality comparisons per broadcast (5 stations × sink + source) by arithmetic from the published counts — a CAM-style associative match, one comparator per tag field. The comparators' circuit form, matchline organisation and the number of result buses are not published.
- **Operand muxes (value-or-tag selection)** — At issue, each source operand is either copied from the register file (if ready) or replaced by its producer's tag — a 2:1 selection per operand between a 64-bit value and a 4-bit tag. At capture, a station selects between the CDB broadcast and the register file. The mux tree structure, widths and fan-in are not published.
- **FLOS queue (8-deep instruction FIFO)** — The floating-point operation stack holds up to 8 instructions waiting for issue (Fig. 1) — the in-order queue that feeds FLOS decode and the reservation stations. It is the front of the issue window: 8 FLOS entries plus 5 stations is the roughly 13–14-instruction window the machine looks ahead across. The entry width and the queue's pointer organisation are not published.
- **Load/store buffers as one-operand reservation stations** — Six floating-point load buffers (FLB) and three store data buffers (SDB) — the paper's own words: "The fetch and store buffers can be considered as specialized, one-operand reservation stations." Each holds one operand or result plus its tag and a FULL/EMPTY control bit; the load buffer's bit is set FULL by the Main Storage Control Element and EMPTY when the buffer is used. Their storage cell form is not published.
- **Control FSM + FULL/EMPTY and busy bits** — The sequencing is control logic, not datapath: a busy bit per reservation station, a busy bit per FP register (in addition to its tag), and FULL/EMPTY bits on the six load buffers, all set and cleared by FLOS decode, the storage control element and CDB broadcasts. The FSM's state count and its next-state logic are not published; the paper describes the control behaviour (decode hold-up on a busy sink register, buffer-full forwarding) without a state diagram.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the papers publish the station counts (3 add, 2 multiply/divide), the FLOS depth (8), the buffer counts (6 FLB, 3 SDB), the four FP registers and the 17 four-bit tag registers. Below that level — the internal comparator organisation, the mux tree structure, the FLOS entry width, any gate-level detail — the Model 91 papers publish nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. The Model 91 was built from discrete-transistor SLT modules, and no transistor counts are claimed for it.

#### Down to the primitives: The common data bus — one broadcast, every consumer

Decomposed in broadcast order — a unit finishes and requests the bus, drives result and tag onto it, every consumer compares at once, and dependents fire on the next cycle. The paper publishes the bus timing and the one-result-per-cycle limit, but no driver circuit, no arbitration policy and no gate-level detail. Where a number below is computed from published geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **Broadcast bus (data + tag)** — One shared bus carrying a 64-bit result and a 4-bit tag — the data path plus the tag that says whose it is. The bus runs on the 60 ns machine cycle and the paper states only 30 ns of the interval is required to perform all CDB functions, so the broadcast fits inside a cycle with time to spare. The bus width beyond data+tag, its loading and its driver count are not published.
- **Result muxes / bus drivers** — Both execution units — the adder and the multiply/divide unit — drive results onto the one bus, so each unit's output passes through a driver/mux onto the shared wires, and only one unit drives at a time. The driver circuit, the mux tree and the tri-state or wired-OR form are not published.
- **CDB request + arbitration logic** — A unit requests the CDB when its result is ready — the paper's worked timing shows an adder requesting the bus mid-execution — and one result crosses per cycle, so requests must be arbitrated. The arbitration policy (fixed priority, round-robin or otherwise) is not published, and no request-queue depth is claimed.
- **Consumer-side tag comparators** — The same CAM-style comparator primitive as the reservation-station block, replicated at every consumer: each of the five stations, the four FP registers and the three store data buffers compares its tags against the broadcast tag. Twelve consumers listen (5 + 4 + 3), each with at least one 4-bit comparator, by arithmetic from the published consumer list. The comparator circuit form is not published.
- **Sink/source pipeline registers** — Two additional registers — one sink, one source — feed each execution circuit, the paper's Fig. 1 datapath: the sink register holds the destination-side operand, the source register the incoming operand, so the unit's inputs are stable while it computes. Each is a 64-bit register by the paper's double-precision rule. Their cell form is not published.
- **Tag-valid / busy-bit control** — The precedence rule is enforced by bits, not by the bus: a floating-point register may not participate in an operation while it is the sink of another incompleted instruction — the paper's cardinal principle — implemented as the busy bit carried with each register's tag. When the producing station broadcasts, the bit clears and the register becomes usable. The bit count is published (one per register, per station, per buffer); the gating logic is not.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the paper publishes the 60 ns cycle, the 30 ns of CDB function inside it, the 64-bit double-precision operand width, the 4-bit tag width and the one-result-per-cycle limit. Below that level — the bus driver circuit, the request/arbitration policy, any gate-level detail — the paper publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing.

#### Down to the gates: The reservation station — where instructions wait for data

The Model 91 was built from IBM SLT (Solid Logic Technology) — hybrid modules of discrete transistors on ceramic substrates, not integrated standard cells — so there is no CMOS gate netlist to quote. What follows is the logical construction of each primitive in the primer's standard-cell terms, labelled standard construction throughout; the transistor counts are the textbook cells, not Model 91 facts. A gate-term search of the 1967 papers this run found no transistor, flip-flop or gate-level content.

- **Reservation-station array (operand storage)** — Storage is flip-flops: each 64-bit operand slot is 64 D flip-flops, a D flip-flop being two cross-coupled latch stages, about 20–28 transistors in a standard-cell library. Arithmetic: five stations × two operand slots × 64 bits × 20–28 transistors is 12,800–17,920 transistors of operand storage, plus the op and busy-bit flops — a large number for 1967, which is why there are only five stations. The array could equally be a small SRAM, but the paper gives no cell form, so no SRAM claim is made. Standard construction.
- **Tag registers (17 × 4-bit)** — 68 D flip-flops in total (17 registers × 4 bits), about 20–28 transistors each — 1,360–1,904 transistors by arithmetic. Each tag is a 4-bit value (station numbers 8–12 fit in four bits: 8 = 1000, 12 = 1100), and the register is written at issue and cleared on broadcast. Standard construction.
- **Tag comparators (CAM-style match)** — A 4-bit equality comparator is four XNOR gates (one per bit) feeding an AND tree — three AND gates for four bits. Per station that is two comparators (sink and source), ten comparators across the five stations, forty XNOR gates and thirty AND gates by arithmetic. At gate level this is the CAM cell's match logic (SRAM cell + XOR match) with the storage stripped out: the tag lives in a register, the comparator is pure combinational match. The matchline organisation is not published. Standard construction.
- **Operand muxes (value-or-tag selection)** — A 2:1 mux is a transmission gate per input leg (two transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree; a 64-bit 2:1 mux is 64 such legs, about 128 transistors as transmission gates by arithmetic. The issue-time selection is one such mux per operand (value vs tag); the capture selection is another. The paper does not publish the mux tree, so no total is claimed for the block. Standard construction.
- **FLOS queue (8-deep instruction FIFO)** — A queue is storage plus pointers: eight entries of flip-flop storage (the entry width is not published, so no bit total is claimed) with a 3-bit write counter and a 3-bit read counter (8 entries need 3 bits) and full/empty comparators on the pointers. A counter is D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer — a full adder is two half adders, five gates (2 XOR + 2 AND + 1 OR) — so a 3-bit counter is three flip-flops plus three full adders by arithmetic. Standard construction.
- **Load/store buffers as one-operand reservation stations** — Same construction as the station array, one operand each: six load buffers and three store data buffers, each a 64-bit flip-flop register plus a 4-bit tag register plus one FULL/EMPTY flip-flop — 64 + 4 + 1 = 69 flip-flops per buffer, 621 across the nine buffers, about 20–28 transistors each by arithmetic. The FULL bit is set by the storage control element and cleared on use — a set/reset latch, two cross-coupled NAND gates. Standard construction.
- **Control FSM + FULL/EMPTY and busy bits** — Control is a finite-state machine built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the busy bits, the FULL/EMPTY bits and the CDB tag matches. The busy bits themselves are single flip-flops — one per station, one per register, one per buffer. The FSM's state count is not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

**Honesty.** Honesty: the Model 91 papers publish the station counts, the FLOS depth, the buffer counts, the four FP registers and the 17 four-bit tag registers — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — comparator organisation, mux trees, FLOS entry width, any SLT schematic — IBM publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Every gate form above is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive from the primer's bottom layer, never a claim about the Model 91's circuits.

#### Down to the gates: The common data bus — one broadcast, every consumer

The bus at gate level is wires, drivers and comparators; as with the reservation-station block, the 1967 hardware was discrete-transistor SLT, so all gate detail here is textbook-standard construction from the primer, not a Model 91 netlist. The paper publishes the bus timing (60 ns cycle, 30 ns of CDB function) and the one-result-per-cycle limit; it publishes no driver circuit, no arbitration policy and no SLT schematic.

- **Broadcast bus (data + tag)** — A bus is wires plus drivers, not gates: 64 data wires and 4 tag wires shared by all consumers, with a driver per source. The timing is the published fact — 30 ns of the 60 ns cycle for all CDB functions — and it is a timing budget, not a gate count: the broadcast is a single-cycle transfer because the tag compare and the data ingate both fit in that 30 ns. No driver transistor count is claimed; in SLT the drivers were discrete-transistor circuits. Standard construction.
- **Result muxes / bus drivers** — Each unit's output reaches the shared wires through a driver: in standard-cell terms a tri-state buffer or a transmission-gate mux, one per bit per driver — 64 bits × 2 units = 128 driver legs by arithmetic, each a transmission gate of two transistors (256 transistors) if built as muxes. Only one unit drives at a time, so the drivers are mutually exclusive by the arbitration logic. The actual SLT driver circuit is not published. Standard construction.
- **CDB request + arbitration logic** — Arbitration is a priority encoder over the units' request lines: two requesters (adder, multiply/divide) need one bit of priority — a single AND/OR decision — but the policy (which unit wins a tie) is not published, so no encoder width beyond the two requesters is claimed. The request itself is a flip-flop set when the unit finishes and cleared when the bus is granted. Standard construction.
- **Consumer-side tag comparators** — The same 4-bit equality comparator as the station block — four XNOR gates plus a three-AND tree — replicated at every consumer: five stations × two tags, four registers × one tag, three store buffers × one tag, seventeen comparators in total by arithmetic from the published consumer list, or 68 XNOR gates and 51 AND gates. A match ingates the data into the consumer's register in the same cycle. The matchline organisation is not published. Standard construction.
- **Sink/source pipeline registers** — Two 64-bit registers per execution unit — one sink, one source — each 64 D flip-flops, about 20–28 transistors each: 128 flip-flops per unit, 256 across the two units, 5,120–7,168 transistors by arithmetic. They hold the unit's inputs stable while it computes, which is what lets the adder pipeline a new add every cycle. Standard construction.
- **Tag-valid / busy-bit control** — One flip-flop per busy bit — per register, per station, per buffer — gated by AND/OR logic against the CDB tag match: when the tag matches, the bit clears and the register becomes usable. The cardinal precedence principle (no floating-point register may participate in an operation if it is the sink of another, incompleted instruction) is, at gate level, one AND gate per register combining 'not busy' with the issue enable. The gating logic's exact form is not published. Standard construction.

**Honesty.** Honesty: the paper publishes the bus timing (60 ns cycle, 30 ns of CDB function) and the one-result-per-cycle limit — and the arithmetic below is derived from the published consumer list (5 stations, 4 registers, 3 store buffers) and the published 64-bit operand width. Below that level — driver circuits, arbitration policy, any SLT schematic — IBM publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Every gate form above is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive from the primer's bottom layer, never a claim about the Model 91's circuits.

- [verified] **Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)** — Planning latencies: multiply 6 cycles, divide 18, add 2; achieved times of 3, 12 and 2. Source: Tomasulo 1967, Introduction.
- [verified] **Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)** — CDB worked loop: 17 cycles without the CDB, 11 with it — about one-third faster. Source: Tomasulo 1967, worked example, pp. 32–33.
- [verified] **Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)** — Only 30 ns of the 60 ns CDB interval is required for all CDB functions. Source: Tomasulo 1967, worked example.
- [verified] **Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)** — Six floating-point buffers and three store data buffers: the instruction unit maps all of storage into them so FLOS sees only pseudo-register-to-register operations. Source: Tomasulo 1967, Definitions and data paths.
- [verified] **Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)** — The fetch and store buffers can be considered as specialized, one-operand reservation stations. Source: Tomasulo 1967.
- [verified] **Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)** — Four architectural floating-point registers (FLR). Source: Tomasulo 1967, Definitions and data paths.
- [verified] **Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)** — FLOS holds up to 8 instructions waiting for issue. Source: Tomasulo 1967, Fig. 1 (figure, not prose — no verbatim sentence quoted).
- [verified] **Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)** — First delivery to NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in October–November 1967, regular operations from January 1968. Source: Michal Brennek, "IBM System/360 Model 91" research file, citing Wikipedia "IBM System/360 Model 91" and Padegs (1981).
- [disputed] **Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)** — How many Model 91s were built: Wikipedia says only 15 ever produced, four for IBM internal use, but concedes the number is also authoritatively stated as 10, 11, 12, 14, 15 or 20. Source: Michal Brennek, "IBM System/360 Model 91" research file, §4.1, citing Wikipedia.
- [verified] **Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)** — Imprecise interrupts: because instructions could complete out of order, an FP exception's architectural PC no longer pointed at the offending instruction. Source: Michal Brennek, "IBM System/360 Model 91" research file, §1.6, citing Smotherman and Padegs, IBM J. Res. Dev. 25(5), Sept 1981.
- [verified] **Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)** — Commercial revival with Intel's P6 (Pentium Pro), launched 1 November 1995, after ~28 years dormant. Source: Michal Brennek, "IBM System/360 Model 91" research file, §2.6, citing Wikipedia "Pentium Pro" and Hennessy & Patterson.
- [verified] **Out-of-Order Execution & Tomasulo's Algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91)** — Robert Tomasulo received the Eckert–Mauchly Award in 1997 for his work on the algorithm. Source: Wikipedia, "Tomasulo's algorithm".

## AI accelerators

### Google TPU v5p

**Added: 2026-11-22** (deepened: Building blocks breakdown added to the wiki entry; the wiki card existed at launch)

**What it is / why it matters.** Google's performance-tier fifth-generation TPU, announced 6 December 2023 and built for Gemini-era training: the large-scale training chip to v5e's cost-efficient sibling. It is the generation where Google's bet became explicit — the pod, not the chip, is the machine. A full v5p pod wires 8,960 chips into one 3D torus, and the chip itself was redesigned so that one device serves the whole large model, dense layers and embeddings alike.

**Building blocks.** Seven named pieces, and the connections between them are the design:
- **TensorCore ×2** — each of the two compute cores on the chip: four 128×128 systolic MXUs, one vector unit and one scalar unit — eight MXUs per chip, twice v5e's one TensorCore.
- **MXU — systolic array** — a 128×128 grid of MACs; weights sit still, activations flow through, each partial sum passes to a neighbour — BF16 multiplies with FP32 accumulation.
- **Vector unit** — activations, normalisation, softmax and everything that isn't a dense matmul, one per TensorCore.
- **Scalar unit** — a small control core sequencing the MXU and vector unit and the XLA-generated schedule.
- **SparseCore ×4 (2nd gen)** — dataflow processors for embedding gather/scatter — the irregular, sparse half of recommendation and large-vocabulary models.
- **95 GiB HBM + ICI links** — HBM at 2,765 GB/s per chip, plus Inter-Chip Interconnect wiring chips into a 3D torus — 1,200 GB/s bidirectional per chip.
- **Optical circuit switch** — reconfigurable light paths rewire the pod topology per job without moving a cable — inherited from v4, now across 8,960 chips.

**The piece that makes it special:** the dense-plus-sparse pairing at pod scale. v4 proved the systolic MXU; v5p keeps its two TensorCores per chip and pairs them with four second-generation SparseCores, so one chip serves the whole large model — dense transformer layers on the MXUs, embedding and vocabulary layers on the SparseCores — while the 3D torus and optical switches scale that pairing to 8,960 chips. The bet is that the pod, not the chip, is the machine: Google claims over 2× the FLOPS and 3× the HBM capacity of v4 (published peaks give 1.67× the FLOPS; HBM bandwidth is 2.3×), with the interconnect to keep 6,144-chip jobs fed.

Note: v5p's MXUs are the same 128x128 systolic shape as TPU v4's, whose entry already carries a full MXU Level-2 block, so this entry deepens the SparseCore and the pod interconnect instead.

#### Inside the signature block: Second-generation SparseCore — the dataflow engine for embeddings

**Inside it.** Four SparseCores per v5p chip. Each SparseCore is a tiled dataflow processor: 16 compute tiles per SparseCore, with a single SparseCore sequencer orchestrating tasks across all 16 tiles in lockstep (OpenXLA spec table confirms 16 tiles and SIMD width 8 for v5p — unchanged from v4). Each tile, in the structure the ISCA 2023 paper discloses for v4 and which v5p inherits, holds a Fetch Unit, a programmable 8-wide SIMD vector unit (scVPU, which reuses the TensorCore VPU's ALUs), and a Flush Unit, plus the tile's slice of the Sparse Vector Memory (spmem) — 2.5 MiB per SparseCore organised as 16 banks on v4; Google has not published v5p's spmem size. Each tile has its own associated HBM channel and supports multiple outstanding memory accesses. Five cross-channel units sit across all 16 spmem banks and execute CISC-like, variable-length embedding operations (deduplication, reduction) whose runtime is data-dependent. Embedding tables live in HBM and are mod-sharded across every SparseCore in the pod; the host pre-processes each batch into COO form (row_ids, col_ids) and XLA statically sizes the spmem buffers from per-partition limits (max_ids_per_partition, max_unique_ids_per_partition). What Google has not published: any internal change that makes this SparseCore "second generation" — tiles, SIMD width and tile structure are all identical to v4's on the published record, so the only published gen-2 delta is the system-level claim of 1.9x faster embedding-dense training.

**Trace — one unit of work.**
1. **Host prepares the batch.**The host CPU converts the batch's categorical features into COO sparse tensors (row_ids, col_ids), deduplicates repeated IDs within a sample, and validates the counts against the compiled per-partition limits.
2. **IDs are mod-sharded.**Each col_id is assigned to its owning SparseCore by target_sc_id = col_id % num_total_sparse_cores, so the lookup for one feature fans out across many SparseCores, often on other chips.
3. **Fetch Units gather from HBM.**Each tile's Fetch Unit issues multiple outstanding, uncoalesced reads against its HBM channel and stages the returned embedding rows into its slice of spmem.
4. **scVPUs and cross-channel units reduce.**The 8-wide scVPUs process the gathered vectors while the five cross-channel units dedupe repeated IDs and reduce vectors across all 16 spmem banks into pooled per-sample vectors.
5. **All-to-all returns the pooled vectors.**The pooled vectors cross the ICI torus in a variable-length all-to-all to the chips whose TensorCores own those samples, and join the dense bottom-MLP computation on the MXUs.
6. **Backward pass flushes updates.**Gradients flow back through the same path, the scVPUs apply the optimizer update, and the Flush Units write the updated embedding rows back to HBM; with TensorCore/SparseCore pipelining the SparseCore is already working the next step while the TensorCore finishes this one.

**Bottleneck.** Relieves the dense engines and the host of latency-bound gather/scatter work: embeddings run at memory latency, not FLOPS, and placing them on the TensorCore or on host CPUs — through the CPU DRAM interface, shared four chips to one host — throttles the whole step; on v4 the SparseCore accelerates embeddings 5-7x for about 5% of die area and power. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: pod-wide all-to-all traffic that strains torus bisection bandwidth far more than all-reduce; load imbalance from hot IDs, since a few frequent values skew compute, memory and network together; and the spmem budget itself — limits set too low force mini-batching or drop IDs, limits set too high fail compilation when the buffers no longer fit.

**Numbers.** 4 SparseCores per chip; 16 compute tiles per SparseCore; 8-wide SIMD (scVPU) per tile; embedding-dense models 1.9x faster than v4 (Google claim, launch blog now offline — unverifiable beyond secondary reporting); v4-inherited: 2.5 MiB spmem per SparseCore in 16 banks, five cross-channel units, embeddings 5-7x faster for about 5% of die area and power; v5p spmem size and any internal second-generation changes not published by Google.

**Source.** Google Cloud docs, "TPU v5p" and "TPU architecture" (docs.cloud.google.com); OpenXLA, "A deep dive into SparseCore for Large Embedding Models (LEM)" (openxla.org/xla/sparsecore); Jouppi et al., "TPU v4: An Optically Reconfigurable Supercomputer for Machine Learning with Hardware Support for Embeddings", ISCA 2023, section 3.5 (v4-inherited internals).

#### Inside the signature block: The pod-scale interconnect — ICI 3D torus and the optical circuit switch

**Inside it.** The pod is built from 4x4x4 cubes of 64 chips (16 hosts, 4 chips per host); a full v5p pod holds 140 cubes. Inside a cube, neighbouring chips connect over high-speed copper ICI links; the cube's boundary links leave through optical links to Google's Palomar optical circuit switches, which stitch the cubes into a 3D torus — or a twisted 3D torus — with no physical recabling, the topology reprogrammed in the OCS routing tables per job. Palomar is a 3D MEMS-mirror switch (v4 paper: 136x136, 128 ports plus 8 spares; mirrors switch in milliseconds; circulators send light both ways down one fibre, halving ports and cables); v4's supercomputer used 48 OCSes for 64 cubes, and Google has not published the OCS count for a v5p pod. A twisted torus option is offered for slice shapes where each dimension is equal to or twice the smallest; ICI resiliency (on by default for slices of one cube or larger) reroutes ICI connections around failed OCSes and optical links at the cost of temporary ICI degradation. Beyond a single slice, Multislice extends a job across slices over the 50 Gbps-per-chip data-centre network.

**Trace — one unit of work.**
1. **XLA inserts the collective.**The compiled program issues the collective (all-reduce for dense gradients, all-to-all for embedding vectors) and the data moves from HBM onto the chip's ICI links.
2. **Copper hops inside the cube.**The packet travels chip to chip over copper ICI within the 4x4x4 cube, each hop a direct neighbour link with no switch in the path.
3. **Electrical to optical at the cube edge.**At the cube boundary the signal converts to light at the tray's fibre connector and enters the optical link.
4. **The OCS forwards it.**The Palomar switch, its MEMS mirrors pre-set to the job's topology (regular or twisted torus), reflects the light to the fibre of the destination cube — no packet switch, no store-and-forward, just a mirror.
5. **Optical to electrical, copper to the chip.**The light converts back at the destination tray and the packet finishes over copper ICI hops to the destination chip.
6. **Reduction and return.**The destination reduces or pools the arriving data with its local slice and the result retraces the path, so a 6,144-chip all-reduce completes as a sequence of neighbour exchanges rather than a trip through a central switch.

**Bottleneck.** Relieves the scale and availability wall: without reconfigurable optics a 4,096-chip machine could not tolerate hosts failing 0.1-1.0% of the time, and a fixed topology could not be reshaped per workload — the OCS lets the scheduler route around dead hosts and links and pick twisted topologies for all-to-all-heavy jobs. Creates a bisection-bandwidth bottleneck instead: embedding all-to-all traffic grows with the pod and strains the torus bisection (a 3D torus scales as N to the 2/3), so at large slices the network, not the MXUs, sets the step time; the twisted torus and ICI resiliency only buy back part of it, and resiliency rerouting temporarily degrades ICI performance.

**Numbers.** 8,960 chips per pod (140 cubes of 64); largest single slice 6,144 chips (16x16x24, 96 cubes); Multislice to 18,432 chips; 1,200 GB/s bidirectional ICI per chip (600 GB/s per direction, 4,800 Gbps per direction); 50 Gbps data-centre network per chip; twisted 4x4x8 slice about 70% higher theoretical bisection bandwidth than untwisted, 4x8x8 about 40%; near-linear scaling, 11.97x throughput for a 12x slice-size increase (512 to 6,144 chips); v4-inherited: OCS and optics under 5% of system cost and under 3% of power, Palomar 136x136 with 128 ports plus 8 spares, 48 OCSes per 4,096-chip v4 supercomputer, twisted torus 1.63x/1.31x all-to-all throughput on 4x4x8/4x8x8 slices; v5p OCS count not published.

**Source.** Google Cloud docs, "TPU v5p" (docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/v5p); Google Cloud blog, "What's new with Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer architecture", April 2024; Jouppi et al., "TPU v4: An Optically Reconfigurable Supercomputer for Machine Learning with Hardware Support for Embeddings", ISCA 2023, section 2 (v4-inherited OCS and torus mechanisms).

**The architecture.** Work arrives as an XLA-compiled graph, tiled to the 128×128 MXU shape and sharded across the pod before the first chip runs. A weight tile enters an MXU and stays stationary in the PEs while activations systolic-flow past it, partial sums accumulating PE to PE. Embedding lookups and sparse gathers run on the four SparseCores while the MXUs stay on dense matmul; softmax, layernorm and residuals run on the vector units while the MXU starts the next tile. Between chips, ICI plus optical circuit switches move activations across the 3D torus as if the pod were one accelerator. Pods are built from 64-chip cubes (4×4×4 across 16 hosts); only a full cube or larger gets genuine 3D-torus wraparound, and ICI resiliency reroutes optical links around faults. Each 4-chip host VM carries 208 vCPUs and 448 GB of RAM.

**Key numbers.** Announced 6 December 2023; 459 TFLOPS BF16 and FP8 per chip, 918 TOPS INT8; 95 GiB HBM at 2,765 GB/s per chip; 2 TensorCores (8 MXUs) and 4 SparseCores per chip; 1,200 GB/s bidirectional ICI per chip; 3D torus; 8,960 chips per pod (~4.1 exaFLOPS BF16), largest single job 6,144 chips. Google's headline launch claim is 2.8× faster LLM training than v4 — but that chart measured v5p on INT8 against v4 on BF16, and Google's like-for-like BF16 figure is 67% faster (1.67×, matching the 459/275 peak-FLOPS ratio). Embedding-dense models are claimed 1.9× faster via the second-generation SparseCores, but the launch post is offline and the figure is unverifiable beyond secondary reporting. (Process node and HBM generation are not disclosed by Google and are omitted.)

**Signature ideas.**
1. **Two TensorCores per chip** — doubled dense compute over v5e, with the MXU count to match.
2. **Second-generation SparseCores** — sparse embedding acceleration on the same die as the dense matmul engines.
3. **8,960-chip 3D-torus pods with optical rewiring** — topology reshaped per job by optical circuit switches.
4. **XLA compiler co-design** — the chip, the compiler and the data-centre topology designed as one artefact.

**Limits & tradeoffs.** Flexibility and access. Control flow, dynamic shapes and small models underuse the array, and the whole stack assumes XLA/JAX-style compilation — peak efficiency demands the workload be re-expressed as large, regular matmuls. And the pod is a cloud machine, not a part you buy: you rent slices (up to 6,144 chips per job), so the architecture's scale is only available inside Google's data centres.

**Lineage.** Descended from TPU v4 (2021), which introduced the 3D torus, optical circuit switching and the first SparseCores; v5p keeps v4's two TensorCores per chip (doubling v5e's one), triples HBM capacity (HBM bandwidth is 2.3×) and more than doubles pod size. Its sibling v5e (2023) is the cost-efficient single-TensorCore variant for inference and smaller training. Succeeded by Trillium / TPU v6e (2024), which doubles per-chip BF16 compute again to 918 TFLOPS.

**One-line summary.** TPU v5p pairs two systolic TensorCores with four SparseCores on one chip and scales the pair to 8,960-chip optically rewired pods — Google's statement that for frontier training, the pod is the machine.
