## GPUs

### Intel Ponte Vecchio (Xe-HPC)

**Added: 2026-11-22** (deepened: Building blocks breakdown added to the wiki entry)

**What it is / why it matters.** Intel's maximalist HPC and AI GPU, sold as the Intel Data Center GPU Max series and built as the compute engine of the Aurora exascale supercomputer at Argonne National Laboratory. Disclosed in 2021–22 and launched in January 2023, it is less notable for any single compute unit than for how it is put together: 47 functional tiles on three different process nodes, stacked with Foveros 3D packaging and stitched with EMIB bridges — the most heterogeneous package ever shipped in a GPU, and a statement that architecture now lives as much in the packaging as in the ALU.

**Building blocks.** Six named pieces, and the connections between them are the design:
- **Compute tile (TSMC N5)** — the compute building block: 8 Xe-cores plus 4 MB of L1 per tile, stacked by Foveros 3D onto the base tile. Sixteen of them make the 128 Xe-cores of a full OAM module.
- **Xe-core** — each core packs 8 vector engines (XVE, 512-bit, native FP64/FP32) and 8 matrix engines (XMX, 4096-bit) plus one ray-tracing unit, for 128 RT units across the package.
- **XMX matrix engine** — the AI FLOPS engine: 2048 TF32 / 4096 FP16 / 4096 BF16 operations per clock per Xe-core, for 839 TFLOPS of BF16/FP16 across the full OAM.
- **Rambo cache tile** — a dedicated SRAM tile holding a slice of the 408 MB L2 close to the compute tiles, so the working set rarely has to leave the package for HBM.
- **Base tile (Intel 7, Foveros)** — the package's nervous system: 144 MB of L2 per base tile, the HBM2e controllers, the PCIe Gen5 host interface, and the Modular Die Fabric (MDFI) that routes traffic between tiles.
- **Xe Link tile (TSMC N7)** — scale-out: 8 Xe Links per tile through an 8-port embedded switch on up to 90G SerDes, wiring up to 8 OAMs into one fabric.

**The piece that makes it special:** the package itself. The compute is conventional for its class; what is radical is assembling 47 tiles on three process nodes (TSMC N5 compute, Intel 7 base, TSMC N7 link) with Foveros 3D stacking and EMIB bridges, totalling over 100 billion transistors. The base tile is the trick: it carries the L2, the HBM controllers and the die-to-die fabric, so the compute tiles stay small, high-yielding and swappable.

**The architecture.** Work arrives from the host over PCIe Gen5; the base tile's host interface hands kernels to the compute tiles through the MDFI fabric. Each Xe-core runs vector work on its 8 XVEs and matrix work on its 8 XMX engines, with operands held in the 64 MB of L1 across the package. The 408 MB L2 — Rambo tiles plus the base tiles' 144 MB each — absorbs reuse before traffic reaches HBM. Eight HBM2e stacks feed the package with up to 128 GB at about 3.2 TB/s in the Max 1550 configuration. Multi-GPU collectives leave through the Xe Link tiles' 8-port switch, so up to 8 OAMs act as one fabric. Three SKUs shipped: Max 1100 (56 Xe-cores, 48 GB HBM2e, 300 W PCIe), Max 1350 (112 Xe-cores, 96 GB, 450 W OAM) and Max 1550 (128 Xe-cores, 128 GB, 600 W OAM).

**Key numbers.** 47 functional tiles (63 including thermal tiles), over 100 billion transistors; 128 Xe-cores, 1024 vector engines and 1024 matrix engines; 52 TFLOPS FP64/FP32, 419 TFLOPS TF32, 839 TFLOPS BF16/FP16, 1678 TFLOPS INT8 (two-stack OAM, Hot Chips 34); 64 MB L1, 408 MB L2, up to 128 GB HBM2e at ~3.2 TB/s; package 77.5 × 62.5 mm; 600 W (Max 1550 OAM).

**Signature ideas.**
1. **Foveros 3D + EMIB heterogeneous integration** — three process nodes in one package, compute stacked on the base tile, bridges between tiles.
2. **Rambo cache tiles** — a dedicated SRAM die as a first-class tile, not cache bolted onto the compute die.
3. **XMX matrix engines with native FP64 vector** — one core that does both HPC's FP64 and AI's low-precision matrix math.
4. **Xe Link scale-out fabric** — an embedded switch tile turning up to 8 OAMs into one fabric for Aurora.

**Limits & tradeoffs.** Yield, power and software. Forty-seven tiles mean 47 dice to test, bin and assemble; the 600 W Max 1550 OAM needs liquid cooling in practice, and the part shipped late — Aurora's schedule slipped with it. The Xe-HPC software stack (oneAPI/SYCL) had to be built from scratch against CUDA's incumbency, and Intel has since narrowed its discrete data-center GPU ambitions. Ponte Vecchio is a packaging landmark more than a market winner.

**Lineage.** Descended from Intel's Xe family (Xe-LP in Tiger Lake, Xe-HPG in Arc Alchemist) scaled up to the Xe-HPC branch for data centers. Its packaging approach — Foveros 3D stacking plus EMIB bridges, with cache and I/O as separate tiles — carried into Intel's later data-center parts and into the industry's chiplet mainstream. It remains the GPU of the Aurora exascale system.

**One-line summary.** Ponte Vecchio bet that the future of GPUs is packaging: 47 tiles on three process nodes, stacked and bridged into one 100-billion-transistor device whose cleverest block is the base tile holding it all together.


## Drill-down completion — all remaining entries deepened (2026-11-22)

The final 36 catalogue entries that still carried generic class-pattern breakdowns were replaced with hand-written, chip-specific breakdowns (DEEP map 61 → 97 of 97; zero entries remain at class-pattern level). Each entry below mirrors the wiki deep dive: named blocks of that specific design, the starred special piece, the accepted trade-off, and a fact check under Sai's standard (source: primary where possible; quote: the exact sentence; status: verified / corrected / disputed / unverifiable). One JSON record per fact is stored in files/fact-records.json.

### Tesla Dojo D1

**Specs (wiki card).** 7 nm · 50B transistors · 354 training nodes per die · 25 dies per training tile

**Building blocks.**
- **Training node ×354** — The repeating unit of the die: a small programmable core with its own scalar unit, a 64-byte-wide SIMD vector/matrix unit (8×8×4 matrix multiply), and 4-way SMT — 354 of them tile the 645 mm² die in a 2D array
- **1.25 MB SRAM per node** — Each node's private, software-managed scratchpad — 440 MB across the die. There are deliberately no caches, no virtual memory and no coherence: software moves every byte explicitly
- **2D mesh NoC** — Nearest-neighbour mesh wiring the nodes on-die, extended off-die by high-speed SerDes on all four edges so dies butt-join into a 5×5 training tile with no switch chip in between
- **Configurable FP8 / BF16 datapaths** — Tesla's own CFP8/BF16 formats sized for video training — the node's vector unit does 64-byte SIMD in these formats, reaching 362–376 TFLOPS per die (see Fact check — the two published figures disagree)
- **Dojo Interface Processor (DIP)** — I/O dies at the training-tile edges holding the shared DRAM pool (160 GB per tile) and host/Ethernet interfaces, so the D1 die itself carries no DRAM controllers
- **TTPoE transport** — Tesla Transport Protocol over Ethernet — Tesla's custom, trimmed Ethernet protocol for tile-to-tile traffic, later open-sourced and taken to the Ultra Ethernet Consortium

**The piece that makes it special.** The node, not the array. Where a TPU bets on one giant systolic array, D1 bets on 354 small CPU-like training nodes, each with private SRAM and SMT, joined by a mesh that extends seamlessly across 25 dies into a training tile and 3,000 dies into an ExaPOD. The special piece is the seam — or its absence: the same mesh programming model runs on one node, one die, or a cabinet, because the die edges are just more mesh.

**How work flows.** Compiler places the model: Layers are mapped onto nodes; weights and activations are written into per-node SRAM explicitly — there is no cache to hide a bad placement. Nodes compute locally: Each node runs its scalar schedule and fires its SIMD/matrix unit on the tile of the network it owns. Activations cross the mesh: Results move node-to-node on-die, then die-to-die across tile edges at multi-TB/s aggregate bandwidth. DIPs feed the tile: Interface processors stream the next batch from the tile's shared DRAM pool and handle host traffic. ExaPOD scales the pattern: Tiles rack into cabinets; TTPoE carries inter-tile traffic over Ethernet with the same send/receive model.

**Trade-off accepted.** Programmability for peak. A mesh of small cores only reaches its FLOPS when the compiler and kernels keep 354 nodes fed with balanced work, and the formats (CFP8) and stack are Tesla-only. Tesla publishes no datasheet for D1 — every number here traces to its Hot Chips 34 disclosure and AI Day, and the programme itself was wound down in 2025 in favour of the AI4/AI5 inference line.

**Fact check.**
- [verified] 354 training nodes per D1 die; 440 MB SRAM per die — Source: Tesla, Hot Chips 34 (2022), Dojo microarchitecture talk. Quote: "Each chip has 354 DOJO processing nodes per die and 440MB of SRAM."
- [corrected] Spec line previously read “354 training tiles per system tile” — Source: Tesla, Hot Chips 34 (2022). Was: 354 training tiles per system tile; now: 354 training nodes per D1 die — 25 dies form one training tile. Quote: "Each node has 1.25MB of SRAM."
- [disputed] Peak BF16/CFP8 throughput per die — Source: Tesla Hot Chips 34 vs later Tesla-derived summaries. Note: 362 TFLOPS and 376 TFLOPS both circulate from Tesla-derived material; the wiki states the range instead of picking one.
- [unverifiable] 50 billion transistors — Source: Secondary reporting of Tesla AI Day 2021. Note: Widely reported, but not stated in the Hot Chips 34 deck.

### AWS Inferentia2 & Trainium

**Specs (wiki card).** NeuronCore-v2 · NeuronLink interconnect

**Building blocks.**
- **NeuronCore-v2 ×2** — The whole chip is two identical cores; each is a self-contained heterogeneous accelerator with its own sequencers, SRAMs and DMA — Trainium and Inferentia2 share the same core, differing in links and clocks
- **Tensor Engine** — A power-optimised systolic array for GEMM, convolution and transpose — over 90 BF16 TFLOPS per core, FP32 accumulation, with cFP8/TF32 support
- **Vector Engine** — Wide vector unit for reductions, normalisation, pooling and activations — the non-matmul residue of a transformer layer
- **Scalar Engine** — Element-wise ops and control: biases, ReLU, index math — small, but it keeps the tensor engine from stalling on glue work
- **GpSimd Engine** — Eight fully programmable 512-bit SIMD processors per core running ordinary C code against the on-chip SRAM — the escape hatch for operators the fixed engines can't express
- **SBUF + PSUM SRAMs** — Two software-managed scratchpads, no caches anywhere: a 24 MiB state buffer (SBUF) staging operands and a 2 MiB partial-sum buffer (PSUM) dedicated to tensor-engine accumulation
- **CC cores + NeuronLink-v2** — Six collective-communication cores and NeuronLink-v2 device links run all-reduce and friends off the compute cores' critical path

**The piece that makes it special.** The GpSimd engine. Every other accelerator in this class forces odd operators onto a host CPU or a slow path; NeuronCore-v2 embeds eight programmable 512-bit cores inside the accelerator itself, programmed in C through the Neuron Kernel Interface, so a custom operator runs where the data already lives. The four engines run four independent instruction streams in parallel, synchronised by hardware semaphores — a tiny heterogeneous SoC per core.

**How work flows.** Neuron compiler tiles the graph: The SDK lowers the model to the four engines, tiling tensors to the 128-partition SBUF layout before anything runs. DMA stages SBUF: 32 DMA engines move weights and activations from the 32 GiB HBM into SBUF; nothing is cached or fetched on demand. Tensor engine sweeps: GEMMs run systolically, partial sums accumulating in PSUM at FP32. Vector/scalar finish the layer: Softmax, norms and element-wise ops run on the vector and scalar engines; exotic ops spill to GpSimd — all without leaving the core. Collectives overlap: CC cores and NeuronLink move gradients/activations to peer chips while the next tile computes.

**Trade-off accepted.** Software burden. With no caches and four asynchronous engines, performance lives or dies in the compiler and in explicit synchronisation; models that don't tile to the SBUF's partition geometry leave the systolic array idle. You also buy into one cloud: the chips exist only inside AWS instances.

**Fact check.**
- [verified] NeuronCore-v2 has four heterogeneous compute engines (Tensor, Vector, Scalar, GpSimd) — Source: AWS Neuron documentation — Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI. Quote: "A NeuronCore-v2 consists of four heterogeneous compute engines (Tensor, Vector, Scalar, and GpSimd), each designed to accelerate different types of operators in modern machine learning models."
- [verified] 24 MiB SBUF + 2 MiB PSUM, software-managed — Source: AWS Neuron documentation — Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI. Quote: "Memory-wise, a NeuronCore-v2 consists of two software-managed on-chip SRAMs, a 24MiB SBUF as the main data storage and a 2MiB PSUM as a dedicated accumulation buffer for Tensor Engine."
- [verified] Two NeuronCore-v2 per device; 32 GiB HBM at 820 GB/s — Source: AWS Neuron documentation — Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI. Quote: "2 NeuronCores (v2). 2 HBM stacks with a total device memory capacity of 32GiB and bandwidth of 820 GB/s."

#### Inside the signature block: The Tensor Engine and its two SRAMs — a 128x128 systolic array fed by a 24 MiB SBUF and drained into a 2 MiB PSUM

**Inside it.** The 128x128 systolic array is the heart: 16,384 processing elements, one multiply-accumulate per cycle each, arranged so the stationary operand [K,M] is loaded once by a LoadStationary instruction and cached in the array's internal storage, while the moving operand [K,N] streams through one column per cycle under MultiplyMoving and the partial sums fall down the columns into PSUM — the PSUM partition dimension is rotated 90 degrees against SBUF exactly because of this flow. The SBUF is the 24 MiB staging SRAM: 128 partitions of 192 KiB, a two-dimensional memory whose partition axis is the parallel dimension (128 elements per cycle across partitions) and whose free axis is the time dimension, with hard start-partition alignment rules (0 for 65-128 partitions, 0 or 64 for 33-64, 0/32/64/96 for 1-32). The PSUM is the 2 MiB landing buffer: 128 partitions of 16 KiB, each split into 8 banks of 512 FP32 values, writable only by the Tensor Engine, with near-memory read-accumulate-write on every 4-byte element so a K>128 contraction accumulates in place across a matmul accumulation group — up to eight groups outstanding, one per bank, so the Tensor Engine can move to the next group without waiting for VectorE or ScalarE to drain the last one. Around the array sit the three companion engines: the Vector Engine, 128 lanes at 1.12 GHz organised as four Reshape banks (each wired to 32 SBUF/PSUM partitions, doing 32x32 transposes and 32-partition shuffles) feeding four Compute banks of 32 lanes; the Scalar Engine, 128 lanes at 1.4 GHz with hardware non-linear functions (GELU, sqrt and friends) and a fused per-lane scale/bias multiply-add before the function and an optional FP32 reduction after it, so a softmax-style activation plus its max-subtraction folds into one instruction; and the GpSimd Engine, eight fully programmable 512-bit vector processors at 1.4 GHz, each with 64 KiB of tightly-coupled memory at 3-cycle latency and a 512-bit read/write interface to its own 16 SBUF partitions — the escape hatch for operators the fixed engines cannot express. Each of the four engines has its own sequencer with private 32-bit scalar registers for fetch, decode and issue, plus a fifth Sync Engine that triggers DMA transfers without disturbing compute scheduling; the four instruction streams run asynchronously in parallel and are synchronised by atomic semaphores in hardware. Two access rules serialize the engines against each other: VectorE and GpSimdE cannot touch SBUF in parallel, and VectorE and ScalarE cannot touch PSUM in parallel — the compiler enforces the serialisation. AWS publishes no SRAM bank organisation beyond the partition counts, no per-PE circuit detail and no sequencer queue depths, so this is the array's contract, not its circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one nc_matmul [M=128, K=128, N=512] BF16 through the Tensor Engine.**
1. **DMA stages the tiles.** The compiler has tiled the layer's [128,128] weight matrix and [128,512] activation matrix to the SBUF geometry before anything runs; 16 DMA engines per core move them from the 32 GiB HBM into SBUF as scatter-gather lists — the 128x512 FP32 activation tile goes as 16 transfers, one per engine, each carrying 8 DMA buffers, because every SBUF partition's slice is non-contiguous in the address map. The K dimension sits on the partition axis (128 partitions), the free dimensions stream in time.
2. **LoadStationary parks the weights.** The Tensor Engine's sequencer issues LoadStationary, which reads the [128,128] stationary tile out of SBUF and caches it in the array's internal storage — one weight per processing element, 16,384 weights parked. LoadStationary is pure data movement, up to 4x faster than a MultiplyMoving at the same free-axis size, and the next tile's LoadStationary can already run in the background while the current tile computes.
3. **MultiplyMoving sweeps the activation through.** The sequencer issues MultiplyMoving: the [128,512] moving tile streams through the array one column per cycle, each processing element multiplying its parked weight by the value arriving from the left and adding the partial sum from the element above. The initiation interval is roughly max(N, 64) Tensor Engine cycles — 512 cycles for N=512 — and several LoadStationary/MultiplyMoving pairs can be in flight at once because the engine is deeply pipelined.
4. **Partial sums land in PSUM, not SBUF.** Each column's 128 partial sums drain into one PSUM bank — 512 FP32 values per partition, one bank per accumulation group. If the contraction dimension K exceeds 128, the next K-tile's MultiplyMoving accumulates its output onto the same PSUM bank in place, in FP32, without ever reading the partials back into SBUF; up to eight accumulation groups can be outstanding at once.
5. **Vector and Scalar finish the layer.** With the matmul done, the Vector Engine streams the [128,512] FP32 result out of PSUM at 128 elements per cycle — a layer norm or a reduction across the free dimension, its four Reshape banks transposing or shuffling partitions where the layout demands it — and the Scalar Engine applies the fused scale, bias and non-linear function (GELU, say) in a single instruction, its reduction accumulator catching the running sum for free. The two engines cannot touch PSUM in parallel, so the compiler serialises them; the Tensor Engine has already moved on to the next accumulation group.
6. **The next tile is already in flight.** While the companion engines drain PSUM, the Sync Engine has triggered the DMA engines to stage the next layer's weights into SBUF, and the background LoadStationary for the next matmul is loading — the whole point of the design is that the systolic array never waits for HBM. If the next tile's free dimension is small, the LoadStationary/MultiplyMoving alternation becomes the bound instead, and the array idles between instructions — the shape ceiling, not the arithmetic, is what the compiler is really optimising against.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves two walls at once: the weight re-fetch wall — with the stationary operand parked inside the 128x128 array, each processing element reuses its weight for every column of the moving operand instead of fetching it from SRAM once per multiply; and the K-tile round-trip wall — PSUM's near-memory accumulation folds a K>128 tile's partial sums in place at FP32, so a long contraction never reads its own partials back out of SRAM and rewrites them. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the tile-shape ceiling — one nc_matmul is capped at M=128, K=128 and N=512 by the array width, the SBUF partition count and the PSUM bank depth, so any larger shape must be re-tiled and re-issued, and the LoadStationary/MultiplyMoving alternation becomes the bound whenever the stationary tile is small; the partition-alignment ceiling — a tensor's partitions must start at a legal boundary (0, or 0/64, or 0/32/64/96 by size), and no cross-partition movement is possible at all when a tensor spans more than 64 partitions, so the compiler's layout choices are load-bearing; and the FP32 tax — an FP32 matmul costs roughly 4x the initiation interval of a BF16 one, and the shared-port rules serialize VectorE against GpSimd on SBUF and VectorE against ScalarE on PSUM, so the four engines are only independent until they touch the same SRAM.

**Governing numbers.** 128x128 processing elements = 16,384 MACs per cycle; Tensor Engine clock 2.8 GHz; 92 TFLOPS maximum BF16/FP16/TF32/cFP8 per core, 23 TFLOPS FP32; accumulation always FP32; SBUF 24 MiB = 128 partitions x 192 KiB; PSUM 2 MiB = 128 partitions x 16 KiB, 8 banks x 512 FP32 values per partition; tile limits per nc_matmul: stationary free axis (M) at most 128, partition axis (K) at most 128, moving free axis (N) at most 512; MultiplyMoving initiation interval roughly max(N, 64) Tensor Engine cycles; LoadStationary up to 4x faster than MultiplyMoving at the same free-axis size; background LoadStationary loads the next stationary tile while the current one computes; tensor access overhead about 60 cycles per engine access; SBUF/PSUM read/write interface peak 128 elements per cycle at 1.4 GHz; Vector Engine 128 lanes at 1.12 GHz, 2.3 FP32 TFLOPS, free dimension up to 64K elements on SBUF and 4K on PSUM; Scalar Engine 128 lanes at 1.4 GHz, 2.9 FP32 TFLOPS, fused scale/bias plus non-linear function plus optional FP32 reduction in one instruction, ActReadAccumulator about 64 Scalar Engine cycles; GpSimd eight 512-bit processors at 1.4 GHz, 64 KiB tightly-coupled memory per processor, 3-cycle TCM latency, 512-bit SBUF read/write per cycle per processor, 16 SBUF partitions wired to each processor; Vector Engine four Reshape banks x 32 partitions and four Compute banks x 32 lanes; 32x32 transpose and 32-partition shuffle inside each Reshape bank; up to eight outstanding matmul accumulation groups, one per PSUM bank; two Tensor Engines per chip, chip rated 190 FP16/BF16 TFLOPS (two times 92 TFLOPS is 184 TFLOPS by arithmetic — the guide does not explain the gap).

**Primary source.** AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI — device composition, four engines and sequencers, Tensor Engine systolic array and LoadStationary/MultiplyMoving instructions, tile limits, initiation-interval cost model, background and fast LoadStationary, Vector Engine reshape/compute banks, Scalar Engine fused activation and reduction, GpSimd TCM and SBUF connectivity, DMA engines, SBUF/PSUM address maps, PSUM near-memory accumulation, engine access restrictions, tensor-access overhead (read live, full guide); AWS Neuron, NeuronCore-v2 Architecture — Vector Engine 2.3 FP32 TFLOPS, Scalar Engine 2.9 FP32 TFLOPS, Tensor Engine over 90 TFLOPS; AWS Neuron, Trainium Architecture and Inferentia2 Architecture — 190 FP16/BF16 TFLOPS per chip, 32 GiB HBM at 820 GiB/s, 1 TB/s DMA bandwidth.

#### Inside the signature block: DMA, the CC cores and NeuronLink-v2 — the movement fabric that keeps two cores and sixteen chips fed

**Inside it.** The movement fabric has three layers. At the bottom, each NeuronCore carries 16 DMA engines — 32 per device — each able to run one transfer at a time at a peak 27 GiB/s, moving data between any addressable memories in the system, in practice between the 32 GiB HBM and the core's SBUF. A transfer is a scatter-gather list of DMA buffers, and a buffer must be contiguous in the address map — which is why SBUF's two-dimensional layout matters: HBM is a flat one-dimensional space, but SBUF is 128 partitions laid out free-dimension-first, so a tensor spanning P partitions needs at least P buffers, and a slice that is itself non-contiguous in the free dimension needs more. The Sync Engine triggers these transfers without disturbing the compute engines' scheduling, and the DMA engines run in parallel with computation, so staging and computing overlap by design. In the middle, the HBM itself: two stacks, 32 GiB, 820 GiB/s shared by both cores, with inline compression and decompression on the DMA path — the device-level DMA bandwidth is rated at 1 TB/s. At the top, the collective layer: six CC cores per device whose job is collective communication, and NeuronLink-v2 device links — two on Inferentia2, four on Trainium — carrying gradients and activations chip-to-chip so that a 16-chip Trn1 instance can run tensor-parallel inference or data-parallel training without the host CPU ever touching a gradient. AWS publishes no CC-core internals (no queue depths, no arbitration, no reduction datapath), no NeuronLink signalling rate and no per-link bandwidth — the collective layer is documented at the level of counts and purpose, and this section does not invent the rest.

**Trace — one unit of work: one 128x512 FP32 weight tile into SBUF and its gradient back out over the collective fabric.**
1. **The weight tile leaves HBM.** A training step needs its [128,512] FP32 weight tile in SBUF. The Sync Engine triggers the transfer and the 16 DMA engines on the core split it: 16 transfers, one per engine, each a scatter-gather list of 8 DMA buffers — 128 buffers in total, one per SBUF partition, each carrying a 2 KiB slice (512 FP32 values). The buffers are sized to amortise their own overhead: the guide's rule is a free dimension of 4 KiB or above across ideally all 128 partitions, and this tile meets it.
2. **The tile lands in SBUF, partitioned.** Each buffer's slice lands in its partition at the same free-dimension offset — the SBUF address map runs free-dimension-first within a partition, then advances to the next partition — so the tile is whole again only when read across all 128 partitions at once. The DMA engines finish and the Tensor Engine's LoadStationary can park the tile in the systolic array while the DMA engines move on to the next tile; compute and staging never wait on each other.
3. **The backward pass produces gradients in PSUM.** After the forward matmuls and the backward pass, the tile's gradients sit in PSUM/SBUF on this core. They are the collective's payload: every chip in the 16-chip Trn1 instance holds its own shard of the same gradient, and no chip can take its optimiser step until all sixteen shards have been summed.
4. **The CC cores take the collective.** The six CC cores pick up the gradient tile and drive it out over the chip's NeuronLink-v2 links — four on Trainium, two on Inferentia2 — toward the peer chips, while the Tensor Engine is already starting the next tile's matmul. AWS publishes no CC-core internals, so what is documented is the division of labour, not the mechanism: the collectives run off the compute cores' critical path, and the compiler schedules them to overlap compute rather than serialise behind it.
5. **Peers reduce and return.** Each peer chip's CC cores receive the incoming gradient shards into its SBUF, where the receiving core's own engines perform the reduction — the same Vector Engine that does layer norms does the all-reduce's adds — and the summed gradient goes back out over NeuronLink to the chips that need it. The round trip is the step's synchronisation point: a chip that is still waiting on a shard cannot advance, which is why the link-count asymmetry between Inferentia2 (2 links) and Trainium (4 links) is a real ceiling on scale-out, not a packaging detail.
6. **Weights restage for the next step.** With the optimiser step applied, the updated weights stream back through the DMA engines from HBM into SBUF — 1 TB/s of device DMA bandwidth against 820 GiB/s of HBM, shared by both cores — and the next step's first LoadStationary is already queued. The fabric's bill comes due here: if the next layer's tensors are skinny (few partitions, short free dimension), the DMA buffer and transfer overheads dominate the move, and the Tensor Engine waits — the movement fabric, not the systolic array, sets the step time.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves two walls at once: the host-CPU collective wall — the six CC cores and NeuronLink-v2 run all-reduce and friends off the compute cores' critical path, so a training step's gradient exchange overlaps the next tile's matmul instead of stalling it; and the HBM-latency wall — 32 DMA engines stage tiles explicitly from HBM into SBUF in parallel with compute, so there are no cache misses and no demand-fetch stalls anywhere in the machine. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the buffer-count wall — every SBUF tensor crossing the DMA boundary must be cut into at least as many DMA buffers as it has partitions (128 for a full-width tile), and each buffer and each transfer carries overhead that is only amortised by moving at least 4 KiB per free-dimension slice across all 128 partitions, so small or skinny tensors pay a disproportionate tax; the link-count asymmetry — Inferentia2 carries 2 NeuronLink-v2 links and Trainium 4, so the same two NeuronCores hit a different scale-out ceiling depending on which chip they are packaged in, and AWS publishes no per-link rate, so the fabric's true bandwidth is a matter of conflicting secondary estimates; and the shared-HBM wall — both cores share one 820 GiB/s HBM pool, so the two Tensor Engines' appetites add up against a single memory, and the DMA engines' 1 TB/s of aggregate bandwidth is the ceiling on how fast weights can be restaged between layers.

**Governing numbers.** 32 DMA engines per device, 16 per NeuronCore, each driving one transfer at a time at a peak 27 GiB/s; 1 TB/s device DMA bandwidth with inline memory compression/decompression; 32 GiB HBM in 2 stacks, 820 GiB/s; 6 CC cores per device for collective communication; NeuronLink-v2: 2 links on Inferentia2, 4 on Trainium; DMA optimisation rule: free dimension 4 KiB or above, partition dimension ideally 128; a 128x512 FP32 HBM tensor loads into SBUF as 16 DMA transfers, one per engine, each moving a scatter-gather list of 8 DMA buffers; 16 Trainium chips per Trn1 instance; SBUF tensor needs at least as many DMA buffers as it has partitions; 32 DMA engines x 27 GiB/s = 864 GiB/s against the rated 1 TB/s DMA bandwidth; NeuronLink-v2 per-chip bandwidth is not published by AWS — secondary estimates range from 192 GiB/s to about 800 GB/s per chip (disputed, see fact records).

**Primary source.** AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI — 32 DMA engines, 16 per core at 27 GiB/s each, scatter-gather DMA buffers, SBUF two-dimensional address map, the 128x512 FP32 load example (16 transfers x 8 buffers), the 4 KiB / 128-partition optimisation rule, 6 CC cores, NeuronLink-v2 link counts, Sync Engine DMA triggering (read live, full guide); AWS Neuron, Trainium Architecture — 1 TB/s DMA bandwidth with inline compression/decompression, 16 chips per Trn1 instance, 32 GiB HBM at 820 GiB/s; AWS Neuron, Inferentia2 Architecture — identical per-chip compute/memory numbers, NeuronLink-v2 for collective compute.

### SambaNova SN40L

**Specs (wiki card).** Reconfigurable Dataflow Unit · three-tier memory (SRAM/DRAM/HBM class)

**Building blocks.**
- **Pattern Compute Unit (PCU) ×1,040** — A multi-stage reconfigurable SIMD pipeline; each PCU is configured at compile time to execute one innermost loop body — configurable as systolic array or vector unit, BF16/FP32/INT32/INT8, with a cross-lane reduction tree
- **Pattern Memory Unit (PMU) ×1,040** — Distributed scratchpad SRAM — 520 MB in total — programmer-managed, fragmentable, with its own address-generation pipeline (4 addresses/cycle) and alignment crossbars for transpose and layout changes in flight
- **Mesh switches (3 networks)** — Separate packet-switched networks for vector data, scalar addresses/metadata and control, wiring PCUs and PMUs into a spatial fabric — operators pass tensors directly, never via memory
- **AGCU** — Address Generation and Coalescing Unit — the portal off-chip: generates and coalesces accesses to HBM, DDR and peer RDUs, including sparse and graph-shaped patterns
- **HBM tier — 64 GB** — Co-packaged HBM as the middle tier: a software-managed cache between SRAM and the DDR reservoir
- **DDR tier — up to 1.5 TB** — Pluggable DRAM attached to the accelerator itself, not the host — the tier that lets a socket hold trillion-parameter models and swap experts in milliseconds

**The piece that makes it special.** The three-tier memory, attached to the accelerator. GPUs force a choice: fit in HBM or stream from host memory over PCIe. SN40L stacks 520 MB of SRAM, 64 GB of HBM and up to 1.5 TB of DDR on the RDU itself, and the SambaFlow compiler places every tensor in a tier deliberately. That is what makes its party trick — a Composition-of-Experts serving 150+ models from one rack — possible: experts live in DDR and are promoted through HBM into SRAM-resident dataflow graphs.

**How work flows.** SambaFlow maps the whole graph: The compiler spatially assigns every operator to PCUs, every tensor to PMUs, and every route to the mesh — the binary (PEF) is the schedule. Weights stream up the tiers: The active model's weights move DDR → HBM → PMU SRAM ahead of the tokens that need them. Data flows spatially: Activations stream PCU to PCU through the mesh; fused operators never round-trip to memory between layers. AGCU handles the irregular: Sparse gathers and off-chip accesses are generated and coalesced at the fabric edge. Model switches are memory moves: Serving a different expert is a tier promotion, not a reload from a host — SambaNova quotes sub-10 ms switches for an 8B model.

**Trade-off accepted.** Compile-time rigidity. A spatial map is optimal for the graph it was compiled for and brittle for dynamic shapes and control flow; the RDU's peak (638 BF16 TFLOPS) is inseparable from SambaFlow's whole-graph compilation, and the ecosystem is a single vendor's rack, not a card you buy.

**Fact check.**
- [verified] 1,040 PCUs and 1,040 PMUs per socket — Source: SambaNova, Hot Chips 2024 — SN40L RDU presentation. Quote: "1040 PCUs and PMUs PCU: Compute unit PMU: Memory unit S: Mesh switches AGCU: Portal to off-chip memory and IO"
- [verified] Three-tier memory: 520 MB SRAM / 64 GB HBM / 1.5 TB DDR; 638 BF16 TFLOPS; 102B transistors, TSMC 5 nm — Source: SambaNova, Hot Chips 2024 — SN40L RDU presentation. Quote: "5nm TSMC 3-tier Dataflow Memory … 520 MB On-Chip Memory, 64 GB High Bandwidth Memory, 1.5 TB High Capacity Memory, 638 TFLOPS (bf16), 102B Transistors."

#### Inside the signature block: The PCU/PMU tile pair and the three-fabric RDN — the reconfigurable spatial fabric

**Inside it.** The RDU tile is a coarse-grained reconfigurable array of Pattern Compute Units, Pattern Memory Units and Address Generation and Coalescing Units wired by the Reconfigurable Dataflow Network (RDN), a two-dimensional mesh of non-blocking switches. A PCU is a multi-stage reconfigurable SIMD pipeline in three sections — a header that consumes incoming dataflows and drives the body, a body configurable either as an output-stationary systolic array or as a pipelined SIMD core with multiple stages of vector compute, and a tail that performs special element-wise functions and drives the output FIFOs. As a systolic array the PCU streams its inputs left-to-right and top-to-bottom through a broadcast buffer and drains accumulated results left-to-right to the output FIFOs through the tail; as a SIMD core each stage supports arithmetic, logical and bitwise operations in FP32, BF16 and INT32 (the Hot Chips deck adds INT8 compute types), with an optional cross-lane reduction network and lane-wise reductions. Counters in the PCU track loop iterations and generate control events when they reach the programmed maximum, and the tail supports transcendental functions, random number generation, stochastic rounding and format conversions, fusable and pipelined with the body's compute. A PMU is the tile's memory: a programmer-managed scratchpad organised as an array of SRAM instances supporting concurrent reads and writes, with its own scalar ALU pipeline of several stages of integer ALUs that generates read and write addresses concurrently — including special instructions for bitfield extraction and shift-and-set — and can be partitioned into independent read and write address-generation pipelines with a software-configured number of stages each. The PMU's data alignment unit handles transpose, cross-lane vector permute, vector-unaligned accesses, lookup tables and data format and layout conversions, and tensors written in a diagonally striped format across the scratchpad banks can be read back in transposed form at full bandwidth. The RDN itself is three physical fabrics: a packet-switched vector fabric carrying tensor data, a packet-switched scalar fabric carrying addresses and metadata (and sometimes data or control), and a circuit-switched control fabric — a bundle of individually routable single-bit wires carrying flow-control tokens and graph-orchestration tokens, typically the PCU counters' loop-done events. Inbound scalar and vector packets land in input FIFOs and exit through output FIFOs, with credit-based flow control at every hop and end-to-end flow control between units through coarse-grained software tokens, fine-grained hardware credits and forward-progress guarantees in hardware. Routing is either dynamic two-dimensional dimension-order routing or software-controlled static flow routing, in which a flow ID carried with the packet stream is decoded and reassigned at every switch port and supports multicasting; vector packets also carry a sequence ID that lets many sources feed one destination in a software-defined order, with the PMU using the sequence ID to compute the write addresses that reorder the packets. SambaNova publishes no PCU lane count (the deck says only 'M lanes'), no PCU stage count, no PMU bank count or organisation, no RDN switch radix or port counts, and no FIFO depths, so this is the fabric's contract, not its circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one matmul tile through a PCU chain.**
1. **Weights are staged in the PMU, laid out for the sweep.**The compiler has placed the matmul's weight tile in one or more PMUs — a single logical tensor may span several PMUs for capacity or bandwidth, with each PMU programmed with its valid address range or a predicate bit per generated address, and bank bits placed by software. If the tile must be read transposed, it was written in the diagonally striped format so the transpose costs no extra pass.
2. **The PMU's scalar ALU pipeline generates the addresses.**The address-generation pipeline produces up to four addresses per cycle, with its stages split between independent read and write pipelines as the compiler configured them; complex address math can be spread across PMUs because the pipeline ingests scalars from the scalar fabric and emits computed scalars back onto it. The read addresses pull the weight and activation vectors out of the scratchpad banks while a write pipeline stages the next tile.
3. **Vectors enter the PCU header through the RDN input FIFOs.**The activation and weight vectors arrive on the vector fabric and land in the PCU's input FIFOs; the header consumes them and drives the body. Credit-based flow control at every hop and end-to-end software tokens keep the producer PMU from overrunning the PCU — the schedule, not a runtime arbiter, decides when each vector moves.
4. **The systolic sweep multiplies and accumulates in place.**Configured as an output-stationary systolic array, the PCU streams its inputs left-to-right and top-to-bottom through the broadcast buffer, each element meeting its weight and accumulating into the stationary partial sum; a matmul too large for one PCU is parallelised across several, data-parallel, tensor-parallel or pipeline-parallel, with the partials joined downstream. In SIMD configuration the same tile runs as a pipelined multi-stage vector operation instead.
5. **The tail finishes the tile — reduction, activation, rounding.**The accumulated results drain left-to-right through the tail, which applies the element-wise finish: the cross-lane reduction tree reduces along the vectorised dimension where the operator needs it, transcendental functions and format conversions run here, and stochastic rounding is applied — all fused and pipelined with the body's compute so the finish costs no extra pass. The PCU's counters fire a loop-done control event onto the control fabric when the programmed iteration count is reached.
6. **The result streams on to the next PCU — or back to a PMU — with no memory round-trip.**The finished tile leaves through the output FIFOs onto the vector fabric toward the next PCU in the fused chain, or into a PMU for staging; fused operators never materialise intermediates to memory between layers. If several PCUs feed one PMU, their packets' sequence IDs tell the PMU the logical order, and it computes the write addresses that reassemble the tile in order.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves two walls at once: the kernel-launch wall — a whole fused graph runs as one spatially scheduled kernel, so the hundreds of operator launches and intermediate materialisations a GPU pays per layer disappear; and the operand-delivery wall — weights sit in PMU scratchpads beside the PCUs and stream through the broadcast buffer once, instead of being re-fetched from DRAM per multiply. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the static-schedule wall — every route, flow ID, sequence ID and credit arrangement is fixed at compile time by the compiler's place-and-route, so data-dependent routing and dynamic shapes cannot be expressed in the fabric; the PMU-capacity wall — a tile must fit in roughly 0.5 MiB of scratchpad per PMU, so large tensors must be sharded across PMUs with predication and bank-bit bookkeeping that costs address-generation stages; and the flow-control wall — a deep PCU chain is only as fast as its slowest credit return, so a stalled consumer back-pressures the whole chain through the FIFOs rather than letting the producer run ahead.

**Governing numbers.** 1,040 PCUs and 1,040 PMUs per socket; 520 MiB of PMU SRAM in total (the Hot Chips deck states 520 MB) — 0.5 MiB per PMU by arithmetic from the published totals; PMUs in aggregate provide hundreds of TBps of on-chip memory bandwidth with bank-level parallelism within and across PMUs; PMU address-generation pipeline produces 4 addresses per cycle; PCU compute data types BF16, FP32, INT32 and INT8 (INT8 from the Hot Chips deck); clock under 2 GHz; die under 650 mm²; 2 Reconfigurable Dataflow Dies per socket; PCU lane count 'M' not published; PCU stage count, PMU bank count and organisation, RDN switch radix and port counts, and input/output FIFO depths not published.

**Primary source.** Prabhakar et al., "SambaNova SN40L: Scaling the AI Memory Wall with Dataflow and Composition of Experts", arXiv:2405.07518 — §IV-A PCU, §IV-B PMU, §IV-C RDN (read live, full paper); Prabhakar, "SambaNova SN40L RDU: Breaking the Barrier of Trillion+ Parameter Scale Gen AI Computing", Hot Chips 2024 — SN40L PCU slide, SN40L PMU slide, SN40L Unit-Level Interconnect slide (read live, full deck); Prabhakar et al., "Plasticine: A Reconfigurable Architecture for Parallel Patterns", ISCA 2017 — lineage only: PCU as multi-stage reconfigurable SIMD pipeline, PMU as banked scratchpad with configurable address decoders, three static interconnects.

#### Inside the signature block: The three-tier memory system and the AGCU at the fabric edge — DDR → HBM → PMU SRAM promotion

**Inside it.** The memory system is three software-managed tiers on the accelerator itself: 520 MiB of distributed PMU SRAM on the dies (the Hot Chips deck states 520 MB), 64 GiB of co-packaged HBM at 1.8 TB/s per socket (the paper's text rounds this to 'about 2 TB/s'), and up to 1.5 TiB of pluggable DDR DRAM at over 200 GB/s per socket — an order of magnitude slower than HBM, which is why the compiler treats the tiers as a placement problem rather than a cache hierarchy. A single SN40L Node holds eight RDU sockets and a host, and models load from DDR to HBM at over 1 TB/s in one node; the Hot Chips deck quotes the switching bandwidth as 1,600 GB/s with a Llama 3.1 8B switch in under 0.01 s — the arithmetic of 16 GB of BF16 weights at 1.6 TB/s. The portal between the tile fabric and the off-chip tiers is the Address Generation and Coalescing Unit: on the tile side it looks like any other dataflow core, exposing RDN vector, scalar and control ports, and on the Top Level Network side it generates read and write requests and coalesces the responses, with its own scalar address-generation pipeline and counters — the PMU's address logic without the SRAM — plus an address-translation layer, which the Hot Chips deck names as a Segment Lookaside Buffer for virtual-to-physical translation and memory-access management. The AGCU also speaks peer-to-peer: its P2P protocol streams data directly between RDU tiles on different sockets without touching DDR or HBM, which is what collective operations such as AllReduce are built on, and it owns kernel-launch orchestration — a three-command sequence of Program Load, Argument Load and Kernel Execute — in either software-orchestrated form, where the host schedules kernels, or hardware-orchestrated form, where a static kernel schedule is offloaded to dedicated hardware in the AGCUs. Above the AGCU sits the Top Level Network, a hybrid mesh/ring packet-switched interconnect with four physical networks — Data, Request, Response and Credit — routed by Y-X dimension-order routing with all traffic managed by end-to-end credits or guaranteed consumption to avoid deadlocks; the two dies of a socket also stream data directly between each other over a die-to-die interface without going through off-chip memory, and the host attaches over PCIe with DMA between host and device memory and direct host-to-tile communication. None of this is a cache: the compiler manages the tiers explicitly, defaulting to HBM and using DDR for spilling and for holding inactive Composition-of-Experts models, with static lifetime analysis standing in for garbage collection — the programming model has no dynamic allocation and no pointer aliasing, so symbols whose lifetimes do not overlap can share device virtual addresses, and symbols are spilled smallest-bandwidth-first by aggregate transfer size, weights first to stay in HBM. SambaNova publishes no AGCU queue depths or coalescing window, no TLN link rates, no die-to-die bandwidth, and no PMU-bank organisation, so this is the memory system's contract, not its circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one expert-model switch, router to running expert.**
1. **The router runs from HBM-resident weights.**The prompt arrives and the router model — small, always resident in HBM — runs on the RDU's PCUs and picks the expert for this prompt. The router and the KV cache never leave HBM; only experts move between tiers.
2. **The CoE runtime activates the chosen expert.**The runtime checks whether the expert's HBM segments are already resident; if the HBM region for the current expert is full it evicts the least-recently-used model, and read-only weight symbols are never copied back to DDR on eviction. Each compiled model binary declares in advance exactly how much HBM and DDR space it needs, so the activation is a planned copy, not a demand fault.
3. **The AGCU generates the DDR reads and coalesces the replies.**The AGCU's scalar address-generation pipeline produces the DDR read requests for the expert's weight segments, translating device virtual addresses through the Segment Lookaside Buffer, and issues them onto the Top Level Network; as responses return it coalesces them into streams for the tile fabric. The requests cross the Request network and the data returns on the Data network, with the Credit network carrying the end-to-end flow control.
4. **The expert's weights stream DDR → HBM at node bandwidth.**Sixteen gigabytes of BF16 weights for an 8B expert cross from DDR into HBM at over 1 TB/s per node — the deck's 1,600 GB/s figure puts the copy under 0.01 s. The DDR tier is nine times slower than HBM, so the copy is the switch: everything after it is fast because the weights are now in the fast tier.
5. **Weights are promoted HBM → PMU SRAM ahead of the tokens.**The AGCU streams the expert's active weight tiles from HBM into the PMUs' scratchpads ahead of the tokens that need them, staged tile by tile so the first decoder layer can start while later tiles are still promoting. Activations never leave the fabric between layers; only weights climb the tiers.
6. **The expert decodes, re-reading its weights from HBM at over 85 percent of bandwidth.**In the autoregressive decode loop each token's pass re-reads the weights from HBM — the model-level temporal locality the tiering exploits — and the measured HBM utilisation exceeds 85 percent, against rarely over 50 percent for optimised GPU implementations on weights and KV cache. The next prompt's expert can already be staging in DDR while this one decodes, because the switch is a tier promotion, not a host reload.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves two walls at once: the model-switch wall — 150 experts live in DDR on the accelerator, so switching models is a DDR-to-HBM promotion at over 1 TB/s per node instead of a host reload over PCIe, which the paper measures as 15× to 31× faster switching than a DGX baseline; and the capacity wall — 1.5 TiB of DDR per socket holds a trillion-parameter Composition-of-Experts that no HBM-only socket could host. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the DDR-bandwidth wall — at just over 200 GB/s per socket the DDR tier is an order of magnitude slower than HBM, so every expert switch pays a promotion whose cost grows with the expert, and a request pattern that thrashes the HBM working set re-pays the copy on every switch; the HBM-capacity wall — only the active expert or experts fit in 64 GiB, so the LRU eviction policy, not hardware, decides what stays fast; and the software-management wall — with no hardware cache anywhere, every symbol's tier, lifetime and spill order is the compiler and runtime's job, and a placement mistake is a slowdown no hardware mechanism recovers.

**Governing numbers.** 520 MiB PMU SRAM (deck: 520 MB); 64 GiB HBM at 1.8 TB/s per socket (paper text: 'about 2 TB/s'); up to 1.5 TiB DDR at over 200 GB/s per socket; both tiers software-managed; SN40L Node is 8 RDU sockets plus one host; models load DDR → HBM at over 1 TB/s in a single node; Hot Chips deck: 1,600 GB/s switching bandwidth, under 0.01 s for a Llama 3.1 8B switch (16 GB of BF16 weights at 1.6 TB/s by arithmetic); decode uses over 85 percent of HBM bandwidth; hardware-orchestrated kernel launches speed autoregressive decoding 1.4× to 8× over software orchestration, and prefill/training by at most 1.1×; operator fusion speedups 2× to 13× over the unfused baseline on 8 sockets; AGCU queue depths, coalescing window, TLN link rates and die-to-die bandwidth not published.

**Primary source.** Prabhakar et al., "SambaNova SN40L: Scaling the AI Memory Wall with Dataflow and Composition of Experts", arXiv:2405.07518 — §IV RDN/AGCU/TLN, Table II chip parameters, §V software memory management and CoE runtime, §VI measured fusion, orchestration and Llama 3.1 results (read live, full paper); Prabhakar, "SambaNova SN40L RDU: Breaking the Barrier of Trillion+ Parameter Scale Gen AI Computing", Hot Chips 2024 — 3-tier Memory System slide, SN40L AGCU slide, SN40L Top-Level Interconnect slide (read live, full deck).

### Intel Gaudi 2 (Habana)

**Specs (wiki card).** 7 nm · 96 GB HBM2e · 24 TPCs + MME

**Building blocks.**
- **Matrix Multiplication Engine (MME) ×2** — The GEMM engine: a large output-stationary systolic array (256×256 MAC structure) handling everything that lowers to matrix multiplication — fully connected, convolution, batched GEMM — and the two units can merge into one wider engine
- **Tensor Processor Core (TPC) ×24** — Fully programmable VLIW SIMD cores, programmed in TPC-C, for everything the MME can't do — normalisation, softmax, custom operators. This programmability is Gaudi's founding idea: no operator needs a host fallback
- **Shared SRAM — 48 MB** — The meeting point: MME, TPCs, DMAs and NICs all operate against one 48 MB SRAM complex in parallel, rather than private buffers with copies between them
- **DMA + transpose engines** — Multiple DMAs coupled to a transpose engine reshape tensors on the fly and stream non-contiguous multi-dimensional tensors between HBM and SRAM
- **96 GB HBM2e** — Six stacks delivering 2.45 TB/s — capacity sized so training models fit without aggressive sharding
- **24× 100 GbE RoCE v2 NICs** — Scale-out integrated on the die itself: 2.4 Tb/s of RDMA-over-Ethernet, no separate NIC card, scaling through standard Ethernet switches

**The piece that makes it special.** Ethernet on the die, and a programmable core beside the matrix engine. Gaudi 2's two heterodoxies compound: the TPC cluster means the accelerator never waits for a GPU-style kernel library to support a new operator, and the 24 integrated RoCE ports mean scale-out uses commodity Ethernet instead of a proprietary fabric — the chip is designed to make a thousand-accelerator cluster a networking commodity purchase.

**How work flows.** Graph compiler splits the work: SynapseAI lowers matmul-shaped ops to the MME and everything else to TPC kernels, scheduling both against shared SRAM. DMAs stage tensors: Weights and activations stream from HBM into SRAM, transposed into MME layout in flight. MME sweeps the GEMMs: Matrix work runs on the systolic array while TPCs concurrently run the layer's non-matmul ops on the previous tile. Collectives leave by Ethernet: Gradients and activations move chip-to-chip over the on-die RoCE ports, overlapped with compute. Results write back: Outputs return to HBM; the SRAM complex turns over to the next layer.

**Trade-off accepted.** Ecosystem gravity. The architecture is competitive — ISCA 2025 benchmarking found Gaudi 2 trading wins with the A100 — but CUDA's library moat meant the heterogeneous split had to be re-proven model by model, and Intel's commitment to the line wavered. The design lesson (programmable companion cores + integrated Ethernet) outlived the product's market position.

**Fact check.**
- [verified] Two compute engines: MME + programmable TPC cluster; 96 GB HBM2e at 2.45 TB/s; 48 MB SRAM — Source: Intel/Habana, Intel Gaudi2 AI Accelerators white paper (v2.0, Oct 2023). Quote: "The Intel Gaudi2 Memory subsystem includes 96 GB of HBM2E memories delivering 2.45 TB/sec bandwidth, in addition to a 48 MB of local SRAM with sufficient bandwidth to allow MME, TPC, DMAs and RDMA NICs to operate in parallel."
- [verified] 24 TPCs; 24×100 GbE RoCE v2 integrated — Source: Intel/Habana, Gaudi2 HL-225H datasheet (Oct 2022). Quote: "The Intel Gaudi2 AI accelerator offers unmatched scalability of 2.4 Terabits networking capacity with native integration of 24x100 GbE RoCE v2 RDMA ports"
- [verified] MME is a 256×256 MAC output-stationary systolic array; Gaudi 2 has two MMEs and 24 TPCs — Source: Debunking the CUDA Myth, ISCA 2025 (architecture background, citing Habana). Quote: "Gaudi-2 features two MMEs and 24 TPCs, which together provide high throughput by pipelining computations between the MMEs and TPCs."

#### Inside the signature block: The MME — a 256x256 output-stationary systolic array that stays full on small GEMMs

**Inside it.** Gaudi 2 carries two Matrix Multiplication Engines, each a 256x256 MAC output-stationary systolic array — 65,536 MACs per MME, 131,072 per chip — with FP32 accumulators for every data type. Output-stationary means the partial sums stay in place in the MAC cells while the two operands stream past, so a finished tile drains only once, at the end of the sweep. The two MMEs are dynamically reconfigurable at runtime: two separate 256x256 units, or one 512x256 unit, one 1024x128 unit, and other shapes, with the Gaudi graph compiler choosing the configuration for each GEMM from the shape of its input and output matrices. The MME is not directly programmable — the programmer reaches it only through the graph compiler, and its job is matrix multiplication and nothing else. Feeding one big array is cheap: it needs 512 input elements per cycle (256 per operand) to stay fully utilized, against 8,192 for 256 small 16x16 arrays doing the same compute — a 16x difference in read bandwidth toward first-level memory. An internal pipeline keeps the array fed at full rate, and because one big array needs so little operand bandwidth, the 48 MB SRAM can pipeline activations and the MME stays full on GEMMs as small as m=n=k=512.

**Trace — one unit of work: one 256x256 output tile of a linear layer, BF16.**
1. **The graph compiler picks the MME shape for this GEMM.** For a linear layer the compiler looks at the GEMM shape and reconfigures the two MMEs — one wide 512x256 unit for a wide output tile, two separate 256x256 units for two independent GEMMs, or another shape — then slices the layer into tiles that fit the chosen window. The slicing is what makes the overlap below possible: each slice is an independent unit of work for the MME and the TPCs.
2. **DMAs stage the A and B tiles into shared SRAM, transposed in flight.** The DMA engines coupled to the transpose engine stream the weight and activation tiles from HBM into the 48 MB shared SRAM, reshaping them into the MME's layout on the fly so no separate transpose pass is needed. Staging runs ahead of compute: while the MME sweeps one tile, the DMAs are already landing the next.
3. **Operands stream into the array, 256 elements per cycle per side.** The A tile streams in from one edge and the B tile from the other, 256 elements per cycle each — 512 elements per cycle in total — and the wavefront sweeps across the 256x256 grid. Because the array is one big unit rather than hundreds of small ones, this modest feed rate is enough to keep all 65,536 MACs busy.
4. **The systolic sweep multiplies and accumulates in place, in FP32.** Each MAC cell multiplies its streaming operands and adds the product into its stationary partial sum, in FP32 whatever the input type — BF16, FP16 or FP8 in, FP32 accumulated. No partial sum leaves the array mid-sweep, so the only traffic is the two operand streams in and the finished tile out.
5. **The finished tile drains to SRAM while the TPC runs the previous tile's epilogue.** Once the sweep completes, the 256x256 output tile drains into the shared SRAM. The TPC cluster is already working the previous tile's non-GEMM ops — bias, activation, normalisation — from the same SRAM, so the MME's drain and the TPC's epilogue overlap instead of serialising.
6. **The next slice starts with no idle gap.** The compiler's sliced schedule hands the MME the next tile as soon as the previous one drains, with the DMAs having staged it ahead of time. The measured result is 429 TFLOPS on a square 8192-cubed BF16 GEMM — 99.3 percent of the 432 TFLOPS peak — and full utilisation on GEMMs far smaller than a GPU needs.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves two walls at once: the small-GEMM utilisation wall — a GPU needs a GEMM of m=n=k=~3K to use 80 percent of its many small matrix units, while Gaudi 2 is 100 percent utilised at m=n=k=1K, and at m=n=k=512 when activations are pipelined through the 48 MB SRAM, needing roughly 25x to 200x fewer MACs in a GEMM to be fully utilised; and the operand-bandwidth wall — one big array needs 512 input elements per cycle where 256 small 16x16 arrays need 8,192, leaving most of the SRAM and HBM bandwidth free for the TPCs, the DMAs and the NICs. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the shape-sensitivity wall — utilisation depends on the compiler picking the right reconfiguration for each GEMM shape, and tall-skinny GEMV-like shapes stay memory-bound whatever the configuration; the MME-only-does-matmul wall — every non-GEMM operation must fit through the 11-TFLOPS TPC cluster, so a layer with a heavy non-matmul share is capped by the weaker engine; and the tile-window wall — output-stationary means a tile must fit the 256x256 window, so large GEMMs are sliced and re-staged through SRAM, and the slicing schedule is the compiler's job, not hardware's.

**Governing numbers.** Two MMEs, each 256x256 MACs = 65,536 MACs per MME, 131,072 per chip; 64K MACs per cycle per MME for BF16 and FP8; 432 BF16 TFLOPS peak, 429 TFLOPS measured at M=K=N=8192 (99.3 percent of peak); 512 input elements per cycle to utilise the array, against 8,192 for 256 small 16x16 arrays (16x less read bandwidth); m=n=k=1K sufficient for 100 percent utilisation, m=n=k=512 sufficient when activations are pipelined via the 48 MB SRAM; modern GPUs need m=n=k=~3K for 80 percent utilisation; Intel Gaudi2 needs ~25x-~200x fewer MACs in a GEMM to be utilised 100 percent than modern GPUs at 80 percent; all data types accumulate into FP32; reconfiguration shapes include a single 512x256 and a single 1024x128 MAC unit, chosen per GEMM by the graph compiler; MME internal pipeline depth and staging buffer sizes not published.

**Primary source.** Intel/Habana, "Intel Gaudi2 AI Accelerators" white paper v2.0 (Oct 2023) — section II chip architecture, Figures 6-9 (read live, full document); Lee et al., "Debunking the CUDA Myth: Towards GPU-based AI Systems", ISCA 2025, arXiv:2501.00210v2 — section 2.1 hardware architecture, section 3.2 GEMM microbenchmarks (read live, full paper).

#### Inside the signature block: The TPC cluster and the 48 MB shared SRAM — programmable vector cores that never wait for a DMA

**Inside it.** Gaudi 2 carries 24 fourth-generation Tensor Processor Cores, fully programmable VLIW SIMD processors that handle everything the MME cannot — normalisation, softmax, custom operators. Each TPC has four execution slots that issue in parallel: a Load slot, a scalar slot (SPU), a vector slot (VPU) and a Store slot, with a 256-byte (2,048-bit) SIMD vector unit in the VPU. Each TPC has its own private local memory: 1 KB of scalar local memory, read and written in aligned 4-byte chunks, and 80 KB of vector local memory, read and written in aligned 128- or 256-byte chunks — dropping to 16 KB when the kernel uses special functions such as tanh, sin or cos. Local memory can be read from or written to on every cycle with no bandwidth constraint, while a 2,048-bit vector can be loaded from or stored to global memory every four cycles on average. The pipeline is exposed: each instruction has a predefined latency, four cycles being the most prevalent, so the compiler unrolls loops — typically by a factor of four — to hide it. The programming model is DMA-free: the TPC reads global memory directly through tensor descriptors instead of waiting for a DMA to stage operands into local memory, and execution between kernels is bubble-free, so the TPC stays utilised even on very short kernels. Global memory — the 48 MB shared SRAM and the HBM behind it — is not coherent with program execution, so a read-after-write across engines needs an atomic semaphore operation, and the minimum global access granularity is 256-byte chunks. The 48 MB shared SRAM is the compiler's scratchpad and the meeting point: MME, TPCs, DMAs and RoCE NICs all operate against it in parallel, and the graph compiler uses it as the intermediate buffer when it pipelines an MME operation into a following TPC operation. Several DMA engines coupled to a transpose engine stage tensors between HBM and SRAM, reshaping them on the fly; Habana publishes no DMA engine count.

**Trace — one unit of work: one fused epilogue kernel — bias + activation + normalisation — on the previous GEMM slice while the MME works the next.**
1. **The graph compiler slices the layer and fuses the epilogue into one TPC kernel.** For a transformer layer the compiler breaks the GEMM-plus-activation pair into smaller independent sub-operations: the MME takes the GEMM slices, and the bias, activation and normalisation of each slice are fused into a single TPC kernel by the MLIR-based fuser. The fused kernel is one program, partitioned across the TPCs by index space — up to five dimensions — with each TPC taking an indivisible unit of work.
2. **The TPC loads 2,048-bit vectors straight from shared SRAM.** The kernel's loop loads its operands directly from the shared SRAM through tensor descriptors — no DMA staging step, no copy into local memory first. Each load pulls a 2,048-bit vector, aligned to the 256-byte global-memory granularity, and the local memory holds only the working set the kernel chooses to keep: partial reductions, lookup tables, constants.
3. **All four VLIW slots fire in parallel on an unrolled loop.** The loop body is unrolled by four so that Load, scalar, vector and Store instructions overlap and hide the four-cycle average instruction latency. While the VPU crunches one vector, the Load slot is already fetching the next, the SPU is computing addresses and predicates, and the Store slot is writing back the previous result — the exposed pipeline is kept full by the schedule, not by hardware interlocks.
4. **Vector math runs in the VPU; scalars and addresses run beside it.** The 256-byte-wide VPU applies the activation and normalisation element-wise across the vector while the SPU handles the scalar bookkeeping — loop counters, masks, address arithmetic — in the same VLIW word. Special functions such as tanh run through the TPC's special-function path, which is when the vector local memory shrinks to 16 KB.
5. **Results store back to shared SRAM in 256-byte chunks; a semaphore marks the tile done.** The finished vectors store back into the shared SRAM at the 256-byte global granularity, ready for the next layer's MME slice or for the RoCE NICs to carry off-chip. Because global memory is not coherent, the kernel issues an atomic semaphore operation where a read-after-write must be visible before the next consumer reads the tile back.
6. **The next kernel starts with no bubble — and the MME never waited.** Kernel-to-kernel execution is bubble-free, so the next fused kernel begins the moment this one ends, and the whole epilogue ran overlapped with the MME's next GEMM slice rather than after it. The measured cost of the programmable side is small in FLOPS — 11 BF16 TFLOPS against the MME's 432 — but it is what lets a new operator run at all without a host fallback.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves two walls at once: the operator-fallback wall — any operator can be written as a TPC kernel in TPC-C, so no new model waits for a GPU-style kernel library to support it and no operator needs a host fallback; and the kernel-launch and bubble wall — the DMA-free model and bubble-free execution between kernels keep the TPC at 100 percent utilisation on tensor processing even for very short kernels, regardless of whether inputs live in SRAM or HBM. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the TPC-throughput wall — 11 BF16 TFLOPS of vector compute against the MME's 432, so a layer whose non-GEMM share is large becomes TPC-bound, and the ISCA paper measures Gaudi-2's vector compute at 0.3x the A100's SIMD cores; the private-memory wall — local memory belongs to one TPC only, so all sharing goes through the shared SRAM or HBM at 256-byte granularity with semaphore synchronisation and no hardware coherence; and the exposed-pipeline wall — with no caches and no hardware multithreading to hide latency, the compiler must unroll loops to hide the four-cycle instruction latency, and a kernel that misses its unroll factor stalls on the latency and the global-memory round trip.

**Governing numbers.** 24 TPCs, fourth generation; 256-byte (2,048-bit) SIMD wide; four VLIW execution slots — Load, SPU, VPU, Store; 80 KB vector local memory per TPC (16 KB when special functions such as tanh, sin or cos are used), 1 KB scalar local memory; local memory readable or writable every cycle with no bandwidth constraint; a 2,048-bit vector loads from or stores to global memory every four cycles on average; average TPC instruction latency 4 processor cycles; TPC vector compute 11 BF16 TFLOPS in total; index space divisible into up to five dimensions; global memory minimum access granularity 256-byte chunks; 48 MB shared SRAM; DMA engine count and transpose-engine internals not published.

**Primary source.** Intel/Habana, "Intel Gaudi2 AI Accelerators" white paper v2.0 (Oct 2023) — section II chip architecture (read live, full document); Intel/Habana, TPC User Guide, Processor Architectural Overview, Gaudi Documentation v1.14.0 (docs.habana.ai — read via search-verified excerpts; the docs site did not resolve in the live browser this run); Lee et al., "Debunking the CUDA Myth: Towards GPU-based AI Systems", ISCA 2025, arXiv:2501.00210v2 — sections 2.1-2.2 (read live, full paper).
