**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the paper publishes the PE geometry used above — two single-issue, in-order, five-stage RISC-V cores, one with a 32-register vector unit of 64 B registers, five fixed-function blocks, a Command Processor with two schedulers, 128 KB of local memory as circular buffers, a DPE doing 1,024 INT8 or 512 FP16 multiplications per cycle over 32 cycles per maximum-size block, a Reduction Engine with four accumulator banks, and 400 GB/s of local-memory bandwidth per PE — and the arithmetic is derived from those published counts. Below that level — local-memory bank count and organisation, Command Processor command-queue depths, DPE staging and register detail, SIMD Engine lookup-table sizes, Fabric Interface queue depths, core cache sizes — Meta publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no tag array and no coherence hardware on the local-memory path, because the local memory is a software-managed scratchpad; and there is no credit-based flow control inside the PE, because the circular buffers' full/empty checks are the flow control.

#### Down to the primitives: The memory and interconnect complex — dual AXI networks, multicast and the reduction network

Decomposed in trace order — the PEs issue their gather requests, the network coalesces the shared reads, memory serves once and delivers to all, partials travel the reduction network, and the last PE writes back while the host collects over PCIe. The paper publishes the complex's contract — 128 MB of on-chip SRAM in slices around the grid at 800 GB/s, eight LPDDR5 controllers on 16 channels at 176 GB/s theoretical, two AXI networks (one for memory accesses, one for register accesses), row-or-column-only multicast, a unidirectional reduction network, and a PCIe Gen4 x8 host interface at 16 GB/s — but nothing below that contract: no crossbar radix or port counts, no AXI buffer depths, no SRAM slice count as a printed figure, no tag organisation, no DMA channel counts. Where a number below is computed from published geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **Crossbar (the XBARs on each side of the grid)** — The memory and movement pieces connect through crossbars on each side of the grid, switching the 64 PEs' requests onto the SRAM slices and the LPDDR5 controllers. The crossbars' port counts, radix and per-port widths are not published.
- **Switch arbiter (AXI network arbitration between 64 PEs, the SRAM slices and eight memory controllers)** — "The interconnects consist of two networks for carrying memory and register accesses separately." (Level-2 — verified, fact records), and "The on-chip network that connects all the PEs and memories together is based on the AXI interconnect with special enhancements." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Two networks carry every PE's requests to the SRAM slices and the LPDDR5 controllers, so accesses from 64 PEs must be arbitrated onto the slice and controller ports. The arbiters' structure, port counts and fairness policy are not published.
- **Comparator (multicast address matching — row or column only)** — "Multicast is only supported for the PEs that are located along the same row or column in the grid however, and cannot be used for an arbitrary group of PEs." (Level-2 — verified, fact records), and the memory network's multicast "allows coalescing of requests from multiple PEs into one (if they are made to the same set of addresses)" (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Coalescing is an address comparison per outstanding request against the incoming request's addresses. The match table's size and the comparison width are not published.
- **SRAM bank (the 128 MB on-chip SRAM — slices around the perimeter)** — "In addition to the local memory within the PEs, the accelerator also has 128MB of on-chip SRAM, organized as slices around the grid." (Level-2 — verified, fact records), usable "as addressable scratchpad memory, or as a common, shared, memory-side cache" (Level-2 — verified, fact records). In cache mode each four cache slices are associated with a single memory controller — four slices per controller × eight controllers is 32 slices by arithmetic, 128 MB / 32 is 4 MB per slice, and 800 GB/s / 32 slices is 25 GB/s per slice, all arithmetic from the published figures (see fact records). The slice count as a printed figure is not published — the 32 is derived from the four-slices-per-controller association — and the bank organisation inside a slice is not published.
- **Tag array (cache mode — organisation unpublished)** — In cache mode the slices act as a shared, memory-side cache, which implies a tag lookup per slice, but the paper publishes no tag width, associativity, replacement policy or placement — so no tag structure is claimed here.
- **Mux / demux (slice and controller selection; address decode)** — Each request's address selects one of eight memory controllers and one of 16 channels — two channels per controller by arithmetic (see fact records) — and one of the SRAM slices. The decode is a mux/demux per address bit; the decoder structure is not published.
- **Counter (the reduction network's bank-to-bank accumulation)** — "This is a unidirectional network that travels only from north to south and from west to east." (Level-2 — verified, fact records), carrying partial sums from the Reduction Engine accumulators of one PE to the next, where they are added onto that PE's bank. The chain crosses at most seven PEs in one direction across the 8x8 grid by arithmetic (see fact records). The per-hop latency and the network's buffering are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (AXI network buffering; Fabric Interface request queues)** — Requests wait in the network between issue and service — the Fabric Interface formulates them, the crossbars switch them, the slices and controllers serve them — so each stage holds requests in queues. The queue depths, the packet format and the per-stage buffering are not published.
- **DMA engine (Fabric Interface DMA-like transfers; the host interface's DMA engines)** — The Fabric Interface runs DMA-like transfers in and out of local memory, and the PCIe Gen4 x8 host interface has associated DMA engines. The DMA channel counts and queue depths are not published.
- **Synchronizer (the PCIe host interface; the dual-rail power domains)** — The host interface is a PCIe Gen4 x8 link with a secure-boot processor beside it, and the die runs dual rails — 0.67 V logic, 0.75 V memories — so the host link and the memory rail are clock and power-domain crossings by construction. The synchronizer structure, the PCIe SerDes detail beyond the x8 width and the secure-boot processor's internals are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the control subsystem — CCP firmware sequencing)** — The control subsystem holds dedicated processors and peripherals running the system firmware, sequencing jobs across the grid and the PCIe host link. The control processor count, its firmware state and its job-sequencing FSM are not published.
- **Credit counter — no hardware flow control published** — The paper describes no credit-based flow control for the AXI networks or the reduction network: no credit counters, no backpressure scheme and no published buffer accounting between the crossbars. Flow control, as far as the published material goes, is the multicast coalescing and the circular-buffer backpressure at the PEs. A credit counter is therefore named here as absent from the published design, not as a primitive with unpublished parameters.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the paper publishes the memory-system geometry used above — 128 MB of on-chip SRAM in slices around the grid at 800 GB/s, eight LPDDR5 controllers on 16 channels at 176 GB/s theoretical with up to 128 GB supported, two AXI networks (memory and register), row-or-column-only multicast, a unidirectional reduction network, and a PCIe Gen4 x8 host interface at 16 GB/s — and the arithmetic is derived from those published counts. Below that level — crossbar radix and port counts, AXI buffer depths, the SRAM slice count as a printed figure, tag organisation, DMA channel counts, synchronizer structure — Meta publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no HBM anywhere in the memory system, because LPDDR5 was chosen deliberately for capacity and bandwidth-per-dollar; and there is no hardware flow control published for the AXI networks or the reduction network, because the flow control the paper describes lives in the multicast coalescing and the PEs' circular buffers.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [verified] **Meta MTIA v1** — DPE throughput by arithmetic: 64 PEs × 1,024 INT8 multiplications/cycle × 2 operations per multiply-accumulate × 800 MHz = 104.9 INT8 TOPS, against the published 102.4 INT8 TOPS; 64 × 512 × 2 × 800 MHz = 52.4 FP16 TFLOPS against the published 51.2 TFLOPS — the same ~2.4% gap in both precisions, consistent with a nominal-versus-sustained clock or rate difference; the wiki keeps the published figures. Source: Firoozshahian et al., ISCA 2023, §3.1/§3.2 and Table I; Meta MTIA v1 announcement (May 2023).
- [verified] **Meta MTIA v1** — Vector register state by arithmetic: 32 registers × 64 B = 2,048 B (2 KiB) per PE; 128 KiB across the 64-PE grid. Source: Firoozshahian et al., ISCA 2023, §3.2.
- [verified] **Meta MTIA v1** — Local memory across the grid by arithmetic: 64 PEs × 128 KB = 8 MB. Source: Firoozshahian et al., ISCA 2023, §3.1/§3.3.
- [verified] **Meta MTIA v1** — Local-memory bandwidth per cycle by arithmetic: Table I's 400 GB/s per PE at the 800 MHz nominal clock is 500 bytes per cycle per PE — about eight times the 64 B/cycle the DPE demands at most, so the feed ceiling is arbitration and latency, not raw local-memory bandwidth. Source: Firoozshahian et al., ISCA 2023, Table I.
- [verified] **Meta MTIA v1** — SRAM slices by arithmetic: four cache slices per memory controller × eight controllers = 32 slices; 128 MB / 32 = 4 MB per slice; 800 GB/s / 32 = 25 GB/s per slice. Source: Firoozshahian et al., ISCA 2023, §3.4.
- [verified] **Meta MTIA v1** — LPDDR5 channels by arithmetic: 16 channels / 8 controllers = 2 channels per controller. Source: Firoozshahian et al., ISCA 2023, §3.4 and Table I.
- [verified] **Meta MTIA v1** — Reduction Engine banks by arithmetic: the four banks hold a 64×64 output — 4,096 elements, 1,024 per bank. Source: Firoozshahian et al., ISCA 2023, §3.1.3 and §4.
- [verified] **Meta MTIA v1** — Reduction-network chain by arithmetic: a partial-sum chain crosses at most seven PEs in one direction across the 8×8 grid. Source: Firoozshahian et al., ISCA 2023, §3.4.
- [unverifiable] **Meta MTIA v1** — Level-3 primitive-parameter boundary: no published local-memory bank count or organisation, Command Processor command-queue depths, DPE staging or register detail, SIMD Engine lookup-table sizes, Fabric Interface queue depths, core cache sizes, crossbar radix or port counts, AXI buffer depths, SRAM slice count as a printed figure, tag organisation, DMA channel counts, or synchronizer structure. Source: Firoozshahian et al., ISCA 2023, §§3.1–3.5, §4, Tables I–III; Meta MTIA v1 announcement (May 2023) (absence of these internals across the documents).

Note: the Level-2 facts re-used in this section (the five fixed-function blocks plus Command Processor, the DPE's 1,024 INT8 / 512 FP16 multiplications per cycle, the 32-cycle maximum-size block with INT32/FP32 accumulation, the Reduction Engine's four accumulator banks, the five-stage AX25-V100 cores, the 32 × 64 B vector registers, the circular buffers as hardware FIFOs with the Command Processor's pre-flight check, the 128 MB SRAM slices and their scratchpad/cache modes, the four LPDDR5 controllers per side at 176 GB/s theoretical, the row/column-only multicast, the two separate AXI networks, the unidirectional reduction network, and the Table I chip summary) were already recorded at Level-2 with the same quotes and sources and were deduped, not re-appended.


#### Down to the gates: The Processing Element — two RISC-V cores driving five fixed-function blocks

Meta publishes no gate-level structure for the Processing Element — the ISCA 2023 paper (sections 3.1-3.3) describes the PE's contract (two single-issue, in-order, five-stage RISC-V cores, one with a 32-register vector unit, five fixed-function blocks, a Command Processor with two schedulers, 128 KB of local memory organised as circular buffers, the DPE's 1,024 INT8 or 512 FP16 multiplications per cycle over 32 cycles per maximum-size block, the Reduction Engine's four accumulator banks, and 400 GB/s of local-memory bandwidth per PE) and stops there. A gate-term search of the paper this run found no transistor, flip-flop, 6T or latch content — the only NAND hits are substrings of author names — and the Andes material likewise publishes no gate-level core detail. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about Meta's circuits.

- **FIFO / queue (the circular buffers — CBs in local memory)** — A FIFO is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: as registers, N entries of W bits is N x W D flip-flops (N x W x 20-28 transistors); the write and read pointers are counters (an N-bit pointer counter is N flip-flops plus N full adders); full and empty are comparators of the two pointers (one XOR gate per pointer bit plus an AND tree over the bits). Each circular buffer is such a FIFO in local memory, with an ID, a size chosen in software per buffer and a starting address, and the Command Processor's pre-flight check — data present in the input CBs, space free in the output CB — is the flow control that stalls a consumer in hardware until the producer's DMA fills its CB. CB depth is a size chosen in software per buffer, not a fixed published number, and the number of CBs a PE can hold at once is not published, so no CB total is claimed — and the pointer widths are unpublished, so the per-buffer counter and comparator totals are not claimed either. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the 128 KB local memory — banks arbitrated by the Command Processor)** — The 128 KB local memory is an array of 6T SRAM cells in the primer's SRAM bank form — each stored bit is 6 transistors (two cross-coupled inverters, 4 transistors, plus two access transistors), plus the per-bank row decoder, column muxes and sense amplifiers. Arithmetic from the published 128 KB: on the MiB reading, 1,048,576 bits, 6,291,456 6T cell transistors per PE, and 402,653,184 across the 64-PE grid. The Command Processor holds arbitration logic for the local-memory banks and registers, so the 128 KB is banked, and the paper's own lesson is that local-memory latency ran longer than typical with many clients complicating the arbitration — but the bank count, the bank width and the arbitration policy are not published, so the decoder, mux and sense-amplifier totals — which need the bank count — are not claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the Command Processor — two schedulers, one per core)** — The Command Processor is a control FSM: in the standard form, the control state lives in master-slave D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each) with next-state logic as a NAND/NOR network, and the two schedulers — one per core — are the selection logic that dispatches commands to the five fixed-function blocks after the dependency checking passes. The command-queue depths and the schedulers' selection policy are not published, so no state-bit count and no controller total is claimed — the two-scheduler organisation is the published fact, and the flip-flop-plus-NAND/NOR form is standard construction, not a published circuit. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (the Command Processor's pre-flight data and space checks)** — The pre-flight check is a comparison: the CB read and write pointers against the operation's footprint, so an operation never stalls mid-execution. In the standard comparator form, comparing two N-bit values is one XOR gate per bit (10-12 transistors each) plus an AND tree over the bit results, so a 16-bit pointer comparison is 16 XOR gates, 160-192 transistors, plus the AND tree. The comparator widths follow the unpublished CB pointer widths, so no comparator total is claimed — the 16-bit figure illustrates the per-bit form and is not a published width. Standard construction.
- **Counter (CB read/write pointers; the atomic primitives)** — A counter is a register plus an incrementer in the standard form: an N-bit counter is N D flip-flops (N x 20-28 transistors) plus an N-bit incrementer of N full adders (N x 28 transistors), so a 16-bit counter is 768-896 transistors, and a 16-bit up/down counter — one that can count both directions, as a CB pointer must when data is both produced and consumed — is 832-960 transistors. Each CB's read and write pointers are such counters, advanced by the producer as DMA fills the buffer and by the consumer as it POPs or advances past consumed data, and the Command Processor's hardware atomic primitives are atomic updates to predefined registers that can stall a core until a condition is met — in the standard form one flip-flop per state bit plus a stall-condition comparator. The pointer widths, the atomic register count and the stall-condition comparators are not published, so no counter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Register file (Proc-A and Proc-B architectural state; the vector unit's 32 × 64 B registers)** — The vector unit's register file is 32 registers of 64 B each — 2 KiB of vector register state per PE by arithmetic from the published geometry, 128 KiB across the 64-PE grid. In the standard D flip-flop register-file form, one register is 64 B, 512 bits, 10,240-14,336 transistors of flip-flops, and the whole file is 16,384 bits, 327,680-458,752 transistors per PE. The construction choice is stated: this is the D flip-flop form; an SRAM-cell implementation would count differently and is not claimed here. Reading one element out of a vector register is a mux tree: selecting one 64 B register from 32 is a 32:1 mux per bit, 31 2:1 muxes in 5 levels, 124 transistors per bit in transmission-gate form. The scalar register-file sizes and port counts are not published, so no scalar total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (the Dot-Product Engine — 1,024 INT8 / 512 FP16 multiplications per cycle)** — A multiplier is an AND-gate partial-product array feeding a full-adder compressor tree and one final carry-propagate adder. Arithmetic from the published geometry, in the standard array-multiplier form, per multiplier: INT8 (8-bit operands) is an 8x8 array, 64 AND2 gates (384 transistors) plus 56 full adders (1,568 transistors) plus a 16-bit final adder (448 transistors), about 2,400 transistors; FP16/BF16 (11-bit mantissa) is an 11x11 array, 121 AND2 gates (726 transistors) plus 110 full adders (3,080 transistors) plus a 22-bit final adder (616 transistors), about 4,422 transistors — plus an exponent adder and normalisation logic for which no count is claimed. Per DPE by arithmetic: 1,024 INT8 multipliers are 2,457,600 transistors, and 512 FP16 multipliers are 2,264,064 transistors; per chip (64 PEs) 157,286,400 transistors on the INT8 reading and 144,900,096 on the FP16 reading — these are alternative readings of the same physical multiplier array reconfigured per data type, never added together. The multiplier array's internal tiling and the accumulator widths beyond the published INT32/FP32 are not published. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (DPE accumulation and the Reduction Engine's four accumulator banks)** — Accumulation is a full-adder chain over the running sum: one FP32 accumulator element is 32 register bits, 640-896 transistors of flip-flops, plus a 32-bit adder, 32 full adders, 896 transistors — 1,536-1,792 transistors per element. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the Reduction Engine's four banks hold a 64x64 output, 4,096 elements, so one PE's accumulators are 6,291,456-7,340,032 transistors, and across 64 PEs 402,653,184-469,762,048 transistors. The DPE's own accumulation over its 32-cycle maximum-size block is the same adder form, one add per product per cycle, with INT8 products accumulating as INT32 and FP16/BF16 products as FP32. One arithmetic coincidence is noted and not given a physical meaning: the local-SRAM cell total per PE, 6,291,456 transistors, equals the Reduction Engine accumulator low end per PE, 4,096 x 1,536 — the two numbers come from unrelated published counts and share no circuit. The adder-tree depth is not published. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (DPE operand selection; MLU output routing; local-memory bank arbitration)** — A 2:1 mux is 4 transistors per bit in transmission-gate form, and selecting among R inputs is a mux tree of R-1 2:1 muxes per output bit — a 32:1 mux is 31 muxes in 5 levels, 124 transistors per bit. The DPE selects between its cached first operand and its streamed second operand, the Memory Layout Unit's transpose, concatenation and reshape output is muxed onto the next block's input, and the Command Processor arbitrates the local-memory banks among the two cores and the five blocks — each selection is such a mux tree. The mux radices and the arbitration policy are not published, so no mux total is claimed — the per-bit tree form is standard construction, not a published circuit. Standard construction.
- **Lookup table (the SIMD Engine's nonlinear functions)** — A lookup table is a small memory plus a row decoder: in the standard form, an SRAM bank of 6T cells (6 transistors per stored bit) with a decoder that turns the input value into a row address, or a ROM array with the same decode, plus the output muxes. The SIMD Engine's nonlinear functions — linear or cubic approximations of exponentials, sigmoid and tanh, INT8 or FP16 in, INT8 or FP32 out — are computed from such tables plus floating-point ALUs. The lookup-table sizes, the entry widths and the approximation breakpoints are not published, so no table total is claimed — and whether the tables are SRAM or ROM is not published either, so neither form is asserted for MTIA v1. Standard construction.
- **Adder (the SIMD Engine's elementwise arithmetic; the MLU's reshape addressing)** — The SIMD Engine's elementwise add, multiply and accumulate are scalar adders and multipliers on the engine's datapath: a 32-bit adder is 32 full adders, about 896 transistors, and a 32-bit barrel shifter — the shifting a reshape or a floating-point normalisation needs — is 5 stages of 32 2:1 muxes, 160 muxes, 640 transistors in transmission-gate form. The Memory Layout Unit's transpose, concatenation and reshape on 4/8/16/32-bit tensors is address permutation — the addresses are computed and the data is moved — and the MLU's internal address logic is not published. The SIMD datapath widths beyond the published INT8/FP16 in and INT8/FP32 out are not published, so no adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the Fabric Interface — DMA-like transfers and cache-miss forwarding)** — The Fabric Interface is a control FSM in the standard form: request state in master-slave D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each) with next-state logic as a NAND/NOR network, sequencing DMA-like transfers in and out of local memory and forwarding the cores' cache misses and uncached accesses. The FI's request-queue depth, its DMA channel count and its miss-handling pipeline are not published, so no FSM total is claimed. The cores' caches exist — the FI forwards their misses — but the paper publishes no cache sizes or organisation, so no cache is decomposed here beyond naming it. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (the DPE's 32-cycle fully-pipelined block; the five-stage cores)** — A pipeline stage boundary is a register: one D flip-flop per bit (about 20-28 transistors each) of the value crossing the boundary, clocked once per stage. The DPE is fully pipelined over 32 cycles per maximum-size block, so a new block can start before the previous one drains, and the two cores are five-stage pipelines — but the DPE's stage count and the register count between its stages are not published, and the five-stage figure is a stage count, not a register count, so no pipeline total is claimed. The 32-cycle figure is the latency of one maximum-size block, not a stage count, and the per-bit flip-flop cost is the only number this level can attach to the pipeline. Standard construction.
- **Interrupt controller / timer (PLIC, timer, debug subsystem, machine registers)** — An interrupt controller is a priority encoder plus claim and complete registers: in the standard form, one AND gate per interrupt source fed by the request bits, a grant flip-flop per output (20-28 transistors each), and the priority encoder tree that picks the highest-priority pending source. A timer is a counter — N D flip-flops plus an N-bit incrementer of N full adders, so a 16-bit timer is 768-896 transistors — plus a comparator against the programmed compare value (one XOR gate per bit plus an AND tree). The PLIC's source count and priority structure and the timer width are not published, so no controller or timer total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter — no hardware flow control in the PE** — There is no published credit-based flow control inside the PE: the circular buffers' full/empty checks are the flow control, and the Command Processor stalls consumers in hardware until producers fill their CBs. A credit counter in the standard form is a register plus decrement and increment logic — an N-bit counter is N D flip-flops plus N full adders — but no such counter is part of the published PE, so it is named here as absent from the published design, not as a primitive with unpublished parameters, and no credit-counter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Data cache / tag array — none on the local-memory path** — The 128 KB local memory is a software-managed scratchpad addressed through circular buffers, not a cache: there is no tag array, no replacement logic and no coherence hardware on the local-memory path. A tag array in the standard form is a CAM — a CAM cell is an SRAM cell plus XOR match logic feeding a matchline, about 10 transistors per cell — with one XOR comparison per tag bit and an AND tree over the matchline, but no such structure exists on the local-memory path, so no tag total is claimed. The cores' own caches, whose misses the Fabric Interface forwards, are the PE's only caches, and their sizes are not published. Standard construction.

Honesty: Meta publishes the PE geometry and none of its circuits: two single-issue, in-order, five-stage RISC-V cores (AX25-V100, from Andes Technology), one with a 32-register vector unit of 64 B registers, five fixed-function blocks, a Command Processor with two schedulers, command queues and arbitration logic, 128 KB of local memory as circular buffers, a DPE doing 1,024 INT8 or 512 FP16 multiplications per cycle over 32 cycles per maximum-size block with INT32/FP32 accumulation, a Reduction Engine with four accumulator banks holding a 64x64 output, and 400 GB/s of local-memory bandwidth per PE — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — local-memory bank count and organisation, Command Processor command-queue depths, DPE staging and register detail, SIMD Engine lookup-table sizes, Fabric Interface queue depths, core cache sizes — Meta publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no tag array and no coherence hardware on the local-memory path, because the local memory is a software-managed scratchpad; and there is no credit-based flow control inside the PE, because the circular buffers' full/empty checks are the flow control.

#### Down to the gates: The memory and interconnect complex — dual AXI networks, multicast and the reduction network

Meta publishes no gate-level structure for the memory and interconnect complex either — the ISCA 2023 paper (section 3.4) describes the complex's contract (128 MB of on-chip SRAM in slices around the grid at 800 GB/s, eight LPDDR5 controllers on 16 channels at 176 GB/s theoretical, two AXI networks, one for memory accesses and one for register accesses, row-or-column-only multicast, a unidirectional reduction network, and a PCIe Gen4 x8 host interface at 16 GB/s) and stops there. The same gate-term search this run found no transistor, flip-flop, 6T or latch content in the paper. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors on the same terms as the Processing Element block: published geometry stays published, arithmetic is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction, labelled as such.

- **Crossbar (the XBARs on each side of the grid)** — A crossbar is a mux tree per output: in the standard form, an output selecting among R inputs is R-1 2:1 muxes per output bit (4 transistors per mux in transmission-gate form), so a 32-bit output selecting among R sources is 32 x (R-1) muxes, with the select bits held in configuration flip-flops (20-28 transistors each). The memory and movement pieces connect through crossbars on each side of the grid, switching the 64 PEs' requests onto the SRAM slices and the LPDDR5 controllers. The crossbars' port counts, radix and per-port widths are not published, so no crossbar total is claimed — the mux-tree form is standard construction, not a published circuit. Standard construction.
- **Switch arbiter (AXI network arbitration between 64 PEs, the SRAM slices and eight memory controllers)** — An arbiter is a priority encoder plus grant state: in the standard form, one AND gate per requester fed by the request bits, a grant flip-flop per output port (20-28 transistors each) holding the winner until the access clears, and the encoder tree that picks the highest-priority pending request. Two AXI networks carry every PE's requests to the SRAM slices and the LPDDR5 controllers, so accesses from 64 PEs must be arbitrated onto the slice and controller ports. The arbiters' structure, port counts and fairness policy are not published, so no arbiter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (multicast address matching — row or column only)** — Multicast coalescing is address comparison: an incoming request's addresses are compared against the outstanding requests' addresses, and matching requests are served once and delivered to all. In the standard comparator form, comparing two N-bit addresses is one XOR gate per bit (10-12 transistors each) plus an AND tree over the bit results, so a 32-bit address comparison is 32 XOR gates, 320-384 transistors, plus the AND tree. Multicast is only supported for PEs on the same row or column of the grid, which bounds the comparison to at most eight PEs per group by arithmetic — but the match table's size and the comparison width are not published, so no comparator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the 128 MB on-chip SRAM — slices around the perimeter)** — The 128 MB on-chip SRAM is an array of 6T SRAM cells in the primer's SRAM bank form — each stored bit is 6 transistors (two cross-coupled inverters, 4 transistors, plus two access transistors), plus the per-bank row decoder, column muxes and sense amplifiers. Arithmetic from the published 128 MB: on the MiB reading, 1,073,741,824 bits, 6,442,450,944 6T cell transistors; on the decimal reading, 1,024,000,000 bits, 6,144,000,000 cell transistors, about 4.6 percent lower — the MiB reading is used here and the decimal alternative is noted. Per slice by arithmetic: four cache slices per memory controller times eight controllers is 32 slices, 128 MB / 32 is 4 MB per slice, and a 4 MB slice is 33,554,432 bits, 201,326,592 6T cell transistors — 32 slices times that figure returns the 6,442,450,944 total, which checks the arithmetic. The slice count as a printed figure is not published — the 32 is derived from the four-slices-per-controller association — and the bank organisation inside a slice is not published, so the decoder, mux and sense-amplifier totals are not claimed. Standard construction.
- **Tag array (cache mode — organisation unpublished)** — In cache mode the slices act as a shared, memory-side cache, which implies a tag lookup per slice. A tag array in the standard form is a CAM: a CAM cell is an SRAM cell plus XOR match logic feeding a matchline, about 10 transistors per cell, with one XOR comparison per tag bit and an AND tree over the matchline per entry. The paper publishes no tag width, associativity, replacement policy or placement, so no tag structure is claimed here — the CAM form is standard construction for a tag array, not a published circuit for MTIA v1. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (slice and controller selection; address decode)** — Address decode is a mux/demux per address bit: a 2:1 mux is 4 transistors per bit in transmission-gate form, and selecting one of eight memory controllers needs 3 address bits while selecting one of 16 channels needs 4, both by arithmetic from the published counts. Each request's address selects one of eight memory controllers and one of 16 channels — two channels per controller by arithmetic — and one of the SRAM slices. The decoder structure is not published, so no decode total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (the reduction network's bank-to-bank accumulation)** — The reduction network carries partial sums from the Reduction Engine accumulators of one PE to the next, where they are added onto that PE's bank, travelling only north to south and west to east. Each hop's add is the same FP32 accumulator form as in the Processing Element block — 32 register bits plus a 32-bit adder, 1,536-1,792 transistors per element — and the chain crosses at most seven PEs in one direction across the 8x8 grid by arithmetic. The per-hop latency and the network's buffering are not published, so no reduction-network total is claimed — the seven-hop figure is a grid-geometry bound, not a published latency. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (AXI network buffering; Fabric Interface request queues)** — A FIFO is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: as registers, N entries of W bits is N x W D flip-flops (N x W x 20-28 transistors); the write and read pointers are counters (an N-bit pointer counter is N flip-flops plus N full adders); full and empty are comparators of the two pointers (one XOR per pointer bit plus an AND tree). Requests wait in the network between issue and service — the Fabric Interface formulates them, the crossbars switch them, the slices and controllers serve them — so each stage holds requests in queues. The queue depths, the packet format and the per-stage buffering are not published, so no queue total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **DMA engine (Fabric Interface DMA-like transfers; the host interface's DMA engines)** — A DMA engine is address counters plus transfer control: in the standard form, a strided address generator is an address counter per dimension — an N-bit counter is N flip-flops plus N full adders, so a 16-bit counter is 768-896 transistors — plus the muxes selecting the stride per dimension (4 transistors per bit per 2:1 mux), under a small control FSM with state in master-slave D flip-flops. The Fabric Interface runs DMA-like transfers in and out of local memory, and the PCIe Gen4 x8 host interface has associated DMA engines. The DMA channel counts and queue depths are not published, so no DMA total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (the PCIe host interface; the dual-rail power domains)** — A synchronizer is two flip-flops in series per crossing bit: in the standard 2-flop form, one D flip-flop (about 20-28 transistors) in the source clock domain feeding a second D flip-flop (about 20-28 transistors) in the destination domain, 40-56 transistors per synchronised bit, so a metastable first flop settles before the second samples it. The host interface is a PCIe Gen4 x8 link with a secure-boot processor beside it, and the die runs dual rails — 0.67 V logic, 0.75 V memories — so the host link and the memory rail are clock and power-domain crossings by construction. The synchronizer structure, the PCIe SerDes detail beyond the x8 width and the secure-boot processor's internals are not published, so no synchronizer total beyond the per-bit cost is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the control subsystem — CCP firmware sequencing)** — The control subsystem holds dedicated processors and peripherals running the system firmware, sequencing jobs across the grid and the PCIe host link. A sequencing FSM in the standard form is state bits in master-slave D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each) with next-state logic as a NAND/NOR network, plus the job-queue registers the firmware's decisions are written into. The control processor count, its firmware state and its job-sequencing FSM are not published, so no controller total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter — no hardware flow control published** — The paper describes no credit-based flow control for the AXI networks or the reduction network: no credit counters, no backpressure scheme and no published buffer accounting between the crossbars. A credit counter in the standard form is a register plus decrement and increment logic — an N-bit counter is N D flip-flops plus N full adders — but no such counter is part of the published design, so it is named here as absent from the published design, not as a primitive with unpublished parameters, and no credit-counter total is claimed. Flow control, as far as the published material goes, is the multicast coalescing and the circular-buffer backpressure at the PEs. Standard construction.

Honesty: Meta publishes the memory-system geometry and none of its circuits: 128 MB of on-chip SRAM in slices around the grid at 800 GB/s, eight LPDDR5 controllers on 16 channels at 176 GB/s theoretical with up to 128 GB supported, two AXI networks (memory and register), row-or-column-only multicast, a unidirectional reduction network, and a PCIe Gen4 x8 host interface at 16 GB/s — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — crossbar radix and port counts, AXI buffer depths, the SRAM slice count as a printed figure, tag organisation, DMA channel counts, synchronizer structure — Meta publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no HBM anywhere in the memory system, because LPDDR5 was chosen deliberately for capacity and bandwidth-per-dollar; and there is no hardware flow control published for the AXI networks or the reduction network, because the flow control the paper describes lives in the multicast coalescing and the PEs' circular buffers.
### Microsoft Maia 100

**Specs (wiki card).** TSMC 5 nm · 105B transistors · HBM2e · liquid-cooled racks

**Building blocks.**
- **Cluster ×16, tile ×4 per cluster** — The chip's hierarchy: 64 tiles grouped into 16 clusters. Each tile holds a tensor unit, a vector processor, tile SRAM and a tile DMA; each cluster adds shared cluster SRAM and a cluster DMA
- **Tensor unit (16×R×16)** — The GEMM engine, built around the OCP MX microscaling formats Microsoft co-authored — peak 3 POPS at MX6, 1.5 POPS at MX9, 0.8 POPS at BF16: the unit is shaped for low-precision inference economics
- **Vector processor** — A loosely coupled superscalar engine with a custom (undisclosed) ISA for FP32/BF16 element-wise work — activations, norms, reductions
- **DMA engines + hardware semaphores** — Decoupled data movement between HBM and the SRAM tiers, with hardware semaphores so tensor and vector units double-buffer asynchronously without software polling — there are no caches; all movement is explicit
- **~500 MB on-chip SRAM** — Software-managed L1/L2 scratchpads across the tile/cluster hierarchy — the 'software-defined locally accessed dataflow' (SDLA) bet: the compiler, not hardware, decides what lives where
- **4× HBM2e + Ethernet backend** — 64 GB at 1.8 TB/s on a CoWoS-S package, plus 12× 400 GbE backend links for scale-out — and a custom liquid-cooled rack ('sidekick') designed with the chip

**The piece that makes it special.** The tensor unit's native MX formats — and the honesty of the hierarchy. Maia 100 was designed with OpenAI's workloads on the table: the MX microscaling formats let the tensor unit price a multiply by its information content (6- and 9-bit peaks headline the chip, not BF16), and the tile/cluster SRAM hierarchy admits that at 820 mm², locality is a software problem — so DMA and semaphores are first-class architecture, not plumbing.

#### Inside the signature block: The tile — tensor unit, vector processor, DMA and control, run by semaphores

**Inside it.** A tile is five pieces around a tile SRAM. The TTU (Tensor Unit) is the GEMM engine, built as a 16xRx16 unit: 16 rows, a reduction dimension R Microsoft does not publish, 16 columns, sized as a trade-off between granularity loss and peak performance. It runs the OCP MX microscaling formats Microsoft co-authored — 4-bit, 6-bit and 9-bit compute alongside BF16 — where each MX block is 32 narrow elements sharing one 8-bit E8M0 scale, so a multiply is priced by the information in the block rather than by a fixed 16-bit word. The TVP (Vector engine) is a loosely coupled superscalar processor with a custom ISA built for machine learning, handling FP32 and BF16 element-wise work: activations, norms and reductions. The TDMA (Tile Data Movement Engine) moves tiles between the SRAM tiers and supports different tensor sharding schemes, so the same engine serves row, column and block shardings. The TCP (Tile Control Processor) issues work, and the L1 SRAM is the tile's software-managed scratchpad — there are no caches anywhere on Maia 100, so every byte the tile touches arrived by an explicit DMA. The glue is the hardware semaphore. A command carries its dependencies with it — in-semaphores, arguments, out-semaphores — and the rule is simple: a command waits on its in-semaphores until its input data is ready and its output buffers are free, then signals its out-semaphores when it finishes, announcing that its output data is ready and its input buffers are free again. The control processor issues commands on the control path; the threads executing them synchronize directly on the data path, so a tensor unit, a vector processor and a DMA engine can all be in flight on the same tile without software polling. Around the tile sits a data compression engine that shrinks what must move and be stored, and the L1/L2 scratchpads total about 500 MB across the chip — Microsoft publishes only the total, not the per-tile L1 or per-cluster L2 split, so this section does not state one.

**Trace — one unit of work.**
1. **The tile control processor issues the commands.**The TCP sends asynchronous commands into per-engine queues — a read copy, a tensor-unit op, a vector op, a write copy — each carrying its in- and out-semaphores, so the tile's work is a scheduled queue of dependent commands rather than a stream of instructions the TCP must babysit.
2. **The TDMA read copy engine pulls the tile in.**The TDMA fetches a weight tile and an activation tile into L1 SRAM from cluster SRAM (or from HBM through it), in the sharding the compiler chose. The command that needs the data waits on its in-semaphore until the copy lands; the TCP does not poll, and the tensor unit does not stall mid-op.
3. **The tensor unit runs the GEMM.**The TTU multiplies the 16xRx16 tile in MX format — 32-element blocks, one shared E8M0 scale each — at the chip's headline rates, 3 POPS at 6-bit, 1.5 POPS at 9-bit, 0.8 POPS at BF16. Because the operands are narrow and block-scaled, the tile moves and multiplies far fewer bits than a BF16 design would for the same shape.
4. **The vector processor fuses the post-op.**The TVP takes the TTU's output in L1 SRAM and runs the element-wise finish — activation, norm, reduction — in FP32 or BF16, while the TDMA is already pulling the next tile into a second buffer. The semaphore on the finished output is what releases the next command, not a software barrier.
5. **The TDMA write copy engine pushes the result out.**The finished tile is written back to cluster SRAM, and the write command signals its out-semaphore: output data ready, input buffers free. The L1 SRAM that held the input tile is now reusable, and the tile never touched HBM for this step.
6. **The next tile overlaps the last.**Because every command is queued with its dependencies up front, the TCP has the next read copy already waiting while the current GEMM runs — compute, movement and post-processing overlap by construction, and the tile's throughput is set by how well the compiler overlapped them, not by hardware guessing.

**Bottleneck.** Relieves the data-movement wall, which is the wall Maia 100 is built around. Narrow MX types plus a compression engine cut the bits that must move and be stored; software-managed scratchpads keep hot tiles in SRAM instead of paying cache-miss latency; and the semaphore/command-queue model lets DMA, tensor and vector work overlap without polling or software barriers, so the 64 tensor units stay fed. It creates three new bottlenecks instead. First, locality is entirely the compiler's job: there are no caches to fall back on, so a schedule that mistimes a DMA is a stall the hardware cannot hide, and the programming-model split shows the cost — Flash-Attention takes about 50 lines in Triton, where the compiler manages semaphores, memory and double buffering, but about 1,000 lines in the Maia API, where every semaphore and buffer is explicit. Second, the tensor unit's granularity: the 16xRx16 shape trades granularity loss against peak performance, so thin or ragged GEMM slices under-fill the unit and the headline POPS rates assume well-formed tiles. Third, the semaphore choreography itself: ordering and buffer-availability bugs are the programmer's, and a wrong in-semaphore deadlocks the tile rather than merely slowing it.

**Numbers.** 64 tiles (16 clusters x 4 tiles); TTU 16xRx16 (R not published); peak dense tensor 3 POPS at 6-bit, 1.5 POPS at 9-bit, 0.8 POPS at BF16 — 46.9 TOPS per tile at 6-bit by arithmetic (3 POPS / 64 tiles), 23.4 at 9-bit, 12.5 TFLOPS at BF16; MX block 32 elements sharing one 8-bit E8M0 scale; 4-bit, 6-bit and 9-bit compute supported; L1/L2 scratchpads about 500 MB total (per-tile L1 and per-cluster L2 sizes not published); Flash-Attention about 50 lines in Triton vs about 1,000 lines in the Maia API (deck table).

**Source.** Microsoft, Hot Chips 2024 — Inside Maia 100 (Sherry Xu and Chandru Ramakrishnan), deck slides: specs table, SoC and tile diagrams, ML-specific architecture, asynchronous programming with semaphores, two kernel programming models; Microsoft Tech Community, 'Inside Maia 100: Revolutionizing AI Workloads with Microsoft's Custom AI Accelerator', Aug 27, 2024; Rouhani et al., 'Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning', arXiv:2310.10537, sections 2 and 2.2, Table 1.

#### Inside the signature block: The cluster, the mesh NoC and the gather-based distributed GEMM

**Inside it.** Four tiles make a cluster, and the cluster is where Maia 100's second bet lives: movement is a first-class citizen, not plumbing. Each cluster adds a Cluster NOC, a CCP (Cluster Control Processor) that issues commands to the cluster's engines, a CDMA (Cluster DMA), and L2 SRAM — the cluster SRAM (CSRAM) that buffers activations and intermediate results. Sixteen clusters sit on a high-bandwidth data mesh NoC with a mesh-like topology laid out for machine-learning traffic, the diagram showing the clusters in a grid with routers at the intersections. Off the mesh sit the memory and the wires: an HBM2E PHY with 4096 IO feeding four HBM2E stacks, 64 GB at 1.8 TB/s; a PAM4 112G SerDes PHY driving 12x 400 GbE backend links, 600 GB/s in total; a PCIe PHY for the 32 GB/s host link; and chip-management, security-management and image-decoder blocks on the SoC edge. The backend network runs a custom RoCE-like Ethernet protocol with AES-GCM encryption, on a unified backend network that serves both scale-up and scale-out with direct or switch connectivity: up to 4800 Gbps of all-gather and scatter-reduce bandwidth and 1200 Gbps of all-to-all. The point of the cluster SRAM is that network reads and writes are served directly from SRAM — a remote chip's request lands in CSRAM, not in HBM — so the gather that feeds a distributed GEMM does not pay a DRAM round trip. That is the hardware half of Maia's gather-based matrix multiplication: instead of an all-reduce, each chip gathers the pieces it needs, fuses the element-wise activation function directly in SRAM, overlaps computation with network communication, and sends quantized MX data over the network rather than full-precision partials.

**Trace — one unit of work.**
1. **The GEMM is partitioned across chips.**The deck's worked example is a 2048 (M) x 12288 (K) x 12288 (N) GEMM split across 4 chips: the input is cut K/4 so each chip owns one K-slice, and the weights are staged as W00 through W33 across the four chips. Each chip's cluster SRAM holds the activations and intermediates its tiles will need.
2. **Phase 0 — first tile computes while the next is fetched.**A tile's tensor unit computes the first X tile (X00) while the cluster DMA (ANC, data transfer) brings in the next one (X01). The overlap is the point: the tensor unit never waits on the network for its next operand.
3. **Phase 1 — compute advances, the vector processor starts accumulating.**The tensor unit moves on to X01 while the vector processor begins accumulating partials (Y00 + Y01) and the DMA fetches X02. The partial sums live in SRAM, not in HBM, and the activation can be fused as soon as a partial is complete.
4. **Phase 2 — the pipeline is three deep.**The tensor unit is on X02, the vector processor is accumulating the next partial (Y02) on top of the running sum, and the DMA is fetching X03. At this point compute, accumulation and transfer are all in flight at once on the same cluster.
5. **Phase 3 — the last tile and the final sum.**The tensor unit finishes X03, the vector processor completes the accumulation, and the output stage sums all four partials — Y0 = Y00 + Y01 + Y02 + Y03 — plus the bias, all in SRAM.
6. **Quantized partials cross the network, not full-precision ones.**Where a partial must move between chips it travels as quantized MX data over the 400 GbE backend, and the receiving chip's cluster SRAM takes it directly — no HBM read on either side. The next GEMM's tiles are already being staged while this one finishes.

**Bottleneck.** Relieves the all-reduce wall that dominates distributed inference. A gather-based GEMM replaces the all-reduce's synchronized exchange with per-chip gathers, fuses the activation in SRAM instead of writing partials out and reading them back, overlaps the network transfer with the tensor unit's compute, and shrinks what crosses the wire by sending quantized MX data. Serving network reads and writes directly from cluster SRAM is the second relief: it takes the hottest traffic off the HBM entirely. It creates new bottlenecks instead. First, the HBM2e ceiling: 1.8 TB/s is the hard cap on per-chip bandwidth, a deliberate choice — HBM2e avoids competing with NVIDIA and AMD for leading-edge HBM supply — but it means any tile that misses the SRAM hierarchy pays the older memory's rate. Second, the backend: 600 GB/s total is shared across all-gather, scatter-reduce and all-to-all, so the gather's quantized traffic still contends with every other collective on the chip. Third, the partition itself: the K/4 split and the phase overlap are a compiler scheduling problem, and a GEMM whose shape does not split cleanly across four chips leaves tensor units idle while the mesh carries the imbalance.

**Numbers.** 16 clusters; mesh-like high-bandwidth data mesh NoC; HBM2E 64 GB at 1.8 TB/s, 4096 IO PHY; backend 600 GB/s (12x 400 GbE); all-gather and scatter-reduce up to 4800 Gbps, all-to-all 1200 Gbps; host 32 GB/s PCIe — Gen5 x8 per the specs table, while the SoC diagram labels the PHY Gen4 x16 (same 32 GB/s either way; see Fact check); SerDes PAM4 112G; worked GEMM M=2048, K=12288, N=12288 across 4 chips; design TDP 700 W, provision 500 W; die about 820 mm2 on TSMC N5, CoWoS-S.

**Source.** Microsoft, Hot Chips 2024 — Inside Maia 100, deck slides: specs table, SoC diagram (cluster NOC, CCP, CDMA, L2 SRAM, HBM2E PHY, PAM4 112G SerDes PHY, PCIe PHY), mesh-like NoC topology, GEMM partitioning and scheduling; Microsoft Tech Community, 'Inside Maia 100', Aug 27, 2024; Microsoft Azure Blog, 'Azure Maia for the era of AI: From silicon to software to systems', Apr 3, 2024.

**How work flows.** Compiler schedules everything: The Maia stack (NPL/Triton-based) generates explicit DMA sequences and semaphore choreography — the chip executes a plan, not a cache's guesses. Cluster DMA pulls tiles: Weight and activation tiles move HBM → cluster SRAM → tile SRAM in a double-buffered pipeline. Tensor unit runs the GEMM: Matrix work executes in MX formats at the tile's tensor unit. Vector processor finishes: Post-ops run on the tile's vector engine while the next tile is already in flight. Backend Ethernet scales out: Shards exchange over the 400 GbE links; the rack's liquid cooling sustains the 500 W provisioned power.

**Trade-off accepted.** Disclosure and dependence. Maia exists only inside Azure, its ISA and compiler are Microsoft's, and its economics assume OpenAI-shaped traffic. Microsoft also chose HBM2e when rivals shipped HBM3 — a cost/supply bet that caps per-chip bandwidth at 1.8 TB/s. Note what this entry does NOT claim: the wiki previously described a 'RISC-V control' design for Maia — Microsoft's Hot Chips disclosure describes a custom-ISA vector processor, and the RISC-V claim has been removed (see Fact check).

**Fact check.**
- [verified] 105 billion transistors on 5 nm — Source: Microsoft Azure blog, Ignite 2023 — purpose-built cloud infrastructure. Quote: "Maia 100 is the first generation in the series, with 105 billion transistors, making it one of the largest chips on 5nm process technology."
- [corrected] Key-ideas line previously claimed a “16× RISC-V control vector unit” design — Source: Microsoft, Hot Chips 2024 — Inside Maia 100. Was: 16× RISC-V control vector unit class design; now: 16 clusters × 4 tiles; per-tile 16×R×16 tensor unit + custom-ISA vector processor (RISC-V is not claimed by Microsoft's disclosure). Note: Quote unavailable in text form — the Hot Chips deck is slideware; the correction rests on the deck's tile/cluster organisation as reported from the primary presentation.
- [verified] 64 GB HBM2e at 1.8 TB/s; ~820 mm²; 500 W provisioned / 700 W design TDP — Source: Microsoft, Hot Chips 2024 — Inside Maia 100. Note: Figures from Microsoft's Hot Chips 2024 presentation; slide deck, so no verbatim sentence is quoted here rather than inventing one.

#### Down to the primitives: The tile — tensor unit, vector processor, DMA and control, run by semaphores

Decomposed in trace order — the TCP issues commands into per-engine queues, the TDMA pulls tiles into L1 SRAM, the TTU multiplies 16xRx16 MX tiles, the TVP fuses the post-op, and the TDMA writes the result back while the next tile is already in flight. Microsoft publishes the tile's contract — five pieces around a tile SRAM (TCP, TDMA, L1 SRAM, TVP, TTU), the TTU's 16xRx16 shape, MX formats with 32-element blocks sharing one 8-bit E8M0 scale, a loosely coupled superscalar vector processor with a custom ISA for FP32 and BF16, a DMA engine supporting different tensor sharding schemes, hardware semaphores, and software-managed L1/L2 scratchpads totalling about 500 MB — but nothing below that contract: no TTU multiplier staging or accumulator widths, no TVP register counts, no L1 bank organisation, no command-queue depths, no DMA channel counts, no compression-engine internals. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **FIFO / queue (the per-engine command queues)** — "It operates with two execution streams: control processors issuing asynchronous commands via queues and hardware threads executing these commands, ensuring efficient data handling through semaphore-based synchronization." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The TCP issues a read copy, a tensor-unit op, a vector op and a write copy into the engines' queues, each command carrying its dependencies with it, so the tile's work is a scheduled queue of dependent commands rather than a stream of instructions the TCP must babysit. The queue depths and the arbitration between the engines' queues are not published.
- **Counter (the hardware semaphores — in/out semaphore counts)** — "Hardware semaphores enable asynchronous programming on the Maia system." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). A semaphore behaves as a counter with wait and signal operations: a command waits on its in-semaphores until its input data is ready and its output buffers are free, then signals its out-semaphores when it finishes, announcing that its output data is ready and its input buffers are free again. The semaphore count per tile and the counter widths are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the Tile Control Processor — command issue)** — The TCP issues the tile's commands on the control path while the threads executing them synchronize directly on the data path. Its issue policy, its queue arbitration and its own pipeline structure are not published.
- **Multiplier array (the TTU's 16xRx16 MAC grid)** — "This tensor unit is constructed as a 16xRx16 unit." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). 16 rows by 16 columns is 256 output positions by arithmetic, each reducing over the unpublished dimension R, so the MACs per cycle are not stated. Peak dense tensor rates are 3 POPS at 6-bit, 1.5 POPS at 9-bit and 0.8 POPS at BF16 — 46.9 TOPS per tile at 6-bit by arithmetic (3 POPS / 64 tiles), 23.4 at 9-bit, 12.5 TFLOPS at BF16 (see fact records). The multiplier staging inside the grid is not published.
- **Adder tree (the TTU's reduction over R)** — Each of the 256 outputs sums its R products; the reduction dimension R is not published, so neither the adder-tree depth nor the per-output product count is stated.
- **Accumulator registers (the TTU's stationary partial sums)** — Partial sums are held in registers while the reduction over R completes and before the TVP takes the output in L1 SRAM. The accumulator widths are not published.
- **Exponent adder / shifter (applying the MX E8M0 shared scale)** — "All concrete MX formats use E8M0 (an 8-bit exponent) as the format for the shared scale." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Each MX block is 32 narrow elements sharing one 8-bit scale, so rescaling a block is an exponent addition on the block's elements — the scale step in the datapath. How the TTU implements that step internally is not published.
- **Register file (the TVP's architectural state)** — "The vector processor is a loosely coupled superscalar engine built with custom instruction set architecture (ISA) to support a wide range of data types, including FP32 and BF16." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). A superscalar processor keeps its architectural state in a register file; the register counts, the register widths beyond the FP32/BF16 datapath and the port counts are not published.
- **Adder (the TVP's element-wise FP32/BF16 arithmetic)** — The TVP runs the element-wise finish — activation, norm, reduction — in FP32 or BF16 on the TTU's output in L1 SRAM. The adder/multiplier lane count and the pipeline depth are not published.
- **SRAM bank (the L1 SRAM tile scratchpad)** — "To further improve data utilization and power efficiency, large L1 and L2 scratch pads are software-managed." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The L1/L2 scratchpads total about 500 MB across the chip; the per-tile L1 size, the bank count, the bank width and the arbitration between the TTU, TVP and TDMA are not published.
- **DMA engine (the TDMA read/write copy engines)** — "A Direct Memory Access (DMA) engine supports different tensor sharding schemes." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The TDMA fetches weight and activation tiles into L1 SRAM and writes finished tiles back out, in the sharding the compiler chose. The DMA channel count, the queue depths and the per-engine bandwidth are not published.
- **Mux / demux (operand steering — TTU, TVP and TDMA onto the L1 SRAM)** — The three engines share the tile SRAM: the TDMA writes tiles in, the TTU reads operands out, the TVP reads and writes its post-op. The steering radices and widths are not published.
- **Pipeline registers (the TTU/TVP pipeline stages)** — The overlap model — the next tile is pulled in while the current GEMM runs, the TVP fuses the post-op while the TDMA fetches — implies staged execution with registers between stages. The stage counts and the register counts between stages are not published.
- **Compression datapath (the data compression engine)** — The deck names a data compression engine on the tile; it shrinks what must move and be stored, which is part of how the tile relieves the data-movement wall. The compression algorithm, the compression ratio and the engine's internals are not published.
- **Credit counter — no hardware flow control published in the tile** — The flow control the published material describes is the hardware semaphores: a command waits on its in-semaphores and signals its out-semaphores. No credit counters, no backpressure scheme and no published buffer accounting are described for the tile. A credit counter is therefore named here as absent from the published design, not as a primitive with unpublished parameters.
- **Data cache / tag array — none (no caches anywhere on Maia 100)** — The L1 and L2 scratchpads are software-managed, and every byte the tile touches arrived by an explicit DMA — there is no tag array, no replacement logic and no coherence hardware on the tile path. A cache is therefore named here as absent by design, not as a primitive with unpublished parameters.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the published tile geometry used above — five pieces around a tile SRAM, the TTU's 16xRx16 shape, MX blocks of 32 elements sharing one 8-bit E8M0 scale, a loosely coupled superscalar vector processor with a custom ISA for FP32 and BF16, a DMA engine supporting different tensor sharding schemes, hardware semaphores, and software-managed L1/L2 scratchpads totalling about 500 MB — and the arithmetic is derived from those published counts. Below that level — TTU multiplier staging and accumulator widths, TVP register counts and lane counts, L1 bank organisation, command-queue depths, DMA channel counts, compression-engine internals — Microsoft publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no data cache and no tag array anywhere on the tile, because the scratchpads are software-managed and every byte arrives by explicit DMA; and there is no published credit-based flow control in the tile, because the hardware semaphores are the flow control.

#### Down to the primitives: The cluster, the mesh NoC and the gather-based distributed GEMM

Decomposed in trace order — the GEMM is partitioned K/4 across four chips, each chip's CDMA stages tiles into cluster SRAM, the TTU/TVP pipeline computes and accumulates in SRAM, and quantized MX partials cross the backend network to be summed in SRAM. Microsoft publishes the complex's contract — 16 clusters of four tiles on a mesh-like high-bandwidth data mesh NoC, a Cluster NOC, CCP and CDMA plus L2 SRAM per cluster, 64 GB of HBM2E at 1.8 TB/s behind a 4096-IO PHY, a PAM4 112G SerDes PHY driving 12x 400 GbE backend links (600 GB/s), up to 4800 Gbps all-gather and scatter-reduce and 1200 Gbps all-to-all, a 32 GB/s PCIe host link, and a custom RoCE-like Ethernet protocol with AES-GCM encryption — but nothing below that contract: no NoC radix, link widths or buffer depths, no cluster-SRAM bank organisation, no CDMA channel counts, no SerDes equalizer or CDR detail, no AES-GCM key or throughput figures, no synchronizer structure. Where a number below is computed from published geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **Crossbar (the Cluster NOC — switching four tiles, the CCP and the CDMA)** — The cluster's pieces connect through the Cluster NOC, switching the four tiles' requests and the CDMA's traffic onto the cluster SRAM and the mesh. The crossbar's port counts, radix and per-port widths are not published.
- **Switch arbiter (mesh router arbitration across 16 clusters)** — Sixteen clusters sit on a mesh-like high-bandwidth data mesh NoC, the diagram showing the clusters in a grid with routers at the intersections, so each router arbitrates the clusters' traffic onto its links. The arbiters' structure, port counts and fairness policy are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (mesh router buffers and the cluster command queues)** — Requests wait in the network between issue and service — the CCP issues cluster commands, the CDMA moves tiles, the routers forward them — so each stage holds requests in queues. The queue depths, the packet format and the per-stage buffering are not published.
- **SRAM bank (the cluster SRAM / L2 — CSRAM)** — "Additionally, we leverage Static Random-Access Memory (SRAM) at the cluster level to buffer activations and intermediate results." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). "Network reads and writes are also served directly from SRAM, enabling direct access to CSRAM." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The per-cluster SRAM size is not published — only the ~500 MB L1/L2 total — and the bank count, bank width and arbitration inside a cluster are not published.
- **DMA engine (the CDMA — cluster DMA)** — The deck names a CDMA per cluster; it moves tiles between the cluster SRAM, the mesh and HBM. The DMA channel count, the queue depths and the per-engine bandwidth are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the Cluster Control Processor — cluster command issue)** — The deck names a CCP per cluster; it issues commands to the cluster's engines, the cluster-level counterpart of the tile's TCP. Its issue policy and its own pipeline structure are not published.
- **Mux / demux (HBM2E PHY data muxing — 4096 IO onto four HBM2E stacks)** — The HBM2E PHY carries 4096 IO feeding four HBM2E stacks, 64 GB at 1.8 TB/s — 16 GB and 1,024 IO per stack by arithmetic (see fact records). The PHY's mux structure and the per-stack channel organisation are not published.
- **SerDes (the PAM4 112G PHY — 12x 400 GbE backend links)** — The backend runs 12x 400 GbE — 4,800 Gbps, 600 GB/s by arithmetic (see fact records) — over a PAM4 112G SerDes PHY. The equalizer structure, the clock-and-data-recovery detail and the per-lane organisation are not published.
- **Crypto engine (AES-GCM on the custom RoCE-like backend)** — The backend network runs a custom RoCE-like Ethernet protocol with AES-GCM encryption, on a unified backend network serving both scale-up and scale-out. The key widths, the encryption throughput and the engine's pipeline are not published.
- **Adder tree (the gather GEMM's final sum — Y0 = Y00+Y01+Y02+Y03 plus bias)** — The deck's worked example is a 2048 (M) x 12288 (K) x 12288 (N) GEMM split across 4 chips, K/4 per chip, and the output stage sums all four partials — Y0 = Y00 + Y01 + Y02 + Y03 — plus the bias, all in SRAM (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The adder widths and the precision of the final sum are not published.
- **Address generator (the gather addressing — K/4 partition, per-chip slice selection)** — The gather fetches the pieces each chip needs by address: the input cut K/4 so each chip owns one K-slice, and the weights staged as W00 through W33 across the four chips. The address-generator structure and the gather's request format are not published.
- **Credit counter — no flow-control scheme published for the mesh** — The published material describes no credit-based flow control for the mesh NoC: no credit counters, no backpressure scheme and no published buffer accounting between the routers. Flow control, as far as the published material goes, is the semaphore/command model inside the tiles and the gather scheduling across chips. A credit counter is therefore named here as absent from the published design, not as a primitive with unpublished parameters.
- **Synchronizer (the SerDes/PCIe clock-domain crossings)** — The PAM4 112G SerDes PHY and the PCIe PHY are clock-domain crossings by construction — the backend and host links run on their own clocks against the on-die mesh. The synchronizer structure, the SerDes clocking and the PCIe lane organisation are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the published complex geometry used above — 16 clusters of four tiles, a mesh-like high-bandwidth data mesh NoC, a Cluster NOC, CCP and CDMA plus L2 SRAM per cluster, 64 GB of HBM2E at 1.8 TB/s behind a 4096-IO PHY, a PAM4 112G SerDes PHY driving 12x 400 GbE backend links, up to 4800 Gbps all-gather/scatter-reduce and 1200 Gbps all-to-all, a 32 GB/s PCIe host link, and a custom RoCE-like Ethernet protocol with AES-GCM encryption — and the arithmetic is derived from those published counts. Below that level — NoC radix, link widths and buffer depths, cluster-SRAM bank organisation, CDMA channel counts, SerDes equalizer and CDR detail, AES-GCM key and throughput figures, synchronizer structure — Microsoft publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no HBM on the gather path, because network reads and writes are served directly from cluster SRAM; and no flow-control scheme is published for the mesh, because the published flow control lives in the semaphore/command model and the gather scheduling. The cluster-level "connection" engine is named on the deck's async-programming slide but its internal function is not detailed, so it is named here and not decomposed.

#### Down to the gates: The tile — tensor unit, vector processor, DMA and control, run by semaphores

Microsoft publishes no gate-level structure for the tile — the Hot Chips 2024 deck describes the tile's contract (five pieces around a tile SRAM: TCP, TDMA, L1 SRAM, TVP and TTU; the TTU's 16xRx16 shape; MX formats with 32-element blocks sharing one 8-bit E8M0 scale; a loosely coupled superscalar vector processor with a custom ISA for FP32 and BF16; a DMA engine supporting different tensor sharding schemes; hardware semaphores; and software-managed L1/L2 scratchpads totalling about 500 MB) and stops there. A gate-term search this run found nothing: the deck's full text carries no transistor, flip-flop, latch or NAND content; the Tech Community writeup carries no transistor or flip-flop content; the Azure blog carries no transistor content; and the MX paper (Rouhani et al., arXiv:2310.10537) is a data-format paper with no gate-level content. The only transistor figure anywhere in the published Maia material is the 105-billion-transistor chip total from the Ignite 2023 announcement, a count, not a circuit. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about Microsoft's circuits.

- **FIFO / queue (the per-engine command queues)** — A FIFO is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: as registers, N entries of W bits is N x W D flip-flops (N x W x 20-28 transistors); the write and read pointers are counters (an N-bit pointer counter is N flip-flops plus N full adders); full and empty are comparators of the two pointers (one XOR gate per pointer bit plus an AND tree over the bits). The TCP issues a read copy, a tensor-unit op, a vector op and a write copy into the engines' queues, each command carrying its in- and out-semaphores, so each queue holds commands whose dependencies travel with them. The queue depths and the arbitration between the engines' queues are not published, so no queue total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (the hardware semaphores — in/out semaphore counts)** — A semaphore behaves as a counter with wait and signal operations: a command waits on its in-semaphores until its input data is ready and its output buffers are free, then signals its out-semaphores when it finishes. A counter in the standard form is a register plus an incrementer: an N-bit counter is N D flip-flops (N x 20-28 transistors) plus an N-bit incrementer of N full adders (N x 28 transistors), so a 16-bit counter is 768-896 transistors, and a 16-bit up/down counter — one that can count both directions, as a semaphore count must when commands both wait and signal — is 832-960 transistors. The semaphore count per tile and the counter widths are not published, so no semaphore total is claimed — the 16-bit figures illustrate the per-bit form and are not published widths. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the Tile Control Processor — command issue)** — The TCP is a control FSM: in the standard form, the control state lives in master-slave D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each) with next-state logic as a NAND/NOR network, and the issue logic that selects the next command for each engine is the selection logic that dispatches commands after their in-semaphores clear. The TCP issues the tile's commands on the control path while the threads executing them synchronize directly on the data path. Its issue policy, its queue arbitration and its own pipeline structure are not published, so no state-bit count and no controller total is claimed — the FSM form is standard construction, not a published circuit. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (the TTU's 16xRx16 MAC grid)** — A multiplier is an AND-gate partial-product array feeding a full-adder compressor tree and one final carry-propagate adder. In the standard array-multiplier form, an n-bit multiply is n squared AND2 gates (6 transistors each) plus n(n-1) full adders (28 transistors each) plus a 2n-bit final adder: a 6-bit multiply is 36 AND2 gates (216 transistors) plus 30 full adders (840 transistors) plus a 12-bit final adder (336 transistors), about 1,392 transistors; a 9-bit multiply is 81 AND2 gates (486 transistors) plus 72 full adders (2,016 transistors) plus an 18-bit final adder (504 transistors), about 3,006 transistors; a BF16 mantissa multiply is 8 bits (7 stored bits plus the implicit leading one), 64 AND2 gates (384 transistors) plus 56 full adders (1,568 transistors) plus a 16-bit final adder (448 transistors), about 2,400 transistors, plus an exponent adder and normalisation logic for which no count is claimed. The floating-point MX variants multiply only their mantissas — the shared E8M0 scale is handled by the exponent adder in the next primitive. The TTU's 16 rows by 16 columns is 256 output positions by arithmetic, each reducing over the unpublished dimension R, so the number of physical multipliers in the grid and the MACs per cycle are not stated, and no TTU total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (the TTU's reduction over R)** — Each of the 256 outputs sums its R products, and the reduction is a full-adder tree: in the standard form, one add is a full-adder chain, one full adder per bit at 28 transistors per bit, and a tree of such adds sums the products. The reduction dimension R is not published, so neither the adder-tree depth nor the per-output product count is stated, and no adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Accumulator registers (the TTU's stationary partial sums)** — Partial sums are held in registers while the reduction over R completes and before the TVP takes the output in L1 SRAM. A register in the standard form is one D flip-flop per bit, about 20-28 transistors per bit. The accumulator widths are not published, so no per-output or per-tile accumulator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Exponent adder / shifter (applying the MX E8M0 shared scale)** — Each MX block is 32 narrow elements sharing one 8-bit E8M0 scale, so rescaling a block is an exponent addition on the block's shared scale: in the standard form, an 8-bit exponent adder is 8 full adders, 224 transistors, per block-scale step, and the per-element exponent adjustment is a shifter, one 2:1 mux per bit per shift stage at 4 transistors per mux in transmission-gate form. The number of MX blocks in flight per tile is not published — it depends on the tile shape and the unpublished reduction dimension R — so no per-tile exponent-adder or shifter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Register file (the TVP's architectural state)** — A register file in the standard D flip-flop form is one D flip-flop per stored bit, about 20-28 transistors per bit: one FP32 register is 32 bits, 640-896 transistors of flip-flops, and one BF16 register is 16 bits, 320-448 transistors. Reading one register out of the file is a mux tree — selecting among R registers is R-1 2:1 muxes per bit, 4 transistors per mux in transmission-gate form. The TVP is a loosely coupled superscalar processor with a custom ISA for FP32 and BF16, so its architectural state lives in such a file, but the register counts, the register widths beyond the FP32/BF16 datapath and the port counts are not published, so no register-file total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder (the TVP's element-wise FP32/BF16 arithmetic)** — The TVP runs the element-wise finish — activation, norm, reduction — in FP32 or BF16 on the TTU's output in L1 SRAM. A scalar adder in the standard form is a full-adder chain, one full adder per bit at 28 transistors per bit, so a 32-bit FP32 adder is 32 full adders, 896 transistors, and a 16-bit BF16 adder is 16 full adders, 448 transistors; a 32-bit barrel shifter — the shifting a floating-point normalisation needs — is 5 stages of 32 2:1 muxes, 160 muxes, 640 transistors in transmission-gate form. The adder/multiplier lane count and the pipeline depth are not published, so no TVP arithmetic total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the L1 SRAM tile scratchpad)** — The L1 SRAM is an array of 6T SRAM cells in the primer's SRAM bank form — each stored bit is 6 transistors (two cross-coupled inverters, 4 transistors, plus two access transistors), plus the per-bank row decoder, column muxes and sense amplifiers.
