#### Down to the gates: The Cognitive ISP — semantic segmentation inside the capture pipeline

Qualcomm publishes no gate-level structure for Spectra — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 ISP or video path. The deepest published description is the Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 and 8s Gen 3 Product Briefs, which describe the pipeline stages, the capture configurations and the codec features at block level, and the codec specifications (HEVC), which define the algorithms the silicon must implement. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published spec geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about Qualcomm's circuits.

- **SRAM bank / line buffers (frame store for multi-frame alignment and per-layer working buffers)** — The frame store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. The published structure is the workload: multi-frame noise reduction aligns several frames and averages them, and each of the up to 12 semantic layers gets its own treatment, so the store must hold frames and per-layer working data while the pipeline works them — but the store's capacity in frames, its banking and its port count are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Whether the store is one bank or one bank per pipeline or per layer is not published. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (RAW ingest per 18-bit pipeline, frame output, segmentation-result handoff)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each, incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The ingest path per 18-bit pipeline, the frame output path and the handoff of the segmentation result from the Hexagon NPU back into the ISP are FIFOs of this form, but their depths and widths are not published, so the pointer widths — and therefore the counter and comparator totals — are not claimed. The three pipelines ingest in parallel, which is a demux steering one sensor stream to each pipeline, counted in the mux primitive below. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree + comparator (HDR fusion accumulation, MFNR frame averaging, 3A statistics accumulation, face-detection scoring)** — An accumulation is an adder tree in the standard form: full adders (about 28 transistors each — two half adders, two XOR plus two AND plus one OR) arranged pairwise so the tree depth is log2 of the operand count, collapsing the values to one sum, with a carry-propagate adder finishing each stage. The published geometry is the depth: HDR fusion adds several exposures of the same frame at 18-bit depth, so the adders in the fusion tree are 18 bits wide plus carry — but the number of exposures fused, the number of frames averaged by multi-frame noise reduction and the scoring thresholds are not published, so no adder-tree total is claimed. The best-exposure and best-face-score selection is a comparator (one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree) holding the best value so far, with a register holding the winning exposure or score. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (demosaic interpolation, tone-mapping and colour-correction matrix math)** — Each interpolated sample and each colour-matrix output is a weighted sum, so the multiplier array is in the standard form: AND gates form the partial products, a full-adder compressor tree collapses them, and one final carry-propagate adder finishes. The published structure is the workload: demosaic interpolates the Bayer sensor pattern into full colour, and tone mapping and colour correction apply per-layer matrix math at full 18-bit depth — but the coefficient and sample widths, the tap parallelism and the multiplier count are not published, so no multiplier total is claimed. As an illustrative width only — not Spectra's — a 16-bit by 16-bit array multiplier is 256 AND gates (1,536 transistors) plus 240 full adders (6,720 transistors) plus a 32-bit final adder (896 transistors), about 9,152 transistors per multiplier. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (pipeline sequencer, AI 3A control loop, Sensing Hub wake controller)** — A finite-state machine at gate level is state registers plus next-state logic plus output decode: the state is held in D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, two cross-coupled latch stages), the next state is a NAND/NOR gate network over the current state and the inputs, and the outputs are decoded from the state by another gate network. The pipeline sequencer, the AI 3A control loop and the Sensing Hub wake controller are FSMs of this form — the wake controller watches the two always-sensing ISPs and wakes the main triple ISP only when a face or QR code appears — but their state counts, the loop's arithmetic and the stage timing are not published, so no flip-flop or gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (per-layer treatment routing, three-pipeline select)** — A mux at gate level is transmission gates (2 transistors per input leg) or a NAND/NOR gate tree, selected by a decode of the select bits. The published geometry is the routing: each of the up to 12 semantic layers is routed to its own treatment path and recombined, and the three 18-bit pipelines are selected per sensor — a three-way select needs 2 select bits by arithmetic (2 to the power 2 is 4, which covers 3), and a twelve-way layer select needs 4 select bits (2 to the power 4 is 16, which covers 12). The mux radix, the layer-routing logic and whether the routing is transmission-gate or NAND/NOR-tree are not published, so no transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Register file (per-layer treatment parameters)** — The per-layer state is a register file in the standard form: one D flip-flop per stored bit (about 20–28 transistors each), written by a decoder over the layer index and read through a mux tree over the entries. The published geometry is the layer count: up to 12 semantic layers, so the layer index needs 4 bits by arithmetic (2 to the power 4 is 16, which covers 12) — but the entry width (exposure, white balance, tone curve and noise-reduction strength per layer), the entry count beyond the 12 layers and the banking are not published, so no flip-flop total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (inter-stage latches between the published stages)** — A pipeline register at gate level is a row of D flip-flops — two cross-coupled latch stages each, about 20–28 transistors per flip-flop in a standard-cell library — one flip-flop per latched bit, clocked together so a whole stage's worth of data moves in one cycle. Work is latched between ingest, 3A statistics, segmentation, per-layer treatment, HDR fusion, multi-frame noise reduction and output so the pipeline sustains 30 fps across three cameras at once, but the stage count, the latch widths and the stage latencies are not published, so no flip-flop total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Qualcomm publishes the Spectra ISP at stage level only — three 18-bit RAW pipelines, 3A statistics and NPU-backed semantic segmentation, per-layer treatment, HDR fusion and multi-frame noise reduction (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the block appears in any Qualcomm source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Qualcomm's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable).

### Chips&Media WAVE Codec IP

**Specs (wiki card).** Licensable multi-standard codec IP · 8K

**Building blocks.**
- **Video Coding Engine (VCE)** — The codec core proper: block-level processing through stream generation for AV1/HEVC/AVC encode and AV1/HEVC/AVC/VP9 decode, in single-core (4K60) or dual-core (8K60/4K240) configurations
- **On-the-fly entropy engine** — CABAC/context entropy coding fused into the VCE pipeline instead of a separate pass — Chips&Media's stated reason the architecture stays small: the entropy stage never becomes a store-and-forward bottleneck
- **CFrame™ frame-buffer compression** — The signature block: proprietary lossless compression of reference frames in external memory, cutting DRAM bandwidth — the resource codec IP actually starves for — roughly in half on typical content (vendor characterisation)
- **Embedded control processor** — A small in-IP CPU sequencing host commands and firmware, so the host SoC's load is near zero and the same RTL drops into any vendor's SoC
- **Pre/post processor** — Scaling, rotation and format handling bundled with the codec — the subsystem pieces an SoC team would otherwise build itself
- **AXI/APB host interface** — Standard AMBA attach (128-bit AXI data, APB control): the entire product is a licensable block, so the interface IS an architectural feature

**The piece that makes it special.** CFrame. A codec IP vendor can't out-run the standards — everyone implements the same AV1 — so WAVE differentiates where the memory system bleeds: reference frames. Losslessly compressing them in flight cuts the external bandwidth every decode/encode depends on, which is why the same WAVE6 core can be sold into a phone SoC and a transcoding server. The architecture is a business model rendered in RTL: one verified block, configurable tiers, dozens of licensees' chips.

**How work flows.** Host queues a stream: The SoC's driver programs the IP over APB; bitstream and frames move over AXI. VCE processes coding units: Prediction, transform and reconstruction run block by block in the core. Entropy codes on the fly: Symbols are arithmetic-coded as they are produced — no separate entropy pass. CFrame compresses references: Reconstructed frames are losslessly compressed into DRAM and decompressed on reference fetch. Bitstream/pixels exit: Decoded frames flow to display/ISP; encoded streams return to the host.

**Trade-off accepted.** A licensee's ceiling is the licensor's roadmap. WAVE's quality tuning is Chips&Media's, its VVC/AV2 support arrives on their schedule, and licensees publish almost nothing about which configuration they bought — so 'WAVE inside' guarantees a standards list, not a quality level. Public material names the VCE, entropy engine and CFrame; finer internal stages are not disclosed.

**Fact check.**
- [verified] WAVE6/WAVE627: single core compresses 4K60 at 500 MHz; AV1+HEVC+AVC encode — Source: Chips&Media WAVE627 launch release (June 2021). Quote: "This IP core is based on a more defined architecture design and delivers sophisticated encoding quality with a single core to compress 4K60fps@500MHz on the proven architecture of Chips&Media."
- [verified] On-the-fly entropy engine inside the VCE — Source: Chips&Media WAVE627 launch release (June 2021). Quote: "The Video Coding Engine (VCE) incorporates an on-the-fly entropy engine for simpler architecture and minimum control."
- [verified] CFrame integrated frame-buffer compression block — Source: Chips&Media WAVE627 launch release (June 2021). Quote: "Like other IPs by Chips&Media, a specialized hardware block called CFrameTM is integrated into the video IP."



#### Inside the signature block: The Video Coding Engine and its on-the-fly entropy engine — one 4K AV1 frame through the encode pipeline

**Inside it.** The Video Coding Engine (VCE) is the codec core proper, and the WAVE6 generation rebuilt it around a single architectural decision: the frame pipeline is gone, replaced by an on-the-fly architecture. Chips&Media's January 2021 WAVE6 announcement states the change directly — the series moves from frame pipeline to a more advanced on-the-fly architecture to deliver ultra-low latency — and the WAVE627 release explains what that buys: the VCE takes full advantage of the engine for the entire encoding process from block-level processing to stream generation, with the entropy engine incorporated inside the VCE rather than bolted on as a separate pass. The pipeline the releases name is: an on-the-fly pre-processor (rotation and mirror, RGB-to-YUV colour-space conversion, 422/444 to 420 format conversion, bit-depth conversion, crop, and sub-frame sync for ultra-low-delay encoding) feeding the VCE; the VCE itself doing block partition, prediction, transform and reconstruction; the on-the-fly entropy engine arithmetic-coding symbols as they are produced; and an on-the-fly post-processor (down-scaler to about one eighth, YUV-to-RGB, 422 to 420, bit-depth conversion, crop) on the output side. A small embedded processor sequences host commands, so the host SoC's load is near zero — the Gen2+ release repeats the point, that the embedded processor manages HOST commands requiring an extremely low HOST CPU load. The VPU runs in two clock domains, one for the video engine core and one for the entropy engine, which the Gen2+ release names as a practical synthesis and performance choice: the entropy engine paces the pipeline, so it gets its own clock. The product family the VCE ships in is the WAVE6 series: WAVE627, the AV1/HEVC/AVC encoder; WAVE637, the AV1/HEVC/AVC codec; WAVE617, the AV1/HEVC/AVC decoder; WAVE618 and WAVE638, the VVC decoder and codec; and WAVE677, the dual-core codec. The WAVE5 generation it replaced began with WAVE510, the HEVC decoder that was the first rollout of the new WAVE5 series, followed by WAVE512, the second-generation VP9/HEVC decoder, and WAVE515, the industry's first AVS2 decoder; WAVE510A followed as the world's first commercial AV1 hardware decoder IP. The family has shipped at scale: Chips&Media's video codec IP has powered over 3,000,000,000 units, adopted by more than 150 semiconductor companies, and the WAVE6 core itself entered the global mobile market in August 2025. The current head of the line, WAVE6 Gen2+, is a performance-enhanced single core targeting 8K30, adds AV2 and VVC decode, and is being prepared for ISO 26262 ASIL-B automotive use with release scheduled for the second quarter of 2026. Chips&Media publishes no internal sub-block diagram for the VCE — no stage latencies, queue depths, reference-store sizes or buffer geometry — so this block describes the published pipeline stages and the codec-mandated order, and invents no circuits inside them.

**Trace — one unit of work: one 4K AV1 frame through the WAVE627 encoder.**
1. **Frame in through the on-the-fly pre-processor. **A raw 4K frame arrives over the 128-bit AXI interface; the pre-processor rotates or mirrors it, converts RGB to YUV, drops 422 or 444 chroma to 420, converts bit depth and crops — all on the fly, with no full-frame staging buffer. Sub-frame sync lets encoding start before the whole frame has arrived, which is where the ultra-low-delay claim comes from.
2. **Superblock partition and mode decision. **The VCE splits the frame into AV1 superblocks of 128x128 or 64x64 luma samples, recursively partitioned down to 4x4 blocks, and chooses intra or inter prediction per block — the codec-mandated structure the encoder must implement, not a Chips&Media invention.
3. **Motion estimation against reference frames. **For inter blocks the engine searches motion against up to seven AV1 reference frames held in the decoded picture buffer — REFS_PER_FRAME 7 in the AV1 specification — the most expensive stage of the pipeline, and the one whose bandwidth CFrame exists to feed.
4. **Prediction, transform, quantise, reconstruct. **Motion compensation forms the residual, which is transformed and quantised under rate control — FixedQP, CBR, VBR or CVBR, at frame level and CU level, with a Custom map feature — and the block is reconstructed so it can serve as a future reference.
5. **On-the-fly entropy coding. **As each block's symbols are produced, the entropy engine inside the VCE arithmetic-codes them into the bitstream — the WAVE627 release's on-the-fly entropy engine for simpler architecture and minimum control — with no separate entropy pass and no store-and-forward buffer in between; in Gen2+ this engine runs on its own clock domain.
6. **Bitstream out; reconstructed frame to CFrame. **The finished bitstream leaves over AXI to the host, the reconstructed frame is handed to CFrame for compression into DRAM as a future reference, and the embedded processor sequences the next frame's host commands — the host SoC does almost nothing per frame.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the frame-pipeline tax: the old WAVE5 frame pipeline staged whole frames between stages, which cost latency, area and firmware complexity; the on-the-fly VCE removes the staging, so latency falls to the sub-frame level, the architecture shrinks, and firmware only sequences host commands through the embedded processor — the WAVE6 release lists ultra-low latency, bandwidth and memory-footprint saving, area saving and a simple architecture with reduced firmware complexity as the four gains. Creates a single-core throughput ceiling instead: one core compresses 4K60 at 500 MHz, so 8K60 needs the dual-core WAVE677 at 1 GHz or the Gen2+ single core at 550 MHz, and the entropy engine now sits on the critical path of every symbol — Gen2+ gives it its own clock domain precisely because it paces the pipeline. And the reference-fetch problem is not solved here, only moved: motion estimation still reads up to seven reference frames from external memory, which is why the VCE is paired with CFrame. Quality is the licensor's, too: WAVE6's visual-quality gains over WAVE5 were measured by PSNR and SSIM after tuning the major encoding factors, so a licensee inherits Chips&Media's quality curve, not its own.

**Governing numbers.** WAVE627 encoder, WAVE637 codec and WAVE617 decoder: 4K60 at 500 MHz (AV1, HEVC, AVC); WAVE618 decoder and WAVE638 codec: VVC at 4K60 at 500 MHz; WAVE677 codec: dual-core 8K60 at 1 GHz for HEVC and AV1, single-core 4K120 at 1 GHz for AVC; WAVE6 Gen2+ single core: 8K30 encode at 550 MHz, 8K30 decode at 500 MHz; resolution range WAVE6 256x128 to 8192x4320, Gen2+ to 8192x8192; bit depth 8-/10-bit (WAVE6), 8-/10-/12-bit (Gen2+); AV1 superblocks 128x128 or 64x64 luma samples, partitions down to 4x4, up to 7 reference frames per frame; interface APB 32-bit address/32-bit data, AXI 40-bit address/128-bit data; VPU two clock domains (video engine core, entropy engine). Internal stage latencies, queue depths and buffer geometry: not published.

**Primary source.** Chips&Media, 'Chips&Media Adds Extraordinary Features in the Next-Generation Video Codec IPs, introducing the WAVE6 Series' (press release, January 14, 2021, via Design-Reuse) — on-the-fly architecture, cFrame up to 50% bandwidth saving, WAVE6 product list and the four series benefits; Chips&Media, 'Silicon IP Provider Chips&Media Launches AV1 Video Encoder Hardware IP for 4K/UHD Video Resolutions and Beyond' (press release, June 17, 2021, via AnySilicon) — WAVE627, VCE on-the-fly entropy engine, CFrame; Chips&Media, 'Silicon IP Provider, Chips&Media Unveils New Multi Video Codec IP, WAVE6 Gen2+' (press release, October 23, 2024, via Design-Reuse) — 8K30 at 550/500 MHz, two clock domains, embedded processor, CFrame10, pre/post-processor features, rate control, interface and resolution tables; Chips&Media, 'Chips&Media's WAVE IP Successfully Enters the Global Mobile Market' (August 27, 2025, via Design-Reuse) — WAVE6/Gen2+ comparison table, 3 billion units, 150+ semiconductor companies; AOMedia, 'AV1 Bitstream and Decoding Process Specification' v1.0.0 with Errata 1 — superblock definition and REFS_PER_FRAME 7; libaom, 'AV1 Encoder Guide' — block partitions 128x128 down to 4x4; Nas Chung (Chips&Media), '[PATCH v2 0/8] Add support for Wave6 video codec driver' (Linux kernel mailing list, April 22, 2025, via LWN) — Wave6 a completely different hardware architecture from Wave5, VPU Control and VPU Core regions on NXP i.MX, WAVE633C.

#### Down to the primitives: The Video Coding Engine and its on-the-fly entropy engine — one 4K AV1 frame through the encode pipeline

The VCE runs the published on-the-fly pipeline — pre-processor, block partition, prediction, transform and reconstruction, the on-the-fly entropy engine, post-processor — with the embedded processor sequencing host commands and the entropy engine on its own clock domain, and each stage is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (pre-processor to VCE, VCE to entropy engine, bitstream output)** — The on-the-fly architecture replaces the old frame pipeline with a streaming one: the pre-processor hands pixels to the VCE, the VCE hands symbols to the entropy engine, and the entropy engine hands the bitstream out — each handoff is a FIFO decoupling a producer stage from a consumer stage that runs at a different rate. Because there is no full-frame staging buffer (verified — WAVE6 release: on-the-fly architecture, ultra-low latency; already recorded at Level 2), these are shallow block- or symbol-level queues, not frame stores. Their depths and widths are not published.
- **SRAM bank / line buffers (working superblock neighbourhood and reference-block window)** — Prediction and reconstruction work on one superblock at a time — AV1 superblocks of 128x128 or 64x64 luma samples, partitioned down to 4x4 (verified — AV1 specification; already recorded at Level 2) — so the VCE must hold the current superblock, its neighbouring reconstructed pixels for intra prediction, and the fetched reference blocks for motion compensation on chip while it works them. The reference frames themselves live in external DRAM, compressed by CFrame, so this is a working window store, not a frame store. Its capacity, banking and port count are not published. Standard construction for the store itself; the superblock sizes are spec facts.
- **Adder tree + comparator (motion-estimation SAD and best-match selection)** — Inter prediction scores each candidate displacement against up to seven AV1 reference frames (verified — AV1 specification, REFS_PER_FRAME 7; already recorded at Level 2) by a sum of absolute differences: per-pixel subtractors feeding an adder tree, with a comparator keeping the lowest-cost candidate as the search proceeds. Motion estimation is the most expensive stage of the pipeline and the one whose bandwidth CFrame exists to feed (already recorded at Level 2). The candidate set, the search range, the block sizes the search covers and the SAD datapath width are not published. Standard construction for the SAD arithmetic.
- **Multiplier array (codec transform and motion-compensation interpolation)** — The prediction residual is transformed and quantised on encode — AV1 uses DCT, ADST, flipped ADST and identity transforms in combinations along the horizontal and vertical axes — and motion compensation interpolates reference samples to sub-pixel accuracy. Each transform coefficient and each interpolated sample is a weighted sum, so a multiplier array feeding an adder tree. The transform and motion-compensation stages are codec-mandated parts of the AV1 encode the VCE implements. The multiplier count, the transform set the silicon covers and the interpolation tap structure are not published. Standard construction for the arithmetic; the stages are codec facts, not WAVE silicon facts.
- **Register file (CABAC context models and AV1 CDF tables)** — The entropy stage keeps its probability state in tables. For the HEVC/AVC path that is CABAC: each probability model can take one out of 127 different states with associated probability values p ranging in the interval [0.01875, 0.98125] (verified — Fraunhofer HHI, CABAC; already recorded for NVENC, Xe Media Engine, Apple Media Engine and Spectra). For the AV1 path the coder is different: AV1 does not use CABAC, it uses a non-binary multi-symbol arithmetic coder (verified — AV1 multi-symbol arithmetic coder, up to 16 symbols per step; new fact record this run), whose cumulative distribution functions are held in tables the coder reads and updates per symbol. The tables are a register file (or small SRAM) indexed by syntax element and context. The table count, entry count and banking are not published.
- **FSM / controller (VCE pipeline sequencer and CABAC probability-estimation FSM)** — The VCE pipeline sequencer steps each block through partition, prediction, transform, quantisation, reconstruction and entropy coding, and the embedded processor sequences host commands so the host SoC's load is near zero (verified — WAVE6 Gen2+ release; already recorded at Level 2). Inside the entropy engine, probability estimation in CABAC is based on a table-driven estimator using a finite-state machine approach with tabulated transition rules (verified — Fraunhofer HHI; already recorded for Apple Media Engine and Spectra). The sequencer's state count, the FSM's state count and the stage timing are not published.
- **Synchronizer / CDC (video-engine clock domain to entropy-engine clock domain)** — The VPU runs in two clock domains, one for the video engine core and one for the entropy engine (verified — WAVE6 Gen2+ release; already recorded at Level 2), because the entropy engine paces the pipeline and gets its own clock. Every symbol the VCE produces must therefore cross from the video-engine clock domain into the entropy-engine clock domain, and every control signal back must cross the other way — a clock-domain-crossing synchronizer, built in standard construction from two-flop synchronizers or an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers. The synchronizer depth, the FIFO depth and the clock frequencies are not published. This is the one primitive in the VCE whose existence is a published WAVE fact rather than a mapping from a codec stage.
- **Barrel shifter (entropy-code bit packing and bit-depth conversion)** — The entropy engine packs variable-length arithmetic-coded symbols into the bitstream, and the pre- and post-processors convert bit depth (8-/10-bit in WAVE6, 8-/10-/12-bit in Gen2+; already recorded at Level 2) — variable-length packing is a barrel-shifter operation: bits shifted into the stream by a code-dependent amount, and read back out by the same amount on decode. The shift width and the bitstream buffer depth are not published. Standard construction for the shifter; the entropy-coding and bit-depth stages are published pipeline facts.
- **Mux / demux (intra/inter prediction select, pre/post-processor path select)** — Each block chooses intra or inter prediction per block (already recorded at Level 2), so the prediction stage is a mux selecting between the intra predictor and the motion-compensated predictor; the pre-processor selects between rotation or mirror, RGB-to-YUV conversion, 422/444 to 420 conversion, bit-depth conversion and crop (verified — WAVE6 Gen2+ release; already recorded at Level 2), and the post-processor selects between the down-scaler, YUV-to-RGB, 422 to 420 and bit-depth paths. Each selection is a mux/demux steering the frame through the chosen path. The mux radix and the path-selection logic are not published.
- **Pipeline registers (inter-stage latches between the published stages)** — Work is latched between the pre-processor, block partition, prediction, transform, reconstruction, entropy coding and post-processor so the pipeline sustains 4K60 at 500 MHz from a single WAVE627 core (verified — WAVE627 release; already recorded at Level 2). The stage count, latch widths and stage latencies are not published.
- **Counter (rate-control and frame/CU sequencing)** — Rate control runs at frame level and CU level — FixedQP, CBR, VBR or CVBR, with a Custom map feature (verified — WAVE6 Gen2+ release; already recorded at Level 2) — so the VCE counts frames and coding units as they pass through the pipeline and tracks the bit budget consumed against the target rate. The counter widths, the budget arithmetic and the sequencing policy are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Chips&Media publishes no internal sub-block diagram for the VCE — no stage latencies, queue depths, reference-store sizes or buffer geometry — so the primitives above are mapped from the published pipeline stages and the codec specifications, not from a die diagram. Every number in this block that comes from a codec spec is a spec fact (the algorithm the silicon must implement); no parameter of the VCE itself is claimed. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Inside the signature block: CFrame — one reference frame through compress, DRAM and decompress-on-fetch

**Inside it.** CFrame is Chips&Media's proprietary frame-buffer compression block, integrated into the video IP alongside the VCE. Its job is narrow and total: every reconstructed frame that must survive as a reference is compressed before it is written to external memory and decompressed when it is fetched back, so the DRAM traffic of the codec — the resource a codec IP actually starves for — falls. The WAVE6 series release quantifies it: cFrame is embedded within the WAVE6 series and therefore saves up to 50% of the bandwidth access to memory. The WAVE510A release says the same thing from the decoder's side: with the compression of reconstructed frames for future reference, the VPU can significantly reduce the bus bandwidth by 50% on average while accessing frame data effectively in the external memory. The WAVE627 release adds the mechanism in one line: with compression of reference frames, this IP core can significantly reduce bus transactions while accessing extensive frame data effectively in the external memory. The current generation, CFrame10 in WAVE6 Gen2+, improves bandwidth efficiency by 5-10% over the WAVE6 series, and Gen2+ also supports third-party frame compression — AFBC and PVRIC — for source and output images, so a licensee is no longer locked to the proprietary format for the frames that leave the codec. The compression is lossless for reference frames: a reference must be bit-identical when it is fetched back, or the decoder's reconstruction would drift from the encoder's. That constraint is what makes CFrame a compression block rather than a codec: it cannot trade quality for ratio on the reference path. How often the win compounds is set by the codec: an AV1 frame can reference up to seven earlier frames, so one compressed reference frame is fetched many times over its life in the decoded picture buffer — one compress on write, many decompresses on fetch. Chips&Media publishes no CFrame algorithm, block size, compression ratio by content, buffer geometry or decompression latency — no sub-block diagram, no queue depths — so this block describes the published compress-store-fetch contract and invents no circuits inside it.

**Trace — one unit of work: one reference frame through CFrame, DRAM and back.**
1. **Reconstruction finishes a frame. **The VCE completes a 4K frame; it is a future reference for the inter frames that follow, so it must be stored in external memory rather than discarded — an uncompressed 4K frame is more than ten megabytes the AXI bus would have to carry.
2. **CFrame compresses the frame on the fly. **The reconstructed frame passes through CFrame as it leaves the VCE; the block losslessly compresses it before it ever touches external memory, with no frame-sized staging buffer in between — the same on-the-fly discipline as the rest of WAVE6.
3. **Compressed frame written to DRAM. **The compressed frame goes out over the 128-bit AXI interface into external memory at up to half the bytes an uncompressed frame would need — the WAVE6 release's up to 50% saving of memory bandwidth access, measured across read and write.
4. **Motion estimation asks for a reference block. **The next frame's inter prediction needs a block from this reference frame; the fetch goes to DRAM for the compressed bytes, not to an on-chip copy — there is no large on-chip reference store, which is the point of the block.
5. **Decompress on fetch. **CFrame decompresses the fetched region as it returns from DRAM, restoring the exact pixels — lossless, so the reference is bit-identical to what the VCE reconstructed, and the decoder's prediction matches the encoder's.
6. **Pixels feed prediction; the cycle repeats. **The decompressed reference pixels feed motion compensation for the new frame, whose own reconstruction will in turn pass through CFrame — every reference frame pays one compress and as many decompresses as the frames that reference it.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the bandwidth wall: reference traffic is the codec's largest DRAM consumer — every inter frame reads several reference frames — so halving it is what lets a single WAVE6 core hold 4K60 at 500 MHz and lets the same core sell into a phone SoC and a transcoding server alike. Creates a decompress-on-fetch dependency on the prediction critical path instead: every motion-compensation fetch now waits on decompression, so CFrame's throughput and latency bound the motion search, and the compression ratio is content-dependent — noisy or finely detailed content compresses worse — so the bandwidth budget must be sized for the worst case, not the up-to-50% average. And the stored format is proprietary: frames compressed by CFrame can only be read back through CFrame, so a licensee's SoC cannot reuse them elsewhere without it — Gen2+ answers this for source and output images with AFBC and PVRIC support, but the reference path stays proprietary.

**Governing numbers.** Up to 50% saving of memory bandwidth access with cFrame embedded in the WAVE6 series; 50% bus bandwidth reduction on average with compression of reconstructed frames for future reference (WAVE510A); CFrame10 in WAVE6 Gen2+ improves bandwidth efficiency 5-10% over the WAVE6 series; Gen2+ area 130-140% of the WAVE6 single core, WAVE637DV Gen2+ about two-thirds the area of the WAVE6 dual-core version; third-party frame compression (AFBC, PVRIC) supported for source and output images in Gen2+. CFrame compression ratio by content, compression algorithm, block size, buffer geometry and decompression latency: not published.

**Primary source.** Chips&Media, 'Chips&Media Adds Extraordinary Features in the Next-Generation Video Codec IPs, introducing the WAVE6 Series' (press release, January 14, 2021, via Design-Reuse) — cFrame embedded, up to 50% memory bandwidth saving; Chips&Media, 'Silicon IP Provider Chips&Media Launches AV1 Video Encoder Hardware IP for 4K/UHD Video Resolutions and Beyond' (press release, June 17, 2021, via AnySilicon) — CFrame integrated, compression of reference frames reduces bus transactions; Chips&Media, 'Chips&Media Delivers The World's First Commercial AV1 Hardware Decoder IP, WAVE510A' (press release, October 22, 2019, via Design-Reuse) — 50% bus bandwidth reduction on average; Chips&Media, 'Silicon IP Provider, Chips&Media Unveils New Multi Video Codec IP, WAVE6 Gen2+' (press release, October 23, 2024, via Design-Reuse) — CFrame10, 5-10% bandwidth efficiency improvement, AFBC/PVRIC support, area figures; AOMedia, 'AV1 Bitstream and Decoding Process Specification' v1.0.0 with Errata 1 — REFS_PER_FRAME 7.

#### Down to the primitives: CFrame — one reference frame through compress, DRAM and decompress-on-fetch

CFrame runs the published compress-store-fetch contract — compress the reconstructed frame on the fly, write it to DRAM over the 128-bit AXI interface, decompress it on fetch — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (reconstructed-frame ingest, compressed-byte staging to AXI, fetch-return path)** — The reconstructed frame passes through CFrame as it leaves the VCE, with no frame-sized staging buffer in between (already recorded at Level 2), so the ingest path is a FIFO decoupling the VCE's block-rate output from the compressor; the compressed bytes are staged into a FIFO before they are written out over the 128-bit AXI interface; and on fetch, the compressed bytes return from DRAM through a FIFO into the decompressor. Their depths and widths are not published.
- **SRAM bank / line buffers (working store for the region being compressed or decompressed)** — Compression and decompression work on a region of the frame at a time, not on the whole frame — the block compresses on the fly as the frame leaves the VCE — so CFrame must hold the region currently being processed on chip while it works it, a working store built from SRAM banks or line buffers. The region size, the store's capacity and its port count are not published. Standard construction for the store itself; the on-the-fly contract is a published pipeline fact.
- **Barrel shifter (variable-length packing and unpacking of the compressed stream)** — A lossless compressor emits variable-length codes, so the compressed stream must be packed into bytes by shifting each code in by a code-dependent amount — a barrel-shifter operation — and on fetch the same shifter unpacks the codes back out before decompression. The shift width and the compressed-byte buffer depth are not published. Standard construction for the shifter; the variable-length nature of the compressed stream follows from the lossless-compression contract.
- **Mux / demux (CFrame vs AFBC/PVRIC path select, compressed vs uncompressed path)** — WAVE6 Gen2+ supports third-party frame compression — AFBC and PVRIC — for source and output images (verified — WAVE6 Gen2+ release; already recorded at Level 2), so the frame path is a mux selecting between the proprietary CFrame path and the third-party format path for frames that leave the codec, while the reference path stays on CFrame. The mux radix and the path-selection logic are not published.
- **Register file (compressed-region address and layout table)** — Compressed frames are variable-length, so the block must remember where each compressed region was written in DRAM — otherwise a fetch for a reference block cannot find the right bytes. That layout is held in a register file (or small SRAM) indexed by frame region, written when a frame is compressed and read when a reference block is fetched. The entry count, entry width and banking are not published. The table's existence follows from the variable-length storage contract; its organisation is not published.
- **Adder tree (compressed-offset address arithmetic)** — Because compressed regions are variable-length, the DRAM address of a region is not a fixed stride from the frame base — it is the accumulation of the sizes of the regions before it. Computing those addresses is an adder-tree operation over the region sizes held in the layout table. The accumulation width and the region granularity are not published. Standard construction for the address arithmetic; the variable-length layout follows from the lossless-compression contract.
- **Counter (frame-region sequencing and outstanding AXI transaction tracking)** — Frames are sequenced through CFrame region by region on both the compress and the decompress side, and the compressed writes and fetches go out over AXI as bursts whose completion must be tracked — the counters that track which region is in flight and how many AXI transactions are outstanding. The counter widths and the sequencing policy are not published.
- **Credit counter (AXI flow control for variable-length compressed bursts)** — Compressed frames are variable-length, so the bursts CFrame writes to DRAM over the 128-bit AXI interface (verified — WAVE6 Gen2+ release; already recorded at Level 2) vary in length from region to region, and the block must not overrun the memory system — a credit counter tracking how many AXI write or read credits are outstanding and throttling the compressor or the fetch side when the budget is exhausted. The credit budget and the throttling policy are not published. Standard construction for the credit counter; the 128-bit AXI interface is a published fact.
- **FSM / controller (compress-on-write / decompress-on-fetch sequencer)** — The sequencer steps each frame through compress, write, fetch and decompress, and enforces the lossless round-trip: a reference must be bit-identical when it is fetched back, or the decoder's reconstruction would drift from the encoder's (already recorded at Level 2). The state count, the stage timing and the decompression latency are not published.
- **Pipeline registers (inter-stage latches between the compress and decompress stages)** — Work is latched between the ingest, compress, AXI-write, AXI-read and decompress steps so the block sustains the up to 50% bandwidth saving the WAVE6 release claims (verified — WAVE6 release: cFrame saves up to 50% of the bandwidth access to memory; already recorded at Level 2) across the read and write traffic of a 4K60 stream. The stage count, latch widths and stage latencies are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Chips&Media publishes no CFrame algorithm, block size, compression ratio by content, buffer geometry or decompression latency — no sub-block diagram, no queue depths — so the primitives above are mapped from the published compress-store-fetch contract, not from a die diagram. The compression algorithm itself is proprietary and unpublished; the primitives describe what any lossless compress-store-fetch block must contain to honour that contract, labelled as such. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Down to the gates: The Video Coding Engine and its on-the-fly entropy engine — one 4K AV1 frame through the encode pipeline

Chips&Media publishes no gate-level structure for WAVE — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the VCE, the entropy engine or CFrame. The deepest published description is the WAVE6, WAVE627 and WAVE6 Gen2+ releases, which describe the pipeline stages, the configurations and the codec features at block level, and the codec specifications (AV1, HEVC, AVC), which define the algorithms the silicon must implement. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published spec geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about Chips&Media's circuits.

- **FIFO / queue (pre-processor to VCE, VCE to entropy engine, bitstream output)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each, incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The pre-processor-to-VCE handoff, the VCE-to-entropy-engine handoff and the bitstream output are FIFOs of this form, decoupling stages that run at different rates in the on-the-fly pipeline — but their depths and widths are not published, so the pointer widths — and therefore the counter and comparator totals — are not claimed. The on-the-fly contract is the published part: no full-frame staging buffer sits between the stages. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank / line buffers (working superblock neighbourhood and reference-block window)** — The working window is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. The published geometry is the workload: prediction and reconstruction work on one superblock at a time — AV1 superblocks of 128x128 or 64x64 luma samples, partitioned down to 4x4 — so the store must hold the current superblock, its neighbouring reconstructed pixels for intra prediction and the fetched reference blocks for motion compensation while the VCE works them; a 4K frame is 510 full 128x128 superblocks by arithmetic (30 across, 17 down with the bottom row partial), so the store turns over 510 times per frame — but the store's capacity, banking and port count are not published, so no cell total is claimed. The reference frames themselves live in external DRAM, compressed by CFrame, so this is a working window store, not a frame store. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree + comparator (motion-estimation SAD and best-match selection)** — A sum of absolute differences is subtractors, absolute-value logic and an adder tree: each per-pixel difference is a subtractor (one full adder per bit, about 28 transistors each, with the sign bit selecting the two's-complement negation through a mux), the absolute value is a conditional invert-and-increment, and the adder tree collapses the per-pixel differences pairwise — a tree of adders whose depth is log2 of the block size, so a 4x4 block's SAD tree is 4 deep by arithmetic and a full 128x128 superblock's is 14 deep by arithmetic. The best-match selection is a comparator (one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree) holding the lowest cost so far, with a register holding the winning displacement. The published geometry is the search: up to seven AV1 reference frames per frame (REFS_PER_FRAME 7), each scored by SAD — but the candidate set, the search range, the block sizes the search covers and the SAD datapath width are not published, so no adder-tree or comparator total is claimed — only the form. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (codec transform and motion-compensation interpolation)** — Each transform coefficient and each interpolated sample is a weighted sum, so the multiplier array is in the standard form: AND gates form the partial products, a full-adder compressor tree collapses them, and one final carry-propagate adder finishes. The published structure is the workload: AV1 uses DCT, ADST, flipped ADST and identity transforms in combinations along the horizontal and vertical axes, and motion compensation interpolates reference samples to sub-pixel accuracy — but the coefficient and sample widths, the tap parallelism, the transform set the silicon covers and the multiplier count are not published, so no multiplier total is claimed. As an illustrative width only — not WAVE's — a 16-bit by 16-bit array multiplier is 256 AND gates (1,536 transistors) plus 240 full adders (6,720 transistors) plus a 32-bit final adder (896 transistors), about 9,152 transistors per multiplier. Standard construction.
- **Register file (CABAC context models and AV1 CDF tables)** — The entropy tables are a register file in the standard form: one D flip-flop per stored bit (about 20–28 transistors each), written by the probability-update logic and read by the symbol coder, with a decoder over the context index on write and a mux tree over the entries on read. The published geometry is the state count: each CABAC probability model can take one out of 127 different states, so the state index needs 7 bits by arithmetic (2 to the power 7 is 128, which covers 127), with associated probability values p ranging in the interval [0.01875, 0.98125]; the AV1 path's multi-symbol arithmetic coder takes up to 16 symbols per step, so its symbol index needs 4 bits by arithmetic (2 to the power 4 is 16) — but the table count, the entry count and the banking are not published, so no flip-flop total is claimed. Spec facts about the tables; nothing about WAVE's table storage is published. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (VCE pipeline sequencer and CABAC probability-estimation FSM)** — A finite-state machine at gate level is state registers plus next-state logic plus output decode: the state is held in D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, two cross-coupled latch stages), the next state is a NAND/NOR gate network over the current state and the inputs, and the outputs are decoded from the state by another gate network. The VCE pipeline sequencer steps each block through partition, prediction, transform, quantisation, reconstruction and entropy coding, the embedded processor sequences host commands, and inside the entropy engine the CABAC probability estimator is itself a table-driven finite-state machine with tabulated transition rules — all FSMs of this form — but their state counts and the stage timing are not published, so no flip-flop or gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer / CDC (video-engine clock domain to entropy-engine clock domain)** — A clock-domain crossing at gate level is two-flop synchronizers or an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers: a control signal crosses on two D flip-flops in series in the receiving clock domain (about 20–28 transistors each), so a metastable first flop has a full cycle to settle before the second samples it; a multi-bit data path crosses through an asynchronous FIFO whose read and write pointers are Gray-coded — only one bit changes per increment, so a pointer sampled across the boundary is never more than one count stale — with the full/empty flags computed from the synchronized pointers. The published geometry is the boundary itself: the VPU runs in two clock domains, one for the video engine core and one for the entropy engine, because the entropy engine paces the pipeline — but the synchronizer depth, the FIFO depth and the clock frequencies are not published, so no flip-flop total is claimed. This is the one primitive in the VCE whose existence is a published WAVE fact rather than a mapping from a codec stage. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (entropy-code bit packing and bit-depth conversion)** — A barrel shifter at gate level is log2(N) stages of 2-to-1 muxes for an N-bit shift, each stage shifting by a power of two selected by one bit of the shift amount — each mux a transmission-gate pair (2 transistors) or a NAND/NOR gate tree, so an N-bit shifter is N times log2(N) muxes in the standard form. The entropy engine packs variable-length arithmetic-coded symbols into the bitstream by shifting each code in by a code-dependent amount, and the pre- and post-processors convert bit depth — 8-/10-bit in WAVE6, 8-/10-/12-bit in Gen2+ — which is the same shift-and-pack operation at the sample level — but the shift width and the bitstream buffer depth are not published, so no mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (intra/inter prediction select, pre/post-processor path select)** — A mux at gate level is transmission gates (2 transistors per input leg) or a NAND/NOR gate tree, selected by a decode of the select bits. The published geometry is the path count: each block chooses intra or inter prediction — a two-way select needing 1 select bit by arithmetic — and the pre-processor selects between rotation or mirror, RGB-to-YUV conversion, 422/444 to 420 conversion, bit-depth conversion and crop, while the post-processor selects between the down-scaler, YUV-to-RGB, 422 to 420 and bit-depth paths. The mux radix, the path-selection logic and whether the routing is transmission-gate or NAND/NOR-tree are not published, so no transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (inter-stage latches between the published stages)** — A pipeline register at gate level is a row of D flip-flops — two cross-coupled latch stages each, about 20–28 transistors per flip-flop in a standard-cell library — one flip-flop per latched bit, clocked together so a whole stage's worth of data moves in one cycle. Work is latched between the pre-processor, block partition, prediction, transform, reconstruction, entropy coding and post-processor so the pipeline sustains 4K60 at 500 MHz from a single WAVE627 core — 500 million cycles a second for 60 frames, about 8.33 million cycles per frame by arithmetic — but the stage count, the latch widths and the stage latencies are not published, so no flip-flop total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (rate-control and frame/CU sequencing)** — A counter at gate level is N D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) holding the count plus an incrementer of N full adders (about 28 transistors each) adding one on each clock, with a comparator (one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree) detecting the terminal count. Rate control runs at frame level and CU level — FixedQP, CBR, VBR or CVBR, with a Custom map feature — so the VCE counts frames and coding units as they pass through the pipeline and tracks the bit budget consumed against the target rate — but the counter widths, the budget arithmetic and the sequencing policy are not published, so no flip-flop or adder total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Chips&Media publishes the VCE at stage level only — pre-processor, block partition, prediction, transform and reconstruction, the on-the-fly entropy engine, post-processor, two clock domains and the embedded processor (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the block appears in any Chips&Media source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Chips&Media's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable).

#### Down to the gates: CFrame — one reference frame through compress, DRAM and decompress-on-fetch

CFrame runs the published compress-store-fetch contract — compress the reconstructed frame on the fly, write it to DRAM over the 128-bit AXI interface, decompress it on fetch — and each step is built from the primitives below. As with the VCE, Chips&Media publishes no gate-level structure for CFrame either, so the decompositions below are the textbook-standard constructions of the Level-3 primitives, with published spec geometry kept published and arithmetic from it labelled as arithmetic.

- **FIFO / queue (reconstructed-frame ingest, compressed-byte staging to AXI, fetch-return path)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each, incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The reconstructed-frame ingest path, the compressed-byte staging path to AXI and the fetch-return path are FIFOs of this form, decoupling the VCE's block-rate output from the compressor and the compressor from the memory system — but their depths and widths are not published, so the pointer widths — and therefore the counter and comparator totals — are not claimed. The on-the-fly contract is the published part: no frame-sized staging buffer sits between the VCE and CFrame. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank / line buffers (working store for the region being compressed or decompressed)** — The working store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. The published geometry is the workload: compression and decompression work on a region of the frame at a time, not on the whole frame, so the store must hold the region currently being processed on chip while it works it — but the region size, the store's capacity and its port count are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Whether the store is one bank or one bank per direction is not published. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (variable-length packing and unpacking of the compressed stream)** — A barrel shifter at gate level is log2(N) stages of 2-to-1 muxes for an N-bit shift, each stage shifting by a power of two selected by one bit of the shift amount — each mux a transmission-gate pair (2 transistors) or a NAND/NOR gate tree, so an N-bit shifter is N times log2(N) muxes in the standard form. A lossless compressor emits variable-length codes, so the compressed stream is packed into bytes by shifting each code in by a code-dependent amount, and on fetch the same shifter unpacks the codes back out before decompression — but the shift width and the compressed-byte buffer depth are not published, so no mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (CFrame vs AFBC/PVRIC path select, compressed vs uncompressed path)** — A mux at gate level is transmission gates (2 transistors per input leg) or a NAND/NOR gate tree, selected by a decode of the select bits. The published geometry is the path count: WAVE6 Gen2+ supports third-party frame compression — AFBC and PVRIC — for source and output images, so the frame path selects between the proprietary CFrame path and the third-party format path, while the reference path stays on CFrame — a three-way select needing 2 select bits by arithmetic (2 to the power 2 is 4, which covers 3) — and each frame also selects between the compressed and uncompressed paths. The mux radix, the path-selection logic and whether the routing is transmission-gate or NAND/NOR-tree are not published, so no transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Register file (compressed-region address and layout table)** — The layout table is a register file in the standard form: one D flip-flop per stored bit (about 20–28 transistors each), written by the compressor when a frame is compressed and read by the fetch side when a reference block is requested, with a decoder over the region index on write and a mux tree over the entries on read. The published geometry is the contract: compressed frames are variable-length, so the block must remember where each compressed region was written in DRAM — otherwise a fetch for a reference block cannot find the right bytes — but the entry count, the entry width and the banking are not published, so no flip-flop total is claimed. The table's existence follows from the variable-length storage contract; its organisation is not published. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (compressed-offset address arithmetic)** — An accumulation is an adder tree in the standard form: full adders (about 28 transistors each — two half adders, two XOR plus two AND plus one OR) arranged pairwise so the tree depth is log2 of the operand count, collapsing the values to one sum, with a carry-propagate adder finishing each stage. The published geometry is the address rule: because compressed regions are variable-length, the DRAM address of a region is not a fixed stride from the frame base — it is the accumulation of the sizes of the regions before it, read out of the layout table — but the accumulation width and the region granularity are not published, so no adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (frame-region sequencing and outstanding AXI transaction tracking)** — A counter at gate level is N D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) holding the count plus an incrementer of N full adders (about 28 transistors each) adding one on each clock, with a comparator (one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree) detecting the terminal count. Frames are sequenced through CFrame region by region on both the compress and the decompress side, and the compressed writes and fetches go out over AXI as bursts whose completion must be tracked — the counters track which region is in flight and how many AXI transactions are outstanding — but the counter widths and the sequencing policy are not published, so no flip-flop or adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (AXI flow control for variable-length compressed bursts)** — A credit counter at gate level is an up/down counter plus a limit comparator: N D flip-flops holding the outstanding-credit count, an incrementer of N full adders adding one when a burst is issued and a decrementer subtracting one when its completion returns, and a comparator (one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree) against the credit budget that throttles the compressor or the fetch side when the budget is exhausted. The published geometry is the interface: compressed frames are variable-length, so the bursts CFrame writes to DRAM over the 128-bit AXI interface vary in length from region to region — but the credit budget and the throttling policy are not published, so no flip-flop or adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (compress-on-write / decompress-on-fetch sequencer)** — A finite-state machine at gate level is state registers plus next-state logic plus output decode: the state is held in D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, two cross-coupled latch stages), the next state is a NAND/NOR gate network over the current state and the inputs, and the outputs are decoded from the state by another gate network. The CFrame sequencer steps each frame through compress, write, fetch and decompress, and enforces the lossless round-trip — a reference must be bit-identical when it is fetched back, or the decoder's reconstruction would drift from the encoder's — but the state count, the stage timing and the decompression latency are not published, so no flip-flop or gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (inter-stage latches between the compress and decompress stages)** — A pipeline register at gate level is a row of D flip-flops — two cross-coupled latch stages each, about 20–28 transistors per flip-flop in a standard-cell library — one flip-flop per latched bit, clocked together so a whole stage's worth of data moves in one cycle. Work is latched between the ingest, compress, AXI-write, AXI-read and decompress steps so the block sustains the up to 50% bandwidth saving the WAVE6 release claims across the read and write traffic of a 4K60 stream — but the stage count, the latch widths and the stage latencies are not published, so no flip-flop total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Chips&Media publishes no CFrame algorithm, block size, compression ratio by content, buffer geometry or decompression latency — no sub-block diagram, no queue depths — and no gate-level structure for any part of the block appears in any Chips&Media source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Chips&Media's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable).


### Ambarella CV3 / CVflow

**Specs (wiki card).** 5 nm · CVflow NPU + ISP · automotive & cameras

**Building blocks.**
- **Neural Vector Processor (NVP) ★** — The CVflow engine: a neural vector processor rated up to 500 eTOPS across the CV3 family, executing compiled CNN/transformer graphs — and, unusually, radar perception (Oculii adaptive algorithms) on the same engine
- **General Vector Processor (GVP)** — A floating-point vector engine taking classical computer-vision and radar math off both the NVP and the CPUs — the middle tier between neural and scalar work
- **ISP — 12 physical / 20 virtual cameras** — Ambarella's heritage block: HDR ISP feeding the perception stack directly, sized for a full surround suite (10 cameras + 5 radar + ultrasonics in a typical L2+ fit)
- **Stereo + dense optical-flow engines** — Dedicated depth/motion hardware beside the ISP — geometry the neural nets would otherwise spend their budget re-deriving
- **Arm Cortex-A78AE ×16 + R52 lockstep safety pairs** — Up to 16 application cores (12 A78AE + 3 dual-core lockstep R52 pairs on the AD685) run the driving stack, with an ASIL-D safety island supervising
- **Video encoder (H.264/H.265) + automotive GPU + HSM** — Recording/streaming encode, surround-view rendering GPU, and a hardware security module with crypto acceleration, TRNG and DRAM scrambling

**The piece that makes it special.** One chip, whole sensor suite — with radar on the neural engine. CV3's bet is consolidation at the perception layer: the NVP doesn't just run camera networks, it runs the Oculii radar algorithms too, so vision and radar fuse on one engine's tensors instead of across chips. Paired with an ISP that ingests a dozen cameras and lockstep safety cores, the CVflow pitch is that a domain controller is an ISP with a neural engine attached — Ambarella's camera lineage is the architecture.

**How work flows.** Sensors stream in: Cameras hit the ISP; radar returns hit the NVP/GVP path; ultrasonics and vehicle signals land on the safety cores. ISP conditions the frames: HDR merge and correction produce perception-grade frames at line rate. NVP runs the networks: Detection, segmentation and radar perception execute as compiled CVflow graphs. GVP + CPUs fuse and plan: Classical CV and fusion run on the GVP; the A78AE cluster runs tracking, prediction and path planning under R52 supervision. Vehicle outputs + recording: Control commands exit via the safety island; the encoder records the surround streams for logging.

**Trade-off accepted.** A domain, not a platform. CVflow's efficiency comes from compiling networks to one vendor's engine — portability is deliberately traded away, TOPS are quoted as 'eTOPS' (equivalent, sparsity-assisted) rather than dense, and the family spans wide power/performance points under one name, so 'CV3' alone specifies little. Ambarella publishes capabilities, not die internals.

**Fact check.**
- [verified] CV3: next-generation CVflow with on-chip NVP up to 500 eTOPS; up to 16 Cortex-A78AE cores — Source: Ambarella CV3 launch release (CES 2022), via VentureBeat. Quote: "The company said this drove the development of the on-chip neural vector processor (NVP), with up to 500 eTOPS of AI compute"
- [verified] CV3-AD685: 12 Cortex-A78AE + 3 dual-core lockstep Cortex-R52 pairs; Samsung 5 nm; ASIL-D safety island — Source: Ambarella CV3-AD685 announcement (CES 2023), via Electronic Specifier. Quote: "Twelve Arm Cortex A78AE CPUs and 3 dual-core, lockstep pairs of Cortex-R52 CPUs are included. CV3-AD685 is targeting ASIL-B on the chip level, with an ASIL-D safety island."
- [verified] ISP supports up to 12 physical or 20 virtual cameras simultaneously — Source: Ambarella CV3 launch material. Quote: "By simultaneously supporting up to 12 physical or 20 virtual cameras, a single CV3 can process the entire sensor suite"

#### Inside the signature block: The CVflow NVP + GVP — one vector engine for camera nets and radar

**Inside it.** The third-generation CVflow engine is two vector processors, not one. The neural vector processor (NVP) runs neural-network inference — detection, segmentation, path-planning networks, and, unusually, the Oculii adaptive AI radar-perception algorithms. The general vector processor (GVP) is a floating-point vector engine that offloads classical computer vision and radar processing from the NVP engines, and floating-point-intensive algorithms from the Arm CPUs — Ambarella's launch release states the split explicitly, and the point of the split is that the NVP can be further optimized for convolution and matrix work once the floating-point work leaves it. Both blocks are in-house Ambarella IP, and both carry radar-specific signal-processing enhancements for the centralized 4D imaging radar. The engine is fed camera frames by the ISP and raw radar returns from the radar front-ends, and its outputs go to the A78AE cluster for fusion and planning. Ambarella publishes no NVP block diagram — no MAC-array dimensions, no vector width, no SRAM sizes, no queue depths, no per-stage latencies — so the organization above is the split the launch material names, not a die photograph.

**Trace — one unit of work: one radar frame through the centralized 4D imaging radar path.**
1. **Raw radar returns arrive. **The radar front-ends send raw chirp data to the CV3 instead of pre-processed point clouds — the centralized architecture moves the radar processing onto the SoC, where the full compute budget lives.
2. **The GVP conditions the signal. **Classical radar signal processing — the floating-point range and Doppler work — runs on the GVP, offloaded from both the NVP and the Arm CPUs, as the launch release describes the GVP's role.
3. **Oculii adaptive algorithms run on the NVP. **The Oculii adaptive AI software — virtual-aperture imaging that synthesizes a larger aperture from the radar array — executes on the neural vector processor, which Ambarella says is enhanced to run advanced radar perception software.
4. **Perception nets run on the same engine. **Camera detection and segmentation networks execute on the NVP alongside the radar work, so one engine time-multiplexes across modalities instead of vision and radar living on separate chips.
5. **Fusion and planning run on the CPUs. **The A78AE cluster fuses the radar point cloud with camera perception and plans the path, under the supervision of the lockstep R52 safety pairs.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the per-sensor-processor wall: radar used to be processed at the edge, inside each radar module's own DSP, and camera perception on separate chips — centralizing both on one NVP/GVP complex removes the chip-to-chip fusion hop and the duplicated processors, which is the whole point of the domain-controller bet. Creates a scheduling wall in its place: a single engine must time-multiplex up to 20 camera streams plus radar, so the compiler's schedule and the engine's utilization set the real throughput — and the headline 500 eTOPS is an equivalent figure, sparsity-assisted, so dense-network throughput is lower than the headline. The engine is also a compile target: networks must be compiled to CVflow, so portability is traded away for efficiency.

**Governing numbers.** NVP up to 500 eTOPS at 8-bit precision, 1,000 eTOPS at 4-bit (EE Times reporting Ambarella); 42× the AI performance of Ambarella's prior automotive family; CV3-High about 50 W (EE Times). Oculii centralized 4D imaging radar: 0.5-degree angular resolution, a dense point cloud of tens of thousands of points per frame, detection range over 500 metres, up to 100× the performance of traditional edge radar processors (Ambarella via All About Circuits). The GVP is floating-point; no TOPS figure is published for it.

**Primary source.** Ambarella, 'Ambarella Launches AI Domain Controller SoC Family for Single-Chip Multi-Sensor Perception, Fusion and Path Planning in ADAS to L4 Autonomous Vehicles' (Jan 4, 2022, ambarella.com) — next-generation CVflow debut, NVP up to 500 eTOPS, GVP offload role, Oculii radar on the NVP, 42× AI and 30× CPU generational claims; EE Times, 'Ambarella Targets AV Domain Controllers with Next-Gen AI Engine' — 500 eTOPS 8-bit / 1,000 eTOPS 4-bit, CV3-High about 50 W; All About Circuits, 'Ambarella Disrupts 4D Imaging Automotive Radar with Centralized Approach' — centralized 4D imaging radar, 0.5-degree resolution, tens of thousands of points per frame, over 500 m range, up to 100× vs edge radar processors.

#### Down to the primitives: The CVflow NVP + GVP — one vector engine for camera nets and radar

The NVP and GVP run the published five-step flow — raw radar chirp ingest, GVP floating-point conditioning, Oculii adaptive algorithms on the NVP, perception nets time-multiplexed on the same engine, fusion and planning on the CPUs — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (radar chirp ingest, camera-frame ingest from the ISP, NVP-to-GVP handoff, compiled-graph task queue)** — The engine ingests two very different streams — raw radar chirp data from the front-ends and conditioned camera frames from the ISP — and the NVP and GVP hand work back and forth as the pipeline moves from conditioning to perception, so each boundary is a FIFO decoupling a producer from a consumer that runs at a different rate. The compiled CVflow graphs the NVP executes are themselves a queue of tasks the compiler scheduled: one engine time-multiplexes up to 20 camera streams plus radar, so the next graph task waits in a queue while the current one runs. The queue depths, the ingest widths and the task-queue depth are not published.
- **SRAM bank / register file (NVP weight and activation working store; GVP vector register file)** — A neural engine holds the weights and activations of the layer it is currently executing on chip — the NVP working store — and a floating-point vector engine holds its vector operands in a vector register file. Both are SRAM banks or register files: the weights arrive from DRAM, the activations are produced and consumed layer by layer, and the GVP range and Doppler operands sit in vector registers while the FP lanes work them. Their capacities, banking, port counts and widths are not published.
- **Multiplier array (MAC array for convolution and matrix work on the NVP; FP multiply-add lanes on the GVP)** — Convolution and matrix multiplication are multiply-accumulate work, so the NVP core is a multiplier array: each multiply-accumulate unit takes a weight and an activation and produces a partial product, and the array works many of them in parallel across a layer. The GVP classical radar work is floating-point multiply-add — range and Doppler processing over chirp samples — so its lanes are floating-point multiplier arrays of the same shape in a different number format. The array dimensions, the lane count, the operand widths and the accumulation precision are not published. Standard construction for the multiplier array itself; the NVP/GVP split of the work is a published fact.
- **Adder tree (partial-product accumulation on the NVP; range and Doppler accumulation on the GVP)** — A multiplier array produces partial products that must be summed before the result is usable — an adder tree reduces many partial products to one sum per output, and the same tree shape accumulates the range and Doppler sums in the GVP radar conditioning. The tree depth, the adder widths and the number of partial products reduced per cycle are not published. Standard construction for the adder tree; the convolution and matrix role on the NVP and the range and Doppler role on the GVP follow from the published split.
- **Comparator (activation thresholding; sparsity gating)** — Neural inference thresholds activations — a comparator deciding whether a value passes the activation function or is zero — and the headline 500 eTOPS figure is sparsity-assisted, so a zero-skip role for the comparator (skipping multiply-accumulates whose operand is zero) is the standard construction for how a sparsity-assisted engine reaches its headline figure. That zero-skip role is standard construction, NOT a published CV3 fact: Ambarella publishes no sparsity mechanism, no sparsity ratio and no dense-network throughput for the NVP. The comparator thresholds and the gating policy are not published.
- **Barrel shifter (fixed-point scaling in radar signal processing; FP exponent alignment in the GVP)** — Fixed-point radar processing rescales values as they move between stages — a barrel shifter moving a value by a variable number of bits in one cycle — and floating-point addition aligns exponents before the mantissas can be added, which is also a shift. Both roles are standard construction for the arithmetic the published pipeline requires: the GVP range and Doppler work is floating-point and the radar chain is fixed-point in places, but Ambarella publishes no datapath widths, no shift amounts and no rounding policy. Standard construction; the pipeline stages are published facts.
- **Priority encoder / arbiter (NVP, GVP and CPUs sharing memory bandwidth; scheduler picking the next compiled graph task)** — One engine time-multiplexes up to 20 camera streams plus radar, and the NVP, GVP, ISP and A78AE cluster all share one memory system, so something must decide who gets the memory next and which compiled graph task runs next — a priority encoder or arbiter picking the highest-priority requester or the next scheduled task. The arbitration policy, the requester count and the scheduler priority scheme are not published. Standard construction for the arbiter; the time-multiplexing and the shared memory system are published facts.
- **FSM / controller (CVflow compiler-scheduled execution sequencer; radar processing state machine)** — The NVP executes compiled CVflow graphs, so a sequencer steps the engine through the compiled schedule — load weights, run a layer, write activations, move to the next layer — and the radar chain steps through its own states from chirp ingest to point-cloud output. That sequencer is a finite-state machine or controller. Its state count, the schedule format and the stage timing are not published. The compiled-graph execution model is a published fact; the sequencer construction is standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (between NVP stages; GVP vector pipeline stages)** — Work is latched between the NVP stages — ingest, multiply-accumulate, activation, write-back — and between the GVP vector pipeline stages, so the engine sustains its throughput instead of stalling between stages. The stage count, the latch widths and the per-stage latencies are not published.
- **Counter (frame and stream sequencing, radar chirp counting)** — The engine must know which camera stream a frame belongs to, which chirp of a radar frame is being processed and where it is in a compiled graph — counters sequencing frames, streams, chirps and graph steps. The counter widths and the sequencing policy are not published.
- **Mux / demux (camera-net vs radar-perception mode select on the shared NVP; NVP/GVP input select)** — One NVP runs both camera networks and Oculii radar perception, so the engine input is a mux selecting between the camera path and the radar path for each scheduled task, and the GVP input is a mux selecting between classical vision work and radar conditioning. The mux radix and the mode-selection logic are not published. The shared-engine, dual-modality role is a published fact; the mux construction is standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (radar front-end clock domain vs SoC domain; ISP-to-NVP handoff)** — Radar front-ends and the ISP run in their own clock domains, and the CVflow engine in its own, so every chirp sample and every camera frame crossing into the NVP must cross a clock-domain boundary — a synchronizer, built in standard construction from two-flop synchronizers or an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers. The domain count, the synchronizer depth and the clock frequencies are not published. Standard construction; the multi-source ingest is a published fact.
- **Credit counter (shared DRAM bandwidth budgeting between NVP, GVP, ISP and CPUs)** — The NVP, GVP, ISP and the A78AE cluster all draw on one DRAM, and the Level-2 bottleneck is exactly that shared bandwidth — 12 high-resolution streams plus radar at frame rate — so the memory system must budget bandwidth between requesters, and a credit counter tracking outstanding requests and throttling a requester when its budget is exhausted is the standard construction for that budgeting. The credit budget, the throttling policy and the requester weights are not published. Standard construction; the shared-bandwidth bottleneck is a published Level-2 fact.
