**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Ambarella publishes no CVflow block diagram — no MAC-array dimensions, no vector width, no SRAM sizes, no queue depths, no per-stage latencies — so the primitives below are mapped from the published NVP/GVP split and the five-step pipeline the launch material names, not from a die diagram. The 500 eTOPS 8-bit and 1,000 eTOPS 4-bit figures are already recorded at Level 2; no new chip-specific number is claimed here. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Inside the signature block: The next-generation ISP — twelve cameras, one pipe

**Inside it.** Ambarella's heritage block, scaled to a domain controller: one ISP ingesting up to 12 physical cameras — or 20 virtual cameras — simultaneously, so a single CV3 processes the entire sensor suite. The launch release's typical L2+ fit is 10 cameras, five radar modules and numerous ultrasonic sensors. Beside the ISP sit higher-performance stereo and dense optical-flow engines that compute depth and motion in hardware — geometry the neural nets would otherwise spend their budget re-deriving. The ISP feeds perception-grade frames directly to the NVP; the encoder records the surround streams for logging and the automotive GPU renders the 3D surround view. Ambarella publishes no ISP block diagram, no per-camera line buffers, no queue depths and no HDR merge stage counts, so the stage order below is the pipeline the launch material names plus the ISP-mandated order, not a die photograph.

**Trace — one unit of work: one surround-camera frame through the next-generation ISP.**
1. **Twelve sensors stream RAW. **Up to 12 physical cameras feed the ISP at the same time — 20 virtual cameras when streams are split or merged — so the whole surround suite arrives in one clock domain.
2. **HDR merge and correction condition each frame. **The ISP merges exposures and corrects each frame, producing perception-grade frames at line rate for the machine-vision stack as well as for viewing.
3. **Stereo and optical flow compute geometry. **The stereo engine derives depth from camera pairs and the dense optical-flow engine derives per-pixel motion, both in dedicated hardware beside the ISP.
4. **Perception-grade frames reach the NVP. **Conditioned frames, depth and motion flow to the CVflow engine, where detection and segmentation networks run on them.
5. **Recording and viewing split off. **The encoder records the surround streams for logging while the GPU renders the 3D surround view from the same frames.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the sensor-count bottleneck: previously each camera needed its own ISP channel or its own chip, and fusion had to reconcile unsynchronized streams — one ISP ingesting the whole suite means fusion sees synchronized frames from one clock domain. Creates a bandwidth bottleneck in its place: 12 high-resolution streams plus radar must cross the memory system and the ISP-to-NVP handoff at frame rate, so the memory controller and the NVP's ingest rate set the ceiling on how many streams can actually run at full resolution. And the ISP's HDR, stereo and optical-flow stages are fixed-function at tape-out, so a new sensor mode waits for new silicon.

**Governing numbers.** Up to 12 physical or 20 virtual cameras simultaneously; typical L2+ deployment 10 cameras, five radar modules and numerous ultrasonic sensors. CV3-AD685, the family's first production version (Jan 2023): 12 Cortex-A78AE cores plus 3 dual-core lockstep Cortex-R52 pairs, Samsung 5 nm, ASIL-B at chip level with an ASIL-D safety island (verified at launch).

**Primary source.** Ambarella, CV3 launch release (Jan 4, 2022, ambarella.com) — ISP camera counts, typical L2+ sensor suite, stereo and dense optical-flow engines; Ambarella, CV3-AD685 announcement (Jan 5, 2023), via Electronic Specifier — 12 Cortex-A78AE, 3 dual-core lockstep Cortex-R52 pairs, ASIL-B chip level with ASIL-D safety island (recorded at launch).

#### Down to the primitives: The next-generation ISP — twelve cameras, one pipe

The ISP runs the published five-step pipeline — twelve sensors streaming RAW, HDR merge and correction, stereo and dense optical flow computing geometry, perception-grade frames to the NVP, recording and viewing splitting off — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (per-camera line ingest, frame output to the NVP, encoder and GPU split-off)** — Twelve sensors stream RAW into one ISP at the same time, so each camera's lines arrive through a FIFO decoupling the sensor's line rate from the ISP processing rate; conditioned frames leave through a FIFO to the NVP, and the same frames split off through FIFOs to the encoder for recording and to the GPU for the 3D surround view. The queue depths, the line widths and the per-camera buffering are not published.
- **SRAM bank / line buffers (HDR merge working store, stereo disparity window, optical-flow neighbourhood)** — HDR merge must hold the exposures of one line while it combines them, stereo matching must hold a window of pixels from both cameras of a pair while it searches for correspondence, and dense optical flow must hold a neighbourhood of pixels while it estimates motion — each is a working store built from SRAM banks or line buffers, holding a line or a window, not a frame. The line-buffer depths, the window sizes, the banking and the port counts are not published.
- **Adder tree + comparator (HDR exposure merge weighting, stereo SAD matching, optical-flow block matching)** — HDR merge weights and sums exposures, stereo matching scores candidate disparities by a sum of absolute differences, and optical-flow block matching scores candidate motion vectors the same way — each is an adder tree summing per-pixel differences, with a comparator keeping the lowest-cost candidate as the search proceeds. The candidate sets, the search ranges, the block sizes and the SAD datapath widths are not published. Standard construction for the SAD arithmetic; the HDR, stereo and optical-flow stages are published facts.
- **Multiplier array (demosaic interpolation weights, colour-correction matrix, lens shading)** — Demosaic reconstructs a full-colour pixel from its neighbours by weighted interpolation, colour correction multiplies each pixel by a 3x3 matrix, and lens shading multiplies each pixel by a position-dependent gain — each is a weighted sum, so a multiplier array feeding an adder tree. The multiplier count, the interpolation kernel and the matrix coefficients are not published. Standard construction for the arithmetic; the stages are ISP-mandated parts of the pipeline the launch material names.
- **Barrel shifter (bit-depth scaling, HDR tone-mapping shifts, pixel packing)** — Sensor data arrives at one bit depth and leaves at another, HDR tone mapping rescales merged exposures into the output range, and pixels are packed into memory words — each is a shift by a variable amount, a barrel-shifter operation. The shift widths, the tone-mapping curve and the packing format are not published. Standard construction for the shifter; the HDR and correction stages are published facts.
- **Mux / demux (12 physical vs 20 virtual camera stream select; HDR exposure-path select)** — One ISP ingests 12 physical cameras or 20 virtual cameras, so the input is a mux selecting which sensor stream feeds which pipeline lane, and the HDR path is a mux selecting between exposure streams for the merge. The mux radix and the stream-selection logic are not published. The 12/20 camera counts are already recorded at Level 2; the mux construction is standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (ISP pipeline sequencer per camera; exposure and white-balance control loop)** — The ISP sequencer steps each camera's frames through RAW ingest, HDR merge, demosaic and correction in order, and the 3A control loop — auto-exposure and auto-white-balance — reads frame statistics and adjusts the sensor settings for the next frame. Both are finite-state machines or controllers. Their state counts, the stage timing and the control-loop policy are not published.
- **Pipeline registers (between ISP stages: RAW, HDR merge, demosaic, correction)** — Work is latched between the ISP stages — RAW ingest, HDR merge, demosaic, correction — so the pipeline sustains line rate across up to 12 simultaneous streams instead of stalling between stages. The stage count, the latch widths and the per-stage latencies are not published.
- **Counter (line and frame counters per camera, exposure timing)** — The ISP must know which line and which frame of which camera it is processing, and how long each exposure ran — line and frame counters per camera, and exposure-timing counters feeding the 3A loop. The counter widths and the sequencing policy are not published.
- **Synchronizer (sensor clock domains vs ISP domain)** — Twelve sensors each run in their own clock domain and the ISP in its own, so every line crossing from a sensor into the ISP crosses a clock-domain boundary — a synchronizer, built in standard construction from two-flop synchronizers or an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers. The Level-2 bottleneck notes that fusion sees synchronized frames from one clock domain; the synchronizer role at the sensor/ISP boundary is standard construction, not a published ISP fact. The domain count, the synchronizer depth and the clock frequencies are not published.
- **Credit counter / arbiter (12 streams sharing DRAM bandwidth)** — Twelve high-resolution streams plus radar must cross the memory system at frame rate, so the ISP DRAM traffic must be budgeted against the NVP, GVP and CPUs — a credit counter tracking outstanding requests and an arbiter picking which camera stream's request goes next when several are ready. The credit budget, the arbitration policy and the requester weights are not published. Standard construction; the shared-bandwidth bottleneck is a published Level-2 fact.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Ambarella publishes no ISP block diagram, no per-camera line buffers, no queue depths and no HDR merge stage counts, so the primitives below are mapped from the published pipeline stages and the ISP-mandated order, not from a die diagram. The 12 physical / 20 virtual camera counts are already recorded at Level 2; no new chip-specific number is claimed here. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Down to the gates: The CVflow NVP + GVP — one vector engine for camera nets and radar

Ambarella publishes no gate-level structure for CVflow — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the NVP, the GVP or the ISP. The deepest published description is the January 4, 2022 CV3 launch release, which names the NVP/GVP split, the compiled-graph execution model and the Oculii radar role, plus the January 5, 2023 CV3-AD685 announcement. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors using the primer's bottom layer — the universal gates, the latch and the flip-flop, the 6T SRAM cell, the CAM cell and the full adder — and every gate or transistor figure is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, not a claim about Ambarella's actual netlist. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, no total is claimed.

- **FIFO / queue (radar chirp ingest, camera-frame ingest from the ISP, NVP-to-GVP handoff, compiled-graph task queue)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each, incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The radar chirp ingest, the camera-frame ingest from the ISP, the NVP-to-GVP handoff and the compiled-graph task queue are FIFOs of this form, decoupling producers from consumers that run at different rates — but their depths and widths are not published, so the pointer widths — and therefore the counter and comparator totals — are not claimed. The published part is the decoupling: raw chirp data arrives from the front-ends, frames arrive from the ISP, and one engine time-multiplexes up to 20 camera streams plus radar. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank / register file (NVP weight and activation working store; GVP vector register file)** — The working store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers; the GVP vector register file is the same storage built as a multi-ported register file of D flip-flops, about 20–28 transistors per bit per port pair, so a register file costs far more per bit than the SRAM bank and is used where the GVP needs several operands at once. The NVP working store holds the weights and activations of the layer currently executing; the GVP register file holds the vector operands of the range and Doppler work — but their capacities, banking, port counts and widths are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (MAC array for convolution and matrix work on the NVP; FP multiply-add lanes on the GVP)** — A multiplier array is partial-product generation plus an adder tree: each multiply-accumulate unit generates partial products with AND gates — one AND gate per bit-pair — and reduces them through full adders, 28 transistors each in the standard-cell form, two half adders of XOR, AND and OR gates. The NVP convolution and matrix work is this array in integer form at 8-bit and 4-bit precision — the published 500 eTOPS 8-bit and 1,000 eTOPS 4-bit figures already recorded at Level 2 — and the GVP floating-point multiply-add lanes are the same array with an exponent adder, a mantissa multiplier and a normalizer wrapped around it. The array dimensions, the lane count, the operand widths and the accumulation precision are not published, so no multiplier total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (partial-product accumulation on the NVP; range and Doppler accumulation on the GVP)** — An adder tree is full adders arranged in a binary reduction: partial products reduce one stage per halving of their count, each full adder two half adders — 2 XOR, 2 AND and 1 OR gates, about 28 transistors in a standard cell. The NVP partial-product accumulation and the GVP range and Doppler accumulation are adder trees of this form, one sum per output per cycle — but the tree depth, the adder widths and the number of partial products reduced per cycle are not published, so no adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (activation thresholding; sparsity gating)** — A comparator is an XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree: equal is all XOR outputs zero, greater-than is a priority chain over the most-significant differing bit. Neural inference thresholds activations through comparators of this form, and the sparsity-assisted headline figure implies a zero-skip role — a comparator per operand deciding whether a multiply-accumulate is skipped when the operand is zero — but that zero-skip role is the textbook construction, NOT a published CV3 fact: Ambarella publishes no sparsity mechanism, no sparsity ratio and no dense-network throughput for the NVP. The comparator thresholds and the gating policy are not published, so no comparator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (fixed-point scaling in radar signal processing; FP exponent alignment in the GVP)** — A barrel shifter is a mux tree: shifting an N-bit value by a variable amount takes log2(N) stages of 2:1 muxes, each mux a transmission-gate pair (2 transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree. Fixed-point radar processing rescales values between stages through shifters of this form, and floating-point addition aligns exponents before the mantissas can be added — the alignment shift is a barrel shifter, and the exponent difference is computed by a subtractor of full adders. Ambarella publishes no datapath widths, no shift amounts and no rounding policy, so no shifter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Priority encoder / arbiter (NVP, GVP and CPUs sharing memory bandwidth; scheduler picking the next compiled graph task)** — A priority encoder is a tree of OR gates with a priority chain: N request lines reduce to a grant index naming the highest-priority active request, with a round-robin variant adding a rotating priority register of D flip-flops. One engine time-multiplexes up to 20 camera streams plus radar, and the NVP, GVP, ISP and A78AE cluster share one memory system, so an arbiter of this form picks which requester gets the memory next and which compiled graph task runs next — but the arbitration policy, the requester count and the scheduler priority scheme are not published, so no encoder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (CVflow compiler-scheduled execution sequencer; radar processing state machine)** — A finite-state machine is state bits plus next-state logic plus output logic: the state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and the next-state and output logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the current state and the inputs. The CVflow execution sequencer steps the engine through the compiled schedule — load weights, run a layer, write activations, move to the next layer — and the radar chain steps through its own states from chirp ingest to point-cloud output; both are state machines of this form. The state count, the schedule format and the stage timing are not published, so no state-bit total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (between NVP stages; GVP vector pipeline stages)** — A pipeline register is one D flip-flop per bit — about 20–28 transistors each, two cross-coupled latch stages — latched between stages so the next stage can start while the current stage's result is held. Work is latched between the NVP stages — ingest, multiply-accumulate, activation, write-back — and between the GVP vector pipeline stages, so the engine sustains throughput instead of stalling between stages — but the stage count, the latch widths and the per-stage latencies are not published, so no register total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (frame and stream sequencing, radar chirp counting)** — A counter is N D flip-flops plus N full adders in a ripple or look-ahead chain, incrementing on each clock, with a comparator resetting it at the terminal count. The engine sequences frames, streams, chirps and graph steps with counters of this form: 20 camera streams need a 5-bit stream counter (2 to the power 5 is 32, which covers 20) and 12 physical cameras need a 4-bit camera counter (2 to the power 4 is 16, which covers 12) — arithmetic from the published stream counts — a 5-bit counter being 5 D flip-flops (100–140 transistors) plus 5 full adders (140 transistors), a 4-bit counter 4 D flip-flops (80–112 transistors) plus 4 full adders (112 transistors). The counter widths beyond the published counts and the sequencing policy are not published. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (camera-net vs radar-perception mode select on the shared NVP; NVP/GVP input select)** — A mux is a transmission-gate tree or a NAND/NOR tree: a 2:1 mux is 2 transistors per input leg as transmission gates, and an N:1 mux is N minus 1 2:1 muxes arranged as a tree, selected by a decoder. One NVP runs both camera networks and Oculii radar perception, so the engine input is a mux selecting between the camera path and the radar path for each scheduled task, and the GVP input is a mux selecting between classical vision work and radar conditioning — but the mux radix and the mode-selection logic are not published, so no mux total is claimed. The shared-engine, dual-modality role is a published fact; the mux itself is the textbook construction. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (radar front-end clock domain vs SoC domain; ISP-to-NVP handoff)** — A synchronizer is two D flip-flops in series — about 20–28 transistors each — the first sampling the incoming signal in the new clock domain and the second re-sampling it a cycle later so metastability resolves before the value is used; a multi-bit crossing is an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers, the pointers changing one bit at a time so a sampled pointer is never more than one count stale. Radar front-ends and the ISP run in their own clock domains and the CVflow engine in its own, so every chirp sample and every camera frame crossing into the NVP passes through synchronizers of this form. The domain count, the synchronizer depth and the clock frequencies are not published, so no synchronizer total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (shared DRAM bandwidth budgeting between NVP, GVP, ISP and CPUs)** — A credit counter is a down-counter of D flip-flops and full adders with a comparator: it starts at the budget, decrements on each issued request and increments on each returned credit, and a comparator blocks new requests when the count reaches zero. The NVP, GVP, ISP and the A78AE cluster all draw on one DRAM, and the Level-2 bottleneck is exactly that shared bandwidth — 12 high-resolution streams plus radar at frame rate — so the memory system budgets bandwidth between requesters with credit counters of this form. The credit budget, the throttling policy and the requester weights are not published, so no counter total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Ambarella publishes the CVflow engine at the split level only — NVP for neural and radar-perception work, GVP for floating-point classical vision and radar work, compiled CVflow graphs as the execution model (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the engine appears in any Ambarella source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Ambarella's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable).

### Google Tensor G3 ISP + HDR+ Pipeline

**Specs (wiki card).** Tensor G3 · computational photography pipeline

**Building blocks.**
- **Custom ISP front-end** — The RAW pipeline on Tensor G3 — black level, shading, demosaic and the statistics feeding 3A — whose output the rest of the Pixel stack treats as ground truth. (Google publishes no ISP block diagram; the stages named here are the ones its research and product material describe.)
- **HDR+ burst pipeline ★** — The defining algorithm-as-architecture: every shutter press captures a burst of short, underexposed RAW frames; the pipeline aligns them (FFT/gradient-based alignment in Google's published HDR+ paper) and merges in the temporal domain — trading time for dynamic range and noise, so the sensor's limits stop being the image's limits
- **Custom DSP ('Callisto' in reporting)** — A dedicated image DSP beside the ISP handling depth and imaging ML stages Google moved off the GPU — Photo Unblur and depth mapping among them (codename and assignment are secondary reporting; Google has not published the block)
- **Edge TPU (in-SoC)** — The Tensor G3's TPU runs the learned stages: Night Sight's merge/tone decisions, Magic Eraser segmentation, Best Take face selection — models scheduled as pipeline stages, not app features
- **Video Boost / Night Sight Video path** — Video extends the same bargain off-device: frames are captured on-phone and finished with data-centre HDR+ processing — the pipeline's last stage is literally in the cloud, an architectural admission about phone thermals

**The piece that makes it special.** The burst is the sensor. HDR+ inverted ISP design: instead of one perfectly exposed frame processed perfectly, capture many imperfect frames and let alignment + merge statistics do what optics can't. Everything in the Tensor imaging stack — the DSP, the TPU stages, even a cloud finishing step — exists to serve that one decision, which is why Pixel image quality tracks Google's algorithms more than its silicon generations.

**How work flows.** Burst capture: The shutter fires a rapid RAW burst, each frame deliberately underexposed to protect highlights. Align: Frames are aligned to a reference frame despite hand shake and subject motion. Merge: Aligned frames merge in the temporal domain — noise averages down, dynamic range stacks up. Learned stages run: TPU/DSP stages apply Night Sight tone decisions, unblur and segmentation features. Finish: Tone-mapped output exits — or, for Video Boost, uploads for cloud finishing and returns.

**Trade-off accepted.** Latency and light. Burst merging needs several frames of still-ish scene; fast motion ghosts, and the best video path leaves the device entirely. And disclosure: Google publishes the HDR+ algorithm (its 2016 paper) but not the Tensor G3 ISP's hardware organisation — block-level claims beyond the paper's stages would be invention, so this entry stays at the pipeline level Google documents.

**Fact check.**

#### Inside the signature block: The HDR+ burst pipeline — align and merge in the frequency domain

**Inside it.** The pipeline the 2016 paper publishes has five stages, and Google publishes no Tensor G3 ISP hardware diagram — no block diagram, no queue depths, no stage counts, no per-stage latencies — so these are the paper's stages, not a die photograph. (1) Burst capture: the hardware ISP's viewfinder (1.6 Mpix at 15–30 fps) suspends at the shutter press and a burst of up to 8 deliberately underexposed Bayer RAW frames is captured at up to 30 fps and held in main memory. (2) Reference selection: lucky imaging — the sharpest of the first 3 frames, picked by a gradient metric on the green channel of the RAW input, so perceived shutter lag stays low. (3) Alignment: coarse-to-fine on four-level Gaussian pyramids of the RAW downsampled to gray (2×2 Bayer blocks averaged, so alignment runs on 3 Mpix gray instead of 12 Mpix RAW), FFT-accelerated L2 matching at coarse scales with a subpixel fit, pixel-level L1 matching at the finest scale, and multi-hypothesis upsampling when a coarse alignment straddles a motion boundary. (4) Merge: a pairwise frequency-domain Wiener temporal filter on 16×16 Bayer tiles (32×32 for very dark scenes), tiles overlapped by half, each reference tile merged with one tile from each alternate frame, the per-frequency contribution set by a noise model whose variance is Ax + B for signal x — the Poisson photon-counting model, with A and B set by the shot's gain. (5) Finish: exposure-fusion tone mapping, demosaic, chroma denoise (an approximate bilateral filter, a sparse 3×3 tap kernel in two YUV passes), colour correction with a 3×3 matrix supplied by the ISP, dehaze and global tone adjustment — a single 8-bit 12 Mpix photograph out.

**Trace — one unit of work: one shutter press in daylight HDR.**
1. **Viewfinder running. **The hardware ISP shows a 1.6 Mpix preview at 15–30 fps while the photographer frames the shot.
2. **Shutter: burst captured. **The viewfinder suspends and a burst of up to 8 constant-exposure, deliberately underexposed Bayer RAW frames is captured at up to 30 fps and stored temporarily in main memory.
3. **Reference picked. **The sharpest of the first 3 frames is chosen by a green-channel gradient metric — lucky imaging — so the composition and the sharpest frame are the same frame.
4. **Tiles aligned. **Each alternate frame is aligned to the reference tile by tile on the four-level Gaussian pyramid, FFT-accelerated at coarse scales and pixel-level at the finest, with displacements kept to multiples of 2 pixels so displaced Bayer samples keep coincident colours.
5. **Tiles merged in the frequency domain. **Each 16×16 reference tile is merged with its aligned alternate tiles by the pairwise Wiener filter: frequency content that differs from the reference by no more than the modelled noise is kept, and content that cannot be ascribed to noise falls back to the reference — so a failed alignment costs noise, not a ghost.
6. **Finished and stored. **Exposure-fusion tone mapping, demosaic, chroma denoise and sharpen produce a single 8-bit 12 Mpix photograph in about 4 seconds on device — on the paper's Snapdragon 810 a low-light shot breaks down as 1 s to capture, 500 ms to align, 1,200 ms to merge and 1,600 ms to finish.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the photon bottleneck: a phone's small aperture and small pixels cap the light each frame can gather, so HDR+ trades time (a burst) and compute for light — noise averages down across frames and dynamic range stacks up, without a bigger lens or sensor. Creates a compute-and-robustness bottleneck in its place: as much as 104 Mpix must be stored and processed per output photograph (8 frames × 13 Mpix), the whole merge has to finish on-device in about 4 seconds, and alignment can fail on occlusions, non-rigid motion or lighting changes — the merge is deliberately conservative, falling back to the reference tile, so a failure degrades to noise rather than a ghost. And the reference frame's own motion blur is never removed — the paper does no deblurring — so lucky imaging is the only defence against a blurred reference.

**Governing numbers.** Burst of up to 8 frames; 12–13 Mpix sensors, as much as 104 Mpix stored and processed per output photograph. Bayer RAW input at full sensor resolution at up to 30 fps; viewfinder 1.6 Mpix at 15–30 fps. Alignment runs at 24 ms per Mpix; four-level Gaussian pyramid; finest-level tiles 32×32 pixels with a maximum displacement of 64 pixels, the method supporting displacements up to 169 pixels. Merge tiles typically 16×16, 32×32 for very dark scenes, overlapped by half in each dimension. On a Snapdragon 810 the time to produce an output photograph ranges from 2.5 to 4 seconds depending on burst size — a low-light shot breaks down as 1 s capture, 500 ms alignment, 1,200 ms merge, 1,600 ms finish; a daylight shot as 100 ms capture, 250 ms alignment, 580 ms merge, 1,600 ms finish. The paper's own Halide FFT runs five times faster than FFTW on an ARM phone for the small DFTs in the pipeline.

**Primary source.** Hasinoff et al., 'Burst photography for high dynamic range and low-light imaging on mobile cameras', SIGGRAPH Asia 2016 (ACM Transactions on Graphics 35(6), Article 192) — constant-exposure underexposed burst, Bayer RAW start, FFT-based alignment, hybrid 2D/3D Wiener merge, 4 seconds on device for a 12 Mpix image, up to 8 frames, 104 Mpix per photograph, Snapdragon 810 timing breakdown, Halide FFT 5× FFTW; Google Research. Google publishes no Tensor G3 ISP block diagram, queue depths or per-stage latencies, so the stages above are the paper's, not a die photograph.

#### Down to the primitives: The HDR+ burst pipeline — align and merge in the frequency domain

The pipeline the 2016 HDR+ paper publishes has five stages — burst capture, reference selection, alignment, merge and finish — and each stage is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (burst frame ingest staging, viewfinder frame queue, tile queues between alignment and merge)** — The burst is stored temporarily in main memory, so the on-chip FIFO is the ingest staging between the sensor and DRAM: up to 8 Bayer RAW frames arrive at up to 30 fps and are staged into the frame store, the 1.6 Mpix viewfinder stream runs through its own frame queue at 15-30 fps, and tiles queue between the alignment stages and the merge so a slow merge does not stall the aligner. The FIFO depths and the ingest widths are not published.
- **SRAM bank / register file (tile working store; Gaussian pyramid levels)** — The merge holds one reference tile and its aligned alternate tiles while the Wiener filter runs — 16x16 tiles, 32x32 for very dark scenes — and the alignment holds the four Gaussian pyramid levels, the gray base at 3 Mpix quartering per level, so by arithmetic from the published figures the levels hold 3 Mpix, 750K, 187.5K and about 47K pixels. That pixel-count arithmetic is derived from the published 3 Mpix base, not a published buffer size. The tile-buffer sizes, the banking and the port counts are not published.
- **Multiplier array (FFT butterfly complex multiplies; Wiener per-frequency weighting; 3x3 colour-correction matrix; demosaic interpolation weights)** — The FFT-accelerated alignment is butterfly work — each butterfly is a complex multiply — the Wiener merge weights each frequency by a per-frequency factor, the finish multiplies each pixel by the ISP-supplied 3x3 colour-correction matrix, and demosaic interpolates each missing colour by weighted neighbours. Each is a multiplier array feeding an adder tree. The array dimensions, the lane count and the operand widths are not published. Standard construction for the multiplier array; the FFT, Wiener, matrix and demosaic stages are published facts.
- **Adder tree (FFT butterfly additions; 2x2 Bayer averaging; Wiener accumulation across alternate frames; bilateral 3x3 tap sums)** — Each FFT butterfly adds as well as multiplies, the gray pyramid is built by averaging 2x2 Bayer blocks, the Wiener merge accumulates the per-frequency contributions across the alternate frames, and the chroma denoise sums a sparse 3x3 tap kernel in two YUV passes. Each is an adder tree reducing many partial sums to one result per output. The tree depth, the adder widths and the number of terms reduced per cycle are not published. Standard construction for the adder tree; the stages are published facts.
- **Comparator (reference-frame sharpness pick; Wiener keep-or-fall-back decision; L1 best-match selection)** — Reference selection picks the sharpest of the first 3 frames by a gradient metric on the green channel — a comparator deciding which frame's metric is highest — the Wiener merge keeps frequency content that differs from the reference by no more than the modelled noise and falls back to the reference otherwise, and the finest-level L1 matching keeps the lowest-cost displacement. The metric thresholds, the noise-model constants A and B per shot and the L1 search policy are set by the shot's gain or are not published.
- **Barrel shifter (pyramid downsample by 2x per level; displacement multiples of 2 pixels; bit-depth scaling to 8-bit output)** — Each pyramid level is the level above downsampled by 2x in each dimension, alignment displacements are kept to multiples of 2 pixels so displaced Bayer samples keep coincident colours, and the finish scales the RAW bit depth down to the 8-bit output photograph — each is a shift by a variable amount, a barrel-shifter operation. The shift widths and the scaling policy are not published. Standard construction for the shifter; the downsample factor, the displacement rule and the 8-bit output are published facts.
- **Mux / demux (reference vs alternate frame select; Bayer colour-plane select; FFT coarse-scale vs L1 finest-scale path select)** — Each merge step selects between the reference tile and an alternate tile, the merge draws its tiles from the Bayer RAW colour planes so the colour-plane select is a mux, and the alignment selects between the FFT-accelerated L2 path at coarse scales and the pixel-level L1 path at the finest scale. The mux radix and the path-selection logic are not published. The reference-vs-alternate merge, the Bayer-plane tiles and the two matching paths are published facts; the mux construction is standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (pipeline sequencer capture to reference to align to merge to finish; coarse-to-fine level controller with multi-hypothesis upsampling state)** — The pipeline sequencer steps the burst through capture, reference selection, alignment, merge and finish in order, and the alignment controller steps the pyramid from coarse to fine, holding the multi-hypothesis upsampling state when a coarse alignment straddles a motion boundary. That sequencer is a finite-state machine or controller. Its state count, the stage timing and the upsampling policy are not published. The five-stage pipeline and the multi-hypothesis upsampling are published facts; the sequencer construction is standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (between alignment stages — pyramid, FFT, L1 match — and merge stages — tile fetch, Wiener weighting, write-back)** — Work is latched between the alignment stages — pyramid build, FFT matching, L1 matching — and between the merge stages — tile fetch, Wiener weighting, write-back — so the pipeline sustains its throughput instead of stalling between stages. The stage count, the latch widths and the per-stage latencies are not published.
- **Counter (frame counter; tile counter; pyramid level counter)** — The pipeline must know which frame of the burst it is merging, which tile of the frame it is working and which pyramid level it is aligning: a frame counter for up to 8 frames — a 3-bit counter, since 2 to the power 3 is 8 — a tile counter for the 16x16 tiles overlapped by half, step 8 pixels, so about 187,500 tile positions in a 12 Mpix frame, 12 Mpix divided by 64 square pixels per 8-pixel step, edge effects aside — an 18-bit counter, since 2 to the power 18 is 262,144 — and a pyramid level counter for the 4 levels — a 2-bit counter. All three widths are arithmetic derived from the published figures and labelled as such; the counter widths themselves are not published.
- **Synchronizer (sensor/ISP clock domain vs compute domain; viewfinder stream crossing)** — The sensor and the hardware ISP run in their own clock domain and the compute that aligns and merges in its own, so every burst frame crossing from the ISP into the merge pipeline crosses a clock-domain boundary, and the viewfinder stream crosses the same boundary — a synchronizer, built in standard construction from two-flop synchronizers or an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers. The domain count, the synchronizer depth and the clock frequencies are not published. Standard construction; the burst ingest and the viewfinder stream are published facts.
- **Priority encoder / arbiter (tile scheduler picking the next tile; DRAM arbiter between burst ingest, alignment reads, merge reads and writes and the viewfinder)** — Tiles must be scheduled in order across the merge, and the burst ingest, the alignment reads, the merge reads and writes and the viewfinder all share one main memory, so something must decide which tile runs next and which memory request goes next — a priority encoder or arbiter picking the highest-priority ready requester. The arbitration policy, the requester count and the scheduler priority scheme are not published. Standard construction for the arbiter; the shared main-memory frame store is a published fact.
- **Credit counter (DRAM bandwidth budgeting — as much as 104 Mpix per photograph moves through main memory)** — As much as 104 Mpix must be stored and processed per output photograph, so the memory system must budget DRAM bandwidth between burst ingest, alignment traffic and merge traffic, and a credit counter tracking outstanding requests and throttling a requester when its budget is exhausted is the standard construction for that budgeting. The credit budget, the throttling policy and the requester weights are not published. Standard construction; the 104 Mpix figure is a published Level-2 fact already recorded.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Google publishes no Tensor G3 ISP block diagram — no queue depths, no tile-buffer sizes, no FFT-array dimensions, no per-stage latencies — so the primitives below are mapped from the published five-stage pipeline of the 2016 HDR+ paper and the Tensor G3 product blog, not from a die diagram. The burst size, tile sizes, pyramid levels and timing figures are already recorded at Level 2; no new chip-specific number is claimed here. The only new numbers are arithmetic derived from those published figures and labelled as such. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Inside the signature block: Night Sight motion metering — and Video Boost, the pipeline's cloud stage

**Inside it.** The low-light extension of the same pipeline, published in the 2019 Night Sight paper, plus the Tensor G3 product blog's cloud stage. (1) Motion metering: before the shutter press, viewfinder frames measure scene and camera motion — the flow field's magnitude is estimated in 3 ms — and gyroscope-based stability analysis caps the exposure time; the meter then picks the per-frame exposure time and the frame count (6–13) that best trade noise against motion blur. (2) Motion-robust merge: the 2016 pairwise merge extended so each alternate frame contributes more in static regions and less where motion blur is possible. (3) Learned auto white balance: a learning-based colour-constancy model, trained for low light, whose gains are computed from the reference frame downsampled. (4) Illusionistic tone mapping: shadows brightened, blacks crushed, the scene kept reading as dark — detail the eye could not see, without the photograph pretending it was daylight. (5) Video Boost: Pixel 8 Pro's cloud stage — frames are captured on-phone and finished in Google's data centres, which apply the HDR+ processing (colour, lighting, stabilisation, graininess) and enable Night Sight Video; the finished video returns to the phone. The Tensor G3 blog confirms the chip's new ISP and Imaging DSP and next-gen TPU behind these stages, but gives no block diagram, so again the stages above are the published pipeline, not hardware internals.

**Trace — one unit of work: one Night Sight press at ~0.4 lux.**
1. **Motion metered before the press. **Viewfinder frames feed motion metering, which estimates the flow field's magnitude in 3 ms and, with gyroscope stability limits, sets the exposure ceiling for the burst.
2. **Schedule set. **The meter picks a longer exposure and more frames because scene motion is low — in the paper's 0.4 lux example, per-frame exposure extended from 0.14 s to 0.33 s and the burst from 6 to 13 frames.
3. **Burst captured. **The 6–13 frame burst is captured over 1–6 seconds after the shutter press, each frame at the metered exposure.
4. **Merged with motion-robust weighting. **Frames are aligned and merged with per-region weighting — static regions get the full temporal denoise, regions with possible motion blur get less, so moving subjects stay sharp.
5. **White balance and tone set. **The learned colour-constancy model sets white-balance gains from the downsampled reference, and illusionistic tone mapping brightens shadows while keeping the night dark.
6. **Finished — on device, or in the cloud. **The photograph is finished in under 2 seconds on the phone; for Video Boost, the frames upload to Google's data centres for HDR+ finishing and Night Sight Video, and the finished video returns.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the read-noise wall: at 0.3 lux the signal is so low that read noise dominates, so Night Sight trades capture time — up to 6 seconds — for light, the same bargain HDR+ makes in daylight, stretched further. Creates a time-and-motion bottleneck in its place: the whole capture-plus-processing budget is 8 seconds maximum, and any subject motion forces shorter exposures and fewer frames — the hardest scenes get the least light to work with. And for video the bargain leaves the device entirely: Video Boost's cloud round trip is the price of the best low-light video, and the phone's thermals are the reason the last stage lives in a data centre instead of on the SoC.

**Governing numbers.** Works in light as low as about 0.3 lux. Burst of 6–13 frames; total capture 1–6 seconds; processing under 2 seconds; motion metering estimates the flow field's magnitude in 3 ms; maximum total capture and processing time 8 seconds. Paper's 0.4 lux example: per-frame exposure 0.14 s extended to 0.33 s, 6 frames extended to 13. Tensor G3 (product blog): more than twice as many machine-learning models run on-device as on the first-generation Tensor (Pixel 6); on-device generative AI is 150 times more complex than the most complex model on Pixel 7.

**Primary source.** Liba et al., 'Handheld Mobile Photography in Very Low Light', SIGGRAPH Asia 2019 (ACM Transactions on Graphics 38(6), Article 164) — 0.3 lux floor, motion metering, 6–13 frame bursts, 1–6 s capture, under 2 s processing, 3 ms flow estimate, 8 s maximum, learned auto white balance, illusionistic tone mapping, launched November 2018 as Night Sight; Google, 'Google Tensor G3: Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro's AI-first processor' (The Keyword, Oct 4, 2023) — new ISP and Imaging DSP, next-gen TPU, more than twice as many on-device ML models as Tensor G1, generative AI 150× more complex than Pixel 7's most complex model, Live HDR; Google, 'Meet Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro' (The Keyword, Oct 5, 2023) — Video Boost pairs Tensor G3 with Google's data centres and enables Night Sight Video.

#### Down to the primitives: Night Sight motion metering — and Video Boost, the pipeline's cloud stage

The low-light extension the 2019 Night Sight paper publishes has four on-device stages — motion metering, motion-robust merge, learned auto white balance and illusionistic tone mapping — plus the Tensor G3 product blog's cloud stage, Video Boost, and each stage is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (viewfinder frame queue feeding motion metering; burst frame queue; Video Boost upload queue)** — Viewfinder frames queue into motion metering before the shutter press, the 6-13 frame burst queues into the merge over 1-6 seconds of capture, and Video Boost frames queue for upload while the finished video queues back down — each boundary is a FIFO decoupling a producer from a consumer that runs at a different rate. The queue depths, the ingest widths and the upload buffering are not published.
- **SRAM bank / register file (motion-metering flow-field working store; downsampled reference frame store for learned auto white balance; tone-mapping look-up tables)** — Motion metering holds the flow field while it estimates its magnitude in 3 ms, learned auto white balance holds the reference frame downsampled while the colour-constancy model reads it, and illusionistic tone mapping holds its tone curves as look-up tables — each is a working store built from SRAM banks or register files. Their capacities, banking, port counts and widths are not published.
- **Multiplier array (motion-estimation and optical-flow multiply-accumulates; learned auto-white-balance model multiply-accumulates; tone-curve application)** — Estimating the flow field is multiply-accumulate work over viewfinder frames, the learned colour-constancy model is multiply-accumulate work over the downsampled reference — a learned stage, and the entry's building blocks put the learned stages on the TPU — and applying a tone curve multiplies each pixel by its mapped value. Each is a multiplier array feeding an adder tree. The array dimensions, the lane count and the operand widths are not published. Standard construction for the multiplier array; the metering, the learned model and the tone mapping are published facts.
- **Adder tree (flow-field magnitude accumulation across the frame; per-region merge weight sums)** — The flow field's magnitude is accumulated across the frame to produce the single motion estimate the meter acts on, and the motion-robust merge sums the per-region merge weights across the burst — each is an adder tree reducing many per-pixel or per-region terms to one sum. The tree depth, the adder widths and the number of terms reduced per cycle are not published. Standard construction for the adder tree; the flow estimate and the per-region weighting are published facts.
- **Comparator (motion magnitude vs exposure ceiling; gyroscope stability limit; 8 s total-budget watchdog)** — The meter picks the per-frame exposure time and the frame count by comparing the estimated motion against thresholds, gyroscope-based stability analysis caps the exposure time, and the 8 s maximum total capture and processing time is a watchdog comparing elapsed time against the budget. The thresholds, the stability limits and the watchdog policy are not published.
- **Barrel shifter (reference-frame downsampling for auto white balance; exposure-time scaling)** — The learned auto white balance reads the reference frame downsampled, and the meter scales the per-frame exposure time between the 0.14 s and 0.33 s of the paper's 0.4 lux example — each is a shift by a variable amount, a barrel-shifter operation. The shift widths and the scaling policy are not published. Standard construction for the shifter; the downsampled reference and the exposure range are published facts.
- **Mux / demux (on-device finish vs cloud finish select — Video Boost; per-region merge weight select — static vs motion regions)** — A photograph finishes on device while a Video Boost clip finishes in the cloud, so the output path is a mux selecting between the on-device finish and the upload path, and the motion-robust merge selects per region between the full temporal-denoise weight for static regions and the reduced weight where motion blur is possible. The mux radix and the selection logic are not published. The on-device vs cloud finish and the per-region weighting are published facts; the mux construction is standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (Night Sight capture sequencer meter to schedule to capture to merge to finish; Video Boost upload and download state machine)** — The Night Sight sequencer steps the shot through motion metering, schedule selection, burst capture, motion-robust merge and finish in order, and the Video Boost path steps through upload, cloud processing and download — each is a finite-state machine or controller. Their state counts, the stage timing and the upload policy are not published. The capture sequence and the cloud stage are published facts; the sequencer construction is standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (between metering, capture, merge and finish stages)** — Work is latched between the metering, capture, merge and finish stages so the pipeline sustains its throughput instead of stalling between stages, and the Video Boost upload path latches frames between capture and upload. The stage count, the latch widths and the per-stage latencies are not published.
- **Counter (frame-count counter; exposure-time counter; 3 ms flow-estimate timing; 8 s total-budget counter)** — The meter must count the frames of the burst, time each exposure, time the 3 ms flow estimate and watch the 8 s total budget: a frame-count counter for 6-13 frames — a 4-bit counter, since 2 to the power 4 is 16, which covers 13 — an exposure-time counter for the metered per-frame exposure, a timing counter for the 3 ms flow estimate and a budget counter for the 8 s maximum. The counter widths are arithmetic derived from the published frame count and labelled as such; the timing-counter widths and the budget policy are not published.
- **Synchronizer (gyroscope data crossing into the imaging pipeline clock domain; cloud upload and download boundary)** — Gyroscope samples arrive in their own clock domain and the imaging pipeline runs in its own, so the stability data crosses a clock-domain boundary into the meter, and the Video Boost frames cross the on-device to cloud boundary — a synchronizer, built in standard construction from two-flop synchronizers or an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers. The domain count, the synchronizer depth and the clock frequencies are not published. Standard construction; the gyroscope stability analysis and the cloud stage are published facts.
- **Credit counter (DRAM bandwidth budgeting for the longer burst — up to 13 frames — and the upload path)** — The Night Sight burst runs up to 13 frames over up to 6 seconds, longer than the daylight burst, and the Video Boost upload path draws on the same memory system, so the memory system must budget DRAM bandwidth between the longer burst, the merge traffic and the upload — a credit counter tracking outstanding requests and throttling a requester when its budget is exhausted is the standard construction for that budgeting. The credit budget, the throttling policy and the requester weights are not published. Standard construction; the 6-13 frame burst and the cloud upload are published facts.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Google publishes no Tensor G3 ISP block diagram — no queue depths, no flow-field buffer sizes, no per-stage latencies — so the primitives below are mapped from the published Night Sight pipeline of the 2019 paper and the Tensor G3 product blogs, not from a die diagram. The frame counts, capture times and 3 ms flow estimate are already recorded at Level 2; no new chip-specific number is claimed here. The only new numbers are arithmetic derived from those published figures and labelled as such. The learned auto white balance model runs on the TPU, per the entry's building blocks. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Down to the gates: The HDR+ burst pipeline — align and merge in the frequency domain

Google publishes no gate-level structure for the Tensor G3 ISP — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the HDR+ pipeline, the Night Sight meter or the Video Boost path. The deepest published description is the 2016 HDR+ paper, which publishes the five-stage pipeline and its figures, the 2019 Night Sight paper, which publishes the motion-metering pipeline and its figures, and the Tensor G3 product blog, which names Video Boost as the pipeline's cloud stage. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors using the primer's bottom layer — the universal gates, the latch and the flip-flop, the 6T SRAM cell, the CAM cell and the full adder — and every gate or transistor figure is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, not a claim about Google's actual netlist. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, no total is claimed.

- **FIFO / queue (burst frame ingest staging, viewfinder frame queue, tile queues between alignment and merge)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is a register file of D flip-flops or a small SRAM bank, the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each, incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. Up to 8 Bayer RAW frames arrive at up to 30 fps and are staged into the frame store, the 1.6 Mpix viewfinder stream runs through its own frame queue at 15-30 fps, and tiles queue between the alignment stages and the merge so a slow merge does not stall the aligner — each boundary is a FIFO of this form, decoupling a producer from a consumer that runs at a different rate. The FIFO depths and the ingest widths are not published, so the pointer widths — and therefore the counter and comparator totals — are not claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank / register file (tile working store; Gaussian pyramid levels)** — The working store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. The merge holds one reference tile and its aligned alternate tiles while the Wiener filter runs — 16x16 tiles, 256 pixels each, 32x32 tiles, 1,024 pixels each, for very dark scenes — and the alignment holds the four Gaussian pyramid levels, the gray base at 3 Mpix quartering per level, so by arithmetic from the published figures the levels hold 3 Mpix, 750K, 187.5K and about 47K pixels. The tile-buffer sizes, the banking and the port counts are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (FFT butterfly complex multiplies; Wiener per-frequency weighting; 3x3 colour-correction matrix; demosaic interpolation weights)** — A multiplier array is partial-product generation plus an adder tree: each multiply generates partial products with AND gates — one AND gate per bit-pair — and reduces them through full adders, 28 transistors each in the standard-cell form, two half adders of XOR, AND and OR gates. The FFT-accelerated alignment is butterfly work — each butterfly is a complex multiply, four real multiplies and two real adds in the textbook form, plus additions — the Wiener merge weights each frequency by a per-frequency factor, the finish multiplies each pixel by the ISP-supplied 3x3 colour-correction matrix, nine multiplies and six adds per pixel by arithmetic, and demosaic interpolates each missing colour by weighted neighbours. Each is a multiplier array feeding an adder tree. The array dimensions, the lane count and the operand widths are not published, so no multiplier total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (FFT butterfly additions; 2x2 Bayer averaging; Wiener accumulation across alternate frames; bilateral 3x3 tap sums)** — An adder tree is full adders arranged in a binary reduction: partial sums reduce one stage per halving of their count, each full adder two half adders — 2 XOR, 2 AND and 1 OR gates, about 28 transistors in a standard cell. Each FFT butterfly adds as well as multiplies, the gray pyramid is built by averaging 2x2 Bayer blocks — three adds and a shift by 2 per block, by arithmetic — the Wiener merge accumulates the per-frequency contributions across the alternate frames, and the chroma denoise sums a sparse 3x3 tap kernel in two YUV passes, nine taps reducing through eight adds per pass by arithmetic. Each is an adder tree reducing many partial sums to one result per output. The tree depth, the adder widths and the number of terms reduced per cycle are not published, so no adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (reference-frame sharpness pick; Wiener keep-or-fall-back decision; L1 best-match selection)** — A comparator is an XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree for equality, or a subtractor of full adders whose sign bit decides magnitude: equal is all XOR outputs zero, greater-than is a priority chain over the most-significant differing bit. Reference selection picks the sharpest of the first 3 frames by a gradient metric on the green channel — a comparator deciding which frame's metric is highest, a three-way maximum being two comparators plus a mux by arithmetic — the Wiener merge keeps frequency content that differs from the reference by no more than the modelled noise and falls back to the reference otherwise, and the finest-level L1 matching keeps the lowest-cost displacement. The metric thresholds, the noise-model constants A and B per shot and the L1 search policy are set by the shot's gain or are not published, so no comparator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (pyramid downsample by 2x per level; displacement multiples of 2 pixels; bit-depth scaling to 8-bit output)** — A barrel shifter is a mux tree: shifting an N-bit value by a variable amount takes log2(N) stages of 2:1 muxes, each mux a transmission-gate pair (2 transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree. Each pyramid level is the level above downsampled by 2x in each dimension, alignment displacements are kept to multiples of 2 pixels so displaced Bayer samples keep coincident colours, and the finish scales the RAW bit depth down to the 8-bit output photograph — each is a shift by a variable amount through shifters of this form. The shift widths and the scaling policy are not published, so no shifter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (reference vs alternate frame select; Bayer colour-plane select; FFT coarse-scale vs L1 finest-scale path select)** — A mux is a transmission-gate tree or a NAND/NOR tree: a 2:1 mux is 2 transistors per input leg as transmission gates, and an N:1 mux is N minus 1 2:1 muxes arranged as a tree in log2(N) stages, selected by a decoder. Each merge step selects between the reference tile and an alternate tile — a 2:1 select per tile — the merge draws its tiles from the Bayer RAW colour planes, so the colour-plane select is a 4:1 mux, 3 2:1 muxes in 2 stages by arithmetic from the four-plane Bayer pattern, and the alignment selects between the FFT-accelerated coarse-scale path and the pixel-level L1 path at the finest scale. The mux radix beyond the published colour planes and the path-selection logic are not published, so no further mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (pipeline sequencer capture to reference to align to merge to finish; coarse-to-fine level controller with multi-hypothesis upsampling state)** — A finite-state machine is state bits plus next-state logic plus output logic: the state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and the next-state and output logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the current state and the inputs. The pipeline sequencer steps the burst through capture, reference selection, alignment, merge and finish in order, and the alignment controller steps the pyramid from coarse to fine, holding the multi-hypothesis upsampling state when a coarse alignment straddles a motion boundary. That sequencer is a state machine of this form. Its state count, the stage timing and the upsampling policy are not published, so no state-bit total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (between alignment stages — pyramid, FFT, L1 match — and merge stages — tile fetch, Wiener weighting, write-back)** — A pipeline register is one D flip-flop per bit — about 20–28 transistors each, two cross-coupled latch stages — latched between stages so the next stage can start while the current stage's result is held. Work is latched between the alignment stages — pyramid build, FFT matching, L1 matching — and between the merge stages — tile fetch, Wiener weighting, write-back — so the pipeline sustains its throughput instead of stalling between stages. The stage count, the latch widths and the per-stage latencies are not published, so no register total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (frame counter; tile counter; pyramid level counter)** — A counter is N D flip-flops plus N full adders in a ripple or look-ahead chain, incrementing on each clock, with a comparator resetting it at the terminal count. The pipeline must know which frame of the burst it is merging, which tile of the frame it is working and which pyramid level it is aligning: a frame counter for up to 8 frames — a 3-bit counter, since 2 to the power 3 is 8, being 3 D flip-flops (60–84 transistors) plus 3 full adders (84 transistors) — a tile counter for the 16x16 tiles overlapped by half, step 8 pixels, so about 187,500 tile positions in a 12 Mpix frame, 12 Mpix divided by 64 square pixels per 8-pixel step, edge effects aside — an 18-bit counter, since 2 to the power 18 is 262,144, being 18 D flip-flops (360–504 transistors) plus 18 full adders (504 transistors) — and a pyramid level counter for the 4 levels — a 2-bit counter, being 2 D flip-flops (40–56 transistors) plus 2 full adders (56 transistors). All three widths are arithmetic derived from the published figures and labelled as such; the counter widths themselves are not published. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (sensor/ISP clock domain vs compute domain; viewfinder stream crossing)** — A synchronizer is two D flip-flops in series — about 20–28 transistors each — the first sampling the incoming signal in the new clock domain and the second re-sampling it a cycle later so metastability resolves before the value is used; a multi-bit crossing is an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers, the pointers changing one bit at a time so a sampled pointer is never more than one count stale. The sensor and the hardware ISP run in their own clock domain and the compute that aligns and merges in its own, so every burst frame crossing from the ISP into the merge pipeline crosses a clock-domain boundary, and the viewfinder stream crosses the same boundary — a synchronizer of this form at each crossing. The domain count, the synchronizer depth and the clock frequencies are not published, so no synchronizer total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Priority encoder / arbiter (tile scheduler picking the next tile; DRAM arbiter between burst ingest, alignment reads, merge reads and writes and the viewfinder)** — A priority encoder is a tree of OR gates with a priority chain: N request lines reduce to a grant index naming the highest-priority active request, with a round-robin variant adding a rotating priority register of D flip-flops. Tiles must be scheduled in order across the merge, and the burst ingest, the alignment reads, the merge reads and writes and the viewfinder all share one main memory, so something must decide which tile runs next and which memory request goes next — a priority encoder or arbiter of this form picking the highest-priority ready requester. The arbitration policy, the requester count and the scheduler priority scheme are not published, so no encoder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (DRAM bandwidth budgeting — as much as 104 Mpix per photograph moves through main memory)** — A credit counter is a down-counter of D flip-flops and full adders with a comparator: it starts at the budget, decrements on each issued request and increments on each returned credit, and a comparator blocks new requests when the count reaches zero. As much as 104 Mpix must be stored and processed per output photograph, so the memory system must budget DRAM bandwidth between burst ingest, alignment traffic and merge traffic, and a credit counter of this form tracking outstanding requests and throttling a requester when its budget is exhausted is the standard construction for that budgeting. The credit budget, the throttling policy and the requester weights are not published, so no counter total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Google publishes the HDR+ pipeline at stage level only — burst capture, reference selection, alignment, merge and finish (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the pipeline appears in any Google source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Google's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable).

#### Down to the gates: Night Sight motion metering — and Video Boost, the pipeline's cloud stage

What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors using the primer's bottom layer, and every gate or transistor figure is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, not a claim about Google's actual netlist. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, no total is claimed.

Viewfinder frames queue into motion metering before the shutter press, the 6-13 frame burst queues into the merge over 1-6 seconds of capture, and Video Boost frames queue for upload while the finished video queues back down — each boundary is a FIFO of this form decoupling a producer from a consumer that runs at a different rate. The queue depths, the ingest widths and the upload buffering are not published, so the pointer widths — and therefore the counter and comparator totals — are not claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank / register file (motion-metering flow-field working store; downsampled reference frame store for learned auto white balance; tone-mapping look-up tables)** — The working store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. - **Multiplier array (motion-estimation and optical-flow multiply-accumulates; learned auto-white-balance model multiply-accumulates; tone-curve application)** — A multiplier array is partial-product generation plus an adder tree: each multiply generates partial products with AND gates — one AND gate per bit-pair — and reduces them through full adders, 28 transistors each in the standard-cell form, two half adders of XOR, AND and OR gates. Estimating the flow field is multiply-accumulate work over viewfinder frames, the learned colour-constancy model is multiply-accumulate work over the downsampled reference — a learned stage, and the entry's building blocks put the learned stages on the TPU — and applying a tone curve multiplies each pixel by its mapped value. - **Adder tree (flow-field magnitude accumulation across the frame; per-region merge weight sums)** — An adder tree is full adders arranged in a binary reduction: partial sums reduce one stage per halving of their count, each full adder two half adders — 2 XOR, 2 AND and 1 OR gates, about 28 transistors in a standard cell. ### Sony BIONZ XR + AI Processing Unit (α7R V)

**Specs (wiki card).** Camera ISP + dedicated AI unit · subject-recognition AF

**Building blocks.**
- **AI Processing Unit ★** — A separate processor beside BIONZ XR, dedicated to AI-based image recognition — the first in an Alpha camera. It runs deep-learning subject recognition and human pose estimation: it tracks bodies and heads, not just faces and eyes, so AF holds a subject who turns away
- **BIONZ XR image engine** — The main pipeline — up to 8× the processing power of the previous generation (Sony's figure for the XR engine) — running demosaic, noise reduction and colour on the 61 MP stream at 10 fps bursts
- **61 MP Exmor R BSI sensor interface** — The front of the pipe: full-frame back-illuminated readout feeding both processors; the AI unit works from the same data the image engine develops
- **Real-time Eye AF / Recognition AF control loop** — The AI unit's output steers the Fast Hybrid AF system — recognition results select and hold the focus point across 693 phase-detection points (α7R V configuration)
- **RAW + video paths** — Lossless compressed RAW stills and 8K/4K movie recording paths through BIONZ XR; the AI unit also informs auto white balance (recognising the scene, e.g. a subject in shadow) and exposure

**The piece that makes it special.** A second brain that only looks. Sony's split is the point: image development (BIONZ XR) and image understanding (the AI unit) are different silicon with different jobs, so recognition can deepen — pose estimation, animal/vehicle/insect classes — without touching the debayer pipeline photographers trust. It is the phone industry's ISP+NPU pattern arriving in a dedicated camera, with the twist that the AI block never touches a pixel of the final image; it only decides where focus and exposure go.

**How work flows.** Sensor reads out: The 61 MP stream enters both the image engine and the AI unit. AI unit recognises: Pose estimation and subject classification identify what and where the subject is — person, animal, vehicle, insect. AF/AE act on it: Focus locks to the recognised subject's eye/body; exposure and white balance adjust to the recognised scene. BIONZ XR develops: The frame is demosaiced, noise-reduced and written as RAW/JPEG/HEIF or encoded as video.

**Trade-off accepted.** A black box by design. Sony publishes what the AI unit achieves, not what it is — no TOPS, no process, no block diagram — so this entry names only the functions Sony documents and flags the rest as undisclosed. Recognition classes and pose models are firmware-defined: the hardware's ceiling is whatever Sony's models learn next, and older bodies can't be upgraded to it.
