#### Inside the signature block: The AI Processing Unit — deep-learning recognition pipeline

**Inside it.** Sony documents six functions of the AI Processing Unit, and publishes no block diagram, no TOPS, no process node and no per-stage latency — so these are the documented functions in pipeline order, not die sub-blocks. (1) Deep-learning subject recognition: the unit interprets 'significant amounts of data' to recognise subjects and a wider range of subject types, using learned human forms and poses. (2) Human pose estimation: it recognises not just eyes but body and head position with high precision, using learned human forms and postures, so a subject facing away from the camera or wearing a mask can still be locked onto and tracked. (3) Subject-class selection: the photographer picks one of seven settings — Human, Animal/Bird, Animal, Bird, Insect, Car/Train, Airplane — and heads and bodies are recognised in addition to eyes for the Human, Animal and Bird settings. (4) Real-time Recognition AF: the recognition result selects and holds the focus point on the Fast Hybrid AF grid — up to 693 phase-detection points covering approximately 79% of the image area, with AF precision down to EV -4.0 in AF-S mode. (5) Real-time Tracking: for stills and movies, the recognised subject is held across frames; even with subject recognition OFF, touch operation acquires and tracks subjects based on colour, pattern (luminance) and distance (depth). (6) Auto white balance assist: alongside the Visible Light + IR sensor on the front of the body, the AI unit helps achieve more accurate white balance in difficult lighting, such as when the subject is in shadow.

**Trace — one unit of work: one frame's recognition, from sensor data to AF-point selection.**
1. **Sensor readout reaches both processors. **The 61 MP Exmor R frame (9504 × 6336) is read out and enters BIONZ XR for development and the AI Processing Unit for recognition at the same time — the AI unit works from the same data the image engine develops.
2. **Subject class selected. **The photographer has picked one of the seven subject settings — say Human — so the unit knows which learned model to run; Sony warns the camera may not accurately recognise all specified subjects in all conditions.
3. **Pose estimated. **The unit runs its learned human-form and pose model on the frame: it locates the body's and head's position, not just the eyes, so the subject is found even turned away from the camera or wearing a mask.
4. **Eye, head or body target chosen. **Recognition picks the target — eye where visible, otherwise head or body — with approximately 60% better human-eye recognition than the α7R IV, and the AF system drives focus to that point on the 693-point grid.
5. **Tracking holds the lock. **Real-time Tracking holds the recognised subject across frames, using colour, pattern and distance data, while the shutter fires at up to 10 fps with AF/AE tracking.
6. **Recognition feeds exposure and white balance. **The same recognition result informs auto exposure and auto white balance — the AI unit plus the Visible Light + IR sensor set white balance for the recognised scene, for example a subject in shadow — while BIONZ XR develops the frame.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the face-and-eye-only wall: earlier Real-time Eye AF needed a visible face and eye, so a subject who turned away, wore a mask, or presented only a back or a body lost focus. Pose estimation tracks the body and head as well as the eye, so the lock survives the turn-away. Creates a firmware-defined-classes bottleneck in its place: recognition only covers the seven subject settings Sony ships (Human, Animal/Bird, Animal, Bird, Insect, Car/Train, Airplane), and Sony itself warns the camera may not accurately recognise all specified subjects in all conditions and may erroneously recognise a subject type other than the one specified — so the ceiling of the hardware is whatever Sony's models learn next, and older bodies cannot be upgraded to it. And the unit is a black box by design: Sony publishes no TOPS, no process node, no block diagram and no per-stage latency for it, so its behaviour can only be judged by what it achieves, not by what it is.

**Governing numbers.** 693 phase-detection AF points in a high-density array covering approximately 79% of the image area; AF precision down to EV -4.0 in AF-S mode. Seven subject settings: Human, Animal/Bird, Animal, Bird, Insect, Car/Train, Airplane. Approximately 60% improvement in human eye recognition compared to the α7R IV. Continuous shooting at up to 10 fps with AF/AE tracking, up to 8 fps with AF/AE tracking when shooting with live view.

**Primary source.** Sony Electronics press release — Alpha 7R V (Oct 26, 2022) — AI processing unit dedicated to AI-based image recognition, a first in any Alpha camera; human form and pose estimation; subject types including animals, vehicles and insects; continuous shooting at up to 10 fps with AF/AE tracking; subject settings footnote. Sony α7R V product page (Sony Electronics) — 'Real-time Recognition AF for human' (approximately 60% improvement in human eye recognition compared to the α7R IV; pose estimation locks onto a subject facing away or wearing a mask), 'Real-time Recognition AF for wider range of subjects', 'AI processing unit for advanced subject recognition', and the AWB note (AI unit plus Visible Light + IR sensor for white balance in difficult lighting, such as a subject in shadow) — read via Adorama's verbatim reproduction of Sony's product copy, since the live Sony product page returned only its FAQ in this run. Sony α7R V product page FAQ (electronics.sony.com, read live) — 693 phase-detection AF points. Sony publishes no TOPS, process node, block diagram or per-stage latency for the AI Processing Unit, so the sub-functions above are Sony's documented functions, not hardware sub-blocks.

#### Inside the signature block: BIONZ XR image engine — the 61 MP develop pipeline

**Inside it.** Sony documents the develop pipeline as product functions, and publishes no BIONZ XR block diagram, queue depths, stage latencies or bit depths — so these are the documented functions in pipeline order, not die sub-blocks. (1) Sensor readout interface: the 35mm full-frame back-illuminated Exmor R CMOS sensor delivers approximately 61.0 effective megapixels (9504 × 6336) to the engine in real time. (2) Develop: demosaic, noise reduction and colour — 'processed in real time to the fullest extent by the advanced BIONZ XR processing engine' — including in-camera Creative Look settings (10 presets) for stills and video. (3) RAW path: lossless compressed RAW with three selectable pixel counts — L (60M), M (26M), S (15M) — plus uncompressed and compressed RAW; continuous bursts run to 583 compressed RAW images at high speed. (4) JPEG/HEIF output: high-quality HEIF images with high compression efficiency, alongside JPEG. (5) Video encode: XAVC HS (MPEG-H HEVC/H.265) for 8K 24/25p, XAVC S-I all-intra and XAVC HS for 4K, 10-bit 4:2:2 recording, S-Log3 and S-Cinetone picture profiles; 16-bit RAW output to an external recorder via HDMI. (6) Pixel Shift Multi Shooting: the in-body stabilisation system shifts the sensor in small increments for 4- or 16-image composites (approximately 240.8 million pixels for 16 images), composited on a computer with Imaging Edge Desktop. (7) Heat management: an improved heat-dissipation structure for extended recording times, the video branch's limiter.

**Trace — one unit of work: one 61 MP frame through the develop pipeline at 10 fps.**
1. **Readout: one 61 MP frame in. **The Exmor R sensor reads out a 9504 × 6336 frame and hands it to BIONZ XR — at 10 fps in a burst, roughly 610 million pixels a second to develop while AF/AE tracking stays live.
2. **Develop: demosaic, denoise, colour. **BIONZ XR demosaics the Bayer data, applies noise reduction and colour (including the selected Creative Look) in real time — the stage Sony's eight-times processing-power figure exists to pay for.
3. **RAW written — or JPEG/HEIF. **The developed frame is written as lossless compressed RAW at the selected size (L 60M, M 26M or S 15M), or as JPEG/HEIF, to the CFexpress Type A / SDXC media slots.
4. **Burst depth spent. **The burst continues at up to 10 fps with AF/AE tracking until the buffer fills — up to 583 compressed RAW images at high speed on Sony's CFexpress Type A card.
5. **Video branch: encode. **For movies the same engine encodes instead of writing stills: 8K 24/25p in XAVC HS (HEVC/H.265) from the approximately 1.2x-cropped region, or 4K 60p from the same cropped region, or 4K oversampled from 6.2K in Super 35mm mode — all 10-bit 4:2:2, with 16-bit RAW available over HDMI.
6. **Heat is the limiter. **Extended video recording is bounded by heat, not by the encode pipeline — Sony's improved heat-dissipation structure is what buys the longer recording times.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the 61 MP × 10 fps data-rate wall: a 9504 × 6336 frame is about 61 million pixels, and at 10 fps the engine must develop roughly 610 million pixels a second while keeping AF/AE tracking live — the job BIONZ XR's eight-times processing power (Sony's figure, versus BIONZ X, from the Alpha 1 launch) exists for. Lossless compressed RAW keeps the resulting files manageable, and the burst can run to 583 compressed RAW images. Creates a format-and-crop bottleneck in its place: the burst depth is media- and format-bound (583 compressed RAW at high speed; fewer uncompressed), and the video branch trades sensor width for frame rate — 8K 24/25p and 4K 60p both come from a roughly 1.2x-cropped region, with full-width 4K only up to 30p — while heat dissipation is the video limiter, which Sony answers with an improved heat-dissipation structure for extended recording times.

**Governing numbers.** 61.0 effective megapixels (9504 × 6336); BIONZ XR with eight times more processing power than BIONZ X (Sony's Alpha 1 figure). Continuous shooting at up to 10 fps with AF/AE tracking; up to 583 compressed RAW images at high speed; up to 8 fps with AF/AE tracking when shooting with live view. Lossless RAW with three selectable pixel counts — L (60M), M (26M), S (15M). 8K 24/25p video (approximately 1.2x angle of view), 4K video oversampled from 6.2K without binning, MPEG-H HEVC/H.265 codec, all-intra recording, 10-bit 4:2:2 recording; 4K 60p from the 1.24x-cropped region, full-width 4K up to 30p. Sensitivity ISO 100 to ISO 32000 for stills and movies; 15 stops of dynamic range for stills.

**Primary source.** Sony Electronics press release — Alpha 7R V (Oct 26, 2022) — 61.0 MP Exmor R sensor and BIONZ XR; ISO 100–32000 and 15 stops for stills; 10 fps with AF/AE tracking; up to 583 compressed RAW images; Lossless RAW image compression and selectable RAW sizes; 8K 24/25p, 4K oversampled from 6.2K without binning, MPEG-H HEVC/H.265, all-intra, 10-bit 4:2:2; improved heat dissipation for extended recording times. Sony Electronics press release — Alpha 1 (Jan 26, 2021) — BIONZ XR with eight times more processing power, compared to BIONZ X; 759 phase-detection points covering approximately 92% of the image area (the Alpha 1 figure — see the corrected fact record). Sony α7R V product page (Sony Electronics) — lossless RAW pixel counts L (60M), M (26M), S (15M); 16-bit RAW output via HDMI — read via verbatim retailer reproductions of Sony's product copy. DPReview, 'Sony a7R V in-depth review' — 8K/24p or 4K/60p video, both with a 1.24x crop; full-width 4K up to 30p. Sony publishes no BIONZ XR block diagram, queue depths, stage latencies or bit depths, so the stages above are the product-documented functions in pipeline order, not die sub-blocks.

#### Down to the primitives: The AI Processing Unit — deep-learning recognition pipeline

The AI Processing Unit runs Sony's six documented functions in pipeline order — subject recognition, pose estimation, subject-class selection, Recognition AF, tracking, and white-balance assist — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (frame ingest staging; recognition-result queue feeding the Fast Hybrid AF grid)** — The 61 MP frame reaches the AI unit at the same time as BIONZ XR, so a frame-ingest FIFO stages the readout while the recognition pipeline works the previous frame, decoupling the sensor readout rate from the inference rate. At the other end, the recognition result waits in a queue feeding the Fast Hybrid AF grid: the unit recognises, then the AF system drives focus to the chosen point, and the queue absorbs the rate mismatch between recognition and the lens drive. The queue depths and ingest widths are not published.
- **SRAM bank / register file (learned-model weight store; feature-map working store; subject-class config registers)** — The learned human forms and poses live in on-chip weights, so the model the unit runs is held in an SRAM weight store, read out layer by layer as a frame is recognised, with a feature-map working store holding the intermediate activations while the frame is in flight. The photographer's pick of the seven subject settings lives in config registers that steer which learned model runs. The weight-store capacity, banking, port counts and widths are not published.
- **Multiplier array (learned-model multiply-accumulates; pose keypoint scoring)** — Recognition is a deep-learning inference pass, so the compute heart is a multiplier array: each multiply-accumulate unit takes a weight and an activation and produces a partial product, and the array works many of them in parallel across a layer. Pose estimation scores keypoints the same way, weighting learned body and head features against the frame. The array dimensions, lane count and number format are not published.
- **Adder tree (MAC accumulation across the weight array; feature-map summation)** — The partial products the multiplier array produces have to be summed into one score per output, so an adder tree collapses them layer by layer — the standard construction for a MAC array — and feature-map values are summed the same way when a stage combines its inputs. The tree depth and width are not published.
- **Comparator (eye/head/body target selection; subject-class match thresholds; EV -4.0 low-light AF precision floor)** — Choosing a target is a comparison: the highest recognition score wins, so comparators rank the eye, head and body candidates and pick the winner, and the subject-class match is checked against the thresholds of the selected setting. The AF precision floor Sony publishes — down to EV -4.0 in AF-S mode — is itself a comparator threshold on the low-light side. The comparator count and widths are not published.
- **Priority encoder / arbiter (AF-point selection on the 693-point grid; subject priority when several candidates are recognised)** — The recognition result picks one focus point on the 693-point Fast Hybrid AF grid, so a priority encoder turns the winning candidate into a point index, and when several subjects are recognised an arbiter decides which one gets the lock first. The encoder width follows from the published grid: 693 points need a 10-bit index (arithmetic — 2 to the 10th is 1024, the smallest power of two above 693), not a Sony figure. The arbiter policy is not published.
- **Mux / demux (subject-class model select among seven learned models; eye vs head vs body target select)** — One of seven learned models runs, chosen by the photographer's subject setting, so a mux steers the frame to the Human, Animal/Bird, Animal, Bird, Insect, Car/Train or Airplane model, and a second mux selects between the eye, head and body outputs once recognition has scored them. The mux widths and select encoding are not published.
- **FSM / controller (recognition pipeline sequencer ingest to recognise to pose to select to track; subject-class state machine)** — The six documented functions run in order, so a controller sequences the pipeline — ingest, recognise, pose, select, track — and a subject-class state machine holds the photographer's setting across frames until it is changed. The state count and sequencing are not published.
- **Pipeline registers (between recognition stages — frame ingest, model inference, pose estimation, target selection)** — Each recognition stage hands its result to the next through pipeline registers, so frame ingest, model inference, pose estimation and target selection can overlap on successive frames instead of running one frame end to end. The register widths and stage count are not published.
- **Counter (frame counter at up to 10 fps tracking; AF-point index counter over the 693-point grid)** — Tracking holds the lock across frames, so a frame counter tracks the sequence at up to 10 fps with AF/AE tracking — a 4-bit counter covers the ten frames in a second (arithmetic, not a Sony figure) — and the AF-point index counter steps across the 693-point grid, 10 bits wide by the same arithmetic as the priority encoder. No other counter width is claimed.
- **Synchronizer (sensor readout clock domain vs AI-unit domain; recognition result crossing to BIONZ XR and the lens drive)** — The sensor readout, the AI unit and the lens drive do not share one clock, so synchronizers carry the frame into the AI unit's domain and the recognition result out again to BIONZ XR and the AF system, in the standard two-flop construction. The domain frequencies and synchronizer depths are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Sony publishes no AI-unit block diagram, no TOPS, no process node, no queue depths, no stage counts, no per-stage latencies and no bit depths, so the primitives below are mapped from the documented functions in pipeline order of the Oct 26, 2022 press release and the α7R V product page, not from a die diagram. Every press-release and product-page figure is already recorded at Level 2; no new chip-specific number is claimed here. The only new numbers are counter widths computed from published figures and labelled arithmetic. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Down to the primitives: BIONZ XR image engine — the 61 MP develop pipeline

BIONZ XR runs Sony's seven documented develop functions in pipeline order — sensor readout, develop, RAW path, JPEG/HEIF output, video encode, Pixel Shift and heat management — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (sensor readout staging; burst buffer to media; line queues between develop stages)** — The 9504 by 6336 frame streams in at up to 10 fps, so a readout FIFO stages it while the develop stages work the previous frame, and line queues sit between demosaic, denoise and colour so each stage runs at its own rate. At the far end a burst buffer queues developed frames for the CFexpress Type A and SDXC media slots — up to 583 compressed RAW images at high speed — absorbing the gap between the engine's output rate and the media write rate. The queue depths and widths are not published.
- **SRAM bank / line buffers (demosaic working neighbourhood; noise-reduction window store; Pixel Shift reference-frame store)** — Demosaic interpolates each pixel from a small window of its Bayer neighbours, so line buffers hold the rows the interpolation window needs, and noise reduction keeps a similar window store while it averages across neighbouring pixels. Pixel Shift Multi Shooting needs the earlier frames held while the sensor shifts in small increments for its 4- or 16-image composite, so a reference-frame store holds them until the composite is built on a computer. The buffer capacities, banking and widths are not published.
- **Multiplier array (demosaic interpolation weights; 3x3 colour-correction matrix; HEVC transform coefficients; tone-curve scaling for S-Log3 and S-Cinetone)** — Develop is multiply work throughout: demosaic weights neighbouring Bayer samples, the 3x3 colour-correction matrix multiplies each pixel's colour vector, the HEVC transform multiplies by its coefficients, and the S-Log3 and S-Cinetone tone curves scale values — all of it landing on multiplier arrays. The array dimensions, lane count and number format are not published.
- **Adder tree (demosaic gradient sums; noise-reduction weighted sums; HEVC inverse-transform accumulation)** — The products the multiplier arrays produce have to be summed: demosaic adds its gradient terms, noise reduction adds its weighted neighbourhood samples, and the HEVC inverse transform accumulates its coefficients — each an adder tree collapsing many products into one output value, in the standard construction. The tree depth and width are not published.
- **Comparator (Pixel Shift frame-alignment check; lossless-RAW predictor residual handling; exposure and white-balance thresholds from the AI unit's recognition result)** — The Pixel Shift composite only works if the shifted frames line up, so comparators check frame alignment before the composite is built; lossless RAW compression compares each pixel against its predictor and handles the residual; and the exposure and white-balance thresholds the AI unit's recognition result sets are comparator thresholds on the developed values. The comparator count and widths are not published.
- **Barrel shifter (bit-depth scaling from RAW sensor data to 8-bit JPEG and 10-bit 4:2:2 video; Pixel Shift sub-pixel alignment)** — Sensor RAW data has to be scaled to the output bit depth — 8-bit JPEG and 10-bit 4:2:2 video — so a barrel shifter shifts each value by a variable amount in one step, and Pixel Shift alignment shifts samples by sub-pixel amounts when the sensor has moved in small increments. The shifter width is not published.
- **Mux / demux (still vs video path select; Creative Look preset select across 10 presets; L/M/S RAW size select)** — One engine serves two paths, so a mux steers the developed frame to the stills write path (RAW, JPEG or HEIF) or the video encode path (XAVC), a second mux selects among the 10 Creative Look presets, and a third selects the Lossless RAW size — L (60M), M (26M) or S (15M). The mux widths and select encoding are not published.
- **FSM / controller (develop pipeline sequencer readout to demosaic to denoise to colour to write or encode; Pixel Shift capture sequencer for 4 or 16 frames; video encode state machine)** — The develop functions run in order, so a controller sequences readout, demosaic, denoise, colour and then write or encode; a Pixel Shift sequencer counts the 4 or 16 captures and steps the sensor shift between them; and a video encode state machine walks the XAVC HS and XAVC S-I modes through their frame states. The state counts and sequencing are not published.
- **Pipeline registers (between demosaic, denoise, colour and encode stages)** — Each develop stage hands its result to the next through pipeline registers, so demosaic, denoise, colour and encode can overlap on successive frames — the structure that lets the engine sustain roughly 610 million pixels a second at 10 fps. The register widths and stage count are not published.
- **Counter (pixel counter over the 9504 by 6336 frame; burst frame counter up to 583 frames; Pixel Shift image counter for 4 or 16 images)** — The engine counts what it processes: a pixel counter steps across the 9504 by 6336 frame — 60,217,344 pixels, so 26 bits wide (arithmetic — 2 to the 26th is 67,108,864, the smallest power of two above the pixel count); a burst frame counter runs to 583 compressed RAW images, 10 bits wide by the same arithmetic; and the Pixel Shift image counter runs to 4 or 16 images, 4 bits covering sixteen values (arithmetic). No other counter width is claimed.
- **Synchronizer (sensor readout clock domain vs engine domain; HDMI output domain for 16-bit RAW)** — The sensor readout, the engine and the HDMI output do not share one clock, so synchronizers carry the frame into the engine's domain and the 16-bit RAW stream out to the external recorder's domain, in the standard two-flop construction. The domain frequencies and synchronizer depths are not published.
- **Credit counter (DRAM bandwidth budgeting at roughly 610 million pixels a second; media-write budgeting for the 583-frame burst)** — At 10 fps the engine must develop roughly 610 million pixels a second (61.0 MP times 10 fps — arithmetic, not a Sony figure) while AF/AE tracking stays live, so a credit counter budgets DRAM reads and writes between the develop traffic, the video encode traffic and the AI unit's share of the same frame; a second credit counter budgets media writes so the 583-frame burst does not outrun the CFexpress Type A and SDXC slots. The credit limits and counter widths are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Sony publishes no BIONZ XR block diagram, no queue depths, no stage latencies and no bit depths, so the primitives below are mapped from the documented functions in pipeline order of the Oct 26, 2022 press release and the α7R V product page, not from a die diagram. Every press-release and product-page figure is already recorded at Level 2; no new chip-specific number is claimed here. The only new numbers are counter widths and a pixel rate computed from published figures and labelled arithmetic. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Down to the gates: The AI Processing Unit — deep-learning recognition pipeline

Sony publishes no gate-level structure for the AI Processing Unit — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the recognition pipeline, the pose estimator or the AF-point selector. The deepest published description is the Oct 26, 2022 press release, which documents the six functions in pipeline order, and the α7R V product page, which publishes the 693-point AF grid, the seven subject settings and the roughly 60% human-eye recognition improvement. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors using the primer's bottom layer — the universal gates, the latch and the flip-flop, the 6T SRAM cell, the CAM cell and the full adder — and every gate or transistor figure is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, not a claim about Sony's actual netlist. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, no total is claimed.

- **FIFO / queue (frame ingest staging; recognition-result queue feeding the Fast Hybrid AF grid)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is a register file of D flip-flops or a small SRAM bank, the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each, incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The 61 MP frame reaches the AI unit at the same time as BIONZ XR, so a frame-ingest FIFO stages the readout while the recognition pipeline works the previous frame, decoupling the sensor readout rate from the inference rate, and at the other end the recognition result waits in a queue feeding the Fast Hybrid AF grid while the AF system drives focus to the chosen point, absorbing the rate mismatch between recognition and the lens drive. The queue depths and the ingest widths are not published, so the pointer widths — and therefore the counter and comparator totals — are not claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank / register file (learned-model weight store; feature-map working store; subject-class config registers)** — The working store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. The learned human forms and poses live in on-chip weights, so the model the unit runs is held in an SRAM weight store read out layer by layer as a frame is recognised, with a feature-map working store holding the intermediate activations while the frame is in flight, and the photographer's pick of the seven subject settings lives in config registers — small register files of D flip-flops, about 20–28 transistors each — that steer which learned model runs. The weight-store capacity, the banking, the port counts and the widths are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (learned-model multiply-accumulates; pose keypoint scoring)** — A multiplier array is partial-product generation plus an adder tree: each multiply generates partial products with AND gates — one AND gate per bit-pair — and reduces them through full adders, 28 transistors each in the standard-cell form, two half adders of XOR, AND and OR gates. Recognition is a deep-learning inference pass, so the compute heart is a multiplier array: each multiply-accumulate unit takes a weight and an activation and produces a partial product, and the array works many of them in parallel across a layer, and pose estimation scores its keypoints the same way, weighting learned body and head features against the frame. Each is a multiplier array feeding an adder tree. The array dimensions, the lane count and the number format are not published, so no multiplier total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (MAC accumulation across the weight array; feature-map summation)** — An adder tree is full adders arranged in a binary reduction: partial sums reduce one stage per halving of their count, each full adder two half adders — 2 XOR, 2 AND and 1 OR gates, about 28 transistors in a standard cell. The partial products the multiplier array produces have to be summed into one score per output, so an adder tree collapses them layer by layer — the standard construction for a MAC array — and feature-map values are summed the same way when a stage combines its inputs. The tree depth and the width are not published, so no adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (eye/head/body target selection; subject-class match thresholds; EV -4.0 low-light AF precision floor)** — A comparator is an XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree for equality, or a subtractor of full adders whose sign bit decides magnitude: equal is all XOR outputs zero, greater-than is a priority chain over the most-significant differing bit. Choosing a target is a comparison: the highest recognition score wins, so comparators rank the eye, head and body candidates and pick the winner, and the subject-class match is checked against the thresholds of the selected setting. The AF precision floor Sony publishes — down to EV -4.0 in AF-S mode — is itself a comparator threshold on the low-light side. The comparator count and the widths are not published, so no comparator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Priority encoder / arbiter (AF-point selection on the 693-point grid; subject priority when several candidates are recognised)** — A priority encoder is a tree of OR gates with a priority chain: N request lines reduce to a grant index naming the highest-priority active request, with a round-robin variant adding a rotating priority register of D flip-flops. The recognition result picks one focus point on the 693-point Fast Hybrid AF grid, so a priority encoder turns the winning candidate into a point index — a 10-bit index by arithmetic, since 2 to the power 10 is 1024, the smallest power of two above 693 — and when several subjects are recognised an arbiter decides which one gets the lock first. The encoder width follows from the published grid; the arbiter policy is not published, so no further encoder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (subject-class model select among seven learned models; eye vs head vs body target select)** — A mux is a transmission-gate tree or a NAND/NOR tree: a 2:1 mux is 2 transistors per input leg as transmission gates, and an N:1 mux is N minus 1 2:1 muxes arranged as a tree in log2(N) stages, selected by a decoder. One of seven learned models runs, chosen by the photographer's subject setting, so a mux steers the frame to the Human, Animal/Bird, Animal, Bird, Insect, Car/Train or Airplane model — a 7:1 select, 6 2:1 muxes in 3 stages by arithmetic — and a second mux selects between the eye, head and body outputs once recognition has scored them, a 3:1 select, 2 2:1 muxes in 2 stages by arithmetic. The mux widths and the select encoding are not published, so no further mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (recognition pipeline sequencer ingest to recognise to pose to select to track; subject-class state machine)** — A finite-state machine is state bits plus next-state logic plus output logic: the state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and the next-state and output logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the current state and the inputs. The six documented functions run in order, so a controller sequences the pipeline — ingest, recognise, pose, select, track — and a subject-class state machine holds the photographer's setting across frames until it is changed. That sequencer is a state machine of this form. Its state count and the sequencing are not published, so no state-bit total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (between recognition stages — frame ingest, model inference, pose estimation, target selection)** — A pipeline register is one D flip-flop per bit — about 20–28 transistors each, two cross-coupled latch stages — latched between stages so the next stage can start while the current stage's result is held. Each recognition stage hands its result to the next through pipeline registers, so frame ingest, model inference, pose estimation and target selection can overlap on successive frames instead of running one frame end to end. The register widths and the stage count are not published, so no register total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (frame counter at up to 10 fps tracking; AF-point index counter over the 693-point grid)** — A counter is N D flip-flops plus N full adders in a ripple or look-ahead chain, incrementing on each clock, with a comparator resetting it at the terminal count. Tracking holds the lock across frames, so a frame counter tracks the sequence at up to 10 fps with AF/AE tracking — a 4-bit counter, since 2 to the power 4 is 16, which covers ten, being 4 D flip-flops (80–112 transistors) plus 4 full adders (112 transistors) — and the AF-point index counter steps across the 693-point grid, 10 bits wide by the same arithmetic as the priority encoder, being 10 D flip-flops (200–280 transistors) plus 10 full adders (280 transistors). Both widths are arithmetic derived from the published figures and labelled as such; the counter widths themselves are not published. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (sensor readout clock domain vs AI-unit domain; recognition result crossing to BIONZ XR and the lens drive)** — A synchronizer is two D flip-flops in series — about 20–28 transistors each — the first sampling the incoming signal in the new clock domain and the second re-sampling it a cycle later so metastability resolves before the value is used; a multi-bit crossing is an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers, the pointers changing one bit at a time so a sampled pointer is never more than one count stale. The sensor readout, the AI unit and the lens drive do not share one clock, so synchronizers carry the frame into the AI unit's domain and the recognition result out again to BIONZ XR and the AF system, in the standard two-flop construction. The domain frequencies and the synchronizer depths are not published, so no synchronizer total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Sony publishes the AI Processing Unit at function level only — subject recognition, pose estimation, subject-class selection, Real-time Recognition AF, Real-time Tracking and white-balance assist (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the unit appears in any Sony source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Sony's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable).

#### Down to the gates: BIONZ XR image engine — the 61 MP develop pipeline

Sony publishes no gate-level structure for BIONZ XR — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the develop pipeline, the RAW path or the video encode path. The deepest published description is the Oct 26, 2022 press release, which documents the develop functions in pipeline order, and the α7R V product page, which publishes the 61.0 MP frame, the Lossless RAW sizes, the 583-frame burst and the 8K and 4K video modes. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors using the primer's bottom layer — the universal gates, the latch and the flip-flop, the 6T SRAM cell, the CAM cell and the full adder — and every gate or transistor figure is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, not a claim about Sony's actual netlist. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, no total is claimed.

- **FIFO / queue (sensor readout staging; burst buffer to media; line queues between develop stages)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is a register file of D flip-flops or a small SRAM bank, the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each, incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The 9504 by 6336 frame streams in at up to 10 fps, so a readout FIFO stages it while the develop stages work the previous frame, and line queues sit between demosaic, denoise and colour so each stage runs at its own rate. At the far end a burst buffer queues developed frames for the CFexpress Type A and SDXC media slots — up to 583 compressed RAW images at high speed — absorbing the gap between the engine's output rate and the media write rate. The queue depths and the widths are not published, so the pointer widths — and therefore the counter and comparator totals — are not claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank / line buffers (demosaic working neighbourhood; noise-reduction window store; Pixel Shift reference-frame store)** — The working store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. Demosaic interpolates each pixel from a small window of its Bayer neighbours, so line buffers hold the rows the interpolation window needs, and noise reduction keeps a similar window store while it averages across neighbouring pixels. Pixel Shift Multi Shooting needs the earlier frames held while the sensor shifts in small increments for its 4- or 16-image composite, so a reference-frame store holds them until the composite is built on a computer. The buffer capacities, the banking and the widths are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (demosaic interpolation weights; 3x3 colour-correction matrix; HEVC transform coefficients; tone-curve scaling for S-Log3 and S-Cinetone)** — A multiplier array is partial-product generation plus an adder tree: each multiply generates partial products with AND gates — one AND gate per bit-pair — and reduces them through full adders, 28 transistors each in the standard-cell form, two half adders of XOR, AND and OR gates. Develop is multiply work throughout: demosaic weights neighbouring Bayer samples, the 3x3 colour-correction matrix multiplies each pixel's colour vector — nine multiplies and six adds per pixel by arithmetic — the HEVC transform multiplies by its coefficients, and the S-Log3 and S-Cinetone tone curves scale values — all of it landing on multiplier arrays. Each is a multiplier array feeding an adder tree. The array dimensions, the lane count and the number format are not published, so no multiplier total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (demosaic gradient sums; noise-reduction weighted sums; HEVC inverse-transform accumulation)** — An adder tree is full adders arranged in a binary reduction: partial sums reduce one stage per halving of their count, each full adder two half adders — 2 XOR, 2 AND and 1 OR gates, about 28 transistors in a standard cell. The products the multiplier arrays produce have to be summed: demosaic adds its gradient terms, noise reduction adds its weighted neighbourhood samples, and the HEVC inverse transform accumulates its coefficients — each an adder tree collapsing many products into one output value, in the standard construction. The tree depth and the width are not published, so no adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (Pixel Shift frame-alignment check; lossless-RAW predictor residual handling; exposure and white-balance thresholds from the AI unit's recognition result)** — A comparator is an XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree for equality, or a subtractor of full adders whose sign bit decides magnitude: equal is all XOR outputs zero, greater-than is a priority chain over the most-significant differing bit. The Pixel Shift composite only works if the shifted frames line up, so comparators check frame alignment before the composite is built; lossless RAW compression compares each pixel against its predictor and handles the residual; and the exposure and white-balance thresholds the AI unit's recognition result sets are comparator thresholds on the developed values. The comparator count and the widths are not published, so no comparator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (bit-depth scaling from RAW sensor data to 8-bit JPEG and 10-bit 4:2:2 video; Pixel Shift sub-pixel alignment)** — A barrel shifter is a mux tree: shifting an N-bit value by a variable amount takes log2(N) stages of 2:1 muxes, each mux a transmission-gate pair (2 transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree. Sensor RAW data has to be scaled to the output bit depth — 8-bit JPEG and 10-bit 4:2:2 video — so a barrel shifter shifts each value by a variable amount in one step, and Pixel Shift alignment shifts samples by sub-pixel amounts when the sensor has moved in small increments. The shifter width is not published, so no shifter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (still vs video path select; Creative Look preset select across 10 presets; L/M/S RAW size select)** — A mux is a transmission-gate tree or a NAND/NOR tree: a 2:1 mux is 2 transistors per input leg as transmission gates, and an N:1 mux is N minus 1 2:1 muxes arranged as a tree in log2(N) stages, selected by a decoder. One engine serves two paths, so a mux steers the developed frame to the stills write path (RAW, JPEG or HEIF) or the video encode path (XAVC), a second mux selects among the 10 Creative Look presets — a 10:1 select, 9 2:1 muxes in 4 stages by arithmetic — and a third selects the Lossless RAW size — L (60M), M (26M) or S (15M), a 3:1 select, 2 2:1 muxes in 2 stages by arithmetic. The mux widths and the select encoding are not published, so no further mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (develop pipeline sequencer readout to demosaic to denoise to colour to write or encode; Pixel Shift capture sequencer for 4 or 16 frames; video encode state machine)** — A finite-state machine is state bits plus next-state logic plus output logic: the state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and the next-state and output logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the current state and the inputs. The develop functions run in order, so a controller sequences readout, demosaic, denoise, colour and then write or encode; a Pixel Shift sequencer counts the 4 or 16 captures and steps the sensor shift between them; and a video encode state machine walks the XAVC HS and XAVC S-I modes through their frame states. Each is a state machine of this form. The state counts and the sequencing are not published, so no state-bit total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (between demosaic, denoise, colour and encode stages)** — A pipeline register is one D flip-flop per bit — about 20–28 transistors each, two cross-coupled latch stages — latched between stages so the next stage can start while the current stage's result is held. Each develop stage hands its result to the next through pipeline registers, so demosaic, denoise, colour and encode can overlap on successive frames — the structure that lets the engine sustain roughly 610 million pixels a second at 10 fps. The register widths and the stage count are not published, so no register total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (pixel counter over the 9504 by 6336 frame; burst frame counter up to 583 frames; Pixel Shift image counter for 4 or 16 images)** — A counter is N D flip-flops plus N full adders in a ripple or look-ahead chain, incrementing on each clock, with a comparator resetting it at the terminal count. The engine counts what it processes: a pixel counter steps across the 9504 by 6336 frame — 60,217,344 pixels, so 26 bits wide, since 2 to the power 26 is 67,108,864, the smallest power of two above the pixel count, being 26 D flip-flops (520–728 transistors) plus 26 full adders (728 transistors) — a burst frame counter runs to 583 compressed RAW images, 10 bits wide by the same arithmetic, being 10 D flip-flops (200–280 transistors) plus 10 full adders (280 transistors) — and the Pixel Shift image counter runs to 4 or 16 images, 4 bits covering sixteen values, being 4 D flip-flops (80–112 transistors) plus 4 full adders (112 transistors). All three widths are arithmetic derived from the published figures and labelled as such; the counter widths themselves are not published. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (sensor readout clock domain vs engine domain; HDMI output domain for 16-bit RAW)** — A synchronizer is two D flip-flops in series — about 20–28 transistors each — the first sampling the incoming signal in the new clock domain and the second re-sampling it a cycle later so metastability resolves before the value is used; a multi-bit crossing is an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers, the pointers changing one bit at a time so a sampled pointer is never more than one count stale. The sensor readout, the engine and the HDMI output do not share one clock, so synchronizers carry the frame into the engine's domain and the 16-bit RAW stream out to the external recorder's domain, in the standard two-flop construction. The domain frequencies and the synchronizer depths are not published, so no synchronizer total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (DRAM bandwidth budgeting at roughly 610 million pixels a second; media-write budgeting for the 583-frame burst)** — A credit counter is a down-counter of D flip-flops and full adders with a comparator: it starts at the budget, decrements on each issued request and increments on each returned credit, and a comparator blocks new requests when the count reaches zero. At 10 fps the engine must develop roughly 610 million pixels a second (61.0 MP times 10 fps — arithmetic, not a Sony figure) while AF/AE tracking stays live, so a credit counter budgets DRAM reads and writes between the develop traffic, the video encode traffic and the AI unit's share of the same frame; a second credit counter budgets media writes so the 583-frame burst does not outrun the CFexpress Type A and SDXC slots. The credit limits and the counter widths are not published, so no counter total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Sony publishes the BIONZ XR develop pipeline at function level only — sensor readout, develop (demosaic, noise reduction, colour), RAW path, JPEG/HEIF output, video encode and Pixel Shift Multi Shooting (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the engine appears in any Sony source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Sony's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable).

### Canon DIGIC X

**Specs (wiki card).** EOS R5/R3 generation · 8K RAW video

**Building blocks.**
- **DIGIC X image pipeline** — Canon's single-chip engine (debuted in the EOS-1D X Mark III, then the R5/R6/R3): sensor readout, demosaic, noise reduction and JPEG/HEIF development at 45 MP and 20 fps in the R5 — Canon publishes capabilities, not an internal block diagram, and this entry invents none
- **Dual Pixel CMOS AF II data path ★** — Every pixel split into two photodiodes: the sensor delivers phase-difference data across ~100% of the frame (1,053 automatic AF zones in the R5) alongside the image — focus information is a by-product of capture, computed in the same readout
- **Deep-learning subject detection** — DIGIC X runs Canon's trained detection for people (eye/face/head/body) and animals (dogs, cats, birds) — notable as inference inside the AF loop of a 2020 camera, before 'AI chip' was a camera marketing line
- **8K RAW video path** — The pipeline's stress test: 8K DCI RAW internal recording at up to 29.97 fps (12-bit) and 4K/120p 4:2:2 10-bit — sustained throughput that made the R5's thermal limits famous
- **In-body stabilisation coordination (IBIS)** — DIGIC X fuses gyro data with lens IS for coordinated control (up to 8 stops with select RF lenses) — a control loop sharing the processor with imaging

**The piece that makes it special.** Focus data for free. Dual Pixel CMOS AF is the architectural idea: by splitting every pixel, the sensor produces a phase map with the photograph, so DIGIC X never hunts — it measures defocus directly, everywhere in the frame, and spends its deep-learning budget on what to focus on rather than where focus is. The 8K RAW path then shows the cost of the whole arrangement: the pipeline's sustained throughput, not its peak, is the product — and in the R5, thermals set it.

**How work flows.** Dual Pixel readout: The 45 MP sensor streams image + phase-difference data simultaneously. Detection runs: Deep-learning models find eyes, faces, heads and animal subjects in the AF data. AF drives the lens: Measured defocus (not contrast hunting) moves the lens directly to focus; IBIS coordinates sensor and lens shift. Image develops / video records: Stills develop to JPEG/HEIF/RAW; video encodes up to 8K RAW or 4K120 4:2:2 internally — until the thermal budget says stop.

**Trade-off accepted.** Thermals and opacity. The R5's 8K recording limits were a launch controversy precisely because the architecture's constraint is sustained heat, not peak capability — Canon later eased limits via firmware and the R5 C added a fan. Canon discloses no DIGIC X internals (no core counts, no process, no TOPS): any finer breakdown would be fiction, so this entry stops at the documented functional blocks.

#### Inside the signature block: Dual Pixel CMOS AF II + EOS iTR AF X — the focus pipeline

**Inside it.** Canon publishes no DIGIC X block diagram, core counts, process node or per-stage latency — so these are Canon's documented functions in pipeline order, not die sub-blocks. (1) Dual Pixel sensor readout: every pixel on the 45 MP sensor is split into two photodiodes, so each pixel yields both image data and a phase-difference signal — Canon's Dual Pixel CMOS AF technology 'uses every pixel on the imaging sensor to detect focus, and also to capture actual image information'. (2) Phase-difference measurement: the disparity between the two half-pixel signals gives defocus direction and magnitude directly — the system measures focus instead of hunting for it by contrast. (3) AF zone grid: 1,053 automatic AF areas when Face + Tracking or auto selection is active, and 5,940 manually selectable positions for stills (4,500 for movies), covering approximately 100% of the frame horizontally and vertically with select RF and EF lenses — approximately 80% with older EF lenses or Extender types I and II. (4) EOS iTR AF X subject recognition: deep-learning models detect people (eye, face, head) and animals — 'the whole body, face, or eye of cats, dogs, or birds' — and track them regardless of size, posture or face orientation. (5) Servo AF and lens drive: the measured defocus drives the lens directly to focus, and tracking holds the subject across frames at up to 20 fps with the electronic shutter (12 fps mechanical). (6) Low-light floor: the AF system operates down to EV -6, so the loop keeps working in near darkness.

**Trace — one unit of work: one frame of a bird in flight, from readout to lens drive.**
1. **Readout: image and phase data together. **The 45 MP sensor reads out a frame and, in the same readout, the split-pixel pairs deliver a phase-difference signal for every pixel — focus data is a by-product of the photograph, not a separate measurement.
2. **Phase map computed. **DIGIC X turns the half-pixel disparities into a defocus map across the frame: each of the 1,053 automatic AF areas knows how far out of focus it is and in which direction, with no contrast-hunting pass.
3. **Detection runs. **The deep-learning models scan the frame for the trained subjects — a bird's eye, face or body — and pick the target; Canon's animal detection tracks the whole body, face or eye of cats, dogs or birds regardless of size, posture or face orientation.
4. **Target zone chosen. **The AF system selects the zone on the bird's eye (or head, or body where the eye is hidden) from the approximately 100% frame coverage, and Servo AF takes over the tracking.
5. **Lens driven to focus. **The measured defocus moves the lens directly to the focus position — one move, no hunting — and the loop repeats on the next frame at up to 20 fps with the electronic shutter.
6. **Tracking holds across frames. **As the bird crosses the frame, the recognised subject stays locked while the shutter fires; the same loop runs in video, where Dual Pixel CMOS AF is available in all 8K and 4K modes.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the contrast-hunt wall: a contrast AF system must sweep the lens back and forth to find peak sharpness, burning time and frames on every focus change; here focus is measured from the phase map in a single readout, so the lens moves once, directly to focus, anywhere in the frame. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the model-defined subject ceiling — detection only covers the classes Canon trained (people; cats, dogs, birds), and Canon's own footnote warns detection varies with the subject, so the loop's ceiling is the trained model rather than the optics; the everywhere-at-once cost — phase data for the whole frame must be read and processed on every frame at up to 20 fps, which is part of the sensor-plus-processor power that ends up as heat in the 8K story below; and the coverage shrink — with older EF lenses or Extender types I and II the AF area falls to approximately 80% horizontally and vertically, so the 'focus anywhere' promise is lens-dependent.

**Governing numbers.** 1,053 automatic AF areas (Face + Tracking / auto selection); 5,940 manually selectable AF positions for stills, 4,500 for movies; AF coverage approximately 100% horizontal and 100% vertical with select RF and EF lenses, approximately 80% with older EF lenses or Extender types I and II; AF working range down to EV -6 (at 23°C and ISO 100); continuous shooting up to 20 fps with the electronic shutter, up to 12 fps with the mechanical shutter, with AF tracking.

**Primary source.** Canon EOS R5 product page (Canon U.S.A.) — Dual Pixel CMOS AF II 1,053 Automatic AF zones; approximately 100% x 100% AF area coverage; EV -6 low-light autofocus; animal detection developed using deep learning technology; up to 12 fps mechanical and 20 fps electronic shutter; Dual Pixel CMOS AF available in all 8K and 4K modes. Canon EOS R5 C product page (Canon U.S.A.) — 'Canon's Dual Pixel CMOS AF technology uses every pixel on the imaging sensor to detect focus, and also to capture actual image information'. Canon EOS R5 specifications (Canon UK) — AF point selection: 1,053 available AF areas when automatically selected; manual selection 5,940 (stills) / 4,500 (movie) AF positions; AF working range EV -6 – 20.

#### Inside the signature block: The 8K RAW video path — the throughput stress test

**Inside it.** Canon publishes no DIGIC X block diagram, so these are the documented functions of the video path in pipeline order, not die sub-blocks. (1) Full-width sensor readout: the 45 MP sensor reads out the full frame for 8K DCI (8192 x 4320), uncropped, at up to 29.97 fps. (2) RAW stream formation: DIGIC X passes the 12-bit RAW stream through at approximately 2,600 Mbps — about 325 MB/s — with a lighter RAW (Light) variant at approximately 1,700 Mbps. (3) HEVC encode branch: the same readout can instead be encoded in camera as H.265/HEVC — 8K ALL-I at approximately 1,300 Mbps or IPB at approximately 470 Mbps, 10-bit 4:2:2 with Canon Log or HDR PQ; 4K up to 119.88 fps, with 4K ALL-I at approximately 1,880 Mbps. (4) CFexpress Type B write path: the high-bitrate stream is written to the CFexpress Type B card, the camera's high-speed slot, beside a UHS-II SD slot. (5) Overheat control: the camera monitors internal temperature, displays the estimated remaining recording time on standby, and offers an Overheat control setting that conserves battery and can prolong recording.

**Trace — one unit of work: one second of 8K RAW, from readout to the thermal limit.**
1. **Thirty frames read out. **The 45 MP sensor reads out 30 full frames in one second — roughly 1.35 billion pixels a second (45 MP x 30 fps, arithmetic) — each frame carrying both image and Dual Pixel phase data, with autofocus live throughout.
2. **RAW stream formed. **DIGIC X forms the 12-bit RAW stream at approximately 2,600 Mbps, about 325 MB/s, and hands it to the card interface; the lighter RAW (Light) variant runs at approximately 1,700 Mbps.
3. **CFexpress write. **The stream lands on the CFexpress Type B card — the high-speed slot Canon fits for exactly this data rate — while the SD slot takes lower-rate material.
4. **Temperature climbs. **Sensor and processor dissipation heats the fanless body; the camera's remaining-time estimate on standby shrinks as the internal temperature rises, and the Overheat control setting trades battery and standby heat for recording time.
5. **The limit trips. **After approximately 20 minutes of 8K at 23°C from a cold start, the camera stops recording on temperature; ten minutes powered off buys approximately three more minutes of 8K RAW, twenty minutes buys eight.
6. **The 4K120 branch. **The same pipe at 4K 119.88 fps — ALL-I at approximately 1,880 Mbps — stops after approximately 15 minutes on the same thermal budget, while ordinary 4K 29.97 fps carries no temperature restriction at all.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the '8K in a stills body' wall: internal uncropped 8K RAW in a mirrorless camera, with autofocus live in every mode — a capability that had belonged to cinema cameras with fans. Creates the thermal wall in its place: the product is sustained throughput, not peak — approximately 20 minutes of 8K at 23°C, then a cool-down that returns only minutes of recording, and a 29-minute-59-second hard cap above that. The R5 C's answer was a fan; the R5's answer is the recording-time estimate on the standby screen and the Overheat control setting. The architecture's famous constraint is therefore not a missing block but a missing heat path — a fanless body can only shed so much heat.

**Governing numbers.** 8K DCI 8192 x 4320, uncropped, up to 29.97 fps; 12-bit RAW; 8K RAW approximately 2,600 Mbps, 8K RAW (Light) approximately 1,700 Mbps; 8K ALL-I approximately 1,300 Mbps, 8K IPB approximately 470 Mbps; 4K up to 119.88 fps, 4K ALL-I approximately 1,880 Mbps; continuous recording at 23°C from a cold start: 8K (all formats) approximately 20 minutes, 4K 119.88 fps approximately 15 minutes, 4K 29.97 fps no temperature restriction; recovery: 10 minutes powered off returns approximately 3 minutes of 8K RAW, 20 minutes returns approximately 8 minutes; recording stops automatically at 29 minutes 59 seconds.

**Primary source.** Canon EOS R5 product page (Canon U.S.A.) — 8K movies uncropped at up to 29.97 fps; 4K video up to 119.9 fps in 4:2:2 10-bit (H.265) Canon Log; Dual Pixel CMOS AF available in all 8K and 4K modes. Canon EOS R5 specifications (Canon UK) — 8K DCI 8192 x 4320 RAW at 29.97/25/24/23.98 fps; bitrates: 8K RAW approximately 2,600 Mbps, 8K RAW (Light) approximately 1,700 Mbps, 8K ALL-I approximately 1,300 Mbps, 8K IPB approximately 470 Mbps, 4K (119.9p/100p) ALL-I approximately 1,880 Mbps; storage: 1x CFexpress Type B, 1x SD UHS-II. Canon EOS R5 specifications (Canon Iceland) — '8K RAW: 12bit CRM'. Canon support article, 'Precautions about the Camera's Internal Temperature Increases due to Movie Recording (EOS R5/EOS R6)' (sg.canon) — 8K 29.97 fps approximately 20 minutes, 4K 119.88 fps approximately 15 minutes at 23°C; 10 minutes standby returns approximately 3 minutes of 8K, 20 minutes returns approximately 8 minutes; recording stops automatically at 29 min. 59 sec.

#### Down to the primitives: Dual Pixel CMOS AF II + EOS iTR AF X — the focus pipeline

The focus pipeline runs Canon's six documented functions in pipeline order — Dual Pixel sensor readout, phase-difference measurement, the AF zone grid, EOS iTR AF X subject recognition, Servo AF and lens drive, and the EV -6 low-light floor — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (sensor readout staging — image + phase data; AF-result queue to the lens drive)** — The 45 MP sensor reads out image and phase-difference data together, so a readout FIFO stages the frame while the phase map and the detection models work the previous frame, decoupling the sensor readout rate from the AF pipeline's rate — at up to 20 fps the stills burst moves 45 MP x 20 fps, 900 million pixels a second (arithmetic). At the other end the focus decision waits in a queue for the lens drive: the measured defocus is computed in the camera, the lens moves on the mount, and the queue absorbs the rate mismatch between the AF loop and the lens motor. The queue depths and the readout width are not published.

- **SRAM bank / register file (AF-zone defocus store; subject-class config registers; deep-learning weight store)** — The phase map is 1,053 zones of defocus data, so the zone grid lives in an on-chip store — each zone's defocus direction and magnitude held until Servo AF reads it — with config registers holding the photographer's AF mode (Face + Tracking, auto selection, or manual 1-point) and the subject setting (people or animals). The deep-learning models that recognise eyes, faces, heads and animal subjects live in learned weights, held in an SRAM weight store read out as each frame is recognised. The store capacities, banking, port counts and widths are not published.

- **Multiplier array (phase-difference correlation per zone; deep-learning multiply-accumulates)** — Defocus is measured, not hunted: the disparity between each pixel's two half-pixel signals is correlated zone by zone, a multiply-accumulate workload across the 1,053 zones, and the deep-learning subject detection is a second MAC workload — each multiply-accumulate unit taking a weight and an activation and producing a partial product, the array working many in parallel across a layer. The array dimensions, lane count and number format are not published.

- **Adder tree (phase-disparity sums within a zone; MAC accumulation in detection)** — The half-pixel disparities inside one AF zone have to be combined into a single defocus value for that zone, so an adder tree collapses them — the standard construction — and the detection models' partial products are summed the same way into one score per subject candidate. The tree depth and width are not published.

- **Comparator (defocus direction and magnitude; detection-score thresholds; EV -6 low-light floor)** — Choosing where to focus is a comparison: the defocus magnitude in each zone is compared against the in-focus threshold, the detection scores are compared against the subject-class thresholds, and the highest-scoring subject wins. The AF working range Canon publishes — down to EV -6 at 23°C and ISO 100 — is itself a comparator threshold on the low-light side, below which the loop stops trusting the phase signal. The comparator count and widths are not published.

- **Priority encoder / arbiter (AF-zone selection among 1,053 areas; subject priority when several candidates are recognised)** — The focus decision picks one zone, so a priority encoder turns the winning defocus measurement into a zone index — 1,053 zones need an 11-bit index (arithmetic — 2 to the 10th is 1024, below 1,053, and 2 to the 11th is 2048, the smallest power of two above it), not a Canon figure — and when several subjects are recognised an arbiter decides which one gets the lock first. The arbiter policy is not published.

- **Mux / demux (AF-mode select; subject-class select; eye vs face vs head vs body target select)** — One pipeline serves three AF modes, so a mux steers the zone grid to Face + Tracking, auto selection or manual 1-point AF, a second mux selects between the people and animal detection models, and a third selects among the eye, face, head and body outputs once recognition has scored them. The mux widths and select encoding are not published.

- **FSM / controller (AF pipeline sequencer readout to phase map to detect to select to drive to track; Servo AF tracking state machine)** — The six documented functions run in order, so a controller sequences the pipeline — readout, phase map, detection, zone selection, lens drive, tracking — and a Servo AF state machine holds the tracked subject across frames until it is lost or changed. The state count and sequencing are not published.

- **Pipeline registers (between phase-map, detection, selection and lens-drive stages)** — Each AF stage hands its result to the next through pipeline registers, so phase-map computation, detection, zone selection and lens drive can overlap on successive frames instead of running one frame end to end — the structure that lets the loop sustain up to 20 fps with the electronic shutter. The register widths and stage count are not published.

- **Counter (AF-zone index counter over 1,053 zones; manual-position index over 5,940 positions; frame counter at up to 20 fps)** — The pipeline counts what it processes: the AF-zone index counter steps across the 1,053 automatic areas — 11 bits wide by the same arithmetic as the priority encoder — the manual-position index runs to 5,940 selectable positions for stills (4,500 for movies), 13 bits wide by the same arithmetic (2 to the 12th is 4096, below 5,940, and 2 to the 13th is 8192), and a frame counter tracks the sequence at up to 20 fps — 5 bits covering the twenty frames in a second (arithmetic). No other counter width is claimed.

- **Adder (gyro-rate integration for IBIS sensor-shift coordination)** — The AF loop shares the processor with stabilisation: DIGIC X fuses gyro data with lens IS for coordinated control (up to 8 stops with select RF lenses), and the gyro-rate samples are integrated — added, sample by sample — into the sensor-shift position the IBIS loop holds. The integrator width and the gyro sample rate are not published.

- **Synchronizer (sensor readout clock domain vs DIGIC X domain; lens-drive command crossing to the RF/EF mount)** — The sensor readout, DIGIC X and the lens drive do not share one clock, so synchronizers carry the frame into the processor's domain and the focus command out again to the lens, in the standard two-flop construction. The domain frequencies and synchronizer depths are not published.

- **Credit counter (readout-bandwidth budgeting between image data and phase data at up to 20 fps)** — Every frame carries both image and phase data, so a credit counter budgets the shared sensor-readout bandwidth between the two streams at up to 20 fps with the electronic shutter — the everywhere-at-once cost the Level-2 bottleneck section names — holding back one stream when the other's budget is spent. The credit limit and the counter width are not published, so no counter total is claimed. Standard construction.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Canon publishes no DIGIC X block diagram, no core counts, no process node, no TOPS, no queue depths, no stage latencies and no per-stage bit depths, so the primitives below are mapped from the documented functions in pipeline order of the Canon EOS R5 product page, the EOS R5 specifications and the EOS R5 C product page, not from a die diagram. Every product-page, specification-table and support-article figure is already recorded at Level 2; no new chip-specific number is claimed here. The only new numbers are counter widths and a pixel rate computed from published figures and labelled arithmetic. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Down to the primitives: The 8K RAW video path — the throughput stress test

The video path runs Canon's five documented functions in pipeline order — full-width sensor readout, RAW stream formation, the HEVC encode branch, the CFexpress Type B write path and overheat control — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (sensor readout staging at roughly 1.06 billion pixels a second; RAW stream buffer to the CFexpress card)** — The 45 MP sensor reads out 30 full frames a second, so a readout FIFO stages the frame while the RAW formatter and the encoder work the previous one, decoupling the sensor rate from the encode rate. At the far end a stream buffer holds the formed RAW stream for the CFexpress Type B card — the high-speed slot Canon fits for exactly this data rate — absorbing the gap between the engine's output rate and the card's write rate. The queue depths and widths are not published. Arithmetic from published figures: one 8K DCI frame is 8192 x 4320 = 35,389,440 pixels, so 29.97 fps is roughly 1.06 billion pixels a second; at 12 bits per pixel the uncompressed image stream alone is roughly 12.7 Gbps, and the approximately 2,600 Mbps recorded CRM stream is the compression that packs it — about a 4.9:1 reduction, arithmetic, not a Canon figure.

- **SRAM bank / line buffers (RAW working store; HEVC reference-frame store for the IPB branch)** — The RAW stream passes through a working store while it is formed, and the HEVC encode branch needs the frames it predicts from: the IPB mode encodes some frames by reference to others, so a reference-frame store holds the earlier frames until the prediction is done. The store capacities, banking and widths are not published.

- **Multiplier array (HEVC transform coefficients; Canon Log and HDR PQ tone-mapping scaling)** — Encode is multiply work throughout: the HEVC transform multiplies by its coefficients, and the Canon Log and HDR PQ tone curves scale values before the 10-bit 4:2:2 output — all of it landing on multiplier arrays. The array dimensions, lane count and number format are not published.

- **Adder tree (HEVC inverse-transform accumulation; motion-estimation SAD sums for the IPB branch)** — The products the multiplier arrays produce have to be summed: the HEVC inverse transform accumulates its coefficients, and the IPB branch's inter prediction sums absolute differences between the current block and its reference — the SAD that motion estimation is built from — an adder tree collapsing many terms into one score, in the standard construction. The tree depth, the search range and the block sizes are not published.

- **Comparator (thermal-limit threshold; stream-buffer full threshold; bitrate-mode thresholds)** — Recording stops on a comparison: the internal temperature is compared against the thermal limit, and the camera's remaining-time estimate on standby is that comparison made visible. The stream buffer's full flag is a comparator on its fill level, and the choice between the RAW, RAW (Light), ALL-I and IPB branches is a set of thresholds on the requested bitrate. The comparator count and widths are not published; the thermal figures themselves — approximately 20 minutes of 8K, approximately 15 minutes of 4K 119.88 fps at 23°C — are already recorded at Level 2.

- **Barrel shifter (bit-depth scaling from 12-bit RAW to 10-bit 4:2:2 HEVC)** — The 12-bit RAW stream has to be scaled to the 10-bit 4:2:2 HEVC output, so a barrel shifter shifts each value by a variable amount in one step. The shifter width is not published.

- **Mux / demux (RAW vs HEVC path select; ALL-I vs IPB mode select; RAW vs RAW (Light) select; CFexpress vs SD slot select)** — One readout serves several record paths, so a mux steers the stream to the RAW recorder or the HEVC encoder, a second selects ALL-I or IPB inside the encoder, a third selects the full RAW or the lighter RAW (Light) variant, and a fourth steers the finished stream to the CFexpress Type B slot or the UHS-II SD slot. The mux widths and select encoding are not published.

- **FSM / controller (video pipeline sequencer readout to RAW form to encode to write; thermal state machine record to warn to stop to recover)** — The video functions run in order, so a controller sequences readout, RAW formation, encode and write; a thermal state machine walks record, warn, stop and recover — after the limit trips, ten minutes powered off returns approximately three minutes of 8K recording and twenty minutes returns approximately eight. The state counts and sequencing are not published.

- **Pipeline registers (between readout, RAW formation, encode and card-write stages)** — Each video stage hands its result to the next through pipeline registers, so readout, RAW formation, encode and card write can overlap on successive frames instead of running one frame end to end — the structure that sustains roughly 1.06 billion pixels a second at 29.97 fps. The register widths and stage count are not published.

- **Counter (frame counter to the 29-minute-59-second cap; recording-time counter; thermal-recovery timer)** — The camera counts what it records: the 29-minute-59-second automatic stop is a frame counter — 1,799 seconds at 29.97 fps is approximately 53,916 frames, so a 16-bit counter covers it (arithmetic — 2 to the 16th is 65,536, the smallest power of two above it) — and the thermal-recovery intervals of ten and twenty minutes powered off are a second timer in the same controller. No other counter width is claimed.

- **Synchronizer (sensor readout clock domain vs encode domain; card-interface domain)** — The sensor readout, the encode engine and the CFexpress card interface do not share one clock, so synchronizers carry the frame into the encoder's domain and the finished stream out again to the card, in the standard two-flop construction. The domain frequencies and synchronizer depths are not published.

- **Credit counter (CFexpress write-bandwidth budgeting at approximately 325 MB/s; SD-slot budgeting for lower-rate material)** — The approximately 325 MB/s RAW stream (2,600 Mbps divided by 8 — arithmetic, already recorded at Level 2) must not outrun the card, so a credit counter budgets card writes between the RAW stream, the HEVC stream and the SD slot's lower-rate material, holding back the encoder when the write budget is spent. The credit limits and the counter widths are not published, so no counter total is claimed. Standard construction.
