#### Down to the gates: Dual Pixel CMOS AF II + EOS iTR AF X — the focus pipeline

Canon publishes no gate-level structure for DIGIC X — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the focus pipeline, the AF zone grid or the lens-drive loop. The deepest published description is the EOS R5 product page, which documents the six functions in pipeline order, and the EOS R5 specifications, which publish the 1,053-zone AF grid, the 5,940 manual positions, the EV -6 floor and the 20 fps electronic-shutter rate. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors using the primer's bottom layer — the universal gates, the latch and the flip-flop, the 6T SRAM cell, the CAM cell and the full adder — and every gate or transistor figure is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, not a claim about Canon's actual netlist. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, no total is claimed.

- **FIFO / queue (sensor readout staging — image + phase data; AF-result queue to the lens drive)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is a register file of D flip-flops or a small SRAM bank, the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each, incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The 45 MP sensor reads out image and phase-difference data together, so a readout FIFO stages the frame while the phase map and the detection models work the previous frame, decoupling the sensor readout rate from the AF pipeline's rate — at up to 20 fps the stills burst moves 45 MP x 20 fps, 900 million pixels a second (arithmetic). At the other end the focus decision waits in a queue for the lens drive: the measured defocus is computed in the camera, the lens moves on the mount, and the queue absorbs the rate mismatch between the AF loop and the lens motor. The queue depths and the readout width are not published, so the pointer widths — and therefore the counter and comparator totals — are not claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank / register file (AF-zone defocus store; subject-class config registers; deep-learning weight store)** — The working store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. The phase map is 1,053 zones of defocus data, so the zone grid lives in an on-chip store — each zone's defocus direction and magnitude held until Servo AF reads it — with config registers holding the photographer's AF mode (Face + Tracking, auto selection, or manual 1-point) and the subject setting (people or animals), small register files of D flip-flops, about 20–28 transistors each. The deep-learning models that recognise eyes, faces, heads and animal subjects live in learned weights, held in an SRAM weight store read out as each frame is recognised. The store capacities, banking, port counts and widths are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (phase-difference correlation per zone; deep-learning multiply-accumulates)** — A multiplier array is partial-product generation plus an adder tree: each multiply generates partial products with AND gates — one AND gate per bit-pair — and reduces them through full adders, 28 transistors each in the standard-cell form, two half adders of XOR, AND and OR gates. Defocus is measured, not hunted: the disparity between each pixel's two half-pixel signals is correlated zone by zone, a multiply-accumulate workload across the 1,053 zones, and the deep-learning subject detection is a second MAC workload — each multiply-accumulate unit taking a weight and an activation and producing a partial product, the array working many in parallel across a layer. Each is a multiplier array feeding an adder tree. The array dimensions, lane count and number format are not published, so no multiplier total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (phase-disparity sums within a zone; MAC accumulation in detection)** — An adder tree is full adders arranged in a binary reduction: partial sums reduce one stage per halving of their count, each full adder two half adders — 2 XOR, 2 AND and 1 OR gates, about 28 transistors in a standard cell. The half-pixel disparities inside one AF zone have to be combined into a single defocus value for that zone, so an adder tree collapses them — the standard construction — and the detection models' partial products are summed the same way into one score per subject candidate. The tree depth and width are not published, so no adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (defocus direction and magnitude; detection-score thresholds; EV -6 low-light floor)** — A comparator is an XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree for equality, or a subtractor of full adders whose sign bit decides magnitude: equal is all XOR outputs zero, greater-than is a priority chain over the most-significant differing bit. Choosing where to focus is a comparison: the defocus magnitude in each zone is compared against the in-focus threshold, the detection scores are compared against the subject-class thresholds, and the highest-scoring subject wins. The AF working range Canon publishes — down to EV -6 at 23°C and ISO 100 — is itself a comparator threshold on the low-light side, below which the loop stops trusting the phase signal. The comparator count and widths are not published, so no comparator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Priority encoder / arbiter (AF-zone selection among 1,053 areas; subject priority when several candidates are recognised)** — A priority encoder is a tree of OR gates with a priority chain: N request lines reduce to a grant index naming the highest-priority active request, with a round-robin variant adding a rotating priority register of D flip-flops. The focus decision picks one zone, so a priority encoder turns the winning defocus measurement into a zone index — 1,053 zones need an 11-bit index (arithmetic — 2 to the 10th is 1024, below 1,053, and 2 to the 11th is 2048, the smallest power of two above it) — and when several subjects are recognised an arbiter decides which one gets the lock first. The arbiter policy is not published, so no further encoder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (AF-mode select; subject-class select; eye vs face vs head vs body target select)** — A mux is a transmission-gate tree or a NAND/NOR tree: a 2:1 mux is 2 transistors per input leg as transmission gates, and an N:1 mux is N minus 1 2:1 muxes arranged as a tree in log2(N) stages, selected by a decoder. One pipeline serves three AF modes, so a mux steers the zone grid to Face + Tracking, auto selection or manual 1-point AF — a 3:1 select, 2 2:1 muxes in 2 stages by arithmetic — a second mux selects between the people and animal detection models, a 2:1 select, and a third selects among the eye, face, head and body outputs once recognition has scored them — a 4:1 select, 3 2:1 muxes in 2 stages by arithmetic. The mux widths and select encoding are not published, so no further mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (AF pipeline sequencer readout to phase map to detect to select to drive to track; Servo AF tracking state machine)** — A finite-state machine is state bits plus next-state logic plus output logic: the state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and the next-state and output logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the current state and the inputs. The six documented functions run in order, so a controller sequences the pipeline — readout, phase map, detection, zone selection, lens drive, tracking — and a Servo AF state machine holds the tracked subject across frames until it is lost or changed. That sequencer is a state machine of this form. Its state count and the sequencing are not published, so no state-bit total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (between phase-map, detection, selection and lens-drive stages)** — A pipeline register is one D flip-flop per bit — about 20–28 transistors each, two cross-coupled latch stages — latched between stages so the next stage can start while the current stage's result is held. Each AF stage hands its result to the next through pipeline registers, so phase-map computation, detection, zone selection and lens drive can overlap on successive frames instead of running one frame end to end — the structure that lets the loop sustain up to 20 fps with the electronic shutter. The register widths and the stage count are not published, so no register total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (AF-zone index counter over 1,053 zones; manual-position index over 5,940 positions; frame counter at up to 20 fps)** — A counter is N D flip-flops plus N full adders in a ripple or look-ahead chain, incrementing on each clock, with a comparator resetting it at the terminal count. The pipeline counts what it processes: the AF-zone index counter steps across the 1,053 automatic areas — 11 bits wide by the same arithmetic as the priority encoder, being 11 D flip-flops (220–308 transistors) plus 11 full adders (308 transistors) — the manual-position index runs to 5,940 selectable positions for stills (4,500 for movies), 13 bits wide by the same arithmetic (2 to the 12th is 4096, below 5,940, and 2 to the 13th is 8192), being 13 D flip-flops (260–364 transistors) plus 13 full adders (364 transistors) — and a frame counter tracks the sequence at up to 20 fps — 5 bits covering the twenty frames in a second, being 5 D flip-flops (100–140 transistors) plus 5 full adders (140 transistors). All three widths are arithmetic derived from the published figures and labelled as such; the counter widths themselves are not published. Standard construction.
- **Adder (gyro-rate integration for IBIS sensor-shift coordination)** — An adder is a chain of full adders — each full adder two half adders, 2 XOR, 2 AND and 1 OR gates, about 28 transistors in a standard cell — adding two values bit by bit with the carry rippling or looking ahead from the least-significant bit. The AF loop shares the processor with stabilisation: DIGIC X fuses gyro data with lens IS for coordinated control (up to 8 stops with select RF lenses), and the gyro-rate samples are integrated — added, sample by sample — into the sensor-shift position the IBIS loop holds. The integrator width and the gyro sample rate are not published, so no adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (sensor readout clock domain vs DIGIC X domain; lens-drive command crossing to the RF/EF mount)** — A synchronizer is two D flip-flops in series — about 20–28 transistors each — the first sampling the incoming signal in the new clock domain and the second re-sampling it a cycle later so metastability resolves before the value is used; a multi-bit crossing is an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers, the pointers changing one bit at a time so a sampled pointer is never more than one count stale. The sensor readout, DIGIC X and the lens drive do not share one clock, so synchronizers carry the frame into the processor's domain and the focus command out again to the lens, in the standard two-flop construction. The domain frequencies and synchronizer depths are not published, so no synchronizer total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (readout-bandwidth budgeting between image data and phase data at up to 20 fps)** — A credit counter is a down-counter of D flip-flops and full adders with a comparator: it starts at the budget, decrements on each issued request and increments on each returned credit, and a comparator blocks new requests when the count reaches zero. Every frame carries both image and phase data, so a credit counter budgets the shared sensor-readout bandwidth between the two streams at up to 20 fps with the electronic shutter — the everywhere-at-once cost the Level-2 bottleneck section names — holding back one stream when the other's budget is spent. The credit limit and the counter width are not published, so no counter total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Canon publishes the Dual Pixel CMOS AF II pipeline at function level only — sensor readout, phase-difference measurement, the AF zone grid, EOS iTR AF X subject recognition, Servo AF and lens drive, and the EV -6 low-light floor (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the pipeline appears in any Canon source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Canon's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable).

#### Down to the gates: The 8K RAW video path — the throughput stress test

Canon publishes no gate-level structure for the 8K RAW video path — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the readout staging, the RAW formatter, the HEVC encode branch or the CFexpress write path. The deepest published description is the EOS R5 product page, which documents the five functions in pipeline order, and the EOS R5 specifications, which publish the 8K DCI frame, the 12-bit RAW stream, the approximately 2,600 Mbps bitrate and the 29-minute-59-second cap, with the Canon support article publishing the approximately 20-minute thermal limit and the recovery intervals. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors using the primer's bottom layer — the universal gates, the latch and the flip-flop, the 6T SRAM cell, the CAM cell and the full adder — and every gate or transistor figure is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, not a claim about Canon's actual netlist. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, no total is claimed.

- **FIFO / queue (sensor readout staging at roughly 1.06 billion pixels a second; RAW stream buffer to the CFexpress card)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is a register file of D flip-flops or a small SRAM bank, the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each, incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The 45 MP sensor reads out 30 full frames a second, so a readout FIFO stages the frame while the RAW formatter and the encoder work the previous one, decoupling the sensor rate from the encode rate. At the far end a stream buffer holds the formed RAW stream for the CFexpress Type B card — the high-speed slot Canon fits for exactly this data rate — absorbing the gap between the engine's output rate and the card's write rate. The queue depths and widths are not published, so the pointer widths — and therefore the counter and comparator totals — are not claimed. Arithmetic from published figures: one 8K DCI frame is 8192 x 4320 = 35,389,440 pixels, so 29.97 fps is roughly 1.06 billion pixels a second; at 12 bits per pixel the uncompressed image stream alone is roughly 12.7 Gbps, and the approximately 2,600 Mbps recorded CRM stream is the compression that packs it — about a 4.9:1 reduction, arithmetic, not a Canon figure. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank / line buffers (RAW working store; HEVC reference-frame store for the IPB branch)** — The working store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. The RAW stream passes through a working store while it is formed, and the HEVC encode branch needs the frames it predicts from: the IPB mode encodes some frames by reference to others, so a reference-frame store holds the earlier frames until the prediction is done. The store capacities, banking and widths are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (HEVC transform coefficients; Canon Log and HDR PQ tone-mapping scaling)** — A multiplier array is partial-product generation plus an adder tree: each multiply generates partial products with AND gates — one AND gate per bit-pair — and reduces them through full adders, 28 transistors each in the standard-cell form, two half adders of XOR, AND and OR gates. Encode is multiply work throughout: the HEVC transform multiplies by its coefficients, and the Canon Log and HDR PQ tone curves scale values before the 10-bit 4:2:2 output — all of it landing on multiplier arrays. Each is a multiplier array feeding an adder tree. The array dimensions, lane count and number format are not published, so no multiplier total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (HEVC inverse-transform accumulation; motion-estimation SAD sums for the IPB branch)** — An adder tree is full adders arranged in a binary reduction: partial sums reduce one stage per halving of their count, each full adder two half adders — 2 XOR, 2 AND and 1 OR gates, about 28 transistors in a standard cell. The products the multiplier arrays produce have to be summed: the HEVC inverse transform accumulates its coefficients, and the IPB branch's inter prediction sums absolute differences between the current block and its reference — the SAD that motion estimation is built from — an adder tree collapsing many terms into one score, in the standard construction. The tree depth, the search range and the block sizes are not published, so no adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (thermal-limit threshold; stream-buffer full threshold; bitrate-mode thresholds)** — A comparator is an XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree for equality, or a subtractor of full adders whose sign bit decides magnitude: equal is all XOR outputs zero, greater-than is a priority chain over the most-significant differing bit. Recording stops on a comparison: the internal temperature is compared against the thermal limit, and the camera's remaining-time estimate on standby is that comparison made visible. The stream buffer's full flag is a comparator on its fill level, and the choice between the RAW, RAW (Light), ALL-I and IPB branches is a set of thresholds on the requested bitrate. The comparator count and widths are not published, so no comparator total is claimed; the thermal figures themselves — approximately 20 minutes of 8K, approximately 15 minutes of 4K 119.88 fps at 23°C — are already recorded at Level 2. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (bit-depth scaling from 12-bit RAW to 10-bit 4:2:2 HEVC)** — A barrel shifter is a mux tree: shifting an N-bit value by a variable amount takes log2(N) stages of 2:1 muxes, each mux a transmission-gate pair (2 transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree. The 12-bit RAW stream has to be scaled to the 10-bit 4:2:2 HEVC output, so a barrel shifter shifts each value by a variable amount in one step — a 12-bit shifter is 4 stages of 2:1 muxes by arithmetic, since 2 to the power 4 is 16, the smallest power of two above 12. The shifter width is not published, so no shifter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (RAW vs HEVC path select; ALL-I vs IPB mode select; RAW vs RAW (Light) select; CFexpress vs SD slot select)** — A mux is a transmission-gate tree or a NAND/NOR tree: a 2:1 mux is 2 transistors per input leg as transmission gates, and an N:1 mux is N minus 1 2:1 muxes arranged as a tree in log2(N) stages, selected by a decoder. One readout serves several record paths, so a mux steers the stream to the RAW recorder or the HEVC encoder, a second selects ALL-I or IPB inside the encoder, a third selects the full RAW or the lighter RAW (Light) variant, and a fourth steers the finished stream to the CFexpress Type B slot or the UHS-II SD slot — four 2:1 selects by arithmetic. The mux widths and select encoding are not published, so no further mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (video pipeline sequencer readout to RAW form to encode to write; thermal state machine record to warn to stop to recover)** — A finite-state machine is state bits plus next-state logic plus output logic: the state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and the next-state and output logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the current state and the inputs. The video functions run in order, so a controller sequences readout, RAW formation, encode and write; a thermal state machine walks record, warn, stop and recover — after the limit trips, ten minutes powered off returns approximately three minutes of 8K recording and twenty minutes returns approximately eight. Each is a state machine of this form. The state counts and sequencing are not published, so no state-bit total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (between readout, RAW formation, encode and card-write stages)** — A pipeline register is one D flip-flop per bit — about 20–28 transistors each, two cross-coupled latch stages — latched between stages so the next stage can start while the current stage's result is held. Each video stage hands its result to the next through pipeline registers, so readout, RAW formation, encode and card write can overlap on successive frames instead of running one frame end to end — the structure that sustains roughly 1.06 billion pixels a second at 29.97 fps. The register widths and the stage count are not published, so no register total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (frame counter to the 29-minute-59-second cap; recording-time counter; thermal-recovery timer)** — A counter is N D flip-flops plus N full adders in a ripple or look-ahead chain, incrementing on each clock, with a comparator resetting it at the terminal count. The camera counts what it records: the 29-minute-59-second automatic stop is a frame counter — 1,799 seconds at 29.97 fps is approximately 53,916 frames, so a 16-bit counter covers it (arithmetic — 2 to the 16th is 65,536, the smallest power of two above it), being 16 D flip-flops (320–448 transistors) plus 16 full adders (448 transistors) — and the thermal-recovery intervals of ten and twenty minutes powered off are a second timer in the same controller. No other counter width is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (sensor readout clock domain vs encode domain; card-interface domain)** — A synchronizer is two D flip-flops in series — about 20–28 transistors each — the first sampling the incoming signal in the new clock domain and the second re-sampling it a cycle later so metastability resolves before the value is used; a multi-bit crossing is an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers, the pointers changing one bit at a time so a sampled pointer is never more than one count stale. The sensor readout, the encode engine and the CFexpress card interface do not share one clock, so synchronizers carry the frame into the encoder's domain and the finished stream out again to the card, in the standard two-flop construction. The domain frequencies and synchronizer depths are not published, so no synchronizer total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (CFexpress write-bandwidth budgeting at approximately 325 MB/s; SD-slot budgeting for lower-rate material)** — A credit counter is a down-counter of D flip-flops and full adders with a comparator: it starts at the budget, decrements on each issued request and increments on each returned credit, and a comparator blocks new requests when the count reaches zero. The approximately 325 MB/s RAW stream (2,600 Mbps divided by 8 — arithmetic, already recorded at Level 2) must not outrun the card, so a credit counter budgets card writes between the RAW stream, the HEVC stream and the SD slot's lower-rate material, holding back the encoder when the write budget is spent. The credit limits and the counter widths are not published, so no counter total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Canon publishes the 8K RAW video path at function level only — full-width sensor readout, RAW stream formation, the HEVC encode branch, the CFexpress Type B write path and overheat control (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the path appears in any Canon source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Canon's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable).

### MediaTek Imagiq 790 (Dimensity 9000)

**Specs (wiki card).** 18-bit HDR ISP · 9 Gpixel/s · 320 MP max

**Building blocks.**
- **Triple 18-bit HDR-ISP pipelines ★** — Three ISP pipelines running 18-bit HDR simultaneously — the first design to record HDR video on three cameras at once (three exposures per frame), so wide/tele/ultrawide capture the same HDR moment instead of taking turns
- **9 Gpixel/s throughput engine** — The sizing figure MediaTek leads with: 9 billion pixels per second through the pipeline, enabling a single 320 MP capture — the largest sensor support in a phone at launch
- **RGBW sensor path** — Native handling of RGBW sensors on the following generation's variant aside, the 790's front-end is built for exotic CFA layouts alongside Bayer — reconstructing full colour without a wasteful intermediate conversion (RGBW fusion is specified for the 790 in MediaTek's Dimensity 9000 material as part of its sensor support)
- **AI-NR block (with APU 590)** — AI noise reduction executed with the SoC's APU: 4K HDR video with AI-NR, and photo AI-NR twice as fast as the previous generation — denoising as a learned stage inside the ISP's budget
- **AI 3A + Video EIS/HDR stages** — AI-AE/AF/AWB statistics, video bokeh, EIS and AI shutter as named pipeline functions in MediaTek's specification

**The piece that makes it special.** Three cameras, one HDR instant. Rival ISPs time-sliced their HDR pipelines between lenses; Imagiq 790's triple-pipeline design records three 18-bit HDR streams simultaneously, which quietly changes multi-camera UX — zoom transitions stop re-exposing. The correction below matters for the record: Imagiq 790 belongs to the Dimensity 9000 (2021); the Dimensity 9200 line moved to Imagiq 890, and this wiki previously filed the 790 under the 9200+.

**How work flows.** Three sensors stream: Wide, main and tele cameras feed the three 18-bit pipelines concurrently. Per-frame HDR fusion: Three exposures per frame fuse in-pipeline at 18-bit depth. AI stages apply: APU-assisted noise reduction and AI 3A tune each stream. One moment, three focal lengths: All streams record simultaneously — switching views in the final video needs no exposure ramp.

**Trade-off accepted.** Spec-sheet maximalism. 320 MP support and 9 Gpixel/s are ceilings no shipping phone of the generation used in full, and 'simultaneous triple HDR' needs three HDR sensors fitted — the architecture enables a camera system most OEMs only partially built. MediaTek publishes features and ceilings, not the ISP's internal block diagram.

#### Inside the signature block: Triple 18-bit HDR-ISP pipelines — three cameras, one HDR instant

**Inside it.** MediaTek publishes no Imagiq 790 block diagram, no per-stage latency, no queue depths and no per-stage bit depths — so these are MediaTek's documented functions in pipeline order, not die sub-blocks. (1) Three sensor front-ends: the wide, standard and zoom cameras each feed one of three 18-bit HDR-ISP pipelines, so three streams enter concurrently instead of taking turns. (2) Three-exposure HDR fusion: each pipeline merges three exposures into each frame at 18-bit depth — MediaTek's blog puts it as 'the chip can record frames with three exposures merged into each frame for accurate HDR' and 'each pixel captures 18 bits of data'. (3) AI 3A statistics: AI-AE, AI-AF and AI-AWB tune exposure, focus and white balance per stream, with AI-HDR and AI-FD (face detection) as named functions in MediaTek's camera-features list. (4) Video EIS and video bokeh: stabilisation and background-blur stages run in the pipeline on the fused stream. (5) AI shutter: the capture-timing stage that picks the frame. (6) 2X lossless zoom: the crop path that reaches into the high-resolution stream for a 2x zoom without a digital-zoom quality collapse. (7) 4K output: the fused streams exit to the video encoder at a maximum video-capture resolution of 4K (3840 x 2160).

**Trace — one unit of work: one frame of triple-camera HDR video at a concert — wide, standard and zoom.**
1. **Three sensors expose at once. **The wide, standard and zoom cameras each capture three exposures for the same instant — nine exposures in total (3 x 3, arithmetic) — and feed them into the three 18-bit pipelines concurrently; no camera waits for another's pipeline slot.
2. **Nine exposures enter the pipelines. **Each pipeline takes its camera's three exposures at 18-bit depth — 18 bits of data per pixel — inside the shared 9 Gpixel/s throughput budget, so the three streams are in flight at the same time rather than time-sliced.
3. **Three exposures fuse per frame. **Inside each pipeline the three exposures merge into one HDR frame at 18-bit depth, recovering highlight and shadow detail a single exposure would clip — the fusion MediaTek describes as three exposures merged into each frame for accurate HDR.
4. **AI 3A tunes each stream. **AI-AE sets exposure, AI-AF holds focus and AI-AWB sets white balance per camera, with AI-HDR and AI-FD shaping the frame — the learned statistics stage that replaces fixed 3A tables.
5. **EIS, bokeh and shutter apply. **Video EIS stabilises the fused stream, video bokeh separates the subject where requested, and the AI shutter picks the capture instant — all before the frame leaves the ISP.
6. **Three HDR streams exit together. **All three cameras' HDR video records simultaneously at up to 4K, so the editor — or the livestream viewer picking a camera — can switch between wide, standard and zoom without an exposure ramp, because every focal length captured the same HDR instant.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the time-sliced HDR wall: a single-pipeline ISP can only run HDR on one camera at a time, so multi-camera video re-exposed on every lens switch and the 'other' cameras recorded flat or waited; here three pipelines run at once, so the same HDR instant exists at three focal lengths and switching views costs nothing. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the shared throughput budget — 9 Gpixel/s is one budget split three ways, so resolution, frame rate and camera count trade against each other and the 320 MP ceiling is a stills figure, not a three-camera video figure; the 4K ceiling — despite the 320 MP sensor support, maximum video capture is 4K (3840 x 2160), so the triple-HDR video story is a 4K story and there is no 8K video path; and the sensor-fit wall — the feature needs three HDR-capable sensors fitted, and most Dimensity 9000 phones only partially built the three-camera system the architecture enables.

**Governing numbers.** 9 Gpixel/s ISP throughput; 18 bits of data per pixel; three cameras recording simultaneously, three exposures per frame; 320 MP maximum single-camera sensor; maximum video capture 4K (3840 x 2160); 2X lossless zoom.

**Primary source.** MediaTek Dimensity 9000 product page (MediaTek) — 'A flagship 18-bit HDR-ISP design gives users the first opportunity to capture video on three cameras simultaneously'; 'Most Powerful 9Gpixel/s ISP'; 'World's 1st simultaneous triple camera 18-bit HDR video recording (three cameras recording with three exposures per frame)'; 'World's 1st 320MP camera support for smartphones'; 'AI-NR photo – twice as fast as the previous generation'; '4K HDR Video + AI-NR'; '2X lossless zoom'; 'Unique APU-ISP fusion delivers unparalleled capture speeds and image quality.' MediaTek blog, '19 Best Features of the Dimensity 9000' — 'The 18-bit HDR ISP design enables users to capture HDR video from three cameras simultaneously. With a remarkable 9Gpixel/s ISP, the chip can record frames with three exposures merged into each frame for accurate HDR. Each pixel captures 18 bits of data, offering professional-grade raw details.'

#### Down to the primitives: Triple 18-bit HDR-ISP pipelines — three cameras, one HDR instant

The triple-pipeline block runs MediaTek's seven documented functions in pipeline order — three sensor front-ends, three-exposure HDR fusion, AI 3A statistics, video EIS and bokeh, the AI shutter, 2X lossless zoom and the 4K output — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (sensor readout staging — three streams in flight; HDR-frame queue to the video encoder)** — Three cameras expose at once, so a readout FIFO stages each stream while the fusion stage works the previous frame, decoupling the sensor readout rate from the fusion rate — the three pipelines are in flight at the same time rather than time-sliced. At the far end the fused HDR frame waits in a queue for the video encoder, absorbing the rate mismatch between the ISP and the encoder. The queue depths and the readout width are not published. Arithmetic from published figures: one 4K frame is 3840 x 2160 = 8,294,400 pixels, so three exposures per frame is 24,883,200 pixel-equivalents per camera, and three cameras together move 74,649,600 pixel-equivalents per instant — at 30 fps that is roughly 2.24 Gpixel/s, at 60 fps roughly 4.48 Gpixel/s, both inside the 9 Gpixel/s budget MediaTek publishes.

- **SRAM bank / line buffers (per-pipeline exposure-frame store for three-exposure fusion; 320 MP stills staging)** — Each pipeline merges three exposures into one frame, so the exposures live in an on-chip store until the fusion is done — the short exposure, the mid exposure and the long exposure held side by side at 18-bit depth — and a single 320 MP still needs the same store to hold the frame while it is processed. The store capacities, banking, port counts and widths are not published. Arithmetic from published figures: one 320 MP frame at 18 bits of data per pixel is 5,760,000,000 bits, 720 MB, before any compression.

- **Multiplier array (HDR fusion exposure weighting; tone-mapping scaling)** — Fusing three exposures is multiply work: each exposure is weighted before the merge — the long exposure scaled down where it saturates, the short exposure scaled up where it is dark — and the merged 18-bit frame is tone-mapped down toward the output, another scaling pass. The array dimensions, lane count and number format are not published.

- **Adder tree (three-exposure merge sums per pixel; AI 3A statistics accumulation)** — The weighted exposures inside one pixel have to be combined into a single HDR value for that pixel, so an adder tree collapses them — the standard construction — and the AI 3A statistics stage accumulates its exposure, focus and white-balance measurements the same way across the frame. The tree depth and width are not published.

- **Comparator (highlight and shadow clip thresholds; exposure-selection thresholds; stills vs video path thresholds)** — Choosing which exposure contributes to a pixel is a comparison: the long exposure is clipped where it saturates, the short exposure where it falls into noise, and the merge keeps the exposure that is valid at that pixel. The 320 MP stills ceiling against the 4K video ceiling is a second threshold — the same pipelines serve a stills path and a video path, and the mode selects between them. The comparator count and widths are not published.

- **Priority encoder / arbiter (three-pipeline arbitration over the shared 9 Gpixel/s budget; camera-stream priority)** — Three pipelines share one 9 Gpixel/s budget, so an arbiter decides which pipeline's pixels move next when all three are ready at once — the shared-budget cost the Level-2 bottleneck section names — and a priority encoder turns the winning pipeline's request into the stream index the downstream stages see. Split evenly the budget is 3 Gpixel/s per pipeline (arithmetic), but MediaTek publishes no allocation policy, so no fixed split is claimed. The arbiter policy is not published.

- **Mux / demux (camera select wide vs standard vs zoom; exposure select; stills vs video path select; 2X zoom crop select)** — One set of pipelines serves three cameras, so a mux steers each sensor front-end to its pipeline, a second selects among the three exposures inside the fusion, a third steers the fused stream to the stills path or the 4K video path, and a fourth selects the 2X lossless-zoom crop out of the high-resolution stream. The mux widths and select encoding are not published.

- **FSM / controller (per-pipeline sequencer expose to fuse to 3A to EIS to output; triple-pipeline synchronisation controller)** — The seven documented functions run in order, so a controller sequences each pipeline — expose, fuse, 3A, EIS and bokeh, shutter, zoom, output — and a second controller keeps the three pipelines on the same instant, so the wide, standard and zoom streams stay frame-aligned for the editor or the livestream viewer switching between them. The state count and sequencing are not published.

- **Pipeline registers (between fusion, 3A, EIS and output stages)** — Each ISP stage hands its result to the next through pipeline registers, so exposure fusion, AI 3A, EIS and output can overlap on successive frames instead of running one frame end to end — the structure that lets the triple-pipeline block sustain its share of the 9 Gpixel/s budget. #### Down to the gates: Triple 18-bit HDR-ISP pipelines — three cameras, one HDR instant

MediaTek publishes no gate-level structure for Imagiq 790 — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the triple-pipeline block, the HDR fusion stage or the AI 3A statistics. The deepest published description is the Dimensity 9000 product page, which documents the seven functions in pipeline order, and the Dimensity 9000 specifications, which publish the 9 Gpixel/s ISP throughput, the 18-bit depth, the 320 MP sensor ceiling and the 4K maximum video-capture resolution. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors using the primer's bottom layer — the universal gates, the latch and the flip-flop, the 6T SRAM cell, the CAM cell and the full adder — and every gate or transistor figure is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, not a claim about MediaTek's actual netlist. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, no total is claimed.

- **FIFO / queue (sensor readout staging — three streams in flight; HDR-frame queue to the video encoder)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is a register file of D flip-flops or a small SRAM bank, the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each, incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. Three cameras expose at once, so a readout FIFO stages each stream while the fusion stage works the previous frame, decoupling the sensor readout rate from the fusion rate — the three pipelines are in flight at the same time rather than time-sliced. At the far end the fused HDR frame waits in a queue for the video encoder, absorbing the rate mismatch between the ISP and the encoder. The queue depths and the readout width are not published, so the pointer widths — and therefore the counter and comparator totals — are not claimed. Arithmetic from published figures: one 4K frame is 3840 x 2160 = 8,294,400 pixels, so three exposures per frame is 24,883,200 pixel-equivalents per camera, and three cameras together move 74,649,600 pixel-equivalents per instant — at 30 fps that is roughly 2.24 Gpixel/s, at 60 fps roughly 4.48 Gpixel/s, both inside the 9 Gpixel/s budget MediaTek publishes. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank / line buffers (per-pipeline exposure-frame store for three-exposure fusion; 320 MP stills staging)** — The working store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. Each pipeline merges three exposures into one frame, so the exposures live in an on-chip store until the fusion is done — the short exposure, the mid exposure and the long exposure held side by side at 18-bit depth — and a single 320 MP still needs the same store to hold the frame while it is processed. The store capacities, banking, port counts and widths are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Arithmetic from published figures: one 320 MP frame at 18 bits of data per pixel is 5,760,000,000 bits, 720 MB, before any compression. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (HDR fusion exposure weighting; tone-mapping scaling)** — A multiplier array is partial-product generation plus an adder tree: each multiply generates partial products with AND gates — one AND gate per bit-pair — and reduces them through full adders, 28 transistors each in the standard-cell form, two half adders of XOR, AND and OR gates. Fusing three exposures is multiply work: each exposure is weighted before the merge — the long exposure scaled down where it saturates, the short exposure scaled up where it is dark — and the merged 18-bit frame is tone-mapped down toward the output, another scaling pass. Each is a multiplier array feeding an adder tree. The array dimensions, lane count and number format are not published, so no multiplier total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (three-exposure merge sums per pixel; AI 3A statistics accumulation)** — An adder tree is full adders arranged in a binary reduction: partial sums reduce one stage per halving of their count, each full adder two half adders — 2 XOR, 2 AND and 1 OR gates, about 28 transistors in a standard cell. The weighted exposures inside one pixel have to be combined into a single HDR value for that pixel, so an adder tree collapses them — the standard construction — and the AI 3A statistics stage accumulates its exposure, focus and white-balance measurements the same way across the frame. The tree depth and width are not published, so no adder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (highlight and shadow clip thresholds; exposure-selection thresholds; stills vs video path thresholds)** — A comparator is an XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree for equality, or a subtractor of full adders whose sign bit decides magnitude: equal is all XOR outputs zero, greater-than is a priority chain over the most-significant differing bit. Choosing which exposure contributes to a pixel is a comparison: the long exposure is clipped where it saturates, the short exposure where it falls into noise, and the merge keeps the exposure that is valid at that pixel. The 320 MP stills ceiling against the 4K video ceiling is a second threshold — the same pipelines serve a stills path and a video path, and the mode selects between them. The comparator count and widths are not published, so no comparator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Priority encoder / arbiter (three-pipeline arbitration over the shared 9 Gpixel/s budget; camera-stream priority)** — A priority encoder is a tree of OR gates with a priority chain: N request lines reduce to a grant index naming the highest-priority active request, with a round-robin variant adding a rotating priority register of D flip-flops. Three pipelines share one 9 Gpixel/s budget, so an arbiter decides which pipeline's pixels move next when all three are ready at once — the shared-budget cost the Level-2 bottleneck section names — and a priority encoder turns the winning pipeline's request into the stream index the downstream stages see — a 3-way select needs a 2-bit index (arithmetic — 2 to the 1st is 2, below 3, and 2 to the 2nd is 4, the smallest power of two above it). Split evenly the budget is 3 Gpixel/s per pipeline (arithmetic), but MediaTek publishes no allocation policy, so no fixed split is claimed. The arbiter policy is not published. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (camera select wide vs standard vs zoom; exposure select; stills vs video path select; 2X zoom crop select)** — A mux is a transmission-gate tree or a NAND/NOR tree: a 2:1 mux is 2 transistors per input leg as transmission gates, and an N:1 mux is N minus 1 2:1 muxes arranged as a tree in log2(N) stages, selected by a decoder. One set of pipelines serves three cameras, so a mux steers each sensor front-end to its pipeline — a 3:1 select, 2 2:1 muxes in 2 stages by arithmetic — a second selects among the three exposures inside the fusion, also a 3:1 select, a third steers the fused stream to the stills path or the 4K video path, a 2:1 select, and a fourth selects the 2X lossless-zoom crop out of the high-resolution stream, a 2:1 select — six 2:1 muxes in total by arithmetic. The mux widths and select encoding are not published, so no further mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (per-pipeline sequencer expose to fuse to 3A to EIS to output; triple-pipeline synchronisation controller)** — A finite-state machine is state bits plus next-state logic plus output logic: the state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and the next-state and output logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the current state and the inputs. The seven documented functions run in order, so a controller sequences each pipeline — expose, fuse, 3A, EIS and bokeh, shutter, zoom, output — and a second controller keeps the three pipelines on the same instant, so the wide, standard and zoom streams stay frame-aligned for the editor or the livestream viewer switching between them. Each is a state machine of this form. The state count and sequencing are not published, so no state-bit total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (between fusion, 3A, EIS and output stages)** — A pipeline register is one D flip-flop per bit — about 20–28 transistors each, two cross-coupled latch stages — latched between stages so the next stage can start while the current stage's result is held. Each ISP stage hands its result to the next through pipeline registers, so exposure fusion, AI 3A, EIS and output can overlap on successive frames instead of running one frame end to end — the structure that lets the triple-pipeline block sustain its share of the 9 Gpixel/s budget. The register widths and stage count are not published, so no register total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (exposure index over 3 exposures; camera index over 3 cameras; pixel counter to the 320 MP ceiling; frame counter)** — A counter is N D flip-flops plus N full adders in a ripple or look-ahead chain, incrementing on each clock, with a comparator resetting it at the terminal count. The pipeline counts what it processes: the exposure index steps across the three exposures per frame — 2 bits wide (arithmetic, 2 to the 1st is 2, below 3, and 2 to the 2nd is 4, the smallest power of two above it), being 2 D flip-flops (40–56 transistors) plus 2 full adders (56 transistors) — the camera index steps across the three pipelines, also 2 bits by the same arithmetic, being 2 D flip-flops (40–56 transistors) plus 2 full adders (56 transistors) — and the pixel counter runs to the 320 MP ceiling, 29 bits wide (arithmetic — 2 to the 28th is 268,435,456, below 320,000,000, and 2 to the 29th is 536,870,912), being 29 D flip-flops (580–812 transistors) plus 29 full adders (812 transistors). All three widths are arithmetic derived from the published figures and labelled as such; the counter widths themselves are not published. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (18-bit internal depth to 10-bit 4K HDR output scaling)** — A barrel shifter is a mux tree: shifting an N-bit value by a variable amount takes log2(N) stages of 2:1 muxes, each mux a transmission-gate pair (2 transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree. The fused frame is 18 bits per pixel inside the pipeline, but the 4K HDR video output is a narrower depth, so a barrel shifter shifts each value by a variable amount in one step to scale the depth down — an 18-bit shifter is 5 stages of 2:1 muxes by arithmetic, since 2 to the power 4 is 16, below 18, and 2 to the power 5 is 32, the smallest power of two above it. The shifter width is not published, so no shifter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (three sensor clock domains vs ISP domain; APU handoff crossing to the APU 590)** — A synchronizer is two D flip-flops in series — about 20–28 transistors each — the first sampling the incoming signal in the new clock domain and the second re-sampling it a cycle later so metastability resolves before the value is used; a multi-bit crossing is an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers, the pointers changing one bit at a time so a sampled pointer is never more than one count stale. The three sensors, the ISP and the APU 590 do not share one clock, so synchronizers carry each frame into the ISP's domain and the frame for AI-NR out again to the APU, in the standard two-flop construction. The domain frequencies and synchronizer depths are not published, so no synchronizer total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (shared 9 Gpixel/s budget allocation across the three pipelines)** — A credit counter is a down-counter of D flip-flops and full adders with a comparator: it starts at the budget, decrements on each issued request and increments on each returned credit, and a comparator blocks new requests when the count reaches zero. The 9 Gpixel/s budget is one budget split three ways, so a credit counter allocates throughput credits to the three pipelines — at 18 bits per pixel the budget is 162 Gbit/s of pixel data (arithmetic, 9 Gpixel/s x 18 bits), and one 4K frame at 18 bits is roughly 149.3 Mbit (arithmetic, 8,294,400 pixels x 18 bits) — holding back a pipeline when its credits are spent so the other two keep their share. The credit limits and the counter widths are not published, so no counter total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: MediaTek publishes the triple 18-bit HDR-ISP pipelines at function level only — three sensor front-ends, three-exposure HDR fusion, AI 3A statistics, video EIS and bokeh, the AI shutter, 2X lossless zoom and the 4K output (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the block appears in any MediaTek source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about MediaTek's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable).

#### Inside the signature block: AI-NR + APU 590 fusion — the learned denoise stage

**Inside it.** MediaTek publishes no Imagiq 790 block diagram and no APU-ISP interface detail — so these are the documented functions in pipeline order, not die sub-blocks. (1) AI-NR photo stage: learned noise reduction for stills, twice as fast as the previous generation. (2) 4K HDR video + AI-NR: the same learned denoise running on the video path at 4K HDR. (3) APU 590, the 5th-generation AI processor: a multi-core NPU that performs INT8, INT16 and FP16 calculations and works 'together as coprocessor such as AI-ISP, AI-GPU and AI-Video' — the compute partner the ISP hands frames to. (4) AI 3A + AI-HDR + AI-FD: the learned statistics functions (AI-AE/AF/AWB, AI-HDR, AI-FD) that tune each stream around the denoise. (5) Power-efficiency envelope: the APU 590 carries up to a 4X power-efficiency upgrade compared with the last generation, which is what makes per-frame learned denoise affordable on a phone's power budget.

**Trace — one unit of work: one low-light 4K HDR video frame.**
1. **A noisy 18-bit frame arrives. **In low light the small phone sensor runs at high gain, so the frame the HDR fusion produces is dominated by noise in the shadows — exactly the frame a fixed-function filter would smear.
2. **Hand-off to the APU. **The frame goes to the APU 590, which MediaTek positions as an AI-ISP coprocessor — the ISP's learned stage lives on the NPU, not in fixed-function ISP logic, under the 'Unique APU-ISP fusion' the product page leads with.
3. **Learned denoise runs. **The AI-NR model separates signal from noise across the frame — a learned operation that recovers detail a bilateral or temporal filter would trade away — running on the APU's INT8/INT16/FP16 datapaths.
4. **Denoise meets HDR. **The denoised result is applied to the HDR frame, so the 18-bit dynamic range survives the denoise instead of being flattened by it; AI-HDR and AI-FD shape the final frame.
5. **A 4K HDR frame exits. **The cleaned frame leaves for the encoder at up to 4K — the '4K HDR Video + AI-NR' MediaTek promises for 'the highest quality results even in extreme low-light scenarios' — and the loop repeats on the next frame.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the small-sensor noise wall: phone sensors are tiny, so low light is mostly noise, and a fixed-function denoise filter can only trade detail for smoothness; a learned model recovers detail the filter would destroy, which is why MediaTek sells AI-NR as the low-light feature rather than a checkbox. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the APU-dependency wall — ISP throughput is now gated by APU availability, because every frame's denoise is an inference that must fit the phone's power budget, and the APU is shared with gaming, social video and every other AI workload; the model ceiling — denoise quality is bounded by the trained model, not the optics, so a scene the model was not trained on gets the generic treatment; and the photo/video split — photo AI-NR runs twice as fast as the previous generation while video AI-NR runs at 4K HDR, so the two paths carry different speed and quality budgets and the stills gain does not transfer to video.

**Governing numbers.** AI-NR photo twice as fast as the previous generation; 4K HDR video + AI-NR; APU 590 (5th-generation, multi-core) with INT8, INT16 and FP16 calculations; APU up to 4X power-efficiency upgrade compared with the last generation.

**Primary source.** MediaTek Dimensity 9000 product page (MediaTek) — 'Unique APU-ISP fusion delivers unparalleled capture speeds and image quality.'; 'AI-NR photo – twice as fast as the previous generation'; '4K HDR Video + AI-NR'. MediaTek Dimensity 9000 launch press release (PR Newswire, Dec. 16, 2021) — 'The powerful 9Gpixel/s ISP also supports 4K HDR Video + AI noise reduction that enables the highest quality results even in extreme low-light scenarios.' MediaTek Dimensity 9000 product page, MediaTek NPU 590 section — 'Featuring our most powerful 5th generation AI processor, the MediaTek NPU 590 is specifically designed to address the latest AI trends, achieving Maximum Effective Performance in AI-multimedia, -gaming, -camera, and social video experiences.'; 'Up to 4X power efficiency upgrade compared to last generation'. MediaTek Dimensity 9000 tablet product page, NPU 590 section — 'With its capacity to perform INT8, INT16, and FP16 calculations, MediaTek's NPU can work on targeted tasks or together as coprocessor such as AI-ISP, AI-GPU and AI-Video, to provide new functions, performance and power-efficiency gains that are ideal for everyday use.'

The AI-NR fusion block runs MediaTek's five documented functions in pipeline order — the AI-NR photo stage, 4K HDR video with AI-NR, the APU 590 as the compute partner, the AI 3A and AI-HDR and AI-FD statistics, and the power-efficiency envelope — and each step is built from the primitives below. The register widths and stage count are not published.
