#### Inside the signature block: The family 9 GPU shader core — Dynamic Caching, hardware ray tracing and mesh shading

**Inside it.** Apple publishes no die floorplan, per-core ALU counts, register-file sizes or ray-tracing throughput for the A17 Pro GPU, so these are Apple's documented functions and pipeline stages, not die sub-blocks. The Apple family 9 GPU is composed of several building blocks: compute and vertex command processors that parse Metal command buffers, a rasterizer that dispatches fragment shaders for execution, and a hierarchy of caches, including the GPU last level cache that services all GPU memory traffic. Central to the GPU are its shader cores — each can run thousands of threads in parallel — and each shader core is paired with a texture unit that can sample and write texture resources, as well as a brand new ray tracing unit that accelerates ray intersection requests. A shader core subdivides into execution pipelines for FP32, FP16 and integer math plus memory pipelines for texture and buffer reads and writes, a pool tracking the SIMDgroups running on the core, a scheduler choosing which SIMDgroup executes next, and on-chip memories: registers for variables, threadgroup and tile memory for data shared across a compute threadgroup or across the tile, and a cache for stack and buffer accesses. Three advancements define this core. (1) Dynamic shader core memory: on-chip register memory is now dynamically allocated and deallocated over the lifetime of a shader according to what each part of the program actually uses — before family 9, a SIMDgroup allocated its maximum register usage up front and held it for its whole lifetime, so a register-hungry shader capped the core at about four concurrent SIMDgroups; the register file is now a cache instead of permanent storage, so more registers can be used than can be stored on chip. (2) Flexible on-chip memory: register, threadgroup, tile, stack and buffer data are all cached on chip, redesigned into fewer larger caches that service all memory types — on-chip storage is dynamically assigned to the memory types a shader actually uses instead of sitting unused, and the shader core dynamically monitors behaviour and adjusts occupancy to keep data on chip and prevent spills to the next cache level or main memory. (3) High-performance ALU pipelines: FP16, FP32 and integer instructions can now execute in parallel to a greater degree than ever before, delivering up to 2x ALU performance compared with prior Apple GPUs — but only when instructions come from multiple SIMDgroups, so occupancy drives ALU utilisation. Hardware-accelerated ray tracing adds a fixed-function intersector: the intersector object traverses the acceleration structure to find a candidate primitive, invokes an intersection function to test the ray against it, and repeats until the closest intersection is found — and in family 9 the hardware intersector runs each traversal completely independently in fixed-function hardware, the rays being sent to the hardware instead of executing in line with the GPU function, with ray and payload communicated through on-chip memory (the RT scratch); a reorder stage then groups intersection-function calls from rays that originated in separate SIMDgroups into coherent SIMDgroups, removing the execution divergence that used to make every thread wait for the longest traversal. Hardware-accelerated mesh shading replaces the vertex stage with two compute-like shaders: object shaders do coarse-grain processing of whole mesh objects and spawn mesh groups, mesh shaders process a constituent piece — a meshlet — and output a Metal mesh object of vertices and primitives; the hardware schedules object and mesh threadgroups to keep intermediate meshlet data on chip, supports encoding draw-mesh commands into indirect command buffers, and raises the maximum threadgroups per mesh grid from 1,024 to over 1 million.

**Trace — one unit of work: one ray-traced frame — command buffer to pixels.**
1. **Command buffers are parsed. **The compute and vertex command processors parse the game's Metal command buffers, and the rasterizer dispatches fragment shaders for execution; the GPU last level cache services all of the GPU's memory traffic as the frame begins.
2. **Mesh shading builds the geometry. **Object shaders do coarse-grain processing of each mesh object and spawn mesh groups; mesh shaders process each meshlet and emit a Metal mesh object of vertices and primitives, with the hardware keeping the intermediate meshlet data on chip instead of spilling it to memory.
3. **Shaders run with dynamic registers. **The shader core's scheduler picks SIMDgroups to feed the FP32, FP16 and integer execution pipelines; registers are allocated and deallocated over each SIMDgroup's lifetime rather than at the program's maximum, so more SIMDgroups run concurrently and occupancy rises — and with it, ALU parallelism, since FP16, FP32 and integer work can now overlap.
4. **A ray leaves the shader for the RT unit. **For a reflective surface the shader creates an intersector object and calls intersect; the ray and its payload are written to on-chip RT scratch memory, and the hardware intersector traverses the acceleration structure in fixed-function hardware, independently per ray, instead of the traversal executing in line with the shader.
5. **The reorder stage re-groups the work. **Intersection-function calls from rays that started in separate SIMDgroups are grouped into coherent SIMDgroups, so the divergence that used to make every thread idle while waiting for the longest traversal is reduced or eliminated; the closest intersection is returned to the calling shader for shading.
6. **The shaded fragment lands in tile memory. **The shader shades from the returned hit and writes through the flexible on-chip cache — registers, threadgroup, tile, stack and buffer data all cached on chip — to the GPU last level cache and unified memory; the tile's colour attachment data was held in on-chip tile memory throughout, and the finished frame is ready for the display.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the occupancy wall: before family 9, a SIMDgroup held its maximum register allocation for its whole lifetime, so a register-hungry shader — Apple's example is a ray-tracing kernel whose glass-shading path uses many more registers than the rest of the program — capped the core at about four concurrent SIMDgroups, starving the ALU pipelines; dynamic allocation plus the unified on-chip cache lets many more SIMDgroups run, and the hardware intersector removes the traversal divergence that used to idle threads. Creates two new bottlenecks instead: the RT scratch traffic — every ray's payload crosses on-chip memory to and from the intersector, so ray-heavy frames are bounded by scratch bandwidth and by the reorder stage's grouping window, since rays must reach it in close proximity and time to regroup; and the occupancy governor — the core dynamically throttles occupancy to keep data on chip, so a shader whose working set exceeds the on-chip cache spills to the next cache level or main memory and gives back the occupancy it gained.

**Governing numbers.** 6-core GPU; up to 20 percent faster peak performance than the A16 GPU; hardware-accelerated ray tracing 4x faster than software-based ray tracing; FP16, FP32 and integer ALU parallelism up to 2x compared with prior Apple GPUs; mesh grid threadgroups from 1,024 to over 1 million; each shader core runs thousands of threads in parallel. Per-core ALU counts, register-file sizes, RT-unit throughput in rays per second, queue depths and port counts are not published.

**Primary source.** Apple Developer, 'Explore GPU advancements in M3 and A17 Pro' (Tech Talks 111375, November 2023) — 'The Apple family 9 GPUs are composed of several building blocks such as compute and vertex command processors that parse your Metal command buffers, a rasterizer that dispatches fragment shaders for execution, and a hierarchy of caches, including the GPU last level cache that services all GPU memory traffic.'; 'The shader core is also paired with a texture unit that can sample and write your texture resources, as well as a brand new ray tracing unit that accelerates ray intersection requests.'; 'On-chip register memory is now dynamically allocated and deallocated over the lifetime of the shader according to what each part of the program actually uses.'; 'The hardware intersector is able to run each traversal completely independently using fixed function hardware.'; 'The second API enhancement expands the maximum number of threadgroups per mesh grid from 1,024 to over 1 million.' Apple Newsroom, 'Apple unveils iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max' (September 12, 2023) — 'The pro-class GPU is up to 20 percent faster and unlocks entirely new experiences, featuring a new 6-core design that increases peak performance and energy efficiency.'; 'Now with hardware-accelerated ray tracing — which is 4x faster than software-based ray tracing — iPhone 15 Pro offers smoother graphics, as well as more immersive AR applications and gaming experiences.'

#### Down to the primitives: The family 9 GPU shader core — Dynamic Caching, hardware ray tracing and mesh shading

The family 9 shader core runs Apple's documented pipeline in order — command processors parse Metal command buffers, the rasterizer dispatches fragment shaders, mesh shading builds the geometry, the scheduler feeds SIMDgroups to the FP32, FP16 and integer pipelines, the hardware intersector handles ray traversal with a reorder stage, and the flexible on-chip caches hold registers, threadgroup, tile, stack and buffer data — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (Metal command-buffer staging; SIMDgroup ready pool; RT ray queue to the intersector; reorder-stage grouping queue)** — The compute and vertex command processors parse Metal command buffers, so a queue stages the parsed commands while the rasterizer dispatches fragment shaders — decoupling command parsing from shader dispatch. The shader core's pool of running SIMDgroups is itself a queue the scheduler draws from, and a ray leaves the shader for the RT unit through a queue into the intersector, with its payload carried in on-chip RT scratch memory; the reorder stage then holds intersection-function calls in a grouping queue until rays from separate SIMDgroups that arrived close together in time can be re-formed into coherent SIMDgroups. The queue depths and widths are not published.

- **Register file (dynamically allocated SIMDgroup registers — the register file as a cache)** — On-chip register memory is now dynamically allocated and deallocated over the lifetime of a shader according to what each part of the program actually uses, so the register file is the block's working store: a SIMDgroup draws registers as its code path needs them and releases them as it moves on, instead of holding its maximum allocation for its whole lifetime. Before family 9 a register-hungry shader capped the core at about four concurrent SIMDgroups; the dynamic register file is what lifts that cap. The register-file size, port count and per-SIMDgroup allocation granularity are not published.

- **SRAM bank (flexible on-chip caches — registers, threadgroup, tile, stack and buffer data; GPU last level cache)** — Register, threadgroup, tile, stack and buffer data are all cached on chip, redesigned into fewer larger caches that service all memory types — so the on-chip store is one banked SRAM structure dynamically assigned to whichever memory type a shader actually uses, instead of fixed partitions sitting idle. The GPU last level cache is the same kind of banked SRAM at the next level, servicing all GPU memory traffic between the six shader cores and unified memory. The cache capacities, banking, line sizes and port counts are not published.

- **CAM / tag compare (register-cache tags; last-level-cache tags)** — The register file is now a cache instead of permanent storage, and a cache needs tags: a tag store with a comparator per entry decides whether a register a SIMDgroup asks for is resident on chip or has spilled to the next cache level or main memory — the hit-or-spill decision the occupancy governor watches. The GPU last level cache carries the same tag-compare structure for its own lines. This is the standard construction of the cache Apple describes; Apple publishes no tag geometry, associativity or tag widths.

- **Priority encoder / arbiter (SIMDgroup scheduler; FP32/FP16/integer pipeline arbitration; shader-core arbitration for the last level cache)** — The shader core's scheduler chooses which SIMDgroup executes next, so a priority encoder turns the ready SIMDgroups' requests into the next group to issue — and because FP16, FP32 and integer instructions can now execute in parallel, an arbiter also decides which pipeline's ready instructions move when several are ready at once. At the SoC level the six shader cores arbitrate for the GPU last level cache, which services all GPU memory traffic. The arbitration policy and the encoder widths are not published.

- **Counter (occupancy counters; mesh-grid threadgroup count; ray count)** — The shader core dynamically monitors behaviour and adjusts occupancy to keep data on chip, so counters track how many SIMDgroups are resident, how much on-chip storage each holds and how close the core is to spilling. The mesh-shading hardware counts threadgroups per mesh grid — the maximum rose from 1,024 to over 1 million, a roughly 977x expansion (arithmetic, 1,000,000 divided by 1,024 is about 977) — and a counter over 1,000,000 threadgroups is 20 bits wide (arithmetic — 2 to the 19th is 524,288, below 1,000,000, and 2 to the 20th is 1,048,576, the smallest power of two above it). No other counter width is claimed.

- **FSM / controller (occupancy governor; mesh-shading scheduler; command-processor parser)** — The occupancy governor is a controller: it watches the shader core's behaviour, throttles occupancy when a working set threatens to spill, and releases it when data fits on chip — the dynamic control loop behind the flexible on-chip memory. A second controller schedules object and mesh threadgroups so intermediate meshlet data stays on chip, and the compute and vertex command processors are parser state machines walking the Metal command buffers. The state counts and sequencing are not published.

- **Multiplier array (FP32/FP16 fused multiply-add in the ALU pipelines; texture filtering; ray-triangle intersection)** — Shader math is multiply-accumulate work, so the FP32, FP16 and integer execution pipelines are built on multiplier arrays — the up-to-2x ALU performance Apple reports comes from these arrays running in parallel across SIMDgroups. The texture unit's filtering multiplies texel weights the same way, and the hardware intersector's ray-triangle tests are multiply work on the ray and edge vectors. The array dimensions, lane counts and number formats are not published.

- **Adder tree (FP accumulation; intersection edge-function sums; texture filter sums)** — Each multiply needs its products summed, so adder trees sit behind the multiplier arrays — accumulating the partial products of a fused multiply-add, summing the edge-function terms of a ray-triangle intersection test, and collapsing the weighted texels of a texture filter into one sampled value. The tree depths and widths are not published.

- **Barrel shifter (FP normalisation shifts in the ALU pipelines; texture address computation)** — Floating-point work needs variable shifts — normalising a result after a multiply, aligning operands before an add — so the ALU pipelines shift by a variable amount in one step through barrel shifters, and the texture unit shifts addresses the same way when it walks a mip level. The shifter widths are not published.

- **Mux / demux (register-port steering per SIMDgroup; memory-type steering to the flexible caches; meshlet routing to object vs mesh shaders)** — Registers are allocated dynamically, so muxes steer each SIMDgroup's register ports to the slice of the register file it currently owns; a second set of muxes steers register, threadgroup, tile, stack and buffer traffic into the flexible on-chip caches according to what each shader actually uses; and a third routes meshlet data to the object-shader or mesh-shader path the hardware scheduled. The mux widths and select encodings are not published.

- **Comparator (occupancy thresholds; ray-box and ray-triangle intersection tests; RT queue full/empty)** — The occupancy governor's decisions are comparisons — a shader's working set against the on-chip capacity, a counter against the spill threshold — and the hardware intersector tests each ray against bounding boxes and triangles with comparators, keeping the closest intersection found so far. The RT scratch queues carry full/empty comparators of the same form. The comparator counts and widths are not published.

- **Pipeline registers (between ALU pipeline stages; rasterizer to fragment-shader dispatch; intersector to reorder stage)** — Each ALU pipeline stage hands its result to the next through pipeline registers, so FP32, FP16 and integer work overlaps across SIMDgroups — the structure behind the up-to-2x ALU figure, which only appears when instructions come from multiple SIMDgroups. The rasterizer hands dispatched fragment shaders to the cores the same way, and the intersector hands each completed traversal to the reorder stage through registers. The register widths and stage counts are not published.

- **Credit counter (shader-core to last-level-cache flow control; RT scratch bandwidth budgeting)** — Six shader cores share one GPU last level cache, so a credit counter rations cache bandwidth — a core issues requests while it holds credits and waits when they are spent, the standard flow control for a shared cache. The same counter form budgets the RT scratch traffic the Level-2 bottleneck section names: every ray's payload crosses on-chip memory to and from the intersector, so ray-heavy frames are bounded by scratch bandwidth. The credit limits and counter widths are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Apple publishes no die floorplan, per-core ALU counts, register-file sizes, ray-tracing throughput, queue depths or port counts for the A17 Pro GPU, so the primitives below are mapped from the documented functions and pipeline stages in Apple Developer Tech Talks 111375 and the iPhone 15 Pro newsroom release, not from a die diagram. Every published figure is already recorded at Level 2; no new chip-specific number is claimed here. The only new numbers are counter widths and a mesh-grid expansion factor computed from published figures and labelled arithmetic. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Down to the gates: The family 9 GPU shader core — Dynamic Caching, hardware ray tracing and mesh shading

Apple publishes no die floorplan, gate netlist, standard-cell library or transistor counts for the A17 Pro GPU, so there is no Apple gate-level schematic to quote. What follows is the gate-level construction of each Level-3 primitive in the primer's bottom-layer terms (NAND/NOR, latch and flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder), labelled standard construction throughout; the transistor counts are the textbook cells, not A17 Pro facts. No chip-specific gate or transistor total is claimed.

- **FIFO / queue (Metal command-buffer staging; SIMDgroup ready pool; RT ray queue to the intersector; reorder-stage grouping queue)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each (a full adder is two half adders — two XOR plus two AND plus one OR — about 28 transistors in static CMOS), incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XNOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The command-buffer staging queue, the SIMDgroup ready pool, the ray queue into the intersector and the reorder-stage grouping queue are all FIFOs of this form; their depths and widths are not published, so no pointer width and no transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Register file (dynamically allocated SIMDgroup registers — the register file as a cache)** — A register file at gate level is an array of storage bits with a write decoder and read-port muxes: each stored bit is a D flip-flop — two cross-coupled latch stages, about 20–28 transistors in a standard-cell library — or a 6T SRAM cell where the array is built as SRAM, with the write address decoded through a NAND/NOR row-decoder tree and each read port a transmission-gate mux tree (two transistors per input leg). Dynamic allocation adds valid and tag bits per entry — more flip-flops — and the tag compare of the next primitive. The register-file size, port count and per-SIMDgroup allocation granularity are not published, so no bit total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (flexible on-chip caches — registers, threadgroup, tile, stack and buffer data; GPU last level cache)** — An SRAM bank at gate level is 6T cells — two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (two transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers (a cross-coupled inverter pair with enable transistors). The flexible on-chip caches are banks of this form, dynamically assigned to whichever memory type a shader uses, and the GPU last level cache is a larger bank of the same cells. The cache capacities, banking, line sizes and port counts are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **CAM / tag compare (register-cache tags; last-level-cache tags)** — A CAM cell is a 6T SRAM storage cell plus XOR match logic feeding a matchline — a NOR CAM cell adds four match transistors (ten transistors in total) and a NAND CAM cell adds three (nine in total), textbook-standard — with the matchline precharged and sensed per row. A plain tag compare is the same match without the storage: one XNOR gate per tag bit feeding an AND tree that asserts on a full match. The register-cache tags that decide hit-or-spill and the last-level-cache tags are comparators of this form. Apple publishes no tag geometry, associativity or tag widths, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Priority encoder / arbiter (SIMDgroup scheduler; FP32/FP16/integer pipeline arbitration; shader-core arbitration for the last level cache)** — A priority encoder at gate level is an OR/NAND tree that turns a one-hot ready vector into the binary index of the highest-priority set bit — a 2^n-to-n encoder is a tree of OR gates, one per output bit, fed by the ready lines. The SIMDgroup scheduler is an encoder of this form over the ready SIMDgroups; round-robin fairness adds a rotating priority register (D flip-flops holding the last grant) that reorders the encoder's inputs. The FP32/FP16/integer pipeline arbiter and the six-core arbitration for the last level cache are the same tree form with different widths. The arbitration policy and the encoder widths are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (occupancy counters; mesh-grid threadgroup count; ray count)** — A counter at gate level is D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer — one flip-flop and one full adder (about 28 transistors, two half adders) per bit — so a counter's transistor cost is roughly its bit width times the flip-flop-plus-adder cost. The mesh-grid threadgroup counter is 20 bits wide by arithmetic from the published over-1,000,000 maximum (2 to the 19th is 524,288, below 1,000,000; 2 to the 20th is 1,048,576, the smallest power of two above it) — 20 flip-flops plus 20 full adders by arithmetic. The occupancy and ray-counter widths are not published, so no other counter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (occupancy governor; mesh-shading scheduler; command-processor parser)** — A controller at gate level is a finite-state machine built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the inputs — the occupancy counters, the spill comparators and the scheduler state — with the outputs decoded from the state flops through another NAND/NOR network. The occupancy governor is an FSM of this form whose next-state logic compares a shader's working set against the on-chip capacity; the mesh-shading scheduler and the command-processor parser are FSMs of the same form. The state counts and sequencing are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (FP32/FP16 fused multiply-add in the ALU pipelines; texture filtering; ray-triangle intersection)** — A multiplier array at gate level is AND gates forming the partial products — one AND gate per product bit — feeding an adder tree of full adders (about 28 transistors each) that collapses the partials into the product. A fused multiply-add is this array plus one more adder tree for the accumulate, and the FP32, FP16 and integer pipelines are arrays of this form running in parallel across SIMDgroups; the texture unit's filtering and the hardware intersector's ray-triangle tests are multiply work of the same form. The array dimensions, lane counts and number formats are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (FP accumulation; intersection edge-function sums; texture filter sums)** — An adder tree at gate level is full adders arranged pairwise so the tree depth is log2 of the operand count: each full adder is two half adders — two XOR plus two AND plus one OR, about 28 transistors in static CMOS — so an N-operand tree is N−1 full adders by arithmetic. The FP accumulation behind the multiplier arrays, the edge-function sums of a ray-triangle intersection test and the weighted-texel sums of a texture filter are trees of this form. The tree depths and widths are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (FP normalisation shifts in the ALU pipelines; texture address computation)** — A barrel shifter at gate level is log2(N) stages of 2:1 muxes for an N-bit word — each 2:1 mux a transmission gate per input leg (two transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree — so an N-bit shifter is N times log2(N) mux legs by arithmetic, shifting by any amount in one step. The FP normalisation shifts after a multiply and the operand alignment shifts before an add are shifters of this form, as is the texture unit's address shifting across mip levels. The shifter widths are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (register-port steering per SIMDgroup; memory-type steering to the flexible caches; meshlet routing to object vs mesh shaders)** — A mux at gate level is a transmission gate per input leg (two transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree, with the select lines decoded from the control bits through a NAND/NOR decoder. The register-port steering that gives each SIMDgroup the slice of the register file it currently owns, the memory-type steering into the flexible on-chip caches and the meshlet routing to the object- or mesh-shader path are mux trees of this form; a demux is the same tree run in reverse. The mux widths and select encodings are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (occupancy thresholds; ray-box and ray-triangle intersection tests; RT queue full/empty)** — A comparator at gate level is XNOR gates — one per compared bit — feeding an AND tree for equality, or a subtractor (a chain of full adders, about 28 transistors each) whose sign bit decides magnitude. The occupancy governor's threshold checks are magnitude comparators of this form; the hardware intersector's ray-box and ray-triangle tests compare coordinates the same way, keeping the closest intersection found so far; and the RT scratch queues carry full/empty comparators over their pointer values. The comparator counts and widths are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (between ALU pipeline stages; rasterizer to fragment-shader dispatch; intersector to reorder stage)** — Pipeline registers at gate level are D flip-flops — two cross-coupled latch stages, about 20–28 transistors each — one per bit of the value carried across the stage boundary, clocked together so a whole stage's result moves in one cycle. The ALU pipeline stages hand results to each other through registers of this form, which is what lets FP32, FP16 and integer work overlap across SIMDgroups; the rasterizer-to-core dispatch and the intersector-to-reorder handoff are registers of the same form. The register widths and stage counts are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (shader-core to last-level-cache flow control; RT scratch bandwidth budgeting)** — A credit counter at gate level is an up/down counter: D flip-flops holding the credit balance plus a full-adder incrementer/decrementer (about 28 transistors per bit) that adds on a credit return and subtracts on an issue, with a zero comparator (XNOR per bit plus an AND tree) that stalls the core when the balance is spent. The shader-core-to-last-level-cache rationing and the RT scratch bandwidth budgeting of the Level-2 bottleneck section are counters of this form. The credit limits and counter widths are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.

**Parameter honesty.** Construction honesty: all gate/transistor detail here is textbook-standard construction from the primer's bottom layer (NAND/NOR, latch/flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder), labelled as such in every primitive. Apple publishes no A17 Pro GPU die floorplan, gate netlist, standard-cell library or transistor counts, so no gate or transistor total is claimed for the chip itself. The only new number is a 20-bit counter width computed from the published mesh-grid maximum and labelled arithmetic.

#### Inside the signature block: The media engine and USB 3 path — ProRes, AV1 and the first 10 Gb/s iPhone I/O

**Inside it.** Apple publishes no media-engine block diagram, no encoder throughput in pixels per second and no queue depths for the A17 Pro, so these are Apple's documented functions in pipeline order, not die sub-blocks. (1) ProRes encode and decode: the media engine records ProRes video directly to external storage, enabling higher recording options up to 4K at 60 fps, with a new option for Log encoding, and iPhone 15 Pro is the first smartphone in the world to support ACES, the Academy Color Encoding System. (2) Dedicated AV1 decoder: A17 Pro includes a dedicated AV1 decoder for more efficient, high-quality video experiences from streaming services — new this generation. (3) HEVC and H.264 encode and decode for the rest of the camera and playback catalogue, shared with the ProRes path through the same media engine. (4) 48MP stills path: the 48MP Main camera's super-high-resolution 24MP default and 48MP ProRAW and HEIF captures are computed by the Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion and Smart HDR stages that feed the media engine, and 48MP ProRAW images can be shot and instantly transferred to a Mac with Capture One. (5) New USB controller: a new USB controller enables USB 3 speeds on iPhone for the first time, supporting much higher transfer speeds and video output up to 4K at 60 fps HDR; iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max support USB 3 for data transfer speeds up to 10 gigabits per second, up to 20x faster than before, with an optional USB 3 cable. (6) Unified memory: every engine on the SoC — CPU, GPU, Neural Engine, media engine — reads the same 8 GB LPDDR5 pool, so frames pass between ISP, media engine and USB controller by pointer, not by copy.

**Trace — one unit of work: one ProRes 4K60 clip — sensor to external SSD.**
1. **The sensor exposes a frame. **The 48MP Main camera exposes a frame; the Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion and Smart HDR stages compute it, and the video path hands the finished frame to the media engine — the stills path would instead write a 24MP default or a 48MP ProRAW file.
2. **The media engine encodes ProRes. **The ProRes encoder compresses the frame intra-frame — each frame independently of the others — with the Log encoding option and ACES colour available; at 4K60 the ProRes 422 HQ target data rate is about 1,768 Mbps, so the encoder must sustain roughly 221 MB/s before anything leaves the phone.
3. **The stream is buffered in unified memory. **The encoded stream lands in the shared 8 GB LPDDR5 pool, not in a private media memory; the media engine, GPU, CPU and Neural Engine all read the same pool, so the frame is never copied between engines.
4. **The USB 3 controller moves it out. **The new USB controller streams the ProRes file over USB-C to the external drive at up to 10 Gb/s — about 5.6 times the 1,768 Mbps stream (arithmetic) — so the link itself is not the bottleneck; the phone's internal write path and its thermal envelope are.
5. **AV1 decode runs the other way. **While the ProRes stream leaves, a streamed title arrives the other way: the dedicated AV1 decoder decodes it for playback, and HEVC and H.264 titles share the media engine's decode path — the AV1 decoder is new this generation.
6. **The clip is a file on the drive. **The ProRes file sits on the external SSD ready for the edit, and the phone's own storage never held it — which is what makes 4K60 ProRes practical at all, since an hour of ProRes 422 HQ at 4K60 is about 795 GB by the white paper's target rates, more than most of the phone's storage.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the internal-storage wall: a 4K60 ProRes stream runs at about 1,768 Mbps, so an hour of it is about 795 GB — more than most of the phone's storage — and recording straight to an external drive removes that ceiling entirely, which is what turns the phone into a camera that can stay on a set. Creates two new bottlenecks instead: the 10 Gb/s USB 3 link is shared with everything on the port — display output up to 4K at 60 fps HDR, charging and data — so a monitor plus a drive plus a ProRes stream contend on one controller; and sustained-write thermals — a phone chassis cannot shed heat like a camera body, so long 4K60 ProRes takes are bounded by the phone's thermal envelope, not by the encoder or the link.

**Governing numbers.** USB 3 up to 10 Gb/s, up to 20x faster than USB 2; ProRes video recording directly to external storage, up to 4K at 60 fps; video output up to 4K at 60 fps HDR; ProRes 422 HQ target data rate at 4K60 about 1,768 Mbps (about 795 GB per hour) — Apple ProRes white paper, April 2022; 48MP ProRAW stills, 24MP super-high-resolution default; first smartphone to support ACES; dedicated AV1 decoder. Media-engine block diagram, encoder throughput in pixels per second, queue depths and port counts are not published.

**Primary source.** Apple Newsroom, 'Apple unveils iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max' (September 12, 2023) — 'A17 Pro includes a dedicated AV1 decoder, enabling more efficient, high-quality video experiences for streaming services.'; 'a new USB controller enables USB 3 speeds on iPhone for the first time, now supporting much higher transfer speeds and video output up to 4K at 60 fps HDR.'; 'ProRes video can be recorded directly to external storage, enabling higher recording options up to 4K at 60 fps, and greater flexibility on set when using iPhone as the main camera.'; 'iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max support USB 3 for data transfer speeds up to 10 gigabits per second, up to 20x faster than before.'; 'iPhone 15 Pro also introduces a new option for Log encoding and is the first smartphone in the world to support ACES, the Academy Color Encoding System, a global standard for color workflows.' Apple, Apple ProRes White Paper (April 2022), appendix Target Data Rates — 4K (3840 x 2160) at 60 fps, ProRes 422 HQ: 1,768 Mbps, 795 GB per hour; 'The target data rate of Apple ProRes 422 HQ is approximately 220 Mbps at 1920 x 1080 and 29.97 fps.'

#### Down to the primitives: The media engine and USB 3 path — ProRes, AV1 and the first 10 Gb/s iPhone I/O

The media-engine block runs Apple's documented functions in pipeline order — the ProRes encoder writing 4K60 straight to external storage, the dedicated AV1 decoder, the shared HEVC and H.264 path, the 48MP stills path feeding the media engine, and the new USB 3 controller moving the stream out at up to 10 Gb/s — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (frame ingest from the ISP; encoded bitstream buffer to USB; AV1 bitstream ingest; USB transmit/receive queues)** — Frames arrive from the Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion and Smart HDR stages, so an ingest FIFO stages each frame while the encoder works the previous one, decoupling the sensor rate from the encode rate. The encoded ProRes stream waits in a bitstream buffer for the USB controller, absorbing the rate mismatch between the encoder's roughly 221 MB/s output and the link's up-to-10 Gb/s bursts; the AV1 decoder's incoming bitstream queues the same way, and the USB controller carries transmit and receive queues for the two directions at once. The queue depths and widths are not published.

- **SRAM bank / line buffers (ProRes frame store; AV1 reference-frame store; stills-path frame store)** — ProRes encodes each frame independently, so the frame under encode lives in an on-chip store until its coefficients are written out; the AV1 decoder keeps its reference frames in the same kind of banked store while it predicts from them, and the 48MP stills path stages its 24MP-default and 48MP ProRAW frames in it on the way to the media engine. The store capacities, banking, port counts and widths are not published. Arithmetic from published figures: one 4K frame is 3840 x 2160 = 8,294,400 pixels, so at 60 fps the ProRes encoder must sustain roughly 497,664,000 pixels per second, about 0.5 Gpixel/s.

- **Multiplier array (ProRes transform; AV1 inverse transform; Log and ACES colour-matrix math)** — ProRes compresses with a transform — each block of pixels multiplied through a coefficient matrix — and the AV1 decoder inverts its own transform the same way, so both paths are multiplier arrays. The Log encoding option and the ACES colour workflow are matrix math on every pixel, another multiply pass over the frame. The array dimensions, lane counts and number formats are not published.

- **Adder tree (transform accumulation; AV1 loop-restoration and CDEF filter sums; deblocking filter sums)** — Each transform coefficient is a sum of products, so adder trees collapse the multiplier arrays' partial products; the AV1 decoder's loop-restoration and CDEF filters accumulate neighbouring-pixel sums the same way, and the HEVC and H.264 deblocking filters sum across block edges. The tree depths and widths are not published.

- **Comparator (entropy-decoding symbol comparisons; ProRes coefficient thresholding; stills vs video path thresholds)** — Entropy decoding is comparison work — each incoming bit narrows a range until the symbol is decided — so the AV1, HEVC and H.264 decoders compare ranges against thresholds on every symbol, and the ProRes encoder thresholds coefficients before it packs them. The same comparison form picks the stills path against the video path. The comparator counts and widths are not published.

- **Barrel shifter (variable-length bitstream packing and unpacking; Log/ACES bit-depth scaling)** — Codec bitstreams are variable-length codes, so the ProRes encoder packs and the AV1 decoder unpacks symbols by shifting a bit buffer by a variable amount in one step — a barrel shifter's job — and the Log encoding and ACES colour paths scale bit depths the same way. The shifter widths are not published.

- **FSM / controller (media-engine pipeline sequencer; USB 3 link-training and power-state controller; DMA engine controller)** — The media engine sequences each frame — ingest, transform, quantise, entropy, output — through a pipeline controller, and the new USB controller runs its own state machines for link training, power states and the data-vs-display-output sharing of the one port. A DMA controller moves the encoded stream from unified memory to the USB controller without the CPU. The state counts and sequencing are not published.

- **Counter (frame counter; ProRes byte counter; 4K pixel counter; USB transfer counter)** — The encoder counts what it processes: the frame counter steps per frame, the byte counter tracks the ProRes stream against its roughly 221 MB/s rate, and the pixel counter runs to the 4K frame — 8,294,400 pixels, 23 bits wide (arithmetic — 2 to the 22nd is 4,194,304, below 8,294,400, and 2 to the 23rd is 8,388,608, the smallest power of two above it). The USB controller counts bytes transferred against the 10 Gb/s link. No other counter width is claimed.

- **Mux / demux (ProRes vs HEVC vs H.264 vs AV1 path select; encode vs decode routing; USB data vs display-output routing)** — One media engine serves four codecs, so muxes steer each frame to the ProRes, HEVC, H.264 or AV1 path and route the result to encode or decode; a second set steers the 48MP stills path against the video path; and the USB controller's muxes share the one port between the ProRes stream to the external drive, the 4K60 HDR display output and charging. The mux widths and select encodings are not published.

- **Pipeline registers (between codec pipeline stages — ingest, transform, quantise, entropy)** — Each codec stage hands its result to the next through pipeline registers, so ingest, transform, quantisation and entropy coding overlap on successive frames instead of running one frame end to end — the structure that lets the ProRes encoder sustain its roughly 221 MB/s. The register widths and stage counts are not published.

- **Credit counter (unified-memory bandwidth allocation between engines; USB controller flow control)** — Every engine on the SoC — CPU, GPU, Neural Engine, media engine — reads the same 8 GB LPDDR5 pool, so a credit counter allocates memory bandwidth among them, holding back an engine when its credits are spent so the others keep their share; the USB controller carries the same counter form for its own flow control on the port. The credit limits and counter widths are not published.

- **Synchronizer (ISP clock domain to media-engine domain; media-engine to USB controller domain)** — The sensor and ISP, the media engine and the USB controller do not share one clock, so synchronizers carry each frame into the media engine's domain and the encoded stream out again to the USB controller, in the standard two-flop construction. The domain frequencies and synchronizer depths are not published.

- **Priority encoder / arbiter (unified-memory arbitration between CPU, GPU, Neural Engine and media engine; USB port sharing arbitration)** — Four engines share one 8 GB LPDDR5 pool, so an arbiter decides whose memory request moves next when several are ready at once — the media engine's ProRes stream against the GPU's frame traffic and the Neural Engine's model traffic — and a priority encoder turns the winning request into the access the memory controller sees. The USB port carries a second arbiter for the display, storage and data traffic sharing the one controller. The arbitration policies and encoder widths are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Apple publishes no media-engine block diagram, no encoder throughput in pixels per second, no queue depths and no port counts for the A17 Pro, so the primitives below are mapped from the documented functions in pipeline order in the iPhone 15 Pro newsroom release and the Apple ProRes White Paper, not from a die diagram. Every published figure is already recorded at Level 2; no new chip-specific number is claimed here. The only new numbers are pixel rates and counter widths computed from published figures and labelled arithmetic. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Down to the gates: The media engine and USB 3 path — ProRes, AV1 and the first 10 Gb/s iPhone I/O

Apple publishes no media-engine block diagram, gate netlist, standard-cell library or transistor counts for the A17 Pro, so there is no Apple gate-level schematic to quote. What follows is the gate-level construction of each Level-3 primitive in the primer's bottom-layer terms (NAND/NOR, latch and flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder), labelled standard construction throughout; the transistor counts are the textbook cells, not A17 Pro facts. No chip-specific gate or transistor total is claimed.

- **FIFO / queue (frame ingest from the ISP; encoded bitstream buffer to USB; AV1 bitstream ingest; USB transmit/receive queues)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each (a full adder is two half adders — two XOR plus two AND plus one OR — about 28 transistors in static CMOS), incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XNOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The frame-ingest FIFO from the ISP, the encoded bitstream buffer waiting on the USB controller, the AV1 bitstream ingest queue and the USB controller's transmit and receive queues are all FIFOs of this form; their depths and widths are not published, so no pointer width and no transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank / line buffers (ProRes frame store; AV1 reference-frame store; stills-path frame store)** — An SRAM bank at gate level is 6T cells — two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (two transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers (a cross-coupled inverter pair with enable transistors). The ProRes frame store, the AV1 reference-frame store and the 48MP stills-path frame store are banks of this form. The store capacities, banking, port counts and widths are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (ProRes transform; AV1 inverse transform; Log and ACES colour-matrix math)** — A multiplier array at gate level is AND gates forming the partial products — one AND gate per product bit — feeding an adder tree of full adders (about 28 transistors each) that collapses the partials into the product. The ProRes transform and the AV1 inverse transform are arrays of this form, and the Log encoding option and the ACES colour workflow are matrix math — another multiply pass over every pixel — of the same form. The array dimensions, lane counts and number formats are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (transform accumulation; AV1 loop-restoration and CDEF filter sums; deblocking filter sums)** — An adder tree at gate level is full adders arranged pairwise so the tree depth is log2 of the operand count: each full adder is two half adders — two XOR plus two AND plus one OR, about 28 transistors in static CMOS — so an N-operand tree is N−1 full adders by arithmetic. Each transform coefficient is a sum of products collapsed by a tree of this form; the AV1 decoder's loop-restoration and CDEF filters and the HEVC and H.264 deblocking filters accumulate neighbouring-pixel sums the same way. The tree depths and widths are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (entropy-decoding symbol comparisons; ProRes coefficient thresholding; stills vs video path thresholds)** — A comparator at gate level is XNOR gates — one per compared bit — feeding an AND tree for equality, or a subtractor (a chain of full adders, about 28 transistors each) whose sign bit decides magnitude, or — for a threshold against a constant — an AND/NAND network with the constant's bits tied off. Entropy decoding compares ranges against thresholds on every symbol, the ProRes encoder thresholds coefficients before packing them, and the stills-vs-video path choice is a comparison of the same form. The comparator counts and widths are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (variable-length bitstream packing and unpacking; Log/ACES bit-depth scaling)** — A barrel shifter at gate level is log2(N) stages of 2:1 muxes for an N-bit word — each 2:1 mux a transmission gate per input leg (two transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree — so an N-bit shifter is N times log2(N) mux legs by arithmetic, shifting by any amount in one step. The ProRes encoder packs and the AV1 decoder unpacks variable-length symbols by shifting a bit buffer through a shifter of this form, and the Log encoding and ACES colour paths scale bit depths the same way. The shifter widths are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (media-engine pipeline sequencer; USB 3 link-training and power-state controller; DMA engine controller)** — A controller at gate level is a finite-state machine built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the inputs, with the outputs decoded from the state flops through another NAND/NOR network. The media-engine pipeline sequencer that steps each frame through ingest, transform, quantise, entropy and output is an FSM of this form; the USB controller's link-training and power-state machines are FSMs of the same form, and the DMA controller that moves the encoded stream from unified memory to the USB controller is counters plus an FSM. The state counts and sequencing are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (frame counter; ProRes byte counter; 4K pixel counter; USB transfer counter)** — A counter at gate level is D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer — one flip-flop and one full adder (about 28 transistors, two half adders) per bit. The 4K pixel counter is 23 bits wide by arithmetic from the published frame size (3840 x 2160 = 8,294,400 pixels; 2 to the 22nd is 4,194,304, below 8,294,400, and 2 to the 23rd is 8,388,608, the smallest power of two above it) — 23 flip-flops plus 23 full adders by arithmetic. The frame, byte and USB-transfer counter widths are not published, so no other counter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (ProRes vs HEVC vs H.264 vs AV1 path select; encode vs decode routing; USB data vs display-output routing)** — A mux at gate level is a transmission gate per input leg (two transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree, with the select lines decoded from the control bits through a NAND/NOR decoder. The muxes that steer each frame to the ProRes, HEVC, H.264 or AV1 path and route the result to encode or decode, the muxes that steer the 48MP stills path against the video path, and the USB controller's muxes that share the one port between the ProRes stream, the 4K60 HDR display output and charging are all trees of this form; a demux is the same tree run in reverse. The mux widths and select encodings are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (between codec pipeline stages — ingest, transform, quantise, entropy)** — Pipeline registers at gate level are D flip-flops — two cross-coupled latch stages, about 20–28 transistors each — one per bit of the value carried across the stage boundary, clocked together so a whole stage's result moves in one cycle. Ingest, transform, quantisation and entropy coding hand results to each other through registers of this form, which is what lets the ProRes encoder overlap successive frames and sustain its roughly 221 MB/s. The register widths and stage counts are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (unified-memory bandwidth allocation between engines; USB controller flow control)** — A credit counter at gate level is an up/down counter: D flip-flops holding the credit balance plus a full-adder incrementer/decrementer (about 28 transistors per bit) that adds on a credit return and subtracts on an issue, with a zero comparator (XNOR per bit plus an AND tree) that stalls the requester when the balance is spent. The unified-memory bandwidth allocation among the CPU, GPU, Neural Engine and media engine and the USB controller's own flow control are counters of this form. The credit limits and counter widths are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (ISP clock domain to media-engine domain; media-engine to USB controller domain)** — A synchronizer at gate level is two D flip-flops in series per crossing bit — the standard two-flop synchronizer: the first flop may go metastable on a clock-domain crossing, and the second samples it a cycle later, so each bit crossing a domain costs two flip-flops by arithmetic. The sensor and ISP, the media engine and the USB controller do not share one clock, so the frame handoff into the media engine's domain and the encoded stream's handoff out to the USB controller are synchronizers of this form. The domain frequencies and synchronizer depths are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Priority encoder / arbiter (unified-memory arbitration between CPU, GPU, Neural Engine and media engine; USB port sharing arbitration)** — A priority encoder at gate level is an OR/NAND tree that turns a one-hot ready vector into the binary index of the highest-priority set bit — a 2^n-to-n encoder is a tree of OR gates, one per output bit, fed by the ready lines. The unified-memory arbiter that decides whose request moves next when the CPU, GPU, Neural Engine and media engine are ready at once is an encoder of this form, with a rotating priority register (D flip-flops holding the last grant) where fairness is round-robin; the USB port's arbiter for display, storage and data traffic is the same tree form. The arbitration policies and encoder widths are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

**Parameter honesty.** Construction honesty: all gate/transistor detail here is textbook-standard construction from the primer's bottom layer (NAND/NOR, latch/flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder), labelled as such in every primitive. Apple publishes no A17 Pro media-engine block diagram, gate netlist, standard-cell library or transistor counts, so no gate or transistor total is claimed for the chip itself. The only new number is a 23-bit pixel counter width computed from the published 4K frame size and labelled arithmetic.

### Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

**Added: 2026-11-22** (deepened to Level-2/3/4 standard: 2026-11-27)

**Specs (wiki card).** TSMC 4 nm · Kryo (X4) · Adreno 750 · Hexagon NPU

**Building blocks.**
- **Kryo CPU — 1+5+2** — One Cortex-X4 prime (up to 3.3 GHz in the standard brief; 3.39 GHz 'for Galaxy' variant), five A720 performance cores and two A520 efficiency cores — Qualcomm's answer to all-big-core: keep the little cores, outnumber them
- **Hexagon NPU — fused accelerator ★** — Scalar + vector + tensor accelerators fused on one die area with a shared memory path and Hexagon Direct Link to the other engines; upgraded micro-tile inferencing slices models so LLM layers stream through the tensor array — the block that runs 10B-parameter models at 20 tokens/s on a phone
- **Adreno 750 GPU** — Hardware ray tracing with global illumination, Adreno Frame Motion Engine 2.0 frame generation, and the AI Engine's third leg — the AI Engine is explicitly CPU+GPU+NPU, not the NPU alone
- **Spectra Cognitive ISP** — Triple 18-bit ISPs with NPU-in-the-loop semantic segmentation (see its own entry) — listed here because on this SoC the camera is a first-class AI workload, not a peripheral
- **Sensing Hub — dual micro NPUs** — Always-on audio/sensor inference at microwatts, 3.5× the prior generation — personalisation context (location, activity) gathered without waking the big engines
- **X75 Modem-RF + FastConnect 7800** — Integrated 5G (10 Gbps peak down) and Wi-Fi 7 — on an SoC, the radios are blocks too, sharing the LPDDR5X (up to 24 GB, 4,800 MHz) memory system with everything above

**The piece that makes it special.** The fused AI engine. Snapdragon 8 Gen 3's architecture document leads with AI because the silicon does: the Hexagon's scalar/vector/tensor trio is one fused accelerator with its own power delivery upgrade, and micro-tile inferencing exists specifically so transformer layers — too big for the NPU's local memory — stream in tiles without CPU orchestration. The SoC is the argument that a phone chip is now an AI part with a phone attached.

**How work flows.** Request arrives: A GenAI prompt, a photo, a game frame — the workload enters through the OS scheduler. AI Engine triages: LLM inference lands on the Hexagon tensor path in micro-tiles; vision splits between NPU and Adreno; glue code runs on Kryo. Camera runs concurrently: Spectra pipelines pull NPU segmentation mid-capture while the modem streams — all sharing LPDDR5X bandwidth under one power budget. Sensing Hub never sleeps: Context keeps updating at microwatts so the next wake starts already knowing the scene.

**Trade-off accepted.** Integration opacity. Qualcomm publishes a superb product brief and no microarchitecture: Hexagon internals, Adreno organisation and cache sizes are undisclosed, and headline AI rates depend on the precision mix (INT4 support headlines the TOPS story). The brief is the boundary of honest description.

**Fact check.**
- [verified] Hexagon NPU: fused scalar/vector/tensor accelerators, Hexagon Direct Link, upgraded micro-tile inferencing; INT4/8/16 + FP16 — Source: Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 Product Brief (87-71408-1 Rev G). #### Inside the signature block: The Hexagon NPU — fused scalar/vector/tensor accelerator with micro-tile inferencing

**Inside it.** Qualcomm publishes no Hexagon block diagram, shared-memory capacity, micro-tile dimensions, queue depths or per-accelerator widths, so these are the vendor's documented functions and pipeline stages, not die sub-blocks. The Hexagon NPU is three accelerators fused onto one die area with one shared memory path. (1) Scalar accelerator — the DSP-descended control core: it breaks networks into micro-tiles, schedules work across the vector and tensor accelerators, and runs the elementwise and control code of each layer. (2) Vector accelerator (Hexagon Vector eXtensions, HVX) — wide SIMD for activations, normalisation and the vector half of each layer. (3) Tensor accelerator — the matrix engine for convolutions, fully-connected layers and transformer attention; native INT4 support doubles its throughput on INT4 layers, and dedicated transformer-acceleration hardware speeds multi-head attention. (4) Large shared memory — one pool shared by all three accelerators, so tiles move between scalar, vector and tensor work without leaving the NPU; its bandwidth doubled in the Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 generation. (5) Hexagon Direct Link — the NPU's direct path to the other AI Engine processors, so data moves between the NPU, CPU, GPU and Sensing Hub without CPU orchestration. (6) Power delivery — a dedicated power rail for the NPU that adapts delivery to the workload (since the Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 generation), plus a second dedicated rail added in the 8 Gen 3 generation for the tensor accelerator alone, so scalar, vector and tensor work can be powered at different levels.

**Trace — one unit of work: one token of Llama 2-7B generation.**
1. **Weights stream in. **The model's INT4-quantised weights stream from LPDDR5X — 4,800 MHz, 77 GB/s — into the NPU. Token generation is memory-bound, so the whole design is organised around moving fewer bytes per token.
2. **Scalar slices the layer. **The scalar accelerator breaks the transformer layer into micro-tiles small enough to execute independently — micro-tile inferencing, upgraded in the 8 Gen 3 generation for generative-AI workloads and reduced memory bandwidth.
3. **Tensor does the matmul. **Each micro-tile's matrix multiply runs on the tensor accelerator at INT4, double the throughput of INT8 layers; attention scores run on the dedicated transformer-acceleration hardware.
4. **Vector finishes the layer. **Activations, normalisation and elementwise operations run on the vector accelerator, while the scalar unit handles control flow and token sampling.
5. **Results stay on chip. **The micro-tile's output stays in the large shared memory and feeds the next layer directly — micro-tile inferencing eliminates the memory traffic between as many as 10 or more layers, so a whole stack of layers runs without a round trip to LPDDR5X.
6. **Next token. **The sampled token is the output; the key-value cache for the next step lives in shared memory and LPDDR5X, and the cycle repeats — at up to 20 tokens per second for Llama 2-7B in Qualcomm's demo.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the memory wall for LLM inference: token generation is memory-bound, and micro-tile inferencing plus INT4 quantisation plus the doubled shared-memory bandwidth attack exactly that — weights are read once per stack of layers instead of once per layer, and INT4 halves the bytes per weight. Creates two new bottlenecks instead: the shared memory's capacity — only as many layers as fit in the NPU's local memory can run without DRAM traffic, so larger models or longer contexts spill back to LPDDR5X and the token rate falls toward the memory-bandwidth ceiling; and the tensor accelerator's power envelope — the dedicated rail lets it sprint, but sustained generation is thermally capped, which is why Qualcomm quotes sustained-inference figures (98% faster, 40% better performance-per-watt) rather than a peak TOPS number.

**Governing numbers.** 98% faster sustained AI inference and 40% improved performance-per-watt versus the Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 Hexagon NPU; micro-tile inferencing eliminates memory traffic between as many as 10 or more layers; INT4 doubles tensor throughput on INT4 layers; transformer acceleration up to 4.35x faster on certain MobileBERT use cases; large shared-memory bandwidth doubled versus the 8 Gen 2 generation; Llama 2-7B at up to 20 tokens per second; Fast Stable Diffusion 512x512 in less than 0.6 seconds; LPDDR5X at 4,800 MHz, 77 GB/s. NPU TOPS, shared-memory capacity, micro-tile dimensions, queue depths and per-accelerator widths are not published.

**Primary source.** Qualcomm, 'Unlocking on-device generative AI with an NPU and heterogeneous computing' (whitepaper, February 2024) — 'Microtile inferencing leverages the Hexagon NPU scalar capacity to break networks into small microtiles that can be executed independently. This eliminates memory traffic between as many as 10 or more layers, maximizes utilization of the scalar, vector, and tensor accelerators within the Hexagon NPU, and minimizes power consumption.'; 'Our latest Hexagon NPU in Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 was designed for generative AI and is our best yet, delivering 98% faster performance and 40% improved performance-per-watt for sustained AI inferencing.'; 'In addition, a dedicated power rail was added to the Hexagon Tensor Accelerator to enable maximum performance and efficiency for AI models that require different levels of scalar, vector, and tensor processing. The large shared memory also doubled its bandwidth.'; 'Memory bandwidth is the bottleneck for LLM token generation, which means that performance is limited by memory bandwidth rather than processing.'; 'On Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, our personal assistant demo ran Llama 2-7B at up to 20 tokens per second.'; 'Fast Stable Diffusion generated a 512x512 image in less than 0.6 seconds without losing much accuracy.'; 'Native 4-bit integer (INT4) support enables improved power and memory bandwidth efficiency while doubling tensor throughput of INT4 layers and networks.'; 'The transformer network acceleration dramatically sped up inference for multi-head attention, which is used throughout generative AI, resulting in a staggering AI performance up to 4.35X faster on certain use cases with the MobileBERT model.' Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 Mobile Platform Product Brief (87-71408-1 Rev G) — 'Fused AI accelerator architecture • Hexagon scalar, vector, and tensor accelerators • Hexagon Direct Link • Upgraded Micro Tile Inferencing • Support for all precisions (INT4, INT8, INT16, FP16)'.

#### Inside the signature block: The Kryo CPU cluster — 1+5+2 on the DSU-120

**Inside it.** The cluster is Arm's Total Compute Solution 2023 configuration, assembled by Qualcomm: one Cortex-X4 prime, five Cortex-A720 performance cores and two Cortex-A520 efficiency cores in a merged-core complex, all joined by the DynamIQ Shared Unit DSU-120 with a shared L3. (1) Cortex-X4 prime — the widest Arm core to date: 10-wide decode and 10-wide rename/dispatch, a 384-entry reorder buffer, 21 execution ports including eight integer ALUs and three branch units, 64 KB I-cache plus 64 KB D-cache, and up to 2 MB of private L2; the micro-op cache of the X3 generation is removed, so every instruction pays the decode cost each time it executes. (2) Five Cortex-A720 — the sustained-performance middle: 5-wide decode out-of-order cores with a new L2 spatial-prefetch engine, 9-cycle L2 latency (down from 10), up to twice the memset(0) bandwidth in L2, and 20% more power efficiency than the A715; three run at up to 3.2 GHz and two at up to 3.0 GHz. (3) Two Cortex-A520 in a merged-core complex — the efficiency pair: 3-wide decode, two ALU instructions issued per cycle (one of its three ALU pipelines removed versus the A510), sharing one L2 cache, one L2 TLB and one vector datapath between the two cores; 22% more power efficient than the A510 and 8% faster. (4) DSU-120 — the cluster hub: scales to 14 cores and up to 32 MB of shared L3, with intelligent per-core power modes; Qualcomm configures it with 12 MB of shared L3 on this SoC per most secondary reporting — Notebookcheck lists 8 MiB, so the size is disputed, see Fact check. (5) Per-core clock domains — prime at up to 3.3 GHz, performance cores at 3.2 and 3.0 GHz, efficiency cores at 2.3 GHz; the first 64-bit-only Qualcomm flagship cluster.

**Trace — one unit of work: one instruction through the prime core.**
1. **Fetch. **The prime core fetches from its 64 KB I-cache; a miss goes to the private L2 (up to 2 MB) or the shared DSU-120 L3.
2. **Decode 10-wide. **Up to 10 instructions decode per cycle — the X4 has no micro-op cache, so every instruction pays the decode cost each time it executes, and the width is the compensation.
3. **Rename and dispatch. **Up to 10 micro-ops per cycle are renamed onto physical registers and dispatched into the 384-entry reorder buffer — the out-of-order window that lets the core look nearly 400 instructions ahead for independent work.
4. **Issue and execute. **The scheduler issues ready micro-ops to 21 execution ports — eight integer ALUs, three branch units and the FP/NEON pipelines — so independent work overlaps in the same cycle.
5. **Retire in order. **Results commit in program order from the reorder buffer; a branch mispredict flushes the window and the front end refills from the correct path.
6. **Cluster placement. **The OS scheduler — not the hardware — decides which core runs the thread: a single-threaded burst goes to the X4 at 3.3 GHz, sustained multi-threaded work spreads across the five A720s, and background work drops to the A520 complex, where the two cores share an L2 and a vector unit and sip power.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves two walls: the single-thread wall — the X4's 10-wide front end and 384-entry window are the widest Arm has shipped, so one thread gets more per-cycle work than any prior Kryo; and the middle-core wall — five A720s instead of three little cores mean sustained multi-threaded work no longer queues behind one prime core. Creates two new bottlenecks instead: the shared L3 and the LPDDR5X link — when all eight cores fire at once, the shared L3 and the 77 GB/s memory link are the contention point, so the cluster's peak is a memory-system peak as much as a core peak; and the thermal wall on the prime — the X4 at 3.3 GHz is the hottest spot on the die, so sustained single-thread performance throttles toward the A720s' clocks and the 'prime' advantage narrows under load.

**Governing numbers.** Cortex-X4: 10-wide decode, 10-wide rename/dispatch, 384-entry reorder buffer, 21 execution ports, 8 integer ALUs, 3 branch units, 64 KB I-cache plus 64 KB D-cache, up to 2 MB private L2; Arm claims 15% more performance and 40% better power efficiency than the Cortex-X3 (SPECRate2017_int_base). Cortex-A720: 5-wide decode, 9-cycle L2 latency, new L2 spatial-prefetch engine, up to 2x memset(0) bandwidth in L2, 20% more power efficient than the A715. Cortex-A520: 3-wide decode, 2 ALU instructions issued per cycle, 22% more power efficient and 8% faster than the A510. DSU-120: up to 14 cores, up to 32 MB shared L3. Cluster clocks: 3.3 GHz (X4), 3.2 and 3.0 GHz (A720), 2.3 GHz (A520). Shared L3: 12 MB per most secondary reporting; Notebookcheck lists 8 MiB — disputed. Qualcomm's own figures: Kryo CPU 30% faster and 20% more power efficient than the Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 CPU. Per-core L2 sizes as configured by Qualcomm, L3 latency and DSU-120 queue depths are not published.

**Primary source.** Arm, 'Arm Cortex-A720 and Cortex-A520 CPUs' (Arm Community blog, May 2023) — 'Cortex-A720 is the industry-leading IP for sustained premium performance, delivering 20 percent more power efficiency compared to the previous generation Arm Cortex-A715'; 'Cortex-A520, our latest LITTLE core, has an unrelenting focus on delivering the very best power efficiency in the smallest silicon footprint, with improvements of 22 percent over the previous generation Cortex-A510'; 'Building on the merged-core architecture introduced two years ago with Cortex-A510, these high efficiency improvements are made possible through additional microarchitecture-level changes, particularly around data prefetching and branch prediction.'; 'Integrating both CPUs with the new DynamIQ Shared Unit, the DSU-120, provides intelligent power-saving features, enhanced PPA and even greater scalability.'
