#### Down to the primitives: The Hexagon NPU — fused scalar/vector/tensor accelerator with micro-tile inferencing

The NPU runs Qualcomm's documented pipeline in order — INT4 weights stream from LPDDR5X into the large shared memory, the scalar accelerator slices each layer into micro-tiles, the tensor accelerator runs the matrix multiplies at INT4, the vector accelerator finishes activations and normalisation, the tile's output stays in shared memory and feeds the next layer directly, and Hexagon Direct Link moves data to the other AI Engine processors without CPU orchestration — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (micro-tiles waiting for the tensor and vector accelerators; weight and activation staging)** — The scalar accelerator breaks each network layer into micro-tiles and schedules them across the vector and tensor accelerators, so a queue holds the tiles waiting for an accelerator to free up — decoupling slicing from execution, which is what lets the three accelerators stay busy on different tiles at once. Weights and activations stage through queues on their way from LPDDR5X into the shared memory. The queue depths and widths are not published.

- **SRAM bank (large shared memory — one pool for the scalar, vector and tensor accelerators)** — The large shared memory is the block's working store: one pool shared by all three accelerators, so a micro-tile's output moves from tensor work to vector work to the next layer without leaving the NPU — the physical reason micro-tile inferencing eliminates the memory traffic between as many as 10 or more layers. Its bandwidth doubled in the Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 generation. The capacity, banking, line size and port count are not published.

- **Multiplier array + adder tree (tensor accelerator — the matrix engine; INT4 doubling)** — The tensor accelerator is a multiplier array feeding adder trees that reduce partial products into one result per output element — the matrix multiply at the heart of every convolution, fully-connected layer and attention score. Qualcomm states INT4 doubles tensor throughput on INT4 layers; in standard construction that is a MAC array whose lanes each process two 4-bit operands per cycle in place of one 8-bit operand. The array dimensions, MAC count and lane width are not published.

- **Wide SIMD register file (HVX vector accelerator — activations, normalisation, elementwise work)** — The vector accelerator (Hexagon Vector eXtensions, HVX) runs the activations, normalisation and elementwise operations of each layer, and its wide register file holds the vector operands those operations stream through. The HVX width for this generation is not published.

- **Crossbar / mux network (Hexagon Direct Link; shared-memory arbitration between the three accelerators)** — Hexagon Direct Link is the NPU's direct path to the other AI Engine processors, so data moves between the NPU, CPU, GPU and Sensing Hub without CPU orchestration — a mux/crossbar-style interconnect between the three accelerators, the shared memory and the external engines. Inside the NPU the same kind of arbitration decides which accelerator's request reaches the shared memory each cycle, since all three share one memory path. The link width, topology and arbitration policy are not published.

- **Address generator / counter (micro-tile slicing — tile coordinates and base addresses)** — Slicing a layer into micro-tiles is address arithmetic: counters step through tile coordinates and compute each tile's base address in shared memory, so the scalar accelerator can hand the tensor and vector accelerators a stream of independent tiles. The counter widths and tile dimensions are not published.

- **FSM / controller (scalar accelerator — the NPU's scheduler; dedicated power-rail control)** — The scalar accelerator is the NPU's control core: a finite-state controller that slices networks, schedules tiles across the vector and tensor accelerators and runs the elementwise and control code of each layer. The dedicated power rails are managed by a second controller that adapts delivery to the workload — a separate rail for the tensor accelerator alone in this generation — so scalar, vector and tensor work can be powered at different levels. Neither controller's state structure is published.

- **Activation-function unit (transformer acceleration; group convolution; activation acceleration)** — The whitepaper documents additional special hardware for transformer acceleration, improved group convolution and activation-function acceleration — the units that compute attention scores and the non-linear functions (softmax, GELU and their relatives) that a pure MAC array cannot do. In standard construction these are lookup tables plus adder trees for normalisation; Qualcomm publishes no unit counts, table sizes or latencies.

- **Credit counter / flow control (shared-memory bandwidth shared by three accelerators; LPDDR5X pacing)** — Three accelerators share one memory path and one 77 GB/s LPDDR5X link, so access is rationed — credit counters are the standard mechanism, granting an accelerator memory slots only while it holds credits, which is what keeps the tensor array from starving the scalar scheduler. The credit limits and counter widths are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Qualcomm publishes no Hexagon block diagram, shared-memory capacity, micro-tile dimensions, queue depths or per-accelerator widths for the Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 NPU, so the primitives below are mapped from the documented functions and pipeline stages in the February 2024 whitepaper and the product brief, not from a die diagram. Every published figure is already recorded at Level 2; no new chip-specific number is claimed here. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Down to the primitives: The Kryo CPU cluster — 1+5+2 on the DSU-120

The cluster runs Arm's documented pipeline in order — fetch from the 64 KB I-cache, 10-wide decode on the Cortex-X4 prime, rename onto physical registers, dispatch into the 384-entry reorder buffer, issue to 21 execution ports, retire in order, with the DSU-120's Snoop Control Unit and shared L3 keeping all eight cores coherent — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **Register file (physical register file — rename targets; 10-wide rename/dispatch on the X4)** — Rename maps each instruction's architectural registers onto physical registers, and the physical register file is the structure written at dispatch and read at issue — 10 micro-ops per cycle on the Cortex-X4, each taking its operands from this file. The physical register-file size, port count and per-cycle read/write width are not published.

- **FIFO / queue (384-entry reorder buffer — the in-order retirement queue; issue queues / reservation stations)** — The reorder buffer is a 384-entry circular queue holding in-flight micro-ops in program order: instructions dispatch into it, execute out of order, and retire from it in order. In front of the 21 execution ports, issue queues hold micro-ops waiting for their operands to be ready. The ROB depth of 384 entries is published; the issue-queue depths are not.

- **CAM / tag compare (L1 and L2 cache tags; L1 TLBs; DSU-120 snoop filters)** — Every cache lookup is a tag compare: the 64 KB L1 data cache is 4-way set associative, so four tags are compared in parallel on each access, and the L2 and shared L3 carry the same tag-compare structure at their own geometries. The L1 TLBs are fully associative CAM structures that match a virtual address against stored page translations. In the DSU-120, the Snoop Control Unit holds snoop filters — tag RAMs that track which core caches hold which addresses — so the SCU does not need to ask a core cache to look up a line it does not hold. The snoop filter's size is automatically determined from the configured number of cores and cache sizes; the TLB entry counts are not published.

- **SRAM bank (L1 I/D caches; private L2; shared L3 in DSU-120 slices)** — The L1 data cache is a 64 KB, 4-way set-associative SRAM bank with 64-byte lines, ECC protection and an RRIP replacement policy; the L1 instruction cache is 64 KB. Each core's private L2 is configurable to 512 KB, 1 MB or 2 MB, with an ECC granule of 128 or 256 bits. The shared L3 lives in the DSU-120 as up to eight slices, each slice a banked SRAM structure with data, tag, victim and snoop-filter RAMs; the 12 MB size most secondary reporting lists for this SoC is 12-way associative with 64-byte lines and ECC on data and tag RAMs — but the size itself is disputed (Notebookcheck lists 8 MiB, which the DSU-120 manual gives as 16-way), so the associativity is conditional on the 12 MB figure. Per-core L2 sizes as configured by Qualcomm are not published.

- **Priority encoder / arbiter (issue select to 21 execution ports; DSU-120 SCU and L3-slice arbitration)** — Each cycle the scheduler picks ready micro-ops for the Cortex-X4's 21 execution ports — a priority encoder over the issue queues, oldest-ready first in standard construction. In the DSU-120 the Snoop Control Unit arbitrates coherent requests between eight cores, and the L3 slices arbitrate requests from the cores and the main-memory masters. The arbiter structures and port counts are not published beyond the 21 execution ports.

- **Branch predictor structures (BTB tag array; history-predictor counter array; return stack)** — The Cortex-X4's program flow prediction hardware is three structures: a Branch Target Buffer holding the target addresses of previously taken branches — a tag array with one target address per entry; a branch prediction unit that uses previous branch history — a counter array indexed by history; and a return stack holding nested subroutine return addresses, pushed by BL-family instructions and popped by RET. A static predictor and an indirect branch predictor complete the set. The BTB entry count, history-table size and return-stack depth are not published.

- **Adder tree / ALU array (8 integer ALUs; 3 branch units; vector datapath 2x128 or 4x128-bit)** — The Cortex-X4's execution core is eight integer ALUs and three branch units fed by the 21 execution ports, plus an integrated Advanced SIMD and floating-point unit with SVE and SVE2 at a 128-bit vector length. The vector datapath is configurable to 2x128 bits or 4x128 bits; Qualcomm's configuration for this SoC is not published.

- **Multiplier array (integer and FP/SIMD multiply; Int8 dot product)** — The execution pipelines carry multiplier arrays for integer multiply and for floating-point and SIMD multiply, and the core implements the Int8 dot-product instructions that collapse a row of small multiplies into one accumulation. The multiplier array geometry and the number of multiply pipes are not published.

- **Prefetch engine / address generator (L2 spatial-prefetch engine on the A720; hardware data prefetchers on the X4)** — The Cortex-A720 carries a new L2 spatial-prefetch engine with a 9-cycle L2 latency, and the Cortex-X4 includes multiple hardware prefetch engines as part of the L1 and L2 caches, prefetching using a combination of virtual and physical addresses — address generators that predict which lines a thread will touch next and fetch them before the demand miss. The prefetch queue depths and the number of prefetch streams are not published.

- **Counter (PMU event counters — 6 or 31; write-streaming threshold counters)** — The Cortex-X4's Performance Monitoring Unit counts microarchitectural events with counters configurable to 6 or 31, and the write-streaming mode uses threshold counters per cache — L2, L3 and DRAM thresholds that decide when full-line writes stop causing cache allocations. Qualcomm's PMU configuration for this SoC is not published.

- **FSM / controller (exclusive monitor — 2-state open/exclusive FSM; DSU-120 Power Policy Units; MPMM/PDP dispatch block)** — The Cortex-X4's internal exclusive monitor is a 2-state finite-state machine — open and exclusive — that manages Load-Exclusive and Store-Exclusive accesses and Clear-Exclusive instructions, tagging a 16-word block (one cache line) for exclusive access. The DSU-120 integrates Power Policy Units that gate clocks and power per core and per L3 slice, and the X4's Maximum Power Mitigation Mechanism and Performance Defined Power features feed a dispatch-block signal that throttles issue when the power budget is exceeded. The FSM state encodings are not published.

- **Crossbar / interconnect (DSU-120 transport — cores to SCU to L3 slices to 1-4 CHI/AXI main-memory masters)** — The DSU-120's transport links eight cores, the Snoop Control Unit, up to eight L3 slices and the main-memory interface; its topology is automatically determined from the number of cores and L3 slices, and the main-memory interface can be configured as CHI or AXI with 1 to 4 bus master interfaces, plus up to two Accelerator Coherency Ports. The transport path widths are not published.

- **Mux / demux (L1 data-cache port structure; A520 merged-core shared vector datapath)** — The L1 data cache presents 4x64-bit read paths and 4x64-bit write paths to the integer pipeline and 3x128-bit read paths and 2x128-bit write paths to the vector pipeline — muxes selecting which bank serves which port each cycle. In the A520 merged-core complex the two cores share one vector datapath, so a mux selects which core drives it each cycle. The mux select logic is standard construction; the bank count is not published.

- **Synchronizer / clock-domain crossing (per-core clock domains; DSU-120 Q-Channel clock gating)** — The cluster's cores run at different frequencies and voltages — prime at up to 3.3 GHz, performance cores at 3.2 and 3.0 GHz, efficiency cores at 2.3 GHz — so data crossing between a core and the DSU-120 passes through synchronizers, and the DSU-120 gates clocks through Q-Channel requests with individual control of each core's clock. The synchronizer depths are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Arm publishes the Cortex-X4 and DSU-120 microarchitecture in its Technical Reference Manuals, so the primitives below are mapped from those manuals — but the manuals do not publish issue-queue depths, physical-register-file sizes, BTB entry counts, return-stack depth or the DSU-120's queue depths, and Qualcomm publishes no per-core L2 sizes as configured, L3 latency or cluster floorplan. Every published figure is already recorded at Level 2 unless it is a new Level-3 number recorded in the Fact check; no other new chip-specific number is claimed here. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Down to the gates: The Hexagon NPU — fused scalar/vector/tensor accelerator with micro-tile inferencing

Qualcomm publishes no gate-level structure for the Hexagon NPU on the Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the scalar, vector or tensor accelerators, the shared memory or Hexagon Direct Link. The deepest published description is the Qualcomm whitepaper Unlocking on-device generative AI with an NPU and heterogeneous computing (February 2024) and the Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 product brief, which document the fused scalar/vector/tensor pipeline, micro-tile inferencing across 10 or more layers, INT4 doubling tensor throughput, the doubled shared-memory bandwidth, the 77 GB/s LPDDR5X link and the dedicated power rails including a rail for the tensor accelerator alone. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors using the primer’s bottom layer — the universal gates, the latch and the flip-flop, the 6T SRAM cell, the CAM cell and the full adder — and every gate or transistor figure is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, not a claim about Qualcomm’s actual netlist. Where a primitive’s geometry is not published, no total is claimed.

- **FIFO / queue (micro-tiles waiting for the tensor and vector accelerators; weight and activation staging)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is a register file of D flip-flops — two cross-coupled latch stages, about 20–28 transistors each in a standard-cell library — or a small SRAM bank of 6T cells where the queue is deep, the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each (a full adder is two half adders — two XOR plus two AND plus one OR — about 28 transistors in static CMOS), incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XNOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The micro-tile queue that holds tiles waiting for the tensor or vector accelerator to free up is a FIFO of this form, and so are the weight and activation staging queues on the way from LPDDR5X into the shared memory; the decoupling they provide is what lets the three accelerators stay busy on different tiles at once. The queue depths and widths are not published, so no pointer width and no transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **SRAM bank (large shared memory — one pool for the scalar, vector and tensor accelerators)** — An SRAM bank at gate level is 6T cells — two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (two transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers (a cross-coupled inverter pair with enable transistors). The large shared memory is a bank of this form, one pool shared by the scalar, vector and tensor accelerators, so a micro-tile’s output moves from tensor work to vector work to the next layer without leaving the NPU — the physical reason micro-tile inferencing eliminates the memory traffic between as many as 10 or more layers, and the reason its bandwidth doubling in this generation matters: every accelerator’s operand fetch and result store passes through these cells. The capacity, banking, line size and port count are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Multiplier array + adder tree (tensor accelerator — the matrix engine; INT4 doubling)** — A multiplier array at gate level is AND gates forming the partial products — one AND gate per product bit — feeding an adder tree of full adders (about 28 transistors each) that collapses the partials into the product. The tensor accelerator is an array of this form: each multiply of the matrix engine is a partial-product AND plane plus an adder tree, and the INT4 doubling Qualcomm states is, in standard construction, a MAC array whose lanes each process two 4-bit operands per cycle in place of one 8-bit operand — a 4-bit by 4-bit multiply is 16 partial-product AND gates by arithmetic, against 64 for an 8-bit by 8-bit multiply, so the same array area holds twice the INT4 lanes. The array dimensions, MAC count and lane width are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Wide SIMD register file (HVX vector accelerator — activations, normalisation, elementwise work)** — A register file at gate level is an array of storage bits with a write decoder and read-port muxes: each stored bit is a D flip-flop — two cross-coupled latch stages, about 20–28 transistors in a standard-cell library — or a 6T SRAM cell where the array is built as SRAM, with the write address decoded through a NAND/NOR row-decoder tree and each read port a transmission-gate mux tree (two transistors per input leg). The HVX vector accelerator’s wide register file is a file of this form, holding the vector operands that the activations, normalisation and elementwise operations stream through after the tensor accelerator hands each micro-tile over; the write decoder is what lets the tensor result land in the vector file without a trip back to shared memory. The HVX width for this generation is not published, so no bit total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Crossbar / mux network (Hexagon Direct Link; shared-memory arbitration between the three accelerators)** — A mux at gate level is a transmission gate per input leg (two transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree, with the select lines decoded from the control bits through a NAND/NOR decoder, and a crossbar is a grid of such muxes — one per output, each selecting among all inputs. Hexagon Direct Link is a mux/crossbar network of this form, moving data between the NPU, CPU, GPU and Sensing Hub without CPU orchestration, and inside the NPU the same kind of arbitration decides which accelerator’s request reaches the shared memory each cycle, since all three share one memory path — the arbiter is a priority-encoder tree over the three request lines. The link width, topology and arbitration policy are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Address generator / counter (micro-tile slicing — tile coordinates and base addresses)** — An address generator at gate level is counters plus adders: a counter is D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer — one flip-flop and one full adder (about 28 transistors, two half adders) per bit — and the base-address computation is an adder tree over the tile coordinates. Slicing a layer into micro-tiles is address arithmetic of this form: counters step through tile coordinates and an adder computes each tile’s base address in shared memory, so the scalar accelerator can hand the tensor and vector accelerators a stream of independent tiles with no address work left for them. The counter widths and tile dimensions are not published, so no transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **FSM / controller (scalar accelerator — the NPU's scheduler; dedicated power-rail control)** — A controller at gate level is a finite-state machine built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the inputs, with the outputs decoded from the state flops through another NAND/NOR network. The scalar accelerator is an FSM of this form — it slices networks, schedules micro-tiles across the vector and tensor accelerators and runs the elementwise and control code of each layer, so its next-state logic is driven by the tile-queue full/empty flags and the accelerators’ completion signals. The dedicated power-rail controller is a second FSM of the same form, switching the tensor accelerator’s own rail to the level the workload needs. Neither controller’s state structure is published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Activation-function unit (transformer acceleration; group convolution; activation acceleration)** — An activation-function unit at gate level is lookup tables plus adder trees: a table is a small SRAM bank or ROM array of 6T cells (or a NAND/NOR decoder tree over a hardwired bit pattern) holding the function’s sampled values, addressed by the input’s high bits, with an adder tree interpolating between samples, and normalisation is an adder tree plus a divider built from subtractors of full adders. The transformer-acceleration, group-convolution and activation-acceleration hardware Qualcomm documents is units of this form, computing the attention scores and the non-linear functions (softmax, GELU and their relatives) that the pure MAC array of the tensor accelerator cannot do. Qualcomm publishes no unit counts, table sizes or latencies, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Credit counter / flow control (shared-memory bandwidth shared by three accelerators; LPDDR5X pacing)** — A credit counter at gate level is an up/down counter: D flip-flops holding the credit balance plus a full-adder incrementer/decrementer (about 28 transistors per bit) that adds on a credit return and subtracts on an issue, with a zero comparator (XNOR per bit plus an AND tree) that stalls the requester when the balance is spent. The rationing of the shared-memory path and the single 77 GB/s LPDDR5X link between the three accelerators is counters of this form, granting an accelerator memory slots only while it holds credits — which is what keeps the tensor array from starving the scalar scheduler. The credit limits and counter widths are not published, so no transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Qualcomm publishes the Hexagon NPU at function level only — the fused scalar, vector and tensor accelerators, micro-tile inferencing, INT4 tensor throughput, the large shared memory and Hexagon Direct Link (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the NPU appears in any Qualcomm source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer’s bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Qualcomm’s actual netlist. No new chip-specific number is claimed at Level 4 beyond the published figures already recorded at Levels 2 and 3.

#### Down to the gates: The Kryo CPU cluster — 1+5+2 on the DSU-120

Arm publishes the Cortex-X4 and DSU-120 microarchitecture in its Technical Reference Manuals — the pipeline widths, the cache geometries, the 384-entry reorder buffer, the 21 execution ports — but no gate-level structure for any of it: no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the rename logic, the issue queues, the caches or the DSU-120 transport. Qualcomm publishes no per-core L2 sizes as configured, no L3 latency and no cluster floorplan. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors using the primer’s bottom layer — the universal gates, the latch and the flip-flop, the 6T SRAM cell, the CAM cell and the full adder — and every gate or transistor figure is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, not a claim about Arm’s or Qualcomm’s actual netlist. Counter widths computed from published figures are labelled arithmetic; where a primitive’s geometry is not published, no total is claimed.

- **Register file (physical register file — rename targets; 10-wide rename/dispatch on the X4)** — A register file at gate level is an array of storage bits with a write decoder and read-port muxes: each stored bit is a D flip-flop — two cross-coupled latch stages, about 20–28 transistors in a standard-cell library — or a 6T SRAM cell where the array is built as SRAM, with the write address decoded through a NAND/NOR row-decoder tree and each read port a transmission-gate mux tree (two transistors per input leg). The Cortex-X4’s physical register file is a file of this form, written at dispatch and read at issue — 10 micro-ops per cycle, each taking its operands from this file, so the read-port mux trees are what the 10-wide rename and dispatch actually costs in gates. The physical register-file size, port count and per-cycle read/write width are not published, so no bit total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **FIFO / queue (384-entry reorder buffer — the in-order retirement queue; issue queues / reservation stations)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is a register file of D flip-flops or a small SRAM bank, the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each (a full adder is two half adders — two XOR plus two AND plus one OR — about 28 transistors in static CMOS), and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XNOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The 384-entry reorder buffer is a circular queue of this form holding in-flight micro-ops in program order, and its pointers are 9 bits wide by arithmetic from the published 384 entries (2 to the 8th is 256, below 384; 2 to the 9th is 512, the smallest power of two above it) — 9 flip-flops plus 9 full adders per pointer by arithmetic, 180 to 252 transistors of flip-flops plus 252 of adders. The issue queues in front of the 21 execution ports are FIFOs of the same form; their depths are not published, so no other pointer width and no total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **CAM / tag compare (L1 and L2 cache tags; L1 TLBs; DSU-120 snoop filters)** — A CAM cell is a 6T SRAM storage cell plus XOR match logic feeding a matchline — a NOR CAM cell adds four match transistors (ten transistors in total) and a NAND CAM cell adds three (nine in total), textbook-standard — with the matchline precharged and sensed per row. A plain tag compare is the same match without the storage: one XNOR gate per tag bit feeding an AND tree that asserts on a full match. The L1 data cache’s four-way tag compare is four such comparators in parallel on each access, and the L1 TLBs are fully associative CAM structures matching a virtual address against stored page translations, while the DSU-120 snoop filters are tag RAMs whose comparators let the Snoop Control Unit skip asking a core cache about a line it does not hold. The L1 set index is 8 bits by arithmetic from the published 64 KB, 4-way, 64-byte-line geometry (65,536 divided by 4 ways times 64 bytes is 256 sets, and 2 to the 8th is 256), with a 6-bit byte offset inside each 64-byte line by arithmetic. The snoop-filter size and the TLB entry counts are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **SRAM bank (L1 I/D caches; private L2; shared L3 in DSU-120 slices)** — An SRAM bank at gate level is 6T cells — two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (two transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers (a cross-coupled inverter pair with enable transistors). The 64 KB L1 data and instruction caches are banks of this form with 64-byte lines, ECC protection and an RRIP replacement policy, each core’s private L2 is a larger bank of the same cells configurable to 512 KB, 1 MB or 2 MB, and the shared L3 lives in the DSU-120 as up to eight slices, each slice a banked SRAM structure with data, tag, victim and snoop-filter RAMs. The 12 MB size most secondary reporting lists for this SoC is disputed (Notebookcheck lists 8 MiB), so no L3 cell total is computed from it, and the per-core L2 sizes as configured by Qualcomm are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Priority encoder / arbiter (issue select to 21 execution ports; DSU-120 SCU and L3-slice arbitration)** — A priority encoder at gate level is an OR/NAND tree that turns a one-hot ready vector into the binary index of the highest-priority set bit — a 2-to-the-n-to-n encoder is a tree of OR gates, one per output bit, fed by the ready lines. The Cortex-X4’s issue select is an encoder of this form over the issue queues, picking ready micro-ops for the 21 execution ports each cycle, and its port index is 5 bits wide by arithmetic from the published 21 ports (2 to the 4th is 16, below 21; 2 to the 5th is 32, the smallest power of two above it); round-robin fairness adds a rotating priority register (D flip-flops holding the last grant) that reorders the encoder’s inputs. In the DSU-120 the Snoop Control Unit’s arbitration between eight cores and the L3 slices’ arbitration of core and main-memory requests are encoders of the same tree form. The arbiter structures and port counts are not published beyond the 21 execution ports, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Branch predictor structures (BTB tag array; history-predictor counter array; return stack)** — A branch-target buffer at gate level is a tag array — an SRAM bank of 6T cells with a row decoder and sense amplifiers, one target address per entry — plus a tag comparator per entry (one XNOR per tag bit feeding an AND tree) that asserts on a match; a history-predictor counter array is a bank of small saturating counters, each two D flip-flops plus next-state NAND/NOR logic that increments on a taken branch and decrements on a not-taken one; and a return stack is a stack of D flip-flops holding nested subroutine return addresses, with a push/pop pointer counter (D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer) driven by BL-family instructions and RET. The Cortex-X4’s program-flow prediction hardware is these three structures plus a static predictor and an indirect branch predictor, all of the same cell forms. The BTB entry count, history-table size and return-stack depth are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Adder tree / ALU array (8 integer ALUs; 3 branch units; vector datapath 2x128 or 4x128-bit)** — An integer ALU at gate level is a full-adder chain for add and subtract (each full adder two half adders — two XOR plus two AND plus one OR, about 28 transistors in static CMOS), a NAND/NOR network for the logic operations, and a mux tree for the shifts — a barrel shifter of log2(N) stages of 2:1 muxes for an N-bit word. The Cortex-X4’s execution core is eight such ALUs and three branch units — the branch units are magnitude comparators, subtractors of full adders whose sign bit decides the outcome — fed by the 21 execution ports, plus an integrated Advanced SIMD and floating-point unit with SVE and SVE2 at a 128-bit vector length, whose vector datapath is configurable to 2x128 bits or 4x128 bits: each 128-bit lane is a replicated adder and logic array of the same gates. Qualcomm’s vector-datapath configuration for this SoC is not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Multiplier array (integer and FP/SIMD multiply; Int8 dot product)** — A multiplier array at gate level is AND gates forming the partial products — one AND gate per product bit — feeding an adder tree of full adders (about 28 transistors each) that collapses the partials into the product. The Cortex-X4’s execution pipelines carry multiplier arrays of this form for integer multiply and for floating-point and SIMD multiply, and the Int8 dot-product instructions are narrow multipliers of the same form whose partial products feed one accumulation tree, collapsing a row of small multiplies into one accumulation instead of a chain of separate multiply-adds. The multiplier array geometry and the number of multiply pipes are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Prefetch engine / address generator (L2 spatial-prefetch engine on the A720; hardware data prefetchers on the X4)** — A prefetch engine at gate level is address generators plus a small queue: each generator is a counter (D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer) stepping through a stride pattern plus an adder computing the next line address from the current one, and the predicted lines wait in a FIFO of D flip-flops with pointer counters and full/empty comparators before the demand miss arrives. The Cortex-A720’s L2 spatial-prefetch engine is a generator of this form working against the published 9-cycle L2 latency, and the Cortex-X4’s multiple hardware prefetch engines in the L1 and L2 caches are generators of the same form, prefetching with a combination of virtual and physical addresses. The prefetch queue depths and the number of prefetch streams are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Counter (PMU event counters — 6 or 31; write-streaming threshold counters)** — A counter at gate level is D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer — one flip-flop and one full adder (about 28 transistors, two half adders) per bit — so a counter’s transistor cost is roughly its bit width times the flip-flop-plus-adder cost. The Cortex-X4’s Performance Monitoring Unit is counters of this form, configurable to 6 or 31 event counters, and the counter select is 5 bits wide by arithmetic from the published 31 (2 to the 4th is 16, below 31; 2 to the 5th is 32, the smallest power of two above it) — 100 to 140 transistors of flip-flops plus 140 of adders for the select logic by arithmetic. The write-streaming threshold counters are counters of the same form with a magnitude comparator (a subtractor of full adders) that decides when full-line writes stop causing cache allocations. Qualcomm’s PMU configuration for this SoC is not published, so no other counter total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **FSM / controller (exclusive monitor — 2-state open/exclusive FSM; DSU-120 Power Policy Units; MPMM/PDP dispatch block)** — A controller at gate level is a finite-state machine built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the inputs, with the outputs decoded from the state flops through another NAND/NOR network. The Cortex-X4’s internal exclusive monitor is a 2-state FSM of this form — open and exclusive — so it is a single state flip-flop plus the next-state logic for Load-Exclusive, Store-Exclusive and Clear-Exclusive, tagging a 16-word block (one cache line) whose word index is 4 bits wide by arithmetic (2 to the 4th is 16). The DSU-120’s Power Policy Units are FSMs of the same form gating clocks and power per core and per L3 slice, and the X4’s Maximum Power Mitigation Mechanism and Performance Defined Power features feed a dispatch-block signal — a magnitude comparator against the power budget whose output throttles issue. The FSM state encodings are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Crossbar / interconnect (DSU-120 transport — cores to SCU to L3 slices to 1-4 CHI/AXI main-memory masters)** — A crossbar at gate level is a grid of muxes — one per output, each a transmission gate per input leg (two transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree, selecting among all inputs, with the select lines decoded from the control bits through a NAND/NOR decoder — and an interconnect is crossbars plus the arbiters that grant them, priority-encoder trees over the request lines. The DSU-120’s transport is a network of this form linking eight cores, the Snoop Control Unit, up to eight L3 slices and the main-memory interface, configurable as CHI or AXI with 1 to 4 bus master interfaces plus up to two Accelerator Coherency Ports; its topology is automatically determined from the number of cores and L3 slices. The transport path widths are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Mux / demux (L1 data-cache port structure; A520 merged-core shared vector datapath)** — A mux at gate level is a transmission gate per input leg (two transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree, with the select lines decoded from the control bits through a NAND/NOR decoder; a demux is the same tree run in reverse. The L1 data cache’s port structure is mux trees of this form selecting which bank serves which port each cycle — 4x64-bit read paths and 4x64-bit write paths to the integer pipeline and 3x128-bit read paths and 2x128-bit write paths to the vector pipeline — and in the A520 merged-core complex the two cores share one vector datapath, so a mux selects which core drives it each cycle. The mux select logic is standard construction; the bank count is not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Synchronizer / clock-domain crossing (per-core clock domains; DSU-120 Q-Channel clock gating)** — A synchronizer at gate level is two D flip-flops in series per crossing bit — the standard two-flop synchronizer: the first flop may go metastable on a clock-domain crossing, and the second samples it a cycle later, so each bit crossing a domain costs two flip-flops by arithmetic; a multi-bit crossing is an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers, the pointers themselves counters of D flip-flops plus full adders with only one bit changing per step. The cluster’s cores run at different frequencies and voltages — prime at up to 3.3 GHz, performance cores at 3.2 and 3.0 GHz, efficiency cores at 2.3 GHz — so data crossing between a core and the DSU-120 passes through synchronizers of this form, and the DSU-120 gates clocks through Q-Channel requests with individual control of each core’s clock. The synchronizer depths are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Arm publishes the Cortex-X4 and DSU-120 at microarchitecture level only — pipeline widths, cache geometries, the 384-entry reorder buffer, the 21 execution ports, the PMU counter options, the exclusive-monitor state machine and the DSU-120 transport (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the cluster appears in any Arm or Qualcomm source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer’s bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Arm’s or Qualcomm’s actual netlist. The only new numbers are counter widths computed from published figures and labelled arithmetic: 9-bit reorder-buffer pointers from 384 entries, an 8-bit L1 set index from 64 KB, 4-way, 64-byte lines, a 4-bit exclusive-monitor word index from a 16-word block, a 5-bit PMU counter select from 31 counters and a 5-bit issue-port index from 21 ports.

### MediaTek Dimensity 9300

**Added: 2026-11-22** (deepened to Level-2/3/4 standard: 2026-11-28)

**Specs (wiki card).** TSMC 4 nm · all-big-core (4× X4 + 4× A720)

**Building blocks.**
- **All-big-core CPU — 4× X4 + 4× A720 ★** — The gamble itself: four Cortex-X4 (one at 3.25 GHz, three at 2.85 GHz) and four Cortex-A720 at 2.0 GHz — no efficiency cores at all. Idle and light work run on down-clocked big cores, betting the process and scheduler make little cores unnecessary
- **18 MB cache complex** — Enlarged L3 + system-level cache (29% larger than the prior generation per MediaTek) — the quiet enabler of the all-big bet: big cores are only efficient if they aren't waiting on DRAM
- **APU 790 — generative AI engine** — MediaTek's 7th-generation APU with a hardware generative-AI engine: transformer acceleration, INT4 (A16W4) support and a hardware memory-compression path feeding it — specified to run 7B LLMs at 20 tokens/s, scaling to 33B with compression
- **Immortalis-G720 MC12 GPU** — Arm's 12-core flagship GPU with second-generation hardware ray tracing — the gaming leg of the platform
- **Imagiq 990 ISP + MiraVision 990** — The 9300's camera/display pair: Imagiq 990 with a 16-layer AI semantic analysis engine for video, and the MiraVision 990 AI display pipeline
- **LPDDR5T-9600 memory** — First phone SoC on LPDDR5T at 9,600 Mbps — bandwidth bought specifically to feed LLM inference and the all-big cluster

**The piece that makes it special.** Deleting the little core. Every flagship SoC since big.LITTLE assumed efficiency needs a different, smaller core. Dimensity 9300 is the clean controlled experiment against that assumption: eight big cores, a fat cache, fast memory, and DVFS doing the efficiency work. Its results — competitive efficiency in reviews, with sustained-load thermals as the caveat — moved the industry: subsequent flagships shrank, but did not restore, the classic little-core cluster.

**How work flows.** Workload lands: The scheduler sees only big cores; threads place by performance need, not core type. DVFS does the efficiency work: Light tasks run X4/A720 cores at low voltage/frequency points instead of migrating to a little core. LLM inference streams: APU 790 pulls compressed weights from LPDDR5T; its decompression hardware expands them in flight. Cache absorbs the bursts: The 18 MB complex keeps the wide cluster fed so DRAM trips stay rare. Thermals arbitrate: Sustained all-core loads settle where the phone's cooling lets them — the bet's known price.

**Trade-off accepted.** Sustained-load thermals and idle floor. Peak benchmarks flattered the design; long gaming sessions in reviews showed throttling doing the efficiency work the little cores used to do, and there is no ultra-low-power CPU island for the lightest background work (the APU and sensor hub cover some of it). MediaTek publishes clocks and ceilings, not core internals — the X4/A720 blocks themselves are Arm's documented designs.
