#### Inside the signature block: The all-big-core CPU cluster — 4× Cortex-X4 + 4× Cortex-A720 on the DSU-120

**Inside it.** The cluster is Arm's DSU-120 shared logic wrapped around eight cores of two types — the documented parts, not a MediaTek floorplan. (1) Four Cortex-X4 prime cores: the widest Arm core of its generation — 10-wide decode and rename/dispatch, a 384-entry reorder buffer (a 768-instruction window with fused micro-ops), 21 execution ports, eight integer ALUs and three branch units, 64 KB instruction and 64 KB data L1 caches, and a private 512 KB–2 MB 8-way L2 per core. The old MOP cache is gone — fusion moved into the redesigned single instruction cache. (2) Four Cortex-A720 performance cores: 5-wide decode, a 9-cycle L2 latency, a new L2 spatial-prefetch engine, and 20% better power efficiency than the A715 — the cores that do the light and medium work the old little cores used to do. (3) The DSU-120 itself: shared L3, snoop control, power policy and the memory interfaces. (4) One asynchronous CPU bridge per core, between each core's L2 and the DSU-120. (5) MediaTek's own 10 MB system-level cache beyond the DSU-120, which with the 8 MB L3 makes the 18 MB complex.

**Trace — one unit of work: one instruction through the prime core, and one load that misses to L3.**
1. **Fetch.** The instruction is fetched from the 64 KB L1 instruction cache; the redesigned single instruction cache carries the fused-instruction role the old 1,536-entry MOP cache used to play.
2. **Decode — 10 wide.** Eight parallel decoders deliver up to eight instructions per cycle; rename and dispatch move up to 10 micro-ops per cycle into the out-of-order engine.
3. **Wait in the reorder buffer.** The micro-op takes a slot in the 384-entry reorder buffer — a 768-instruction window with fused micro-ops — and waits there until its operands are ready and older instructions have retired.
4. **Issue to 21 ports.** When ready, the micro-op issues to one of 21 execution ports — integer work to one of eight ALUs, branches to one of three branch units, vector work to the 128-bit SVE2 datapath, configurable to 2×128 or 4×128 bits.
5. **Load hits L1.** A load reads the 64 KB, 4-way L1 data cache (64-byte lines, RRIP replacement) through one of four 64-bit integer read paths; on a hit the data returns to the execution pipeline and the instruction retires in order from the reorder buffer.
6. **Miss walks to L3.** On an L1 miss the request checks the private L2 (512 KB–2 MB, 8-way), then crosses the asynchronous CPU bridge over the 256-bit CHI interface into the DSU-120, where the Snoop Control Unit's snoop filters — one per L3 slice — say whether any core already holds the line, so a cache-to-cache transfer can move it directly without touching L3.
7. **L3 or DRAM.** Otherwise the 8 MB, 16-way shared L3 (64-byte lines, ECC on data and tag RAMs) serves the line; on an L3 miss the request leaves through the 256-bit main-memory interface to MediaTek's 10 MB system-level cache and then LPDDR5T at 9,600 Mbps.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the single-thread and scheduling walls at once: the widest Arm core of its generation does the heavy lifting, and with no little cores there is no migration cost, no little-core frequency ceiling and no scheduler guessing which core a thread belongs on. Creates three new bottlenecks instead. First, shared-cache contention: eight big cores share one 8 MB L3 and one memory path, so a multithreaded burst competes harder for the 18 MB complex — and the L3 allocation policy is typically exclusive, so a line lives in exactly one place and a miss pays the full walk to DRAM. Second, power: the efficiency floor is now set by DVFS on big cores, and the DSU-120's six cache power modes with 7% lower L3 dynamic power and 18% lower power from cache misses (Arm's figures) only soften the cost of keeping eight wide cores fed. Third, thermals: sustained all-core loads settle where the phone's cooling lets them, which is why the all-big bet shows up as burst performance first and sustained performance second.

**Governing numbers.** 1× Cortex-X4 at 3.25 GHz, 3× Cortex-X4 at 2.85 GHz, 4× Cortex-A720 at 2.0 GHz; X4 decode 10-wide, dispatch 10 micro-ops per cycle, 384-entry reorder buffer, 21 execution ports, 8 integer ALUs, 3 branch units; L1 64 KB instruction + 64 KB data per core (4-way, 64-byte lines); private L2 512 KB–2 MB per core, 8-way (MediaTek's per-core sizes not published); L3 8 MB, 16-way, 64-byte lines, ECC on data and tag RAMs, up to 8 slices; CHI interface 256 bits wide; main-memory interface up to four 256-bit bus masters; 18 MB total cache complex (8 MB L3 + 10 MB system-level cache), 29% larger than the Dimensity 9200's 14 MB; LPDDR5T at 9,600 Mbps. Not published: per-core L2 sizes and vector datapath width as configured by MediaTek, the number of L3 slices as configured, and L3 latency.

**Primary source.** Arm Cortex-X4 Core Technical Reference Manual (102484_0003_06_en, Issue 06, r0p3) — "The main blocks include: • L1 instruction and L1 data memory systems • L2 memory system • Register rename • Instruction decode • Instruction issue • Execution pipeline • Memory Management Unit (MMU) • Trace unit and trace buffer • Performance Monitoring Unit (PMU) • Activity Monitoring Unit (AMU) • Generic Interrupt Controller (GIC) CPU interface"; "The L1 data memory system includes: • A 64KB, 4-way set associative cache with 64-byte cache lines."; "You can configure the L2 cache to be 512KB, 1024KB, or 2048KB."; "The CHI interface is 256 bits wide." Arm DynamIQ Shared Unit-120 Technical Reference Manual (102547_0201_07_en, Issue 07) — "The cache can be implemented with up to eight cache slices, depending on the specified L3 cache size. Each cache slice consists of data, tag, victim, and snoop filter RAMs and associated logic."; "All caches have 64-byte line cache length. Data and tag RAMs have Error Correcting Code (ECC) protection."; "The SCU contains a set of snoop filters that track the addresses for locations cached in the core caches." MediaTek Dimensity 9300 product page — "4X Cortex-X4 performance cores up to 3.25GHz — 4X Cortex-A720 efficiency cores up to 2.0GHz — 18MB L3 + SLC cache: 29% Larger than previous generation".

#### Inside the signature block: APU 790 — the generative-AI engine and its memory-compression path

**Inside it.** MediaTek publishes no APU 790 block diagram, TOPS figure, internal widths or queue depths, so these are the functions MediaTek itself names, not die sub-blocks. (1) The A16W4 INT4 tensor unit — a mixed-precision tensor engine that runs 16-bit activations against 4-bit weights, halving the bytes per weight against INT8. (2) NeuroPilot memory hardware compression — the compression and decompression hardware between DRAM and the APU: models are pre-compressed before they are stored, then expanded in hardware as they stream into the tensor unit. (3) Transformer operator acceleration — the hardware adaptation of the transformer model for operator acceleration that MediaTek credits with the 8× speedup over the APU 690. (4) NeuroPilot Fusion — the LoRA path that continuously performs low-rank adaptation on-device. (5) The memory path itself — LPDDR5T at 9,600 Mbps feeding the APU, the reason the whole design is organised around moving fewer bytes per token.

**Trace — one unit of work: one decode step of a 7B LLM.**
1. **Weights wait compressed.** The model's weights sit in LPDDR5T in compressed form — in MediaTek's worked example a 13 GB INT8 model is pre-compressed to 5 GB before it ever reaches the chip (reported by Android Authority).
2. **Decompression in flight.** As weights stream toward the APU, the NeuroPilot hardware decompression expands them on the way in — the model is stored compressed and expanded only as it is consumed.
3. **INT4 tensor math.** The A16W4 tensor unit multiplies 16-bit activations against 4-bit weights, halving the bytes per weight against INT8.
4. **Attention accelerated.** Multi-head attention runs through the transformer operator acceleration — the 8× faster path versus the APU 690.
5. **LoRA fused in.** NeuroPilot Fusion applies the low-rank adapter continuously, so personalisation updates ride the same pass instead of a second one.
6. **One token out.** A token emerges at 20 tokens per second for a 7B model; the same path stretches to 13B models inside 16 GB of RAM and 33B models with 24 GB — at 3–4 tokens per second, where the compression and bandwidth budget finally runs out (rates for the larger models as reported by Android Authority).

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the memory wall that makes on-device LLMs impractical: token generation is memory-bound, and INT4 plus hardware decompression attack exactly that — a 13 GB model fits in 5 GB of RAM, and the bytes per token fall with the weight precision. Creates two new bottlenecks instead: decompression throughput — the tensor unit can only eat weights as fast as the decompression hardware expands them, so the ceiling moves from DRAM bandwidth to the decompressor; and the token-rate cliff — 20 tokens per second at 7B parameters falls to 3–4 at 33B, because the compressed model still has to stream through the same LPDDR5T path. Power is the quiet third limit: the APU 790 doubles integer and floating-point performance while cutting power 45% against the APU 690, which is what makes sustained on-device generation possible at all — but it is a budget, not a removal, of the thermal cost.

**Governing numbers.** 2× integer and floating-point operations performance and 45% lower power than the APU 690; 8× faster transformer processing; Stable Diffusion image generation in under one second; 7B-parameter LLM at 20 tokens per second; supports 1B, 7B and 13B models, scalable to 33B; 13B model inside 16 GB of RAM, 33B with 24 GB of RAM at 3–4 tokens per second (secondary reporting); 13 GB INT8 model compressed to 5 GB in MediaTek's worked example (secondary reporting). Not published: APU 790 TOPS, tensor-unit dimensions, decompression throughput, queue depths, or any block diagram.

**Primary source.** MediaTek, "MediaTek's New All Big Core Design for Flagship Dimensity 9300 Chipset Maximizes Smartphone Performance and Efficiency" (press release, Nov 6, 2023) — "The APU 790 doubles the integer and floating-point operations performance, while reducing power consumption by 45%."; "By adapting the Transformer model for operator acceleration, the processing speed of the APU 790 is 8 times faster than the previous generation, with image generation within one second using Stable Diffusion."; "MediaTek has developed mixed-precision INT4 quantization technology, which when combined with the company's NeuroPilot memory hardware compression, can more efficiently utilize memory bandwidth and significantly reduce memory requirements for large AI models."; "The APU 790 provides support for NeuroPilot Fusion, which can continuously perform LoRA low-rank adaptation, and is capable of supporting large language models with 1B, 7B, and 13B parameters, with scalability up to 33B." MediaTek Dimensity 9300 product page — "7B parameters AI LLM speed — 20 tokens/ sec. … Supports from 1B, 7B, 13B to 33B parameter AI LLMs".

#### Down to the primitives: The all-big-core CPU cluster — 4× Cortex-X4 + 4× Cortex-A720 on the DSU-120

The cluster runs Arm's documented pipeline in order — fetch from the L1 instruction cache, decode (10-wide on the Cortex-X4, 5-wide on the Cortex-A720), rename onto physical registers, dispatch into the reorder buffer and issue queues, issue to the execution ports, retire in order, with the DSU-120's Snoop Control Unit and shared L3 keeping all eight cores coherent — and each step is built from the primitives below. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **Register file (rename map / physical register file — 10-wide rename/dispatch on the X4, 5-wide decode on the A720)** — Rename maps each instruction's architectural registers onto physical registers, and the physical register file is the structure written at dispatch and read at issue — 10 micro-ops per cycle on the Cortex-X4 (verified — Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, Issue 06, Register rename: "The register rename unit performs register renaming to facilitate out-of-order execution and dispatches decoded instructions to various issue queues."). The Cortex-A720's rename unit does the same job (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, Register rename: "The register rename unit performs register renaming to facilitate out-of-order execution and dispatches decoded instructions to various issue queues."), at its 5-wide decode width (recorded at Level 2). The physical register-file size, port count and per-cycle read/write width are not published for either core.

- **FIFO / queue (384-entry reorder buffer on the X4; issue queues on both cores)** — The reorder buffer is a 384-entry circular queue holding in-flight micro-ops in program order: instructions dispatch into it, execute out of order, and retire from it in order (verified — secondary sources, recorded at Level 2; the X4 TRM itself never names a reorder buffer). In front of the execution ports, issue queues hold micro-ops waiting for their operands to be ready — the X4's issue unit "includes issue queues for storing instructions pending dispatch to execution pipelines" (verified — Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, Issue 06, Instruction issue) and the A720's issue unit does the same (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, Instruction issue: "It includes issue queues for storing instructions pending dispatch to execution pipelines."). The ROB depth of 384 entries is published; the issue-queue depths are not.

- **CAM / tag compare (L1 and L2 cache tags; fully associative L1 TLBs; DSU-120 snoop filters)** — Every cache lookup is a tag compare: the L1 data caches are 4-way set associative, so four tags are compared in parallel on each access, and the L2 and shared L3 carry the same tag-compare structure at their own geometries. The L1 TLBs are fully associative CAM structures that match a virtual address against stored page translations — the X4 and A720 both use fully associative L1 instruction and data TLBs with native support for 4 KB, 16 KB, 64 KB and 2 MB page sizes (verified — Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, Issue 06; Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04). In the DSU-120, the Snoop Control Unit holds snoop filters — tag RAMs that track which core caches hold which addresses — so the SCU does not need to ask a core cache to look up a line it does not hold (verified — Arm DSU-120 TRM, Issue 07, recorded at Level 2). The snoop filter's size is automatically determined from the configured number of cores and cache sizes; the TLB entry counts are not published.

- **SRAM bank (L1 instruction caches — X4 64 KB; A720 32/64 KB, PLRU, parity option, 32 bytes/cycle to L2)** — The X4's L1 instruction cache is a 64 KB, 4-way set-associative SRAM bank with 64-byte lines, physically indexed and physically tagged, with ECC as an optional configurable feature (verified — Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, Issue 06; recorded under the Cortex-X4 entry). The A720's is configurable to 32 KB or 64 KB, 4-way set associative, physically indexed and physically tagged, optionally protected with parity, with a pseudo-least-recently-used (PLRU) replacement policy and a 32-bytes-per-cycle interface to the L2 memory system (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, Table 7-1: "32KB or 64KB • 4-way set associative • Physically Indexed, Physically Tagged (PIPT) • Optionally protected with parity"; "Cache line length 64 bytes"; "Cache policy Pseudo-Least Recently Used (PLRU) cache replacement policy"; "Interface with L2 memory system 32 bytes per cycle interface"). That geometry is 256 sets with an 8-bit set index at 64 KB (arithmetic from the published geometry). MediaTek's chosen L1 size per core is not published; the replacement policy, banking, port counts and read latency of the X4's L1I are not published.

- **SRAM bank (L1 data caches — X4 64 KB RRIP always-ECC; A720 32/64 KB, 16 banks, pseudo-LRU, optional ECC)** — The X4's L1 data cache is a 64 KB, 4-way set-associative SRAM bank with 64-byte lines, virtually indexed and physically tagged behaving as physically indexed and physically tagged, always ECC-protected, with RRIP replacement (verified — Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, Issue 06; recorded at Level 2). The A720's is configurable to 32 KB or 64 KB, 4-way set associative, 16 banks, virtually indexed and physically tagged behaving as physically indexed and physically tagged, optionally protected with ECC, with a pseudo-LRU replacement policy and 64-byte lines (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, Table 8-1: "32KB or 64KB • 4-way set associative, 16 banks • Virtually Indexed, Physically Tagged (VIPT) behaving as Physically Indexed, Physically Tagged (PIPT) • Optionally protected with Error Correcting Code (ECC)"; "Cache line length 64 bytes"; "Cache policy Pseudo-Least Recently Used (LRU) cache replacement policy"). That geometry is 256 sets with an 8-bit set index at 64 KB (arithmetic from the published geometry). MediaTek's chosen L1 size per core is not published; banking and read latency beyond the published port widths are not published.

- **SRAM bank (private L2 caches — X4 512 KB–2 MB in 4 banks; A720 128–512 KB in 2 banks; both dynamic biased replacement)** — Each core's private L2 is a banked SRAM structure: the X4's is configurable to 512 KB, 1 MB or 2 MB, 8-way set associative, divided into 4 banks, with a dynamic biased replacement policy and optional ECC (verified — Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, Issue 06; recorded under the Cortex-X4 entry). The A720's is configurable to 128 KB, 256 KB or 512 KB, 8-way set associative, 2 banks, physically indexed and physically tagged, optionally protected with ECC, with a dynamic biased cache replacement policy and 64-byte lines (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, Table 9-1: "128KB, 256KB, or 512KB • 8-way set associative, 2 banks • Physically Indexed, Physically Tagged (PIPT) • Optionally protected with Error Correcting Code (ECC)"; "Cache line length 64 bytes"; "Cache policy Dynamic biased cache replacement policy"). Sets: 1,024 at 512 KB, 512 at 256 KB, 256 at 128 KB for the A720 (arithmetic from the published geometry). The two cores differ in inclusion: "The L1 data cache and L2 cache are strictly exclusive. Any data contained in the L1 data cache is never present in the L2 cache" while "The L1 instruction cache and L2 cache are weakly inclusive" (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, L2 cache). Per-core L2 sizes as configured by MediaTek are not published; per-bank port counts, tag/data RAM latencies and the replacement policy's bias table are not published.

- **SRAM bank (shared L3 in DSU-120 slices + MediaTek's 10 MB system-level cache)** — The shared L3 lives in the DSU-120 as up to eight slices, each slice a banked SRAM structure with data, tag, victim and snoop-filter RAMs; the 8 MB size MediaTek configured is 16-way associative with 64-byte lines and ECC on data and tag RAMs (verified — Arm DSU-120 TRM, Issue 07, recorded at Level 2). Beyond the DSU-120 sits MediaTek's own 10 MB system-level cache, which with the 8 MB L3 makes the 18 MB complex — MediaTek publishes its size and the +29% figure, not its internal geometry, banking or port counts. The number of L3 slices as configured by MediaTek is not published.

- **Priority encoder / arbiter (issue select to 21 execution ports on the X4; SCU and L3-slice arbitration in the DSU-120)** — Each cycle the scheduler picks ready micro-ops for the Cortex-X4's 21 execution ports — a priority encoder over the issue queues, oldest-ready first in standard construction. The A720's issue select is the same primitive at its own width, which Arm does not publish. In the DSU-120 the Snoop Control Unit arbitrates coherent requests between eight cores, and the L3 slices arbitrate requests from the cores and the main-memory masters. The arbiter structures and port counts are not published beyond the 21 execution ports.

- **Branch predictor structures (BTB tag array; history-predictor counter array; return stack — identical five structures on both cores)** — Both cores' program-flow prediction hardware is the same five structures: a Branch Target Buffer holding the target addresses of previously taken branches — a tag array with one target address per entry; a branch prediction unit that uses previous branch history — a counter array indexed by history; a return stack holding nested subroutine return addresses, pushed by BL-family instructions and popped by RET; a static predictor; and an indirect branch predictor (verified — Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, Issue 06, recorded at Level 2; verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, §7.3: "Program flow prediction hardware contains the following functionality: • A Branch Target Buffer (BTB) holding the branch target address of previously taken branches • A Branch Prediction (BP) predictor that uses the previous branch history • The return stack, including nested subroutine return addresses • A static branch predictor • An indirect branch predictor"). The BTB entry count, history-table size and return-stack depth are not published for either core.

- **Adder tree / ALU array (X4: 8 integer ALUs, 3 branch units; A720: integer execute — port counts not published)** — The Cortex-X4's execution core is eight integer ALUs and three branch units fed by the 21 execution ports (verified — secondary sources, recorded at Level 2): six simple single-cycle ALUs, one ALU/MAC and one ALU/MAC/DIV unit, each a 64-bit adder plus a logic unit plus a comparator. The A720's integer execute unit "performs arithmetic and logical data processing operations" (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, Integer execute) — the same adder-plus-logic-unit primitive — but Arm publishes no ALU count, port count or issue width for the A720. The branch units resolve branches and perform branch target calculation (verified — Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, Issue 06, Branch execute). The ALU carry-tree depth, logic-unit mux radix and the A720's execution-port count are not published.

- **Multiplier array (X4: two MAC units; A720: vector/SVE2 pipes with optional crypto)** — The X4's ALU/MAC and ALU/MAC/DIV units add a multiplier array to the adder: a Wallace/Dadda tree of full adders reducing the partial products, then a final carry-propagate adder — the standard construction of a 64-bit multiplier. The upgrade from X3's single MAC to two MACs is published (secondary sources, recorded at Level 2). The A720's vector execute unit "performs Advanced SIMD and floating-point operations" and "executes the Scalable Vector Extension (SVE) and Scalable Vector Extension 2 (SVE2) instructions, and optionally executes the cryptographic instructions" (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, Vector execute) — multiplier arrays plus adder trees plus barrel shifters per vector pipe — but Arm publishes no A720 vector-datapath width or pipe count, and MediaTek's configuration is not published. The multiplier array geometry and pipeline depth are not published for either core.

- **Prefetch engine / address generator (A720 spatial streaming + Best Offset/Region/History/Stride/Store Issue; X4 temporal prefetcher)** — The A720's load/store unit "includes hardware prefetcher engines that are responsible for generating prefetches targeting L1, L2, and L3 caches. Specifically, the prefetch engine in the L1 memory subsystem targets the L1 and L2 caches. The prefetch engine in the L2 memory subsystem targets the L2 and L3 caches. The load side prefetcher uses the Virtual Address (VA) and the Program Counter (PC). The store side prefetcher uses the Virtual Address (VA) only." (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, §8.5). The engine set is named in the CPU extended control register: the Global Spatial Memory Streaming Prefetcher — the L2 spatial-prefetch engine recorded at Level 2 — plus the Best Offset, Region, History, Stride and Store Issue prefetchers, and MMU prefetchers for table walks, streams and coalesced entries (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1 bits: "[56] sw_disable_pf_gsms Disable Global Spatial Memory Streaming Prefetcher", "[43] sw_disable_pf_bo Disable Best Offset Prefetcher", "[42] sw_disable_pf_rpf Disable Region Prefetcher", "[41] sw_disable_pf_hpf Disable History Prefetcher"). The X4 adds its own L1 temporal data prefetcher (verified — secondary sources, recorded at Level 2). The prefetch queue depths and the number of prefetch streams are not published.

- **Counter (PMU event counters — X4 6 or 31, A720 6 or 20; write-streaming threshold counters per cache)** — The Cortex-X4's Performance Monitoring Unit counts microarchitectural events with counters configurable to 6 or 31 (verified — Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, recorded at Level 2). The A720's PMU "provides either 6 or 20 performance monitors that can be configured to gather statistics on the operation of each core and the memory system" (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, Performance Monitoring Unit). Both cores share the write-streaming mechanism: "The write streaming threshold defines the number of consecutive cache lines that are fully written without being read before store operations stop causing cache allocations. You can configure the write streaming threshold for each cache (L1, L2, and L3)" (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, §8.2) — one threshold counter per cache. MediaTek's PMU configuration and threshold values for this SoC are not published.

- **FSM / controller (exclusive monitor — 2-state open/exclusive FSM; DSU-120 Power Policy Units; MPMM/PDP dispatch block)** — Both cores' internal exclusive monitor is a 2-state finite-state machine — open and exclusive — that manages Load-Exclusive and Store-Exclusive accesses and Clear-Exclusive instructions, tagging a 16-word block (one cache line) for exclusive access (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, §8.4: "The Cortex-A720 core includes an internal exclusive monitor with a 2-state, open and exclusive state machine that manages Load-Exclusive and Store-Exclusive accesses and Clear-Exclusive (CLREX) instructions."; "A Load-Exclusive instruction tags a small block of memory for exclusive access. CTR_EL0 defines the size of the tagged blocks as 16 words, one cache line."; same construction on the X4, recorded at Level 2). The DSU-120 integrates Power Policy Units that gate clocks and power per core and per L3 slice, and the cores' Maximum Power Mitigation Mechanism and Performance Defined Power features feed a dispatch-block signal that throttles issue when the power budget is exceeded (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, §5; Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, recorded at Level 2). The FSM state encodings are not published.

- **Crossbar / interconnect (DSU-120 transport — cores to SCU to L3 slices to 1–4 CHI/AXI main-memory masters)** — The DSU-120's transport links eight cores, the Snoop Control Unit, up to eight L3 slices and the main-memory interface; its topology is automatically determined from the number of cores and L3 slices, and the main-memory interface can be configured as CHI or AXI with 1 to 4 bus master interfaces, plus up to two Accelerator Coherency Ports (verified — Arm DSU-120 TRM, Issue 07, recorded at Level 2). Each core reaches the DSU-120 over a 256-bit CHI interface (verified — Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, Issue 06; Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, Table 9-1: "One CHI Issue E compliant interfaces with 256-bit read and write channel widths"). The transport path widths beyond the published 256-bit interfaces are not published.

- **Mux / demux (L1 data-cache port structure on both cores; A720 L1I 32 bytes/cycle interface)** — The X4's L1 data cache presents 4x64-bit read paths and 4x64-bit write paths to the integer pipeline and 3x128-bit read paths and 2x128-bit write paths to the vector pipeline — muxes selecting which bank serves which port each cycle (verified — Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, Issue 06, recorded at Level 2). The A720's L1 data cache presents 3×64-bit read paths and 4×64-bit write paths for the integer execute pipeline and 2×128-bit write paths and 3×128-bit read paths for the vector execute pipeline (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, Table 8-1: "3×64-bit read paths and 4×64-bit write paths for the integer execute pipeline • 2×128-bit write paths and 3×128-bit read paths for the vector execute"). The A720's L1 instruction cache feeds its L2 over a 32-bytes-per-cycle interface (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, Table 7-1). The mux select logic is standard construction; the bank count beyond the A720 L1D's published 16 banks is not published.

- **FIFO / queue (transaction queues — A720: 120 outstanding writes, 60 reads, 64 snoops, 30 DVM)** — The A720's L2 memory system bounds how much work can be in flight: "Write issuing capability 120 — This is the maximum number of outstanding write transactions"; "Read issuing capability 60 — This is the maximum number of outstanding read transactions"; "Snoop acceptance capability 64 — This is the maximum number of outstanding snoops accepted"; "DVM issuing capability 30 — This is the maximum number of outstanding DVM operation transactions" (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, Table 9-2). These caps are the depths of the transaction queues between the core, the DSU-120 and the memory system — a queue of 120 write entries, 60 read entries, 64 snoop entries and 30 DVM entries, by the manual's own definition. The X4's corresponding caps and the L2 Transaction Queue's depth are not published.

- **Synchronizer / clock-domain crossing (asynchronous CPU bridge per core; DSU-120 Q-Channel clock gating; per-core DVFS)** — The cluster's cores run at different frequencies and voltages — X4 primes at up to 3.25 GHz, the other X4s at 2.85 GHz, A720s at 2.0 GHz — so data crossing between a core and the DSU-120 passes through synchronizers. "In a cluster, there is one CPU bridge between each Cortex-A720 core and the DSU-120. The CPU bridge controls buffering and synchronization between the core and the DSU-120. The CPU bridge is asynchronous to allow different frequency, power, and area implementation points for each core." (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, CPU bridge); the X4's bridge is the same asynchronous construction (verified — Arm Cortex-X4 TRM, Issue 06, recorded at Level 2). The DSU-120 gates clocks through Q-Channel requests with individual control of each core's clock, and each core supports per-core DVFS (verified — Arm Cortex-A720 TRM, Issue 04, §4–§5). The synchronizer depths are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** The Arm TRMs publish the X4's 64 KB L1I (4-way, 64-byte lines, PIPT, optional ECC) and 64 KB L1D (4-way, 64-byte lines, VIPT-behaving-as-PIPT, always ECC, RRIP, 4x64-bit read / 4x64-bit write integer and 3x128-bit read / 2x128-bit write vector interfaces); the A720's 32/64 KB L1I (4-way, 64-byte lines, PIPT, optional parity, PLRU, 32 bytes/cycle to L2) and 32/64 KB L1D (4-way, 16 banks, VIPT-behaving-as-PIPT, optional ECC, pseudo-LRU, 3x64-bit read / 4x64-bit write integer and 2x128-bit write / 3x128-bit read vector interfaces); the X4's private L2 (512 KB–2 MB, 8-way, 4 banks, dynamic biased replacement) and the A720's (128–512 KB, 8-way, 2 banks, dynamic biased replacement, PIPT, optional ECC); the A720's L1D/L2 strict exclusivity and L1I/L2 weak inclusivity; the A720's transaction caps (120 outstanding writes, 60 reads, 64 snoops, 30 DVM); the five-structure branch predictor on both cores; the A720's prefetcher engines (L1 targets L1/L2, L2 targets L2/L3, load VA+PC, store VA only) and the named GSMS/Best Offset/Region/History/Stride/Store Issue engines; the PMU counts (X4 6 or 31, A720 6 or 20) and the per-cache write-streaming thresholds; the 2-state exclusive monitor tagging a 16-word block; the asynchronous CPU bridge per core and the 256-bit CHI interfaces; and the DSU-120's up-to-eight L3 slices, snoop filters, 1–4 bus-master main-memory interface and up-to-two ACPs. They publish no issue-queue depths, physical-register-file sizes, TLB entry counts, BTB entry counts, history-table sizes, return-stack depth, ALU carry-tree depths, multiplier geometry, prefetcher queue depths, L2 per-bank port counts, synchronizer depths, DSU-120 queue depths or L3 latency — and this decomposition invents none of them. MediaTek's per-core L1/L2 sizes, vector-datapath width and L3 slice count as configured are not published.

#### Down to the primitives: APU 790 — the generative-AI engine and its memory-compression path

MediaTek publishes no APU 790 block diagram, TOPS figure, internal widths or queue depths, so the primitives below are mapped from the functions MediaTek itself names in its press release and product page, in the order a token passes through them — compressed weights stream in from LPDDR5T, the decompression hardware expands them, the INT4 tensor unit multiplies, the transformer acceleration finishes attention, and NeuroPilot Fusion folds the LoRA update into the same pass. Where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (compressed-weight staging; weight and activation queues into the tensor unit)** — Weights arrive compressed and are expanded only as they are consumed, so a queue stages the compressed weights on their way from LPDDR5T into the decompression hardware and another stages the expanded weights and activations into the tensor unit — decoupling the memory stream from the compute, which is what lets the tensor unit stay busy while the decompressor works ahead. The queue depths and widths are not published.

- **SRAM bank (on-chip working store — one pool for the tensor unit, the transformer acceleration and the LoRA path)** — The APU's working store is the block's SRAM: one pool holding the expanded weights, the activations and the LoRA adapter for the current layer, so a token's work stays on-chip between the tensor multiply, the attention step and the LoRA fusion instead of round-tripping to LPDDR5T — the physical reason the compression path saves bandwidth rather than merely moving the bottleneck. Its capacity, banking, line size and port count are not published.

- **Multiplier array + adder tree (A16W4 tensor unit — 16-bit activations against 4-bit weights)** — The A16W4 tensor unit is a multiplier array feeding adder trees that reduce partial products into one result per output element — the matrix multiply at the heart of every transformer layer. MediaTek states the mixed-precision INT4 quantization "when combined with the company's NeuroPilot memory hardware compression, can more efficiently utilize memory bandwidth and significantly reduce memory requirements for large AI models" (verified — MediaTek press release, Nov 6, 2023, recorded at Level 2): 16-bit activations against 4-bit weights halve the bytes per weight against INT8. The tensor unit's dimensions, lane count and array geometry are not published.

- **Adder tree (NeuroPilot Fusion — the LoRA low-rank update added into the same pass)** — NeuroPilot Fusion "can continuously perform LoRA low-rank adaptation" (verified — MediaTek press release, Nov 6, 2023, recorded at Level 2): the low-rank adapter's update is added into the layer's output by an adder tree, so personalisation rides the same pass as the base model instead of a second one. The adapter's rank, the adder tree's width and the update's precision are not published.

- **FSM / controller + codec (NeuroPilot memory hardware compression — the decompression engine between DRAM and the APU)** — The compression hardware is a codec driven by a controller: models are pre-compressed before they are stored, then expanded in hardware as they stream into the tensor unit — the decompression engine is the block that turns the stored 5 GB back into the 13 GB the tensor unit actually multiplies (figures from MediaTek's worked example, secondary reporting, recorded at Level 2). The codec's algorithm, throughput, dictionary size and the controller's state machine are not published.

- **FIFO / queue + synchronizer (LPDDR5T interface — 9,600 Mbps streaming into the APU)** — The memory path is a streaming FIFO across the LPDDR5T interface at 9,600 Mbps: compressed weights flow in at the memory rate and the decompressor and tensor unit drain the queue at their own rates, with synchronizers crossing whatever clock domains separate the memory controller from the APU. The interface width, FIFO depth and synchronizer implementation are not published.

- **Mux / demux (precision select — INT4, INT8 and floating-point paths)** — The APU runs mixed precision — INT4 weights against 16-bit activations, INT8 for other layers, floating-point for the operations that need it — so a mux network selects which datapath each layer's operands take, and a demux routes each result back to the working store or the next stage. The mux radix and the per-layer precision assignment are not published.

- **Counter (token-rate governor — the 20-tokens-per-second budget and the 45% power cut)** — The APU's output rate is the token counter: 20 tokens per second for a 7B model (verified — MediaTek product page, recorded at Level 2), falling to 3–4 tokens per second at 33B where the compression and bandwidth budget runs out (secondary reporting, recorded at Level 2). Behind it is the power budget — the APU 790 doubles integer and floating-point performance while cutting power 45% against the APU 690 (verified — MediaTek press release, recorded at Level 2) — which is what makes sustained on-device generation possible at all. The governor's counter widths and the power-management state machine are not published.

- **Crossbar / interconnect (APU to memory path; transformer operator acceleration datapath)** — The transformer operator acceleration is the datapath that moves a token's attention work through the APU — the hardware adaptation of the transformer model that MediaTek credits with the 8× speedup over the APU 690 (verified — MediaTek press release, recorded at Level 2). In primitive terms it is an interconnect: the crossbar that carries expanded weights, activations and attention scores between the working store, the tensor unit and the LoRA adder without each stage touching LPDDR5T. Its topology, width and arbitration are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** MediaTek publishes the APU 790's functions and rates — the A16W4 INT4 tensor unit, NeuroPilot memory hardware compression, transformer operator acceleration at 8× over the APU 690, NeuroPilot Fusion LoRA, 20 tokens per second for a 7B model, 2× integer/floating-point performance at 45% lower power than the APU 690, and the LPDDR5T 9,600 Mbps memory path — and this decomposition maps primitives onto those functions only. It publishes no APU 790 block diagram, TOPS figure, tensor-unit dimensions, decompression throughput, queue depths, working-store capacity, codec algorithm or per-accelerator widths, and this decomposition invents none of them.

#### Down to the gates: The all-big-core CPU cluster — 4× Cortex-X4 + 4× Cortex-A720 on the DSU-120

Arm publishes the Cortex-X4, Cortex-A720 and DSU-120 microarchitectures in its Technical Reference Manuals — the pipeline widths, the cache geometries, the 384-entry reorder buffer, the 21 execution ports, the transaction caps — but no gate-level structure for any of it: no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the rename logic, the issue queues, the caches or the DSU-120 transport. MediaTek publishes no per-core L1/L2 sizes as configured, no L3 latency and no cluster floorplan. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors using the primer’s bottom layer — the universal gates, the latch and the flip-flop, the 6T SRAM cell, the CAM cell and the full adder — and every gate or transistor figure is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, not a claim about Arm’s or MediaTek’s actual netlist. Counter widths computed from published figures are labelled arithmetic; where a primitive’s geometry is not published, no total is claimed.

- **Register file (rename map / physical register file — 10-wide rename/dispatch on the X4, 5-wide decode on the A720)** — A register file at gate level is an array of storage bits with a write decoder and read-port muxes: each stored bit is a D flip-flop — two cross-coupled latch stages, about 20–28 transistors in a standard-cell library — or a 6T SRAM cell where the array is built as SRAM, with the write address decoded through a NAND/NOR row-decoder tree and each read port a transmission-gate mux tree (two transistors per input leg). The rename map and physical register file are a file of this form: the rename map is a small array of D flip-flops indexed by architectural register number, written at rename with the physical register tag and read to supply the tag, and the physical register file is the wide array written at dispatch and read at issue — 10 micro-ops per cycle on the Cortex-X4, each taking its operands from this file, so the read-port mux trees are what the 10-wide rename and dispatch actually costs in gates. The physical register-file size, port count and per-cycle read/write width are not published, so no bit total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **FIFO / queue (384-entry reorder buffer on the X4; issue queues on both cores)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is a register file of D flip-flops or a small SRAM bank, the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each (a full adder is two half adders — two XOR plus two AND plus one OR — about 28 transistors in static CMOS), and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XNOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The 384-entry reorder buffer is a circular queue of this form holding in-flight micro-ops in program order, and its pointers are 9 bits wide by arithmetic from the published 384 entries (2 to the 8th is 256, below 384; 2 to the 9th is 512, the smallest power of two above it) — 9 flip-flops plus 9 full adders per pointer by arithmetic, 180 to 252 transistors of flip-flops plus 252 of adders. The issue queues in front of the 21 execution ports are FIFOs of the same form; their depths are not published, so no other pointer width and no total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **CAM / tag compare (L1 and L2 cache tags; fully associative L1 TLBs; DSU-120 snoop filters)** — A CAM cell is a 6T SRAM storage cell plus XOR match logic feeding a matchline — a NOR CAM cell adds four match transistors (ten transistors in total) and a NAND CAM cell adds three (nine in total), textbook-standard — with the matchline precharged and sensed per row. A plain tag compare is the same match without the storage: one XNOR gate per tag bit feeding an AND tree that asserts on a full match. The L1 data cache’s four-way tag compare is four such comparators in parallel on each access, and the L1 TLBs are fully associative CAM structures matching a virtual address against stored page translations, while the DSU-120 snoop filters are tag RAMs whose comparators let the Snoop Control Unit skip asking a core cache about a line it does not hold. The L1 set index is 8 bits by arithmetic from the published 64 KB, 4-way, 64-byte-line geometry (65,536 divided by 4 ways times 64 bytes is 256 sets, and 2 to the 8th is 256), with a 6-bit byte offset inside each 64-byte line by arithmetic. The snoop-filter size and the TLB entry counts are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **SRAM bank (L1 instruction caches — X4 64 KB; A720 32/64 KB, PLRU, parity option, 32 bytes/cycle to L2)** — An SRAM bank at gate level is 6T cells — two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (two transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers (a cross-coupled inverter pair with enable transistors). The X4’s 64 KB L1 instruction cache is a bank of this form with 64-byte lines, physically indexed and physically tagged, with optional ECC; the A720’s is the same cell form at 32 KB or 64 KB with optional parity, pseudo-LRU replacement and a 32-bytes-per-cycle interface to the L2 — 256 bits per cycle by arithmetic — so the fetch unit’s instruction stream is a wordline read plus a column mux plus a sense amplifier per cycle. The set index is 8 bits by arithmetic at 64 KB (256 sets), with a 6-bit byte offset inside each 64-byte line. MediaTek’s chosen L1 size per core is not published; the replacement policy, banking, port counts and read latency of the X4’s L1I are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **SRAM bank (L1 data caches — X4 64 KB RRIP always-ECC; A720 32/64 KB, 16 banks, pseudo-LRU, optional ECC)** — An SRAM bank at gate level is 6T cells — two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (two transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers (a cross-coupled inverter pair with enable transistors), with ECC protection adding extra 6T cells per word plus an XOR-tree encoder and decoder. The X4’s 64 KB L1 data cache is a bank of this form with 64-byte lines, virtually indexed and physically tagged behaving as physically indexed and physically tagged, always ECC-protected, with RRIP replacement; the A720’s is the same cell form at 32 KB or 64 KB with optional ECC, pseudo-LRU replacement and 16 banks — a 4-bit bank select by arithmetic — so a load or store picks its bank, reads its wordline, and the column muxes steer the 64-bit integer or 128-bit vector result to the right port. The set index is 8 bits by arithmetic at 64 KB (256 sets), with a 6-bit byte offset inside each 64-byte line. MediaTek’s chosen L1 size per core is not published; banking and read latency beyond the published port widths are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **SRAM bank (private L2 caches — X4 512 KB–2 MB in 4 banks; A720 128–512 KB in 2 banks; both dynamic biased replacement)** — An SRAM bank at gate level is 6T cells — two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (two transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers (a cross-coupled inverter pair with enable transistors), with ECC protection adding extra 6T cells per word plus an XOR-tree encoder and decoder. Each core’s private L2 is a banked SRAM structure of this form: the X4’s configurable to 512 KB, 1 MB or 2 MB in 4 banks, the A720’s configurable to 128 KB, 256 KB or 512 KB in 2 banks, both 8-way set associative with dynamic biased replacement. The set indices are arithmetic from the published geometries: the X4’s is 10 bits at 512 KB (1,024 sets), 11 bits at 1 MB (2,048 sets) and 12 bits at 2 MB (4,096 sets); the A720’s is 8 bits at 128 KB (256 sets), 9 bits at 256 KB (512 sets) and 10 bits at 512 KB (1,024 sets), each with a 6-bit byte offset inside the 64-byte line. The dynamic biased replacement policy is counters plus a comparator per set in standard construction, but its bias table is not published. Per-core L2 sizes as configured by MediaTek are not published; per-bank port counts, tag/data RAM latencies and the replacement policy’s bias table are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **SRAM bank (shared L3 in DSU-120 slices + MediaTek's 10 MB system-level cache)** — An SRAM bank at gate level is 6T cells — two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (two transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers (a cross-coupled inverter pair with enable transistors), with ECC protection adding extra 6T cells per word plus an XOR-tree encoder and decoder. The shared L3 in the DSU-120 is banks of this form: up to eight slices, each slice a banked SRAM structure with data, tag, victim and snoop-filter RAMs, and the 8 MB size MediaTek configured is 16-way associative with 64-byte lines and ECC on data and tag RAMs — a 13-bit set index by arithmetic (8,388,608 divided by 16 ways times 64 bytes is 8,192 sets, and 2 to the 13th is 8,192), with a 6-bit byte offset inside each 64-byte line. Beyond the DSU-120 sits MediaTek’s own 10 MB system-level cache, whose internal geometry, banking and port counts are not published. The number of L3 slices as configured by MediaTek is not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Priority encoder / arbiter (issue select to 21 execution ports on the X4; SCU and L3-slice arbitration in the DSU-120)** — A priority encoder at gate level is an OR/NAND tree that turns a one-hot ready vector into the binary index of the highest-priority set bit — a 2-to-the-n-to-n encoder is a tree of OR gates, one per output bit, fed by the ready lines. The Cortex-X4’s issue select is an encoder of this form over the issue queues, picking ready micro-ops for the 21 execution ports each cycle, and its port index is 5 bits wide by arithmetic from the published 21 ports (2 to the 4th is 16, below 21; 2 to the 5th is 32, the smallest power of two above it); round-robin fairness adds a rotating priority register (D flip-flops holding the last grant) that reorders the encoder’s inputs. In the DSU-120 the Snoop Control Unit’s arbitration between eight cores and the L3 slices’ arbitration of core and main-memory requests are encoders of the same tree form. The arbiter structures and port counts are not published beyond the 21 execution ports, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Branch predictor structures (BTB tag array; history-predictor counter array; return stack — identical five structures on both cores)** — A branch-target buffer at gate level is a tag array — an SRAM bank of 6T cells with a row decoder and sense amplifiers, one target address per entry — plus a tag comparator per entry (one XNOR per tag bit feeding an AND tree) that asserts on a match; a history-predictor counter array is a bank of small saturating counters, each two D flip-flops plus next-state NAND/NOR logic that increments on a taken branch and decrements on a not-taken one; and a return stack is a stack of D flip-flops holding nested subroutine return addresses, with a push/pop pointer counter (D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer) driven by BL-family instructions and RET. Both cores’ program-flow prediction hardware is these three structures plus a static predictor and an indirect branch predictor, all of the same cell forms. The BTB entry count, history-table size and return-stack depth are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Adder tree / ALU array (X4: 8 integer ALUs, 3 branch units; A720: integer execute — port counts not published)** — An ALU at gate level is a 64-bit adder — a carry-propagate chain of full adders, each two half adders, about 28 transistors in static CMOS — plus a logic unit of NAND/NOR gates and a comparator of XNOR gates feeding an AND tree, with a result mux (transmission gates, two transistors per leg) selecting between them. The Cortex-X4’s eight integer ALUs are eight such units fed by the 21 execution ports: six simple single-cycle ALUs, one ALU/MAC and one ALU/MAC/DIV unit; the three branch units are adders of the same form computing branch targets, and the A720’s integer execute unit is the same adder-plus-logic-unit primitive at its own width, which Arm does not publish. The ALU carry-tree depth, logic-unit mux radix and the A720’s execution-port count are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Multiplier array (X4: two MAC units; A720: vector/SVE2 pipes with optional crypto)** — A multiplier array at gate level is AND gates forming the partial products — one AND gate per product bit — feeding an adder tree of full adders (about 28 transistors each) that collapses the partials into the product; a Wallace/Dadda tree reduces the partials in logarithmic stages before a final carry-propagate adder. The X4’s two MAC units are arrays of this form: a 64-bit by 64-bit multiply is 4,096 partial-product AND gates by arithmetic, reduced by the adder tree — and the upgrade from the X3’s single MAC to two MACs is a second array of the same form. The A720’s vector/SVE2 pipes are multiplier arrays plus adder trees plus barrel shifters per vector pipe — a barrel shifter is a tree of transmission-gate muxes, one level per shift bit. Arm publishes no A720 vector-datapath width or pipe count, and MediaTek’s configuration is not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Prefetch engine / address generator (A720 spatial streaming + Best Offset/Region/History/Stride/Store Issue; X4 temporal prefetcher)** — An address generator at gate level is counters plus adders: a counter is D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer — one flip-flop and one full adder (about 28 transistors) per bit — and the prefetch address computation is an adder tree over the base address and the stride or offset. The A720’s prefetch engines are address generators of this form: the spatial streaming prefetcher steps through neighbouring lines with a counter, the Best Offset, Region, History and Stride prefetchers each hold a stride register (D flip-flops) and add it to the demand address, and the load-side engine indexes on the virtual address and program counter while the store-side engine uses the virtual address only. The X4’s temporal prefetcher is the same counter-plus-adder form with a history table of 6T SRAM cells. The prefetch queue depths and the number of prefetch streams are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Counter (PMU event counters — X4 6 or 31, A720 6 or 20; write-streaming threshold counters per cache)** — A counter at gate level is D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer — one flip-flop and one full adder (about 28 transistors) per bit — with a zero or threshold comparator (XNOR per bit plus an AND tree) that asserts when the count is reached. The X4’s PMU counters are counters of this form, 6 or 31 of them, and the counter select is 5 bits wide by arithmetic from the published 31 (2 to the 4th is 16, below 31; 2 to the 5th is 32, the smallest power of two above it); the A720’s 6 or 20 counters are the same form with a 5-bit select by arithmetic from 20. The write-streaming threshold is one threshold counter per cache — a counter plus a comparator that stops cache allocation once the configured number of consecutive fully-written lines is reached. MediaTek’s PMU configuration and threshold values for this SoC are not published, so no transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **FSM / controller (exclusive monitor — 2-state open/exclusive FSM; DSU-120 Power Policy Units; MPMM/PDP dispatch block)** — A controller at gate level is a finite-state machine built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network driven by the inputs, with the outputs decoded from the state flops through another NAND/NOR network. The exclusive monitor is a 2-state FSM of this form — one state flip-flop holding open versus exclusive — with the next-state logic driven by Load-Exclusive, Store-Exclusive and Clear-Exclusive instructions, and the tagged block is a 16-word address register whose word index is 4 bits wide by arithmetic (2 to the 4th is 16). The DSU-120 Power Policy Units are FSMs of the same form gating clocks and power per core and per L3 slice, and the MPMM/PDP dispatch block is a comparator (XNOR per bit plus an AND tree) over a power counter that throttles issue when the budget is exceeded. The FSM state encodings are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Crossbar / interconnect (DSU-120 transport — cores to SCU to L3 slices to 1–4 CHI/AXI main-memory masters)** — A crossbar at gate level is a grid of muxes — one per output, each selecting among all inputs — where a mux is a transmission gate per input leg (two transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree, with the select lines decoded from the control bits through a NAND/NOR decoder, and the arbitration is a priority-encoder tree over the request lines. The DSU-120 transport is a crossbar of this form linking eight cores, the Snoop Control Unit, up to eight L3 slices and the main-memory interface: each core reaches the DSU-120 over a 256-bit CHI interface — 32 bytes per cycle by arithmetic — and the main-memory interface can be configured as CHI or AXI with 1 to 4 bus master interfaces plus up to two Accelerator Coherency Ports. The transport path widths beyond the published 256-bit interfaces are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Mux / demux (L1 data-cache port structure on both cores; A720 L1I 32 bytes/cycle interface)** — A mux at gate level is a transmission gate per input leg (two transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree, with the select lines decoded from the control bits; a demux is the same structure reversed, one input fanned out through transmission gates to the selected output. The X4’s L1 data-cache port structure is muxes of this form: 4×64-bit read paths and 4×64-bit write paths for the integer pipeline and 3×128-bit read paths and 2×128-bit write paths for the vector pipeline, each path a mux selecting which bank serves which port each cycle; the A720’s is the same form at 3×64-bit read and 4×64-bit write integer plus 2×128-bit write and 3×128-bit read vector, with its 16-bank L1 data cache needing a 4-bit bank select by arithmetic. The A720’s L1 instruction cache feeds its L2 over a 32-bytes-per-cycle interface — 256 bits per cycle by arithmetic — through a mux of the same form. The mux select logic is standard construction; the bank count beyond the A720 L1D’s published 16 banks is not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **FIFO / queue (transaction queues — A720: 120 outstanding writes, 60 reads, 64 snoops, 30 DVM)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is a register file of D flip-flops — two cross-coupled latch stages, about 20–28 transistors each in a standard-cell library — or a small SRAM bank of 6T cells where the queue is deep, the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each (a full adder is two half adders — two XOR plus two AND plus one OR — about 28 transistors in static CMOS), and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XNOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The A720’s L2 transaction queues are FIFOs of this form, and their pointer widths are arithmetic from the published caps: 120 outstanding writes need 7 bits (2 to the 6th is 64, below 120; 2 to the 7th is 128, the smallest power of two above it), 60 outstanding reads need 6 bits, 64 outstanding snoops need 6 bits, and 30 outstanding DVM operations need 5 bits. The X4’s corresponding caps and the L2 Transaction Queue’s depth are not published, so no other pointer width and no total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Synchronizer / clock-domain crossing (asynchronous CPU bridge per core; DSU-120 Q-Channel clock gating; per-core DVFS)** — A synchronizer at gate level is a chain of D flip-flops — two cross-coupled latch stages each, about 20–28 transistors in a standard-cell library — clocked by the receiving domain, so a metastable first stage has a full cycle to settle before the second stage samples it; a two-flop synchronizer is the standard construction, and a multi-bit crossing adds a FIFO or a Gray-coded pointer (a counter whose successive values differ in one bit) so the receiving domain never samples a half-changed word. The asynchronous CPU bridge between each core and the DSU-120 is a synchronizer of this form, letting each core run at its own frequency and voltage — X4 primes at up to 3.25 GHz, the other X4s at 2.85 GHz, A720s at 2.0 GHz — and the DSU-120’s Q-Channel clock gating is a handshake of the same form, with per-core DVFS changing the clock the synchronizer must cross. The synchronizer depths are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Arm publishes the Cortex-X4, Cortex-A720 and DSU-120 microarchitectures in its Technical Reference Manuals — the pipeline widths, the cache geometries, the 384-entry reorder buffer, the 21 execution ports, the transaction caps — but no gate-level structure for any of it: no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the rename logic, the issue queues, the caches or the DSU-120 transport. MediaTek publishes no per-core L1/L2 sizes as configured, no L3 latency and no cluster floorplan. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer’s bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Arm’s or MediaTek’s actual netlist. The only new numbers are counter widths computed from published figures and labelled arithmetic: 9-bit reorder-buffer pointers from 384 entries, an 8-bit L1 set index from 64 KB, 4-way, 64-byte lines, 10/11/12-bit X4 L2 set indices from 512 KB/1 MB/2 MB, 8/9/10-bit A720 L2 set indices from 128/256/512 KB, a 13-bit L3 set index from 8 MB, 16-way, 64-byte lines, a 4-bit exclusive-monitor word index from a 16-word block, a 5-bit PMU counter select from 31 or 20 counters, a 5-bit issue-port index from 21 ports, 7/6/6/5-bit transaction-queue pointers from 120 writes, 60 reads, 64 snoops and 30 DVM operations, and a 4-bit bank select from the A720 L1 data cache’s 16 banks.

#### Down to the gates: APU 790 — the generative-AI engine and its memory-compression path

MediaTek publishes no gate-level structure for the APU 790 — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the tensor unit, the working store, the compression hardware or the memory path. The deepest published description is the MediaTek press release and product page, which document the A16W4 tensor unit, NeuroPilot memory hardware compression, transformer operator acceleration, NeuroPilot Fusion LoRA, 20 tokens per second for a 7B model and the LPDDR5T 9,600 Mbps path. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors using the primer’s bottom layer — the universal gates, the latch and the flip-flop, the 6T SRAM cell, the CAM cell and the full adder — and every gate or transistor figure is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, not a claim about MediaTek’s actual netlist. Where a primitive’s geometry is not published, no total is claimed.

- **FIFO / queue (compressed-weight staging; weight and activation queues into the tensor unit)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is a register file of D flip-flops — two cross-coupled latch stages, about 20–28 transistors each in a standard-cell library — or a small SRAM bank of 6T cells where the queue is deep, the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each (a full adder is two half adders — two XOR plus two AND plus one OR — about 28 transistors in static CMOS), incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XNOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The compressed-weight staging queue is a FIFO of this form, holding compressed weights on their way from LPDDR5T into the decompression hardware, and so are the weight and activation queues feeding the tensor unit — the decoupling they provide is what lets the tensor unit stay busy while the decompressor works ahead. The queue depths and widths are not published, so no pointer width and no transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **SRAM bank (on-chip working store — one pool for the tensor unit, the transformer acceleration and the LoRA path)** — An SRAM bank at gate level is 6T cells — two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (two transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers (a cross-coupled inverter pair with enable transistors). The APU’s working store is a bank of this form, one pool holding the expanded weights, the activations and the LoRA adapter for the current layer, so a token’s work stays on-chip between the tensor multiply, the attention step and the LoRA fusion instead of round-tripping to LPDDR5T — the physical reason the compression path saves bandwidth rather than merely moving the bottleneck. Its capacity, banking, line size and port count are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Multiplier array + adder tree (A16W4 tensor unit — 16-bit activations against 4-bit weights)** — A multiplier array at gate level is AND gates forming the partial products — one AND gate per product bit — feeding an adder tree of full adders (about 28 transistors each) that collapses the partials into the product; a Wallace/Dadda tree reduces the partials in logarithmic stages before a final carry-propagate adder. The A16W4 tensor unit is an array of this form: each multiply of the matrix engine is a partial-product AND plane plus an adder tree, and a 16-bit activation against a 4-bit weight is 64 partial-product AND gates by arithmetic — half the 128 of a 16-bit by 8-bit multiply and a quarter of the 256 of a 16-bit by 16-bit multiply — which is the physical reason INT4 halves the bytes per weight and the multiply work per weight against INT8. The tensor unit’s dimensions, lane count and array geometry are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Adder tree (NeuroPilot Fusion — the LoRA low-rank update added into the same pass)** — An adder tree at gate level is full adders arranged in a binary tree — each full adder two half adders, about 28 transistors in static CMOS — collapsing N partial sums into one result in log2(N) stages, with pipeline registers (D flip-flops) between stages where the tree is deep. NeuroPilot Fusion’s LoRA update is an adder tree of this form: the low-rank adapter’s update is added into the layer’s output in the same pass, so the addition rides the tensor unit’s output registers instead of a second pass through the memory path — personalisation costs an adder tree, not another DRAM round trip. The adapter’s rank, the adder tree’s width and the update’s precision are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **FSM / controller + codec (NeuroPilot memory hardware compression — the decompression engine between DRAM and the APU)** — A codec at gate level is a lookup table plus a state machine: the table is a small SRAM bank of 6T cells or a ROM array of NAND/NOR-decoded hardwired bits holding the codebook, addressed by the compressed symbols, and the controller is an FSM — state bits in master-slave D flip-flops with next-state NAND/NOR logic — stepping through fetch, decode, expand and emit. The NeuroPilot memory hardware compression is a codec of this form: models are pre-compressed before storage, then expanded in hardware as they stream into the tensor unit — the decompression engine is what turns the stored 5 GB back into the 13 GB the tensor unit actually multiplies (figures from MediaTek’s worked example, secondary reporting, recorded at Level 2). The codec’s algorithm, throughput, dictionary size and the controller’s state machine are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **FIFO / queue + synchronizer (LPDDR5T interface — 9,600 Mbps streaming into the APU)** — A streaming FIFO across a clock-domain crossing is a FIFO plus synchronizers: the storage is D flip-flops or 6T SRAM cells, the write and read pointers are counters of flip-flops plus full adders, and the pointers cross domains Gray-coded — successive values differing in one bit — through two-flop synchronizers (a chain of D flip-flops clocked by the receiving domain, about 20–28 transistors each) so the receiving side never samples a half-changed pointer. The LPDDR5T interface is a FIFO of this form at 9,600 Mbps: compressed weights flow in at the memory rate and the decompressor and tensor unit drain the queue at their own rates, with the synchronizers crossing whatever clock domains separate the memory controller from the APU. The interface width, FIFO depth and synchronizer implementation are not published, so no pointer width and no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Mux / demux (precision select — INT4, INT8 and floating-point paths)** — A mux at gate level is a transmission gate per input leg (two transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree, with the select lines decoded from the control bits; a demux is the same structure reversed, one input fanned out through transmission gates to the selected output. The precision select is a mux network of this form: INT4 weights against 16-bit activations, INT8 for other layers, floating-point for the operations that need it, so the mux selects which datapath each layer’s operands take and a demux routes each result back to the working store or the next stage — the select bits are the layer’s precision tag, decoded through a NAND/NOR decoder. The mux radix and the per-layer precision assignment are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Counter (token-rate governor — the 20-tokens-per-second budget and the 45% power cut)** — A counter at gate level is D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer — one flip-flop and one full adder (about 28 transistors) per bit — with a threshold comparator (XNOR per bit plus an AND tree) that asserts when the budget is reached. The token-rate governor is a counter of this form: it counts the tokens the APU emits against the 20-tokens-per-second budget for a 7B model, and the power budget behind it — the APU 790 doubling integer and floating-point performance while cutting power 45% against the APU 690 — is the DVFS and power-gating FSM that throttles the count when the budget is spent. The governor’s counter widths and the power-management state machine are not published, so no transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.

- **Crossbar / interconnect (APU to memory path; transformer operator acceleration datapath)** — A crossbar at gate level is a grid of muxes — one per output, each selecting among all inputs — where a mux is a transmission gate per input leg (two transistors per leg) or a NAND/NOR tree, with the select lines decoded from the control bits through a NAND/NOR decoder, and the arbitration is a priority-encoder tree over the request lines. The transformer operator acceleration datapath is a crossbar of this form: it carries expanded weights, activations and attention scores between the working store, the tensor unit and the LoRA adder without each stage touching LPDDR5T — which is the physical reason the 8× speedup over the APU 690 is possible at all. Its topology, width and arbitration are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: MediaTek publishes the APU 790 at function level only — the A16W4 tensor unit, NeuroPilot memory hardware compression, transformer operator acceleration, NeuroPilot Fusion LoRA, 20 tokens per second and the LPDDR5T path (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the APU appears in any MediaTek source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer’s bottom layer; none of it is a claim about MediaTek’s actual netlist. No new chip-specific number is claimed at Level 4 beyond the published figures already recorded at Levels 2 and 3.

### Google Tensor G3

**Specs (wiki card).** Samsung 4 nm · Titan M2 · TPU for Pixel features

**Building blocks.**
- **9-core CPU — 1× X3 + 4× A715 + 4× A510** — An unusual nona-core layout (2.91 / 2.37 / 1.70 GHz): last-generation Arm cores chosen deliberately — Google spends its transistor budget elsewhere and says so by omission. (Configuration is consistent across secondary reporting; Google publishes no spec sheet.)
- **Edge TPU ('Rio' in reporting) ★** — The SoC's reason to exist: the custom TPU running Pixel's speech, translation and imaging models — Google states G3 runs twice as many ML models on-device as the first Tensor. Its internal organisation is undisclosed
- **Mali-G715 GPU (7 cores)** — Arm Immortalis-class graphics with ray tracing — mid-pack by design; the GPU is not where Tensor competes
- **Custom DSP + ISP ('Callisto' in reporting)** — The imaging DSP handling depth and photo stages beside the ISP (see the ISP + HDR+ entry) — again, named only in secondary sources
- **Titan M2 (discrete, on-board)** — The separate RISC-V security chip paired with the SoC (see its own entry), plus the Tensor security core inside the SoC protecting data keys at runtime
- **Exynos 5300 modem + Samsung 4 nm platform** — The honest footnote: Tensor G3 is built with Samsung (4 nm process, Samsung modem) — a platform partnership that defines its radios and its thermal reputation

**The piece that makes it special.** Features over benchmarks, as an architecture. Tensor G3 is the rare SoC whose block diagram is an editorial position: a year-old CPU cluster, a licensed GPU — and the die's ambition concentrated in the TPU and imaging path that power the features Google advertises (call screening, HDR+, speech). Whether that trade is wisdom or excuse depends on the workload, but as a specimen it belongs in this zoo precisely because it refuses the spec-sheet race.

**How work flows.** Feature request arrives: A call to screen, a photo to take, a voice note to transcribe. TPU takes the model: Speech/imaging models run on the Edge TPU on-device — the CPU mostly orchestrates. CPU/GPU handle the app: The 9-core cluster and Mali GPU run Android and the UI at deliberately mid-pack cost. Titan M2 guards the keys: Biometrics and key release stay inside the security boundary throughout.

**Trade-off accepted.** Thermals and modem efficiency in reviews trailed the TSMC-built rivals, and the mid-pack GPU dates quickly. Disclosure is the deeper limit: Google publishes no Tensor G3 datasheet — CPU clocks, TPU organisation and ISP details here are the consensus of secondary reporting and are labelled as such in the Fact check.
