Creates two new ceilings instead: every iteration of a hot loop now re-decodes from scratch — the MOP cache's power and throughput saving is gone, paid in decoder toggles on every pass — and eight decoders plus 10-wide rename cost area and power, about 10% more core area than X3 at equal cache. A wider machine also makes a mispredict more expensive, flushing a 384-entry in-flight window, which is why the predictor and the fetch unit were rebuilt for large instruction footprints rather than benchmark loops.

**Governing numbers.** 8 decoders; rename/dispatch 10 MOPs per cycle (X3: 6-wide decode / 8-wide dispatch); MOP cache 0 entries (X3: 1,536); ROB 384 entries, 768 MOPs in flight with fused pairs (X3: 320 / 640); L1I 64 KB, 4-way, 64-byte lines; L1 I-TLB fully associative (4 KB / 16 KB / 64 KB / 2 MB); pipeline 10 stages; mispredict penalty 10 cycles.

**Primary source.** Arm, Arm Cortex-X4 Core Technical Reference Manual, doc 102484_0002_05_en, Issue 05 (Technical overview — L1 instruction memory system; Instruction decode; Register rename; Instruction issue); Wikipedia, "ARM Cortex-X4" (decode width, rename/dispatch width, ROB, MOP-cache removal — citing WikiChip Fuse, Arm Community and AnandTech); HWCooling, "ARM unveils record-breaking Cortex-X4 core with eight ALUs" (eight decoders, 10-cycle penalty); Android Authority, "Arm Cortex-X4, A720, and A520: 2024 smartphone CPUs deep dive" (redesigned instruction cache, fused instructions, large-footprint tuning).

#### Inside the signature block: The 21-port back end — eight integer ALUs and the 384-entry window

**Inside it.** The back end is where X4 spent its new width: 21 execution ports, up from 15 in X3. The integer cluster is the headline — eight ALUs (six simple single-cycle ALUs, one ALU/MAC and one ALU/MAC/DIV), up from six, with the old MUL unit upgraded to a full MAC so the core now has two integer MAC units where X3 had one; three branch units, up from two; and four address-generation units, up from three, after Arm split one load/store unit into dedicated load and store pipes so the core can sustain up to four memory operations per cycle. Behind them sits the 384-entry reorder buffer — a 768-MOP in-flight window when fused pairs are counted, up from 640 — fed by the 10-wide rename/dispatch stage through per-class issue queues. The vector side deliberately did not widen: the four 128-bit NEON/SVE2 pipes are unchanged from X3 (configurable as 2×128 or 4×128 at build time), though floating-point divide and square root are now pipelined. The memory system around the back end is new L1 temporal data prefetching, an optional doubling of the L1 data TLB, and a private L2 that doubles to a 2 MB option with no added latency — the L2 is private to the core, 8-way set associative, configurable at 512 KB, 1 MB or 2 MB, and reaches the DSU-120 cluster through an asynchronous CPU bridge. The DSU-120 takes up to 14 cores per cluster with up to 32 MB of shared L3.

**Trace — one unit of work: one integer multiply-accumulate instruction.**
1. **Dispatch.** The renamed MOP enters the integer issue queue and takes a slot in the 384-entry ROB.
2. **Wait.** The queue watches for its operands — register-ready, or a forwarded result from an earlier ALU.
3. **Fire.** The MOP issues to one of the two MAC-capable ALU ports; the multi-cycle MAC executes while the six simple ALUs keep taking single-cycle work around it.
4. **Broadcast.** The result returns to the ROB and wakes dependent MOPs waiting in the issue queues.
5. **Commit.** The instruction retires in order from the ROB; up to 768 MOPs may be in flight behind it.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves scalar throughput: integer-heavy phone code — address arithmetic, loop control, UI work — now has eight ALUs, three branch units and four memory ops per cycle instead of six, two and three. Creates the vector imbalance instead: FP/SIMD-heavy code gains little, because the four 128-bit pipes are exactly where X3 left them, so the widening is a scalar bet. And the 768-MOP window means a mispredict or a long-latency load stalls a much bigger in-flight set than X3's 640 — which is why the back end grew a temporal prefetcher, a doubled D-TLB option and a 2 MB L2: the window is only useful if the memory system keeps it fed. Arm's accounting for the whole widening: 13% IPC uplift over X3 at the same process, clock and L3, 15% higher peak performance at 3.4 GHz, and up to 40% lower power at the same performance point.

**Governing numbers.** 21 execution ports (X3: 15); 8 integer ALUs — 6 simple + ALU/MAC + ALU/MAC/DIV (X3: 6, one MAC); 3 branch units (X3: 2); 4 AGUs, up to 4 memory ops per cycle (X3: 3); ROB 384 entries / 768 MOPs in flight (X3: 320 / 640); vector 4×128-bit NEON/SVE2 (2×128 config option); L1D 64 KB, 4-way, 64-byte lines; L1 D-TLB fully associative (4 KB / 16 KB / 64 KB, 2 MB / 512 MB blocks); L2 private, 8-way, 512 KB / 1 MB / 2 MB; DSU-120: up to 14 cores, L3 up to 32 MB; +13% IPC ISO-process, +15% peak performance at 3.4 GHz, up to 40% lower power at the same performance.

**Primary source.** Arm, Arm Cortex-X4 Core Technical Reference Manual, doc 102484_0002_05_en, Issue 05 (Technical overview — L1 data memory system; L2 memory system; Vector execute; configuration options); Wikipedia, "ARM Cortex-X4" (execution ports, ROB, DSU-120, performance claims — citing WikiChip Fuse, Arm Community and AnandTech); Android Authority, "Arm Cortex-X4, A720, and A520: 2024 smartphone CPUs deep dive" (ALU/branch table, 768-MOP window, load/store split, temporal prefetcher, DSU-120 power modes); HWCooling, "ARM unveils record-breaking Cortex-X4 core with eight ALUs" (ALU split, AGU count).

### IBM POWER10

#### Inside the signature block: The eight-slice execution engine — 512-entry instruction table feeding eight slices

**Inside it.** The SMT8 core is two SMT4 halves side by side. Each half has its own 48 KB L1 instruction cache and 32 KB L1 data cache and four 128-bit execution slices; the whole core has eight slices, a private 2 MB L2, an 8 MB region of the 120 MB on-die L3, and a 4,096-entry TLB. Each slice is a self-contained engine: an ALU, an FPU, a branch unit, a load-store unit and a 128-bit VSX SIMD unit, holding up to 20 in-flight instructions. All eight slices are fed from one shared 512-entry instruction table, backed by a 128-entry load queue and an 80-entry store queue (halved per thread when all eight threads run). The front end is the Instruction Fetch Unit (IFU): it fetches, decodes and dispatches every instruction — including 64-bit prefixed instructions and MMA instructions — into the table. Branch prediction accuracy roughly doubled over POWER9, which matters because the table is a 512-entry in-flight window: a mispredict flushes a lot of work. The design point: four vector pipelines per core plus the slice array, aimed at ~30% more core-level throughput than POWER9 at the same clock, and 2.6× the core-level energy efficiency on SPECint.

**Trace — one unit of work: one integer add instruction, steady state.**
1. **Fetch.** The IFU fetches the instruction from the thread's half's 48 KB L1 instruction cache; the I-TLB has already translated the page.
2. **Decode & dispatch.** The instruction is decoded (prefix/fuse handling for 64-bit prefixed forms) and dispatched into the shared 512-entry instruction table, taking one entry.
3. **Wait.** The instruction sits in the table until its operands are ready — register-ready, or a forwarded result from an earlier slice execution.
4. **Issue.** When operands are ready and a slice has a free slot (at most 20 in flight per slice), the instruction issues to one of the eight slices.
5. **Execute.** The slice's ALU runs the add; a load would instead go through the 128-entry load queue to the 32 KB L1 data cache, a store through the 80-entry store queue.
6. **Writeback & complete.** The result is written back and wakes dependent instructions waiting in the table; the instruction completes in program order.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves POWER9's issue bottleneck: eight slices fed by a 512-entry window keep eight SMT threads' work flowing where a narrower core stalled on issue. Creates the shared-table ceiling instead: at full SMT8 all eight threads contend for the same 512 table entries, the same eight slices and the same load/store queues, so per-thread IPC falls as threads are added; and the table's wakeup/select logic is a centralized power and area cost that grows with the window — the reason the per-slice cap is 20 in flight, not unlimited. A long-latency load stalls its slice's 20 slots behind it, which is why the core grew a 2 MB private L2 and a 4,096-entry TLB: the window is only useful if the memory system keeps it fed.

**Governing numbers.** 8 slices (4 per SMT4 half); 512-entry shared instruction table; 20 in-flight instructions per slice; load queue 128 entries / store queue 80 entries (64 / 40 single-threaded); L1I 2×48 KB, L1D 2×32 KB; L2 2 MB private per core; L3 region 8 MB per core, 120 MB per die; TLB 4,096 entries; branch prediction accuracy ~2× POWER9; +30% core-level throughput vs POWER9 at equal clock, 3× at socket level (IEEE Micro); 2.6× core-level energy efficiency on SPECint, up to 3× at socket (ISCA 2021, projected).

**Primary source.** Starke, Thompto, Stuecheli & Moreira, "IBM's POWER10 Processor", IEEE Micro 41(2), 7–14 (2021), DOI 10.1109/MM.2021.3058632; Starke & Thompto, "IBM's POWER10 Processor", Hot Chips 32 (2020), DOI 10.1109/HCS49909.2020.9220618; Qiu et al., "Energy Efficiency Boost in the AI-Infused POWER10 Processor", ISCA 2021; Wikipedia, "Power10" (512-entry table, 20 per slice, 128/80 queues — citing the Hot Chips 32 deck); IT Jungle, "Drilling Down Into The Power10 Chip Architecture" (Aug 24, 2020) (two SMT4 halves, four slices and 48 KB I-cache / 32 KB D-cache per half).

#### Inside the signature block: The Matrix Math Engine — four MMA units, eight 512-bit accumulators

**Inside it.** Four Matrix Math Engines (MME) per SMT8 core execute Power ISA 3.1's Matrix-Multiply Assist (MMA) instructions. The MMA facility adds eight 512-bit accumulator registers, ACC[0:7]; each holds a 4×4 matrix of FP32, a 4×2 matrix of FP64, or a 4×4 matrix of INT32 elements. Each accumulator is associated with a group of four 128-bit vector-scalar registers (VSR[0:31]); while an accumulator is in use its four VSRs must not be used, while VSR[32:63] are never associated with an accumulator and stay free. The accumulators live inside the MME functional unit itself, not in the register file — IBM's stated reason is that keeping the partial sums in the unit significantly reduces switching power. MMA instructions are fetched, decoded and dispatched by the IFU like any other instruction and can overlap fully with other execution in the out-of-order core. The operation is a rank-k update: A ← A + X·Yᵀ, an outer product. For FP64, xvf64ger updates a 4×2 accumulator from a 4-element and a 2-element vector (8 fused multiply-adds, 16 FLOPs); for INT4, xvi4ger8 updates a 4×4 INT32 accumulator from two 4×8 matrices (128 multiply-accumulates, 256 ops). Four engines × 512 result bits = 2,048 result bits per cycle: 64 FP64 FLOPs per cycle, up to ~1,024 INT4 ops per cycle per core. Data types span FP64, FP32, FP16, BF16, INT16, INT8 and INT4.

**Trace — one unit of work: one xvf64ger double-precision outer product through the MME.**
1. **Prime.** xxsetaccz zeroes ACC0 (or xxmtacc assembles it from four VSRs); ACC0 is now primed and its four backing VSRs are locked out until it is deprimed.
2. **Fetch, decode, dispatch.** The IFU fetches the xvf64ger instruction like any other and dispatches it into the 512-entry instruction table.
3. **Wait & issue.** When the two 128-bit operand VSRs (one 4-element, one 2-element FP64 vector) are ready, the instruction issues to one of the four MMEs.
4. **Outer product.** The MME computes A ← A + X·Yᵀ: the 4×2 outer product, 8 fused multiply-adds, added into ACC0 in place — 16 FLOPs from one instruction.
5. **Stay in the unit.** The partial sum never leaves the MME: the next ger in the K-loop accumulates into the same ACC0, so a whole K-slice of the GEMM runs without a register-file write.
6. **Drain.** When the tile is done, xxmfacc moves ACC0 back into its four VSRs (or a paired store writes it to memory); the VSR group is free for reuse.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the BLAS3 wall: one ger instruction replaces a loop of vector FMAs and the register traffic that went with them — 4× the per-core matrix performance of POWER9 at constant frequency, and 10–20× the socket throughput on matrix-intensive work. Creates the accumulator ceiling instead: only eight accumulators, so a GEMM kernel can keep at most eight 4×4/4×2 tiles live, and each live accumulator locks out four VSRs, so accumulator pressure and VSR starvation bound tile size and unrolling. The four MMEs are shared across eight SMT threads, so a second thread's MMA stream halves the per-thread rate; and because the engine is in-core, peak matrix rate is bounded by the core's issue bandwidth and the L1/L2 feed, not by a separate accelerator's memory.

**Governing numbers.** 4 MME units per core; 8 accumulators × 512 bits; accumulator shapes 4×4 FP32 / 4×2 FP64 / 4×4 INT32; 64 VSRs × 128 bits — VSR[0:31] in four-register accumulator groups, VSR[32:63] always free; 2,048 matrix-result bits per cycle; 64 FP64 FLOPs/cycle per core; ~1,024 INT4 ops/cycle per core; 4× per-core matrix performance vs POWER9 at constant frequency; 10–20× matrix-intensive socket throughput vs POWER9; projected 10× FP32 / 21× INT8 socket AI performance on ResNet-50 and BERT-Large.

**Primary source.** Moreira et al., "A matrix math facility for Power ISA™ processors", arXiv:2104.03142 (April 2021); IBM, "Matrix-Multiply Assist Best Practices Guide", Redpaper REDP-5612-00 (April 2021); HPCwire, "IBM Debuts Power10" (Aug 18, 2020) (Thompto's 64 FP64 FLOPs/cycle and ~1K reduced-precision ops/cycle figures); Starke et al., IEEE Micro 41(2) (10–20× matrix-intensive); Qiu et al., ISCA 2021 (10× FP32 / 21× INT8 projections).

### SiFive Performance P670

#### Inside the signature block: The 4-wide rename/dispatch fabric — 160-entry ROB, four dispatch buffers, nine issue queues

**Inside it.** SiFive's own pipeline-overview diagram (launch, November 2022) shows the out-of-order heart as a widened P550 descendant: a front end that fetches up to 8 instructions per cycle from a 32 KB instruction cache, steered by a branch predictor built from four named pieces — a Next Line Predictor, a Branch Direction Predictor, a Return Address Stack and an Indirect Jump Target Predictor. Decode, rename and dispatch run 4-wide into a 160-entry reorder buffer, with rename pools sized per register class: 208 integer renames, 208 floating-point renames and 2×64 vector renames. From there the machine fans out through four dispatch buffers — Integer, Load/Store, Floating Point, Vector — each feeding its own cluster's issue queues: four 16-entry queues in the integer cluster, one 24-entry queue in the load/store cluster, two 16-entry queues in the floating-point cluster and two 16-entry queues in the vector cluster — 152 issue-queue entries in total. The integer cluster has two ALUs and two branch units, with MUL, DIV and int-to-float conversion sitting under the first ALU; the load/store cluster has two address-generation units over two load/store pipes, a 24-entry issue queue fed by two inlets, prefetchers and a 32 KB data cache; the floating-point cluster has two FMAC, two FADD and two FMUL pipes plus int-to-float and FP divide; the vector cluster has two 128-bit ALUs plus DIV and a vector-to-scalar unit. Behind all of it sits a private L2 of up to 512 KB per core and a shared L3 of up to 16 MB, linked at 32 bytes per cycle — the same 32 B/cycle width feeds the instruction cache, the L2-to-L3 link and the data-cache-to-L2 link. SiFive publishes no details beyond the diagram — no load/store queue depths, no branch-predictor table sizes, no cache latencies — and this section stops where the diagram does.

**Trace — one unit of work: one integer ADD, steady state.**
1. **Predict.** The Next Line Predictor and Branch Direction Predictor (with the Return Address Stack covering returns and the Indirect Jump Target Predictor covering indirect jumps) form the fetch address.
2. **Fetch.** Up to 8 instructions stream out of the 32 KB instruction cache in one cycle — twice the 4-wide decode rate, so the fetch buffer absorbs short fetch stalls.
3. **Decode, rename, dispatch.** The ADD is decoded in the 4-wide front end, its architectural registers are renamed against the 208-entry integer rename pool, and it takes a slot in the 160-entry reorder buffer.
4. **Dispatch buffer.** The renamed instruction is routed to the Integer Dispatch Buffer.
5. **Wait.** It sits in one of the four 16-entry integer issue queues until its operands are ready — register-ready, or a forwarded result from an earlier ALU.
6. **Fire.** The queue issues it to one of the two ALUs; a multiply, divide or int-to-float op would instead take the MUL/DIV/I2F path under the first ALU.
7. **Writeback and retire.** The result broadcasts back, wakes dependent instructions waiting in the issue queues, and the ADD retires in program order from the ROB.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the P550's 3-wide ceiling: SiFive widened the whole core to four instructions per cycle and enlarged the buffers throughout, so the front end can sustain 4-wide issue where the P550 capped at three. Creates the 160-entry ceiling instead: the reorder buffer is the in-flight window, modest beside Cortex-X4's 384 entries, so a mispredict flushes up to 160 instructions and a long-latency load stalls the window behind it — which is why the core grew a private L2 with a streaming prefetcher and cache stashing to L3. And the front end is deliberately asymmetric — it fetches 8 per cycle but decodes 4 — so decode, not fetch, is the sustained throughput cap; the fetch margin exists to refill the window fast after a redirect.

**Governing numbers.** Fetch up to 8 instructions/cycle; I-cache 32 KB; decode/rename/dispatch 4-wide; ROB 160 entries; rename pools 208 integer / 208 FP / 2×64 vector; issue queues 4×16 integer, 1×24 load/store, 2×16 FP, 2×16 vector (152 entries total); integer cluster 2 ALU + 2 branch; load/store 2 AGU, 2 LD/ST pipes, D-cache 32 KB; private L2 up to 512 KB; shared L3 up to 16 MB; links 32 B/cycle; pipeline 13 stages; over 3.4 GHz at 5 nm; over 13 SpecINT2k6/GHz (SiFive's current P600 page; the launch figure was over 12).

**Primary source.** SiFive, "SiFive Performance P670 detailed pipeline overview" diagram (November 2022, via CNX Software); SiFive, Performance P670 product brief, rev 1.0 (2025); SiFive, Performance P600 Series product page (sifive.com/cores/performance-p600).

#### Inside the signature block: The dual 128-bit vector cluster — two ALUs, DLEN = VLEN

**Inside it.** The vector cluster is the piece that makes the P670 a different core from its sibling the P650, which is the same scalar machine with the vector unit deleted. The brief specifies it precisely: two 128-bit vector ALUs, DLEN = VLEN — the datapath width equals the architectural vector length of 128 bits — implementing the ratified RISC-V Vector v1.0 specification with vector-length-agnostic operation and dynamic runtime setting of vector lengths, across INT8/16/32/64 and FP16/32/64, plus the vector cryptography extensions (the first RISC-V vector crypto on the market, per SiFive's launch release). The cluster is fed by its own Vector Dispatch Buffer and two 16-entry issue queues, one per ALU, with a DIV unit and a V2S (vector-to-scalar) unit beside the ALUs. Because DLEN equals VLEN, one vector instruction on a full 128-bit register is one pass through one ALU — 16 INT8 lanes, 8 INT16, 4 INT32/FP32, or 2 INT64/FP64 per cycle per ALU — and the two ALUs let two independent vector instructions execute in the same cycle. The vector registers are renamed from a dedicated 2×64-entry pool, separate from the scalar rename pools. What SiFive does not publish: the vector register file's port counts, the DIV latency, and how vector loads move through the load/store cluster — the diagram shows the structure, not the cycle counts.

**Trace — one unit of work: one vector add, `vadd.vv v0, v1, v2`, 16 INT8 elements, VLEN = 128.**
1. **Decode and rename.** The instruction is decoded in the 4-wide front end; its vector registers are renamed against the 2×64 vector rename pool, and the current vl/vtype setting (set dynamically at runtime) is attached to the instruction.
2. **Dispatch.** It is routed to the Vector Dispatch Buffer.
3. **Wait.** It sits in one of the two 16-entry vector issue queues until v1 and v2 are ready.
4. **Fire.** The queue issues it to one of the two 128-bit vector ALUs; all 16 INT8 lanes are added in a single pass, because the 128-bit datapath matches the 128-bit vector length.
5. **Dual issue.** In the same cycle the second ALU can take an independent vector instruction from the other issue queue — two vector ops per cycle, not one wide one.
6. **Writeback and retire.** The 128-bit result lands in the vector register file, wakes dependent vector ops, and the instruction retires in program order from the 160-entry ROB. A vector divide would instead take the DIV path; a move of a vector element to a scalar register takes the V2S path.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the P650's missing-vector gap: AI/ML, media and DSP work that needed a separate accelerator or scalar loops now runs on the core itself, with vector crypto in the same unit — the reason SiFive positions the P670 against the Cortex-A78 for wearables, robotics and networking. Creates the 128-bit width wall instead: with DLEN = VLEN = 128, wider vectors (via LMUL register grouping) cost multiple passes, and a 256-bit-equivalent operation takes two cycles where a 256-bit datapath would take one. And the vector unit shares the scalar machine's oxygen — the 4-wide front end, the 160-entry ROB and the load/store cluster — so a vector-heavy stream competes with scalar work for dispatch slots and for the two load/store pipes feeding it; the streaming prefetcher and cache stashing to L3 exist to keep those pipes from starving.

**Governing numbers.** 2× 128-bit vector ALUs; DLEN = VLEN = 128 bits; vector issue queues 2×16 entries; vector rename pool 2×64; per-cycle per-ALU throughput 16× INT8 / 8× INT16 / 4× INT32 or FP32 / 2× INT64 or FP64 lanes; datatypes INT8–64, FP16/32/64; RVV 1.0 + vector crypto; private L2 up to 512 KB, shared L3 up to 16 MB.

**Primary source.** SiFive, Performance P670 product brief, rev 1.0 (2025) ("2x128-bit ALU, DLEN = VLEN"; datatype list); SiFive, "SiFive Performance P670 detailed pipeline overview" diagram (November 2022, via CNX Software); SiFive press release, "SiFive's New High-Performance Processors Offer a Significant Upgrade for Wearable and Consumer Products" (November 1, 2022).

### NVIDIA Ada Lovelace AD102

#### Inside the signature block: The Ada SM and Shader Execution Reordering — a reorder stage in the ray-tracing pipeline

**Inside it.** The AD10x SM is divided into four processing blocks (partitions). Each partition holds a 64 KB register file, an L0 instruction cache, one warp scheduler and one dispatch unit, 16 CUDA cores dedicated to FP32 and 16 more that execute FP32 or INT32, one fourth-generation Tensor Core, four load/store units and an SFU — 128 FP32 lanes per SM in all, behind 128 KB of L1 that can be configured as data cache or shared memory. SER is not another execution unit: it is a new scheduling system, implemented as an added stage in the ray-tracing pipeline between hit determination and hit shading, with optimisations designed into the SM and the memory system specifically to make thread reordering cheap. It is switched on by the application, through a small API, at the points the developer chooses.

**Trace — one unit of work: one secondary-ray hit through the SER reorder stage.**
1. **Primary rays shade cleanly.** Threads shooting primary rays hit the same objects and run the same shader program — the warp is coherent, execution and data locality are already high, and SER has nothing to fix.
2. **Secondary rays scatter.** Each primary hit spawns secondary rays — reflections, indirect light, path-tracing bounces — that fly off in different directions and strike different objects and materials.
3. **Divergence serialises the warp.** Neighbouring threads now need different shader programs or different code paths (execution divergence) and scattered, uncoalescable data (data divergence); the SM works through the paths one at a time and leaves most of its width idle.
4. **The reorder stage regroups.** Before hit shading runs, the SER stage reorders and groups the pending secondary-hit work on the fly, gathering threads that will execute the same shader onto the same data into the same warps.
5. **Reordered warps execute at width.** The regrouped warps issue through the partitions' schedulers onto coherent code paths; the RT Core keeps traversing while the SM shades the sorted work instead of the scattered work.
6. **Measured payoff.** NVIDIA reports up to 2x on highly divergent RT shaders such as path tracing, and up to 44% overall in Cyberpunk 2077's RT Overdrive mode — the gains live entirely in the shading stage SER reorders.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves divergence, the tax SIMT pays whenever a warp's threads disagree: divergent hit shading serialised execution and thrashed locality even though the RT Core could traverse rays far faster than the SM could shade their hits. Creates an opt-in dependency and a narrower win — SER does nothing unless the application calls its API at the right points, the reorder stage itself costs scheduling work the hardware was designed to minimise, and the benefit is confined to ray-tracing shading; raster and compute divergence are untouched.

**Governing numbers.** 4 partitions per SM, each with 1 warp scheduler, 1 dispatch unit and a 64 KB register file; 128 FP32 operations per clock per SM (16 FP32-only + 16 FP32/INT32 lanes per partition); 128 KB unified L1/shared memory per SM; SER up to 2x on divergent RT shaders, up to 44% in Cyberpunk 2077 RT Overdrive (NVIDIA figures).

**Primary source.** NVIDIA, "NVIDIA Ada GPU Architecture" whitepaper, V2.02 — SM description, "Shader Execution Reordering (SER)" section and Figure 12.

#### Inside the signature block: The Optical Flow Accelerator — a fixed-function engine feeding DLSS 3 frame generation

**Inside it.** The OFA is a standalone fixed-function engine, carried over from Ampere, that computes optical flow: the direction and magnitude of the apparent motion of pixels between two consecutively rendered frames, delivered as a dense flow field. NVIDIA publishes no internal organisation for it — no sub-block breakdown, flow-grid resolution or internal buffering appears in the architecture whitepaper — so what can be described is its contract, not its circuits: frames in, flow field out, at a published rate of 300 TOPS. Its consumer is the DLSS 3 frame-generation network running on the fourth-generation Tensor Cores, which fuses the OFA's flow field with the game engine's own motion vectors and depth to synthesise a frame that was never rendered.

**Trace — one unit of work: one frame pair through DLSS 3 frame generation.**
1. **Two frames are rendered.** The engine renders consecutive frames normally — shaders, RT Cores and Tensor Cores (DLSS super resolution) — and emits per-object motion vectors and depth alongside each.
2. **OFA measures pixel motion.** The accelerator compares the two rendered frames and produces a dense optical-flow field: where each pixel appears to have moved, and by how much — including motion the engine's vectors do not describe.
3. **Two motion estimates are fused.** DLSS 3 combines the engine motion vectors with the OFA flow field; NVIDIA's own diagram reduces it to "Motion Vectors + Optical Flow = Accurate Motion Estimation".
4. **Tensor Cores generate the in-between frame.** The frame-generation network, running on the SMs' fourth-generation Tensor Cores, synthesises an intermediate frame from the fused motion, the two rendered frames and depth.
5. **Frames alternate to the display.** Rendered and generated frames interleave, so the display sees up to twice the frame rate DLSS 2 delivered — including in CPU-bound games such as Microsoft Flight Simulator, where the extra frames bypass the CPU bottleneck entirely (up to 2x there too).

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the render-rate ceiling: historically every displayed frame cost a full pass through rasterisation, ray tracing and shading, and in CPU-bound titles no GPU speedup helped at all; the OFA plus frame generation decouple displayed frames from rendered frames. Creates an epistemic bottleneck instead — the generated frame is an inference, not a simulation: it cannot contain input the player has not yet given, so added latency and occasional flow-estimation artefacts are the price, and the whole path only exists where a game integrates DLSS 3.

**Governing numbers.** OFA throughput 300 TOPS, over 2x the Ampere-generation OFA; DLSS 3 frame generation adds up to 2x frame rate over DLSS 2; 512 fourth-generation Tensor Cores in the RTX 4090 (4 per SM x 128 SMs) deliver 660.6 FP8 TFLOPS dense / 1,321.2 with sparsity per NVIDIA's spec table.

**Primary source.** NVIDIA, "NVIDIA Ada GPU Architecture" whitepaper, V2.02 — "DLSS 3 and Optical Flow Acceleration", Figure 13 and Table 1.

### AMD RDNA 3 — Navi 31

#### Inside the signature block: The dual-issue Work Group Processor — two CUs, four SIMD32s and the VOPD pairing rule

**Inside it.** The WGP is the repeating compute tile of the GCD: 48 of them in Navi 31, each holding two CUs that share a 128 KB local data share (LDS), and four WGPs in a shader array share one 256 KB L1 cache. Each CU has four SIMD32 vector units (128 FP32 lanes per CU), a scalar ALU, a 384 KiB vector register file, a 32 KB L0 vector cache, a 16 KB L0 scalar cache and a 32 KB L0 instruction cache, plus two AI accelerators running WMMA matrix instructions and one second-generation ray accelerator. The LDS is 64 banks of 512 four-byte entries, split into two 32-bank sets, each affiliated with one CU's pair of SIMD32s; in CU mode a wave's LDS space lives in the half belonging to its SIMD pair, in WGP mode the LDS is one contiguous space shared across all four SIMD32s. A WGP holds up to 32 work-groups of up to 1,024 work-items each. The signature trick is dual issue: a VOPD instruction packs two independent VALU operations into one 8-byte instruction, executed in parallel on one SIMD32 — but only in wave32 mode, and only under hard pairing rules enforced by the register-file banks.

**Trace — one unit of work: one VOPD-packed wavefront through a SIMD32.**
1. **A wavefront is resident on one SIMD32.** The wave's state — program counter, EXEC mask, vector registers — lives on one of the CU's four SIMD32 units; in wave32 mode the whole 32-lane wave issues each instruction at most once.
2. **Fetch from the L0 instruction cache.** The next instruction comes from the CU's 32 KB L0 instruction cache; the compiler has already packed two independent FP32 adds into a single 8-byte VOPD instruction.
3. **The pairing rules are checked.** Per AMD's ISA reference the two operations must be independent, wave32-only, with no DPP; the two source-0 operands must come from different VGPR banks and the two source-1 operands from different banks; the two destinations must be one even and one odd VGPR. A pair that breaks a rule does not function — the compiler, not hardware, is responsible for legality.
4. **Operands are read from the banked register cache.** The vector register file has four banks indexed by the low two source bits, and each bank has a cache with three read ports — one each for SRC0, SRC1 and SRC2 — so a bank can serve all three operand positions at once but cannot serve two SRC0 reads at once; that is why same-position operands must live in different banks.
5. **Both operations execute in the same cycle.** The two adds run in parallel on the SIMD32's dual-issue datapath: 64 FP32 results per cycle from one SIMD32, 256 per CU, 24,576 across the 96-CU GCD — at the 2.5 GHz boost clock that is the 61.4 TFLOPS headline figure.
6. **Results write back; the next wave is picked.** Both results write back to the 384 KiB vector register file after the 5-cycle FP32 latency — if one operation reads a VGPR the other writes, the read gets the old value — and the scheduler moves to the next ready wavefront, hiding that latency behind other waves.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the per-WGP throughput wall: RDNA 2's CU issued one wave32 instruction per SIMD32 per cycle, so doubling the lanes would have meant doubling the WGP count and the die; VOPD doubles peak FP32 per SIMD32 with almost no extra control logic — the added hardware is mostly the second datapath and the banked register cache. Creates a compiler-bound bottleneck instead: dual issue only fires when the compiler can find two independent, bank-compatible, even-and-odd-destination operations to pack — FMA, the workhorse behind the headline TFLOPS number, takes three inputs and cannot be a VOPD pair, so measured gains fall far short of the 2x headline (in Chips and Cheese's OpenCL tests convincing dual issue appeared only for FP32 adds, while FMA-heavy code produced very few VOPD instructions), and FP64 throughput was halved to four operations per cycle per WGP.

**Governing numbers.** 48 WGPs / 96 CUs; 4 SIMD32 per CU (128 FP32 lanes), dual-issue to 256 FP32 ops per cycle per CU; 24,576 FP32 ops per cycle across the GCD, 61.4 TFLOPS at 2.5 GHz boost (about 30.7 TFLOPS without dual issue); vector register file 384 KiB per CU; LDS 128 KB per WGP in 64 banks of 512 four-byte entries with 64 integer atomic units, 64 KB maximum per work-group; L0 vector 32 KB, L0 scalar 16 KB, L0 instruction 32 KB per CU; up to 32 work-groups and 1,024 work-items per work-group per WGP; FP32 latency 5 cycles (measured); FP64 4 ops per cycle per WGP; front end 2.5 GHz, shaders 2.3 GHz; 2 AI accelerators and 1 ray accelerator per CU.

**Primary source.** AMD, 'RDNA3' Instruction Set Architecture Reference Guide, 15-Aug-2023 — §1.2.1 Work-group Processor, §1.2.2.1 Local Data Share, §2.1 Wave32 and Wave64, §2.3 Work-groups, §7.6 Dual Issue VALU, §7.9 WMMA; AMD ROCm GPU hardware specifications (RX 7900 XTX: 96 CUs, 384 KiB VGPR file, 32/16/32 KiB L0 caches); Chips and Cheese, 'Microbenchmarking AMD's RDNA 3 Graphics Architecture' (Jan 2023) — VOPD limits, FP32 latency, FP64 halving, 61 TFLOPS basis.

#### Inside the signature block: The Memory Cache Die and Infinity Cache — the last-level cache moved off the die

**Inside it.** Navi 31 splits the memory system off the compute die: six MCDs on TSMC 6 nm ring the 5 nm GCD, each 37.52 mm² with 2.05 billion transistors, holding one 16 MB slice of the second-generation Infinity Cache and two 32-bit GDDR6 PHYs — 96 MB of cache and a 384-bit bus in total. The dies are joined by TSMC InFO-RDL fanout packaging carrying AMD's Infinity Links: four 64-byte channels in each direction per MCD interface, signalling at 9.2 Gbps, for 5.3 TB/s of cumulative peak die-to-die bandwidth at about 10x the bandwidth density of organic package links and up to 80% more efficient. On the GCD side the hierarchy feeding the links is L0 (32 KB vector and 16 KB scalar caches per CU), a 256 KB 16-way L1 per shader array and a 6 MB 16-way L2; the Infinity Cache is the memory-side last-level cache beyond it. AMD quotes 3.5 TB/s of effective memory bandwidth — about 2.5 TB/s from the Infinity Cache plus 960 GB/s from GDDR6 — delivered for under 5% of GPU power. Each MCD also carries unused TSV landing points, so 3D V-Cache stacking was physically possible but never shipped on Navi 31. AMD publishes no internal organisation for the MCD — no cache-controller, tag-array or link-arbiter internals — so what follows is the contract, not the circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one cache-line request from L0 to GDDR6.**
1. **L0: the CU's own caches first.** A vector load checks the CU's 32 KB, 32-way L0 vector cache; a uniform load goes through the 16 KB, 4-way L0 scalar cache instead — the scalar path is the latency-sensitive one, at 15.4 ns load-to-use measured.
2. **L1: the shader array's shared cache.** On an L0 miss the request goes to the 256 KB, 16-way L1 shared across the shader array's four WGPs — doubled from RDNA 2's 128 KB.
3. **L2: the GCD-wide cache.** An L1 miss reaches the 6 MB, 16-way L2 on the GCD, up from 4 MB on RDNA 2; the larger on-die caches exist precisely so fewer requests ever have to leave the GCD.
4. **Across the package: the Infinity Link.** The L2 miss is hashed to one of the six MCDs and crosses the package on an Infinity Fanout link — one of four 64-byte channels per direction at 9.2 Gbps signalling — paying the die-to-die latency a monolithic die would not.
5. **Infinity Cache lookup on the MCD.** The target MCD checks its 16 MB Infinity Cache slice; on a hit the line comes back across the same link. The cache delivers about 2.5 TB/s in aggregate, and measured full-GPU bandwidth is 1.8x RDNA 2's against a 2.7x theoretical claim.
6. **GDDR6 on a miss.** On an Infinity Cache miss the MCD's two 32-bit PHYs fetch the line from GDDR6 — a 384-bit bus at 960 GB/s aggregate — and the line is installed in the cache slice on its way back up the hierarchy.
7. **The occupancy catch.** From a single WGP, Infinity Cache bandwidth is actually lower than RDNA 2's: one WGP cannot generate enough memory-level parallelism to absorb the extra die-to-die latency. The chiplet cache only wins when the whole GPU is loaded.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves two walls at once: the bandwidth wall — a 96-CU GCD needs far more than RDNA 2's 512 GB/s of GDDR6, and the Infinity Cache plus the 384-bit bus deliver 3.5 TB/s effective — and the die-size wall: moving cache and PHYs to 6 nm shrank the GCD to about 300 mm² from Navi 21's 520 mm². Creates a latency tax instead: every L2 miss now pays a die-to-die crossing, Infinity Cache latency is measurably higher than RDNA 2's on-die cache, capacity fell from 128 MB to 96 MB so the hit rate has to be bought back by the wider bus, and the whole cache only pays off at full-GPU occupancy.

**Governing numbers.** 6 MCDs x 16 MB = 96 MB Infinity Cache; 2 x 32-bit GDDR6 PHYs per MCD = 384-bit bus, 960 GB/s; Infinity Fanout link 9.2 Gbps signalling, four 64-byte channels per direction per MCD interface, 5.3 TB/s cumulative peak, about 10x the bandwidth density of organic links, up to 80% more efficient; effective bandwidth 3.5 TB/s (Infinity Cache about 2.5 TB/s plus GDDR6 960 GB/s) for under 5% of GPU power; L1 256 KB 16-way per shader array, L2 6 MB 16-way; L0 vector 32 KB 32-way, L0 scalar 16 KB 4-way, 15.4 ns load-to-use; MCD 37.52 mm², 2.05 billion transistors each; 58 billion transistors in the package.

**Primary source.** AMD press release, 3 Nov 2022 (chiplet design, 54% performance per watt, 5.3 TB/s interconnect, 96 unified compute units, 384-bit GDDR6); AMD ROCm GPU hardware specifications (RX 7900 XTX: Infinity Cache 96 MiB, L2 6 MiB, L1 256 KiB, L0 32/16/32 KiB); AMD, 'RDNA3' ISA Reference Guide §1.2.3 Device Memory (L2 to L1 to L0 read path); PC Gamer, 'AMD's Infinity Links is the unsung hero of RDNA 3' (Nov 2022) — Sam Naffziger, AMD Fellow, on the four 64-byte channels, 9.2 Gbps, 10x density, 80% efficiency and 3.5 TB/s under 5% power; Chips and Cheese, 'Microbenchmarking AMD's RDNA 3 Graphics Architecture' (Jan 2023) — cache sizes, Infinity Cache latency regression, 1.8x measured versus 2.7x theoretical bandwidth, single-WGP shortfall.

### Intel Ponte Vecchio (Xe-HPC)

#### Inside the signature block: The Xe-core — eight vector engines, eight matrix engines and a 512 KB L1 that doubles as scratchpad

**Inside it.** The Xe-core is Ponte Vecchio's compute atom, and Intel's own deck draws it as a small, regular tile: eight 512-bit vector engines (XVE) and eight 4096-bit matrix engines (XMX) — each matrix engine an 8-deep systolic array — plus one ray-tracing unit, a 512 KB L1 data cache that is software-configurable as shared local memory (SLM), an L1 instruction cache, and a wide load/store unit. The deck's published per-core rates make the division of labour plain: the vector engines retire 256 FP32, 256 FP64 and 512 FP16 operations per clock, while the matrix engines retire 2048 TF32, 4096 FP16, 4096 BF16 and 8192 INT8 operations per clock. Eight Xe-cores make one compute tile on TSMC N5 with 4 MB of L1; sixteen tiles make the full OAM — 128 Xe-cores, 1024 vector engines, 1024 matrix engines and 128 ray-tracing units. Intel publishes no scheduler, issue-width or pipeline-stage detail for the Xe-core, so this is the block's contract, not its circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one BF16 matrix-multiply tile through one Xe-core.**
1. **Tile staged in L1/SLM.** A BF16 activation tile and weight tile arrive from the Memory Fabric and are written into the core's 512 KB L1 — or placed there directly as scratchpad by software — so the matrix engines never wait on the package fabric mid-tile.
2. **Load/store feeds at 512 bytes per clock.** The wide load/store unit streams operands from the L1 into the engines at 512 bytes per clock, the rate the ISSCC paper publishes for the core's memory port.
3. **The systolic arrays take the tile.** The eight XMX engines step 4096-bit vector operations through their 8-deep systolic arrays each clock — 4096 BF16 operations per clock for the whole core — with operands flowing through the array rather than being re-fetched per operation.
4. **Vector engines take the residue.** Bias, activation and other element-wise work that is not a matrix multiply runs on the eight 512-bit vector engines at 256 FP32 operations per clock, so the matrix engines are never spent on scalar work.
5. **Results return to L1.** The finished tile is written back to the 512 KB L1/SLM, where the next tile's operands are already staging, and from there out through the load/store unit to the Memory Fabric for the next consumer.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the matrix-throughput wall: one core retires 4096 BF16 operations per clock against 256 FP32 on its vector path — a 16x gap — so dense AI and HPC matmuls run at the matrix rate instead of the vector rate. Creates a feeding wall instead: the only doors into the core are the 512-bytes-per-clock load/store port and the 512 KB L1, so a tile that does not fit L1, or a kernel that cannot keep eight systolic arrays fed, leaves the XMX idle; and the 839 TFLOPS headline exists only at 1.6 GHz with all 128 cores fed at once, which is why the 408 MB second level and its 13 TB/s sit one level up. Non-matrix code gets none of this: it runs at the vector rate, 52 TFLOPS across the whole package.

**Governing numbers.** 8 XVE (512-bit) + 8 XMX (4096-bit, 8-deep systolic) + 1 RT unit per Xe-core; 512 KB L1/SLM per core, 4 MB L1 per compute tile, 64 MB L1 per OAM; 256 FP32 / 256 FP64 / 512 FP16 vector ops per clock per core; 2048 TF32 / 4096 FP16 / 4096 BF16 / 8192 INT8 matrix ops per clock per core; load/store 512 B/clock; 1024 vector + 1024 matrix engines per OAM; 52 TFLOPS FP32/FP64, 419 TF32, 839 BF16/FP16, 1678 INT8 at 1.6 GHz (2-stack OAM, Hot Chips 34).

**Primary source.** Intel, "Ponte Vecchio: A Multi Tile 3D Stacked Processor for Exascale Computing" (Gomes et al., 2022) — Compute Tile / Xe-core slides and Architecture Summary; Intel Hot Chips 34 presentation (Hong Jiang, Aug 2022) for the 1.6 GHz peak rates.

#### Inside the signature block: Rambo and the base tile's Memory Fabric — 408 MB of second-level cache and the die-to-die fabric that feeds it

**Inside it.** The second level of Ponte Vecchio's hierarchy is split across two tile types, and the split is the point. Eight Rambo tiles — "Random Access Memory, Bandwidth Optimized", on Intel 7 — hold four 3.75 MB SRAM banks each: 15 MB per tile, 120 MB in all, built for random-access bandwidth. The two base tiles (Intel 7, 640 mm² each) each carry 144 MB of cache in their Memory Fabric, plus the HBM2e controllers, the PCIe Gen5 host interface and the Modular Die Fabric Interface (MDFI) that routes traffic between tiles. Rambo plus Memory Fabric is the 408 MB of the headline figure. Intel's own slides disagree on what to call it — the summary and base-tile slides say L2, the cache-hierarchy slides and the ISSCC paper call the same structures L3, the base-tile portion a "Memory Fabric" — and the wiki follows the summary's L2 wording. The fabric moves 4096 bytes per cycle. Compute tiles meet the base tile through Foveros at 36 µm bump pitch with over 7,000 Foveros Die Interconnect (FDI) connections per compute tile; HBM and Xe Link tiles attach through EMIB at 55 µm Co-EMIB pitch. Intel publishes no Rambo bank arbitration, replacement policy or tag geometry, so this is the memory system's contract, not its circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one cache line on a load that misses the Xe-core's L1.**
1. **L1 miss in the Xe-core.** A load misses the core's 512 KB L1/SLM; the load/store unit hands the request down instead of stalling the engines on it.
2. **Down through Foveros.** The request crosses the 36 µm-pitch Foveros die interconnect — more than 7,000 FDI connections per compute tile — into the base tile's Modular Die Fabric Interface.
3. **Second-level lookup.** The MDFI routes the request to the 408 MB second level: the eight Rambo tiles (120 MB of bandwidth-optimised SRAM) and the two base tiles' 144 MB Memory Fabric each, served by a fabric moving 4096 bytes per cycle.
4. **HBM on a miss.** On a second-level miss the base tile's HBM controllers fetch the line from one of the eight HBM2e stacks — 128 GB in total, 3.2 TB/s on the Max 1550 — and install it in the second level on the way back.
5. **Back up to the core.** The line returns across Foveros into the Xe-core's L1, and the load/store unit delivers it to the vector or matrix engines.
6. **Scale-out variant.** If the line lives on another OAM, the request leaves through a Xe Link tile instead: an 8-port embedded switch over up to 90G SerDes, with up to eight OAMs fully connected.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the HBM wall: 408 MB of on-package cache at 13 TB/s (Hot Chips 34) absorbs the working sets that would otherwise stream from HBM at 3.2 TB/s — Intel's own Hot Chips slides credit the large second level with large gains on 2D-FFT and DNN cases — and without it the 512 KB-per-core L1s could never keep 1024 matrix engines fed. Creates a packaging wall instead: the cache only exists because the package is two stacks, 47 functional tiles and 16 thermal tiles on a 4,844 mm² substrate, so every miss that does reach HBM pays a Foveros and EMIB crossing, and the "one" 408 MB is physically two structures (Rambo tiles and base-tile Memory Fabric) reached through different paths. The whole level is bought with a 600 W envelope and liquid cooling on the Max 1550.

**Governing numbers.** 408 MB second level (120 MB Rambo + 288 MB Memory Fabric); Rambo: 8 tiles × 4 banks × 3.75 MB; base tile: 2 × 144 MB Memory Fabric, 640 mm² each, Intel 7; second-level bandwidth 13 TB/s (Hot Chips 34); Memory Fabric 4096 B/cycle; Foveros 36 µm bump pitch, >7,000 FDI connections per compute tile; Co-EMIB 55 µm pitch; HBM2e 8 stacks, 128 GB, 3.2 TB/s (Max 1550); package 77.5 × 62.5 mm (4,844 mm²), 3,100 mm² silicon, 4,468 pins; 63 tiles total (47 functional + 16 thermal).

**Primary source.** Intel, "Ponte Vecchio: A Multi Tile 3D Stacked Processor for Exascale Computing" (Gomes et al., 2022) — Base Tile, RAMBO Breakdown, Foveros and Summary slides; Intel ISSCC 2022 paper via eeNews Europe for the Memory Fabric 4096 B/cycle and the L3 naming; Intel Hot Chips 34 (Hong Jiang, Aug 2022) for the 13 TB/s second-level bandwidth, via TweakTown coverage.

### Arm Immortalis-G720

#### Inside the signature block: The Deferred Vertex Shading pipeline — Binning phase, Main phase and the tiler that decides between them

**Inside it.** The 5th Gen front end is built around two independently scheduled phases and the queues that feed them. The Command Stream Front-end (CSF) takes draw calls from the command stream and puts binning-phase jobs on the Binning phase queue and main-phase jobs on the Main phase queue, with a Compute queue alongside them for compute and advanced-geometry work. The Tiler is the fixed-function unit that runs the Binning phase: it coordinates vertex shading, performs primitive culling and bins primitives into per-tile lists. The shader cores do the shading itself: each is a programmable core wrapped in fixed-function hardware, up to 2048 threads in 16-wide warps, with a Main phase front-end that turns a tile list into warps. Between the phases sits only the binning information — positions computed in the Binning phase are thrown away and re-generated in the Main phase — and the finished tile lives in on-chip tile memory until it is written out through the GPU's L2 slices to shared LPDDR. Arm publishes no tiler buffer sizes, binning-list depths, queue depths or culling rates for this front end, so this is the pipeline's contract, not its circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one triangle through Deferred Vertex Shading.**
1. **Command stream in, job queued.** The CSF takes the draw call from the command stream and puts a binning-phase job on the Binning phase queue, which breaks the job into tasks for the tiler and the shader cores.
2. **Position shading only.** For a draw call using basic vertex shading, the shader cores run only the position part of the vertex shader — enough to flatten perspective and find which tiles the primitive covers — and the position values are then thrown away rather than written to memory.
3. **Cull and bin.** The tiler performs primitive culling — frustum, facing, scissor and sample culling — and bins the surviving primitives into per-tile lists. A triangle wholly contained in a tile stays on the deferred path; a triangle spanning tiles, or a draw call using transform feedback, tessellation or geometry shaders, takes the advanced-geometry path and is fully shaded up front, with its outputs written back to main memory.
4. **Main phase, per tile.** When the tile comes up on the Main phase queue, the shader cores re-run the full vertex shader for the binned primitives — regenerating the positions discarded in the Binning phase — then rasterize and fragment-shade from the on-chip tile buffer, and the tile is written back to memory only once.
5. **Tile flush.** The finished tile is written out through the GPU's L2 slices to the shared LPDDR memory, and transaction elimination skips any tile whose CRC matches the previous frame.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the geometry-bandwidth wall: the Binning phase stores only binning information instead of fully shaded vertices, so the handover between phases costs almost no DRAM traffic — Arm claims up to 40% less memory bandwidth overall, 26% less in Fortnite and 33% less in Genshin Impact, against a backdrop where memory access is about a third of the power draw in high-end gaming. Creates a recomputation wall instead: every deferred position is shaded twice — once for binning, once for real — so the saving is bought with extra shader work, and the bargain only holds because compute capability is growing faster than DDR bandwidth; draw calls that cannot defer (transform feedback, tessellation, geometry shaders) pay the old cost in full, and the extra phase costs time before the first fragment, which is why the wiki's trade-off line already notes the latency price.

**Governing numbers.** Tiles up to 64x64 (vs 32x32 on Immortalis-G715); up to 40% less memory bandwidth; 26% less bandwidth in Fortnite, 33% less in Genshin Impact (Arm-measured vs G715); 15% more performance per watt, 15% more sustained and peak performance vs G715; 2x HDR rendering capability with 64bpp texturing; GPU core 2% larger than last generation; 10-16 shader cores; 2 or 4 L2 slices, up to 1,024 KB; per shader core: 2048 threads max in 16-wide warps (1024 threads with 33-64 work registers), 4 arithmetic units, 512 FP16 / 256 FP32 ops per cycle, 4 fragments and 4 pixels per cycle, 8 texels and 8 bilinear samples per cycle, 32 KB load/store cache, 32 KB texture cache, 256 tile bits per pixel.

**Primary source.** Arm, Mali G1 Performance Counter Reference Guide (doc 111042) — 5th Gen execution model, DVS definition, hardware queues and major functional blocks; Arm GPU Best Practices Developer Guide (doc 101897, Issue 11) — DVS pipeline, Binning/Main phases and advanced-geometry path; Arm Immortalis-G720 product page — 64x64 tiles; Android Authority, "A close look at the Arm Immortalis-G720 and its 5th Gen graphics" (May 2023) — 40% bandwidth, 15% perf/W, Fortnite/Genshin figures, 2x HDR; Hot Hardware, "Arm Unveils Cortex-X4 And Immortalis GPU" (May 2023) — 40% bandwidth, 15% sustained/peak performance, larger tiles; Arm, "Mali GPUs" reference sheet (2024) — per-core rates and cache sizes.

#### Inside the signature block: The ray-tracing unit — a fixed-function RTU inside each shader core, power-gated when idle

**Inside it.** The ray-tracing unit is not a separate accelerator: it is a fixed-function block built directly into each shader core, so ray-tracing throughput scales with the shader-core count — 10 to 16 cores in the Immortalis configuration. Inside the RTU are two dedicated test units: a ray-box unit that tests rays against bounding-volume-hierarchy nodes, and a ray-triangle unit that tests rays against the triangles at a hierarchy leaf. Arm's G715-era technical diagrams label these RBOX_UNIT (RT_RAY_BOX) and RTRI_UNIT (RT_RAY_TRI). The shader drives the work through Vulkan ray-query instructions: a ray query is initialised with the acceleration structure, ray flags, cull mask and the ray itself, and traversal proceeds query by query, with the RTU accelerating the box and triangle tests and the shader keeping control of the traversal. Shading and denoising stay on the shader cores, so the render is hybrid — rasterization for primaries, rays for shadows, reflections and ambient occlusion. In the 5th generation the RTU sits on its own power island and can be power-gated, so applications that never trace a ray pay no leakage for it. The RTU is the unit introduced with the Immortalis-G715; Arm announced no new ray-tracing generation for the G720. Arm publishes no ray-test rates, BVH fetch widths, ray-queue depths, traversal-stack depths or a GigaRays/s figure for it — this is the unit's contract, not its circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one ray through the RTU.**
1. **Shader issues a ray query.** A shader in the core initialises a ray query with the acceleration structure (top-level and bottom-level BVHs), ray flags, cull mask, origin, tMin, direction and tMax, using the new ray-query shader instructions; the query runs inline in any shader stage.
2. **Ray-box tests in the RTU.** The RTU's ray-box unit tests the ray against BVH nodes and descends the hierarchy; a missed box prunes the whole subtree beneath it, so most of the scene's triangles are never tested at all.
3. **Ray-triangle tests at the leaf.** At a hierarchy leaf the RTU's ray-triangle unit tests the candidate triangles and returns the closest hit with barycentric coordinates to the shader.
4. **Traversal stays in the shader.** Arm does not accelerate BVH processing itself: the shader drives the traversal step by step through ray-query instructions, calling back into the RTU for each box and triangle test — a smaller, cheaper unit than a console-style full-traversal accelerator, at the cost of more shader involvement per ray.
5. **Shading back on the cores.** The hit result returns to the shader core, which shades the contribution and denoises with the rest of the frame; the render stays hybrid, with rays reserved for shadows, reflections and ambient occlusion. When no ray work is submitted, the RTU sits power-gated on its own island.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the intersection-cost wall: the two fixed-function test units do the ray-box and ray-triangle arithmetic that would otherwise burn FMA cycles on the shader cores, and Arm's benchmarks put the gain at over 300% better ray-tracing performance than software — for less than 4% of the shader core's area. Creates a traversal wall instead: because BVH processing itself is not accelerated, the shader must drive every traversal step through ray-query instructions, so divergent rays cost shader time as well as RTU time; and every BVH node fetch still crosses the memory system, so ray coherence — not raw test rate — decides whether the unit stays fed. The power island is the other half of the bargain: the RTU costs nothing when idle, which is most of the time in a raster-first mobile game.

**Governing numbers.** RTU under 4% of shader-core area; over 300% better ray-tracing performance than software (Arm benchmarks); one RTU per shader core, 10-16 cores in the Immortalis configuration; RTU power-gatable on its own power island; ray queries via Vulkan ray query (inline, any shader stage); hybrid raster plus ray tracing; no published ray-test rate or GigaRays/s figure for the G720.

**Primary source.** Android Authority, "Arm Immortalis-G715 deep dive: Ray tracing graphics for mobile" (2022) — RTU inside the shader core, under 4% area, over 300% faster, box/triangle test units, no BVH acceleration, hybrid rendering; Arm, "Unreal Lumen with Arm Immortalis: The Best Practices of Ray Tracing Content on Mobile" (TGDF 2024) — ray-query instructions, TLAS/BLAS acceleration structures; Hot Hardware, "Arm Unveils Cortex-X4 And Immortalis GPU" (May 2023) — RTU on a power island; Arm Immortalis-G720 product page — power-gateable RTU.

### Imagination PowerVR

#### Inside the signature block: The Tile Accelerator, Parameter Buffer and ISP — the deferred-visibility front end

**Inside it.** The front end is built around one idea: capture the whole scene before shading a single pixel. Vertex processing runs first — the unified shader engine executes the application's vertex shaders, then the results are converted to screen space (clip, project, cull). The Tile Accelerator (TA) then determines which tiles contain each transformed primitive and updates the per-tile lists: each tile's list holds primitive lists containing pointers to the transformed vertex data. Both the tile lists and the transformed vertex data live in an intermediate store called the Parameter Buffer (PB), which resides in system memory and is mostly managed by the hardware — it holds all the information needed to render the tiles. When a tile's turn comes, the Image Synthesis Processor (ISP) fetches the primitive data from the PB and performs Hidden Surface Removal (HSR) along with depth and stencil tests, fetching only screen-space position data for the geometry within the tile. The Tag Buffer records which triangle is on top for each pixel, so by the end of the ISP pass the tile's visible set is fully known. Colour, depth and stencil read-modify-write operations run on fast on-chip memory rather than system memory. The whole GPU is managed by firmware, which handles most high-level graphics events internally instead of leaving them to the CPU-side driver. Imagination publishes no Parameter Buffer sizes, tile-list depths, TA binning rates, ISP depth-test rates or Tag Buffer depths for this front end, so this is the pipeline's contract, not its circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one tile through the deferred-visibility front end.**
1. **Vertex shaders run, geometry to screen space.** The unified shader engine executes the application's vertex shaders, and the resulting data is converted to screen space — clip, project and cull — exactly as the Tiler stage of the TBDR pipeline describes.
2. **The Tile Accelerator bins the primitive.** The TA determines which tiles contain each transformed primitive and updates the per-tile lists, each holding pointers to the transformed vertex data; the tile lists and the vertex data are written into the Parameter Buffer in system memory.
3. **Tile operation begins, list retrieved.** When a tile comes up for rendering, its tile list is retrieved from the Parameter Buffer to identify the screen-space primitive data that needs to be fetched — nothing is shaded yet.
4. **ISP resolves visibility on-chip.** The Image Synthesis Processor fetches the primitive data and performs Hidden Surface Removal along with depth and stencil tests, fetching only screen-space position data for the geometry within the tile; the Tag Buffer records which triangle is on top for each pixel.
5. **Visible set handed to the shader back end.** With the Tag Buffer complete, the tile's visible fragments are known and the Texture and Shading Processor takes over; the front end has done its work without shading a single hidden fragment.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the overdraw wall: because the whole scene is captured before rendering starts, Hidden Surface Removal removes overdraw entirely for completely opaque renders regardless of draw-call submission order — Imagination's Shadowgun capture shows 4.7 fragments coloured per screen pixel without HSR against 1.2 with it, 75% fewer fragments, with the shortfall from 1:1 explained by blended UI elements. Creates a capture-first wall instead: no pixel is shaded until the entire scene has been tiled, so tiling latency sits in front of the first pixel (the wiki's trade-off line already notes this), and the Parameter Buffer lives in system memory, so geometry traffic — tile lists plus transformed vertices — still crosses DRAM. The bargain also has a hole: alpha blending disables the visibility hardware, because an occluded blended fragment can still affect the final image, so transparent-heavy scenes pay the overdraw the architecture exists to remove.

**Governing numbers.** Tiles 32x32 pixels as the classic example size (Imagination: varies by device); HSR removes overdraw entirely for completely opaque renders; Shadowgun capture: 4.7 fragments coloured per screen pixel without HSR, 1.2 with HSR — 75% fewer; Parameter Buffer resides in system memory; colour, depth and stencil read-modify-write on fast on-chip memory; no published Parameter Buffer size, tile-list depth, TA binning rate, ISP depth-test rate or Tag Buffer depth.

**Primary source.** Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers (Rev 1.0, 11/02/2020) — TBDR pipeline, Tiler stages, Tile Accelerator, Parameter Buffer, ISP, Tag Buffer, on-chip buffers, shader engine, firmware, HSR efficiency and the Shadowgun 4.7 to 1.2 measurement; Imagination, Droidcon 2013 slides (Triangles, Gangolells) — 32x32 pixels per tile, for example, varies by device; Series5/5XT 4x MSAA, Series6 8x MSAA.

#### Inside the signature block: The Unified Shading Cluster and TSP — shading only what survived

**Inside it.** The shading back end is the Rogue/Furian Unified Shading Cluster (USC) and the Texture and Shading Processor (TSP) wrapped around it. PowerVR has a unified shader architecture: vertex and fragment shaders run on the same processing modules, so the same USC that ran the vertex work in the Tiler stage now runs the fragment work. Lift the lid on a USC and there are 16 ALU pipelines in parallel, each holding 2 FP32 ALUs, 2 FP16 ALUs and 1 special-function ALU for sine, cosine, log, reciprocals and friends; execution is scalar SIMD, one component per cycle per lane, which keeps utilisation high on the mixed-width data of real shaders. The shader engine is massively multi-threaded and hardware-managed, load-balanced by a data-driven execution model that schedules tasks on data availability and switches between independent tasks to avoid data-dependency stalls. The TSP applies colouring operations — fragment shaders — to the visible pixels only, then alpha testing and alpha blending run, and the finished tile's colour data is written to the frame buffer in system memory exactly once. Texture work goes through a dedicated texture unit (in Furian it has its own cache, so it no longer competes with the USCs for data), and PVRTC textures are decoded on the fly in the texture unit, never existing decompressed in memory. Imagination publishes no USC register-file sizes, thread counts, texture-cache sizes or TSP queue depths, so this is the back end's contract, not its circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one tile's visible fragments through the USC/TSP back end.**
1. **Visible pixels only reach the TSP.** The Texture and Shading Processor takes the tile's visible set from the Tag Buffer and applies colouring operations — fragment shaders — to the visible pixels; hidden fragments never reach this stage.
2. **Fragment shaders run on the USCs.** The unified shader engine runs the fragment programs on the USC pipelines — 16 per cluster, each with 2 FP32, 2 FP16 and 1 special-function ALU — with the hardware's data-driven scheduler keeping the pipelines fed and switching tasks around data-dependency stalls.
3. **Textures fetched and decoded on the fly.** Texture fetches go through the dedicated texture unit, which decodes PVRTC (2 or 4 bits per pixel) in hardware as part of the fetch; the compressed texture is never decompressed into memory, and in Furian the texture unit has its own cache so it does not compete with the USCs.
4. **Alpha and MSAA resolve on-chip.** Alpha testing and then alpha blending run on the tile's on-chip colour, depth and stencil buffers, and the Pixel Back End combines sub-samples for on-chip MSAA — 4x on Series5/5XT, 8x on Series6 — without touching system memory.
5. **Tile flushes once.** Once the tile's render is complete, its colour data is written to the frame buffer in system memory exactly once, and the process repeats for the next tile until the frame buffer is complete.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the shading wall: the back end only ever shades fragments the ISP proved visible, so the most expensive work in the pipeline — fragment shading and texturing — is spent once per visible pixel instead of once per submitted fragment, and the PVR3C triple compression (lossy PVRTC/ASTC textures, lossless PVRIC framebuffer compression, lossless PVRGC geometry compression) keeps the texture and framebuffer traffic that remains small. Creates a throughput wall instead: the whole bargain rests on USC arithmetic rate — a Rogue USC peaks at 64 FP32 FLOPs per cycle, 128 FP16 FLOPs per cycle on Series6XT — so a fragment-heavy scene is bounded by ALU count and clock, and the deferred model concentrates all fragment work into per-tile bursts rather than spreading it across the frame. Furian's answer was to widen the machine (primary ALU pipelines doubled from 16 to 32 per cluster, texture unit doubled to 8 pixels and 8 bilinear texels per clock) rather than change the model.

**Governing numbers.** USC: 16 pipelines, each 2 FP32 + 2 FP16 + 1 special-function ALU; FP32 up to 2 FLOPs/cycle per ALU, 64 FLOPs/cycle per USC; FP16 up to 4 FLOPs/cycle per ALU on Series6XT, up to 128 FLOPs/cycle per USC; up to 8 USCs in a Series6/Series6XT GPU; GX6650: 6 USCs, 192 FP32 ALU cores, 12 pixels per clock; Series7XT GT7900: 16 clusters, 512 ALU cores, up to 1 TFLOP FP32; Furian GT8525: 2 clusters, 8 pixels per clock and 8 bilinear texels per clock (vs 4 for the GT7200), primary ALU pipelines doubled 16 to 32; PVRTC 2bpp (16:1 vs 32bpp) and 4bpp (8:1 vs 32bpp); MSAA 4x on Series5/5XT, 8x on Series6; no published USC register-file size, thread count, texture-cache size or TSP queue depth.

**Primary source.** Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers (Rev 1.0, 11/02/2020) — unified shader architecture, shader engine data-driven scheduling, TSP, alpha test/blend, tile flush to framebuffer, on-chip buffers, PVRTC guidance; Imagination blog, Graphics cores: trying to compare apples to apples (2014) — USC structure, 16 pipelines, 2 FP32 + 2 FP16 + 1 special-function ALU per pipeline, 64 FP32 / up to 128 FP16 FLOPs per cycle per USC, up to 8 USCs, GX6650 6 USCs and 192 FP32 cores; Imagination blog, PowerVR GX6650: redefining performance in mobile with 192 cores (2014) — 12 pixels per clock, PVR3C triple compression; Imagination, The complete guide to PowerVR Rogue GPUs (2014) — PVR3C definition, Series6XT table (GX6650 6 USCs, 192 FP32 / 384 FP16 ALUs); bit-tech, Imagination announces PowerVR Series7 GPUs (2014) — GT7900 16 clusters, 512 ALU cores, up to 1 TFLOP; Imagination blog, PowerVR Series8XT: pushing power efficiency to the next level — Furian texture unit with its own cache, double fill-rate at 8 pixels per clock; Edge AI and Vision Alliance, Imagination Announces First PowerVR Series8XT IP Core Based on New Furian GPU Architecture (2017) — GT8525 8 pixels/clock and 8 texels/clock vs 4 for GT7200, 32-wide ALU cluster; CdrInfo, Imagination Announces PowerVR Series8XT GT8540 GPU (2018) — primary ALU pipelines doubled 16 to 32; Unity Manual, Android 2D Textures Overrides — PVRTC 2 and 4 bits per pixel; Imagination, Droidcon 2013 slides — MSAA 4x Series5/5XT, 8x Series6.

### Graphcore GC200 IPU

#### Inside the signature block: The IPU tile — a barrel-threaded core with 624 KiB of its own SRAM and an AMP

**Inside it.** The die carries 1,472 active tiles of 1,536 physical — the deck's "23/24 tile redundancy" (1,472/1,536 = 23/24, 64 spare tiles for yield) — organised into islands and columns. Each tile is a complete small computer: one barrel-threaded core plus 624 KiB of private SRAM, with no caches and no coherence anywhere on the chip. The core executes 32-bit instructions, single or dual issue, on two execution paths: the MAIN path handles control flow, integer/address arithmetic and multi-load/store to or from either path, while the AUX path handles floating-point arithmetic co-issued with MAIN, including vector and matrix operators with in-line state, plus transcendentals (exp, 2^x, ln, log2, logistic, tanh) and random-number generation. Threading is barrel-style: 7 program contexts share 6 round-robin pipeline slots — the Supervisor program runs in the slots not yielded to Workers, orchestrating vertex updates, and dispatches Workers by RUN instruction; a Worker codelet executes in one slot at 1/6 of the clock and cannot see the pipeline, so its timing is fully predictable to the compiler, and returns its slot with EXIT. Every instruction takes 6 cycles, so each thread effectively runs at 1.325 GHz / 6, about 221 MHz, and never experiences latency. The AMP (Accumulating Matrix Product) unit is the tile's matrix engine: 16×16 FP16×FP16 with FP32 accumulation hits the 250 TFLOP/s peak, 16×8 reaches 125, and 8×8 FP32×FP32 reaches 62; scalar FP32 work without the AMP runs at one FMA per cycle per tile, about 4 TFLOPS across the chip. Each tile generates 128 random bits per cycle from an enhanced xoroshiro128+ PRNG with a 6th-order Irwin-Hall Gaussian shaper, and down-casts are stochastically rounded at full speed. Loads and stores support sparse gather in parallel with arithmetic at full speed via compact pointer lists — 16-bit absolute offsets to a base, or 4-bit cumulative delta offsets — with multi-load/store up to 128-bit quad-register loads. All tiles and SRAM run on a 1.325 GHz global mesochronous clock. Graphcore publishes no tile-SRAM bank organisation, load/store queue depths or AMP pipeline depth, so this is the tile's contract, not its circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one matmul vertex (codelet) through a tile in one compute phase.**
1. **Supervisor dispatches the worker.** The Supervisor program, running in the pipeline slots not yielded to Workers, issues a RUN instruction that hands one of the six round-robin slots to a Worker codelet; the Worker runs at 1/6 of the 1.325 GHz clock and cannot see the pipeline, so its execution time is fully predictable to the compiler.
2. **Operands come from the tile's own SRAM.** The Worker issues multi-load/store instructions against its own 624 KiB SRAM — loads up to 128 bits wide, with sparse gather via 16-bit absolute or 4-bit cumulative-delta pointer lists running in parallel with arithmetic at full speed. Nothing leaves the tile: there is no cache, no coherence and no memory traffic at all in this phase.
3. **The AMP does the multiply-accumulate.** For a 16×16 FP16×FP16 block with FP32 accumulation the AMP unit issues one matrix operation toward the 250 TFLOP/s peak; FP32-only work falls back to the scalar FMA path at one FMA per cycle per tile, and down-casts are stochastically rounded at full speed using the tile's 128 random bits per cycle.
4. **Results stay local; the Worker exits.** Accumulators and activations are written back into the tile's SRAM; the Worker returns its slot to the Supervisor with an EXIT instruction, and the Supervisor moves on to the next vertex in the compute phase's list.
5. **The phase ends at the barrier.** When every tile has finished its vertex list, the hardware barrier fires — about 150 cycles on chip — and the tile hands its outgoing tensors to the exchange.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the memory wall: with the working set in SRAM next to the arithmetic there are no cache misses, no DRAM latency and no memory traffic at all during a compute phase — the 47.5 TB/s of data-side SRAM bandwidth is the whole memory system, and distributed SRAM keeps most on-die transport under 1 mm. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the 624 KiB ceiling — code, data and workspace for one tile must all fit, and the Mk1 lesson was that teams spent their time tuning code and workspace to fit 256 KiB (Mk2's 624 KiB eases it without removing it); the barrier tax — every tile waits for the slowest tile at each superstep, so load imbalance is paid in full at every barrier; and the AMP shape — anything that is not a dense FP16/FP32 matmul runs at the scalar rate of about 4 TFLOPS, roughly 60x below the headline peak, so the compiler's placement and the model's shape decide the real speed.

**Governing numbers.** 1,472 active tiles of 1,536 physical (23/24 redundancy, 64 spare); 624 KiB SRAM per tile; 896 MiB on-die SRAM per the Hot Chips deck (1,472 × 624 KiB = 918,528 KiB = 897 MiB by arithmetic; marketed as 900 MB); 1.325 GHz global mesochronous clock; 7 program contexts, 6 round-robin pipeline slots; 8,832 threads (6 per tile); 250 TFLOP/s FP16, 62.5 TFLOP/s FP32 via AMP, about 4 TFLOPS FP32 scalar FMA; 128 random bits per cycle per tile; 47.5 TB/s data-side SRAM bandwidth (62 TB/s total per the deck headline); 300 W chip TDP per the deck (a Frontiers supplement says 150 W — disputed, see fact records).

**Primary source.** Knowles, "Graphcore Colossus Mk2 IPU", Hot Chips 33, 24 Aug 2021 (hc33.hotchips.org deck) — tile counts, redundancy, clock, tile processor structure, barrel threading, AMP table, RNG, sparse load/store, SRAM bandwidth, TDP; Frontiers in High Performance Computing supplementary material §2, "Technical information of Graphcore IPUs" — tile layout in islands and columns, 624 KB/tile, 918 MB total, 47.5 TB/s, 6-cycle instruction latency, MAIN/AUX pipelines, 128-bit loads, 4 TFLOPS scalar rate (citing Jia et al., "Dissecting the Graphcore IPU Architecture via Microbenchmarking", arXiv:1912.03413, for Mk1 microbenchmarking).

#### Inside the signature block: The IPU-Exchange and BSP synchronisation — a stateless all-to-all fabric

**Inside it.** The exchange is a stateless all-to-all fabric, not a network: an exchange spine of 1600 × 36 bits, with one 36-bit pipelined send channel per tile and IO block, and one 1600-way receive mux per tile. Each tile sends and receives 32 bits per cycle — 4 bytes per cycle, 5.3 GB/s per tile, 7.83 TB/s across all 1,472 tiles. Addressing is by time and select state — there are no queues, arbiters or packet overheads anywhere in the fabric; the Poplar compiler schedules transmit, receive and select at precise cycles from sync, knowing all pipeline delays, so any pattern of data movement is possible and changeable at every clock cycle, with pipelined transport up and down the tile columns. The fabric is physically mesochronous, with 3 cycles of global synchrony drift across the chip. Execution follows bulk-synchronous parallel order — repeat { Sync; Exchange; Compute } — with tiles executing asynchronously until they need to exchange data; the hardware global synchronisation takes about 150 cycles on chip and 15 ns per hop between chips, and there is no overlap between the compute and communication phases. Between chips, 10 IPU-Links give 320 GB/s of aggregate chip-to-chip bandwidth; pairs of IPUs are linked with 12 links at 192 GB/s, and pairs connect in a ladder (closable to a torus) that scales to 64,000 IPUs. The M2000 blade holds 4 IPUs at about 1 PFLOP/s peak with up to 448 GiB of DDR available to the four IPUs as streaming memory, a Gateway link of 32 GB/s to each IPU, and a 100 Gb/s host network.

**Trace — one unit of work: one exchange phase moving a tensor slice from tile A to tile B.**
1. **Sync: the barrier fires.** All 1,472 tiles finish their compute-phase vertex lists; the hardware barrier completes in about 150 cycles on chip and every tile is now at the same superstep boundary — compute and communication never overlap.
2. **Poplar's schedule fires the transmit.** At the cycle the compiler fixed in advance, tile A puts its 32-bit word on its 36-bit pipelined send channel; transmit, receive and select were all scheduled at precise cycles from sync, with every pipeline delay known.
3. **The word travels the spine.** The word moves up or down the tile column on the 1600 × 36-bit exchange spine; the fabric carries no queues, arbiters or packet headers, so the word's arrival cycle is determined by the schedule, not by contention.
4. **Tile B's receive mux selects it.** At the scheduled cycle, tile B's 1600-way receive mux selects the incoming word by time and select state and writes it into B's SRAM; all 1,472 tiles send and receive 4 bytes per cycle simultaneously, 7.83 TB/s in aggregate.
5. **Next compute phase begins.** With the exchange complete, the next superstep's compute phase starts; a tensor that must leave the chip instead goes out over one of the 10 IPU-Links, at 15 ns per hop to the next chip.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the queueing and coherence wall: with no arbiters, no queues and no packet overhead, exchange timing is deterministic — the compiler knows every delay, so there is no contention, no head-of-line blocking and no protocol tax on a 32-bit word. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the barrier tax — the whole chip waits for the slowest tile and the slowest exchange at every superstep, and compute and communication never overlap, so a straggler or a long exchange stalls all 1,472 tiles; the per-tile exchange ceiling — 4 bytes per cycle per tile (5.3 GB/s) means exchange-heavy graphs are fabric-bound long before the AMP is busy; and the inter-chip sync cost — 15 ns per hop and globally synchronised control flow that gets more expensive as more devices join, so the ladder/torus scale-out trades bisection bandwidth (128 GB/s in the ladder configuration) against synchronisation distance.
