### JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1

#### Down to the primitives: The TAP controller — a 16-state machine in every chip

The TAP controller decomposes into eleven primitives: the 16-state FSM that sequences every JTAG operation; the instruction register that holds the current instruction in a shift section plus a hold section; the instruction decoder that selects which data register sits between TDI and TDO; the boundary-scan register — a chain of BC_1 cells, one per pin; the BC_1 cell itself, two D flip-flops with front-end and back-end muxes; the one-bit bypass register; the 32-bit identification register; the TDO output mux and its tri-state driver; and — stated explicitly, because the standard's shape invites the wrong assumption — no counter and no synchronizer, the five-TCK reset guarantee being a property of the state graph and the TAP running entirely on its own clock. JTAG is a standard, not a chip: the IEEE standard mandates behaviour, not circuits, so every implementation detail beyond the standard's own numbers is per-device and unpublished — and this section says so at each primitive instead of inventing numbers.

- **FSM / controller (the 16-state TAP controller, a Moore machine)** — "TMS and TCK (and the optional TRST*) go to a 16-state finite-state machine controller, which produces the various control signals." (verified — Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1, Fig. 33). The tutorial draws the controller as a Moore machine: its outputs are a function of the state alone. "A state transition occurs on the positive edge of TCK and the controller output values change on the negative edge of TCK." (verified — Bennetts, Fig. 34). "The TAP controller initializes in the Test_Logic Reset state ("Asleep" state)." (verified — Bennetts). By arithmetic from the published 16 states the state register is 4 bits wide (2^4 = 16); that width is arithmetic, not a published figure. The controller's outputs are the TAP's whole control vocabulary: dedicated signals to the instruction register (ClockIR, ShiftIR, UpdateIR) and generic signals to all data registers (ClockDR, ShiftDR, UpdateDR), plus Reset, Select and Enable — "Reset is distributed to the Instruction register and to the target Data Register", "Select is distributed to the output multiplexer", "Enable is distributed to the output driver amplifier" (verified — Bennetts, Fig. 33). The state encoding, the next-state logic and the output-decode circuits are not published — the standard fixes the state diagram, not the gates.
- **Shift register (the instruction register — shift section + hold section)** — "An Instruction register (Figure 21) has a shift scan section that can be connected between TDI and TDO, and a hold section that holds the current instruction." (verified — Bennetts). The control signals "either cause a shift-in/shift-out through the Instruction register shift section, or cause the contents of the shift section to be passed across to the hold section (parallel Update operation)" (verified — Bennetts), and at Update-IR the shifted instruction becomes the current instruction and selects its data register. "The Instruction register must be at least two-bits long to allow coding of the four mandatory instructions — Extest, Bypass, Sample, Preload — but the maximum length of the Instruction register is not defined." (verified — Bennetts). "In capture mode, the two least significant bits must capture a 01 pattern." (verified — Bennetts) — the `01` is the infrastructure-test signature the board tester shifts back to prove the chain is intact. "The Bypass instruction must be assigned an all-1s code and when executed, causes the Bypass register to be placed between the TDI and TDO pins." (verified — Bennetts), and "All unused instruction codes must default to Bypass" (verified — Bennetts, Fig. 22). The hold section is the register the rest of the TAP reads; its flop count is the instruction-register length, which the standard leaves to the device.
- **Decoder (instruction decode → data-register select)** — "The data register that actually responds is the one enabled by the conditional control signals generated at the parallel outputs of the Instruction register, according to the particular instruction." (verified — Bennetts). "There may be some decoding logic beyond the hold section depending on the width of the register and the number of different instructions." (verified — Bennetts). "At any time, only one Data register can be connected between TDI and TDO" (verified — Bennetts), so the decoder is a one-hot select: EXTEST/SAMPLE/PRELOAD/INTEST pick the boundary-scan register, BYPASS picks the bypass register, IDCODE/USERCODE pick the identification register, and the generic ClockDR/ShiftDR/UpdateDR signals reach only the selected register. The decoder's circuit form and the number of implemented instructions are per-device and not published.
- **Shift register (the boundary-scan register — BC_1 cells chained)** — "The collection of boundary-scan cells is configured into a parallel-in, parallel-out shift register." (verified — Bennetts). One cell sits on each device primary input and primary output pin (plus cells on the control lines of tristate and bidirectional pins), and the cells are linked Scan_Out-to-Scan_In into a single serial chain between TDI and TDO; "The order of linking within the device is determined by the physical adjacency of the pins and/or by other layout constraints." (verified — Bennetts). The register is selected by the EXTEST, INTEST, SAMPLE and PRELOAD instructions. Its length equals the device's signal-pin count — a per-device number, not a published constant; the standard publishes no fixed length. "Whenever a register is selected to become active between TDI and TDO, it is always possible to perform three operations on the register: parallel Capture followed by serial Shift followed by parallel Update. The order of these operations is fixed by the state-sequencing design of the TAP controller." (verified — Bennetts).
- **D flip-flop pair + muxes (the BC_1 boundary-scan cell)** — "Figure 13 shows a basic universal boundary-scan cell, known as a BC_1. The cell has four modes of operation: normal, update, capture, and serial shift. The memory elements are two D-type flip-flops with front-end and back-end multiplexing of data." (verified — Bennetts). The two flops are the Capture Scan cell and the Update Hold cell, each with a mux in front of it. "During normal mode, Data_In is passed straight through to Data_Out." (verified — Bennetts). "During capture mode, the Data_In signal is routed to the input Capture Scan cell and the value is captured by the next ClockDR. ClockDR is a derivative of TCK." (verified — Bennetts). "During shift mode, the Scan_Out of one Capture Scan cell is passed to the Scan_In of the next Capture Scan cell via a hard-wired path." (verified — Bennetts). "During update mode, the content of the Update Hold cell is passed through to Data_Out." (verified — Bennetts). The Mode signal picks test mode versus normal mode at the output mux. The standard mandates the function, not this circuit: "The IEEE 1149.1 Standard does not mandate the design of the circuit, only its functional specification." (verified — Bennetts) — so the two-flop-plus-muxes form is the standard's example realization, and a device may implement the same four modes differently. The cell's transistor count, mux implementation and drive strength are per-device and not published. For a bidirectional pin, three cells are conceptually needed (input, output, and IO-status control), "In practice, the two IO scan cells are usually combined into a single multifunction cell called a BC_7." (verified — Bennetts).
- **Shift register (the bypass register)** — "It is a 1-bit register, selected by the Bypass instruction and provides a basic serial-shift function." (verified — Bennetts). "There is no parallel output (which means that the Update_DR control has no effect on the register), but there is a defined effect with the Capture_DR control — the register captures a hard-wired value of logic 0." (verified — Bennetts). One bit, one flop, no update stage: a bypassed chip passes the whole board chain in a single TCK, which is the point — BYPASS shortens the chain to the devices actually under test. In Test-Logic-Reset the bypass register is the default selected register when no identification register is present.
- **Shift register (the identification register)** — "The optional Identification register (Figure 36) is a 32-bit register with capture and shift modes of operation." (verified — Bennetts). "Idcode is the instruction to select the Identification register between TDI and TDO, preparatory to loading the internally-held 32-bit identification code and reading it out through TDO. The 32 bits are used to identify the manufacturer of the device, its part number and its version number." (verified — Bennetts). The 32-bit word is laid out as version (4 bits), part number (16 bits), manufacturer identity (11 bits), and a least-significant bit that is always 1: "As specified by the IEEE Std 1149.1, this bit is always 1" (verified — AMD, Versal ACAP TRM, IDCODE Register). The register has no parallel output — it is capture-and-shift only — and IDCODE is the power-up instruction when the register is present, else BYPASS. USERCODE selects the same 32-bit register with an alternative identity word.
- **Mux / demux (the TDO output mux)** — The Select output of the TAP controller "is distributed to the output multiplexer" (verified — Bennetts, Fig. 33): the mux steers the serial output of whichever register the instruction decoder selected — boundary-scan register, bypass register, identification register, or the instruction register itself during Shift-IR — onto the single TDO pin. The mux is one bit wide (TDO is a serial pin); its select encoding is the decoded instruction, and its circuit form is not published.
- **Tri-state driver (the TDO output enable)** — The Enable output of the TAP controller "is distributed to the output driver amplifier" (verified — Bennetts, Fig. 33): TDO is driven only while its device is shifting, and tri-stated otherwise so the next device in the chain can drive the shared board net. "TDO ... is valid on the falling edge of TCK when the internal state machine is in the correct state." (verified — Corelis, JTAG Technical Primer) — the falling-edge validity is what lets the tester sample TDO halfway between the rising-edge shifts, and TDI is "sampled at the rising edge of TCK when the internal state machine is in the correct state" (verified — Corelis). The driver form, drive strength and enable timing are per-device and not published.
- **Counter — none in the TAP** — The one place a counter looks necessary is the reset guarantee, and it is not one: "If TMS is held at logic 1, a maximum of five consecutive TCKs is guaranteed to return the TAP controller to the reset state of Test_Logic Reset." (verified — Bennetts). Five is a property of the state graph — no state is more than five TMS=1 edges from Test-Logic-Reset — not a counted sequence, so the TAP contains no counter primitive at all. The standard also mandates a fail-safe that needs no logic: "The 1149.1 Standard mandates that an open circuit TDI, TMS or TRST* input must go to logic 1." (verified — Bennetts) — an open TMS pulls the TAP to Test-Logic-Reset within five clocks, and an open TDI loads the safe BYPASS instruction.
- **Synchronizer — none in the TAP** — The TAP runs entirely on TCK, and the standard keeps that clock apart from the system clock on purpose: the boundary-scan register's capture-and-shift "has tremendous potential for real-time monitoring of the operational status of a system — a sort of electronic camera taking snapshots — and is one reason why TCK is kept separate from any system clocks." (verified — Bennetts). There is no clock-domain crossing inside the TAP to synchronize: the pins are sampled only on ClockDR (a derivative of TCK), and the values driven onto pins are held levels from the update hold cells, not pulses that must cross into the functional clock domain. The functional logic sees the boundary cells as ordinary combinational paths in normal mode, not as a second clock domain.

**Parameter honesty.** The standard publishes the governing numbers — 16 TAP states; instruction register at least 2 bits with the two least-significant captured bits fixed to `01`; bypass register exactly 1 bit capturing a hard-wired 0; identification register 32 bits (version 4, part number 16, manufacturer identity 11, least-significant bit always 1); boundary-scan register length equal to the device's signal-pin count; at most five TCK cycles with TMS high to reach Test-Logic-Reset; TDO valid on the falling edge of TCK, TDI and TMS sampled on the rising edge. It publishes no state-register encoding, no instruction-register length beyond the 2-bit minimum, no boundary-cell transistor implementation, no TDO driver form, no per-device register length, and no counter, synchronizer, comparator, credit counter, adder tree, multiplier array, SRAM bank or register file anywhere in the TAP — and this decomposition invents none of them.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — The TAP controller is a 16-state finite-state machine (a Moore machine); a state transition occurs on the positive edge of TCK and the controller output values change on the negative edge of TCK; it initializes in the Test-Logic-Reset state. Source: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002), Figs. 33–34.
- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — TAP control outputs are ClockDR, ShiftDR, UpdateDR, ClockIR, ShiftIR, UpdateIR, Reset, Select and Enable; Reset goes to the instruction register and the target data register, Select to the output multiplexer, Enable to the output driver amplifier. Source: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002), Fig. 33.
- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — Synchronous reset: holding TMS at logic 1 for a maximum of five consecutive TCKs is guaranteed to return the TAP controller to Test-Logic-Reset. Source: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002).
- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — The instruction register has a shift scan section that can be connected between TDI and TDO and a hold section that holds the current instruction; control signals shift through the shift section or pass its contents across to the hold section in a parallel Update operation. Source: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002), Fig. 21.
- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — Capture-IR: the two least-significant bits must capture a `01` pattern; BYPASS is assigned the all-1s code; all unused instruction codes must default to Bypass. Source: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002), Figs. 21–22.
- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — EXTEST's code used to be defined as all-0s; that requirement was relaxed in the 1149.1-2001 version; the four mandatory instructions are EXTEST, BYPASS, SAMPLE and PRELOAD. Source: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002).
- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — The BC_1 boundary-scan cell has four modes (normal, update, capture, serial shift) and its memory elements are two D-type flip-flops with front-end and back-end multiplexing of data; the standard does not mandate the design of the circuit, only its functional specification. Source: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002), Fig. 13.
- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — BC_1 mode behaviour: in normal mode Data_In passes straight through to Data_Out; in capture mode Data_In is routed to the Capture Scan cell and captured by the next ClockDR (a derivative of TCK); in shift mode Scan_Out passes to the next cell's Scan_In; in update mode the Update Hold cell's content passes to Data_Out. Source: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002), Fig. 13.
- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — The bypass register is a 1-bit register selected by the BYPASS instruction providing a basic serial-shift function; it has no parallel output and captures a hard-wired value of logic 0. Source: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002), Fig. 35.
- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — The identification register is a 32-bit register with capture and shift modes of operation, selected by the IDCODE (and USERCODE) instructions; its 32 bits identify the manufacturer, part number and version number. Source: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002), Fig. 36.
- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — IDCODE field layout: version 4 bits (31:28), part number 16 bits (27:12), manufacturer identity 11 bits (11:1), least-significant bit always 1. Source: AMD, Versal ACAP TRM, IDCODE Register.
- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — TDO is valid on the falling edge of TCK; TDI is sampled at the rising edge of TCK; TAP state transitions are determined by the state of TMS on the rising edge of TCK. Source: Corelis, JTAG Technical Primer.
- [verified] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — Only one data register can be connected between TDI and TDO at any time, selected by the decoded parallel outputs of the instruction register; a selected register always offers parallel Capture followed by serial Shift followed by parallel Update, in an order fixed by the TAP controller's state sequencing. Source: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002).
- [unverifiable] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — Primitive-level parameters not published: TAP state-register encoding and flop count beyond the 16-state arithmetic, instruction-register length beyond the 2-bit minimum, instruction-decoder circuit form, boundary-scan register length as a constant (it is the per-device pin count), BC_1 transistor implementation, TDO mux and driver form, and the absence of counter, synchronizer, comparator, credit-counter, adder-tree, multiplier-array, SRAM-bank and register-file primitives in the standard TAP. Sources: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002); Corelis, JTAG Technical Primer.

### NVIDIA Ada Lovelace AD102

#### Down to the primitives: The Ada SM and Shader Execution Reordering — a reorder stage in the ray-tracing pipeline

The Ada SM and its SER reorder stage decompose into thirteen primitives: the register file that holds every warp's operands; the muxes that steer operands to the 32 lanes of each partition; the warp-scheduler issue queues and the SER pending-hit queue that hold work waiting to be regrouped; the warp scheduler and dispatch unit that issue one warp instruction per clock per partition, plus the SER reorder controller that decides when a regrouped warp is ready; the comparators that group like-with-like hits and check operand readiness; the fourth-generation Tensor Core's multiplier array and adder tree, with the FP32 datapath's FMA tree beside them; the L0 instruction cache and the 128 KB unified L1/shared store as SRAM banks; the SM crossbar that ties partitions, L1 and the RT Core together; the pipeline registers that latch work between stages; the one-issue-slot-per-clock credit that paces each partition; the warp-reconvergence function inside SER; and the L1 tag compare. The whitepaper publishes the SM geometry generously — the partition layout, the register-file and L1 sizes, the Tensor Core formats and rates, the RT Core engines and their speedups — and stops there: no register-file port count, no SER queue depth or grouping key, no crossbar radix and no Tensor Core or RT Core internal geometry is published, and this section says so at each primitive.

- **Register file (the warp operand store)** — 64 KB per partition (verified — NVIDIA, "NVIDIA Ada GPU Architecture" whitepaper V2.02: "the AD10x SM is divided into four processing blocks (or partitions), with each partition containing a 64 KB register file, an L0 instruction cache, one warp scheduler, one dispatch unit, 16 CUDA Cores that are dedicated for processing FP32 operations (up to 16 FP32 operations per clock), 16 CUDA Cores that can process FP32 or INT32 operations (16 FP32 operations per clock OR 16 INT32 operations per clock), one Ada Fourth-Generation Tensor Core, four Load/Store units, and a Special Function Unit (SFU)"), i.e. 256 KB per SM by arithmetic — and the whitepaper states the SM total directly: "Each SM in AD10x GPUs contain 128 CUDA Cores, one Ada Third-Generation RT Core, four Ada Fourth-Generation Tensor Cores, four Texture Units, a 256 KB Register File, and 128 KB of L1/Shared Memory" (verified — whitepaper). Across the full AD102 die that is 36 MB of register file — "The AD102 GPU contains 18,432 CUDA Cores (70% more CUDA Cores than Ampere), 18 MB of L1 cache, 96 MB of L2 cache (16x more than Ampere), and a large 36 MB register file." (verified — whitepaper, Conclusion) — and the arithmetic checks exactly: 18,432 CUDA cores / 128 per SM = 144 SMs, and 144 x 256 KB = 36,864 KB = 36 MB. The file's banking, read-port count and write-port count are not published.
- **Mux / demux (operand steering and dispatch)** — Each partition's 32 FP32/INT32 lanes take their operands from the register file through muxes, and the dispatch unit steers the one warp instruction issued each clock to its execution units — FP32 lanes, INT32 lanes, Tensor Core, load/store units or SFU. The SFU's transcendental and graphics-interpolation instructions and the four texture units per SM are further consumers of the same select fabric. The mux radix, the operand-collection width and the dispatch steering structure are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (the scheduler issue queues and the SER pending-hit queue)** — One warp scheduler and one dispatch unit per partition (verified — whitepaper, SM partition quote above), so each partition issues at most one warp instruction per clock, and warps wait in the scheduler's queue until selected. SER adds a second queue: pending secondary-hit shading work waits in the reorder stage while it is regrouped — "Shader Execution Reordering adds a new stage in the ray tracing pipeline which reorders and groups the secondary hit shading to have better execution locality" (verified — whitepaper, SER section, Figure 12). The issue-queue depth, the SER queue's depth and its fill/drain policy are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the warp scheduler, the dispatch unit and the SER reorder controller)** — The scheduler and dispatch unit are the SM's issue control: one of each per partition, issuing at most one warp instruction per clock. The SER reorder controller is the control logic of the new pipeline stage: it takes the application's opt-in (verified — whitepaper: "SER is fully controlled by the application through a small API, allowing developers to easily apply reordering where their workload benefits most."), holds the scattered secondary hits, forms regrouped warps and releases them to the schedulers. The controller's state count, its regrouping policy and the API's on-chip signalling are not published.
- **Comparator (the SER grouping key and the operand-readiness check)** — To group like-with-like, the reorder stage must compare a per-hit key — which shader and material each hit needs — and only hits whose keys match can share a regrouped warp. The whitepaper says only that SER "reorders and groups the secondary hit shading to have better execution locality" (verified — whitepaper); the grouping key itself, its width and the comparison circuit are not published. Beside it sits the ordinary readiness check: a warp's instruction issues only when its operands are ready in the register file, and the scoreboard that tracks that readiness is likewise unpublished in form.
- **Multiplier array (the fourth-generation Tensor Core and the RT Core's intersection engines)** — The Tensor Core is the SM's matrix engine: "Ada GPUs include a new Fourth-Generation Tensor Core. The GeForce RTX 4090 offers double the throughput for existing FP16, BF16, TF32, and INT8 formats, and its Fourth-Generation Tensor Core introduces support for a new FP8 tensor format. Compared to FP16, FP8 halves the data storage requirements and doubles throughput." (verified — whitepaper, Conclusion). "Compared to Ampere, Ada delivers more than double the FP16, BF16, TF32, INT8, and INT4 Tensor TFLOPS, and also includes the Hopper FP8 Transformer Engine, delivering over 1.3 PetaFLOPS of tensor processing in the RTX 4090." (verified — whitepaper, Ada Fourth-Generation Tensor Core section). The multiplier array's geometry — its dimensions, partial-product structure and FP8 encoding — is not published. The RT Core's Triangle Intersection Engine is the second multiplier consumer in the block: ray-triangle intersection is multiply-heavy arithmetic, and the whitepaper publishes the engine's name and its speedup — "The Third-Generation RT Core in the Ada architecture provides double the throughput for ray-triangle intersection testing over Ampere (and 4x faster than the first-generation RT Core used in Turing GPUs)." (verified — whitepaper) — but no multiplier geometry inside either the Box Intersection Engine or the Triangle Intersection Engine.
- **Adder tree (Tensor Core accumulation and the FP32 FMA datapath)** — The Tensor Core's products are accumulated into the result matrix, and the SM's ordinary datapath is a fused multiply-add tree: 32 FP32 lanes per partition x 4 partitions = 128 FP32 operations per clock per SM (verified — whitepaper, SM partition quote above; arithmetic). The adder-tree depth, the carry structure and whether Tensor Core accumulation is a tree or a serial chain are not published. The Opacity Micromap Engine and the Displaced Micro-Mesh Engine are further fixed-function consumers in the RT Core — "An Opacity Micromap Engine speeds up ray tracing of alpha-tested geometry by a factor of 2x" and the Displaced Micro-Mesh Engine "reduces BVH build time by a factor of 10x, while reducing BVH storage requirements by a factor of 20x" (verified — whitepaper) — but their internal arithmetic is not published.
- **SRAM bank (the L0 instruction cache and the unified L1/shared store)** — Each partition holds an L0 instruction cache (verified — whitepaper, SM partition quote above); its size is not published. The 128 KB unified L1 per SM is published twice: "The Ada SM contains 128 KB of Level 1 cache. This cache features a unified architecture that can be configured to function as an L1 data cache or shared memory depending on the workload." (verified — whitepaper, Memory Subsystem section), and the die total — "the full AD102 GPU contains 18432 KB of L1 cache (compared to 10752 KB in GA102)" (verified — whitepaper) — checks exactly against the arithmetic: 144 SMs x 128 KB = 18,432 KB = 18 MB, matching the Conclusion's "18 MB of L1 cache". Beyond the SM, the L2 is "98304 KB of L2 cache, an improvement of 16x over the 6144 KB that shipped in GA102" (verified — whitepaper), i.e. 96 MB. The L0 size, the L1 bank count, line size and associativity, and the L2 bank organisation are not published.
- **Crossbar (the SM's internal interconnect)** — The path from each partition to the unified L1/shared store, the dispatch path from each partition's scheduler to its execution units, and the SM-to-RT-Core interface — the RT Core's Box and Triangle Intersection Engines exist precisely so traversal work is offloaded from the SM: "By providing dedicated resources for these highly important ray tracing functions, work is offloaded from the SM, freeing it up to perform other pixel, vertex, and compute shading tasks." (verified — whitepaper, RT Core section). The crossbar's radix, port counts and arbitration policy are not published.
- **Pipeline register (the SM stage latches and the SER stage registers)** — Work is latched between fetch, decode, issue and execute inside each partition, and the SER stage holds its regrouped warps in registers before releasing them to the schedulers. The stage count, the latch widths and the SER stage's own pipeline depth are not published.
- **Credit counter (the one-issue-slot-per-clock throttle)** — Each partition's dispatch unit grants at most one warp instruction per clock (verified — whitepaper: one warp scheduler and one dispatch unit per processing block), so a partition's Tensor Core, FP32 lanes and load/store units share a single issue credit per clock, and a partition busy with FP32/INT32 work issues no Tensor Core work that cycle. Anything beyond the one-per-clock grant — credit widths, issue priority between the Tensor Core and scalar work — is not published.
- **Synchronizer (SER warp reconvergence)** — SER's regrouping is a synchronising operation: threads that scattered across different shaders and materials must be gathered back into same-shader warps before they can execute at width, and the reorder stage is where that gathering happens. NVIDIA calls the payoff historic — "Shader Execution Reordering is as big of an innovation for GPUs as out-of-order execution was for CPUs back in the 1990s, offering 2-3x speedups for some RT workloads." (verified — whitepaper, Conclusion) — but the reconvergence mechanism, its latency and the regrouped warp's formation rule are not published.
- **CAM / TCAM (the L1 tag compare)** — The 128 KB unified L1 is a cache, so every access compares its address against the tag array in parallel before the data is returned; the tag compare is the CAM-shaped primitive at the heart of the store. The L1's associativity, tag-array size and replacement policy are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** The whitepaper publishes the SM geometry in full: four partitions per SM; per partition a 64 KB register file, an L0 instruction cache, one warp scheduler, one dispatch unit, 16 FP32-only and 16 FP32/INT32 CUDA cores, one fourth-generation Tensor Core, four load/store units and one SFU; 128 FP32 operations per clock per SM; 256 KB register file and 128 KB unified L1/shared memory per SM; 18,432 CUDA cores, 18,432 KB of L1, 98,304 KB of L2 and a 36 MB register file across the full AD102 die; 76.3 billion transistors; four Tensor Cores and four texture units per SM; 512 fourth-generation Tensor Cores in the RTX 4090 with 660.6 FP8 TFLOPS dense / 1,321.2 with sparsity; fourth-generation Tensor Core formats FP16, BF16, TF32, INT8, INT4 and the new FP8, at over 1.3 PFLOPS in the RTX 4090; third-generation RT Core with 2x ray-triangle intersection throughput over Ampere (4x over Turing), a 2x-faster Opacity Micromap Engine and a Displaced Micro-Mesh Engine at 10x faster BVH build in 20x less BVH space; SER as an application-controlled new pipeline stage reordering secondary hit shading, up to 2x on divergent RT shaders and up to 44% in Cyberpunk 2077 RT Overdrive. It publishes no register-file port counts or banking, no L0 size, no L1 bank count, line size or associativity, no SM crossbar radix, no SER queue depth, grouping key or reconvergence mechanism, no Tensor Core or RT Core internal geometry, and no issue-priority policy — and this decomposition invents none of them.

#### Down to the primitives: The Optical Flow Accelerator — a fixed-function engine feeding DLSS 3 frame generation

NVIDIA publishes no internal organisation for the OFA — no sub-block breakdown, flow-grid resolution or internal buffering appears in the architecture whitepaper — so this block cannot be decomposed from published Ada facts. What follows names the eight primitives an optical-flow engine of this contract requires, in their standard generic forms: frames in, a dense flow field out, at 300 TOPS. Every primitive below is labelled generic — the inventory itself is not an Ada fact, only the contract is. The published contract: "Starting with the Ampere GPU architecture, NVIDIA's GPUs have had support for a standalone optical flow engine (OFA) that uses state of the art algorithms to ensure high quality results. Ada's OFA unit delivers 300 TeraOPS (TOPS) of optical flow work (over 2x faster than the Ampere generation OFA) and provides critical information to the DLSS 3 network." (verified — whitepaper, DLSS 3 and Optical Flow Acceleration section). Its consumer is the DLSS 3 frame-generation network on the fourth-generation Tensor Cores: "The Ada OFA unit and new motion vector analysis algorithms are fundamental components that enable accurate and performant frame generation capability within the new DLSS 3 technology framework." (verified — whitepaper).

- **SRAM bank (the frame buffers) — generic form** — The engine must hold two consecutive frames while it compares them: the current frame and the previous frame, pixel for pixel. In the standard optical-flow-engine form these are SRAM banks sized by the frame resolution; the OFA's buffer sizes, resolution and banking are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (pixel streaming in, flow field out) — generic form** — Frames stream into the engine and the dense flow field streams out to the DLSS 3 network — one flow vector per pixel, direction and magnitude. In the standard form these are streaming FIFOs decoupling the engine from the frame source and the Tensor Core consumer; their depths and widths are not published.
- **Multiplier array + adder tree (block matching / correlation) — generic form** — Optical-flow estimation compares blocks of pixels between the two frames, scoring each candidate displacement by a sum of differences — the correlation arithmetic at the heart of the engine. The whitepaper says only that the OFA "uses state of the art algorithms"; the algorithm, the block size, the search range and the array geometry are not published, so no multiplier or adder-tree shape is claimed for Ada.
- **Comparator (best-match selection) — generic form** — For each block the engine keeps the candidate displacement with the lowest match cost, comparing costs as they stream out of the correlation array. The candidate set, the cost width and the comparison circuit are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the frame-grid sequencer) — generic form** — The engine steps across the frame's blocks in order, issuing match work and collecting results; in the standard form this is a small sequencer walking X/Y coordinates. Its state count and stepping order are not published.
- **Mux / demux (candidate-vector steering) — generic form** — Candidate displacements are steered into the match units and the winning vector is steered out to the flow-field FIFO. The mux radix and select encoding are not published.
- **Counter (pixel / block coordinates) — generic form** — The sequencer's X and Y position counters, whose widths are log2 of the flow-grid resolution — a resolution NVIDIA does not publish, so no counter width is claimed.
- **Pipeline register (stage latches) — generic form** — Work is latched between the match, select and output stages so the engine sustains its 300 TOPS rate. The stage count and latch widths are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** For the OFA, the whitepaper publishes exactly one number and one contract: 300 TOPS, over 2x the Ampere-generation OFA, frames in and a dense flow field out, fused with the game engine's motion vectors by DLSS 3. It publishes no sub-block breakdown, no flow-grid resolution, no internal buffering, no algorithm, no block size, no search range, no buffer sizes and no stage count — and this decomposition invents none of them. The eight primitives above are the standard construction of an optical-flow engine, labelled generic, not facts about the Ada OFA.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

Source: NVIDIA, Ada GPU Architecture whitepaper V2.02, SM section, Memory Subsystem section and Conclusion.
- [verified] **NVIDIA Ada Lovelace AD102** — L2 cache: 98,304 KB, 16x the 6,144 KB in GA102. Source: NVIDIA, Ada GPU Architecture whitepaper V2.02, Memory Subsystem section.
- [verified] **NVIDIA Ada Lovelace AD102** — Fourth-generation Tensor Core formats: double the throughput for FP16, BF16, TF32 and INT8 versus Ampere, plus the new FP8 format (halves storage requirements and doubles throughput versus FP16); over 1.3 PFLOPS of tensor processing in the RTX 4090. Source: NVIDIA, Ada GPU Architecture whitepaper V2.02, Ada Fourth-Generation Tensor Core section and Conclusion.
- [verified] **NVIDIA Ada Lovelace AD102** — Third-generation RT Core: 2x ray-triangle intersection throughput over Ampere (4x over Turing); Box Intersection Engine and Triangle Intersection Engine; Opacity Micromap Engine at 2x faster alpha traversal; Displaced Micro-Mesh Engine at 10x faster BVH build in 20x less BVH space. Source: NVIDIA, Ada GPU Architecture whitepaper V2.02, Ray Tracing and RT Core sections.
- [verified] **NVIDIA Ada Lovelace AD102** — SER compared to out-of-order execution: as big an innovation for GPUs as out-of-order execution was for CPUs in the 1990s, offering 2–3x speedups for some RT workloads. Source: NVIDIA, Ada GPU Architecture whitepaper V2.02, Conclusion.
- [verified] **NVIDIA Ada Lovelace AD102** — OFA uses "state of the art algorithms"; the Ada OFA unit plus new motion-vector analysis algorithms enable DLSS 3 frame generation. Source: NVIDIA, Ada GPU Architecture whitepaper V2.02, DLSS 3 and Optical Flow Acceleration section.
- [unverifiable] **NVIDIA Ada Lovelace AD102** — Primitive-level parameters not published: SER queue depth and grouping key, register-file port counts and banking, L0 instruction-cache size, L1 bank count / line size / associativity, SM crossbar radix, Tensor Core and RT Core internal geometry, issue-priority policy — and no OFA internals at all (the eight OFA primitives in the section are generic optical-flow-engine forms, not Ada facts). Sources: NVIDIA, Ada GPU Architecture whitepaper V2.02 (all sections above).

### AMD RDNA 3 — Navi 31

#### Down to the primitives: The dual-issue Work Group Processor (WGP) — the banked VGPR file, the banked LDS and the VOPD pairing rule

The WGP decomposes into sixteen primitives: the banked vector register file (and the scalar register file beside it) that holds every wave's operands; the muxes that steer operands to the SIMD32 lanes and swizzle them across lanes under DPP; the wave-scheduler issue queues that hold waves waiting for an issue slot; the wave scheduler and work-group dispatch controller; the comparators that enforce the VOPD bank rules, test the EXEC mask and serialize LDS bank conflicts; the multiplier array and adder tree of the SIMD32 FP32 datapath and the WMMA matrix engine; the LDS and the L0/L1 caches as SRAM banks; the tag compare behind every cache access; the crossbar that ties the four SIMD32s to the LDS banks; the pipeline registers that latch work across the 5-cycle FP32 latency; the counters that track LDS allocation and resident waves; the credit counters that track outstanding memory instructions; the barrier synchronizer that gathers a work-group's waves; the switch arbiter that serializes same-bank LDS accesses; and the barrel shifter in the scalar ALU. The ISA guide publishes the WGP's geometry generously — the bank counts, the cache read ports, the LDS bank RAMs, the work-group limits — and stops there: no scheduler queue depths, no LDS crossbar radix, no SIMD32 pipeline stage count and no ray-accelerator or AI-accelerator internal geometry is published, and this section says so at each primitive.

- **Register file (the banked VGPR file and the SGPR file)** — 384 KiB per CU (verified — AMD ROCm GPU hardware specifications, RX 7900 XTX row, as cited at Level-2). The file is four banks: "There are 4 VGPR banks (indexed by SRC[1:0]), and each bank has a cache" (verified — AMD, "RDNA3" Instruction Set Architecture Reference Guide, 15-Aug-2023, §7.6 Dual Issue VALU) and "Each cache has 3 read ports: one dedicated to SRC0, one dedicated to SRC1 and one for SRC2" (verified — ISA Guide §7.6). The bank cache is what makes dual issue possible: "A cache can read all 3 of them at once, but it can't read two SRC0's at once (or SRC1/2)." (verified — ISA Guide §7.6). The register file's own write-port count, the SGPR file's banking, and how the four SIMD32s share the file are not published.
- **Mux / demux (operand steering, DPP cross-lane select, VOPD destination steering)** — Each SIMD32's lanes take operands from the VGPR banks through muxes; DPP adds a cross-lane mux: "Data Parallel Processing (DPP) operations allow VALU instruction to select operands from different lanes (threads) rather than just using a thread's own data." (verified — ISA Guide §7.7). DPP16: "DPP16 allows selection of data within groups of 16 lanes with a fixed set of predefined swizzles." (verified — ISA Guide §7.7.1). The VOPD destination rule is a steering constraint: "Dest VGPRs: one must be even and the other odd" (verified — ISA Guide §7.6), and the encoding itself enforces it — vdstY's least significant bit is the complement of vdstX[0]. The mux radix, the DPP select width and the operand-collection structure are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (the wave-scheduler issue queues)** — Waves resident on a SIMD32 wait in the scheduler's queue until the issue slot is theirs: "Wave32 waves issue each instruction at most once." (verified — ISA Guide §2.1), so one wave32 instruction occupies one issue slot per cycle per SIMD32. The WGP holds "up to 32 work-groups with a maximum of 1024 work-items per work-group" (verified — ISA Guide §2.3), so the queues hold many waves' worth of state. The issue-queue depth, the per-SIMD32 wave count and the scheduler's selection policy are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the wave scheduler and work-group dispatch)** — The scheduler issues one wave32 instruction per SIMD32 per cycle and the dispatch logic places each work-group's waves: "Waves in a work-group are all issued to the same WGP but can run on any of the 4 SIMD32's and can share data through LDS." (verified — ISA Guide §2.3). Dual issue is not hardware-checked: "This instruction has certain restrictions that must be met - hardware does not function correctly if they are not." (verified — ISA Guide §7.6) — the compiler, not a hardware controller, guarantees legality. The scheduler's state count, its wave-selection policy and the dispatch hardware are not published.
- **Comparator (the VOPD bank-legality check, the EXEC mask, and LDS conflict detection)** — The pairing rules are comparisons on register addresses: "SRCX0 and SRCY0 must use different VGPR banks" and "VSRCX1 and VSRCY1 must use different banks." (verified — ISA Guide §7.6). Every wave carries an EXEC mask: "every wave has an EXECute mask that determines which work-items are active at that moment, and which are dormant." (verified — ISA Guide Ch. 2). In the LDS, same-bank access is detected and serialized: "if, however, more than one access attempt is made to the same bank at the same time, a bank conflict occurs." (verified — ISA Guide §12.1). The comparator widths, the conflict-detection circuit and the EXEC-mask storage are not published.
- **Multiplier array (the SIMD32 FP32 datapath and the WMMA matrix engine)** — Each SIMD32 is a 32-lane multiply-capable datapath; dual issue doubles it to 64 FP32 results per SIMD32 per cycle (256 per CU, 24,576 across the GCD, 61.4 TFLOPS at 2.5 GHz, as published at Level-2). The AI accelerators run WMMA: "Wave Matrix Multiply-Accumulate (WMMA) instructions provide acceleration for common matrix arithmetic operations." (verified — ISA Guide §7.9) and "These perform: A * B + C ⇒ D, where A, B, C and D are matrices." (verified — ISA Guide §7.9). Two AI accelerators per CU. The multiplier array's geometry — its dimensions, partial-product structure and the WMMA tile sizes — is not published.
- **Adder tree (FMA accumulation and WMMA accumulation)** — The SIMD32 datapath is a fused multiply-add tree: each lane's product is added into the accumulator, and the WMMA engine accumulates its matrix products into D. The FP32 latency is 5 cycles (measured — Chips and Cheese, "Microbenchmarking AMD's RDNA 3 Graphics Architecture", Jan 2023, as published at Level-2). The adder-tree depth, the carry structure and whether WMMA accumulation is a tree or a serial chain are not published.
- **SRAM bank (the LDS banks and the L0/L1 caches)** — The LDS is the best-documented SRAM in the block: "There are 128kB of memory per work-group processor split up into 64 banks of DWORD-wide RAMs." (verified — ISA Guide §12.1) and "Each bank is a 512x32 two-port RAM (1R/1W per clock cycle)." (verified — ISA Guide §12.1). The caches are SRAM banks too: 32 KB L0 vector, 16 KB L0 scalar and 32 KB L0 instruction per CU, and a 256 KB L1 per shader array (verified — AMD ROCm GPU hardware specifications, RX 7900 XTX row, as cited at Level-2). The LDS bank count per set is published: "These 64 banks are further sub-divided into two sets of 32-banks each where 32 of the banks are affiliated with a pair of SIMD32's, and the other 32 banks are affiliated with the other pair of SIMD32's within the WGP." (verified — ISA Guide §12.1). The L0/L1 bank counts, line sizes and the LDS sense-amplifier structure are not published.
- **CAM / TCAM (the cache tag compare)** — Every L0 and L1 access compares its address against the tag array in parallel before data is returned; the tag compare is the CAM-shaped primitive at the heart of each cache. The published associativities — L0 vector 32-way, L0 scalar 4-way, L1 16-way, L2 16-way (as published at Level-2) — set the width of the parallel compare. The tag-array size, the replacement policy and the compare circuit are not published.
- **Crossbar (the LDS bank interconnect and the WGP-to-L1 path)** — All 64 LDS banks can be accessed at once: "DWORDs are placed in the banks serially, but all banks can execute a store or load simultaneously." (verified — ISA Guide §12.1), and "it is possible to concurrently execute 32 store or load instructions, each nominally 32-bits" (verified — ISA Guide §12.1) — 32 per 32-bank set. That fan-out from four SIMD32s to 64 banks is a crossbar-shaped fabric, and the read path out of the WGP runs through the shader array's L1: "On the primary read path, the device consists of multiple channels of L2 cache that provides data to read-only L1 caches, and finally to L0 caches per WGP." (verified — ISA Guide §1.2.3). The crossbar's radix, port counts and arbitration policy are not published.
- **Pipeline register (the issue-to-writeback stage latches)** — Work is latched between fetch, issue, operand read, execute and writeback inside each SIMD32, and the FP32 latency is 5 cycles (measured — Chips and Cheese, as published at Level-2), so at least five stages of latching separate issue from writeback. The stage count, the latch widths and the bypass/forwarding network are not published.
- **Counter (LDS allocation registers and resident-wave counts)** — LDS space is tracked per work-group in allocation registers: "LDS space is allocated per work-group or wave (when work-groups not used) and recorded in dedicated LDSbase/size (allocation) registers that are not writable by the shader." (verified — ISA Guide §12.1). A work-group may allocate "up to 64kB of LDS space" (verified — ISA Guide §1.2.2.1). The counter widths, the wave-slot accounting and the barrier resource count are not published.
- **Credit counter (the outstanding-memory-instruction counters)** — Waves stall on counts, not on data: the hardware tracks outstanding VMEM instructions per wave — "but does not skip both halves for VMEM instructions as that would confuse the outstanding-memory-instruction counters" (verified — ISA Guide §2.1) — and LDS loads use their own counter: "LDS_DIRECT_LOAD and LDS_PARAM_LOAD read data from LDS and write it into VGPRs, and they use EXPcnt to track when the instruction has completed and written the VGPRs." (verified — ISA Guide §12.2.1.2). The s_waitcnt instruction waits on these counters. The counter widths and the number of counters per wave are not published.
- **Synchronizer (the work-group barrier)** — The barrier gathers a work-group's waves before any proceeds: "A barrier is a synchronization primitive which makes each wave reach a given point in the shader before any wave proceeds." (verified — ISA Guide §2.3). Single-wave work-groups skip it: they "do not allocate a barrier resource, and barrier ops are treated as S_NOP" (verified — ISA Guide §2.3). The barrier's counter width, its arrival-tracking circuit and the cross-SIMD32 signalling are not published.
- **Switch arbiter (LDS bank arbitration)** — When two accesses collide on one bank, the arbiter serializes them: "for indexed and atomic operations, the hardware is designed to prevent the attempted concurrent accesses to the same bank by turning them into serial accesses." (verified — ISA Guide §12.1). The LDS also carries "64 integer atomic units to enable fast, unordered atomic operations" (verified — ISA Guide §1.2.2.1) — one per bank. The arbiter's policy (round-robin, fixed priority), its grant latency and the atomic-unit arbitration are not published.
- **Barrel shifter (the scalar ALU's shift path)** — The scalar ALU works on one value per wave: "A scalar ALU, which operates on one value per wave (common to all work-items)" (verified — ISA Guide Ch. 2). Shifts, rotates and bit-field operations in that ALU are barrel-shifter work — one shifter that moves a word by any amount in a single pass. The shifter's width, its stage count and whether it is a mux-tree or a logarithmic shifter are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** The ISA guide publishes the WGP geometry in full: 48 WGPs / 96 CUs; 4 SIMD32 per CU; 384 KiB VGPR file per CU (ROCm, as cited at Level-2 — but see the dispute below); 4 VGPR banks indexed by SRC[1:0], each bank cache with 3 read ports (SRC0/SRC1/SRC2); the VOPD rules (wave32-only, no DPP, different banks for the SRC0 pair and the SRC1 pair, even/odd destinations, same-cycle execution, read-gets-old-value); LDS 128 kB per WGP, 64 banks of 512x32 two-port RAM (1R/1W per clock), two 32-bank sets each affiliated with a SIMD32 pair, 64 integer atomic units, 64 kB maximum per work-group; L0 32/16/32 KiB per CU, L1 256 KiB per shader array, L2 6 MiB; up to 32 work-groups and 1,024 work-items per work-group per WGP; FP32 latency 5 cycles (measured); WMMA A\*B+C⇒D; the barrier definition and the single-wave exemption; the outstanding-instruction counters and EXPcnt. It publishes no VGPR write-port count or SGPR banking, no scheduler queue depths or wave-selection policy, no SIMD32 pipeline stage count or bypass network, no LDS crossbar radix or arbitration policy, no L0/L1 bank counts, line sizes or replacement policies, no tag-array geometry, no WMMA tile sizes or multiplier geometry, no ray-accelerator internals, no AI-accelerator internal geometry beyond the WMMA contract, and no barrel-shifter construction — and this decomposition invents none of them. Disputed: AMD's ROCm hardware-specifications table lists VGPR File 768 KiB and SGPR File 16 KiB for the RX 7900 XTX in its 6.3.2 (Dec 2024) edition, against 384 KiB and 20 KiB in the 6.2.2 (Sept 2024) edition the Level-2 values were taken from — the same card, two different AMD tables. This section keeps the Level-2 values and records the dispute; no wiki value was changed.

#### Down to the primitives: The Memory Cache Die and Infinity Cache — the last-level cache moved off the die

AMD publishes no internal organisation for the MCD — no cache-controller, tag-array or link-arbiter internals — so this block cannot be decomposed from published RDNA 3 facts. What follows names the nine primitives an MCD of this contract requires, in their standard generic forms: a 16 MB Infinity Cache slice plus two 32-bit GDDR6 PHYs per MCD, joined to the GCD by four 64-byte Infinity Link channels per direction at 9.2 Gbps. Every primitive below is labelled generic — the inventory itself is not an RDNA 3 fact, only the contract is. The published contract: "You heard the massive numbers tossed out this morning, 5.3 terabytes per second, which means we have on each one of these interfaces [MCDs] four, 64-byte channels going in both directions." (verified — Sam Naffziger, AMD Fellow, quoted in PC Gamer, "AMD's Infinity Links is the unsung hero of RDNA 3", Nov 2022); "The bandwidth density that we achieve is almost 10x" at "9.2 gigabits per second signalling across these interfaces" (verified — PC Gamer, Nov 2022); "up to 80% more efficient than organic package links" (verified — PC Gamer, Nov 2022); and "The end result: 3.5TB/s for less than 5% GPU power consumption." (verified — PC Gamer, Nov 2022).

- **SRAM bank (the 16 MB Infinity Cache slice) — generic form** — The slice is the MCD's bulk store: 16 MB of second-generation Infinity Cache per MCD, 96 MB across six. In the standard form this is a set of SRAM banks interleaved so parallel requests land in different banks; the bank count, line size, associativity and port style are not published.
- **CAM / TCAM (the tag array) — generic form** — Every Infinity Cache access must compare its address against the tags of its set in parallel before the line is returned. In the standard form this is a CAM-shaped tag compare per bank; the associativity, tag width and replacement policy are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (link ingress/egress and GDDR6 request queues) — generic form** — Requests arrive from the GCD over the Infinity Links in bursts and leave for GDDR6 in bursts; the queues decouple the link rate from the cache and DRAM rates. In the standard form these are ingress/egress FIFOs per channel plus a GDDR6 request queue; their depths and widths are not published.
- **Crossbar (the MCD internal switch) — generic form** — The four 64-byte link channels, the cache banks and the two 32-bit PHYs must all reach each other: link traffic to banks, bank misses to PHYs, PHY returns to banks and back to the link. In the standard form this is a small crossbar; its radix and port counts are not published.
- **Switch arbiter (channel and bank arbitration) — generic form** — When two link channels want the same cache bank, or two banks miss to the same PHY, an arbiter grants one per cycle. The policy, requester count and grant latency are not published.
- **Mux / demux (channel select and PHY lane steering) — generic form** — The four 64-byte channels are selected onto the cache banks, and the two 32-bit PHYs steer their lanes onto the GDDR6 bus. The mux radix and select encoding are not published.
- **Credit counter (Infinity Link flow control) — generic form** — The GCD must not overrun the MCD's link queues: in the standard die-to-die form the sender holds a credit count of free receiver slots, spends one per flit and earns credits back as the receiver drains. The credit count, flit width and return latency are not published.
- **Synchronizer (the GCD-to-MCD clock-domain crossing) — generic form** — The GCD and the MCD are different dies on different process nodes (5 nm and 6 nm) with different clocks — the front end runs at up to 2.5 GHz and the shaders at 2.3 GHz, while the MCD's clock is not published — so the link must cross clock domains. In the standard form this is a synchronizer on the link's control and credit signals; its depth and latency are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the cache controller and the GDDR6 controller) — generic form** — One controller owns the Infinity Cache slice (lookup, fill, eviction, writeback) and one owns each GDDR6 PHY (command scheduling, refresh, training). Their state counts, scheduling policies and command queues are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** For the MCD, AMD publishes the contract and nothing inside it: six MCDs on TSMC 6 nm, each 37.52 mm² with 2.05 billion transistors, one 16 MB Infinity Cache slice and two 32-bit GDDR6 PHYs per MCD, 96 MB and a 384-bit bus in total; four 64-byte Infinity Link channels per direction per MCD interface at 9.2 Gbps, 5.3 TB/s cumulative peak, about 10x the bandwidth density of organic links, up to 80% more efficient; 3.5 TB/s effective bandwidth for under 5% of GPU power; the read path L2 to L1 to L0; and unused TSV landing points on each MCD. It publishes no cache-controller, tag-array, link-arbiter, queue-depth, bank-count, associativity, crossbar or clock-domain internals — and this decomposition invents none of them. The nine primitives above are the standard construction of a memory cache die of this contract, labelled generic, not facts about the Navi 31 MCDs.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [verified] **AMD RDNA 3 — Navi 31** — LDS space is allocated per work-group or wave and recorded in dedicated LDSbase/size allocation registers not writable by the shader. Source: AMD, "RDNA3" Instruction Set Architecture Reference Guide, §12.1 Overview.
- [disputed] **AMD RDNA 3 — Navi 31** — VGPR File / SGPR File sizes for RX 7900 XTX: ROCm 6.3.2 (Dec 2024) lists 768 KiB VGPR and 16 KiB SGPR, while ROCm 6.2.2 (Sept 2024) listed 384 KiB VGPR and 20 KiB SGPR for the identical card row. The wiki keeps the Level-2 values (384 KiB / 20 KiB); no wiki value changed. Source: AMD ROCm hardware specifications.
- [unverifiable] **AMD RDNA 3 — Navi 31** — Primitive-level parameters not published: VGPR write-port count and SGPR banking; wave-scheduler queue depths and selection policy; SIMD32 pipeline stage count and bypass network; LDS crossbar radix and arbitration policy; L0/L1 bank counts, line sizes and replacement policies; tag-array geometry; WMMA tile sizes and multiplier geometry; ray-accelerator internals; AI-accelerator internal geometry beyond the WMMA contract; barrel-shifter construction; and no MCD internals at all (the nine MCD primitives in the section are generic memory-cache-die forms, not RDNA 3 facts). Sources: AMD, "RDNA3" Instruction Set Architecture Reference Guide (all sections above); AMD press release 3 Nov 2022; PC Gamer Nov 2022.

Note: nine of the twelve records the builder prepared re-verified facts already recorded at Level-2 with the same quotes and sources (VGPR banks/ports, VOPD rules, LDS geometry, WMMA, Infinity Link contract); those were deduped and not re-appended.

### Intel Ponte Vecchio (Xe-HPC)

#### Down to the primitives: The Xe-core — eight vector engines, eight matrix engines and a 512 KB L1 that doubles as scratchpad

The Xe-core decomposes into sixteen primitives: the register file the deck's diagram draws beside the L1; the 512 KB L1 data cache that doubles as shared local memory and the separate L1 instruction cache; the muxes that steer operands into the sixteen engines; the 8-deep systolic multiplier arrays and the adder trees inside them; the barrel shifter an FP datapath needs for alignment; the tag comparator behind every L1 access; the counters that step the systolic arrays; the dispatch controller Intel never describes; the pipeline registers between engine stages; the crossbar that delivers the load/store unit's 512 bytes per clock; the LSU's request queue and its credit counter to the Memory Fabric; and — stated explicitly, because the block's shape invites the wrong assumption — no synchronizer and no CAM inside the core, the clock-domain crossing living at the tile boundary in the FDI. Intel publishes the core's contract (widths, rates, capacities) and none of its internal geometry, so every primitive below carries its published parameters where they exist and says plainly where they do not.

- **Register file (RF — the operand store beside the L1)** — The deck's Compute Tile diagram labels an "RF" beside the L1 data cache/SLM and the L1 instruction cache ("RF" — verified — Intel, "Ponte Vecchio: A Multi Tile 3D Stacked Processor for Exascale Computing" (Gomes et al., 2022), Compute Tile diagram, slides 8 and 12). The RF is the operand store the sixteen engines read from: each vector engine takes 512-bit operands and each matrix engine 4096-bit operands, so the file must deliver one 512-bit vector operand set or one 4096-bit matrix operand set per engine per clock. Its size, entry count, bank count and port count are not published — the deck draws the label and nothing else.
- **SRAM bank (the 512 KB L1 data cache / shared local memory)** — "L1 Cache 4MB Per Tile" (verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 11), i.e. 512 KB per Xe-core, and "The compute datapath is fed by a wide load/store unit that fetches 512B/clock from a 512KB L1 data cache that is software configurable as a scratchpad memory." (verified — eeNews Europe, "Ponte Vecchio 3D supercomputer processor uses five process nodes", Feb 22, 2022, reporting the ISSCC 2022 paper). The bank is the core's staging store: matrix tiles sit here while the systolic arrays work on them, and the same 512 KB doubles as software-managed scratchpad. Its banking, line size, associativity, port count and tag geometry are not published.
- **SRAM bank (the L1 instruction cache)** — The deck's diagram labels an "L1 Inst cache" ("L1 Inst cache" — verified — Gomes et al., 2022, Multi Tile Architecture diagram, slide 8) beside the data cache, drawn as "I$" in the Compute Tile diagram (slide 12). The instruction cache feeds the core's instruction stream; its size, line size and associativity are not published.
- **Mux / demux (operand select into the engines)** — Each of the eight vector engines takes 512-bit operands and each of the eight matrix engines 4096-bit operands from the RF and L1: "8 Vector Engines 512 bit (XVE) / engine" and "8 Matrix Engines 4096 bit (XMX) / engine" (verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 12). The muxes select which operand set reaches which engine each clock — one 512-bit set per XVE, one 4096-bit set per XMX. Their radix, port count and select encoding are not published.
- **Multiplier array (the XMX 8-deep systolic array)** — "Each core contains 8 vector engines processing 512b floating-point/integer operands and 8 matrix engines with an 8-deep systolic array executing 4096b vector operations/engine/clock." (verified — eeNews Europe, Feb 22, 2022, reporting the ISSCC 2022 paper). The systolic array is the multiplier array: operands step through eight stages, each stage multiplying and accumulating, so one operand fetched is used eight times. By arithmetic from the published rates, the eight XMX engines demand 8 × 4096 bits = 4096 bytes of operands per clock against the load/store unit's 512 bytes per clock — and 4096 / 512 = 8, exactly the systolic depth, so the array's reuse factor is what bridges the feed gap. The array's internal geometry — Booth encoding, compressor-tree structure, partial-product count — is not published.
- **Adder tree (XMX accumulation and the XVE floating-point add)** — The systolic array's accumulation is an adder tree over the stage partials, and the vector engines' 256 FP32 and 256 FP64 operations per clock are add/multiply datapaths: "256 FP32 Ops / Clock", "256 FP64 Ops / Clock", "512 FP16 Ops / Clock" (verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 13). The tree depth, the carry structure and whether the XMX accumulation is a tree or a serial chain are not published.
- **Barrel shifter (FP alignment and normalization in the XVE) — standard form** — A floating-point datapath aligns mantissas before adding and normalizes the result after, and the barrel shifter is the primitive that moves a word by any amount in one pass. Intel publishes no XVE pipeline detail, so this is the standard construction of a floating-point datapath, not a published block of the Xe-core — the section names the primitive and its role only, and claims no shifter width, stage count or placement.
- **Comparator (the L1 tag compare)** — The 512 KB L1 is a cache, so every access compares an address tag before data is returned; the tag compare is the comparator behind each access. The tag width, the associativity, the way count and the replacement policy are not published.
- **Counter (the systolic step counter and the SLM address counters)** — The 8-deep systolic array steps one stage per clock, so a step counter sequences each tile through the array; by arithmetic from the published depth it is 3 bits wide (2³ = 8) — that width is arithmetic, not a published figure. Tile staging in the L1/SLM needs address counters for the same reason. No counter width beyond the 3-bit step arithmetic is published.
- **FSM / controller (the Xe-core dispatch controller)** — Intel publishes no scheduler, issue-width or pipeline-stage detail for the Xe-core (as recorded at Level-2): the controller that dispatches work to eight vector engines, eight matrix engines and one ray-tracing unit must exist, but its form — issue width, scoreboarding, hazard handling, ray-tracing dispatch — is unpublished. The section names the primitive and its role only.
- **Pipeline register (the engine stage registers)** — Work is latched between stages inside the vector and matrix engines, and between the load/store unit and the L1. The stage count, the latch widths beyond the published 512-bit vector and 4096-bit matrix operand widths, and the bypass/forwarding network are not published.
- **Crossbar (the L1-to-engines operand delivery)** — The load/store unit's 512-bytes-per-clock port is the crossbar's published rate: "The compute datapath is fed by a wide load/store unit that fetches 512B/clock from a 512KB L1 data cache that is software configurable as a scratchpad memory." (verified — eeNews Europe, Feb 22, 2022). The crossbar fans that port out to sixteen engines. Its radix, port count and arbitration are not published. (The deck's diagram text reads "512 bit" beside the load/store unit; the wiki keeps 512 B/clock per the eeNews/ISSCC account — already recorded as disputed at Level-2, no new record here.)
- **FIFO / queue (the LSU request queue)** — The load/store unit must queue requests that miss the L1 while the engines keep working on staged tiles, and queue the replies returning from the Memory Fabric. The queue depth and entry width are not published.
- **Credit counter (LSU to Memory Fabric flow control) — standard form** — Requests crossing the Foveros link to the Memory Fabric need credit-based flow control so the LSU cannot overrun the fabric's queues; in the standard form the sender holds a count of free receiver slots, spends one per request and earns credits back as the receiver drains. The credit scheme, the count and the return latency are not published.
- **Synchronizer — none inside the Xe-core** — The core is a single clock domain: its engines, RF, caches and load/store unit all run on the compute tile's clock. The asynchronous crossing lives at the tile boundary in the FDI, where the base tile's level shifters and phase compensation do the work (see the second block). No synchronizer primitive belongs in the core's decomposition.
- **CAM / TCAM — none in the Xe-core** — The only associative lookup in the core is the L1 tag compare, which is a comparator, not a CAM. No content-addressable structure is published for the Xe-core.

#### Down to the primitives: Rambo and the base tile's Memory Fabric — 408 MB of second-level cache and the die-to-die fabric that feeds it

The second level decomposes into twenty primitives: the Rambo SRAM banks with a PLL, clock tap and test block per bank; the base tile's Memory Fabric SRAM banks, each doing one 64-byte operation per clock; the tag comparators behind every bank access; the MDFI crossbar the deck calls the "L3 Switch Fabric" and its arbiter; the FDI's FIFOs, synchronizer and level shifters with their forward and return clocks; the bank-select muxes; the FDI group counters; the HBM and PCIe controllers and the MDFI routing FSM; the address-decode adder tree; the pipeline registers; the credit counters; the die and per-bank PLLs; the Xe Link SerDes and its 8-port switch; the DFT test muxes; and — stated explicitly — no CAM, no multiplier array and no barrel shifter anywhere in the second level. The deck and the ISSCC coverage publish the fabric's geometry generously — the bank sizes, the 4096-bytes-per-cycle fabric rate, the eight FDI groups of 800 lanes — and stop there: no tag geometry, no MDFI radix, no FIFO depths and no controller queue depths are published, and this section says so at each primitive.

- **SRAM bank (Rambo — four 3.75 MB banks per tile)** — "RAMBO Bank Construction" (verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 17): the slide draws each bank with its own PLL, clock tap and test block ("PLL", "CLK", "Tap", "Test" — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 17). Eight Rambo tiles × four banks = 32 banks, 120 MB in all, built for random-access bandwidth: "RAMBO = Random Access Memory, Bandwidth Optimized" (verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 15, as cited at Level-2). Bank arbitration, replacement policy and tag geometry are not published.
- **SRAM bank (the base tile's Memory Fabric — 144 MB per base tile)** — "L2 Cache 144MB" (verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 16), and "the base tile also contains a 144MB L3 cache, called the Memory Fabric (MF), with a complex geometric topology." (verified — eeNews Europe, Feb 22, 2022). "The L3 cache is a large storage that backs up various L1 caches inside the core and is organized as multiple independent banks each of which can perform one 64B read/write operation/clock." (verified — eeNews Europe, Feb 22, 2022). By arithmetic from the two published rates, the fabric's 4096-bytes-per-cycle rate from banks that each do one 64-byte operation per clock implies 64 banks delivering in parallel each cycle (4096 / 64 = 64) — arithmetic, not a published bank count. The bank count, line size, associativity and tag geometry are not published.
- **Comparator (the L3 tag compare)** — Every bank access compares an address tag before the line is returned; the tag compare is the comparator behind each of the 32 Rambo banks and each Memory Fabric bank. The tag width, the associativity, the way count and the replacement policy are not published.
- **Crossbar (the MDFI — the "L3 Switch Fabric")** — The base-tile slide labels the fabric "RAMBO + Cache L3 Switch Fabric" (verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 15), and the base tile carries the "Modular Die Fabric Interface (MDFI)" (verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 16, as cited at Level-2). The crossbar routes between sixteen compute tiles, eight Rambo tiles, two base tiles, the HBM controllers, the PCIe host interface and the Xe Link tiles. Its radix, port count and arbitration are not published.
- **Switch arbiter (MDFI arbitration)** — When several tiles want the same Rambo or Memory Fabric bank in one cycle, the arbiter grants one and queues the rest. The policy — round-robin, fixed priority, age-based — the requester count and the grant latency are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (the FDI transmit and receive FIFOs)** — The FDI slide draws a FIFO on the compute tile and a FIFO on the base tile ("Foveros Die Interconnect: Die 2 Die I/O and Clocking" — verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 26). The FIFOs absorb the rate difference between the two dies and hold requests in flight across the 3D stack. Their depths and widths are not published.
- **Synchronizer (the FDI asynchronous interface — level shifters, phase compensation, forward and return clocks)** — "The transmitter (Tx) and receiver (Rx) circuits of this interface are powered by the compute tile rail and level-shifters on the base tile convert to the supply voltage within the asynchronous interface." (verified — eeNews Europe, Feb 22, 2022). "Each group uses common clocking with phase compensation on the base die to correct for variation between base and compute tiles." (verified — eeNews Europe, Feb 22, 2022) — and the compensation needs two clocks: "This necessitates a base-to-compute tile clock and a return clock going back to the base die to enable clock compensation." (verified — eeNews Europe, Feb 22, 2022). The phase compensation plus the forward and return clocks are the synchronizer's published form.
- **Level shifter (the FDI rail conversion)** — The same eeNews sentence as above: the FDI transmitter and receiver run on the compute tile's rail, and "level-shifters on the base tile convert to the supply voltage within the asynchronous interface" (verified — eeNews Europe, Feb 22, 2022). The level shifter is the primitive that lets two dies on different supply rails talk across the Foveros stack. Its count, width and conversion range are not published.
- **Mux / demux (bank select and SerDes lane steering)** — Address bits select one Rambo or Memory Fabric bank per access, and the SerDes tile steers its lanes onto the 90G links. The mux radix and select encoding are not published.
- **Counter (the FDI group counters and the HBM refresh counters)** — The FDI is "organized as eight groups, with each group consisting of 800 lanes per compute tile" (verified — eeNews Europe, Feb 22, 2022): 8 × 800 = 6,400 data lanes by arithmetic, against the deck's "> 7K FDI Connections" (verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 26, as cited at Level-2) — the larger total including the clock, power and DFT connections the same slide draws. The HBM controllers need refresh counters for their stacks; their widths are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the HBM2e controllers, the MDFI routing FSM, the PCIe Gen5/CXL host interface)** — "The two base die provide a communication network for the stacked tiles and includes SoC infrastructure modules including memory controllers, fully integrated voltage regulators (FIVR), power management and 16 PCIe Gen5/CXL host interface lanes." (verified — eeNews Europe, Feb 22, 2022). The deck's summary adds the I/O totals: "IO 4x16 90G SERDES, 1x16 PCIe Gen5" (verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 33). The controllers' state counts, queue depths, scheduling policies and command queues are not published.
- **Adder tree (the address-to-bank decode)** — Each request's address must be decoded or hashed to pick one of the L3 banks; the decode is an adder/comparator tree over the address bits. The scheme — which bits, what hash, what interleave — is not published; the primitive is named for its role only.
- **Pipeline register (the MDFI stages and the SerDes transmit/receive registers)** — Requests are latched as they cross the fabric, and again as they enter and leave the SerDes; "After traversing the FDI link, signals are decompressed back to full width in the destination Rx domain." (verified — eeNews Europe, Feb 22, 2022) — the decompression is a width change across a register boundary. The stage counts and the register widths beyond the published 64-byte bank operations are not published.
- **Credit counter (FDI, EMIB and HBM flow control) — standard form** — The die-to-die links and the HBM channels need credit-based flow control so a fast sender cannot overrun a slow receiver; in the standard form the sender holds a count of free receiver slots, spends one per flit and earns credits back as the receiver drains. The credit counts, the flit widths and the return latencies are not published.
- **PLL (the die clocks and the per-bank Rambo clocks)** — The FDI slide shows "Compute PLL", "Base PLL", "Link PLL" and "Backup" (verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 26), and each Rambo bank carries its own PLL (slide 17). The PLLs generate the compute, base and link clocks and the per-bank Rambo clocks. Their frequencies and loop parameters are not published.
- **SerDes (the Xe Link tile — up to 90G links and the 8-port embedded switch)** — "Each tile includes an 8-port switch enabling up to 8-way fully connected configuration supporting 90G SerDes links and the SerDes tile supports load/store, bulk data transfers and synchronization semantics that are critical for scaling up HPC and AI applications." (verified — eeNews Europe, Feb 22, 2022). The switch is a crossbar, arbiter and FIFOs in SerDes form, and its three traffic classes — load/store, bulk transfers, synchronization — are the three kinds of work the fabric must carry. The lane count beyond the deck's "4x16 90G SERDES" summary line, the switch radix beyond the 8 ports and the SerDes equalization are not published.
- **DFT / test mux (the FDI test blocks and the Rambo per-bank Test)** — The FDI slide draws "DFT" blocks on both dies (verified — Gomes et al., 2022, slide 26) and each Rambo bank carries a "Test" block (slide 17). The test muxes let the package exercise the die-to-die links and each SRAM bank in isolation — the only way to test 47 tiles after assembly. The test patterns, the scan-chain lengths and the mux forms are not published.
- **CAM / TCAM — none in the second level** — Tag lookup in Rambo and the Memory Fabric is comparator-based; no content-addressable structure is published for either. The L3's "complex geometric topology" (eeNews) is a bank layout, not a CAM.
- **Multiplier array — none in the second level** — This block stores and moves data; it computes nothing. There is no multiply-accumulate anywhere in Rambo, the Memory Fabric, the MDFI or the SerDes tiles.
- **Barrel shifter — none in the second level** — Whole 64-byte lines move through the fabric, and alignment is by address-bit selection at the bank-select muxes, not by a shifter. No barrel shifter is published or implied for the second level.

**Parameter honesty.** Intel publishes the Xe-core's contract and the second level's geometry: the RF and L1 instruction-cache labels in the Compute Tile diagram; 512 KB L1 per core, software-configurable as scratchpad, fed at 512 B/clock (the deck's "512 bit" diagram text against the eeNews/ISSCC 512 B/clock — the dispute recorded at Level-2, wiki keeps 512 B/clock); 8 vector engines at 512 bits and 8 matrix engines at 4096 bits with an 8-deep systolic array; 256 FP32 / 256 FP64 / 512 FP16 vector operations and 2048 TF32 / 4096 FP16 / 4096 BF16 / 8192 INT8 matrix operations per clock per core; Rambo's four 3.75 MB banks per tile with a PLL, clock tap and test block per bank; the base tile's 144 MB Memory Fabric with banks doing one 64-byte read/write per clock and the fabric moving 4096 bytes per cycle; the MDFI and the "L3 Switch Fabric" label; the FDI's eight groups of 800 lanes per compute tile and the deck's "> 7K FDI Connections" total; the FDI's level shifters, phase compensation and forward-plus-return clocks; the deck summary's "4x16 90G SERDES, 1x16 PCIe Gen5"; 16 PCIe Gen5/CXL host lanes; the 24-layer (11-2-11) substrate; and the A0 silicon measurements — over 45 TFLOPS FP32 throughput, over 50 TBps cache bandwidth and over 8 Tbps communication bandwidth. It publishes no RF size, entry count or port count; no L1 banking, line size, associativity or tag geometry; no XMX internal geometry beyond the 8-deep systolic depth; no Xe-core scheduler, issue width or pipeline stages; no LSU queue depth; no MDFI radix, arbitration policy or queue depths; no Rambo or Memory Fabric tag geometry or replacement policy; no HBM controller queue depths or scheduling policy; no FDI FIFO depths or widths; no SerDes lane counts beyond the summary line; and no per-bank clock frequencies — and this decomposition invents none of them. The base-tile area is disputed, not unpublished: the deck says 640 mm² and the ISSCC coverage says 646 mm²; the wiki keeps 640 mm² and records the dispute.
