### Arm Immortalis-G720

#### Down to the primitives: The Deferred Vertex Shading pipeline — Binning phase, Main phase and the tiler that decides between them

Decomposed in trace order — command stream in, tile out. Arm publishes the front end's contract (the two phases, the three queues, the tiler's culling and binning, the per-core thread and rate numbers) but almost none of its circuits: no tiler buffer sizes, no binning-list depths, no queue depths and no culling rates are published for this front end. Where a parameter below comes from Arm's published per-core geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry, not as a published fact; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **FSM / controller (the Command Stream Front-end)** — The CSF is the sequencer at the head of the pipeline: it takes draw calls from the command stream, breaks each job into tasks for the tiler and the shader cores, and issues binning-phase work and main-phase work as independently scheduled jobs — the two-phase structure of DVS exists because this controller keeps the phases separate. Its task-splitting granularity, issue rate and internal state count are not published.

- **FIFO / queue (the Binning phase, Main phase and Compute queues)** — Three hardware queues hold the CSF's jobs: the Binning phase queue feeding position-only vertex work, the Main phase queue feeding per-tile full shading, and the Compute queue carrying compute and advanced-geometry work alongside them. These queues are what let the two phases run independently instead of in lockstep. Arm publishes the queues' existence and roles (Mali G1 Performance Counter Reference Guide, doc 111042); their depths, entry widths and port counts are not published.

- **Switch arbiter / priority encoder (queue selection into the cores)** — Something must choose, each time a shader core frees up, whether the next task comes from the Binning phase queue, the Main phase queue or the Compute queue — an arbitration and priority-select primitive between the three queues and the core array. Its policy (fixed priority, round-robin, or phase-aware), its grant width and its latency are not published.

- **Register file (the shader core's warp thread state)** — Position shading in the Binning phase and full shading in the Main phase both run as warps on the shader cores, and the warp contexts live here. Published per core: up to 2048 threads in 16-wide warps, and 1024 threads when 33-64 work registers are in use. Arithmetic derived from the published geometry: 2048 threads / 16 threads per warp = 128 warps resident per core at most. The register file's banking, port counts and physical organisation are not published.

- **Multiplier array + adder tree (the arithmetic units behind position shading)** — The position part of the vertex shader — the only part run in the Binning phase — is matrix and vector arithmetic executed on the core's arithmetic units, and the same units re-run the full vertex shader in the Main phase, regenerating the positions the Binning phase threw away. Published per core: 4 arithmetic units, 512 FP16 / 256 FP32 ops per cycle. The multiplier array's radix, the adder tree's depth and the pipeline staging between them are not published.

- **Pipeline register (the phase handover that stores almost nothing)** — Between the phases there is deliberately no wide datapath register holding shaded vertices: positions computed in the Binning phase are discarded rather than staged or written out, and only the binning information crosses. The handover is therefore control state and per-tile lists, not vertex data — the primitive-level reason DVS saves bandwidth. The width and form of the binning information itself are not published.

- **Comparator (the tiler's culling tests)** — Inside the tiler, each primitive faces four published culls — frustum, facing, scissor and sample culling — each a set of compares: clip-space position against the frustum planes, signed area for facing, bounds against the scissor rectangle, and sample coverage. Primitives that fail any compare die here, before any Main phase work exists. The comparator count, the tests' parallelism and the achieved culling rates are not published.

- **FSM / controller (the tiler itself)** — The tiler is the fixed-function controller that runs the Binning phase: it coordinates the position shading on the cores, sequences the culling tests and emits the per-tile lists. It is a sequencer wrapped around the comparators and list storage below, not a programmable core. Its state count, clock rate and primitives-per-cycle throughput are not published.

- **SRAM bank (the per-tile binning lists)** — Surviving primitives are binned into per-tile lists held on chip — the only artefact the Binning phase hands to the Main phase. A list per tile, appended as primitives survive culling, is SRAM storage with a write port from the tiler and a read port into the Main phase front-end. Arm publishes no binning-list depths, no per-tile entry format and no total tiler buffer size, so the capacity of this bank is not published.

- **Counter (the per-tile list bookkeeping)** — Each tile's list needs a length or tail pointer that increments as the tiler appends a primitive and is read back when the Main phase drains the list — one counter per open tile list, in the standard construction. The counter width follows the unpublished list depth, so the width is not published either.

- **Mux / demux (the deferred vs advanced-geometry path select)** — Not every draw defers: a triangle spanning tiles still bins per tile, but draw calls using transform feedback, tessellation or geometry shaders take the advanced-geometry path and are fully shaded up front with outputs written to main memory. A path-select mux at the tiler's output steers each draw between the deferred list path and the up-front shading path. The select criteria are published behaviour (GPU Best Practices Developer Guide, doc 101897); the mux structure is not published.

- **Priority encoder / FIFO (the Main phase front-end)** — When a tile comes up on the Main phase queue, this front-end turns the tile's primitive list into warps for the shader cores — walking the list in order, grouping primitives into 16-wide warps and issuing them for the full vertex shader re-run, rasterization and fragment shading. Published warp width: 16 threads. The list-walk rate and the issue queue depth behind it are not published.

- **SRAM bank (the on-chip tile memory)** — Rasterization and fragment shading work out of on-chip tile memory: the finished tile lives here until written out, and the tile is written back to memory only once. Published geometry: tiles up to 64x64 pixels and 256 tile bits per pixel per shader core. Arithmetic derived from the published geometry: 256 bits x 64 x 64 pixels = 1,048,576 bits = 128 KiB of tile storage for a full-size tile — a consequence of the published numbers, not a published capacity. The bank count, banking and port style of the tile memory are not published. The core's published caches sit beside it as SRAM banks of their own: 32 KB load/store cache and 32 KB texture cache per shader core.

- **SRAM bank (the L2 slices on the flush path)** — The finished tile leaves through the GPU's L2 cache, organised as slices between the cores and the shared LPDDR. Published: 2 or 4 L2 slices, up to 1,024 KB total. Per-slice capacity by the published totals is configuration-dependent and not separately published; slice banking and associativity are not published.

- **Comparator (transaction elimination's CRC match)** — On flush, a tile whose CRC matches the previous frame's tile is never written out at all — a comparator over the tile's CRC against the stored previous CRC, gating the LPDDR write. Published behaviour with published effect: up to 40% less memory bandwidth overall, 26% less in Fortnite and 33% less in Genshin Impact (Arm-measured vs G715). The CRC width and the previous-CRC store's size are not published.

- **Credit counter (write-out flow control to LPDDR)** — Tile write-outs cross into the SoC memory system shared with the host, so flushes are paced by the interconnect's flow control — in the standard construction, credit counters that stop the flush path when the memory system cannot accept more. The GPU owns no memory of its own and shares the host SoC's LPDDR5(X); the credit counts, buffer depths and interconnect parameters on this path are not published by Arm.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: Arm publishes the three queues and their roles, the tiler's four culls, the per-core geometry used above (2048 threads, 16-wide warps, 33-64 work registers at the reduced thread count, 4 arithmetic units, 512 FP16 / 256 FP32 ops per cycle, 32 KB load/store and 32 KB texture caches, 256 tile bits per pixel), tiles up to 64x64, and 2 or 4 L2 slices up to 1,024 KB. The two derived figures (128 warps per core; 128 KiB per full-size tile) are arithmetic from those published numbers, labelled as such. Everything else a circuit designer would size — queue depths, binning-list depths, tiler buffer sizes, culling rates, arbiter policy, register-file banking — is not published, and this decomposition invents none of it.

#### Down to the primitives: The ray-tracing unit — a fixed-function RTU inside each shader core, power-gated when idle

Decomposed in trace order — ray query in, closest hit out. Two honesty boundaries govern everything below. First, the RTU does not accelerate BVH traversal: the shader drives every traversal step through Vulkan ray-query instructions, and the RTU is the ray-box and ray-triangle test units only — there is no traversal engine and no traversal stack inside it. Second, instantiation is disputed at Level-2: Arm's G715-era technical diagrams (which label the units RBOX_UNIT / RT_RAY_BOX and RTRI_UNIT / RT_RAY_TRI) show the RTU inside the shader core, but sources differ on one RTU per shader core versus one per core pair, so the per-core count is not asserted as settled here. The G720's RTU is the G715 generation — Arm announced no new ray-tracing generation for the G720 — and its own power island is a 5th-generation feature. Arm publishes no ray-test rates, BVH fetch widths, ray-queue depths, traversal-stack depths or GigaRays/s figure for it.

- **Pipeline register (the ray-query issue state)** — A ray query arrives from the shader as a bundle of state: the acceleration structure (TLAS/BLAS), ray flags, cull mask, origin, tMin, direction and tMax. That bundle is staged in registers at the RTU's input while the query's tests run — the query runs inline in any shader stage via Vulkan ray query. The register count and field widths beyond the query's own parameters are not published.

- **FIFO / queue (the ray queue into the test units)** — Queries from the shader's lanes wait here for the shared test units — the decoupling that lets the shader issue ray work without stalling on every test. Arm publishes no ray-queue depth, entry width or port count, so this queue is named with its role and its parameters are not published.

- **Multiplier array + comparator (the ray-box unit, RBOX_UNIT)** — The ray-box test is the slab method: per axis, multiply the ray's precomputed inverse direction by the box's near and far plane offsets, then compare the resulting t intervals for overlap — a small multiplier array feeding comparators, repeated over the node's box. A missed box prunes the whole subtree beneath it, which is why most of the scene's triangles are never tested. Arm's G715-era diagrams label this unit RBOX_UNIT (RT_RAY_BOX). Its multiplier width, boxes-tested-per-cycle rate and pipeline depth are not published — Arm publishes no ray-test rate for the RTU at all.

- **SRAM bank (the BVH fetch path)** — Every box and triangle test first needs its BVH node or leaf fetched, and those fetches cross the shader core's memory path — the core's published caches (32 KB load/store cache per core) are the on-chip storage the traversal stream passes through. Arm publishes no BVH fetch width, no dedicated BVH buffer and no node-fetch rate, so the fetch datapath's parameters are not published; ray coherence, not a published width, decides whether the test units stay fed.

- **Multiplier array + adder tree (the ray-triangle unit, RTRI_UNIT)** — At a hierarchy leaf, the ray-triangle test solves for the intersection and its barycentric coordinates: cross and dot products over the triangle's edges and the ray — multiplier arrays whose partial products reduce through adder trees — producing a candidate t and the (u, v) barycentrics the shader needs for interpolation. Arm's G715-era diagrams label this unit RTRI_UNIT (RT_RAY_TRI). Its width, triangles-tested-per-cycle rate and pipeline depth are not published.

- **Comparator + mux (closest-hit selection)** — Each candidate triangle's t is compared against the best t so far (and against tMin/tMax); when a candidate wins, a mux swaps its hit record — t plus barycentric coordinates — into the query's result registers. This compare-and-select is what makes the RTU return the closest hit rather than any hit. The comparator count and whether selection is serial or treed are not published.

- **FSM / controller (traversal control — in the shader, not the RTU)** — The traversal loop itself — descend, test children, pop back, advance to the next node — is an FSM executed by the shader through ray-query instructions, one RTU test at a time. It is listed here precisely because it is absent from the RTU: Arm does not accelerate BVH processing, so there is no traversal controller and no hardware traversal stack in the RTU to decompose. Any traversal-stack depth is a property of the shader's own register and memory use, and Arm publishes no traversal-stack depth for this design.

- **Register file (the hit result returning to the shader)** — The closest hit — t and barycentric coordinates — lands back in the shader core's registers, where the shader shades the contribution and denoises with the rest of the frame; shading and denoising never enter the RTU. The result path's width and the query-completion mechanism's details are not published.

- **FSM / controller (the power-island controller)** — In the 5th generation the RTU sits on its own power island: a power controller that gates the island when no ray work is submitted, so raster-only applications pay no leakage for the unit — the primitive-level half of why the RTU costs under 4% of shader-core area (published) yet nothing when idle. The gating latency, retention behaviour and wake-up cost are not published.

- **Synchronizer (the power-island boundary)** — A gated island still has to exchange queries and results with the always-on shader core around it, so the island boundary carries the isolation and synchronisation between the two power domains — queries must not be lost across a gate/ungate transition. The boundary's structure and clock relationship are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: Arm and its launch coverage publish the RTU's composition (ray-box and ray-triangle test units, labelled RBOX_UNIT and RTRI_UNIT in G715-era diagrams), its under-4%-of-core area, over 300% better ray-tracing performance than software (Arm benchmarks), the 5th-generation power island, and the shader-driven ray-query model with no BVH traversal acceleration. They publish no ray-test rates, BVH fetch widths, ray-queue depths, traversal-stack depths or GigaRays/s figure, and the one-RTU-per-core versus one-per-core-pair question is disputed — this decomposition states those silences rather than filling them.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [unverifiable] **Arm Immortalis-G720** — Level-3 decomposition scope boundary: Arm publishes no per-primitive parameters for the Immortalis-G720 DVS front end (no tiler buffer sizes, binning-list depths, queue depths or culling rates) and none for its ray-tracing unit (no ray-test rates, BVH fetch widths, ray-queue depths, traversal-stack depths or GigaRays/s figure); the Level-3 text therefore names those primitives with their roles and marks their parameters unpublished, using only Arm's published per-core geometry plus two figures explicitly labelled as arithmetic derived from that geometry (128 warps per core; 128 KiB per full-size tile). Source: Arm, Mali G1 Performance Counter Reference Guide (doc 111042).

Note: the Level-2 facts re-used in this section (the per-core geometry, the three queues and their roles, the tiler's four culls, the 64x64 tiles, the L2 slice configuration, the RTU's composition, area share and speedup, and the shader-driven ray-query model) were already recorded at Level-2 with the same quotes and sources and were deduped, not re-appended.

### Imagination PowerVR

#### Down to the primitives: The Tile Accelerator, Parameter Buffer and ISP — the deferred-visibility front end

Decomposed in trace order — vertex shader in, visible set out. Imagination publishes the front end's contract (the TA's binning, the Parameter Buffer in system memory, the ISP's Hidden Surface Removal and depth/stencil tests, the Tag Buffer's per-pixel triangle record, the on-chip colour/depth/stencil buffers, the firmware-managed GPU) but none of its circuits: no Parameter Buffer sizes, tile-list depths, TA binning rates, ISP depth-test rates or Tag Buffer depths are published for this front end. Where a parameter below comes from Imagination's published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry, not as a published fact; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **FSM / controller (the Tile Accelerator's binning sequencer)** — The TA is the fixed-function sequencer at the head of the front end: it takes each transformed primitive and determines which tiles contain it, updating the per-tile lists. "The Tile Accelerator (TA) then determines which tiles contain each transformed primitive (Tiling)." (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0). Its binning rate, state count and the number of primitives it can bin per cycle are not published.
- **SRAM bank / memory store (the Parameter Buffer — tile lists and transformed vertices in system memory)** — The tile lists and the transformed vertex data both live in the Parameter Buffer, an intermediate store that "resides in system memory, and is mostly managed by the hardware" (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0): each tile's list holds primitive lists containing pointers to the transformed vertex data. Because the PB is in system memory, the on-chip primitive here is the PB's write/read interface and the pointer-list structure, not an on-chip SRAM array of published size — and Imagination publishes no PB size at all.
- **Counter (per-tile list bookkeeping)** — Each tile list needs a length or tail pointer that increments as the TA appends a primitive and is read back when the ISP drains the list — one counter per open tile list, in the standard construction. The counter width follows the unpublished list depth, so the width is not published either.
- **FIFO / queue (the tile worklist into the ISP)** — Tiles are rendered in turn — "When a tile operation begins, the corresponding tile list is retrieved from the Parameter Buffer (PB) to identify the screen-space primitive data that needs to be fetched." (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0) — so the tiles waiting for the ISP form a worklist queue that decouples binning from rasterization, and "This process is repeated until all tiles have been processed and the frame buffer is complete." (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0). Its depth, entry width and scheduling order are not published.
- **Mux / demux (the ISP's position-only fetch select)** — The ISP fetches only screen-space position data for the geometry within the tile — "The ISP only fetches screen-space position data for the geometry within the tile." (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0). The fetch mux steers position data, not full vertex attributes, into the ISP; its width and the number of primitives fetched per cycle are not published.
- **Comparator (the ISP's depth and stencil tests — Hidden Surface Removal)** — The ISP's core operation is a per-pixel compare: "The Image Synthesis Processor (ISP) fetches the primitive data and performs Hidden Surface Removal (HSR), along with depth and stencil tests." (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0). Each candidate fragment's depth is compared against the stored depth for its pixel, and the stencil test is a further compare against the stored stencil value; the losers never reach the shader back end. The comparator count, the depth-test rate and the stencil-test rate are not published.
- **SRAM bank (the Tag Buffer — one triangle ID per pixel)** — "The Tag Buffer contains information about which triangle is on top for each pixel." (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0). It is a per-pixel store: one triangle identifier per pixel in the tile, written as the ISP resolves visibility and read back as the visible set. Arithmetic derived from the published geometry: at the classic 32x32 example tile size the Tag Buffer holds one entry per pixel for 1,024 pixels — arithmetic from the published example size, not a published Tag Buffer depth, and tile size varies by device. The Tag Buffer's entry width and total depth are not published.
- **SRAM bank (the on-chip colour, depth and stencil buffers)** — Colour, depth and stencil read-modify-write operations run on fast on-chip memory: "Read-Modify-Write operations for the colour, depth and stencil buffers are performed using fast on-chip memory instead of relying on repeated system memory access, as traditional IMRs do." (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0). These are the on-chip SRAM banks the ISP's comparators read and write against; their capacities, banking and port counts are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the firmware event manager)** — "All PowerVR graphics cores are managed by firmware, enabling the graphics processor to handle the majority of high level graphics events internally." (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0). The firmware controller is the sequencer above the TA and ISP: it schedules tiling, starts tile operations and hands the finished visible set to the shader back end, keeping event-handling latency low and driver CPU overhead down. Its event queue depths and handling rates are not published.
- **Credit counter (Parameter Buffer write flow control to system memory)** — The Parameter Buffer lives in system memory, so every TA write and ISP read crosses DRAM; in the standard construction, credit counters pace that traffic against what the memory system can accept, stalling the binning front end when credits run out. The credit counts, PB burst sizes and DRAM interface parameters on this path are not published by Imagination.
- **CAM / TCAM — none in the front end** — The one place a content-addressed store looks necessary is the Tag Buffer, and it is not one: the Tag Buffer is indexed by pixel position — one entry per pixel, written and read at that pixel's address — not searched by content, so no CAM or TCAM appears in the published front-end contract. The per-pixel triangle lookup is an address, not a match.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: Imagination publishes the TA's binning role, the Parameter Buffer's contents and its residence in system memory, the ISP's HSR and depth/stencil tests, the Tag Buffer's per-pixel triangle record, the on-chip colour/depth/stencil buffers, the firmware-managed GPU, and the 32x32 example tile size (tile size varies by device). The one derived figure (1,024 pixels per 32x32 tile) is arithmetic from that published example size, labelled as such. Everything else a circuit designer would size — Parameter Buffer size, tile-list depths, TA binning rate, ISP depth-test rate, Tag Buffer depth and entry width, on-chip buffer capacities, firmware event-queue depths, credit counts — is not published, and this decomposition invents none of it.

#### Down to the primitives: The Unified Shading Cluster and TSP — shading only what survived

Decomposed in trace order — visible set in, finished tile out. Imagination publishes the back end's contract (the unified shader architecture, the USC's 16 pipelines and their ALU mix, the data-driven scheduler, the TSP's colouring of visible pixels only, the Furian texture unit's own cache, the PVRTC formats, the on-chip MSAA resolve, the single tile flush) but none of its circuits: no USC register-file sizes, thread counts, texture-cache sizes or TSP queue depths are published for this back end. Where a parameter below comes from Imagination's published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry, not as a published fact; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **FIFO / queue (visible-fragment dispatch into the USCs)** — The visible set the ISP proved is issued as fragment work to the USC pipelines; this queue is the decoupling between the visibility pass and the shader back end, so the TSP can keep shading while the ISP moves to the next tile. Its depth, entry width and port count are not published.
- **Register file (the USC's warp thread state)** — The shader engine is massively multi-threaded, and the thread contexts live here: "The PowerVR shader engine is based on a massively multi-threaded and multitasking approach. It is hardware-managed and load-balanced by using a data driven execution model to ensure the highest possible utilisation efficiency." (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0). In Furian each pipeline got better access to that state: "the GPU now supports improved simultaneous access to more local memory addresses, which means each ALU pipeline can directly access the memory areas they need without stalls" (verified — Imagination, PowerVR Series8XT blog). The register file's size, thread count, banking and port counts are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the data-driven scheduler)** — The scheduler is the controller that keeps the 16 pipelines fed: it schedules tasks on data availability and switches between independent tasks to avoid data-dependency stalls — "This approach schedules tasks based on data availability, and enables switching between independent processing tasks to ensure that data dependency stalls are avoided at all costs." (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0). Its task-table size, issue rate and scheduling policy details are not published.
- **Priority encoder (task selection among ready tasks)** — When a pipeline frees up, something must pick which ready independent task runs next — a priority-select/arbiter over the ready-task set, the primitive form of the scheduler's choice. Its policy (fixed priority, round-robin, or data-driven), grant width and latency are not published.
- **Multiplier array + adder tree (the FP32/FP16 ALU datapaths)** — Each USC holds 16 ALU pipelines in parallel, each with 2 FP32 ALUs, 2 FP16 ALUs and 1 special-function ALU (verified — Imagination, "Graphics cores: trying to compare apples to apples"); FP32 ALUs do up to 2 FLOPs per cycle for a peak of 64 FLOPs per cycle per USC, FP16 up to 4 per cycle on Series6XT for up to 128 per USC. Inside the pipelines, Rogue's arithmetic is multiply-add: "In Rogue, the pipelines contained two Multiply Adds function blocks (MADs)." (verified — Imagination, PowerVR Series8XT blog), and Furian rebalanced them: "with Furian we instead implemented a MAD and a MUL, offering more performance in the real world, while keeping silicon area cost in check" (verified — Imagination, PowerVR Series8XT blog). Execution is scalar SIMD — one component per cycle per lane: "the USC works on the red component in one cycle, then the blue component in the next, and so on until all components are processed" (verified — Imagination, "Graphics cores: trying to compare apples to apples"). The multiplier array's radix, the adder tree's depth and the pipeline staging between them are not published.
- **Barrel shifter (FP alignment and normalization in the ALU pipes)** — Floating-point add and multiply need their operands aligned and their results normalized — shifters that slide a mantissa by a variable amount, the standard construction inside the FP32/FP16 datapaths above. Shift widths, pipeline placement and whether the shifter sits before or after the adder tree are not published.
- **Multiplier array (the special-function ALU — sine, cosine, log, reciprocal)** — One per pipeline, handling the operations the MAD/MUL datapaths do not: "the special function ALU, which handles more complex arithmetic and trigonometric operations such as sine, cosine, log, reciprocals and friends, on scalar values" (verified — Imagination, "Graphics cores: trying to compare apples to apples"). Its implementation — lookup table, iterative refinement, or polynomial evaluation — its output precisions and its per-operation throughput are not published; the blog notes only that its range of output precisions and performance per operation vary "because of their nature".
- **SRAM bank (the texture unit's own cache — Furian)** — In Furian the texture unit stopped sharing the USCs' data path: "the texture unit now has its own cache, ensuring that it doesn't have to compete with the Unified Shading Clusters (USCs) for access to the data" (verified — Imagination, PowerVR Series8XT blog), and the result is double the fill-rate at eight pixels per clock. The cache's size, associativity, line width and port count are not published.
- **Mux / demux (the PVRTC format select in the texture unit)** — Texture fetches carry a format select: PVRTC comes in 2 bits per pixel and 4 bits per pixel (verified — Unity Manual, already recorded at Level-2), and the texture unit expands the compressed texels as part of the fetch — the compressed form is what sits in the cache: "These textures are also very texture cache efficient as the lower pixel size allows more pixels to fit in the limited amount of cache memory available to the texture units." (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0). The decode datapath's width and the 2bpp/4bpp select encoding are not published.
- **Comparator (alpha test)** — After shading, alpha testing compares each fragment's alpha against the threshold: alpha-tested primitives "cannot write data to the depth buffer until the fragment shader has executed and fragment visibility is known" (verified — Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers, Rev 1.0) — the deferred depth write that makes alpha test expensive on this architecture. The comparator count and width are not published.
- **Adder tree (the Pixel Back End's MSAA sub-sample combine)** — The Pixel Back End combines sub-samples for on-chip MSAA — 4x on Series5/5XT, 8x on Series6 (verified — Imagination, Droidcon 2013 slides, already recorded at Level-2) — and combining 4 or 8 sub-samples into one resolved colour is an adder tree over the samples. The adder width, tree depth and resolve rate are not published.
- **Credit counter (tile-flush flow control to the frame buffer)** — Once the tile's render is complete its colour data is written to the frame buffer in system memory exactly once; in the standard construction, credit counters pace that single burst against what the memory system can accept, so the flush does not stall the next tile's shading. The credit counts and flush burst sizes are not published by Imagination.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: Imagination publishes the USC's pipeline and ALU geometry (16 pipelines, 2 FP32 + 2 FP16 + 1 special-function ALU each; 64 FP32 / up to 128 FP16 FLOPs per cycle per USC), the Rogue two-MAD and Furian MAD+MUL pipeline contents, the scalar-SIMD execution model, the data-driven scheduler, the Furian texture unit's own cache and its 8-pixels-per-clock fill-rate, the PVRTC 2bpp/4bpp formats, the 4x/8x on-chip MSAA, and the single tile flush to the frame buffer. The rate figures used here (64/128 FLOPs per cycle per USC) are arithmetic from the published pipeline geometry, labelled as such at Level-2. Everything else a circuit designer would size — USC register-file size, thread count, texture-cache size and associativity, TSP queue depths, multiplier radix, adder-tree depth, shifter widths, SFU implementation, alpha-test comparator count, MSAA resolve rate, flush credit counts — is not published, and this decomposition invents none of it.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [verified] **Imagination PowerVR** — Furian texture unit has its own cache, so it no longer competes with the USCs for data access; the result is double the fill-rate at eight pixels per clock. Source: Imagination, PowerVR Series8XT blog (2018).
- [verified] **Imagination PowerVR** — Rogue ALU pipelines contain two Multiply Adds function blocks (MADs); Furian pipelines contain one MAD and one MUL. Source: Imagination, PowerVR Series8XT blog (2018).
- [verified] **Imagination PowerVR** — The special-function ALU handles sine, cosine, log, reciprocals and friends on scalar values, with output precisions and per-operation performance that vary by operation. Source: Imagination, "Graphics cores: trying to compare apples to apples" (2014).
- [verified] **Imagination PowerVR** — Scalar SIMD execution: the USC works on one component per cycle per lane (red in one cycle, blue in the next, and so on). Source: Imagination, "Graphics cores: trying to compare apples to apples" (2014).
- [verified] **Imagination PowerVR** — PVRTC textures are very texture-cache efficient: the lower pixel size lets more pixels fit in the limited cache memory available to the texture units. Source: Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers (Rev 1.0, 11/02/2020).
- [verified] **Imagination PowerVR** — Furian supports improved simultaneous access to more local memory addresses, so each ALU pipeline can directly access the memory areas it needs without stalls. Source: Imagination, PowerVR Series8XT blog (2018).

Source: Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers (Rev 1.0, 11/02/2020).

Note: the Level-2 facts re-used in this section (the TA's binning role, the Parameter Buffer's contents and residence in system memory, the ISP's HSR and depth/stencil tests, the Tag Buffer's per-pixel triangle record, the on-chip colour/depth/stencil buffers, the firmware-managed GPU, the 32x32 example tile size, the USC's pipeline and ALU geometry and rates, the up-to-8-USC scaling, the GX6650 configuration, the PVR3C triple compression, the GT7900 and Furian GT8525 configurations, the PVRTC bit rates and the 4x/8x MSAA) were already recorded at Level-2 with the same quotes and sources and were deduped, not re-appended.

### Google TPU v5p

#### Down to the primitives: Second-generation SparseCore — the dataflow engine for embeddings

Decomposed in trace order — host-prepared COO batch in, pooled vectors out to the TensorCores. OpenXLA's deep dive and the ISCA 2023 paper publish the tile geometry (16 tiles, 8-wide SIMD, 2.5 MiB spmem in 16 banks, five cross-channel units) but none of the circuits below it: no queue depths, port counts, arbitration or bank widths are published for this block. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **FSM / controller (the SparseCore sequencer)** — One sequencer per SparseCore orchestrates all 16 tiles in lockstep: "A single SparseCore sequencer orchestrates tasks across all tiles, ensuring synchronized operations." (verified — OpenXLA, A deep dive into SparseCore for Large Embedding Models). It issues the same task stream to every tile, so the tiles stay in step while each works its own slice of the partition. The sequencer's state count, task-queue depth and issue rate are not published.
- **SRAM bank (SPMEM — the Sparse Vector Memory, 16 banks)** — The tile's working memory is compiler-managed SRAM, not a cache: "A relatively small, but very fast, local SRAM that is available exclusively to each SparseCore. It is important to note that SPMEM is not a cache; its usage is explicitly managed and orchestrated by the XLA compiler." (verified — OpenXLA). On the v4 geometry v5p inherits, spmem is 2.5 MiB per SparseCore in 16 banks — "The Fetch Unit reads activations and parameters from the HBM into the tile's slice of a 2.5 MiB Sparse Vector Memory (Spmem)." (verified — Jouppi et al., ISCA 2023). Arithmetic from that geometry: 160 KiB per bank (2.5 MiB / 16), 10 MiB of spmem per chip (4 SparseCores x 2.5 MiB). Google has not published v5p's own spmem size, and no bank widths, port counts or replacement logic are published — spmem is explicitly managed scratchpad, so there is no tag array to decompose.
- **FIFO / queue (the Fetch Unit's outstanding-read queue)** — Each tile's Fetch Unit issues multiple outstanding, uncoalesced reads against its own HBM channel and stages the returned embedding rows into its slice of spmem (v4 structure, ISCA 2023 — verified, fact records). The queue of in-flight reads is what hides HBM latency while the scVPU works the previous batch. The number of outstanding reads per tile, the queue depth and the entry width are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (the Flush Unit's writeback staging)** — The Flush Unit writes updated embedding rows back to HBM on the backward pass (v4 structure, ISCA 2023 — verified, fact records). Its writeback path stages completed updates before they leave the tile, so the scVPU is not stalled on HBM write latency. Queue depth, entry width and the write-combining policy are not published.
- **Multiplier array (the scVPU — 8-wide SIMD per tile)** — Each tile holds "a programmable 8-wide SIMD Vector Processing Unit (scVPU, not to be confused with VPU of the TC in TPU v4)" (verified — Jouppi et al., ISCA 2023), working the 8-element small-vector tasks OpenXLA describes for this hardware version. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 16 tiles x 8 lanes = 128 SIMD lanes per SparseCore, 512 lanes per chip. Per-lane operand widths, the lane interconnect and the ALU pipeline depth are not published.
- **Crossbar (the cross-channel fabric across the 16 spmem banks)** — Five cross-channel units sit across all 16 spmem banks: "In addition, the five Cross-Channel Units (gold boxes in Figure 7) perform specific embedding operations, which their names explain." (verified — Jouppi et al., ISCA 2023). Architecturally that is a crossbar — five consumers, sixteen bank ports — because the units sit across all 16 banks and must reach any bank to dedupe and reduce across the whole partition. The 5x16 radix is derived from the published counts; the arbitration policy, the bank port widths and whether the fabric is a full crossbar or a narrower shared bus are not published.
- **Comparator (deduplication — ID equality)** — The cross-channel units dedupe repeated IDs before reducing (v4 structure — verified, fact records). Deduplication is, at the primitive level, an equality compare on col_ids: two IDs are the same row if and only if the compare matches. The ID width, the number of comparators and whether dedup is done by sorted compare, hashing or a content-addressed structure are not published.
- **Adder tree (the cross-channel reduction)** — The cross-channel units reduce the gathered vectors across all 16 spmem banks into pooled per-sample vectors (Level-2 trace — verified, fact records). That reduction is a vector adder tree: pairwise adds across banks, narrowing to one pooled vector per sample. The tree depth, the adder width and the reduction order are not published beyond the 8-wide SIMD shape.
- **Counter (per-partition limit counters and the index walk)** — XLA sizes the spmem buffers from the compiled limits — "It utilizes the configured operational limits (for example, max_ids_per_partition, max_unique_ids_per_partition, often provided via a limits file specified by flags like xla_sparse_core_max_ids_file) to statically determine the sizes of and allocate on-device memory buffers, particularly within the SPMEM." (verified — OpenXLA). The counting primitive is the index walk itself: the Fetch Unit walks each partition's ID list, and the compiled limits are the bounds it walks against. Counter widths are not published, and the limit values are per-model compile-time constants, not chip parameters.
- **Mux / demux (tile-to-HBM-channel select and spmem bank select)** — Each tile has its own associated HBM channel (Level-2 — verified, fact records), so a channel-select mux steers each tile's reads to its channel, and a bank-select mux steers each tile's spmem accesses to its slice of the 16 banks — a 16-way select derived from the published bank count. The HBM channel count per chip, the mux radix on the HBM side and the bank-select timing are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the OpenXLA deep dive and the ISCA 2023 paper publish the tile geometry used above — 16 tiles, 8-wide SIMD, 2.5 MiB spmem in 16 banks, five cross-channel units — and the arithmetic is derived from those published counts. Below that level — queue depths, port counts, arbitration, bank widths — Google publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. The one synchronizer-shaped question has a negative answer: the 16 tiles run in lockstep under one sequencer in a single clock domain, and the SparseCore-to-TensorCore handoff goes through HBM under XLA's pipeline schedule, so there is no two-flop synchronizer inside the SparseCore to decompose.

#### Down to the primitives: The pod-scale interconnect — ICI 3D torus and the optical circuit switch

Decomposed in trace order — collective issued on the chip, copper hops inside the cube, light across the OCS, copper hops to the destination chip. The Google Cloud docs publish the pod geometry (8,960 chips, 140 cubes, 6,144-chip largest slice, 1,200 GB/s bidirectional ICI, the 3D torus, the twisted-torus gains, ICI resiliency) and the ISCA 2023 paper publishes the Palomar geometry; the 7-port router crossbar and the 18,496-mirror count are arithmetic from those published figures. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **FIFO / queue (the ICI port input queue)** — Packets arriving at a chip wait in per-port input queues before the router forwards them to the next hop — the queueing that makes the hop-by-hop neighbour exchanges of the Level-2 trace possible. Queue depth, entry width and the number of queues per port are not published.
- **Crossbar (the on-chip ICI router switch)** — The topology is a 3D torus — "Interconnect topology | 3D torus" (verified — Google Cloud, TPU v5p docs) — so each chip has six torus neighbours (+x, -x, +y, -y, +z, -z) plus its own local injection port: a 7-port crossbar at the router, derived from the published topology. The twist of a twisted torus changes which node the wrap-around edges connect to, not the degree, so the crossbar stays 7-port and the twist lives in the OCS routing tables. Crossbar radix, arbitration and port widths are not published.
- **Switch arbiter (the router's port arbitrator)** — When several input ports want the same output port in the same cycle, an arbiter grants one and holds the rest in their input queues. The arbitration policy — round-robin, oldest-first, or dimension-priority — and the arbiter's structure are not published.
- **Comparator (the routing decision — coordinate compare)** — Each hop's routing decision is a coordinate compare: the router compares the packet's destination coordinates against its own position to pick the next dimension and direction — the standard construction for a torus router, labelled as such, since Google publishes no router internals. The docs confirm the effect, not the mechanism: twisting gives "Shorter packet routes" (verified — Google Cloud, TPU v5p docs).
- **Crossbar — optical (the Palomar OCS MEMS-mirror array)** — The OCS is itself a crossbar, built from mirrors instead of transistors: "The Palomar OCS is 136x136 (128 ports plus 8 spares for link testing and repairs), so 48 OCSes connect the 48 pairs of cables from 64 4^3 blocks (each 64 chips), yielding the desired total of 4096 TPU v4 chips." (verified — Jouppi et al., ISCA 2023). Arithmetic: 136 x 136 = 18,496 MEMS mirrors, each steering one input fibre to one output fibre; circulators send light both ways down one fibre, halving ports and cables. Mirror switching time is in milliseconds (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The v5p OCS count is not published.
- **Mux / demux (the circulator — splitting both directions off one fibre)** — Each optical link carries traffic both ways down a single fibre, and the circulator is the primitive that splits the two directions apart: outgoing light goes to the fibre, incoming light is routed to the receiver — a 3-port directional mux/demux in optical form (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The circulator's insertion loss, isolation and port count beyond the published 128-plus-8 geometry are not published.
- **SRAM bank / table (the OCS routing table)** — The topology is reprogrammed in the OCS routing tables per job (Level-2 — verified, fact records): the table maps each OCS port to the mirror setting for the job's torus, regular or twisted. The table lives in the OCS controller, not on the TPU chip, and its size, entry width and update latency are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the OCS topology controller and ICI resiliency)** — Two controllers govern the fabric: the OCS controller, which sets the mirror array to the job's topology, and the ICI resiliency logic, which "allows ICI connections to be routed around OCS and optical ICI faults" at the cost of "temporary degradation in ICI performance" (verified — Google Cloud, TPU v5p docs), on by default for slices of one cube or larger. The resiliency reroute latency, the controller's state machine and the failover policy are not published.
- **Synchronizer (the electrical-to-optical clock-domain crossing)** — The cube-edge conversion crosses clock domains — the chip's ICI clock to the optical link's serial clock. Google publishes no SerDes or clocking details for the ICI/optical boundary, so this primitive is stated in its standard construction, labelled as such: a SerDes clock-data-recovery block with an elastic buffer absorbing the phase difference between the two domains. Elastic-buffer depth, SerDes rate and the CDR loop structure are not published.
- **FIFO / queue — none in the optical path** — The one place a queue looks necessary is inside the OCS, and there is none: the OCS is a circuit switch, not a packet switch — light is reflected by a mirror, never stored — so no FIFO or queue exists in the optical path (Level-2 trace — verified, fact records). All queueing in this block lives at the chip's ICI ports.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the Google Cloud docs publish the pod geometry used above — 8,960 chips, 140 cubes, 6,144-chip largest slice, 1,200 GB/s bidirectional ICI, the 3D torus, the twisted-torus gains and ICI resiliency — and the ISCA 2023 paper publishes the Palomar geometry; the 7-port router crossbar and the 18,496-mirror count are arithmetic from those published figures. One primitive is deliberately absent: there is no FIFO/queue in the optical path — the OCS is a circuit switch, light is reflected, never stored, so all queueing in this block lives at the chip's ICI ports. Below the published geometry — queue depths, router internals, SerDes rates, the v5p OCS count — Google publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing.

### Graphcore GC200 IPU

#### Down to the primitives: The IPU tile — a barrel-threaded core with 624 KiB of its own SRAM and an AMP

Decomposed in trace order — Supervisor dispatches the Worker, operands come from the tile's own SRAM, the AMP does the multiply-accumulate, results stay local, the Worker exits. The Hot Chips 33 deck publishes the tile's contract — 1,472 tiles, 624 KiB per tile, 7 contexts on 6 slots, the MAIN/AUX split, the AMP table, the RNG, the sparse load/store — and the Frontiers supplement adds the measured AUX latencies and the no-interleaving result, but neither publishes the circuits below that contract: no SRAM bank organisation, register-file size or port counts, AMP pipeline depth, or PRNG state storage. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **FSM / controller (the barrel-threaded slot scheduler — Supervisor and Worker dispatch)** — The slot scheduler is the tile's traffic cop: 7 program contexts share 6 round-robin pipeline slots — "7 program contexts, 6 round-robin pipeline slots." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 11). The Supervisor program runs in the slots not yielded to Workers and "Dispatches Workers by RUN instruction, yielding that slot." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 11); a Worker "Executes in 1 slot at 1/6 of clock; does not see the pipeline." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 11) and returns the slot with EXIT. The scheduler's state count, slot-rotation logic and RUN/EXIT decode depth are not published.
- **Register file (per-thread architectural state)** — The tile core's register file holds each thread's operands between the SRAM and the execution paths; the load/store path moves them in 32-bit units grouped up to four at a time — "The main pipeline executes all memory load and store instructions up to quad-register wide loads of 128 bit." (verified — Frontiers supplementary material §2.2). The 32-bit instruction width gives 32-bit registers, and the quad-register load is four of them at once. The register count per thread, the number of read/write ports and the bypass network are not published.
- **SRAM bank (the tile's 624 KiB private scratchpad)** — The tile's whole working set lives in its own 624 KiB of SRAM — "Each tile has 624 KB of SRAM, for a total of 918 MB per IPU." (verified — Frontiers supplementary material §2.1) — and the memory is a compiler-managed scratchpad, not a cache, so there is no tag array, no replacement logic and no coherence to decompose. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 624 KiB x 1,472 tiles = 897 MiB on die, which the deck's own structural table confirms at 897 MiB (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 8; see fact records). Locality is the point: "Distributed SRAM keeps most on-die transport to <1mm." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 17), and the data-side bandwidth is 47.5 TB/s (Level-2 — verified, fact records). How the 624 KiB is organised into banks, the bank widths and port counts are not published.
- **Mux / demux (MAIN/AUX operand select and the multi-load/store path)** — With two execution paths issuing in the same cycle, operand steering is a mux problem: the MAIN path handles control flow, integer/address arithmetic and "Multi-load/store, to/from either path." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 10), so a load's 128-bit result must be routable to either path's registers and an AUX result must be storable by MAIN. The 128-bit quad-register load width is published; the mux radix, the operand-select timing and the bypass paths between MAIN and AUX are not published.
- **Multiplier array (the AMP — 16x16 FP16xFP16 with FP32 accumulation)** — The AMP is the tile's matrix engine: a 16x16 array of FP16 multipliers with FP32 accumulation — "16x16 4x4 f32 f16 250" (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 13) — hitting the 250 TFLOP/s peak, with 16x8 at 125 and 8x8 FP32xFP32 at 62 in the same table (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Arithmetic from the published geometry: 16 x 16 = 256 FP16 multipliers per tile AMP, 376,832 across all 1,472 tiles. The deck's structural table also gives the IPU a 64-bit SIMD width (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 8; see fact records). The AMP's pipeline depth, the multiplier array's internal tiling and the accumulator register widths are not published.
- **Adder tree (AMP FP32 accumulation and the scalar FMA)** — The AMP's 256 products narrow to FP32 accumulators through an adder tree — "all intermediates f32" (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 13) — and the same add-then-accumulate shape is the tile's scalar path: one FMA per cycle per tile, about 4 TFLOPS across the chip (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The tree depth, the adder widths and the accumulation order are not published.
- **Counter (the sparse-gather pointer walk — cumulative-delta offsets)** — Sparse gather is a counting problem: load/store instructions walk compact pointer lists — "16b absolute offsets to a base," and "4b cumulative delta offsets to a base." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 12) — and the cumulative-delta form adds each 4-bit delta onto a running base, a counter/adder chain that produces the next gather address while arithmetic runs in parallel at full speed (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The pointer-list depth, the number of parallel gather lanes and the address-generation pipeline depth are not published.
- **Counter and XOR/shift network (the enhanced xoroshiro128+ PRNG)** — Each tile's randomness comes from an enhanced xoroshiro128+ generator — "Each tile can generate 128 random bits per cycle:" and "Enhanced xoroshiro128+ PRNG." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 14) — a counter-state update built from shifts, XORs and an addition, with a "6th-order Irwin Hall Gaussian shaper." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 14) that sums uniform samples into Gaussian ones. The state is private per worker thread — "Private context per worker thread." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 14) — and the algorithm's name gives a 128-bit state per thread. The state storage, the shaper's adder count and the per-thread seeding are not published.
- **Comparator (stochastic-rounding compare)** — Down-casts are rounded by comparing the discarded fraction against fresh random bits — "Stochastically round down-casts at full speed – vital for fast and easy training of f16 models." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 14) — and the compare itself is the primitive: the random bits decide whether the retained value rounds up or stays, which is why the rounding costs no extra cycles. The comparator width and the random-bit consumption per rounded value are not published; the compare-against-random-bits construction is the standard one for stochastic rounding, labelled as such.
- **Comparator (branch and conditional execution)** — Control flow is decided in the MAIN path in a single cycle — "Furthermore, branches and conditional execution are also executed within one cycle." (verified — Frontiers supplementary material §2.2) — so a branch is a condition compare on a register value, evaluated and acted on in the same cycle. There is no branch predictor and no speculation hardware to decompose: "the platform does not have speculative execution or other non-deterministic optimizations often found with CPUs." (verified — Frontiers supplementary material §2.2). The comparator width and the condition-code storage are not published.
- **Pipeline registers (the 6-cycle instruction pipeline)** — Every instruction occupies the 6-stage pipeline for exactly 6 cycles — "IPU instructions, including loads and stores from the local tile memory, take exactly 6 cycles." (verified — Frontiers supplementary material §2.1) — so the pipeline registers hold six in-flight instructions, one per slot, and each thread effectively runs at 1.325 GHz / 6, about 221 MHz (Level-2 — verified, fact records). There is no interleaving and no interlock hardware: "This experiment shows that a long-running instruction bundle blocks both the MAIN and AUX pipelines." (verified — Frontiers supplementary material §2.3), so the compiler counts instructions to determine runtime. The pipeline register count and widths are not published.
- **Multiplier array / lookup table (the AUX transcendental unit)** — The AUX path's transcendentals — "Transcendentals: ex, 2x, ln, log2, logistic, tanh." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 10) — are evaluated by a multiplier-and-table unit on the AUX path, with measured latencies of 3 cycles for div, exp2 and exp, 5 for sqrt and tanh, and 6 for log (verified — Frontiers supplementary material §2.2; see fact records). The table sizes, the polynomial degree and the interpolation hardware are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the Hot Chips 33 deck and the Frontiers supplement publish the tile geometry used above — 1,472 tiles, 624 KiB of SRAM per tile, 7 program contexts on 6 round-robin slots, 32-bit instructions, the MAIN/AUX split, the 16x16 AMP table, 128 random bits per cycle, the 16-bit/4-bit pointer lists and the 128-bit quad-register loads — and the arithmetic is derived from those published counts. Below that level — SRAM bank organisation, register-file size and port counts, AMP pipeline depth, the PRNG's state storage, the transcendental unit's table sizes — Graphcore publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no cache and no speculation hardware anywhere in the tile.

#### Down to the primitives: The IPU-Exchange and BSP synchronisation — a stateless all-to-all fabric

Decomposed in trace order — barrier fires, Poplar's schedule fires the transmit, the word travels the spine, the receiving tile's mux selects it, the next compute phase begins. The Hot Chips 33 deck publishes the fabric's whole contract — the 1600 x 36-bit spine, one 36-bit pipelined send channel per tile, one 1600-way receive mux per tile, 32 bits per cycle per tile, no queues, no arbiters, no packet overheads, mesochronous clocking with 3 cycles of drift, the ~150-cycle on-chip sync and 15 ns per hop — and the Frontiers supplement adds the per-tile rates and the IPU-Link topology, but neither publishes the circuits below that contract: no select-state table size or storage form, no spine column organisation, no SerDes rate, lane count or encoding, no IO-block count. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **Comparator (the hardware global barrier — AND-reduction over all tiles)** — The superstep boundary is a giant AND: the hardware barrier fires only when every tile signals its vertex list done — "Hardware global synchronization in ~150 cycles on chip, 15ns/hop between chips." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 15). At the primitive level that is a completion-compare, an AND-reduction over all 1,472 tiles' done signals, with the inter-chip leg costing 15 ns per hop over the IPU-Links; the reduction is the standard construction for a global barrier, labelled as such. The reduction-tree depth, fan-in and the per-tile completion-signal width are not published.
- **FSM / controller (Poplar's cycle-exact transmit, receive and select schedule)** — Once the barrier fires, a per-tile sequencer runs Poplar's compiled schedule: "The POPLAR® compiler schedules transmit, receive and select at precise cycles from sync, knowing all pipeline delays." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 16), and "Any pattern of data movement, changeable at every clock cycle." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 16). The controller is a cycle counter plus the select state, stepping the tile through its scheduled transmits, receives and mux selects; its state count and the schedule's storage are not published.
- **Pipeline registers (the 36-bit pipelined send channel and column transport)** — The send path is a pipeline, not a wire: "one 36b pipelined send channel per tile and IO block" (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 16), with "pipelined transport up/down columns" (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 16) carrying each word to its destination column. Each tile sends and receives 32 bits per cycle — "Tile 32b/cycle send and receive" (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 16) — so 32 of the 36 channel bits are payload; what the other 4 bits carry is not published. The number of pipeline stages in the channel and the column transport is not published.
- **Crossbar (the 1600 x 36-bit exchange spine)** — The spine is the fabric's switching core: "Exchange spine 1600 x 36b" (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 16) — 1,600 send channels, each 36 bits wide, running the tile columns, with every tile's receive mux able to select any of them. Architecturally that is a crossbar — 1,600 inputs, any tile able to receive from any input — with the selection done in the per-tile receive muxes and the spine itself providing pipelined transport. Arithmetic from the published counts: the spine has 1,600 inputs against 1,536 physical tiles, leaving 64 channels for IO blocks if every physical tile holds a send channel — but Graphcore does not publish the IO-block count, so that split is arithmetic with the assumption stated. The spine's column organisation and the per-column wire counts are not published.
- **Mux / demux (the 1600-way receive mux per tile)** — At the scheduled cycle the receiving tile's 1600-way mux picks one word out of the spine — "One 1600-way receive mux per tile" (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 16) — and writes it into the tile's SRAM. Arithmetic: selecting among 1,600 inputs needs 11 select bits (ceil(log2 1600) = 11). The mux's implementation, its select-line fan-out and its timing relative to the SRAM write are not published; the gate-level form is a Level-4 matter.
- **Register file / table (the per-tile select state)** — Addressing in this fabric is by time and select state — "Addressing is by time and select state – there are no queues, arbiters, or packet overheads," (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 16) — so the state that drives each tile's mux select lines each cycle must be held per tile and advanced every clock cycle. Graphcore publishes neither the storage form of that state (registers vs SRAM) nor its size, so this primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.
- **FIFO / queue — none in the fabric** — The one place a queue looks necessary is in the fabric, and there is none: "there are no queues, arbiters, or packet overheads," (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 16). A word is never stored in flight — it leaves on its scheduled cycle and arrives on its scheduled cycle — so there is no store-and-forward, no head-of-line blocking and no queueing delay to decompose. There are no credit counters either: flow control is the static schedule, not credits.
- **Switch arbiter — none in the fabric** — There is no switch arbiter in the fabric either: "there are no queues, arbiters, or packet overheads," (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 16). Two tiles never contend for the same mux input in the same cycle because Poplar's schedule guarantees it in advance — the arbitration happens at compile time, in the scheduler, not in silicon at run time. That compile-time arbitration is exactly why exchange timing is deterministic.
- **Synchronizer (mesochronous clocking — 3 cycles of drift, no per-link synchronizer)** — The whole chip runs on one mesochronous clock — "Physically mesochronous; 3 cycles global synchrony drift across chip." (verified — Knowles, Hot Chips 33, slide 16) — so the exchange needs no per-link two-flop synchronizer: the 3-cycle drift is absorbed by the cycle-exact schedule, which knows all pipeline delays. The synchronizer-shaped question therefore has a negative answer inside this block; the only clock-domain crossing is at the chip edge, in the IPU-Link SerDes below. The phase-alignment hardware that holds the 3-cycle bound is not published.
- **SerDes (the IPU-Link — chip-to-chip escape)** — A tensor that must leave the chip goes out over one of the 10 IPU-Links — "Each IPU has 10 IPU-links with a total bandwidth of 320 GB/s." (verified — Frontiers supplementary material §2.1) — 32 GB/s per link by arithmetic (320 / 10; see fact records), at 15 ns per hop to the next chip (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Bulk data that must leave the system instead streams through host DDR: the M2000's 448 GB of DRAM is accessible at about 20 GB/s (verified — Frontiers supplementary material §2.1; see fact records). The SerDes rate, lane count, encoding and per-link clocking are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the Hot Chips 33 deck and the Frontiers supplement publish the fabric geometry used above — the 1600 x 36-bit spine, the 36-bit send channel, the 1600-way receive mux, 32 bits per cycle per tile, the ~150-cycle sync, 15 ns per hop, 3 cycles of drift, 10 IPU-Links at 320 GB/s — and the arithmetic is derived from those published counts. Below that level — select-state storage and size, spine column organisation, SerDes rates and encoding, the IO-block count — Graphcore publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two primitives are deliberately absent, and that absence is the design: there is no FIFO/queue and no switch arbiter anywhere in the fabric, because addressing is by time and select state under a statically scheduled exchange.
