### Tesla Dojo D1

#### Down to the primitives: The D1 training node — an 8-wide, 4-way SMT core with 1.25 MB of ECC SRAM and an 8×8×4 matrix unit

Decomposed in trace order — fetch and decode, the scalar schedule runs ahead, the gather engine pulls operands, the matrix unit multiplies, results stay local while another thread communicates. The Hot Chips 34 deck publishes the node's contract — the 32-byte fetch window, the 8-wide decoder on two threads per cycle, the 4-wide 4-way SMT scalar scheduler, the 2-way SMT vector scheduler, the 64-byte SIMD unit and the four 8x8x4 matrix units, the five 64-byte SRAM ports, the 1.25 MB ECC SRAM, the FP32/BF16/CFP8/CFP16 formats and the 2 GHz clock — and the IEEE Micro paper adds the 18x20 array geometry, but neither publishes the circuits below that contract: no SRAM bank organisation, no BTB size, no register-file size or port counts, no vector/matrix pipeline depths, no gather-engine lane count. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **FSM / controller (the branch predictor — BTB in the frontend)** — The frontend predicts the next fetch pointer from a branch target buffer: the deck's pipeline slide shows a BTB in the frontend, and Chips and Cheese notes its capabilities are probably basic, since die area is prioritised for vector execution (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The BTB's size, its prediction scheme and its mispredict handling are not published.
- **SRAM bank (the small instruction cache — 32 bytes per cycle)** — The frontend pulls 32 bytes per cycle from a small instruction cache into the node's per-thread fetch buffers, and the decoder takes its instructions from there — "From the fetch buffers, Dojo's decoder can handle eight instructions per cycle, from two threads." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The instruction cache's size, associativity and line width beyond the 32-byte fetch are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (the per-thread fetch buffers)** — Fetched instructions wait in per-thread fetch buffers between the instruction cache and the decoder, so the 8-wide decoder can take eight instructions from two threads in one cycle — "From the fetch buffers, Dojo's decoder can handle eight instructions per cycle, from two threads." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The buffer depth per thread and the fetch-buffer width are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the 8-wide decoder — two threads per cycle, frontend list parsing)** — The decoder is the node's traffic cop for the frontend: "These instructions are fed to an eight-wide decoder which supports two threads per cycle, followed by a four-wide, four-way SMT scalar scheduler that has two integer units, two address units, and one register file per thread." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). At decode, branches, predicated operations and immediate loads are executed in the frontend and dropped — "At decode, certain instructions like branches, predicated operations, and immediate loads ("list parsing") can be executed within the front end and dropped from the pipeline." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The decoder's internal staging and the list parser's table are not published.
- **Comparator (branch and predicated-operation evaluation in the frontend)** — A branch or predicated operation decided in the frontend is a condition compare on a register value, evaluated and acted on before the instruction enters the pipeline — the frontend execution of branches and predicated operations is the published behaviour (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The comparator width and the condition storage are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the 4-way SMT scalar scheduler)** — The scalar scheduler issues the tile's address arithmetic and runs far ahead of the vector side: "These instructions are fed to an eight-wide decoder which supports two threads per cycle, followed by a four-wide, four-way SMT scalar scheduler that has two integer units, two address units, and one register file per thread." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The integer side executes past stalled vector instructions until a scheduler fills — the scheduler's queue depths and issue-selection policy are not published.
- **Register file (one per thread — scalar architectural state)** — Each of the four SMT threads holds its scalar architectural state in its own register file — "These instructions are fed to an eight-wide decoder which supports two threads per cycle, followed by a four-wide, four-way SMT scalar scheduler that has two integer units, two address units, and one register file per thread." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The register count per thread, the read/write port counts and the bypass network are not published.
- **Adder (the two integer ALUs and two address units)** — The scalar scheduler's execution resources are two integer ALUs and two address units — "These instructions are fed to an eight-wide decoder which supports two threads per cycle, followed by a four-wide, four-way SMT scalar scheduler that has two integer units, two address units, and one register file per thread." (Level-2 — verified, fact records) — the adders that compute the tile's address stream and scalar arithmetic. The ALU pipeline depth is not published.
- **Counter (the list parser and gather engine — address generation at 8- and 16-byte granularity)** — The gather engine is a counting problem: the list parser walks the tile's index list and the gather engine pulls the operand blocks out of SRAM straight into the vector register file — "Each SRAM has a unique list parser that feeds a pair of decoders and a gather engine that feeds the vector register file, which together can directly transfer information across nodes." (Level-2 — verified, fact records) — at 8- or 16-byte gather granularity: "The training node is powered by the Gather engine, offers both 8B and 16B granularity for improved efficiency and performance." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The gather lane count, the list-parser's list depth and the address-generation pipeline depth are not published.
- **SRAM bank (the node's 1.25 MB ECC scratchpad — five 64-byte ports)** — The node's whole memory system is its 1.25 MB of ECC-protected SRAM — "It has optimized matrix multiply units and SIMD (single-instruction, multiple-data) instructions and incorporates 1.25 MB of fast ECC-protected SRAM." (Level-2 — verified, fact records) — with five 64-byte ports: "Tesla says the SRAM has five 512-bit ports (2x load, 1x store, and two to the mesh stop)." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Arithmetic from the published geometry: five 64-byte ports move 320 bytes per cycle on the SRAM side — 640 GB/s at 2 GHz if all five ports fired every cycle (see fact records) — and the two load ports sustain two 512-bit loads per cycle: "It can handle two 512-bit loads per cycle, making its per-cycle bandwidth a match for Intel's CPUs with AVX-512 support." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The load/store rates Tesla stated at AI Day — 400 GB/s load, 270 GB/s store — remain disputed against the port arithmetic: two 64-byte load ports at 2 GHz give 256 GB/s (Level-2 — disputed, fact records). How the 1.25 MB is organised into banks, the port arbitration between the five ports and the ECC granularity are not published.
- **Mux / demux (the five-port SRAM select)** — Five 64-byte ports share one 1.25 MB array, so each port's access must be selected onto the array and each read result routed back to its consumer — the load ports to the vector register file, the store port from the scalar side, the mesh-stop ports to the router. The port count is published; the mux radix, the arbitration policy between the five ports and the timing of a port's access are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the 2-way SMT vector scheduler)** — Vector instructions pass to a dedicated vector scheduler with two-way SMT, which feeds either the 64-byte SIMD unit or the matrix units — "Vector instructions are passed further down the pipeline to a dedicated vector scheduler with two-way SMT, which feeds either a 64-byte SIMD unit or four 8×8×4 matrix multiplication units." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The scheduler's queue depth and its selection policy between the SIMD and matrix pipes are not published.
- **Multiplier array (the four 8×8×4 matrix units — 512 FLOPS/cycle)** — The matrix units are the node's multiply engine: "Vector instructions are passed further down the pipeline to a dedicated vector scheduler with two-way SMT, which feeds either a 64-byte SIMD unit or four 8×8×4 matrix multiplication units." (Level-2 — verified, fact records), running one 8×8×4 multiply per cycle at 512 BF16 FLOPS per cycle per node — "Tesla claims a die with 354 Dojo cores can hit 362 BF16 TFLOPS at 2 GHz, indicating that each core can do 512 BF16 FLOPS per cycle." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Arithmetic from the published geometry: one 8×8×4 multiply is 256 multiply-accumulates, 512 FLOPS (see fact records). Unresolved, stated as published: one 8×8×4 per cycle is exactly 512 FLOPS, so four units each doing a full 8×8×4 per cycle would be 2,048 FLOPS/cycle — either the four units share one 8×8×4 per cycle or the "four" counts something else, and Tesla publishes no division of the work (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The formats are FP32, BF16, CFP8 in 4/3 and 5/2 splits, and CFP16, with up to 16 vector formats usable simultaneously (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The multiplier array's internal tiling, the accumulator widths and the matrix pipeline depth are not published.
- **Adder tree (FP32 accumulation and the 64-byte SIMD unit)** — The matrix unit's 256 products narrow to accumulators through an adder tree, and the same add-then-accumulate shape is the 64-byte SIMD unit — 512 bits wide, which is 32 BF16 lanes by arithmetic (512 / 16; see fact records). An FP32-only tile falls back to the scalar rate of 64 GFLOPS per node (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The adder-tree depth, the accumulator register widths and the SIMD lane organisation are not published.
- **Pipeline registers (the scalar-ahead-of-vector pipeline)** — The pipeline's stages are separated by registers: the frontend feeds the scalar scheduler, the scalar side runs ahead of the vector side, and the vector scheduler feeds the SIMD/matrix pipes — the scalar side executes past stalled vector instructions until a scheduler fills (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The number of pipeline stages and the vector/matrix pipeline depths are not published.
- **Data cache / tag array — none in the node** — There is no data cache anywhere in the node: the 1.25 MB SRAM is a software-managed scratchpad, not a cache, so there is no tag array, no replacement logic and no coherence to decompose — the SRAM's five-port contract is the whole memory system (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The small instruction cache in the frontend is the node's only cache, and its size is not published.
- **TLB / page-walk hardware — none in the node** — There is no virtual memory support and therefore no TLB and no page-walk hardware: "To further cut down on latency, area and core complexity, Dojo has no virtual memory support." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). There is also no in-order retirement logic and no precise exceptions outside debug mode (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The 4-way SMT is for one application's explicit parallelism, not multi-tasking.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the Hot Chips 34 deck and the IEEE Micro paper publish the node geometry used above — 360 physical nodes in an 18x20 array with 354 available, grouped in local blocks of 12, 2 GHz, 32 bytes fetched per cycle, 8-wide decode on two threads, a 4-wide 4-way SMT scalar scheduler with two integer ALUs and two address units, one register file per thread, a 2-way SMT vector scheduler, a 64-byte SIMD unit, four 8x8x4 matrix units at 512 BF16 FLOPS per cycle, 1.25 MB of ECC SRAM with five 64-byte ports, two 512-bit loads per cycle, FP32/BF16/CFP8/CFP16 formats with up to 16 usable simultaneously — and the arithmetic is derived from those published counts. Below that level — SRAM bank organisation, BTB size, register-file size and port counts, vector/matrix pipeline depths, gather-engine lane count — Tesla publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no data cache, no TLB and no virtual memory anywhere in the node, and there is no in-order retirement logic or precise-exception hardware outside debug mode.

#### Down to the primitives: The 2D mesh NoC and die-edge SerDes — a seamless mesh from node to ExaPOD

Decomposed in trace order — the mesh stop reads the tile, the packet hops across the die, crosses the die edge on a SerDes lane, hops across the second die, the destination mesh stop writes it home, and the Z-plane offers the long-route alternative. The Hot Chips 34 deck publishes the fabric's whole contract — one packet in and one packet out in all four directions per node per cycle, one 64-byte mesh-stop read and write per cycle, 64 bytes per cycle per direction, 256 GB/s bidirectional on every row and column, 10 TB/s on-chip, 576 SerDes lanes at 112 Gb/s, about 100 ns die-to-die, no end-to-end ordering with packet counting at the destination, TTPoE at 50 GB/s per link with 30 hops against 4 — and the IEEE Micro paper adds the router's packet rates, but neither publishes the circuits below that contract: no router buffer depths, no arbitration scheme, no packet format or size, no SerDes lane-to-edge assignment. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **SRAM bank (the mesh stop's 64-byte read and write ports)** — The mesh stop is the router's door into the node's SRAM: "It can send one packet in and one packet out in all four directions to/from each neighbor node, along with one 64-byte read and one 64-byte write to local SRAM per clock cycle." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Those are two of the SRAM's five 64-byte ports — "Tesla says the SRAM has five 512-bit ports (2x load, 1x store, and two to the mesh stop)." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Arithmetic: one 64-byte mesh-stop read per cycle at 2 GHz is 128 GB/s into the router, and one 64-byte write per cycle is 128 GB/s out of it (see fact records). A packet merely passing through never touches SRAM at all (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The mesh-stop port arbitration against the load/store ports is not published.
- **FIFO / queue (router input buffering — depth unpublished)** — A packet arriving at a router must be held between its arrival cycle and its departure cycle, so each direction needs at least a one-packet holding register; whether the router holds more — per-direction input FIFOs, their depth, virtual channels — Tesla does not publish. The published contract is the rate, not the buffer: "It can send one packet in and one packet out in all four directions to/from each neighbor node, along with one 64-byte read and one 64-byte write to local SRAM per clock cycle." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The packet format and size are not published either, so no buffer depth can be derived from them.
- **Crossbar (the router's four-direction switch)** — The router switches packets among its four neighbours and the local mesh stop — one packet in and one packet out in all four directions per node per cycle, eight packets per cycle per node (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Architecturally that is a five-input, five-output crossbar — four neighbours plus the local inject, four neighbours plus the local eject — with the selection done per output; the five-by-five form is the standard construction for a router of this port count, labelled as such. Arithmetic from the published counts: 64 bytes per cycle per direction at 2 GHz is 128 GB/s per direction, 512 GB/s aggregate across a node's four directions, and selecting among five inputs needs 3 select bits (see fact records). The crossbar's implementation and the per-direction wire counts are not published.
- **Switch arbiter (output arbitration — scheme unpublished)** — Up to five inputs can want the same output in one cycle, so the router must arbitrate — but Tesla publishes no arbitration scheme, no priority rule and no fairness guarantee for the D1 router. The published contract is the rate: one packet out per direction per cycle (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Any arbitration policy named here would be invention, so none is.
- **FSM / controller (route and direction select)** — Each cycle the router must pick, for each arriving packet, which neighbour it leaves by — the direction toward its destination. The compiler knows the topology, including which of the 360 nodes are unavailable, and places work accordingly (Level-2 — verified, fact records), so routing is at least partly a compile-time decision; the router's own routing algorithm, its direction-select logic and any deadlock-avoidance scheme are not published.
- **Pipeline registers (the one-cycle-per-hop forwarding path)** — Each hop is a pipeline stage: a packet arrives, is switched, and leaves in the next cycle — "The NoC also boasts single cycle per hop in every direction, allowing for efficient communication between nodes." — but that figure is unverifiable in this run: the only textual statement is a secondary blog, and the deck's network-interface slide was read only as a reproduced image (Level-2 — unverifiable, fact records). The pipeline register count and widths follow the unpublished packet size, so they are not published either.
- **SerDes (the 576-lane die edge)** — A packet crossing to a neighbouring die goes out over a SerDes lane: "Each die comprises 576 bi-directional serializer/deserializer (SerDes) channels along the perimeter to link to other dies, and moves 8 TB/sec across all four die edges." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Arithmetic from the published counts: 576 lanes × 112 Gb/s = 64,512 Gb/s = 8,064 GB/s, about 8 TB/s across all four edges, about 2 TB/s per edge with 144 lanes per edge — the lane-to-edge split is arithmetic, not published (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The 4 TB/s-per-edge figure in some AI Day reporting is disputed against that lane arithmetic (Level-2 — disputed, fact records). The SerDes rate per lane (112 Gb/s) is published; the encoding, the lane-to-edge assignment and the per-lane clocking are not.
- **Synchronizer (the die-edge clock-domain crossing)** — Two dies are two clock domains, so the die edge is a clock-domain crossing by construction: the SerDes retiming that bridges it is what the ~100 ns die-to-die latency pays for — "There are IO interfaces around the die edge, which let the die communicate with neighboring dies, with a latency of about 100 ns." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). That is about 200 cycles at 2 GHz by arithmetic (100 ns / 0.5 ns per cycle; see fact records), two orders of magnitude above a single-cycle on-die hop (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The synchronizer's construction, the SerDes' internal pipeline depth and the latency's split between serialisation and retiming are not published.
- **Counter (packet counting at the destination — the synchronisation mechanism)** — Dojo guarantees no end-to-end ordering, so synchronisation is counting: "DOJO does not guarantee end-to-end traffic ordering so packets need to be counted at their destination." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The compiler defines a synchronisation tree over the nodes, and the destination count is what the tree waits on (Level-2 — verified, fact records). At the primitive level that is a counter per expected arrival, incremented as packets land and compared against the expected count — the counter width, the expected-count storage and the compare are not published, and there is no hardware barrier network to decompose instead.
- **FSM / controller (TTPoE — the Z-plane transport)** — For long routes the compiler can send a tile up through the Z-plane instead of across the flat mesh: "Crossing the entire two-dimensional mesh network might take 30 hops, while TTP over Ethernet takes only four hops (at lower bandwidth), reducing vertical latency." (Level-2 — verified, fact records). TTPoE runs at 50 GB/s per link over a single 400 Gb/s Ethernet port (Level-2 — verified, fact records), and standard Ethernet switches can carry it. The TTPoE engine's internal primitives — its packet buffers, its transmit/receive sequencing, its DMA into the tile — are not published.
- **SerDes (the DIP escape — 400 Gb/s NIC and 32 GB HBM per card)** — The tile's escape to the outside world is the Dojo Interface Processor: a PCIe card holding 32 GB of HBM and a 400 Gb/s NIC, five cards per tile edge for 160 GB of shared DRAM and 4.5 TB/s to the host (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The per-DIP rate is disputed — 900 GB/s per The Register's live HC34 reporting against 800 GB/s per Wikipedia citing The Next Platform (Level-2 — disputed, fact records). The DIP sits outside the D1 die, and its internal primitives — the HBM interface, the NIC's SerDes, the PCIe path — are not published.
- **Credit counter — no hardware flow control published** — There is no published hardware flow control in the mesh: no credit counters, no backpressure scheme and no published buffer accounting between routers. Flow control, as far as the published material goes, is the compiler's placement — it knows the topology and the traffic pattern in advance — plus packet counting at the destination (Level-2 — verified, fact records). A credit counter is therefore named here as absent from the published design, not as a primitive with unpublished parameters.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the Hot Chips 34 deck and the IEEE Micro paper publish the fabric geometry used above — one packet in and out in all four directions per node per cycle, one 64-byte mesh-stop read and write per cycle, 64 bytes per cycle per direction, 256 GB/s bidirectional on every row and column, 10 TB/s on-chip, 576 SerDes lanes at 112 Gb/s, about 100 ns die-to-die latency, 50 GB/s TTPoE links over 400 Gb/s Ethernet, 30 mesh hops against 4 Z-plane hops — and the arithmetic is derived from those published counts. Below that level — router buffer depths, arbitration, packet format and size, SerDes lane-to-edge assignment — Tesla publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no hardware ordering guarantee and no hardware barrier network — synchronisation is packet counting under a compiler-defined tree — and there is no switch chip anywhere in the fabric.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [verified] **Tesla Dojo D1** — The node's SRAM moves 320 bytes per cycle across its five 64-byte ports (640 GB/s at 2 GHz if all five ports fired every cycle; arithmetic). Source: Chips and Cheese, "Hot Chips 34 – Tesla's Dojo Microarchitecture".
- [verified] **Tesla Dojo D1** — One 8x8x4 matrix multiply per cycle is 256 multiply-accumulates, i.e. 512 FLOPS (arithmetic). Source: Chips and Cheese, "Hot Chips 34 – Tesla's Dojo Microarchitecture".
- [verified] **Tesla Dojo D1** — The 64-byte (512-bit) SIMD unit processes 32 BF16 elements per cycle (arithmetic). Source: Talpes et al., IEEE Micro 43(3):31–39, 2023, via Wikipedia.
- [verified] **Tesla Dojo D1** — The D1 NoC router switches five inputs (four neighbours plus the local mesh-stop inject) to five outputs; selecting among five inputs needs 3 select bits (arithmetic). Source: Talpes et al., IEEE Micro 43(3):31–39, 2023, via Wikipedia.
- [verified] **Tesla Dojo D1** — The mesh stop's one 64-byte read and one 64-byte write per cycle give 128 GB/s each way at 2 GHz (arithmetic). Source: Talpes et al., IEEE Micro 43(3):31–39, 2023, via Wikipedia.
- [verified] **Tesla Dojo D1** — The ~100 ns die-to-die latency is about 200 cycles at the 2 GHz node clock (arithmetic). Source: Chips and Cheese, "Hot Chips 34 – Tesla's Dojo Microarchitecture".
- [unverifiable] **Tesla Dojo D1** — Level-3 decomposition scope boundary: Tesla publishes no per-primitive parameters for the D1 node or the mesh at Level-3 depth. Source: Talpes, "DOJO: The Microarchitecture of Tesla's Exa-Scale Computer", Hot Chips 34; Talpes et al., IEEE Micro 43(3):31–39, 2023.

Note: the Level-2 facts re-used in this section (the 32-byte fetch window and 8-wide decode on two threads per cycle, the BTB in the frontend, frontend list parsing, the 4-wide 4-way SMT scalar scheduler with two integer ALUs, two address units and one register file per thread, the list parser and gather engine at 8- and 16-byte granularity, the 1.25 MB ECC SRAM, the five 512-bit SRAM ports, two 512-bit loads per cycle, the 2-way SMT vector scheduler feeding the 64-byte SIMD unit or the four 8x8x4 matrix units, 512 BF16 FLOPS per cycle per node, 64 GFLOPS FP32 per node, the FP32/BF16/CFP8/CFP16 formats with up to 16 usable simultaneously, no virtual memory and no precise exceptions outside debug mode, the 360 physical nodes in an 18x20 array with 354 available in 12-node local blocks, the disputed 400 GB/s load / 270 GB/s store rates against the 256 GB/s port arithmetic, the one-packet-in/out in all four directions per node per cycle with one 64-byte mesh-stop read and write per cycle, 128 GB/s per direction, 512 GB/s aggregate per node and 256 GB/s bidirectional per row and column, the 10 TB/s on-chip bandwidth, the 576 SerDes lanes at 112 Gb/s moving 8 TB/s across all four die edges with the disputed 4 TB/s-per-edge figure, the ~100 ns die-to-die latency, no end-to-end ordering with packet counting at the destination under a compiler-defined synchronisation tree, software routing around dead nodes, TTPoE at 50 GB/s per link over 400 Gb/s Ethernet with 30 mesh hops against 4 Z-plane hops, the DIP with 32 GB HBM per card and the disputed 800 vs 900 GB/s per-card rate, five DIPs per tile edge for 160 GB and 4.5 TB/s to the host, and the unverifiable single-cycle-per-hop figure) were already recorded at Level-2 with the same quotes and sources and were deduped, not re-appended.

### AWS Inferentia2 & Trainium

#### Down to the primitives: The Tensor Engine and its two SRAMs — a 128x128 systolic array fed by a 24 MiB SBUF and drained into a 2 MiB PSUM

Decomposed in trace order — the SBUF stages the tile, LoadStationary parks the weights in the array, MultiplyMoving sweeps the activation through, the partial sums land in PSUM, and the companion engines finish the layer while the next tile loads. The NKI guide publishes the block's whole contract — the 128x128 array, the 92 TFLOPS peak, the 128-partition SBUF and PSUM, the tile limits, the initiation-interval cost model, the four engine sequencers and the shared-port rules — and stops there: no SRAM bank organisation, no per-PE circuit detail, no sequencer queue depths, no synchronizer structure. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **SRAM bank (SBUF — 128 partitions of 192 KiB)** — The staging SRAM is the block's memory: "Memory-wise, a NeuronCore-v2 consists of two software-managed on-chip SRAMs, a 24MiB SBUF as the main data storage and a 2MiB PSUM as a dedicated accumulation buffer for Tensor Engine. Both SBUF and PSUM are considered two-dimensional memories with 128 partitions each, i.e., one SBUF partitions has 192KiB of memory while one PSUM partition has 16KiB." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, NeuronCore-v2 Compute Engines section — memory). The partition axis is the parallel dimension — "SBUF/PSUM on NeuronCore-v2 can supply a peak bandwidth of 128 elements/cycle at 1.4 GHz for each tensor read/write interface." (verified — same guide, Data Movement section) — one element per partition, and the free axis is the time dimension, with the hard alignment rules on start partitions (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Arithmetic from the published geometry: 128 partitions x 192 KiB = 24 MiB exactly (see fact records). How a 192 KiB partition is organised into banks, its line width and its port count beyond the 128-element interface are not published.
- **Multiplier array (the 128x128 systolic MAC array)** — The multiply engine is the systolic array itself: "Architecturally, the engine is built around a systolic array with 128 rows and 128 columns of processing elements, which streams input data from SBUF and writes output to PSUM." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Tensor Engine section). Each processing element does one multiply-accumulate per cycle — its parked stationary weight times the moving value arriving from the left, plus the partial sum from the element above — so the array does 16,384 MACs per cycle by arithmetic. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 16,384 MACs x 2 FLOPs per MAC x 2.8 GHz = 91.75 TFLOPS, the guide's 92 TFLOPS maximum for BF16/FP16/TF32/cFP8 inputs (see fact records). The array's internal tiling, the per-PE multiplier width beyond the published data types and the accumulator register widths are not published.
- **Register file (the stationary storage — one weight per processing element)** — LoadStationary "loads the stationary from SBUF and caches it in internal storage of TensorE" (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Tensor Engine section — nc_matmul instruction sequence) — one weight per processing element, 16,384 weights parked for a full [128,128] tile. That internal storage is the array's register file: it holds the stationary operand while the moving operand streams past, which is what makes the weight re-fetch wall disappear. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 16,384 weights at BF16's 16 bits each is 262,144 bits, 32 KiB of stationary storage per array (see fact records). Whether that storage is flip-flops or an SRAM array, and its read/write port count, are not published.
- **Adder (FP32 accumulation — the column add chain and PSUM read-accumulate-write)** — Accumulation is always FP32: "TensorE performs mixed-precision calculations, with accumulations at FP32 precision. Therefore, the output data of a TensorE calculation is always in FP32." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Tensor Engine section — Data Types). Inside the array the accumulation is a column-wise add chain — each processing element adds the partial sum arriving from the element above to its own product — and at the array's foot the partial sums land in PSUM, which "is designed to be a landing buffer for TensorE with near-memory accumulation capabilities that allows read-accumulate-write to every 4B element in memory. Note, this accumulation mechanism can only be controlled by TensorE." (verified — same guide, Near-memory accumulation in PSUM section). One FP32 add per 4-byte element per bank, eight banks per partition, so "with 8 PSUM banks per partition, TensorE can have up to eight outstanding matmul accumulation groups, which allows flexible scheduling of matmul instructions on TensorE." (verified — same guide). The adder widths beyond the published 32-bit element and the pipeline depth of the accumulation path are not published.
- **Mux / demux (SBUF partition select and PSUM bank select)** — Every SBUF/PSUM access selects one partition out of 128 and, inside PSUM, one bank out of eight: "Each partition is further divided into 8 PSUM banks, with each bank holding up to 512 32-bit values." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Near-memory accumulation in PSUM section). Arithmetic from the published geometry: selecting among 128 partitions needs a 7-bit index and selecting among 8 banks needs a 3-bit index (see fact records). The mux radix, the select encoding and the timing of a partition access are not published.
- **Crossbar (VectorE Reshape banks to 32 partitions; GpSimd to 16 partitions)** — The companion engines reach SBUF through fixed crossbars: "VectorE consists of four Reshape and Compute banks: each Reshape Bank connects to 32 SBUF/PSUM partitions and outputs 32 parallel streams of data, while each Compute Bank can process 32 parallel data streams using 32 vector lanes." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Vector Engine section and Cross-partition Data Movement) — and "Each processor connects to 16 SBUF partitions for both reading and writing: processor[0] connected to partition[0:15], processor[1] to partition[16:31] and so on." (verified — same guide, GpSimd Engine section — Memory Hierarchy). Arithmetic from the published geometry: 4 Reshape banks x 32 partitions = 128 partitions and 8 GpSimd processors x 16 partitions = 128 partitions — the two crossbars tile the whole SBUF between them (see fact records). The crossbar radix, the per-output arbitration and the wire counts are not published.
- **Shuffle / permutation network (the Reshape bank's 32x32 transpose and 32-partition shuffle)** — Each Reshape bank does a 32x32 transpose and a 32-partition shuffle inside its group of 32 partitions (Level-2 — verified, fact records) — a permutation of 32 elements across 32 streams, which at the primitive level is a mux network, not a barrel shifter: nothing is shifted by a variable amount, the elements are re-routed. The permutation network's stage count, mux radix and the transpose's buffering are not published. No barrel shifter is published anywhere in this block.
- **FSM / controller (the four engine sequencers and the Sync Engine)** — "A NeuronCore-v2 consists of four heterogeneous compute engines (Tensor, Vector, Scalar, and GpSimd), each designed to accelerate different types of operators in modern machine learning models. Each compute engine has its own sequencer, which is responsible for instruction fetch, decode, and issue. The four compute engines execute four independent instruction streams asynchronously in parallel. Explicit synchronization to satisfy data dependencies between engines is handled through atomic semaphores in hardware." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, NeuronCore-v2 Compute Engines section). Each sequencer carries private 32-bit scalar registers for its fetch, decode and issue, and "Within each NeuronCore, there is also a Sync Engine, which functions as an engine sequencer that can perform the same types of control instructions. The Sync Engine is most commonly used to trigger DMA transfers without interfering with compute engine instruction scheduling and ordering." (verified — same guide). The sequencers' queue depths, issue widths and hazard handling are not published.
- **Counter (initiation-interval, accumulation-group and tensor-access counters)** — The block's timing is counting: "The initiation interval between subsequent MM instructions in this case is roughly max(N, MM_INIT_LATENCY), where MM_INIT_LATENCY is 64 TensorE cycles on NeuronCore-v2, and N is the free axis size of moving of current MM (typically set to 512)." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Tensor Engine section — Performance Consideration / Cost Model), and "Initiating a tensor access request from an engine to its SBUF/PSUM read/write interface incurs a static overhead approximately 60 cycles on NeuronCore-v2." (verified — same guide, Data Movement section — Tensor access overhead). Arithmetic from the published bounds: N is at most 512, so the initiation-interval counter is 9 bits; eight outstanding accumulation groups need a 3-bit group index; the 60-cycle overhead is a 6-bit count (see fact records). The counters' actual widths are arithmetic, not published figures.
- **Comparator (hardware semaphores and partition-alignment checks)** — The four asynchronous instruction streams synchronise through atomic semaphores in hardware — "Explicit synchronization to satisfy data dependencies between engines is handled through atomic semaphores in hardware." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, NeuronCore-v2 Compute Engines section) — and a semaphore test is a compare of a counter against zero. The partition-alignment rules are compares too: a tensor's partitions must start at a legal boundary (0, or 0/64, or 0/32/64/96 by size) (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The semaphore count and widths, and the alignment-check implementation, are not published.
- **Pipeline registers (the deeply pipelined TensorE and VectorE datapaths)** — The engine is deeply pipelined: the guide stresses initiation interval, not end-to-end latency, because the engine is deeply pipelined with several LoadStationary and MultiplyMoving pairs in flight (Level-2 — verified, fact records), and "VectorE consists of 128 parallel vector lanes, each of which can stream data from a SBUF/PSUM partition, perform mathematical operations, and write data back to each SBUF/PSUM partition in a deeply pipelined fashion." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Vector Engine section and Cross-partition Data Movement). The pipeline stage count, the stage latch widths beyond the published 128-element interfaces and the bypass/forwarding network are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (engine instruction streams and sequencer fetch queues)** — Four independent instruction streams run asynchronously in parallel, so each sequencer must queue the instructions it has fetched ahead of issue — but the queue depths, the fetch widths and the semaphore-wait queueing are not published. The SBUF/PSUM read/write interfaces likewise need request queues between the engines and the SRAMs, and their depths are not published either. The published contract is the rate — 128 elements per cycle at 1.4 GHz per interface — not the buffering.
- **Synchronizer (clock-domain crossings — 2.8, 1.4 and 1.12 GHz)** — The block spans three clock domains by construction: Tensor Engine at 2.8 GHz, Vector Engine at 1.12 GHz, Scalar and GpSimd Engines at 1.4 GHz, with the SBUF/PSUM interface at 1.4 GHz (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Data crossing between the 2.8 GHz Tensor Engine and the 1.4 GHz SRAM interface must cross a clock domain, so synchronizers exist somewhere in the block — but AWS publishes no synchronizer structure, no crossing scheme and no latency for the crossings, and this decomposition invents none of them.
- **Switch arbiter — absent by design (compiler-enforced serialisation)** — There is no hardware arbiter for the shared SRAM ports, because the serialisation is done by the compiler: "VectorE and GpSimdE cannot access SBUF in parallel. VectorE and ScalarE cannot access PSUM in parallel. Therefore, VectorE and GpSimdE instructions that access SBUF must be serialized, similarly for VectorE and ScalarE instructions that access PSUM. This is enforced by Neuron Compiler during NKI kernel compilation, so NKI developers are not required to program such serializations." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Data Movement section — memory hierarchy restrictions). A switch arbiter is therefore named here as absent from the published design, not as a primitive with unpublished parameters.
- **CAM / TCAM — none in the block** — There is no associative lookup anywhere in this block: SBUF and PSUM are directly addressed by partition plus free-dimension offset, the stationary weights are indexed by their processing element, and the PSUM banks are indexed by accumulation group. No content-addressable structure is published for the Tensor Engine or its SRAMs.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the NKI guide and the NeuronCore-v2 architecture page publish the geometry used above — 128 rows and 128 columns of processing elements; 92 TFLOPS maximum for BF16/FP16/TF32/cFP8 and 23 TFLOPS for FP32; accumulation always FP32; SBUF 24 MiB in 128 partitions of 192 KiB and PSUM 2 MiB in 128 partitions of 16 KiB; each PSUM partition in 8 banks of 512 32-bit values; tile limits M at most 128, K at most 128, N at most 512; MultiplyMoving initiation interval roughly max(N, 64) Tensor Engine cycles; LoadStationary up to 4x faster than MultiplyMoving; tensor access overhead about 60 cycles; SBUF/PSUM peak 128 elements per cycle at 1.4 GHz; Vector Engine 128 lanes at 1.12 GHz with four Reshape banks of 32 partitions and four Compute banks of 32 lanes; Scalar Engine 128 lanes at 1.4 GHz with fused scale/bias, non-linear function and optional FP32 reduction; GpSimd eight 512-bit processors at 1.4 GHz with 64 KiB TCM at 3-cycle latency and 16 SBUF partitions per processor; each engine with its own sequencer and private 32-bit scalar registers; the Sync Engine triggering DMA; atomic semaphores in hardware; the shared-port rules enforced by the compiler — and the arithmetic is derived from those published counts. Below that level — SRAM bank organisation within a partition, per-PE circuit detail, sequencer queue depths, synchronizer construction, semaphore widths — AWS publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no cache anywhere in the core, so there is no tag array and no coherence to decompose; and there is no hardware arbiter for the shared SRAM ports, because the compiler serialises the conflicting accesses.

#### Down to the primitives: DMA, the CC cores and NeuronLink-v2 — the movement fabric that keeps two cores and sixteen chips fed

Decomposed in trace order — the Sync Engine triggers the transfer, the DMA engines walk their scatter-gather lists, the tile lands partitioned in SBUF, the gradients leave through the CC cores, the peers reduce and return, and the updated weights restage for the next step. The NKI guide publishes the fabric's whole contract — 32 DMA engines at 27 GiB/s each, the 16-transfers-by-8-buffers tiling example, the 4 KiB free-dimension rule, 32 GiB of HBM at 820 GiB/s, 1 TB/s of DMA bandwidth with inline compression/decompression, six CC cores, two NeuronLink-v2 links on Inferentia2 and four on Trainium, 16 chips per Trn1 instance — and stops there: no DMA engine internals, no CC-core internals, no NeuronLink signalling rate, no arbitration scheme. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **FSM / controller (the Sync Engine and the DMA engine controllers)** — The Sync Engine is the fabric's controller: "Within each NeuronCore, there is also a Sync Engine, which functions as an engine sequencer that can perform the same types of control instructions. The Sync Engine is most commonly used to trigger DMA transfers without interfering with compute engine instruction scheduling and ordering." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, NeuronCore-v2 Compute Engines section). Each of the 16 DMA engines per core then runs its transfer — "Each NeuronCore-v2 is equipped by 16 parallel DMA engines that can perform data movement between any addressable memories in the system. Each DMA engine can process one DMA transfer at a time driving a peak bandwidth of 27 GiB/s, but all DMA engines can process different DMA transfers in parallel." (verified — same guide, Data movement between HBM and SBUF using DMAs). The DMA engine's internal state machine — descriptor fetch, scatter-gather list walk, issue sequencing — is not published.
- **FIFO / queue (DMA scatter-gather buffer lists)** — A transfer is a scatter-gather list of DMA buffers, and a buffer must be contiguous in the address map (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The published tiling example is "loading a 128x512 FP32 HBM tensor to SBUF is best done through 16 DMA transfers (one per DMA engine), each moving a scatter-gather list of 8 DMA buffers" (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Data movement between HBM and SBUF using DMAs) — 128 buffers in total, one per SBUF partition. At the primitive level the scatter-gather list is a descriptor queue: the engine walks the list, issues one buffer's move, then the next. The list depth per transfer beyond the published 8-buffer example, the descriptor width and any per-engine buffer queue are not published.
- **Counter (DMA buffer and transfer counting)** — The fabric counts in buffers and transfers: a tensor spanning P partitions needs at least P buffers, and the published example is 16 transfers of 8 buffers each (Level-2 — verified, fact records). Arithmetic from the published geometry: 16 transfers need a 4-bit transfer index per core, 8 buffers per transfer a 3-bit buffer index, and 128 buffers for a full-width tile a 7-bit buffer count (see fact records). The counters' actual widths are arithmetic, not published figures.
- **Mux / demux (DMA engine to SBUF partition routing)** — Sixteen DMA engines per core share one 128-partition SBUF, so each transfer's buffers must be routed to their partitions: the 128x512 FP32 example lands as 128 buffers, one per SBUF partition, each carrying a 2 KiB slice (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The engine-to-partition routing is a mux/demux problem — one engine's buffer stream fans out to eight different partitions per transfer, and sixteen engines' streams interleave across all 128 partitions. The mux radix, the select encoding and the per-cycle routing rate beyond the published 27 GiB/s per engine are not published.
- **Crossbar (the DMA-to-SBUF interconnect)** — "Each NeuronCore-v2 is equipped by 16 parallel DMA engines that can perform data movement between any addressable memories in the system." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Data movement between HBM and SBUF using DMAs), so the interconnect between the 16 engines and the 128 SBUF partitions is architecturally a crossbar — any engine to any partition, one buffer at a time. The published contract is the per-engine rate and the buffer geometry, not the switch: the crossbar's radix, port count, arbitration and wire counts are not published.
- **SRAM bank (SBUF as the DMA landing zone; the two HBM stacks)** — The DMA engines' destination is the SBUF — 128 partitions of 192 KiB, decomposed in the first block — and their source is the HBM: "2 NeuronCores (v2). 2 HBM stacks with a total device memory capacity of 32GiB and bandwidth of 820 GB/s. 32 DMA (Direct Memory Access) engines to move data within and across devices. 6 CC-Cores for collective communication. 2 (Inferentia2) or 4 (Trainium) NeuronLink-v2 for device-to-device collective communication." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Trainium/Inferentia2 device diagram summary). The HBM's internal organisation — channel count, bank count, bank-group structure — is not published by AWS, and the two stacks' split of the 820 GB/s is not published either.
- **Comparator (DMA buffer contiguity and partition-boundary checks)** — A DMA buffer must be contiguous in the address map, and a tensor's partitions must start at a legal boundary (Level-2 — verified, fact records) — both are compares: the buffer's start and length against the partition boundary, and the tensor's start partition against the legal set. The compare implementation, the boundary-check widths and any error signalling are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the six CC cores)** — The collective layer's controllers are the six CC cores: "6 CC-Cores for collective communication." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Trainium/Inferentia2 device diagram summary). AWS publishes no CC-core internals — no queue depths, no arbitration, no reduction datapath — so the CC core's internal primitives cannot be decomposed: the collective layer is documented at the level of counts and purpose, and this section does not invent the rest (Level-2 — unverifiable, fact records). The CC core is named here as a controller with unpublished internals.
- **SerDes (NeuronLink-v2 links)** — The chip-to-chip links are NeuronLink-v2: "2 (Inferentia2) or 4 (Trainium) NeuronLink-v2 for device-to-device collective communication." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium/Inferentia2 Architecture Guide for NKI, Trainium/Inferentia2 device diagram summary). The per-link rate is not published by AWS — secondary estimates range from 192 GiB/s to about 800 GB/s per chip (Level-2 — disputed, fact records). The SerDes lane count per link, the encoding, the signalling rate and the per-link clocking are not published.
- **Synchronizer (the chip-to-chip clock-domain crossing)** — Two chips are two clock domains, so the NeuronLink-v2 link is a clock-domain crossing by construction: the SerDes retiming that bridges it is part of what the collective's latency pays for. AWS publishes no synchronizer structure, no retiming scheme and no link latency, and this decomposition invents none of them.
- **Credit counter — no published flow control** — There is no published hardware flow control for NeuronLink-v2: no credit counters, no backpressure scheme and no published buffer accounting between chips. Flow control, as far as the published material goes, is the compiler's scheduling — the collectives are scheduled to overlap compute rather than serialise behind it (Level-2 — verified, fact records). A credit counter is therefore named here as absent from the published design, not as a primitive with unpublished parameters.
- **Compression engine (inline compression/decompression on the DMA path)** — The device DMA bandwidth is rated at 1 TB/s with inline memory compression/decompression: "Two NeuronCore-v2 delivering 380 INT8 TOPS, 190 FP16/BF16/cFP8/TF32 TFLOPS, and 47.5 FP32 TFLOP. 32 GiB of device memory (for storing model state), with 820 GiB/sec of bandwidth. 1 TB/sec of DMA bandwidth, with inline memory compression/decompression." (verified — AWS Neuron, Trainium Architecture, Trainium chip specification table) — so there is a compression engine on the DMA path, between the HBM and the SBUF. Its algorithm, its compression ratio, its datapath width and whether it sits per DMA engine or shared across the device are not published. The engine is named for its published function only.
- **Adder tree — none in the fabric** — There is no adder tree anywhere in the movement fabric: the all-reduce's adds are done by the receiving core's own engines — the same Vector Engine that does layer norms does the all-reduce's adds (Level-2 — verified, fact records) — not by the fabric. The fabric moves gradients and activations; the engines add them. The Vector Engine's adder tree is decomposed in the first block.
- **Pipeline registers (DMA data-path staging)** — A DMA transfer stages data between two memories at different rates — 27 GiB/s per engine against 820 GB/s of shared HBM — so the data path must be latched as it crosses the HBM interface, the compression engine and the SBUF interface. The stage count, the latch widths and the staging depth are not published.
- **Switch arbiter (HBM arbitration among 32 DMA engines — scheme unpublished)** — Thirty-two DMA engines share one 820 GiB/s HBM pool, so the HBM interface must arbitrate among engines that want the same stack in the same cycle — but AWS publishes no arbitration scheme, no priority rule, no fairness guarantee and no per-engine queue depth for the DMA engines. The published contract is the per-engine rate (27 GiB/s) and the device totals (32 engines, 820 GB/s HBM, 1 TB/s DMA). Any arbitration policy named here would be invention, so none is.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the NKI guide and the Trainium architecture page publish the geometry used above — 16 DMA engines per NeuronCore, each processing one transfer at a time at a peak of 27 GiB/s; the 128x512 FP32 load example as 16 transfers of 8 DMA buffers each; the 4 KiB free-dimension and ideally-128 partition-dimension rule; 2 HBM stacks with 32 GiB and 820 GB/s; 1 TB/s DMA bandwidth with inline memory compression/decompression; 6 CC cores; 2 NeuronLink-v2 links on Inferentia2 and 4 on Trainium; 16 Trainium chips per Trn1 instance — and the arithmetic is derived from those published counts. Below that level — DMA engine internals, scatter-gather list depths, CC-core internals, NeuronLink lane counts and signalling rate, HBM arbitration, the compression engine's algorithm — AWS publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no hardware flow control published for NeuronLink-v2, and there is no adder tree anywhere in the fabric, because the all-reduce's adds are done by the receiving core's Vector Engine, not by the movement fabric.
