### Groq LPU

#### Down to the primitives: The TSP streaming datapath — MXM, VXM and SXM chained as one spatial pipeline

Decomposed in trace order — weights install into the MXM planes, activations stream in on the stream registers, the MXM multiplies, the VXM requantises and activates, the SXM reshapes, and the ICU keeps 144 queues fed in lock-step. The ISCA 2020 paper publishes the datapath's whole contract — the supercell geometry and install rate, the 5,120-ALU mesh, the SXM's shifters, permuter, distributor and transposer, the 144 queues and the 640-byte Ifetch fill, the 35-cycle barrier — and the ALCF deck adds the stream register as a one-cycle hop and the per-hemisphere SXM counts, but neither publishes the circuits below that contract: no multiplier layout inside a supercell, no VXM ALU bit-widths, no permuter or distributor table sizes, no queue depths beyond the Ifetch fill. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **Multiplier array (the MXM supercell MACCs)** — Each of the four MXM planes is a 320x320 array of multiply-accumulate units — "The matrix execution module (MXM) provides four (4) independent 320x320 (Figure 7) planes of multiply-accumulate (MACC) units." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.D). Arithmetic from the published geometry: 320 x 320 = 102,400 MACCs per plane, 409,600 across the four planes. Each plane is built from twenty 16x16 supercells — "Each 320x320 plane is comprised of 20 16x16 supercells that produce a partial-sum each cycle and pass it to the adjacent tile for use in its computation." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.D). The multiplier count and layout inside one supercell are not published, so this entry names the array and its published geometry and does not expand the supercell into a MACC count the paper does not give.
- **Adder tree (MXM partial-sum accumulation)** — The supercells' partial sums are accumulated down the plane into one 320-element dot product per cycle, with accumulation in int32 or fp32 — "features output from the MXM can be accumulated using the accumulators on each int32 or fp32 output stream." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.D) — and the 320-element sum is produced "with only a single rounding step at the end to convert to int32 or fp32 results." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.D). If the contraction is deeper than one tile, the ACC instruction accumulates the plane's output across passes. The adder-tree depth, the accumulation order and the accumulator register widths beyond the int32/fp32 result types are not published.
- **Register file (the installed MXM weights)** — Weights are installed into the planes from streams and then held in place, one per MACC, until the next tile — "It requires 16 streams each with 16 bytes to install 256 8-bit weights (IW) in each supercell on every cycle." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.D) — and "Using all 32 streams in each direction allows us to emplace weights in both MXM planes simultaneously on both MXM hemispheres, loading all 409,600 weights on-chip in less than 40 cycles." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.D). Arithmetic from the published counts: 4 planes x 20 supercells x 256 weights per cycle = 20,480 weights per cycle, so all 409,600 install in 20 cycles, inside the published under-40-cycles bound. The weight registers' circuit form — SRAM cells or flip-flops — is not published.
- **Accumulator registers (the MXM output accumulators)** — Each int32 or fp32 output stream carries its own accumulator — "features output from the MXM can be accumulated using the accumulators on each int32 or fp32 output stream." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.D). Arithmetic from the published geometry: a 320-element output vector per plane across four planes gives 1,280 accumulator registers, each int32 or fp32 wide. The accumulator register implementation and the ACC instruction's accumulation timing are not published.
- **Stream registers (the chip-wide streaming register file)** — Streams are the datapath's only operand transport, implemented as a chip-wide register file — "Streams are implemented in hardware by a chip-wide streaming register file (SR)." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §I.B) — and each stream register is one hop of transit: "Stream Register = 1 hop" (verified — Groq, ALCF deck, interconnect slide). There are 64 logical streams per lane, 32 Eastward and 32 Westward, each element 1 byte, with wider types built from several streams. The execution-time model makes the register file's role explicit: the transit delay is "the distance (in cycles) between SRj and SRi" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III). How many physical stream registers the file holds and how they are banked are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (the 144 instruction queues)** — Each functional slice has its own instruction queue — "144 independent instruction queues (ICUs) on-chip, each can issue one or more instructions per cycle and the compiler has explicit control of the program order in each instruction queue." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §II). An Ifetch fills a queue with "640-bytes (a pair of 320-byte vectors) of instructions." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.A), and "It is imperative that IQs never go empty so that a precise notion of 'logical time' is maintained across the chip." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.A). The queue depth beyond the 640-byte fill and the per-queue issue width are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the ICU dispatch and staggered execution)** — The ICU is the datapath's sequencer: an instruction is issued to the bottom-most tile of a slice and propagates northward one tile per cycle until it has traversed all 20 tiles, while data flows east and west on the stream registers so instruction and operands meet at the compiler-chosen time and place. Each instruction carries temporal parameters — "dfunc functional delay" and "dskew instruction-operand skew" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III) — so the controller is a per-queue issue sequencer plus the stagger pipeline, not a dynamic scheduler. Removing that dynamic scheduling is why the ICU is small: the instruction control unit accounts for "less the 3% of the area." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §II). The sequencer's state count and decode depth are not published.
- **Comparator (the Sync/Notify barrier)** — The one chip-wide synchronisation is a barrier over all 144 queues: "One IQ is designated as the notifier and it issues a Notify instruction while all other IQs are parked on a Sync instruction — receipt of the Notify is broadcast to all the IQs to satisfy the pending Sync and begin processing instructions again." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.A). At the primitive level that is a completion-compare — an AND-reduction over the 143 parked queues' Sync state plus the notifier's Notify — which completes in 35 cycles: "A chip-wide barrier synchronization can be accomplished in 35 clock cycles, from the time the Notify is issued to the time the Sync is satisfied and retired to allow subsequent instructions to flow." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.A). The AND-reduction construction is the standard one for a barrier, labelled as such; the reduction-tree depth and fan-in are not published.
- **Counter (the NOP repeat count and logical time)** — Temporal separation between instructions is counted, not arbitrated: "A NOP has a repeat count 16-bit field which allows 1 NOP to wait from 1 ns up to 65 us for a 1GHz clock." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.A). The repeated NOP "is implemented in the ICU's tile and common to all functional slices" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.A) and lets the slice "turn off the clock enables when NOP-ing for anything longer than a few cycles" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.A). Behind it the compiler "tracks the state of 144 independent program queues on a cycle-by-cycle basis" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.A), so logical time is a counted quantity. The counter's implementation and the clock-gating granularity are not published.
- **Multiplier array (the VXM 4x4 ALU mesh)** — Each superlane is a 4x4 mesh of vector ALUs — "Each superlane implements a 4x4 mesh of vector ALUs capable of doing x16-SIMD computations — 16 vector ALUs per lane." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.C) — for "a total of 5,120 vector ALUs on-chip, capable of 32-bit fixed and floating point operations." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §VII). Arithmetic from the published geometry: 320 lanes x 16 ALUs = 5,120. Each ALU's 32-bit input operands "are organized along naturally aligned quad-stream group (SG4)." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.C). The ALUs "do not produce condition codes or status flags" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.C); instead the VXM provides saturating and modulo variants (add_sat, add_mod, mul_sat, mul_mod). The ALU bit-widths beyond the published data types and the mesh's internal routing are not published.
- **Mux / demux (VXM ALU chaining)** — Two or more ALUs in a lane can be chained so an intermediate result feeds the next ALU directly — "The TSP supports chaining together two or more vector ALUs within each lane, allowing multiple ALU operations to be performed without committing the intermediate results to main memory, saving a write and subsequent read of each intermediate result." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.C). At the primitive level that is a mux per ALU input selecting between the stream register and the previous ALU's output. The chaining mux radix, the bypass timing and the number of chainable stages are not published.
- **Mux / demux (the SXM lane-shifter select)** — The SXM shifts vectors north and south in pairs and selects the wanted elements — "The SXM provides two sets of lane shifters that execute shift instructions (Figure 8) both North and South. The lane-shifters are usually allocated in pairs since we typically shift a vector up or down and select which elements we want from either (i) North-shifted, (ii) South-shifted, or (iii) unshifted data elements" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.E). At the primitive level that is a 3-way mux per lane, fed by the north shifter, the south shifter and the unshifted stream. The shift amounts, the shifter implementation and the select timing are not published.
- **Crossbar (the SXM permuter)** — The permuter remaps whole vectors across the chip's 320 lanes — "the SXM provides a permute instruction which employs a programmed bijection to remap the 320 lanes on a set of similarly indexed streams, one per superlane." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.E). Groq's deck places one permuter/shifter per hemisphere: "Permuter/Shifter: arbitrary mapping of input + mask, shuffling between 320B vector elements" (verified — Groq, ALCF deck, SXM slide). Architecturally that is a crossbar with a programmed select per output lane. The permutation table's size, storage form and select-line fan-out are not published.
- **Mux / demux (the SXM distributor)** — The distributor remaps lanes inside one superlane — "The distributor slice within the SXM is used to arbitrarily remap the 16 lanes within each superlane. As streams pass through the distributor, they can be remapped at full bandwidth, or zero-fill any or all of the 16 elements." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.E). Groq's deck gives four distributors per hemisphere: "Distributor: 4 per hemisphere" (verified — Groq, ALCF deck, SXM slide), each mapping "input + mask to output stream within a 16 byte superlane" (verified — Groq, ALCF deck, SXM slide). The mapping table's size and storage form are not published.
- **Crossbar (the SXM transposer)** — The transposer exchanges rows and columns across 16 streams — "A transpose operation takes 16 incoming streams and produces 16 output streams with the rows and columns exchanged." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.E) — over "a two-dimension transpose of 256 elements organized as 16 streams each with 16 elements" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.E). There are two SXM instances, one per hemisphere, each able to issue two transpose instructions, "yielding a maximum of four (4) simultaneous transpose 16x16 operations." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.E); the deck gives "Transposer: 2 per hemisphere" (verified — Groq, ALCF deck, SXM slide). The transposer's internal storage — registers or SRAM — is not published.
- **Barrel shifter (the SXM rotate)** — Rotate generates every rotation of a small block at once: the ISA table defines Rotate as rotating n x n input data to generate n-squared output streams with all possible rotations, for n=3 or n=4 (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III, instruction table). At the primitive level that is a barrel shifter producing all n rotations of the n-by-n block in parallel, feeding the n-squared output streams. The shifter's implementation and the rotate latency are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the ISCA 2020 paper and the Groq ALCF deck publish the datapath geometry used above — four 320x320 MXM planes, twenty 16x16 supercells per plane, 256 weights installed per supercell per cycle, 5,120 vector ALUs, 64 streams per lane, 144 instruction queues, the 640-byte Ifetch fill, the 35-cycle barrier, the 16-bit NOP repeat count, the four simultaneous 16x16 transposes, the 4 distributors and 2 transposers per hemisphere. Below that level — supercell multiplier layout, VXM ALU bit-widths, permuter and distributor table sizes, instruction-queue depths, the shifter select timing — Groq publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no general-purpose register file and no arbiter anywhere in the datapath, because streams are the only operand transport and the compiler schedules every interception.

#### Down to the primitives: The SRAM-only memory system and the deterministic chip-to-chip fabric — 220 MiB of flat SRAM and software-scheduled RealScale links

Decomposed in trace order — a MEM read creates a 320-byte stream, the vector crosses the chip on stream registers, a Send pushes it onto a C2C link as one flit, the receiving chip emplaces it straight into its SRAM, and the HAC keeps both chips on the same epoch. The two ISCA papers publish the fabric's whole contract — the 88 slices and 2 banks, the 8,192 addresses per slice, the 16 x4 links at 30 Gbps, the 320-byte flit at 97.5 percent encoding efficiency, the 252-cycle HAC epoch, the DESKEW instructions, the measured 216-217-cycle link latency — and the ALCF deck adds the quad timing groups and the 80 TB/s on-die figure, but neither paper publishes the circuits below that contract: no SRAM bank organisation, no SerDes internals, no encoder logic, no per-slice queue depths. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **SRAM bank (the MEM slice pseudo-dual-port SRAM)** — Each MEM slice is two banks of pseudo-dual-port SRAM — "Each MEM slice contains pseudo-dual-port SRAMs that are capable of servicing a pair of read and write requests simultaneously assuming they are not targeting the same bank." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.B) — with "up to 176-way memory concurrency — 88 slices each with 2 banks" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.B). Each slice holds 2.5 MiB in 20 tiles of 8,192 16-byte words, and the deck adds that the slices are "each arranged into quad timing groups" (verified — Groq, ALCF deck, MEM slide). The bank bit is exposed in the ISA so the compiler manages the banks explicitly. How each bank is organised into rows, columns and sense amplifiers, and the bank line widths, are not published.
- **Address decoder (MEM slice row decode)** — A MEM slice holds 8,192 addresses — "88 independent MEM slices with 8192 addresses (220MiB)" (verified — Groq, ALCF deck, MEM slide) — so the slice address is 13 bits by arithmetic (2^13 = 8,192). Reads and writes use direct addressing, "since the address is fully specified in the instruction itself" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.B), while gather and scatter use stream-indirect addressing, where "the physical address comes from the stream value, providing a layer of indirection in the memory referencing." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.B). The decoder's structure — row decoder, column muxes, pre-decode — is not published.
- **Mux / demux (the bank select)** — The pseudo-dual-port behaviour is a bank select: the compiler reads operands from one bank and writes results to the other in the same cycle, because the two banks can be serviced simultaneously "assuming they are not targeting the same bank." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.B). The transpose path uses exactly this: "we take advantage the pseudo-dual-ported SRAM for dual read/write access per slice with a read of inputs from one bank and a write of the results to the opposite bank of the SRAM." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §IV.A). The bank-select mux's radix, timing and conflict handling when both accesses target the same bank are not published.
- **SRAM bank (the instruction-dispatch slices)** — Program text lives in the same SRAM as data: "the compiler reserves several MEM slices to serve as 'instruction dispatch' slices where the machine-coded instructions are stored and supplied on streams to service Ifetch instructions on different functional slices where the instructions will eventually be executed." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §IV). An Ifetch then fills a queue with 640 bytes from those streams. How many slices are reserved for dispatch, and how the compiler lays program text across them, are not published.
- **FIFO / queue — none in the memory system or fabric** — There is no queue anywhere on the data path: a read from a MEM slice creates a 320-byte stream and a write terminates one, and a vector in flight is held in stream registers, not in a buffer. The same holds off-chip — the 2022 paper's flow-control section states the network has no packet headers, no routing tables, no queues, no virtual channels and no backpressure (Level-2 — verified, fact records). A vector is never stored in flight in a queue, so there is no store-and-forward, no head-of-line blocking and no queueing delay to decompose.
- **Switch arbiter — none in the fabric** — There is no switch arbiter in the fabric either: the compiler schedules every vector onto a specific link at a specific cycle, and "the hardware is disallowed from asserting back pressure which would disrupt deterministic operation of the network." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §2.3). Two vectors never contend for the same link in the same cycle because the compiler's schedule guarantees it in advance — the arbitration happens at compile time, in the scheduler, not in silicon at run time. That compile-time arbitration is exactly why multi-chip latency is a contract value rather than a distribution.
- **Crossbar (the X-dimension stream mesh between slices)** — Streams move between slices on a routed mesh — "the on-chip network is implemented as X-dim mesh and Y-dim mesh of tiles with X-Y dimension order routing. Each instruction specifies the first hop direction (East or West), so memory instruction semantics have both an address and a dataflow direction" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §I.B). Streams are "routed in the X-dimension through MEM, and routed in the Y-dimension using the SXM's permuter and laneshifters" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §I.B), one stream-register hop per cycle, and a slice can turn a stream around — streams "can be logically 'turned around' (ie. reverse their direction of flow from East-to-West, or vice versa) at any slice." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §II.E). The mesh's per-tile switching radix and port counts are not published beyond this routing contract.
- **SerDes (the C2C links)** — Each of the sixteen C2C links is four serial lanes — "The first TSP implementation (Figure 5) has a total of sixteen (16) x4 links operating at 30 Gbps each for a total off-chip bandwidth of 16 x4 x30Gb/s x2 directions = 3.84 Tb/s of off-chip pin bandwidth" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §II) — normally operated at 25 Gbps per lane, "with a combined bandwidth of 100 Gbps across the four lanes in a link." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §2.3). The SerDes rate and lane count are published; equalisation, clocking, lane-bonding and the physical-layer coding are not published.
- **Encoder (the flit encoding)** — A whole 320-byte vector goes onto a link as one flit — "a vector is the flow control unit (flit)." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §2.3) — with "an encoding efficiency of 97.5% (320/328 bytes)" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, Fig. 11). Arithmetic from the published figures: 328 - 320 = 8 bytes of overhead per flit. There are no packet headers to encode, because the flit carries no header at all. The encoder's logic and the 8 overhead bytes' contents are not published.
- **Counter (the hardware aligned counter, HAC)** — Each chip keeps its own free-running time reference — "Each TSP maintains a free-running internal hardware aligned counter (HAC) with a low (< 256 cycle) overflow period." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §3.1) — and the epoch is exactly 252 cycles: "the period is the epoch length or 252 clock cycles. The HAC is an 8-bit counter, but 4 values are reserved for special control codes." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §3.1). The counters are "continuously (every 256 cycles) exchanged to maintain a global consensus time" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §3.1), so each link's latency can be measured — measured intra-node latency is about 216-217 cycles. The counter's exchange mechanism and the latency-measurement registers are not published.
- **FSM / controller (DESKEW and RUNTIME_DESKEW)** — DESKEW aligns execution to epoch boundaries — "When a functional unit executes a DESKEW, it will pause issuing subsequent instructions on that functional unit until the next time the HAC overflows or the epoch boundary." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §3.2). Mid-program drift is corrected by RUNTIME_DESKEW: "To reconcile the local vs global time, a RUNTIME_DESKEW instruction is provided in the ISA. The instruction takes a single parameter" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §3.3) — a delay value plus or minus a skew delta, which stalls the TSP by that amount. The DESKEW controller's state and the stall counter's width are not published.
- **Synchronizer (plesiochronous link alignment)** — The chips do not share a clock — the links are plesiochronous, and the SXM's deskew instruction exists to align data across them: the ISA table gives "Deskew: Manage skew across plesiochronous links" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III, instruction table). Alignment is done by the HAC epoch and the DESKEW instructions, not by per-link synchronizer hardware: the papers describe no two-flop synchronizer or phase aligner at the link, and the measured intra-node link latency of about 216-217 cycles is a booked compile-time value, not a synchronizer delay. The deskew logic's implementation is not published.
- **Credit counter — none in the fabric** — There is no credit-based flow control in the fabric: "the hardware is disallowed from asserting back pressure which would disrupt deterministic operation of the network." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §2.3). Instead the compiler schedules every vector onto a specific link at a specific cycle, so the transmitter never overflows and the receiver never underflows by construction — the schedule is the flow control, and there is no credit counter, no buffer-occupancy tracking and no throttle signal to decompose.
- **Pipeline registers (virtual cut-through staging in SRAM)** — A vector travelling more than one hop is staged in the intermediate chip's own SRAM — "a vector is the flow control unit (flit). Since the network path is fully deterministic, a tensor consisting of one or more vector flits can be scheduled using virtual cut through flow control since the receiving TSP can immediately begin sending vectors to the next-hop of the tensor's path." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §2.3). At the destination, a Receive emplaces the vector directly into the destination chip's MEM at the address the compiler chose when it scheduled the transfer, so the vector never passes through a queue or a buffer pool, because there is none (Level-2 — verified, fact records). The staging is the SRAM itself, so the pipeline registers here are the MEM banks, already decomposed above.
- **XOR tree / ECC check (SECDED over SRAM and stream registers)** — Every 128-bit memory word carries 9 check bits — "they are stored alongside the 128-bit memory word as 9-bit ECC, 137-bits in total. The ECC scheme implements SECDED (single-error correction with double-error detection) to allow us to tolerate a single-bit error in the memory word or anywhere along the streaming data path." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §II.D). The check bits are generated only at the producer — "we take advantage of the producer-consumer nature of the stream programming model and generate ECC check bits only at the producer" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §II.D) — which avoids replicating the XOR tree across the wide word, and a consuming slice checks the bits "to ensure data integrity before operating on it" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §II.D). Corrected errors are recorded in a control and status register. The XOR tree's depth and the check-bit generation timing are not published.
- **FSM / controller (source-based Dragonfly routing)** — Each TSP is both endpoint and router — "The TSP acts as both a processing element (endpoint) and network switch for moving tensors across the communication links." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §1) — and routing is source-based and compile-time: "The pin-bandwidth from each TSP is partitioned into 7 local links and 4 global links." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §2.2), with the 7 local links fully connecting the 8 TSPs of a node and the 4 global links building 32-port virtual routers. There is no routing table in silicon: the compiler writes each vector's link and cycle into the program, and the chip executes the schedule. The routing controller's state — the schedule itself, held in the instruction-dispatch slices — is the program text, already decomposed above.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the ISCA 2020 and 2022 papers and the Groq ALCF deck publish the fabric geometry used above — 88 MEM slices, 2 banks per slice, 8,192 addresses per slice, 2.5 MiB per slice, 16 x4 C2C links at 30 Gbps per lane (25 Gbps operating), the 320-byte flit, 97.5 percent encoding efficiency, the 8-bit HAC with a 252-cycle epoch, the 216-217-cycle measured link latency, the 7 local and 4 global links per TSP. Below that level — SRAM bank organisation, address-decoder structure, SerDes equalisation and clocking, encoder logic, per-slice queue depths — Groq publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Three things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no FIFO/queue, no switch arbiter and no credit counter anywhere in the fabric, because flow control is the compiler's static schedule, not hardware.

Source: Groq Language Processing Unit (LPU) Architecture, Architecture Empowering Software — interconnect slide (Eastward and westward paths made up of arrays of stream registers).
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — SXM has 4 distributors and 2 transposers per hemisphere, plus a permuter/shifter per hemisphere. Source: Groq Language Processing Unit (LPU) Architecture, SXM slide (GroqChip v1).
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — Each MEM slice has 8,192 addresses and the slices are arranged into quad timing groups. Source: Groq Language Processing Unit (LPU) Architecture, MEM slide (GroqChip v1).
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — HAC epoch is exactly 252 clock cycles; the HAC is an 8-bit counter with 4 values reserved for special control codes. Source: A Software-defined Tensor Streaming Multiprocessor for Large-scale Machine Learning, Section 3.1 Hardware aligned counters (HAC).
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — Per-TSP hardware aligned counters are continuously (every 256 cycles) exchanged to maintain a global consensus time. Source: A Software-defined Tensor Streaming Multiprocessor for Large-scale Machine Learning, Section 3.1 Hardware aligned counters (HAC).
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — A NOP has a 16-bit repeat count field, allowing one NOP to wait from 1 ns up to 65 us at a 1 GHz clock. Source: Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, Section III.A Instruction control unit (ICU), item 1 (No-op).
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — Each VXM ALU's 32-bit input operands are organised along naturally aligned quad-stream groups (SG4). Source: Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, Section III.C Vector (VXM) processor.
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — SXM Deskew manages skew across plesiochronous links. Source: Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, Section III, instruction table.
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — SXM Rotate rotates n x n input data to generate n-squared output streams with all possible rotations, for n=3 or n=4. Source: Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, Section III, instruction table.
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — 16 streams each with 16 bytes install 256 8-bit weights in each MXM supercell every cycle. Source: Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, Section III.D Matrix execution module (MXM).
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — MXM output features can be accumulated using the accumulators on each int32 or fp32 output stream. Source: Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, Section III.D Matrix execution module (MXM).
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — 1,280 MXM accumulator registers (4 planes x 320-element output vector), each int32 or fp32 wide. Source: Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, Section III.D Matrix execution module (MXM).
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — MEM slice address is 13 bits (2^13 = 8,192 addresses per slice). Source: Groq Language Processing Unit (LPU) Architecture, MEM slide (GroqChip v1).
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — Flit overhead is 8 bytes (328 - 320 bytes per flit). Source: A Software-defined Tensor Streaming Multiprocessor for Large-scale Machine Learning, Section 2.3, Figure 11.
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — The compiler reserves several MEM slices as instruction-dispatch slices, where program text is stored and supplied on streams to service Ifetch instructions. Source: Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, Section IV ResNet50.
- [verified] **Groq LPU** — Streams are implemented in hardware by a chip-wide streaming register file (SR). Source: Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, Section I.B Parallel lanes and streams.
- [unverifiable] **Groq LPU** — No published MXM supercell multiplier layout, no VXM ALU bit-widths beyond the published data types, no SXM permuter or distributor table sizes, no SRAM bank organisation beyond slice/tile/bank counts, no C2C SerDes internals beyond signalling rate and lane count, no instruction-queue depth beyond the 640-byte Ifetch fill, and no per-link synchronizer hardware described in either paper. Source: Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, Whole documents — architecture sections (absence of supercell, ALU, SXM-table, bank, SerDes, queue-depth and synchronizer internals across the documents).

Note: the Level-2 facts re-used in this section (the vertical functional slices and 20-tile stacks, the 320-lane SIMD slice and 16-element minimum vector, the four 320x320 MXM planes and twenty 16x16 supercells per plane, the under-40-cycle weight install, the 5,120 VXM ALUs in a 4x4 mesh per superlane with chaining, the SXM shifters/permuter/distributor/transposer/rotate/deskew, the 64 streams per lane with 1-byte elements, the 144 instruction queues with 640-byte Ifetch fills, the ICU under 3 percent of die area and the 35-cycle chip-wide barrier, the 88 MEM slices of 2.5 MiB with 8,192 16-byte words per tile and pseudo-dual-port 2-bank organisation for 176-way concurrency, the 55 TiB/s SRAM and 20 TiB/s stream-register bandwidth equations, the 16 x4 C2C links at 30 Gbps per lane (25 Gbps operating) carrying 320-byte flits at 97.5 percent encoding efficiency, the HAC epoch and DESKEW/RUNTIME_DESKEW synchronisation, the measured 216-217-cycle intra-node link latency, the software-scheduled Dragonfly topology with 7 local and 4 global links per TSP, the 264-TSP / 56 GiB and 10,440-TSP / 5-hop / under-3-us scale figures, the 50-to-14 GB/s global-bandwidth profile, the disputed 750 INT8 TOPS / 188 FP16 TFLOPS vendor figures and the unverifiable Level-2 scope boundary) were already recorded at Level-2 with the same quotes and sources and were deduped, not re-appended.
### SambaNova SN40L

#### Down to the primitives: The PCU/PMU tile pair and the three-fabric RDN — the reconfigurable spatial fabric

Decomposed in trace order — a matmul tile enters the PCU header, sweeps the systolic body through the broadcast buffer, drains through the tail, and leaves on the vector fabric; the PMU's scalar ALU pipeline generates the addresses, its alignment crossbars reshape the vectors, and the RDN's three fabrics, flow IDs, sequence IDs and credit counters move every packet. The arXiv paper and the Hot Chips deck publish the fabric's whole contract — the header/body/tail datapath, the broadcast buffer, the cross-lane reduction tree, the counters, the tail functions, the SRAM array, the 4-addresses-per-cycle ALU pipeline, the alignment crossbars, the input/output FIFOs, the three fabrics, the flow-ID and sequence-ID mechanisms and the credit flow control — but neither publishes the circuits below that contract: no PCU lane count (the deck says only M lanes), no PCU stage count, no PMU bank count or organisation, no RDN switch radix or port counts, no FIFO depths, no crossbar radices, no SLB entry count. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **Pipeline registers and stage muxes (the PCU header, body and tail)** — The PCU datapath is three sections — "The PCU's datapath consists of a header, body, and tail." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A). "The header consumes incoming dataflows and drives the body section." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A), and "The tail performs special element-wise functions and drives the output FIFOs." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A). The body is "a pipelined SIMD core with multiple stages of vector compute" (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A), so each stage boundary is a pipeline register holding one vector operand per lane, and the body's configuration — systolic array or SIMD core — is selected by stage muxes set at compile time. The PCU stage count is not published, so no register count is claimed.
- **Broadcast buffer (the systolic input staging)** — Systolic inputs are fanned out through the broadcast buffer: "Inputs to the systolic array are streamed left-to-right and top-to-bottom through a structure called broadcast buffer." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A). The buffer stages each input element once and broadcasts it across the systolic lanes, so one fetch feeds many multipliers and the weights are not re-fetched per multiply. Whether the buffer is built from registers or SRAM, and its depth and width, are not published.
- **Multiplier array (the systolic MACCs)** — The PCU body is "configurable as an output stationary systolic array or as a pipelined SIMD core with multiple stages of vector compute" (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A), and "The systolic array accelerates matrix multiplications like Gemm0 and Gemm1" (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A). Each array element multiplies its streamed input by its weight in place. The deck states the PCU is "Configurable as a systolic array or a SIMD vector unit with M lanes" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L PCU slide) — the lane count is M, not published, so no multiplier count is claimed. In SIMD configuration each stage supports "common arithmetic, logical, and bit-wise operations in FP32, BF16, and INT32 formats" (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A), with INT8 added by the deck.
- **Accumulator registers (the output-stationary partial sums)** — In output-stationary mode the partial sums stay in place in the array while inputs stream past, and "Accumulated results are drained left-to-right to output FIFOs through the tail unit." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A). Each stationary sum is an accumulator register, one per systolic element, holding the running total until the tile is finished. The accumulator count and width beyond the published data types are not published.
- **Adder tree and muxes (the cross-lane reduction network)** — Reductions across lanes run through the optional cross-lane network: "The PCU can be configured to implement an optional cross-lane reduction network, shown as the blue triangle in the figure. Lane-wise reductions are also supported, in pure SIMD fashion." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A). The deck calls it "A cross-lane reduction tree (blue) to reduce along the vectorized dimension" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L PCU slide). At the primitive level that is an adder tree across the lanes with muxes selecting which lanes feed it. The tree depth, fan-in and lane count are not published.
- **Counter and FSM (the PCU loop counters and loop-done control events)** — Loop completion is counted, not polled: "Counters track loop iterations and generate control events when they reach the programmed maximum value, indicating that a loop has completed execution." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A). Those events travel on the control fabric: "Control tokens typically correspond to counter 'done' events that indicate the end of a loop, as discussed briefly in Section IV-A." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A). The counter width and the event-generation FSM's state count are not published.
- **Function units (the PCU tail — transcendental, RNG, stochastic rounding, format conversion)** — The tail finishes each tile: "The tail section supports transcendental functions, random number generation, stochastic rounding, and format conversions. A tail operation can be fused and pipelined with compute in the body section." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-A). The deck adds: "Tail stage provides transcendental functions, casting, and stochastic rounding capabilities" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L PCU slide). How the transcendental functions are implemented — tables, iterative logic or otherwise — is not published.
- **SRAM bank (the PMU scratchpad SRAM instances)** — The PMU's memory is an array of SRAM banks: "Each PMU contains a programmer-managed scratchpad memory that is organized as an array of SRAM instances. The SRAM array collectively supports concurrent writes and reads." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-B). The deck repeats it: "Programmer managed scratchpad memory supports concurrent reads and writes" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L PMU slide). Geometry: 520 MiB of PMU SRAM across 1,040 PMUs is 0.5 MiB per PMU by arithmetic from the published totals. The PMU bank count and organisation are not published.
- **Address decoder and comparator (PMU bank-bit decode and address predication)** — Each generated address is decoded to a bank and checked before it is used: "addresses are mapped to scratchpad banks using bank bit locations that can be programmed by software" (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-B), and "each PMU can be programmed with a range of valid addresses for that PMU, or a programmable predicate bit per generated address. An addresses is processed if it is within the programmed range or a valid predicate, and dropped otherwise." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-B). At the primitive level that is a bank-bit decoder plus a range/predicate comparator per generated address. The bank count, the comparator width and the predicate storage are not published.
- **Integer ALU array (the PMU scalar ALU pipeline)** — The PMU generates its own addresses in hardware: "A PMU contains several stages of integer ALUs that can be configured to generate read and write addresses concurrently to flexibly access a tensor in the scratchpad." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-B). "PMU ALUs implement a set of special complex instructions like bitfield extraction and shift-and-set, that are frequently used in address computations." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-B). The deck gives the rate: "Fragmentable, address-generation pipeline that can produce 4 addresses per cycle" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L PMU slide). "It can be partitioned into independent read and write address generation pipelines with a software-configured number of stages allocated to each of them." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-B). The stage count is software-configured and not published as a number, so no ALU count is claimed.
- **Crossbar (the PMU data-alignment crossbars)** — Reshaping happens in the alignment unit, not in the PCU: "The data alignment unit supports common tensor transformation operations like transpose, cross-lane vector permute, vector-unaligned accesses, lookup table (LUT), data format, and data layout conversions." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-B). The deck names the mechanism: "Data alignment crossbars enable high throughput tensor transformations such as transpose, dilation, downcast" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L PMU slide). "Tensors to be transposed are written in a special diagonally striped format across the scratchpad banks that enables reading the same tensor in both regular and transposed format at full bandwidth." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-B). SN40L "augment[s] the data alignment units with high throughput programmable lane shuffles and masking" (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-E). The crossbar radix and the LUT table sizes are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (the RDN input and output FIFOs at every unit)** — Every packet enters and leaves a unit through a FIFO: "inbound scalar and vector packets to units from switches land in input FIFOs, and exit via output FIFOs" (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-C). The PMU deck diagram shows the same FIFOs as PMU components — Scalar In FIFO, Scalar Out FIFO, Vector In FIFO, Vector Out FIFO (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L PMU slide). SN40L adds a use for them: "input FIFOs added support for programmable out-of-order peeks, so that small tensors with a streaming-write-and-reread access pattern can directly be stored in the input FIFO of consumers without consuming a PMU scratchpad." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-E). FIFO depths are not published.
- **Crossbar and switch arbiter (the RDN mesh switches)** — The fabric is a switched mesh, one switch per tile: "The RDN is implemented using a mesh of non-blocking switches." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-C). The deck describes it as a "Mesh Interconnect made of 3 physical networks: Vector: Carries data, Packet Switched; Scalar: Carries addresses, other metadata, Packet Switched; Control: Carries flow control, synchronization and graph orchestration tokens" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L Unit-Level Interconnect slide). At each switch a crossbar moves packets between ports under an arbiter; the switch radix and port counts are not published, and the arbiter structure is not published — non-blocking is the paper's word for the switch behaviour, not a published circuit.
- **Comparator / decoder (flow-ID decode and rewrite at every switch port)** — Static routes are recognised by flow ID at every hop: "In static flow routing, software assigns a flow ID field to a packet stream, which is carried with the packet. The flow ID field is decoded at every switch port and reassigned prior to forwarding the packet to its next destination. The static flow routing mechanism supports packet multi-casting through the switches." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-C). SN40L changed the allocation to a label-swapping scheme: "Each flow is assigned a sequence of flow IDs at compile time, which are programmed into the switch flow tables. As packets flow through switches, the flow ID field in the packet is rewritten using the switch flow tables." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-E). The alternative is dynamic routing: "Routing of packets on the scalar and vector fabrics is done either dynamically using a 2-D dimension order route or as software-controlled static flow routes" (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-C) — the deck calls it "Hardware 2-D dimension order routing (DOR) with software override" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L Unit-Level Interconnect slide). Flow-table sizes and depths are not published.
- **Comparator / address logic (the sequence-ID reorder logic)** — Many-to-one streams are reassembled by sequence ID: "Vector packets contain a metadata field called sequence ID, which is the primary mechanism to support arbitrary many-to-one streams on-chip. Vector output ports of units are equipped with programmable logic to generate sequence IDs for each output vector." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-C). "The sequence ID field is used as an input operand in a PMU to compute the write addresses to reorder the packets." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-C). The sequence-ID width and the reorder logic's implementation are not published.
- **Credit counter (RDN credit-based flow control)** — Flow control is counted at every hop: "Transmissions on the vector and scalar fabric are subject to credit-based flow control at every hop. Packet streams are also end-to-end flow controlled between communicating units on the RDN through a combination of coarse-grained software tokens, fine-grained hardware credits, and forward progress guarantees in hardware." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-C). The deck states it as "Flow control with packet-level E2E credits, or Tensor-level software control tokens" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L Unit-Level Interconnect slide). At the primitive level each hop holds a credit counter per output, decremented on send and incremented on credit return. Counter widths and FIFO depths are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the arXiv paper and the Hot Chips 2024 deck publish the fabric geometry used above — 1,040 PCUs and 1,040 PMUs per socket, 520 MiB of PMU SRAM, the header/body/tail datapath, the broadcast buffer, the cross-lane reduction tree, the 4-addresses-per-cycle PMU address pipeline, the data-alignment crossbars, the three RDN fabrics, the flow-ID and sequence-ID mechanisms, the credit-based flow control. Below that level — PCU lane and stage counts, PMU bank count and organisation, RDN switch radix and port counts, input/output FIFO depths, crossbar radices, flow-table sizes, sequence-ID widths, credit-counter widths — SambaNova publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. One thing is absent by design and is stated as such: there is no dynamic scheduler anywhere in the tile, because the compiler's place-and-route fixes every route, flow ID, sequence ID and credit arrangement at compile time.

#### Down to the primitives: The three-tier memory system and the AGCU at the fabric edge — DDR → HBM → PMU SRAM promotion

Decomposed in trace order — an expert switch starts with the AGCU's address pipeline generating DDR reads, the Segment Lookaside Buffer translating them, the requests crossing the TLN Request network, the weights returning on the Data network, the AGCU coalescing the replies, and the weights promoting DDR to HBM to PMU SRAM ahead of the tokens. The paper and the Hot Chips deck publish the memory system's whole contract — the three tiers and their bandwidths, the AGCU's address pipeline and counters, the Segment Lookaside Buffer, the P2P protocol, the three-command kernel launch, the four TLN networks with Y-X routing and end-to-end credits, the die-to-die interface and the PCIe DMA host link — but neither publishes the circuits below that contract: no AGCU queue depths or coalescing window, no SLB entry count or organisation, no TLN link rates, no die-to-die bandwidth, no DMA queue depths, no memory-controller queue depths. Where a parameter below comes from published geometry it is stated as published; where a number is computed from that geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **Integer ALU array (the AGCU scalar address-generation pipeline)** — The AGCU generates off-chip addresses with the PMU's address logic, minus the memory: "It is equipped with a scalar address generation pipeline and counters, bearing some similarities to the PMU logic (sans SRAM)." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-D). The pipeline produces the DDR and HBM read and write addresses for expert-weight promotions and sparse gathers, instead of the scratchpad addresses the PMU pipeline produces. Its stage count and addresses-per-cycle are not published — the 4-addresses-per-cycle figure belongs to the PMU pipeline, not the AGCU, and is not repeated here.
- **Counter (the AGCU counters)** — The AGCU tracks its own iteration state: "It is equipped with a scalar address generation pipeline and counters, bearing some similarities to the PMU logic (sans SRAM)." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-D). The counters sequence the request streams the AGCU generates for each promotion and each kernel launch, in the same way the PCU counters sequence loop iterations on the tile. Counter widths and counts are not published.
- **CAM / TCAM (the Segment Lookaside Buffer)** — Device virtual addresses are translated at the fabric edge: "It also provides an address translation layer for memory management." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-D). The deck names the structure: "Segment Lookaside Buffer for virtual-physical address translation and memory access management" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L AGCU slide). A lookaside buffer is a lookup keyed by segment, so it is named here as a CAM/TCAM-style lookup — the standard construction for a translation lookaside buffer — but SambaNova publishes no SLB entry count, key width or internal organisation, so no size is claimed and the CAM form is the standard construction, not a published fact about the SN40L.
- **FIFO / queue (the AGCU request-coalescing buffers)** — Replies from off-chip memory are merged at the AGCU: "On the TLN-side, it generates read and write requests and coalesces the responses." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-D). The coalescing buffers hold requests in flight and responses awaiting merge into the streams the tile fabric consumes, so a burst of HBM or DDR replies becomes one ordered weight stream into the PMUs. The coalescing window and the buffer depths are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (the TLN Data, Request and Response network FIFOs)** — The Top Level Network carries three data-bearing packet streams: "Hybrid Mesh/Ring Packet Switched Interconnect with four physical networks: Data: Read and write data; Request: read and write requests; Response: Write acknowledgement and interrupts; Credit: End to end credit exchange" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L Top-Level Interconnect slide). Each of the Data, Request and Response networks queues its packets in FIFOs at the routers — requests out, data and acknowledgements back. FIFO depths and packet widths are not published.
- **Credit counter (the TLN Credit network)** — The TLN's fourth network carries nothing but credits: "Credit: End to end credit exchange" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L Top-Level Interconnect slide), and "All traffic is managed by end-to-end credits or guaranteed consumption to avoid deadlocks" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L Top-Level Interconnect slide). Each sender holds a credit counter per destination, decremented when a packet is sent and incremented when the Credit network returns a credit. Counter widths are not published.
- **Crossbar and FSM (the TLN router — Y-X dimension-order routing)** — TLN packets are switched by Y-X routing: "Routing of packets uses a Y-X DOR mechanism" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L Top-Level Interconnect slide), on a "Hybrid Mesh/Ring Packet Switched Interconnect" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L Top-Level Interconnect slide). At each router a crossbar switches packets between the mesh/ring ports and the local AGCU, host and memory ports, under a Y-X routing FSM that picks the output port from the destination. Router radix, port counts and link rates are not published.
- **Synchronizer and FIFO (the die-to-die interface)** — The two dies of a socket stream directly: "Die-to-Die (D2D) Interface: SN40L tile components can stream data between two dies directly without going through off-chip memory." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV). The two dies are separate clock domains on the CoWoS interposer, so the interface needs clock-domain synchronizers and staging FIFOs at the crossing. Die-to-die bandwidth is not published, and the synchronizer construction is not published.
- **FIFO / queue (the PCIe DMA engine queues)** — The host attaches over PCIe with DMA: "Host Interface: SN40L interfaces with a host x86 CPU using a PCIe link. This interface supports DMA between host and device off-chip memory as well as direct communication between the host and the tile." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV). The DMA engine queues host-to-device and device-to-host transfers, and the direct host-to-tile path lets the host reach a tile without going through device memory. Queue depths and the DMA channel count are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (the HBM and DDR controller request queues)** — Each memory controller queues the AGCUs' requests: "The DDR tier can have a peak memory capacity of 1.5 TiB at a peak bandwidth of over 200 GB/s. The HBM tier has 64 GiB of capacity with a peak bandwidth of about 2 TB/s per socket." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV). Table II gives the HBM figure as 1.8 TB/s; the paper text rounds it to about 2 TB/s. HBM at 1.8 TB/s against DDR at over 200 GB/s is a 9x gap by arithmetic from the published figures, which is why the compiler treats the tiers as a placement problem rather than a cache hierarchy. Controller queue depths and the controller count are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the P2P protocol engine)** — Collectives bypass memory entirely: "The AGCU supports a peer-to-peer (P2P) communication protocol to directly stream data between RDU tiles on different sockets without involving DDR or HBM. The P2P protocol provides the necessary primitives to build collective communication primitives between RDUs such as AllReduce." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-D). The P2P engine is a protocol FSM in the AGCU that opens a direct tile-to-tile stream across the TLN and the inter-socket links. Link rates and the engine's state count are not published.
- **Mux / demux (the AGCU tile-side RDN port selection)** — Tile-side the AGCU looks like any other dataflow core: "On the tile-side, it acts like a dataflow core by exposing RDN vector, scalar, and control ports." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-D). The AGCU multiplexes its three RDN ports onto the tile fabric on one side and the TLN on the other — vector data, scalar addresses and control tokens each take their own port, so the fabric sees the AGCU as a three-port dataflow core. Port widths are not published.
- **FSM / controller (the hardware-orchestrated kernel-launch schedule)** — Kernel launch is a three-command sequence held in the AGCU: "The AGCU implements a kernel launch mechanism which consists of sequence of three commands: Program Load, Argument Load, and Kernel Execute." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-D). "Hardware orchestration offloads a static kernel schedule to the dedicated hardware in the AGCUs, which significantly reduces the overheads." (verified — Prabhakar et al., arXiv:2405.07518, §IV-D). The deck adds: "Graph control interface to load and orchestrate graph execution" and "Enables RDU to orchestrate a schedule of graphs without host involvement" (verified — Prabhakar, Hot Chips 2024, SN40L AGCU slide). The schedule itself is the FSM's state, held in dedicated AGCU hardware; its size is not published. Measured effect, already recorded at Level-2: hardware orchestration speeds autoregressive decoding 1.4x to 8x over software orchestration.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the arXiv paper (Table II and §IV) and the Hot Chips 2024 deck publish the memory geometry used above — 520 MiB PMU SRAM, 64 GiB HBM at 1.8 TB/s per socket, up to 1.5 TiB DDR at over 200 GB/s per socket, 1,600 GB/s switching bandwidth with a Llama 3.1 8B switch under 0.01 s, the AGCU's scalar address-generation pipeline and counters, the Segment Lookaside Buffer, the four TLN networks, Y-X dimension-order routing, end-to-end credits, the die-to-die interface and PCIe DMA. Below that level — AGCU queue depths and coalescing window, SLB entry count and organisation, TLN link rates, die-to-die bandwidth, DMA and memory-controller queue depths — SambaNova publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. One thing is absent by design and is stated as such: there is no hardware cache anywhere in the three tiers, because the compiler manages every symbol's tier, lifetime and spill order explicitly.
