### Google Argos VCU

#### Down to the gates: The encoder core — one 2160p stream per core, ten cores per die

Google publishes no gate-level structure for the Argos encoder core — no netlist, no cell form, no macro organisation, no queue depth, no array banking. What follows takes each of the sixteen Level-3 primitives one level further, into the gates it is built from and the transistors those gates are built from, using the primer's bottom layer (universal NAND/NOR gates, latch and master–slave D flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder). Every gate structure below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled **standard construction**; it is never a claim about Google's actual implementation. The only Argos-specific numbers are the published geometries already recorded at Levels 2–3 and the arithmetic derived transparently from them — and where the paper's own figures don't multiply out, this section says so instead of picking one.

- **SRAM bank (the reference store)** — Rows of 6T SRAM cells (primer, bottom layer): each cell is two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors (2 more), 6 transistors per stored bit. The VP9 store's published geometry is exact: 768 × 192 = 147,456 pixels ("144K"), so assuming 8 bits per stored sample — the paper does not state the store's sample width, and VP9 10-bit content exists, so at 10 bits every total below scales by 10/8 — the store is 147,456 × 8 = 1,179,648 storage bits, i.e. 7,077,888 6T cell transistors for the data alone, before decoders, muxes and sense amplifiers. Behind the array sit a row decoder — a NAND/AND tree from the row address raising one of 192 wordlines, an 8-bit decode (2^7 = 128 < 192 ≤ 256) — transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) selecting the search window's columns, and latch-type differential sense amplifiers on the bitlines. The H.264 configuration needs a flag, not a total: the paper says the store grows to "394K pixels (2048 x 128)", but 2048 × 128 = 262,144, not 394,000 — the two figures don't multiply out. The 1.5× ratio is consistent with counting luma-plus-chroma samples (262,144 × 1.5 = 393,216 ≈ 394K), but the paper doesn't say that, so this section claims no transistor total from the "394K" figure; from the stated geometry alone, 262,144 pixels × 8 bits = 2,097,152 bits = 12,582,912 6T cell transistors, and the H.264 row decode is 7 bits (2^7 = 128 rows). The store evicts by LRU; the standard forms are per-line age counters or a PLRU choice-bit tree, and the paper publishes neither, so no eviction circuit is claimed. Error detection (not full ECC) is likewise standard form only: a parity bit per stored word with an XOR parity tree and a compare — the word width and parity coverage are not published. The store's bank count, port count and read/write turnaround are not published. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (stage decoupling with full backpressure)** — The standard circular-queue construction: entry storage in a D-flip-flop bank or a small SRAM array, plus write and read pointer counters — D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers (about 28-transistor mirror cells, primer) — plus full/empty comparators: XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree, the full flag stalling the upstream stage and the empty flag holding the downstream stage. The pointer width is log2 of the depth, and the depths and widths are not published, so no pointer width or storage-bit total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree + comparator (motion-estimation block matching)** — Scoring a candidate is a per-pixel difference accumulated into a total: each pixel pair passes through a subtractor (full-adder cells) and an absolute-value stage (an XOR/invert plus an incrementer, or a comparator-steered mux), and the differences collapse through an adder tree of full-adder cells — log2 levels deep in the number of pixels scored — into one score per candidate, with a comparator (XNOR per bit feeding an AND tree, or a subtractor whose sign bit is the verdict) keeping the best score so far. Which difference metric the core uses, how many candidates are scored in parallel and the tree depth are not published, so no adder count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (reference-frame selection)** — Selecting among up to three reference frames is a 3:1 mux per pixel bit: transmission gates (2 transistors per input leg) or a NAND/NOR tree, steered by the frame-select bits; VP9's compound prediction, which combines blocks from two frames, is an averaging adder behind the muxes (add the two pixel values, shift right by one). The mux radix, the frame-selection table and the compound-prediction datapath are not published, so no mux count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (bounded recursive partition search)** — A control FSM: state bits in D flip-flops, next-state and output logic as a NAND/NOR network, walking the bounded recursion — descend into a sub-block, score it, decide split-or-stop, backtrack. The recursion bound, the state count and the traversal order are not published, so no state-bit count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree + comparator (the RDO cost comparison)** — Each candidate's cost is distortion plus rate: an adder tree accumulates the distortion, a second addition folds in the rate term, and a comparator keeps the cheapest candidate seen. The programmable round count is a counter in this controller (see Counter): D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer and a terminal-count comparator. The candidate count, the cost widths and the approximate encode/decode datapath are not published, so no adder or comparator count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (transform and 1/8-pixel interpolation)** — The transform is a matrix of coefficient products: a multiplier array (each multiplier a partial-product AND plane feeding a compressor tree of 3:2 and 4:2 full-adder cells, finished by one carry-propagate adder) followed by an adder tree that sums the products, and the 1/8-pixel interpolation is the same shape — a small tap filter, each tap a multiply, the taps summed. The multiplier count, the transform sizes implemented in silicon and the interpolation-filter tap count are not published, so no multiplier or adder count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the loop-filter line buffers)** — A second, smaller SRAM array beside the reference store, same 6T construction: two cross-coupled inverters plus two access transistors per bit, a row decoder raising one wordline, transmission-gate column muxes and differential sense amplifiers. Its size, bank count and port count are not published, so no cell count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (frame buffer compression)** — The compression controller is a control FSM — state bits in D flip-flops, next-state and output logic as a NAND/NOR network — sequencing the per-macroblock compress on write and decompress on read. The algorithm is proprietary and unpublished, so the datapath behind the FSM — what it predicts, what code it emits, how wide its symbols are — is not described here at all: no compression datapath gates are claimed. The ~50% bandwidth saving is the published behaviour, not a circuit. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (the bool coder's range update)** — The one 16-bit multiply per coded bool is, in standard form, a 16×16 unsigned multiplier: 256 partial-product AND gates (16 × 16), a compressor tree of full-adder cells collapsing the partial products in logarithmic depth, and a final carry-propagate adder of about 32 bits — the product of two 16-bit numbers is up to 32 bits. The range itself is a 16-bit register of D flip-flops, renormalised as bits leave: the renormalisation shifter is, in standard form, either a barrel shifter (a log2-depth tree of 2:1 muxes, one level per shift bit) or an iterative single-bit shifter stepped by a small counter — the paper and the VP9 specification publish neither, so no shifter form is claimed. The coder's throughput in bools per clock and its bit-packing width are not published. Standard construction.
- **Register file (probability tables and quantisation tables)** — The staged tables are a register file: each entry a latch/flop cell (a cross-coupled latch pair, primer) or a 6T SRAM cell, written once per operation from DRAM and read out through a mux tree per bit, indexed by the symbol the bool coder is coding. The table sizes, the indexing and the adaptation-update datapath are not published, so no entry count or cell total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (bitstream output)** — The same circular-queue construction as the stage-decoupling FIFOs: D-flip-flop or small-SRAM entry storage, write/read pointer counters with full-adder incrementers, full/empty comparators (XNOR per pointer bit feeding an AND tree), the full flag back-pressuring the entropy stage and the empty flag gating the DRAM writer. Its depth and width are not published. Standard construction.
- **Counter (outstanding memory operations)** — A counter is a D-flip-flop bank holding the count plus a full-adder incrementer/decrementer (about 28-transistor mirror cells, primer) and a terminal-count comparator — XNOR gates per bit feeding an AND tree — that flags when the outstanding-operation limit is reached, so returning data can be matched to the macroblock that asked for it. The width is ⌈log2 of the maximum outstanding count⌉, and the paper says only "dozens": counting to 24 takes 5 bits, to 63 takes 6, to 127 takes 7 — the maximum is unpublished, so no counter width is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Register file (control/status registers)** — The per-operation program lives in D flip-flops behind an address decoder — a NAND/AND tree from the register address raising one write-enable — with a read mux tree returning status bits to the firmware; each control bit is one flop, each status bit one flop (or one latch). The register count, map and widths are not published, so no flop count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline register (inter-stage latches)** — One master–slave D flip-flop per latched bit (about 20–28 transistors, primer), usually with a 2:1 enable mux in front so the stage can stall — the mux + flop pair is the same cell shape as a scan flop, minus the scan input. What crosses between stages is the macroblock (16×16 for H.264) or superblock (64×64 for VP9) with its mode decisions, but the paper publishes no latch widths and no stage latencies, so no flop count is claimed — the latched payload is pixels plus mode data, and only the per-bit cell form is standard construction. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (NoC / DRAM flow control)** — An up/down counter per traffic class: a D-flip-flop bank holding the credit balance, a full-adder incrementer/decrementer adding credits back as operations complete and subtracting them as requests issue, and a zero comparator — a NOR tree over the counter bits — whose empty flag throttles the core when its credits are spent. The published pacing targets are the per-core budget (3.5 GiB/s average at 2160p, ~3 GiB/s worst case, 2 GiB/s typical) against the VCU's four 32b LPDDR4-3200 channels (~36 GiB/s raw). The credit depths, refill rates and the NoC's width and arbitration are not published, so no counter width or credit total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Google publishes no gate-level structure for the Argos encoder core: the ASPLOS 2021 paper publishes the pipeline stages, the reference-store geometry (144K pixels, 768 × 192, LRU eviction; the H.264 raster store at "394K pixels (2048 × 128)"), the 16×16 macroblock / 64×64 superblock unit of work, the exhaustive multi-resolution motion search down to 1/8-pixel against three reference frames, the temporal filter's 16×16 blocks from 3 frames, the ~50% reference-read-bandwidth saving from frame-buffer compression, the per-core DRAM budget, the VCU memory system, the stateless control model and the die provisioning — and nothing below that. The VP9 specification adds the bool coder's construction (one boolean at a time; 16-bit integers and one 16-bit multiply). Every gate and transistor structure above is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer — the generic textbook form of each primitive, never a claim about Google's actual implementation. The only Argos-specific figures in this section are the published geometries and the arithmetic derived from them (768 × 192 = 147,456 pixels × 8 bits = 1,179,648 bits = 7,077,888 6T cell transistors for the VP9 store's data alone, at the stated 8-bit assumption; 2048 × 128 = 262,144 pixels × 8 bits = 2,097,152 bits = 12,582,912 cell transistors for the H.264 geometry; 8-bit row decode for 192 rows, 7-bit for 128; 256 partial products in a 16×16 multiply; counter widths as log2 bounds on the unpublished "dozens"). One published figure is flagged, not used: the paper's "394K pixels (2048 × 128)" does not multiply out (2048 × 128 = 262,144), so no transistor total is claimed from "394K" itself; the 1.5× ratio matches luma-plus-chroma sample counting, but the paper doesn't state that. No per-primitive gate or transistor counts are published, and this decomposition invents none. (New Level-4 fact record: unverifiable.)

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [unverifiable] **Google Argos VCU** — Gate-level structure not published: no Google source discloses the encoder core's per-primitive gate/transistor implementation (reference-store bank/port counts and turnaround; LRU eviction circuit; motion-score circuit and candidates scored in parallel; reference-frame mux radix and compound-prediction datapath; partition-FSM state count and recursion bound; RDO candidate count and cost widths; transform-array geometry and interpolation-filter structure; loop-filter line-buffer sizes; frame-buffer-compression algorithm and datapath; bool-coder throughput, renormalisation-shifter form and bit-packing width; probability-table sizes and adaptation datapath; FIFO depths and widths; outstanding-operation maximum and counter widths; control-register map; pipeline-latch widths and stage latencies; NoC width, arbitration and credit-counter depths). All gate-level detail in the Level-4 decomposition is textbook-standard construction, labelled as such. Sources: Ranganathan et al., 'Warehouse-Scale Video Acceleration: Co-Design and Deployment in the Wild', ASPLOS 2021; Grange, de Rivaz & Hunt, 'VP9 Bitstream & Decoding Process Specification' v0.6, §5.17.

### SK hynix HBM3 / HBM3E

#### Down to the gates: The stack — TSVs, the base die and the 1,024-bit bus

SK hynix and JEDEC publish no gate-level structure for HBM3 or HBM3E — no netlist, no cell form, no macro organisation, no TSV count or pitch, no sense-amplifier or mux radix. What follows takes each of the fourteen Level-3 primitives one level further, into the gates it is built from and the transistors those gates are built from, using the primer's bottom layer (universal NAND/NOR gates, latch and master–slave D flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder). Every gate structure below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled **standard construction**; it is never a claim about SK hynix's actual implementation. One distinction matters before any counting: the DRAM array is **1T1C** — one access transistor plus one storage capacitor per stored bit — not 6T SRAM. The 6T cell counts in the primer describe logic and SRAM, not the DRAM storage array; the base die's logic and PHY are ordinary CMOS, the DRAM dies' storage is 1T1C. The only HBM3-specific numbers in this section are the published geometries already recorded at Levels 2–3 and the arithmetic derived transparently from them.

- **TSV array (the vertical interconnect)** — A TSV is vertical metal, not a gate: a copper-filled hole through thinned silicon, so the gate-level content sits at its two ends — the driver on the sending die and the receiver on the receiving die. Standard construction: each signal's driver is an inverter chain ending in a large output transistor pair, and each receiver is an input buffer (an inverter-based buffer or a differential pair). The 1,024-bit interface alone implies at least 1,024 data TSVs in every die the data signals pass through — a lower bound, not a published count — plus TSVs for command/address, clocks and power, whose counts are not published. The TSV count per die, the TSV pitch and the microbump pitch are not published, so no TSV total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Microbump / interposer interface (the 1,024-bit host bus)** — The 1,024 data bits leave the base die through microbumps onto the interposer. Standard construction: each bit's output driver is an inverter chain driving a large final-stage transistor pair, and each input receiver is a differential comparator or an inverter-based buffer; the published 0.4 V low-swing signalling means the driver swings a fraction of the 1.1 V core supply, with the receiver restoring full CMOS levels. The microbump count, the interposer trace count and the per-signal drive strength are not published, so no bump or driver total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Command/address decoder (the 16 channels / 32 pseudo-channels)** — Each pseudo-channel's decoder turns the host's CA signals into row/column/bank commands. Standard construction: an AND/NAND decode tree — address bits and their complements feeding NAND gates whose outputs select one command path — with the decoded commands latched in D flip-flops (≈20–28 transistors each, primer) before they fan out to the bank arrays. Sixteen channels × two pseudo-channels = 32 independent decoders, one per pseudo-channel (derived from the published channel geometry). The decoder's gate count, its command-queue depth and the CA bus width in pins are not published. Standard construction.
- **Bank-group row decoder (16–64 banks per pseudo-channel)** — Selecting a bank is decode arithmetic: 16 banks need 4 bank-address bits (2^4 = 16) and 64 banks need 6 (2^6 = 64). Standard construction: the row decoder is an AND/NAND tree from the row and bank address raising one wordline, the wordline driving the access transistors of one row of 1T1C cells; a bank-group select mux (transmission gates, 2 transistors per leg) steers the address to the selected bank group. At the published maximum, 32 pseudo-channels × 64 banks = 2,048 banks per stack (16-high) — derived arithmetic, not a published total. The row-decoder radix, the bank-group organisation inside a die and the row-address width are not published, so no wordline count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Sense-amplifier array (the DRAM row read)** — The DRAM row read bottoms out in the sense amplifier and the 1T1C cell. Each stored bit is one access transistor plus one storage capacitor; a 16 Gb die is 2^34 = 17,179,869,184 storage bits, so 17,179,869,184 access transistors in the array of one die — and a 12-high stack of 16 Gb dies holds 12 × 2^34 = 206,158,430,208 storage bits, i.e. 192 Gb = 24 GB (derived; matches the published 24 GB stack). The HBM3E die is 3 GB = 24 Gb = 25,769,803,776 storage bits, so a 12-high HBM3E stack holds 309,237,645,312 bits = 288 Gb = 36 GB (derived; matches the published 36 GB stack). Standard construction for the sense amplifier itself: a cross-coupled latch pair — two inverters, 4 transistors, the same cross-coupled form as the primer's SRAM cell — with bitline precharge/equalization devices (a small set of NMOS transistors holding both bitlines at half-supply before the wordline rises). When the wordline opens a row, each cell shares its charge with its bitline and the cross-coupled pair amplifies the small differential to full swing. The sense-amplifier count, the array segmentation and the bitline length are not published, so no sense-amplifier total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Column mux / demux (the 32-byte burst)** — Standard construction: the column mux is a tree of transmission gates (2 transistors per input leg) or an equivalent NAND-gate mux, steered by the column address, selecting one column's sense-amplifier outputs onto the 32-bit pseudo-channel data path; the demux on writes is the mirror image. The burst arithmetic is exact: 32 bits × 8 beats = 256 bits = 32 bytes per pseudo-channel burst, and across all 32 pseudo-channels one burst moves 32 × 32 = 1,024 bytes = 8,192 bits — the same as the 1,024-bit interface × 8 beats (derived). The mux radix, the column-address width and the prefetch depth inside the die are not published, so no mux count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Base-die PHY (serializers, FIFOs and the DFI bridge)** — Standard construction: the serializer is a shift register — a bank of D flip-flops (≈20–28 transistors each, primer) feeding a mux tree that picks one bit per strobe edge — and the read/write FIFOs are the standard circular-queue construction: entry storage in a flop bank or small SRAM array, write and read pointer counters (D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers, ≈28-transistor mirror cells, primer) and full/empty comparators (XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree). The DFI bridge is the boundary between the controller's digital domain and the PHY: in standard form it is a register slice (D flip-flops) plus the clock-domain crossing covered under Synchronizer. The published DFI 1:1:2 split (controller/DFI/PHY/memory at 1.6 GHz, strobes at 3.2 GHz) is the ratio the serializer bridges. The PHY's serializer ratio, its read/write FIFO depths and its training/calibration logic are not published, so no serializer or FIFO count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the per-channel command sequencer)** — Each channel's controller sequences ACTIVATE, READ, WRITE, PRECHARGE, REFRESH, RFM, self-refresh and power-down — nine distinct command types in the published set (ACTIVATE, READ, WRITE, PRECHARGE, REFRESH, RFM, SREF, PDE, PDX), which need at least ⌈log2 9⌉ = 4 bits to encode (derived). Standard construction: state bits in D flip-flops, next-state and output logic as a NAND/NOR network, the state table mapping each command and its timing constraints to the next state; command issue is gated by counters (see Counter) enforcing the DRAM timing parameters. The controller's state count, its scheduling policy across the 32 pseudo-channels and its queue depths are not published, so no state-bit count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (refresh pacing and Refresh Management)** — Standard construction: a counter is a D-flip-flop bank holding the count plus a full-adder incrementer (≈28-transistor mirror cells, primer) and a terminal-count comparator — XNOR gates per bit feeding an AND tree — that flags when the refresh interval or the RFM threshold is reached; the RFM decision itself is a comparator over the activation counts the DRAM reports. The refresh-counter widths, the RFM threshold counts and the refresh scheduling are not published, so no counter width is claimed. Standard construction.
- **ECC logic (on-die, symbol-based)** — On-die ECC is XOR trees. Standard construction: each of the 32 check bits of the 304-bit code word is the XOR (parity) of a subset of the 272 data bits — a tree of XOR gates (each XOR2 ≈ 10–12 transistors, primer) — so the encoder is 32 XOR trees over the data word; the decoder recomputes the same 32 check bits, XORs them against the stored check bits to form the syndrome, and a small decode network maps the syndrome to the erroneous bit position, corrected by a final XOR. The 32 check bits are 32/304 ≈ 10.5% overhead on the code word (derived). The host side carries its own 2 check bytes per 32-byte burst over the two ECC signals (2 bits × 8 beats = 16 bits, derived). The ECC encoder/decoder gate counts, the symbol size and the correction latency are not published, so no XOR-tree size is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator / severity signals (real-time error reporting)** — Two severity signals per pseudo-channel encode four responses (2^2 = 4: no error, single error corrected, multiple errors corrected, uncorrected error), and 32 pseudo-channels × 2 signals = 64 severity signals per stack (derived). Standard construction: the severity encoder is a small combinational network — AND/OR gates over the syndrome bits — mapping the decoder's error classification onto the two severity bits, which are registered in D flip-flops before they leave the die so they stay aligned with the burst they describe. The comparator implementation behind the severity encoding and the reporting latency are not published. Standard construction.
- **Test access port (IEEE 1500 TAP — ECC transparency)** — Standard construction: the IEEE 1500 TAP controller is the standard's 16-state FSM — state bits in D flip-flops, next-state logic as a NAND/NOR network — sequencing shift/capture/update on the test clock; the ECC transparency registers are scan cells, each a D flip-flop with a 2:1 mux in front (≈ +6–8 transistors over a plain flop, primer) so ECS results shift out through the port. The TAP register widths, the instruction set and the scan-chain organisation are not published, so no register total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (the decoupled clock domains)** — The published clock split is CK at most 1.6 GHz against WDQS/RDQS at 3.2 GHz — one CK period spans two strobe periods (derived). Standard construction: a synchronizer is two D flip-flops in series in the receiving clock domain — the first flop is allowed to go metastable and the chain gives it a full clock period to resolve — and where data (not just control) crosses, the standard form is an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers (only one pointer bit changes per increment, so a sampled pointer is never more than one count wrong) plus the same 2-flop synchronizers on the pointers. The synchronizer structure, the FIFO depth at the clock crossing and the crossing latency are not published, so no flop count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Redundancy / repair logic (the KGSD screen)** — No vendor publishes the repair organisation, so this primitive is named only in conditional standard forms, as with the TLB/directory cases in earlier Level-4 runs: the standard forms are fuse-programmed address comparators — XNOR gates per address bit feeding an AND tree that recognises a faulty row or column address — steering a transmission-gate mux to a spare row or column, with the fuse itself in standard form a one-time-programmable cell (an eFUSE transistor or a laser-blown link). Which form SK hynix uses, how many spare rows and columns each die carries and how the stack-level KGSD screen sequences repair across 12 dies are not published, so no repair circuit is claimed at all. Standard construction (conditional).

Honesty: SK hynix and JEDEC publish the HBM3 stack at channel geometry, clocking and RAS level only — 16 channels, 32 pseudo-channels, the 1,024-bit interface, 6.4 Gb/s per pin for 819 GB/s per device, the 304-bit on-die ECC code word, the two severity signals and their four responses, ECS via the IEEE 1500 TAP, RFM/ARFM row-hammer mitigation, the decoupled clocking (CK 1.6 GHz, WDQS/RDQS 3.2 GHz) and the DFI 1:1:2 split — and the shipping geometry: 16 Gb dies about 30 µm thick in 12-high 24 GB stacks, and HBM3E in a 12-high 36 GB stack at 9.6 Gbps on 3 GB dies 40% thinner. The derived figures in this section check against the published ones exactly: 1,024 pins × 6.4 Gb/s = 6,553.6 Gb/s = 819.2 GB/s; 12 × 16 Gb = 192 Gb = 24 GB; 12 × 3 GB = 36 GB; 32 pseudo-channels × 32 bytes = 1,024 bytes per burst. Every gate and transistor structure above is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer — the generic textbook form of each primitive, never a claim about SK hynix's actual implementation — with one deliberate correction to the primer's vocabulary: the DRAM storage array is 1T1C cells (1 transistor + 1 capacitor per bit), not 6T SRAM cells, so the array's transistor total is one access transistor per stored bit (17,179,869,184 per 16 Gb die), and the 6T cell appears here only in the base die's logic and in the sense amplifier's cross-coupled pair. No TSV count or pitch, microbump pitch, CA bus pin count, row-decoder radix, sense-amplifier count or bitline length, column-mux radix, PHY serializer ratio or FIFO depths, per-channel controller state count or scheduling policy, refresh/RFM counter widths, ECC gate counts or symbol size, TAP register widths, synchronizer depth, or spare-row/column counts are published — and this decomposition invents none of them. (New Level-4 fact record: unverifiable.)

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [unverifiable] **SK hynix HBM3 / HBM3E** — Gate-level structure not published: no SK hynix or JEDEC source discloses HBM3/HBM3E per-primitive gate/transistor implementation (TSV count and pitch; microbump pitch; CA bus pin count; row-decoder radix and bank-group organisation; sense-amplifier count and bitline length; column-mux radix; PHY serializer ratio and FIFO depths; per-channel controller state count and scheduling policy; refresh/RFM counter widths; ECC encoder/decoder gate counts and symbol size; IEEE 1500 TAP register widths; clock-crossing synchronizer depth; spare-row/column repair counts). All gate-level detail in the Level-4 decomposition is textbook-standard construction, labelled as such. The DRAM storage array is 1T1C (one access transistor + one storage capacitor per bit), not 6T SRAM. Sources: JEDEC, 'JEDEC Publishes HBM3 Update to High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) Standard', Jan 27, 2022; Synopsys, 'What Designers Need to Know About HBM3'; SK hynix, 'SK hynix Begins Volume Production of the World's First 12-Layer HBM3E', PR Newswire, Sept 25, 2024.

### Apple Secure Enclave

#### Down to the gates: Memory Protection Engine + the UID-bound AES path

Apple publishes no gate-level structure for the Secure Enclave — that is the central honesty boundary of this section. Everything below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled "standard construction", and is never a claim about Apple's actual netlist. The only transistor arithmetic given is computed from the two published width sets: the AES block is 128 bits (definitional for AES), and the counter lockbox fields are 128-bit salt, 128-bit passcode verifier, 8-bit counter and 8-bit maximum attempt value (272 bits per lockbox, published in the Apple Platform Security guide). Leaf-cell costs come from the primer's bottom layer: inverter = 2 transistors, NAND2 = 4, NOR2 = 4, AND2/OR2 = 6, XOR2 ≈ 10–12, master–slave D flip-flop ≈ 20–28, 6T SRAM cell = 6, transmission-gate mux = 2 transistors per input leg, full adder ≈ 28 transistors (two half adders = XOR/AND/OR gates).

- **AES round datapath (S-box + MixColumns + AddRoundKey)** — The round is the standard AES construction at gate level. The S-box is either a composite-field GF(2^8) inverter — a network of XOR and AND gates — or a 256-entry × 8-bit ROM table (2,048 storage bits: 1 transistor per bit in a mask-ROM array, standard construction); Apple publishes neither form. MixColumns is GF(2^8) multiply-by-2 and multiply-by-3 networks — XOR trees over the state bytes. AddRoundKey is a 128-bit XOR: 128 XOR2 gates ≈ 1,280–1,536 transistors (standard construction, from the definitional 128-bit AES block). Whether the rounds are rolled (one round unit reused) or unrolled (one unit per round) is not published, so no datapath total is claimed.
- **Key schedule (key expansion)** — Round keys are generated inside the engine from the UID/GID-derived master key: S-box substitution on the key words, round-constant XORs, and word rotations — rotations are wiring, not gates. A round-key register held in flops would be 128 D flip-flops ≈ 2,560–3,584 transistors (standard construction). The schedule's depth, width and implementation are not published, so no total is claimed.
- **Key register / fuse array (the UID in fuses)** — The fuse array is one transistor per bit in standard eFuse/antifuse construction: a blown fuse programs one bit, read back through a sense amplifier comparing blown against unblown resistance. No total is claimed — the UID bit-width is unpublished. The hardware key path's working registers are D flip-flops ≈ 20–28 transistors per bit (standard construction), and the keys never leave that path — that is published Apple behaviour, not a gate claim.
- **Mux (hardware/software key select + lockable seed bits)** — The key-select mux is a 2:1 mux per key bit: a transmission-gate mux is 2 transistors per input leg (4 per 2:1 mux per bit), standard construction. The lockable seed bits are D flip-flops with one extra lock latch bit gating the write enable, so a locked seed can never be rewritten. Mux radix and seed-bit count are not published, so no total is claimed.
- **CMAC tag engine** — The tag engine reuses the AES round datapath above, plus an XOR accumulator chaining each block's ciphertext into the tag: a 128-bit XOR = 128 XOR2 gates ≈ 1,280–1,536 transistors (standard construction). Subkey generation is one extra AES encryption plus shifts and XORs. The stored tag width is not published, so the tag register has no claimed size and no engine total is given.
- **XEX tweak (XOR around the encryption)** — The tweak is a 128-bit XOR before encryption and a 128-bit XOR after: 256 XOR2 gates ≈ 2,560–3,072 transistors (standard construction, from the definitional 128-bit AES block). The tweak's derivation is not published and no claim is made about it.
- **Comparator (tag + anti-replay verification)** — Tag verification is an equality check: one XNOR gate per tag bit (≈10–12 transistors each, standard construction) feeding an AND tree, with a mismatch setting an error latch (one D flip-flop plus gating) that halts the enclave until reboot. The comparator is as wide as the tag it checks — and the tag width is unpublished — so only the per-bit structure is given, no total.
- **Anti-replay integrity tree (rooted in dedicated SRAM)** — Each tree node is an authentication value: its storage is a 6T SRAM cell array (6 transistors per bit, primer bottom layer) or a flop register, and each level update is one MAC computation (the AES datapath above) plus one SRAM write. The root register lives in dedicated on-die SRAM inside the enclave — the one piece of the tree that never leaves the chip. Tree arity, depth, node width and hash function are not published, so per-node structure only — no totals.
- **Counter (anti-replay values + counter lockboxes)** — The published counter is the lockbox's 8-bit counter: 8 D flip-flops with a full-adder incrementer (8 full-adder cells at ≈28 transistors each) — the flop bank ≈ 160–224 transistors plus ≈224 for the incrementer (standard construction). The full 272-bit lockbox (128-bit salt + 128-bit passcode verifier + 8-bit counter + 8-bit maximum attempt value) as a flop register would be ≈ 5,440–7,616 transistors, or as a 6T SRAM array = 1,632 cell transistors plus row decoder and sense amplifiers — both candidate forms, standard construction. The Secure Storage Component is a separate device and its actual storage form is unpublished, so neither form is asserted. The anti-replay value's own bit-width is not published, so no total is claimed for it.
- **TRNG (ring oscillators + CTR_DRBG)** — Each ring oscillator is an odd chain of inverters (2 transistors per inverter) closed in a loop, sampled by a D flip-flop (≈20–28 transistors); the CTR_DRBG is a counter (flop bank plus full-adder incrementer) driving the AES datapath above, plus state registers. Oscillator count, sampling structure and DRBG state size are not published — per-oscillator structure only, no total.
- **Boot ROM (mask ROM + hash engine)** — The mask ROM array is 1 transistor per bit (a transistor present = 1, absent = 0, programmed at mask), behind a row decoder (NAND tree) and sense amplifiers — standard construction; ROM size is unpublished, so no total is claimed. The hash engine has no claimable gate form: the hash algorithm Apple uses for sepOS verification is unpublished, so no gate decomposition of it is given here. The sepOS hash lock register (from A10) is D flip-flops ≈ 20–28 transistors per bit (standard construction), its width unpublished.
- **PKA datapath (modular multiplier array)** — A wide modular multiplier at gate level: AND-gate partial products, full-adder compressor trees (≈28-transistor mirror cells) collapsing them, and one final carry-propagate adder; modular reduction adds adder trees, and Montgomery reduction adds quotient-estimation logic (small multipliers plus comparators). Multiplier width, radix and pipeline depth are not published — per-lane structure only, no total.
- **FIFO / queue + interrupt (the mailbox)** — Each mailbox direction is a FIFO: storage (a flop array or a small SRAM) plus write and read pointer counters (D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers) plus full/empty comparators (XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree). The interrupt/doorbell is one set/reset latch bit per direction plus edge-detect logic. Queue depths, message widths and interrupt-controller structure are not published, so no totals are claimed.
- **Synchronizer (the AP–SEP clock-domain crossing)** — The standard two-flop synchronizer: 2 D flip-flops in series per bit in the receiving clock domain ≈ 40–56 transistors per bit (standard construction — Apple publishes only the separate lower SEP clock, not the synchronizer structure). The crossing width is unpublished, so no total is claimed.
- **Secure Storage Component interface (dedicated I2C bus)** — I2C is a two-wire serial interface: open-drain drivers (1 NMOS transistor per line, standard construction) plus shift registers (D flip-flops, ≈20–28 transistors per bit) for serial-to-parallel conversion; the encrypted and authenticated protocol runs on the enclave's crypto engines above. Bus width, the component's crypto-engine internals and its tamper-detection circuits are not published.
- **Power / clock monitor (comparators + clock-gating FSM)** — Voltage and frequency comparators drive a digital trip latch (one D flip-flop) and a clock-gating FSM (state flops plus NAND/NOR next-state logic) that stops the enclave clocks until the next SoC reset. The comparators themselves are analog (differential pairs), which sit below the primer's digital leaf-cell floor and are not decomposed into gates. Monitor thresholds, comparator count and gating logic are not published.
- **Storage DMA AES engine (the sibling AES datapath)** — AES-256: 14 rounds with a 256-bit key (published in the guide). Same round structure as the Secure Enclave AES engine above — S-box + MixColumns + 128-bit AddRoundKey XOR (≈1,280–1,536 transistors per round-key XOR, standard construction) — with a 256-bit key schedule (a key register held in flops would be 256 D flip-flops ≈ 5,120–7,168 transistors, standard construction). Rolled versus unrolled is unpublished, so no datapath total is claimed. The dedicated key-delivery wires are point-to-point routing, not gates.
- **IOMMU / memory-range comparator (Secure Neural Engine access control)** — Access control is address-range comparators against the authorized regions: two comparators per region (lower bound and upper bound), each built from a subtractor (a full-adder chain) plus sign-bit logic, with the region bounds held in D-flip-flop registers (≈20–28 transistors per bit, standard construction). Region count and bounds are not published — per-region structure only, no total.

Honesty: Apple publishes the Secure Enclave's mechanisms and a handful of exact widths, and no gate-level structure for any part of it. Everything in this section is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer except the arithmetic computed from the two published width sets (the 128-bit AES block and the 272-bit lockbox fields); none of it is a claim about Apple's actual netlist.

- [unverifiable] **Apple Secure Enclave** — Gate-level structure not published: no Apple source discloses Secure Enclave per-primitive gate/transistor implementation (AES round implementation, key and tag widths, mailbox queue depths and message widths, integrity-tree geometry, TRNG oscillator count, PKA multiplier width, Boot ROM size and hash algorithm, synchronizer structure, Secure Storage Component internals). All gate-level detail in the Level-4 decomposition is textbook-standard construction, labelled as such. Source: Apple, 'The Secure Enclave', Apple Platform Security guide.

### Memory BIST & Repair (MBIST)

#### Down to the gates: The algorithm engine — running a March test at full speed

No vendor or standard publishes gate-level structure for MBIST — it is a technique applied to memories, and the patents publish block structure only. Everything below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled "standard construction", and is never a claim about any specific chip or MBIST product. Transistor counts are given only as functions of the per-memory parameters — W = memory word width, D = memory depth, S = spare count — computed from the primer's bottom-layer leaf cells: inverter = 2 transistors, NAND2 = 4, NOR2 = 4, AND2/OR2 = 6, XOR2 ≈ 10–12, master–slave D flip-flop ≈ 20–28, 6T SRAM cell = 6, transmission-gate mux = 2 transistors per input leg, full adder ≈ 28 transistors (two half adders = XOR/AND/OR gates). Where the Level-3 text already names gate-level structure, this section carries it down one level: XOR2/OR2 gate counts, counters as D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer, priority encoders as log2 levels of AND/OR gates, register files as D flip-flops, shift registers as daisy-chained D flip-flops.

- **FSM / controller (BIST/BIRA FSM)** — The master BIST controller is a finite-state machine: state registers holding the current phase, plus next-state logic that steps it through the march elements. In standard construction the state register is one D flip-flop per state bit, ≈ 20–28 transistors per bit, and the next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network over the state bits and the control inputs (done, pass/fail, terminal count). The state count is the number of distinct phases in the algorithm library and is not published as a fixed number, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Address generator (up/down counter)** — The address signal generator is an up/down binary counter: log2(D) D flip-flops, ≈ 20–28 transistors per bit, plus a full-adder incrementer of log2(D) full-adder cells at ≈ 28 transistors each, plus a direction mux selecting increment or decrement — derived arithmetic ≈ (20–28 + 28) × log2(D) transistors plus muxing. The row/column split that lets the controller test in fast-row or fast-column order is a wiring choice over the counter bits, not extra gates. Its width is log2 of the memory depth — a per-memory parameter, not a published constant. Standard construction.
- **Data background generator (background register)** — The background register is a W-bit register holding the current background word: W D flip-flops, ≈ 20–28 transistors per bit, so ≈ 20–28 × W transistors derived. All-0s, all-1s and checkerboard patterns are fixed bit values loaded into the register — the checkerboard is an alternating pattern in the register bits, wiring, not gates. Where a programmable controller adds an LFSR for pseudo-random backgrounds, that is W D flip-flops plus a few XOR2 gates (≈ 10–12 transistors each) for the feedback taps — the standard programmable form, not a published detail of any specific MBIST product. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (XOR tree + OR reduction)** — The bit-wise comparator is one XOR2 gate per data bit feeding an OR tree that collapses the per-bit mismatches to the single pass/fail bit: W XOR2 gates at ≈ 10–12 transistors each, so ≈ 10–12 × W transistors, plus W−1 OR2 gates at 6 transistors each for the reduction tree, which is log2(W) levels deep. The single-bit result goes to the memory status register — that is the published behaviour (US Patent 6,560,740 B1); the gate counts are standard construction. W is the memory word width, a per-memory parameter. Standard construction.
- **Fail log / memory status register (FARR)** — Each Failing Address and Repair Register is a register of D flip-flops capturing the encoded failing address: log2(D) D flip-flops per register, ≈ 20–28 transistors per bit, so ≈ 20–28 × log2(D) transistors per register, plus one valid-flag flip-flop. The register count tracks the spare allocation and the depth is a per-memory parameter, not published — so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Fail bitmap (SRAM bank)** — The fail bitmap is a 6T SRAM cell array: 6 transistors per bit, so 6 × D transistors for a cell-level bitmap (or 6 × the word count for a word-level bitmap), behind the standard SRAM bank construction — a row decoder (NAND tree), column muxes (transmission gates, 2 transistors per input leg) and sense amplifiers. The 1D local bitmap form that feeds BIRA is the published efficient form (Tseng, Li & Chang, DATE 2006); its size is the memory's size — per-memory, not published. Standard construction.
- **BIRA solver (counters + threshold comparators + priority encoder)** — The redundancy-analysis engine is one counter per row/column under consideration — each a binary counter of D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer, ≈ (20–28 + 28) transistors per count bit — plus one threshold comparator per counter, an equality/magnitude comparison of the count against the threshold register built from XNOR gates (≈ 10–12 transistors per bit) feeding an AND tree, and a priority encoder that picks which spare to allocate first: log2 levels of AND/OR gates (6 transistors per AND2/OR2) over the flagged-element bits. The count of counters, the counter widths and the threshold values are per-memory parameters, not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Repair registers (register file)** — The repair signature is held in a register file of D flip-flops: S repair registers, each holding an address plus control bits, at ≈ 20–28 transistors per stored bit — so the file is ≈ 20–28 × S × (address width + control bits) transistors, derived. S is the spare count, a per-memory parameter, not published as a fixed number. Standard construction.
- **Address comparators + redirect mux (functional-path remap)** — Each repair register has one equality comparator on the functional path: one XNOR gate per address bit (≈ 10–12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree of log2(D)−1 AND2 gates (6 transistors each), so ≈ 10–12 × log2(D) transistors per comparator plus the AND tree. On a match the redirect mux steers the access to the spare row or column: a 2:1 transmission-gate mux per address bit, 2 transistors per input leg (4 transistors per 2:1 mux per bit). Comparator count equals the repair-register count — per-memory, not published. The match-and-redirect behaviour is the published mechanism (US Patent 6,973,605 B1); the gate counts are standard construction. Standard construction.
- **Mux (test/normal mode select)** — The mode mux is one 2:1 mux per address and data bit, selected by the BIST-enable signal: a transmission-gate mux is 2 transistors per input leg, so 4 transistors per 2:1 mux per bit — derived, ≈ 4 × (address width + data width) transistors for the whole mux. The select behaviour is the published mechanism (multiplexing logic choosing between BIST-controller and system-logic address and data); the transistor count is standard construction. Standard construction.
- **TAP / IJTAG configuration registers (shift registers)** — The configuration register is a shift register chain: one D flip-flop per configuration bit, ≈ 20–28 transistors per bit, daisy-chained through TDI/TDO so the test access port can shift the algorithm selection, target cluster and start/stop commands in serially. Its bit count is implementation-defined, not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (test-clock to memory-clock crossing)** — The standard two-flop synchronizer: 2 D flip-flops in series per bit in the receiving clock domain, ≈ 40–56 transistors per bit (standard construction — no synchronizer depth or structure is published for MBIST). The crossing width is a per-memory parameter, not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **eFuse/OTP interface (fuse controller + shift register)** — The fuse controller is a small FSM — state flip-flops plus NAND/NOR next-state logic, the same standard construction as the BIST FSM above — driving a shift register of one D flip-flop per fuse bit (≈ 20–28 transistors per bit) that shifts the repair signature out to blow the selected fuses. Each fuse cell is one transistor per bit in standard eFuse construction (a blown fuse programs one bit, read back through a sense amplifier comparing blown against unblown resistance). The fuse count equals the repair-signature width, which is not published as a fixed number, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (operation/element counter)** — The element counter is a plain binary counter: one D flip-flop per count bit (≈ 20–28 transistors each) plus a full-adder incrementer of one full-adder cell per bit (≈ 28 transistors each), so ≈ (20–28 + 28) transistors per bit, derived. The address counter's terminal count ends the element — the terminal-count detect is an equality comparison of the counter against its terminal value, XNOR gates per bit feeding an AND tree, the same construction as the redirect comparators above. Both counters are sized to the element length and the memory depth respectively; neither width is published as a fixed number. Standard construction.

Parameter honesty. MBIST is a technique applied to memories, not a chip with a datasheet: every width in this section is a per-memory-instance parameter — the address counter is log2 of the memory depth, the comparator and background register are as wide as the memory word, the fail bitmap is as large as the memory, the FARR depth and the repair-register count track the spare allocation. No vendor publishes gate-level structure or fixed per-primitive parameters for the technique itself, and this section invents none of them. The gate-level forms here are the standard textbook constructions of the named primitives, from the primer's bottom layer; the transistor counts are arithmetic derived from those constructions and the per-memory parameters W, D and S, never published values. The facts specific to the technique are the ones already verified at Level-3: the master BIST controller coupled to a hardwired BIST table, background data generator, address signal generator and control signal generator (US Patent 6,560,740 B1); the comparator's single-bit result to the memory status register; the encoded fail-address register and the functional-path redirect (US Patent 6,973,605 B1); the 1D local bitmap BIRA form (Tseng, Li & Chang, DATE 2006); the threshold-flagging rule (US Patent 6,795,942); and the one-controller-per-shared-bus-cluster rule (Siemens Tessent MemoryBIST white paper).

- [unverifiable] **Memory BIST & Repair (MBIST)** — Gate-level structure not published: no vendor or standard discloses MBIST per-primitive gate/transistor implementation (FSM state count, counter widths, comparator widths, FARR depth, bitmap size, BIRA counter count and thresholds, repair-register widths, mux radix, TAP configuration-register width, synchronizer depth, eFuse count). All gate-level detail in the Level-4 decomposition is textbook-standard construction, labelled as such. Source: US Patents 6,560,740 B1 / 6,973,605 B1 / 6,795,942; Tseng, Li & Chang, DATE 2006; Siemens Tessent MemoryBIST white paper.

### JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1

#### Down to the gates: The TAP controller — a 16-state machine in every chip

IEEE 1149.1 publishes no gate-level structure for the TAP controller — the standard mandates behaviour, not circuits, and the Bennetts tutorial draws functional blocks, not gates. What follows takes each of the eleven Level-3 primitives one level further, into the gates it is built from and the transistors those gates are built from, using the primer's bottom layer (universal NAND/NOR gates, latch and master–slave D flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder). Every gate structure below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled **standard construction**; it is never a claim about any device's actual implementation. The only JTAG-specific numbers are the published geometries already recorded at Levels 2–3 and the arithmetic derived transparently from them.

- **FSM / controller (the 16-state TAP controller, a Moore machine)** — The state register is four master–slave D flip-flops (2^4 = 16 states), ≈ 20–28 transistors each (primer, bottom layer), so ≈ 80–112 transistors for the state register — arithmetic from the published 16 states, not a published figure. The next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network over the four state bits and TMS (plus TRST* where the optional pin is fitted): one next-state function per state bit, each a combinational function of the present state and TMS. The output decode is a second NAND/NOR network over the state bits producing the nine TAP outputs — ClockDR, ShiftDR, UpdateDR, ClockIR, ShiftIR, UpdateIR, Reset, Select and Enable. The tutorial's timing discipline is that "a state transition occurs on the positive edge of TCK and the controller output values change on the negative edge of TCK" (verified — Bennetts, Fig. 34); the state register is clocked on TCK's rising edge, and no published source gives the gate form that realises the falling-edge output change, so no circuit for it is claimed. Test-Logic-Reset is the power-on state: in standard construction the state flops carry an asynchronous set/reset that forces the reset encoding, or the reset is driven through a reset mux in front of the state register. The state encoding itself is not published, so the next-state and output-decode gate counts depend on the encoding and no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Shift register (the instruction register — shift section + hold section)** — The shift section is one D flip-flop per instruction-register bit, daisy-chained TDI→TDO, ≈ 20–28 transistors per bit. The standard fixes only the minimum: the register "must be at least two-bits long", so the shift section is at least 2 flops (≈ 40–56 transistors minimum) and its real length is per-device and unpublished. The hold section is a second bank of one D flip-flop per bit, loaded in parallel from the shift section at Update-IR — another ≈ 20–28 transistors per bit, so the register as a whole is at least 4 flops (≈ 80–112 transistors) at the 2-bit minimum. The parallel load is a 2:1 mux per hold flop (transmission gate, 2 transistors per input leg) or a load-enable flop, in standard form. The `01` capture pattern in the two least-significant bits is tie-offs — one bit tied to ground, one to VDD — wiring, zero gates. Standard construction.
- **Decoder (instruction decode → data-register select)** — The one-hot select is, in standard form, one AND/NAND tree per implemented instruction over the hold-section bits: each decoded output is an AND of the hold bits or their complements (an AND2 is 6 transistors in the primer's construction; a NAND2 is 4), and the decoded output gates the ClockDR/ShiftDR/UpdateDR signals to the selected register only — one AND per register enable. "There may be some decoding logic beyond the hold section depending on the width of the register and the number of different instructions" (verified — Bennetts), and the number of implemented instructions is per-device and not published, so no decoder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Shift register (the boundary-scan register — BC_1 cells chained)** — The register has no flops of its own: each BC_1 cell's Capture Scan flip-flop is the shift element, and the cells chain Scan_Out-to-Scan_In between TDI and TDO. The register's gate total is therefore N × (one BC_1 cell), where N is the device's signal-pin count — a per-device number, not a published constant. Standard construction.
- **D flip-flop pair + muxes (the BC_1 boundary-scan cell)** — Two master–slave D flip-flops — the Capture Scan cell and the Update Hold cell — ≈ 20–28 transistors each, so ≈ 40–56 transistors for the pair. The front-end mux in front of the Capture Scan cell selects between Data_In (capture) and Scan_In (shift): a 2:1 transmission-gate mux, 2 transistors per input leg, 4 transistors per mux. The back-end mux at the output selects between Data_In (normal mode, straight through) and the Update Hold cell's content (update mode), selected by the Mode signal: another 2:1 mux, ≈ 4 transistors. The cell is therefore ≈ 48–64 transistors in standard construction — derived, never a published figure. The standard mandates the function, not this circuit: "The IEEE 1149.1 Standard does not mandate the design of the circuit, only its functional specification" (verified — Bennetts), so a device may realise the four modes differently. For a bidirectional pin the standard's example uses three cells conceptually (input, output, IO-status control), "in practice, the two IO scan cells are usually combined into a single multifunction cell called a BC_7" (verified — Bennetts); the BC_7's gate form is a wider mux tree plus extra flops, and no count is claimed for it. Standard construction.
- **Shift register (the bypass register)** — One D flip-flop, ≈ 20–28 transistors, daisy-chained TDI→TDO — the whole register. There is no hold section and no parallel output, so there is no update mux and no second flop bank. The Capture-DR value is a hard-wired logic 0: a tie-off to ground, zero gates. One bit, one flop: a bypassed chip passes the whole board chain in a single TCK. Standard construction.
- **Shift register (the identification register)** — 32 D flip-flops daisy-chained TDI→TDO, ≈ 20–28 transistors each, so ≈ 640–896 transistors for the shift register — arithmetic from the published 32 bits. The 32-bit code itself is hard-wired: the version (4 bits), part-number (16 bits) and manufacturer-identity (11 bits) fields are fixed 1s and 0s loaded at Capture-IDCODE, i.e. tie-offs to VDD or ground — wiring, zero gates — and the least-significant bit, always 1, is a tie-off to VDD. There is no parallel output and no update stage, so no hold flops and no update muxes. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (the TDO output mux)** — One bit wide (TDO is a serial pin): it steers the serial output of whichever register the instruction decoder selected — boundary-scan register, bypass register, identification register, or the instruction register itself during Shift-IR — onto TDO. In standard form a 4-way select is a tree of three 2:1 transmission-gate muxes (2 transistors per input leg, 4 per 2:1 mux), ≈ 12 transistors, or the equivalent NAND/NOR tree; the select encoding is the decoded instruction. The exact register set varies by device (the identification register is optional), so the 4-way form is the standard construction for the four register families, not a per-device claim. Standard construction.
- **Tri-state driver (the TDO output enable)** — The Enable output of the TAP controller "is distributed to the output driver amplifier" (verified — Bennetts, Fig. 33): in standard form the driver is a tri-state inverter — two PMOS and two NMOS devices in an enable stack, ≈ 4–6 transistors — plus the output driver stage whose size is set by the pad's drive requirement, which is per-device and not published. When Enable is low the driver is high-impedance, so the next device in the chain can drive the shared board net. "TDO ... is valid on the falling edge of TCK when the internal state machine is in the correct state" (verified — Corelis) — the falling-edge validity is the standard's timing discipline, realised through the TAP's Enable output, which changes on the falling edge; no driver timing numbers are published. Standard construction.
- **Counter — none in the TAP** — Zero gates: there is no counter primitive to decompose. The five-TCK reset guarantee is a property of the state graph — no state is more than five TMS=1 edges from Test-Logic-Reset — not a counted sequence. The standard's fail-safe needs no logic either: "The 1149.1 Standard mandates that an open circuit TDI, TMS or TRST* input must go to logic 1" (verified — Bennetts) — in standard pad construction that is one weak pull-up device (one transistor, or a resistor) per input pin, which pulls an open TMS to Test-Logic-Reset within five clocks and loads the safe BYPASS instruction from an open TDI. The pull-up is pad circuitry, not TAP logic.
- **Synchronizer — none in the TAP** — Zero gates: there is no synchronizer primitive to decompose. The TAP runs entirely on TCK, and the standard keeps that clock apart from the system clock on purpose; the pins are sampled only on ClockDR (a derivative of TCK), and the values driven onto pins are held levels from the update hold cells, not pulses that must cross into the functional clock domain. The functional logic sees the boundary cells as ordinary combinational paths in normal mode, not as a second clock domain.

**Parameter honesty.** The standard publishes the governing numbers — 16 TAP states; instruction register at least 2 bits with the two least-significant captured bits fixed to `01`; bypass register exactly 1 bit capturing a hard-wired 0; identification register 32 bits (version 4, part number 16, manufacturer identity 11, least-significant bit always 1); boundary-scan register length equal to the device's signal-pin count; at most five TCK cycles with TMS high to reach Test-Logic-Reset; TDO valid on the falling edge of TCK, TDI and TMS sampled on the rising edge — and nothing below that. It publishes no state-register encoding, no next-state or output-decode gate form, no instruction-register length beyond the 2-bit minimum, no decoder circuit form, no BC_1 transistor implementation, no TDO mux or driver form, no per-device register length, and no counter, synchronizer, comparator, credit counter, adder tree, multiplier array, SRAM bank or register file anywhere in the TAP. Every gate and transistor figure above is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer — the generic textbook form of each primitive, never a claim about any device's actual implementation. The only JTAG-specific figures are the published geometries and the arithmetic derived transparently from them (4-bit state register from 16 states ≈ 80–112 transistors; instruction register at least 4 flops ≈ 80–112 transistors at the 2-bit minimum; BC_1 cell ≈ 48–64 transistors; bypass register 1 flop ≈ 20–28 transistors; identification register 32 flops ≈ 640–896 transistors; TDO mux ≈ 12 transistors in the 4-way transmission-gate form; tri-state driver ≈ 4–6 transistors plus an unpublished driver stage). No per-primitive gate or transistor counts are published, and this decomposition invents none. (New Level-4 fact record: unverifiable.)

- [unverifiable] **JTAG & Boundary Scan — IEEE 1149.1** — Gate-level structure not published: no vendor or standard discloses the TAP controller's per-primitive gate/transistor implementation (state-register encoding and flop count beyond the 16-state arithmetic; next-state and output-decode circuit form; instruction-register length beyond the 2-bit minimum; instruction-decoder circuit form; boundary-scan register length as a constant, it is the per-device pin count; BC_1 transistor implementation; TDO mux and driver form; and the absence of counter, synchronizer, comparator, credit-counter, adder-tree, multiplier-array, SRAM-bank and register-file primitives in the standard TAP). All gate-level detail in the Level-4 decomposition is textbook-standard construction, labelled as such. Sources: Bennetts, Boundary Scan Tutorial v2.1 (2002); Corelis, JTAG Technical Primer.

### AMD RDNA 3 — Navi 31

#### Down to the gates: The dual-issue Work Group Processor — the banked VGPR file, the banked LDS and the VOPD pairing rule

AMD publishes no gate-level structure for Navi 31 — the ISA guide describes the WGP at block level (the VGPR bank counts and read ports, the LDS bank RAMs, the work-group limits, the VOPD pairing rules) and stops there. What follows takes each of the sixteen Level-3 primitives one level further, into the gates it is built from and the transistors those gates are built from, using the primer's bottom layer (universal NAND/NOR gates, latch and master–slave D flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder). Every gate structure below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled standard construction; it is never a claim about AMD's actual netlist. The only RDNA 3-specific numbers are the published geometries already recorded at Levels 2–3 and the arithmetic derived transparently from them.

- **Register file (the banked VGPR file and the SGPR file)** — At gate level a GPU register file is a latch/SRAM-style array: wordline decoders (NAND/AND trees) selecting one row, storage cells holding the bits, per-port column mux trees steering the read data out, and sense amplifiers where the array is SRAM-style. Which cell style AMD uses, and the write-port count, are not published, so both candidate forms are named conditionally and neither is asserted: in 6T-SRAM form the store is 6 transistors per bit — 384 KiB per CU is 3,145,728 bits, i.e. 18,874,368 6T cell transistors per CU by arithmetic, and across the full die 36 MB is 301,989,888 bits, i.e. 1,811,939,328 6T cell transistors; in flip-flop form (about 20–28 transistors per bit, primer bottom layer) the same 384 KiB per CU would be roughly 63–88 million transistors per CU. The arithmetic is from the published geometry, not a published figure. The four banks are indexed by the low two source bits (SRC[1:0], 2 bits by arithmetic), and each bank's cache has three read ports — one each for SRC0, SRC1 and SRC2 — so the port structure is a 3-read-port bank cache, while the write-port count is unpublished. The die-wide totals above rest on the Level-2 value of 384 KiB per CU; ROCm 6.3.2 lists 768 KiB for the same card, and that dispute is recorded at Level-3. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (operand steering, DPP cross-lane select, VOPD destination steering)** — The operand-steering and cross-lane muxes are trees of 2:1 muxes; each 2:1 mux is two transmission gates (one NMOS + one PMOS per leg) or an equivalent NAND-gate cell, with selects decoded by AND trees from the instruction's register fields. DPP adds a cross-lane select: one 2:1 mux per bit per lane choice, steering a neighbouring lane's value into the lane's operand slot. The VOPD destination rule is steering by a single bit: vdstY's least significant bit is the complement of vdstX[0], so the two results are steered to the even and odd VGPR write ports by a 1-bit select — a 2:1 mux per result bit. The mux radix, the DPP select width and the operand-collection structure are not published. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the wave-scheduler issue queues)** — Storage (a flop array or a small SRAM) plus write and read pointer counters — D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers — plus full/empty comparators: XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree. Depths, the per-SIMD32 wave count and the scheduler's selection policy are not published. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the wave scheduler and work-group dispatch)** — State bits are D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer); next-state and output logic are NAND/NOR networks — whatever the synthesis tool maps the state table to in the standard-cell library. Dual issue is not hardware-checked: the compiler, not a hardware controller, guarantees the VOPD pairing rules, so there is no legality-checking state machine to decompose. The scheduler's state count, its wave-selection policy and the dispatch hardware are not published. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (the VOPD bank-legality check, the EXEC mask, and LDS conflict detection)** — The bank-legality check is 2-bit index equality: one XNOR gate per index bit (about 10–12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree, so a pair of source operands from different banks passes only when the two 2-bit bank indices differ — two such checks, one for the SRC0 pair and one for the SRC1 pair. The EXEC mask is a per-lane AND of the EXEC bit with the issue-valid signal — 32 AND2 gates for a wave32 mask. LDS conflict detection is bank-index equality: the bank index is 6 bits by arithmetic (64 banks, 1-bit set select + 5-bit bank-in-set), so one XNOR per index bit feeding an AND tree per pair of accesses, with the arbiter serializing the losers. The comparator widths as circuits, the conflict-detection circuit and the EXEC-mask storage are not published. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (the SIMD32 FP32 datapath and the WMMA matrix engine)** — Each multiplier bottoms out in AND gates forming the partial products from the operand bits, a compressor tree of full adders (about 28-transistor mirror cells, primer bottom layer) collapsing them, and one final carry-propagate adder finishing. Floating-point lanes add an exponent adder (a small lookahead adder), a sign XOR and a normalizer built from a priority encoder and a barrel shifter. The SIMD32 datapath is 32 lanes of this, dual-issued to 64 FP32 results per SIMD32 per cycle — 256 per CU, 24,576 across the GCD, 61.4 TFLOPS at 2.5 GHz, as published at Level-2. The WMMA engine performs A*B+C⇒D; its tile sizes, the multiplier array's dimensions and partial-product structure are not published. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (FMA accumulation and WMMA accumulation)** — A reduction tree whose nodes are the primer's full adder: carry-save compressors (full adders used as 3:2 counters) at the leaves, one carry-propagate adder at the root. FP32 accumulation wraps each add with alignment shifters — log-stage mux arrays — and a rounding incrementer. The WMMA engine accumulates its matrix products into D the same way. Tree depth, the carry structure and whether WMMA accumulation is a tree or a serial chain are not published. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the LDS banks and the L0/L1 caches)** — Rows of 6T SRAM cells (primer, bottom layer) behind a row decoder — a tree of NAND gates selecting one wordline — transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the LDS is 128 KB per WGP, i.e. 1,048,576 bits, i.e. 6,291,456 6T cell transistors per WGP; each bank is 512x32, i.e. 16,384 bits, i.e. 98,304 cells; across 48 WGPs the LDS is 6 MB, i.e. 50,331,648 bits, i.e. 301,989,888 cells. The L0 caches per CU are 32+16+32 = 80 KB, i.e. 655,360 bits, i.e. 3,932,160 cells per CU, and across 96 CUs 7.5 MB, i.e. 62,914,560 bits, i.e. 377,487,360 cells. The L1 is 256 KB per shader array across 12 arrays (96 CUs ÷ 8 per array), i.e. 3 MB, i.e. 25,165,824 bits, i.e. 150,994,944 cells. (Die context only, outside the signature block: the 6 MB L2 would be 50,331,648 bits, i.e. 301,989,888 6T cell transistors in the same form — labelled context, not part of this block.) The LDS bank sense-amplifier form and the L0/L1 bank counts and line sizes are not published. Standard construction.
- **CAM / TCAM (the cache tag compare)** — The tag array is SRAM plus per-bit XNOR match logic: each tag bit is compared against the address bit, and every cell on a row drives one shared, precharged matchline — a wired-NOR of per-bit XNOR results (primer CAM cell, about 10 transistors). The published associativities — L0 vector 32-way, L0 scalar 4-way, L1 16-way, L2 16-way — set the width of the parallel compare. The tag-array size, the replacement policy and the compare circuit are not published, and the tag widths are unpublished (the line sizes are unpublished), so no per-way counts are claimed. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (the LDS bank interconnect and the WGP-to-L1 path)** — One output mux per output fed by all inputs, each mux a tree of transmission-gate legs, plus an arbiter per output: a priority-encoder tree of AND/OR gates with a grant register holding the winner. The published fan-out is 32 concurrent 32-bit accesses per 32-bank set, so the fabric moves 32 DWORDs per cycle per set. The crossbar's radix, port counts and arbitration policy are not published. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline register (the issue-to-writeback stage latches)** — One master–slave D flip-flop per bit (about 20–28 transistors, primer bottom layer), usually with a 2:1 enable mux in front so the stage can stall — the mux + flop pair is the same cell shape as a scan flop, minus the scan input. The FP32 latency is 5 cycles (measured), so at least five stages of latching separate issue from writeback. The stage count, the latch widths and the bypass/forwarding network are not published. Standard construction.
- **Counter (LDS allocation registers and resident-wave counts)** — A binary counter is D flip-flops plus a full-adder incrementer, with a terminal-count comparator — XNOR gates per count bit feeding an AND tree — where the count must stop. The LDSbase/size allocation registers are this form, and the addressing arithmetic is published geometry: 128 KB of LDS is a 17-bit byte address, the 64 KB maximum per work-group is a 16-bit address, and the 64 banks are a 6-bit bank index (1-bit set select + 5-bit bank-in-set). The counter widths, the wave-slot accounting and the barrier resource count are not published. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (the outstanding-memory-instruction counters)** — One counter per wave per instruction class: D flip-flops holding the count, a full-adder incrementer/decrementer that spends a credit on issue and earns it back on completion, and a zero/non-zero comparator — XNOR gates against zero feeding an AND tree — that the s_waitcnt instruction tests before the wave proceeds. The counter widths and the number of counters per wave are not published. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (the work-group barrier)** — There is no synchronizer primitive to decompose here: the barrier is same-clock-domain arrival counting plus an all-arrived AND release, not a clock-domain crossing, so there is no 2-flop synchronizer in this block — zero gates. Its gate content is the arrival counters (item 12's form) plus an AND tree over the arrival flags plus the steering that releases the waiting waves. Single-wave work-groups skip it entirely — their barrier ops are treated as S_NOP. The barrier's counter width, its arrival-tracking circuit and the cross-SIMD32 signalling are not published. Standard construction.
- **Switch arbiter (LDS bank arbitration)** — When two accesses collide on one bank, the arbiter is a priority-encoder tree of AND/OR gates over the request bits, a grant register of D flip-flops holding the winner, and grant muxes steering the winning access to the bank while the losers wait a cycle. The LDS also carries 64 integer atomic units, one per bank, so an atomic on a bank is arbitrated the same way. The arbiter's policy (round-robin, fixed priority), its grant latency and the atomic-unit arbitration are not published. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (the scalar ALU's shift path)** — A 5-stage log shifter for a 32-bit word (log2 32 = 5), one 2:1 mux per bit per stage — 32 bits x 5 stages = 160 2:1 muxes, about 640 transistors in transmission-gate form (4 transistors per 2:1 mux). The scalar registers are 32-bit and the LDS is DWORD-wide, so the 32-bit word is published geometry; the shifter's construction — whether it is a mux-tree or a logarithmic shifter — is not published, and the 5-stage form is the standard log-shifter construction. Standard construction.

Honesty: AMD publishes no gate-level structure for Navi 31 — no register-file cell style or write-port count, no mux radix, no issue-queue depths, no scheduler state count or wave-selection policy, no VOPD comparator circuit form, no SIMD32 or WMMA multiplier geometry or tile sizes, no adder-tree depth or carry structure, no LDS crossbar radix, no pipeline stage count, no tag-array geometry or line sizes, no LDS bank sense-amplifier form, no credit-counter widths, no barrier arrival-circuit form and no barrel-shifter construction. Every gate and transistor figure above is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer — the generic textbook form of each primitive, never a claim about AMD's actual netlist. Disputed: AMD's ROCm hardware-specifications table lists VGPR File 768 KiB and SGPR File 16 KiB for the RX 7900 XTX in its 6.3.2 edition, against 384 KiB and 20 KiB in the 6.2.2 edition the Level-2 values were taken from — the wiki keeps the Level-2 values, and every die-wide register-file total above rests on 384 KiB. The published package anchor is 58 billion transistors, and the wiki states no GCD-specific total (Wikipedia 45.4bn vs Chips and Cheese 45.7bn). The 6T cell totals above — about 1.81 billion for the VGPR file, 0.30 billion for the LDS, 0.38 billion for the L0 caches, 0.15 billion for the L1, 0.30 billion for the L2 and 4.83 billion for the Infinity Cache, roughly 7.8 billion together, about 13% of the 58-billion package total — are a sanity check against that anchor, not a claim about the netlist: the rest of the package is the SIMD32 datapaths, the WMMA and ray accelerators, the MCDs' 12.3 billion transistors, the PHYs, the memory controllers and the I/O. (New Level-4 fact record: unverifiable.)

#### Down to the gates: The Memory Cache Die and Infinity Cache — the last-level cache moved off the die

AMD publishes no internal organisation for the MCD at all — no cache-controller, tag-array or link-arbiter internals — so this block continues the Level-3 position: every primitive below is the standard generic form of a memory cache die of this contract, labelled generic, not an RDNA 3 fact. The published contract is one 16 MB Infinity Cache slice plus two 32-bit GDDR6 PHYs per MCD, joined to the GCD by four 64-byte Infinity Link channels per direction at 9.2 Gbps signalling, for 5.3 TB/s cumulative peak and 3.5 TB/s effective bandwidth at under 5% of GPU power. Each primitive is decomposed into its gate-level structure from the primer's bottom layer; nothing here is a claim about the Navi 31 MCDs' actual implementation.

- **SRAM bank (the 16 MB Infinity Cache slice) — generic form** — The slice is a set of 6T SRAM banks: rows of 6T cells (primer, bottom layer) behind a NAND-tree row decoder, transmission-gate column muxes and latch-type sense amplifiers. Arithmetic from the published contract: a 16 MB slice is 134,217,728 bits, i.e. 805,306,368 6T cell transistors per MCD, and 96 MB across six MCDs is 805,306,368 bits, i.e. 4,831,838,208 cells. The bank count, line size, associativity and port style are not published. Standard construction.
- **CAM / TCAM (the tag array) — generic form** — The tag array is SRAM plus per-bit XNOR match logic: each tag bit is compared against the address bit, and every cell on a row drives one shared, precharged matchline — a wired-NOR of per-bit XNOR results (primer CAM cell, about 10 transistors). The associativity, tag width and replacement policy are not published. Standard construction.
