- **FIFO / queue (link ingress/egress and GDDR6 request queues) — generic form** — Storage (a flop array or a small SRAM) plus write and read pointer counters — D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers — plus full/empty comparators: XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree, as in Block 1 item 3. Depths and widths are not published. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (the MCD internal switch) — generic form** — One output mux per output fed by all inputs, each mux a tree of transmission-gate legs, plus an arbiter per output: a priority-encoder tree of AND/OR gates with a grant register holding the winner. Radix and port counts are not published. Standard construction.
- **Switch arbiter (channel and bank arbitration) — generic form** — A priority-encoder tree of AND/OR gates over the request bits, a grant register of D flip-flops holding the winner, and grant muxes steering the winning request to the bank or PHY. The policy, requester count and grant latency are not published. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (channel select and PHY lane steering) — generic form** — Transmission-gate 2:1 trees, 2 transistors per input leg, selecting the four 64-byte link channels onto the cache banks and steering the two 32-bit PHYs' lanes onto the GDDR6 bus. Radix and select encoding are not published. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (Infinity Link flow control) — generic form** — D flip-flops holding the credit count, a full-adder incrementer/decrementer that spends one credit per flit sent and earns credits back as the receiver drains, and a zero comparator — XNOR gates against zero feeding an AND tree — that stops the sender at zero. The credit count, flit width and return latency are not published. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (the GCD-to-MCD clock-domain crossing) — generic form** — This one IS a real clock-domain crossing: the GCD and the MCD are different dies on different process nodes (5 nm and 6 nm) with different clocks — the front end runs at up to 2.5 GHz and the shaders at 2.3 GHz, while the MCD's clock is not published — so the link's control and credit signals cross domains through the standard two-flop synchronizer: 2 D flip-flops in series per bit in the receiving clock domain, about 40–56 transistors per bit (standard construction). The synchronizer depth and latency are not published. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the cache controller and the GDDR6 controller) — generic form** — State bits are D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer); next-state and output logic are NAND/NOR networks stepping the cache controller through lookup, fill, eviction and writeback, and the GDDR6 controller through command scheduling, refresh and training. State counts, scheduling policies and command queues are not published. Standard construction.

Honesty: AMD publishes the contract and nothing inside it: six MCDs on TSMC 6 nm, each 37.52 mm² with 2.05 billion transistors, one 16 MB Infinity Cache slice and two 32-bit GDDR6 PHYs per MCD, 96 MB and a 384-bit bus in total; four 64-byte Infinity Link channels per direction per MCD interface at 9.2 Gbps, 5.3 TB/s cumulative peak, about 10x the bandwidth density of organic links, up to 80% more efficient; 3.5 TB/s effective bandwidth for under 5% of GPU power; and unused TSV landing points on each MCD. It publishes no cache-controller, tag-array, link-arbiter, queue-depth, bank-count, associativity, crossbar or clock-domain internals — and this decomposition invents none of them. The nine primitives above are the standard construction of a memory cache die of this contract, labelled generic, not facts about the Navi 31 MCDs. (New Level-4 fact record: unverifiable.)

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [unverifiable] **AMD RDNA 3 — Navi 31** — Gate-level structure not published: no AMD source discloses the WGP's, the MCD's or any Navi 31 primitive's per-primitive gate/transistor implementation (register-file cell style and write-port count; mux radix; issue-queue depths; scheduler state count and selection policy; VOPD comparator widths; SIMD32/WMMA multiplier geometry and tile sizes; adder-tree depth and carry structure; LDS crossbar radix; pipeline stage count; tag-array geometry and line sizes; LDS bank sense-amplifier form; credit-counter widths; barrier arrival-circuit form; barrel-shifter construction; and all MCD internals). All gate-level detail in the Level-4 decomposition is textbook-standard construction, labelled as such. Sources: AMD, "RDNA3" Instruction Set Architecture Reference Guide (15-Aug-2023); AMD press release, 3 Nov 2022; AMD ROCm GPU hardware specifications; PC Gamer, "AMD's Infinity Links is the unsung hero of RDNA 3" (Nov 2022); Chips and Cheese, "Microbenchmarking AMD's RDNA 3 Graphics Architecture" (Jan 2023).

### Intel Ponte Vecchio (Xe-HPC)

#### Down to the gates: The Xe-core — eight vector engines, eight matrix engines and a 512 KB L1 that doubles as scratchpad

Intel publishes no gate-level structure for the Xe-core — the deck draws the core at block level (the RF label, the L1 data cache/SLM and instruction cache, the sixteen engines, the load/store unit) and the ISSCC coverage gives its port rate and nothing inside it. What follows takes each of the sixteen Level-3 primitives one level further, into the gates it is built from and the transistors those gates are built from, using the primer's bottom layer (universal NAND/NOR gates, latch and master–slave D flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder). Every gate structure below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled standard construction; it is never a claim about Intel's actual netlist. The only Ponte Vecchio-specific numbers are the published geometries already recorded at Levels 2–3 and the arithmetic derived transparently from them.

- **Register file (RF — the operand store beside the L1)** — At gate level a register file is a storage array — flip-flop/latch cells or 6T SRAM cells — behind wordline decoders (NAND/AND trees) that select one row per port, with per-port column mux trees steering the read data out and sense amplifiers where the array is SRAM-style. The published geometry sets the port widths: each vector engine takes 512-bit operands and each matrix engine 4096-bit operands, so the file must deliver one 512-bit operand set per XVE or one 4096-bit operand set per XMX per clock. Which cell style Intel uses, and the RF's size, entry count, bank count and port count, are not published, so both candidate cell forms are named conditionally and neither is asserted — and no cell total is claimed, since a total needs an entry count the deck never gives. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the 512 KB L1 data cache / shared local memory)** — Rows of 6T SRAM cells (primer, bottom layer) behind a row decoder — a tree of NAND gates selecting one wordline — transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. Arithmetic from the published geometry: a 512 KB L1 is 4,194,304 bits, i.e. 25,165,824 6T cell transistors per Xe-core; per compute tile the 4 MB of L1 is 33,554,432 bits, i.e. 201,326,592 cells; across the full OAM the 64 MB of L1 is 536,870,912 bits, i.e. 3,221,225,472 cells. The SLM mode changes the addressing — software-managed scratchpad instead of hardware-cached lines — not the cell form. The bank count, line size, associativity, port count and tag geometry are not published. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the L1 instruction cache)** — The same 6T form: rows of 6T cells behind a NAND-tree row decoder, transmission-gate column muxes and latch-type sense amplifiers, plus the tag comparator of the next-but-one item. Its size is not published, so no bit or cell total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (operand select into the engines)** — The operand-select muxes are trees of 2:1 muxes; each 2:1 mux is two transmission gates (one NMOS + one PMOS per leg, 4 transistors) or an equivalent NAND-gate cell, with selects decoded by AND trees from the instruction's register fields. Arithmetic from the published operand widths: one 2:1 select stage across a 512-bit XVE operand is 512 muxes, about 2,048 transistors in transmission-gate form; across a 4096-bit XMX operand it is 4,096 muxes, about 16,384 transistors. The mux radix, the port count and the select encoding are not published. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (the XMX 8-deep systolic array)** — Each stage of the systolic array is a multiply-accumulate slice: AND gates forming the partial products from the operand bits, a compressor tree of full adders (about 28-transistor mirror cells, primer bottom layer) collapsing them, and one final carry-propagate adder finishing the sum. Arithmetic from the published 4096-bit operand width: one XMX operand holds 512 INT8 lanes or 256 BF16/FP16 lanes, and the published per-core rates — 1024 INT8 operations and 512 BF16 operations per XMX per clock — are exactly lanes × 2, a multiply plus an accumulate per lane. The Booth encoding, the compressor-tree structure, the partial-product count and how the eight stages split the work are not published. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (XMX accumulation and the XVE floating-point add)** — A reduction tree whose nodes are the primer's full adder: carry-save compressors (full adders used as 3:2 counters) at the leaves, one carry-propagate adder at the root. Floating-point addition wraps each add with an exponent adder (a small lookahead adder), a mantissa alignment shifter (the next-but-one item) and a normalizer built from a priority encoder and a barrel shifter. Arithmetic from the published operand widths: a 512-bit XVE operand holds 16 FP32 lanes, 8 FP64 lanes or 32 FP16 lanes. The tree depth, the carry structure and whether the XMX accumulation is a tree or a serial chain are not published. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (FP alignment and normalization in the XVE) — standard form** — A logarithmic shifter: one 2:1 mux per bit per stage, about 4 transistors per mux in transmission-gate form, with log2 of the shift range stages. A floating-point lane aligns a 24-bit mantissa (23 stored bits plus the implicit leading 1), so the standard form is at most 5 stages (2^5 = 32) of 2:1 muxes per lane. The shifter width, the stage count and the placement inside the XVE pipeline are not published, and this is the standard construction of a floating-point datapath, not a published block of the Xe-core. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (the L1 tag compare)** — One XNOR gate per tag bit (about 10–12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree, so a line is a hit only when every compared bit matches. The tag width, the associativity, the way count and the replacement policy are not published, so no per-way gate count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (the systolic step counter and the SLM address counters)** — A binary counter is D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer) plus a full-adder incrementer, with a terminal-count comparator — XNOR gates per count bit feeding an AND tree — where the count must stop. Arithmetic from the published geometries: the 8-deep systolic array steps one stage per clock, so its step counter is 3 bits wide (2^3 = 8) — about 60–84 transistors for the three flip-flops plus the 3-bit incrementer — and the 512 KB L1/SLM is a 19-bit byte address (2^19 = 524,288). No other counter width is published. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the Xe-core dispatch controller)** — State bits are D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer); next-state and output logic are NAND/NOR networks — whatever the synthesis tool maps the state table to in the standard-cell library. Intel publishes no scheduler, issue width or pipeline-stage detail for the Xe-core, so the controller's state count, its hazard handling and its ray-tracing dispatch are not published, and there is no state machine here to count. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline register (the engine stage registers)** — One master–slave D flip-flop per bit (about 20–28 transistors, primer bottom layer), usually with a 2:1 enable mux in front so the stage can stall — the mux + flop pair is the same cell shape as a scan flop, minus the scan input. Arithmetic from the published operand widths: a 512-bit XVE stage latch is about 10,240–14,336 transistors, and a 4096-bit XMX stage latch about 81,920–114,688 transistors. The stage count, the latch widths beyond the published operand widths and the bypass/forwarding network are not published. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (the L1-to-engines operand delivery)** — One output mux per engine fed by the L1 port, each mux a tree of transmission-gate legs, plus an arbiter per output: a priority-encoder tree of AND/OR gates with a grant register holding the winner. The published rate through the port is 512 bytes per clock — 4096 bits per clock — fanned out to sixteen engines. The crossbar's radix, port count and arbitration policy are not published. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the LSU request queue)** — Storage (a flop array or a small SRAM) plus write and read pointer counters — D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers — plus full/empty comparators: XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree. The queue depth and entry width are not published. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (LSU to Memory Fabric flow control) — standard form** — D flip-flops holding the credit count, a full-adder incrementer/decrementer that spends one credit per request sent and earns credits back as the receiver drains, and a zero comparator — XNOR gates against zero feeding an AND tree — that stops the sender at zero. The credit count and the return latency are not published. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer — none inside the Xe-core** — There is no synchronizer primitive to decompose here: the core is a single clock domain — its engines, RF, caches and load/store unit all run on the compute tile's clock — so there is no 2-flop synchronizer in this block — zero gates. The asynchronous crossing lives at the tile boundary in the FDI, where the base tile's level shifters and phase compensation do the work (see the second block). Standard construction.
- **CAM / TCAM — none in the Xe-core** — There is no CAM primitive to decompose here: the only associative lookup in the core is the L1 tag compare, which is a comparator, not a CAM — zero gates. Standard construction.

Honesty: Intel publishes the Xe-core's contract and none of its circuits: the RF label in the Compute Tile diagram; 512 KB L1 per core, software-configurable as scratchpad, fed at 512 B/clock (the deck's "512 bit" diagram text against the eeNews/ISSCC 512 B/clock — the dispute recorded at Level-2, wiki keeps 512 B/clock); 8 vector engines at 512 bits and 8 matrix engines at 4096 bits with an 8-deep systolic array; 256 FP32 / 256 FP64 / 512 FP16 vector operations and 2048 TF32 / 4096 FP16 / 4096 BF16 / 8192 INT8 matrix operations per clock per core. Every gate and transistor figure above is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer — the generic textbook form of each primitive, never a claim about Intel's actual netlist — and every total is arithmetic from a published geometry, labelled as such. The RF has no claimed cell total because its entry count is unpublished; the L1 instruction cache has none because its size is unpublished. (New Level-4 fact record: unverifiable.)

#### Down to the gates: Rambo and the base tile's Memory Fabric — 408 MB of second-level cache and the die-to-die fabric that feeds it

Intel publishes no gate-level structure for the second level either — the deck and the ISSCC coverage give the fabric's geometry generously (the bank sizes, the 4096-bytes-per-cycle fabric rate, the eight FDI groups of 800 lanes) and stop there. What follows takes each of the twenty Level-3 primitives one level further, into the gates it is built from and the transistors those gates are built from, using the primer's bottom layer. Every gate structure below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled standard construction; it is never a claim about Intel's actual netlist. The only Ponte Vecchio-specific numbers are the published geometries already recorded at Levels 2–3 and the arithmetic derived transparently from them. One distinction the published form forces: the FDI's clock-domain crossing is mesochronous — common clocking with phase compensation and a forward-plus-return clock pair — not a two-flop synchronizer, and the decomposition says so at the synchronizer instead of substituting the familiar form.

- **SRAM bank (Rambo — four 3.75 MB banks per tile)** — Rows of 6T SRAM cells (primer, bottom layer) behind a row decoder — a tree of NAND gates selecting one wordline — transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one 3.75 MB bank is 31,457,280 bits, i.e. 188,743,680 6T cell transistors; across the eight Rambo tiles the 32 banks hold 120 MB, i.e. 1,006,632,960 bits, i.e. 6,039,797,760 cells. Each bank's own PLL, clock tap and test block decompose in the PLL and DFT items below. Bank arbitration, replacement policy and tag geometry are not published. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the base tile's Memory Fabric — 144 MB per base tile)** — The same 6T form: rows of 6T cells behind a NAND-tree row decoder, transmission-gate column muxes and latch-type sense amplifiers. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one base tile's 144 MB is 1,207,959,552 bits, i.e. 7,247,757,312 6T cell transistors; the two base tiles' 288 MB is 2,415,919,104 bits, i.e. 14,495,514,624 cells. The whole second level — Rambo plus Memory Fabric, 408 MB — is 3,422,552,064 bits, i.e. 20,535,312,384 6T cell transistors, about 20.5% of the published 100-billion-transistor package anchor: a sanity check against that anchor, not a claim about the netlist, since the rest of the package is the 128 Xe-cores, the 64 MB of L1, the HBM controllers, the SerDes tiles, the PHYs and the I/O. The bank count, line size, associativity and tag geometry are not published; the 64-banks-in-parallel figure is arithmetic from the two published rates (4096 bytes per cycle ÷ 64 bytes per bank operation), not a published bank count. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (the L3 tag compare)** — One XNOR gate per tag bit (about 10–12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree, so a bank returns a line only when every compared bit matches — one such comparator per bank, 32 across the Rambo tiles plus one per Memory Fabric bank. The tag width, the associativity, the way count and the replacement policy are not published, so no per-bank gate count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (the MDFI — the "L3 Switch Fabric")** — One output mux per destination fed by all sources, each mux a tree of transmission-gate legs, plus an arbiter per output: a priority-encoder tree of AND/OR gates with a grant register holding the winner. The endpoints are the published tile counts: 16 compute tiles, 8 Rambo tiles, 2 base tiles, the HBM controllers, the PCIe host interface and the Xe Link tiles. The crossbar's radix, port count and arbitration policy are not published. Standard construction.
- **Switch arbiter (MDFI arbitration)** — When several tiles want the same Rambo or Memory Fabric bank in one cycle, the arbiter is a priority-encoder tree of AND/OR gates over the request bits, a grant register of D flip-flops holding the winner, and grant muxes steering the winning request to the bank while the losers wait a cycle. The policy — round-robin, fixed priority, age-based — the requester count and the grant latency are not published. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the FDI transmit and receive FIFOs)** — Storage (a flop array or a small SRAM) plus write and read pointer counters — D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers — plus full/empty comparators: XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree. The published Rx behaviour adds a width change across a register boundary — "signals are decompressed back to full width in the destination Rx domain" — which is a demux/register form at the FIFO's read side. The FIFO depths and widths are not published. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (the FDI asynchronous interface — level shifters, phase compensation, forward and return clocks)** — This crossing is mesochronous, not a two-flop synchronizer, and the decomposition keeps the published form: data flops clocked by the forwarded clock, a phase-compensation delay line (an inverter chain or a digitally controlled delay line) that corrects for variation between the base and compute tiles, and a phase detector plus control FSM steering the delay — with the forward clock (base to compute) and the return clock (compute to base) that the compensation needs. There is no 2-flop synchronizer in this block — the standard construction here is the phase-compensated forwarded-clock interface the sources describe, not the generic CDC form. The compensation depth and latency are not published. Standard construction.
- **Level shifter (the FDI rail conversion)** — The standard cross-coupled level shifter: a differential NMOS input pair, a cross-coupled PMOS load and an output inverter — roughly 8–10 transistors per bit in the standard cell form — letting a signal driven on the compute tile's rail be read on the base tile's supply. The count, width and conversion range are not published, and no per-tile total is claimed: the FDI carries 6,400 data lanes by arithmetic (8 groups × 800 lanes) against the deck's "> 7K FDI Connections" total, and the larger total includes the clock, power and DFT connections the same slide draws, so the shifter count is not derivable from either figure. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (bank select and SerDes lane steering)** — Bank select is address decode, not a mux tree: the address bits feed a NAND/AND decoder tree that enables one bank per access, with the 64-byte line gated onto the fabric by that enable. SerDes lane steering is the mux form: transmission-gate 2:1 trees (4 transistors per mux) steering lanes onto the 90G links. The mux radix and the select encoding are not published. Standard construction.
- **Counter (the FDI group counters and the HBM refresh counters)** — A binary counter is D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer) plus a full-adder incrementer, with a terminal-count comparator — XNOR gates per count bit feeding an AND tree — where the count must stop. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the FDI's eight groups are a 3-bit group index (2^3 = 8). The HBM refresh counter widths are not published. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the HBM2e controllers, the MDFI routing FSM, the PCIe Gen5/CXL host interface)** — State bits are D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer); next-state and output logic are NAND/NOR networks — whatever the synthesis tool maps the state table to in the standard-cell library — stepping the HBM controllers through command scheduling and refresh, the MDFI routing FSM through its route table, and the host interface through its 16 published PCIe Gen5/CXL lanes. The state counts, queue depths, scheduling policies and command queues are not published. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (the address-to-bank decode)** — Two candidate standard forms, and the scheme is unpublished so neither is asserted: direct bit-select, where a slice of the address bits indexes the bank through a decoder tree; or an XOR hash, where the bank index is an XOR tree over the address bits (one XOR2 gate, about 10–12 transistors, per tree node) so consecutive lines spread across banks. Which form Intel uses — which bits, what hash, what interleave — is not published; the primitive is named for its role only. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline register (the MDFI stages and the SerDes transmit/receive registers)** — One master–slave D flip-flop per bit (about 20–28 transistors, primer bottom layer), usually with a 2:1 enable mux in front so the stage can stall. Arithmetic from the published bank operation: one 64-byte bank operation is 512 bits per clock, so a stage latch holding one bank's line is about 10,240–14,336 transistors. The stage counts and the register widths beyond the published 64-byte bank operations are not published. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (FDI, EMIB and HBM flow control) — standard form** — D flip-flops holding the credit count, a full-adder incrementer/decrementer that spends one credit per flit sent and earns credits back as the receiver drains, and a zero comparator — XNOR gates against zero feeding an AND tree — that stops the sender at zero. The credit counts, the flit widths and the return latencies are not published. Standard construction.
- **PLL (the die clocks and the per-bank Rambo clocks)** — The standard PLL: a phase-frequency detector (D flip-flops and gates comparing the reference against the divided clock), a charge pump, a loop filter, a voltage-controlled oscillator (a ring of inverters), and a divider (a counter) closing the loop. The FDI slide shows Compute, Base, Link and Backup PLLs, and each of the 32 Rambo banks carries its own PLL. Their frequencies and loop parameters are not published. Standard construction.
- **SerDes (the Xe Link tile — up to 90G links and the 8-port embedded switch)** — The standard SerDes forms: the serializer is a shift register — a chain of D flip-flops — plus a mux tree collapsing parallel data onto one lane; the deserializer is the mirror image, a shift register plus a demux; clock recovery is a phase detector plus loop filter plus VCO; equalization is a feed-forward tapped delay line (flip-flop taps with multiplier/adders) and a decision-feedback path (a decision flop feeding back through taps). Arithmetic from the deck summary: "4x16 90G SERDES" is 64 SerDes lanes. The lane count beyond the summary line, the switch radix beyond the 8 ports and the SerDes equalization are not published. Standard construction.
- **DFT / test mux (the FDI test blocks and the Rambo per-bank Test)** — A scan mux is a 2:1 transmission-gate mux (about 4 transistors) in front of each scannable flop, steering test data in place of functional data; the Rambo per-bank Test block is the MBIST form — a pattern generator plus a comparator, the same algorithm-engine shape as the wiki's Memory BIST & Repair entry — letting each SRAM bank be exercised in isolation, the only way to test 47 tiles after assembly. The test patterns, the scan-chain lengths and the mux forms are not published. Standard construction.
- **CAM / TCAM — none in the second level** — There is no CAM primitive to decompose here: tag lookup in Rambo and the Memory Fabric is comparator-based, and the L3's "complex geometric topology" is a bank layout, not a CAM — zero gates. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array — none in the second level** — There is no multiplier array to decompose here: this block stores and moves data; it computes nothing, and there is no multiply-accumulate anywhere in Rambo, the Memory Fabric, the MDFI or the SerDes tiles — zero gates. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter — none in the second level** — There is no barrel shifter to decompose here: whole 64-byte lines move through the fabric, and alignment is by address-bit selection at the bank-select muxes, not by a shifter — zero gates. Standard construction.

Honesty: Intel publishes the second level's contract and geometry and nothing inside it: Rambo's four 3.75 MB banks per tile with a PLL, clock tap and test block per bank; the base tile's 144 MB Memory Fabric with banks doing one 64-byte read/write per clock and the fabric moving 4096 bytes per cycle; the MDFI and the "L3 Switch Fabric" label; the FDI's eight groups of 800 lanes per compute tile and the deck's "> 7K FDI Connections" total; the FDI's level shifters, phase compensation and forward-plus-return clocks; the deck summary's "4x16 90G SERDES, 1x16 PCIe Gen5"; 16 PCIe Gen5/CXL host lanes; the 24-layer (11-2-11) substrate; and the A0 silicon measurements — over 45 TFLOPS FP32 throughput, over 50 TBps cache bandwidth and over 8 Tbps communication bandwidth. It publishes no Rambo or Memory Fabric tag geometry or replacement policy; no MDFI radix, arbitration policy or queue depths; no HBM controller queue depths or scheduling policy; no FDI FIFO depths or widths; no SerDes lane counts beyond the deck summary line; and no per-bank clock frequencies — and this decomposition invents none of them. Every gate and transistor figure above is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer, and every total is arithmetic from a published geometry, labelled as such; the 20.5% figure is a sanity check against the published 100-billion-transistor package anchor, not a netlist claim. Disputed, not unpublished: the base-tile area is 640 mm² in the deck against 646 mm² in the ISSCC coverage — the wiki keeps 640 mm², recorded at Level-3, no new record here. (New Level-4 fact record: unverifiable.)

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [unverifiable] **Intel Ponte Vecchio (Xe-HPC)** — Gate-level structure not published: no Intel source discloses the Xe-core's, Rambo's, the Memory Fabric's, the MDFI's or the FDI's per-primitive gate/transistor implementation (register-file cell style, size, entry count, bank count and port count; L1 instruction-cache size; mux radix and select encoding; XMX Booth encoding, compressor-tree structure and partial-product count; adder-tree depth and carry structure; barrel-shifter width, stage count and placement; L1/L3 tag widths, associativity and replacement policy; dispatch-controller state count and hazard handling; pipeline stage count and bypass network; crossbar radix and arbitration policy; LSU queue depth; credit counts and return latencies; MDFI radix, arbitration policy and queue depths; HBM controller queue depths and scheduling policy; FDI FIFO depths and widths; SerDes lane counts beyond the deck summary line and equalization; per-bank clock frequencies and PLL loop parameters; scan-chain lengths and test-mux forms). All gate-level detail in the Level-4 decomposition is textbook-standard construction, labelled as such. Sources: Intel, "Ponte Vecchio: A Multi Tile 3D Stacked Processor for Exascale Computing" (Gomes et al., 2022); eeNews Europe, "Ponte Vecchio 3D supercomputer processor uses five process nodes", Feb 22, 2022 (ISSCC 2022).

### Arm Immortalis-G720

#### Down to the gates: The Deferred Vertex Shading pipeline — Binning phase, Main phase and the tiler that decides between them

Arm publishes no gate-level structure for the Deferred Vertex Shading front end — the Mali G1 Performance Counter Reference Guide (doc 111042) and the GPU Best Practices Developer Guide (doc 101897) describe the two phases, the three queues, the tiler's culling and binning and the per-core geometry, and stop there. What follows takes each of the sixteen Level-3 primitives one level further, into the gates it is built from and the transistors those gates are built from, using the primer's bottom layer (universal NAND/NOR gates, latch and master-slave D flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder). Every gate structure below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled standard construction; it is never a claim about Arm's actual netlist. The only Immortalis-specific numbers are the published geometries already recorded at Levels 2–3 and the arithmetic derived transparently from them.

- **FSM / controller (the Command Stream Front-end)** — State bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer); next-state and output logic are NAND/NOR networks — whatever the synthesis tool maps the state table to in the standard-cell library — driving the task-splitting, queue selection and phase sequencing that keep the Binning and Main phases independently scheduled. The CSF's state count, its task-splitting granularity and its issue rate are not published, so no flop count is claimed: a controller's gate total needs a state count Arm never gives. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the Binning phase, Main phase and Compute queues)** — Storage — a flop array or a small SRAM — plus write and read pointer counters, D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers, plus full/empty comparators: XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree, with Gray-coded pointers where a queue crosses clock domains. The three queues are what let the two phases run independently instead of in lockstep, but Arm publishes only their existence and roles; their depths, entry widths and port counts are not published, so no storage total is claimed for any of the three. Standard construction.
- **Switch arbiter / priority encoder (queue selection into the cores)** — A priority-encoder tree of AND/OR gates over the three queue-request bits, a grant register of D flip-flops holding the winner, and grant muxes — transmission-gate 2:1 muxes, about 4 transistors each — steering the winning task toward the core array while the losers wait. The arbitration policy (fixed priority, round-robin, or phase-aware), the grant width and the grant latency are not published, so the encoder's size is not claimed either: three requesters is a small tree, but the policy decides its shape. Standard construction.
- **Register file (the shader core's warp thread state)** — At gate level a register file is a storage array — flip-flop/latch cells or 6T SRAM cells — behind wordline decoders (NAND/AND trees) that select one row per port, with per-port column mux trees steering the read data out and sense amplifiers where the array is SRAM-style. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 2048 threads in 16-wide warps is 128 warps resident per core at most. The register file's banking, port counts and physical organisation are not published, and the work-register width per thread is not published either, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array + adder tree (the arithmetic units behind position shading)** — Each arithmetic unit bottoms out in a gate-level multiplier: AND gates forming the partial products from the operand bits, a compressor tree of full adders (about 28-transistor mirror cells, primer bottom layer) collapsing them, and one final carry-propagate adder finishing the sum. Floating-point lanes add an exponent adder (a small lookahead adder), a sign XOR and a normalizer built from a priority encoder and a barrel shifter. The multiplier array's radix, the adder tree's depth and the pipeline staging between them are not published, so no lane-level gate count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline register (the phase handover that stores almost nothing)** — One master-slave D flip-flop per bit (about 20–28 transistors, primer bottom layer), usually with a 2:1 enable mux in front so the stage can stall. The point of this primitive is how little of it there is: positions computed in the Binning phase are discarded rather than staged or written out, so the phase handover holds control state and per-tile lists, not vertex data — the gate-level reason DVS saves bandwidth. The width and form of the binning information itself are not published, so no handover flop count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (the tiler's culling tests)** — Each cull is a set of compares built the standard way: one XNOR gate per compared bit (about 10–12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree, so a primitive passes only when every compared bit matches — clip-space position against the frustum planes, signed area for facing, bounds against the scissor rectangle, and sample coverage. Four published culls, each a comparator bank of this form. The comparator count, the tests' parallelism and the achieved culling rates are not published, so no per-tiler gate count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the tiler itself)** — State bits are D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer); next-state and output logic are NAND/NOR networks stepping the tiler through its sequence — coordinate the position shading on the cores, run the culling tests, emit the per-tile lists. The tiler's state count, clock rate and primitives-per-cycle throughput are not published, so no flop count is claimed: the sequencer's gate total needs a state count Arm never gives, and the culling comparators it drives are decomposed in the preceding item, not duplicated here. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the per-tile binning lists)** — Rows of 6T SRAM cells (primer, bottom layer) behind a row decoder — a tree of NAND gates selecting one wordline — transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers, with a write port from the tiler and a read port into the Main phase front-end. Arm publishes no binning-list depths, no per-tile entry format and no total tiler buffer size, so no bit or cell total is claimed: a bank's transistor count needs a capacity the sources never give. Standard construction.
- **Counter (the per-tile list bookkeeping)** — A binary counter is D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer) plus a full-adder incrementer, with a terminal-count comparator — XNOR gates per count bit feeding an AND tree — where the count must stop. One such counter tracks each open tile list's length or tail pointer, incrementing as the tiler appends a primitive and read back when the Main phase drains the list. The counter width follows the unpublished list depth, so the width is not published either and no per-counter transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (the deferred vs advanced-geometry path select)** — The path-select muxes are trees of 2:1 muxes; each 2:1 mux is two transmission gates (one NMOS + one PMOS per leg, 4 transistors) or an equivalent NAND-gate cell, with selects decoded by AND trees from the draw's path decision — deferred list path or up-front advanced-geometry shading. The select criteria are published behaviour (GPU Best Practices Developer Guide, doc 101897); the mux structure, radix and select encoding are not published, so no gate count is claimed — the select is a control decision at the tiler's output, and its gate cost is the mux tree the unpublished radix would size. Standard construction.
- **Priority encoder / FIFO (the Main phase front-end)** — The Main phase front-end is a priority encoder plus a FIFO in the standard forms: an AND/OR encoder tree picking the next primitive from the tile's list, and queue storage — a flop array or a small SRAM — with write and read pointer counters (D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers) and full/empty comparators (XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree), grouping primitives into 16-wide warps for issue. The published warp width is 16 threads; the list-walk rate and the issue queue depth behind it are not published. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the on-chip tile memory)** — Rows of 6T SRAM cells (primer, bottom layer) behind a row decoder — a tree of NAND gates selecting one wordline — transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. Arithmetic from the published geometry: a full-size tile is 256 bits x 64 x 64 pixels = 1,048,576 bits = 128 KiB of tile storage, i.e. 6,291,456 6T cell transistors. The core's published caches sit beside it as SRAM banks of their own: each 32 KB cache is 262,144 bits, i.e. 1,572,864 6T cell transistors — load/store cache and texture cache each. The bank count, banking and port style of the tile memory are not published. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the L2 slices on the flush path)** — The same 6T form: rows of 6T cells behind a NAND-tree row decoder, transmission-gate column muxes and latch-type sense amplifiers. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the L2 total of up to 1,024 KB is 8,388,608 bits, i.e. 50,331,648 6T cell transistors. Per-slice capacity is configuration-dependent — 2 or 4 slices — so no per-slice total is asserted, and no per-slice total can be derived from the published total without knowing which configuration a given SoC ships. Slice banking and associativity are not published. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (transaction elimination's CRC match)** — One XNOR gate per CRC bit (about 10–12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree, comparing the finished tile's CRC against the stored previous frame's CRC — a match gates the LPDDR write off entirely, which is the gate-level content of transaction elimination. The CRC width and the previous-CRC store's size are not published, so no per-tile gate count is claimed; the published effect is up to 40% less memory bandwidth overall, 26% less in Fortnite and 33% less in Genshin Impact (Arm-measured vs G715) — the bandwidth the comparator saves, not a gate count. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (write-out flow control to LPDDR)** — D flip-flops holding the credit count, a full-adder incrementer/decrementer that spends one credit per flush sent and earns credits back as the memory system drains, and a zero comparator — XNOR gates against zero feeding an AND tree — that stops the flush path at zero. The GPU owns no memory of its own and shares the host SoC's LPDDR5(X), so this is the standard flow-control form on the write-out path. The credit counts, buffer depths and interconnect parameters on this path are not published by Arm. Standard construction.

Honesty: Arm publishes the front end's contract and geometry and none of its circuits: the three queues and their roles, the tiler's four culls, the per-core geometry (2048 threads, 16-wide warps, 33-64 work registers at the reduced thread count, 4 arithmetic units, 512 FP16 / 256 FP32 ops per cycle, 32 KB load/store and 32 KB texture caches, 256 tile bits per pixel), tiles up to 64x64, and 2 or 4 L2 slices up to 1,024 KB. Every gate and transistor figure above is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer, and every total is arithmetic from a published geometry, labelled as such. The two derived figures from Level-3 (128 warps per core; 128 KiB per full-size tile) are arithmetic, not published facts; the new derived totals here are the 6T cell transistor counts (6,291,456 for a full-size tile, 1,572,864 per 32 KB cache, 50,331,648 for the 1,024 KB L2 total). Queue depths, binning-list depths, tiler buffer sizes, culling rates, arbiter policy and register-file banking are not published, and this decomposition invents none of them.

#### Down to the gates: The ray-tracing unit — a fixed-function RTU inside each shader core, power-gated when idle

Arm publishes no gate-level structure for the ray-tracing unit either — the G715-era technical diagrams label the two test units RBOX_UNIT and RTRI_UNIT, the launch coverage gives the under-4%-of-core area and the over-300% speedup, and the 5th-generation power island is a published feature, but no source opens the RTU. What follows takes each of the ten Level-3 primitives one level further, into the gates it is built from and the transistors those gates are built from, using the primer's bottom layer. Every gate structure below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled standard construction; it is never a claim about Arm's actual netlist. Two honesty boundaries carry over from Level-3: traversal control lives in the shader, not in the RTU, so the traversal FSM decomposes to zero gates inside the unit; and instantiation is disputed — one RTU per shader core versus one per core pair — so no per-GPU RTU total is ever multiplied out.

- **Pipeline register (the ray-query issue state)** — One master-slave D flip-flop per bit (about 20–28 transistors, primer bottom layer), usually with a 2:1 enable mux in front so the stage can stall — the ray query's bundle of state (acceleration structure, ray flags, cull mask, origin, tMin, direction, tMax) staged in registers at the RTU's input while the query's tests run. The register count and field widths beyond the query's own parameters are not published, so no issue-state flop total is claimed: the bundle's bit count is the query's own fields, and Arm publishes no staging width beyond them. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the ray queue into the test units)** — Storage — a flop array or a small SRAM — plus write and read pointer counters, D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers, plus full/empty comparators: XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree. This queue is the decoupling that lets the shader issue ray work without stalling on every test. Arm publishes no ray-queue depth, entry width or port count, so this queue is named with its role and no storage total is claimed: a queue's transistor count needs a depth and an entry width, and neither is published for the RTU. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array + comparator (the ray-box unit, RBOX_UNIT)** — The slab method at gate level: per axis, a multiplier — AND gates forming the partial products from the ray's precomputed inverse direction and the box's near and far plane offsets, a compressor tree of full adders (about 28-transistor mirror cells, primer bottom layer) collapsing them, one final carry-propagate adder — feeding comparators that test the resulting t intervals for overlap, a subtractor of XOR gates and a full-adder borrow chain with a final borrow output. A missed box prunes the whole subtree beneath it. Its multiplier width, boxes-tested-per-cycle rate and pipeline depth are not published. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the BVH fetch path)** — Rows of 6T SRAM cells (primer, bottom layer) behind a row decoder — a tree of NAND gates selecting one wordline — transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. The traversal stream passes through the core's published caches: arithmetic from the published geometry, the 32 KB load/store cache per core is 262,144 bits, i.e. 1,572,864 6T cell transistors. Arm publishes no BVH fetch width, no dedicated BVH buffer and no node-fetch rate, so the fetch datapath's parameters are not published. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array + adder tree (the ray-triangle unit, RTRI_UNIT)** — The ray-triangle test at gate level: cross and dot products over the triangle's edges and the ray — multiplier arrays whose AND-gate partial products reduce through adder trees of full adders (about 28-transistor mirror cells, primer bottom layer), carry-save compressors at the leaves and one carry-propagate adder at the root — producing a candidate t and the (u, v) barycentric coordinates the shader needs for interpolation. Its width, triangles-tested-per-cycle rate and pipeline depth are not published — Arm publishes no ray-test rate for the RTU at all — so no per-unit gate count is claimed, only the standard form of the arithmetic the test performs. Standard construction.
- **Comparator + mux (closest-hit selection)** — Each candidate triangle's t is compared against the best t so far (and against tMin/tMax) by a subtractor — XOR gates forming the difference bits, a chain of full adders propagating the borrow — and when a candidate wins, a mux swaps its hit record into the query's result registers: transmission-gate 2:1 muxes, about 4 transistors each, one per result bit. The comparator count and whether selection is serial or treed are not published, so no per-query gate count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (traversal control — in the shader, not the RTU)** — Zero gates inside the RTU. The traversal loop — descend, test children, pop back, advance to the next node — is an FSM executed by the shader through ray-query instructions, one RTU test at a time; Arm does not accelerate BVH processing, so there is no traversal controller and no hardware traversal stack in the RTU to decompose. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence: the state flops and next-state logic live in the shader core, not in this unit. Any traversal-stack depth is a property of the shader's own register and memory use, and Arm publishes no traversal-stack depth for this design. Standard construction.
- **Register file (the hit result returning to the shader)** — At gate level a register file is a storage array — flip-flop/latch cells or 6T SRAM cells — behind wordline decoders (NAND/AND trees) that select one row per port, with per-port column mux trees steering the read data out and sense amplifiers where the array is SRAM-style. The closest hit — t and barycentric coordinates — lands back in the shader core's registers, where the shader shades the contribution; shading and denoising never enter the RTU. The result path's width and the query-completion mechanism's details are not published, so no cell total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the power-island controller)** — State bits are D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer); next-state and output logic are NAND/NOR networks stepping the controller through its sequence — gate the island when no ray work is submitted, restore it when a ray query arrives — so raster-only applications pay no leakage for the unit, the primitive-level half of why the RTU costs under 4% of shader-core area (published) yet nothing when idle. The gating latency, retention behaviour and wake-up cost are not published, so no controller flop count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (the power-island boundary)** — A gated island still has to exchange queries and results with the always-on shader core around it, so the island boundary is a real clock/power-domain boundary: the standard two-flop synchronizer — two D flip-flops in series in the receiving domain, about 40–56 transistors per bit (2 x 20–28 transistors) — gives the first flop a full clock period to resolve metastability before the value is used, and isolation cells at the boundary hold the island's outputs at safe levels while it is gated. The boundary's structure and clock relationship are not published, so no per-bit total is claimed across the interface. Standard construction.

Honesty: Arm and its launch coverage publish the RTU's composition (ray-box and ray-triangle test units, labelled RBOX_UNIT and RTRI_UNIT in G715-era diagrams), its under-4%-of-core area, over 300% better ray-tracing performance than software (Arm benchmarks), the 5th-generation power island, and the shader-driven ray-query model with no BVH traversal acceleration. They publish no ray-test rates, BVH fetch widths, ray-queue depths, traversal-stack depths or GigaRays/s figure, and the one-RTU-per-core versus one-per-core-pair question is disputed — this decomposition states those silences rather than filling them, and never multiplies any RTU figure by 10–16 cores. Every gate and transistor figure above is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer; the only derived total is the 32 KB load/store cache's 1,572,864 6T cell transistors, arithmetic from a published geometry. The traversal FSM decomposes to zero gates inside the RTU because traversal control lives in the shader.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [unverifiable] **Arm Immortalis-G720** — Level-4 decomposition scope boundary: Arm publishes no gate-level structure for the Immortalis-G720 Deferred Vertex Shading front end or its ray-tracing unit; the Level-4 text therefore decomposes every primitive as the generic textbook construction of that primitive, labelled standard construction, using only Arm's published per-core geometry plus figures explicitly labelled as arithmetic derived from that geometry (128 warps per core; 128 KiB per full-size tile; 6,291,456 6T cell transistors for a full-size tile; 1,572,864 per 32 KB cache; 50,331,648 for the 1,024 KB L2 total). Source: Arm, Mali G1 Performance Counter Reference Guide (doc 111042).

### Imagination PowerVR

#### Down to the gates: The Tile Accelerator, Parameter Buffer and ISP — the deferred-visibility front end

Imagination publishes no gate-level structure for the Tile Accelerator, Parameter Buffer and ISP front end — the Introduction to PowerVR for Developers (Rev 1.0, 11/02/2020) describes the TA's binning, the Parameter Buffer's residence in system memory, the ISP's Hidden Surface Removal and depth/stencil tests, the Tag Buffer's per-pixel triangle record, the on-chip colour/depth/stencil buffers and the firmware-managed GPU, and stops there. What follows takes each of the eleven Level-3 primitives one level further, into the gates it is built from and the transistors those gates are built from, using the primer's bottom layer (universal NAND/NOR gates, latch and master-slave D flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder). Every gate structure below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled standard construction; it is never a claim about Imagination's actual netlist. The only PowerVR-specific numbers are the published geometries already recorded at Levels 2–3 and the arithmetic derived transparently from them.

- **FSM / controller (the Tile Accelerator's binning sequencer)** — State bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer); next-state and output logic are NAND/NOR networks — whatever the synthesis tool maps the state table to in the standard-cell library — stepping the TA through its binning sequence: take a transformed primitive, test it against the tile grid, append it to each tile list it touches. The TA's state count, its binning rate and the number of primitives it can bin per cycle are not published, so no flop count is claimed: a controller's gate total needs a state count Imagination never gives. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank / memory store (the Parameter Buffer — tile lists and transformed vertices in system memory)** — The storage itself is not PowerVR gates at all: the Parameter Buffer resides in system memory, so its bits live in the DRAM device's 1T1C cells (one access transistor plus one storage capacitor per bit, the standard DRAM cell form), not in 6T SRAM on the GPU. What is PowerVR silicon is the Buffer's write/read interface: address registers and data staging registers — master-slave D flip-flops, about 20–28 transistors per bit — plus the pointer-list registers the TA updates as it appends primitives, and the read-side registers that hand a tile's list to the ISP when the tile operation begins. The Parameter Buffer's size, the tile-list depths and the interface widths are not published, so no register total is claimed: an interface's flop count needs a width Imagination never gives. Standard construction.
- **Counter (per-tile list bookkeeping)** — A binary counter is D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer) plus a full-adder incrementer (about 28 transistors per mirror-cell full adder), with a terminal-count comparator — XNOR gates per count bit (about 10–12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree — where the count must stop. One such counter tracks each open tile list's length or tail pointer, incrementing as the TA appends a primitive and read back when the ISP drains the list. The counter width follows the unpublished list depth, so the width is not published either and no per-counter transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the tile worklist into the ISP)** — Storage — a flop array or a small SRAM — plus write and read pointer counters, D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers, plus full/empty comparators: XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree, with Gray-coded pointers where a queue crosses clock domains. The worklist is what decouples binning from rasterization, so the ISP can drain one tile while the TA bins the next frame's primitives. Its depth, entry width and scheduling order are not published, so no storage total is claimed for it: a queue's transistor count needs a depth and an entry width, and neither is published for the tile worklist. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (the ISP's position-only fetch select)** — The fetch muxes are trees of 2:1 muxes; each 2:1 mux is two transmission gates (one NMOS + one PMOS per leg, 4 transistors) or an equivalent NAND-gate cell, with selects decoded by AND trees from the tile's primitive list. The select steers screen-space position data — not full vertex attributes — into the ISP, which is the gate-level content of the position-only fetch: the mux tree's width is the position format's width, not the full vertex width. The fetch width and the number of primitives fetched per cycle are not published, so no mux-tree total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (the ISP's depth and stencil tests — Hidden Surface Removal)** — Each test is a magnitude compare built the standard way: a subtractor of XOR gates forming the difference bits with a chain of full adders propagating the borrow, the final borrow output deciding whether the candidate fragment is in front of the stored depth — or, in equality form, one XNOR gate per compared bit (about 10–12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree, for the stencil test's value match. The losers never reach the shader back end, which is the gate-level content of Hidden Surface Removal: the comparators sit in front of the USC datapaths and gate them. The comparator count, the depth-test rate and the stencil-test rate are not published, so no per-ISP gate count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the Tag Buffer — one triangle ID per pixel)** — Rows of 6T SRAM cells (primer, bottom layer) behind a row decoder — a tree of NAND gates selecting one wordline — transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers, with a write port from the ISP as it resolves visibility and a read port handing the visible set to the TSP. Arithmetic from the published geometry: at the classic 32x32 example tile size the Tag Buffer holds one entry per pixel for 1,024 pixels — arithmetic from the published example size, not a published Tag Buffer depth, and tile size varies by device. The triangle ID's bit width is not published, so no 6T cell total is claimed: the total is 6 × 1,024 × W cell transistors for an unpublished W, and this decomposition asserts no value for W. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the on-chip colour, depth and stencil buffers)** — The same 6T form: rows of 6T cells behind a NAND-tree row decoder, transmission-gate column muxes and latch-type sense amplifiers, with read-modify-write ports the ISP's comparators read and write against instead of going to system memory. Arithmetic from the published geometry: at 8x MSAA each of the 1,024 pixels in a 32x32 example tile carries 8 sub-samples, so the depth buffer alone holds 8,192 depth values per tile — arithmetic from the published 8x rate and the published example tile size, not a published buffer capacity. The depth value's bit width, the colour format's width and the buffers' capacities, banking and port counts are not published, so no 6T cell total is claimed for any of them. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the firmware event manager)** — State bits are D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer); next-state and output logic are NAND/NOR networks stepping the manager through its sequence — schedule tiling, start tile operations, hand the finished visible set to the shader back end — keeping high-level graphics events inside the GPU instead of on the driver CPU. Its event-queue depths and handling rates are not published, so no flop count is claimed: the manager's gate total needs a state count Imagination never gives. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (Parameter Buffer write flow control to system memory)** — D flip-flops holding the credit count, a full-adder incrementer/decrementer that spends one credit per Parameter Buffer burst sent and earns credits back as the memory system drains, and a zero comparator — XNOR gates against zero feeding an AND tree — that stalls the binning front end at zero. The credit counts, PB burst sizes and DRAM interface parameters on this path are not published by Imagination, so no counter width or total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **CAM / TCAM — none in the front end** — Zero gates. The one place a content-addressed store looks necessary is the Tag Buffer, and it is not one: the Tag Buffer is indexed by pixel position — one entry per pixel, written and read at that pixel's address — not searched by content, so there is no matchline, no per-bit XNOR match logic and no CAM or TCAM anywhere in the published front-end contract. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence: the per-pixel triangle lookup is an address decode (a NAND-tree row decoder, the preceding SRAM form), not a match. Standard construction.

Honesty: Imagination publishes the front end's contract and geometry and none of its circuits: the TA's binning role, the Parameter Buffer's contents and its residence in system memory, the ISP's HSR and depth/stencil tests, the Tag Buffer's per-pixel triangle record, the on-chip colour/depth/stencil buffers, the firmware-managed GPU, and the 32x32 example tile size (tile size varies by device). Every gate and transistor figure above is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer, and every total is arithmetic from a published geometry, labelled as such. The new derived figures here are the Tag Buffer's 1,024 entries per 32x32 tile and the 8,192 depth values per tile at 8x MSAA — arithmetic from the published example tile size and the published MSAA rates, not published facts; the Tag Buffer's entry width and the colour/depth/stencil buffer capacities are not published, so no 6T cell total is claimed for any of them. The CAM/TCAM primitive decomposes to zero gates in this block because the Tag Buffer is addressed by pixel position, not searched by content. Parameter Buffer size, tile-list depths, TA binning rate, ISP depth-test rate, firmware event-queue depths and credit counts are not published, and this decomposition invents none of them.

#### Down to the gates: The Unified Shading Cluster and TSP — shading only what survived

Imagination publishes no gate-level structure for the Unified Shading Cluster and TSP back end either — the Introduction to PowerVR for Developers (Rev 1.0) and the Series8XT and 'Graphics cores: trying to compare apples to apples' blogs describe the USC's 16 pipelines and their ALU mix, the data-driven scheduler, the TSP's colouring of visible pixels only, the Furian texture unit's own cache, the PVRTC formats, the on-chip MSAA resolve and the single tile flush, and stop there. What follows takes each of the twelve Level-3 primitives one level further, into the gates it is built from and the transistors those gates are built from, using the primer's bottom layer. Every gate structure below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled standard construction; it is never a claim about Imagination's actual netlist. Two honesty boundaries carry over from Level-3: the USC's register-file size, thread count and texture-cache size are unpublished, so no storage total is claimed for them; and the special-function ALU's implementation is unpublished, so only its candidate standard forms are named, conditionally.

- **FIFO / queue (visible-fragment dispatch into the USCs)** — Storage — a flop array or a small SRAM — plus write and read pointer counters, D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers, plus full/empty comparators: XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree. This queue is the decoupling between the visibility pass and the shader back end, so the TSP can keep shading while the ISP moves to the next tile. Its depth, entry width and port count are not published, so no storage total is claimed: a queue's transistor count needs a depth and an entry width, and neither is published for the dispatch queue. Standard construction.
- **Register file (the USC's warp thread state)** — At gate level a register file is a storage array — flip-flop/latch cells or 6T SRAM cells — behind wordline decoders (NAND/AND trees) that select one row per port, with per-port column mux trees steering the read data out and sense amplifiers where the array is SRAM-style. The thread contexts of the massively multi-threaded shader engine live here, and Furian's improved simultaneous access to more local memory addresses is, in gate terms, more read ports and wider port muxing on this array — more decoders and more column muxes per port, so each ALU pipeline reaches the memory areas it needs without stalls. The register file's size, thread count, banking and port counts are not published, so no cell total is claimed: an array's transistor count needs a capacity Imagination never gives. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the data-driven scheduler)** — State bits are D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer); next-state and output logic are NAND/NOR networks stepping the scheduler through its sequence — watch for data availability, issue a ready independent task to a free pipeline, switch tasks to avoid data-dependency stalls. Its task-table size, issue rate and scheduling policy details are not published, so no flop count is claimed: the scheduler's gate total needs a state count Imagination never gives, and the ready-task selection it drives is decomposed in the next item, not duplicated here. Standard construction.
- **Priority encoder (task selection among ready tasks)** — A priority-encoder tree of AND/OR gates over the ready-task bits, a grant register of D flip-flops holding the winner, and grant muxes — transmission-gate 2:1 muxes, about 4 transistors each — steering the winning task toward the freed pipeline while the losers wait. Its policy (fixed priority, round-robin, or data-driven), grant width and latency are not published, so the encoder's size is not claimed either: the policy decides the tree's shape, and Imagination publishes no policy. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array + adder tree (the FP32/FP16 ALU datapaths)** — Each arithmetic unit bottoms out in a gate-level multiplier: AND gates forming the partial products from the operand bits, a compressor tree of full adders (about 28-transistor mirror cells, primer bottom layer) collapsing them, and one final carry-propagate adder finishing the sum. Floating-point lanes add an exponent adder (a small lookahead adder), a sign XOR and a normalizer built from a priority encoder and a barrel shifter. Arithmetic from the published geometry: a single-precision mantissa multiply is 24x24 bits, i.e. 576 partial-product AND gates before reduction, and a half-precision mantissa multiply is 11x11, i.e. 121 — standard IEEE 754 construction, not a published PowerVR figure. Per USC the published pipeline geometry gives 16 pipelines x 2 FP32 ALUs = 32 FP32 ALUs, 16 x 2 FP16 = 32 FP16 ALUs and 16 x 1 = 16 special-function ALUs; the GX6650's published 192 FP32 cores check exactly against 6 USCs x 32. Rogue's pipelines each hold two Multiply Adds function blocks (MADs); Furian rebalanced them to a MAD and a MUL. The multiplier array's radix, the adder tree's depth and the pipeline staging between them are not published, so no per-USC gate count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (FP alignment and normalization in the ALU pipes)** — A log shifter is stages of 2:1 muxes — one transmission-gate mux (about 4 transistors) per bit per stage, the stage selects decoded from the shift amount. Arithmetic from the standard formats: a 24-bit FP32 mantissa needs 5 stages (log2 24, rounded up) and an 11-bit FP16 mantissa needs 4 stages — standard construction, not a published PowerVR figure. The shift widths, pipeline placement and whether the shifter sits before or after the adder tree are not published, so no per-pipeline mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (the special-function ALU — sine, cosine, log, reciprocal)** — The implementation is unpublished, so only the two candidate standard forms are named, conditionally, and neither is asserted. In table form the SFU is a lookup ROM/SRAM — rows of cells behind a decoder, one entry per input interval — plus an interpolation multiplier and adder refining the table value; in iterative form it is a CORDIC-style datapath — adders and barrel shifters (the preceding items' forms) stepped by a small FSM — converging on the function value over several cycles. Either way it handles sine, cosine, log, reciprocals and friends on scalar values, with output precisions and per-operation performance that vary by operation, as Imagination's blog states. Its table size, iteration count, output precisions and per-operation throughput are not published, so no gate count is claimed for the SFU. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the texture unit's own cache — Furian)** — Rows of 6T SRAM cells (primer, bottom layer) behind a row decoder — a tree of NAND gates selecting one wordline — transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. In Furian this bank sits on the texture unit's own path, so its fills no longer compete with the USCs for data access — the gate-level content of the doubled fill-rate at eight pixels per clock. The cache's size, associativity, line width and port count are not published, so no bit or cell total is claimed: a bank's transistor count needs a capacity Imagination never gives. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (the PVRTC format select in the texture unit)** — The format-select muxes are trees of 2:1 muxes; each 2:1 mux is two transmission gates (one NMOS + one PMOS per leg, 4 transistors) or an equivalent NAND-gate cell, with the select decoded from the texture's format bit — PVRTC at 2 bits per pixel or 4 bits per pixel — steering the fetch down the 2bpp or 4bpp decode path as the compressed texels expand. The decode datapath's width and the 2bpp/4bpp select encoding are not published, so no mux-tree total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (alpha test)** — After shading, alpha testing compares each fragment's alpha against the threshold: one XNOR gate per alpha bit (about 10–12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree for the equality form, or a subtractor — XOR gates forming the difference bits with a full-adder borrow chain — for the magnitude form. The compare is what makes alpha test expensive on this architecture: the fragment cannot write its depth until the shader has executed and visibility is known, so the comparator gates the depth write, not just the colour write. The comparator count and the alpha width are not published, so no per-TSP gate count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (the Pixel Back End's MSAA sub-sample combine)** — Combining sub-samples into one resolved colour is an adder tree over the samples, its nodes the primer's full adder: carry-save compressors at the leaves, one carry-propagate adder at the root. Arithmetic from the published MSAA rates: at 4x MSAA the tree combines 4 sub-samples with 3 adds per channel in 2 levels, and at 8x it combines 8 sub-samples with 7 adds per channel in 3 levels — arithmetic from the published 4x/8x rates, not a published circuit. The colour width, adder width and resolve rate are not published, so no transistor total is claimed for the tree. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (tile-flush flow control to the frame buffer)** — D flip-flops holding the credit count, a full-adder incrementer/decrementer that spends one credit per flush burst sent and earns credits back as the memory system drains, and a zero comparator — XNOR gates against zero feeding an AND tree — that holds the next tile's shading back when the flush path is full. The flush is the tile's single write to the frame buffer in system memory, so this counter is what keeps that one burst from stalling the next tile's shading. The credit counts and flush burst sizes are not published by Imagination, so no counter width or total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Imagination publishes the back end's contract and geometry and none of its circuits: the USC's pipeline and ALU geometry (16 pipelines, 2 FP32 + 2 FP16 + 1 special-function ALU each; 64 FP32 / up to 128 FP16 FLOPs per cycle per USC), the Rogue two-MAD and Furian MAD+MUL pipeline contents, the scalar-SIMD execution model, the data-driven scheduler, the Furian texture unit's own cache and its 8-pixels-per-clock fill-rate, the PVRTC 2bpp/4bpp formats, the 4x/8x on-chip MSAA, and the single tile flush to the frame buffer. Every gate and transistor figure above is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer, and every total is arithmetic from a published geometry, labelled as such. The new derived figures here are the per-USC ALU counts (32 FP32 + 32 FP16 ALUs + 16 special-function ALUs, arithmetic from the published pipeline geometry — the GX6650's published 192 FP32 cores check exactly against 6 USCs x 32), the 576 partial-product AND gates of a 24x24 FP32 mantissa multiply and the 121 of an 11x11 FP16 mantissa multiply (standard IEEE 754 construction), the 5-stage FP32 and 4-stage FP16 log shifters, and the MSAA combine trees (3 adds per channel in 2 levels at 4x, 7 adds in 3 levels at 8x). USC register-file size, thread count, texture-cache size and associativity, TSP queue depths, multiplier radix, adder-tree depth, shifter widths, SFU implementation, alpha-test comparator count and flush credit counts are not published, and this decomposition invents none of them.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [unverifiable] **Imagination PowerVR** — Level-4 decomposition scope boundary: Imagination publishes no gate-level structure for the PowerVR Tile Accelerator/Parameter Buffer/ISP front end or its Unified Shading Cluster/TSP back end; the Level-4 text therefore decomposes every primitive as the generic textbook construction of that primitive, labelled standard construction, using only Imagination's published per-block geometry plus figures explicitly labelled as arithmetic derived from that geometry (1,024 Tag Buffer entries per 32x32 tile; 8,192 depth values per tile at 8x MSAA; 3 adds per channel in 2 levels at 4x MSAA and 7 adds in 3 levels at 8x; 32 FP32 + 32 FP16 ALUs + 16 special-function ALUs per USC, checking exactly against the GX6650's published 192 FP32 cores; 576 partial-product AND gates for a 24x24 FP32 mantissa multiply and 121 for an 11x11 FP16 mantissa multiply; 5-stage FP32 and 4-stage FP16 log shifters). Source: Imagination, Introduction to PowerVR for Developers (Rev 1.0, 11/02/2020).

### Google TPU v5p

#### Down to the gates: Second-generation SparseCore — the dataflow engine for embeddings

Google publishes no gate-level structure for the SparseCore — the OpenXLA deep dive and the ISCA 2023 paper describe the tile geometry (16 tiles, 8-wide SIMD, 2.5 MiB spmem in 16 banks, five cross-channel units), the sequencer's lockstep orchestration, the Fetch and Flush Units and the cross-channel operations, and stop there. What follows takes each of the ten Level-3 primitives one level further, into the gates it is built from and the transistors those gates are built from, using the primer's bottom layer (universal NAND/NOR gates, latch and master-slave D flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder). Every gate structure below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled standard construction; it is never a claim about Google's actual netlist. The only v5p-specific numbers are the published geometries already recorded at Levels 2-3 and the arithmetic derived transparently from them — and the spmem totals below are arithmetic from the v4 2.5 MiB geometry v5p inherits on the published record, since Google has not published v5p's own spmem size.

- **FSM / controller (the SparseCore sequencer)** — State bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each, primer bottom layer); next-state and output logic are NAND/NOR networks — whatever the synthesis tool maps the state table to in the standard-cell library — stepping the sequencer through its task stream and issuing the same tasks to all 16 tiles so they stay in lockstep. The sequencer's state count, task-queue depth and issue rate are not published, so no flop count is claimed: a controller's gate total needs a state count Google never gives. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (SPMEM — the Sparse Vector Memory, 16 banks)** — Rows of 6T SRAM cells (primer, bottom layer) behind a row decoder — a tree of NAND gates selecting one wordline — transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers, with the tile's Fetch Unit writing gathered rows in and the scVPU reading vectors out. The gate-level content of spmem being explicitly managed scratchpad, not a cache, is an absence: there is no tag array, no tag comparators and no replacement logic to decompose — the compiler, not hardware, decides what lives in each bank. Arithmetic from the published geometry: on the v4 geometry v5p inherits, 2.5 MiB per SparseCore is 20,971,520 bits, i.e. 125,829,120 6T cell transistors per SparseCore; per bank 160 KiB is 1,310,720 bits, i.e. 7,864,320 cell transistors; per chip 10 MiB is 83,886,080 bits, i.e. 503,316,480 cell transistors — arithmetic from the v4 geometry, conditional on v5p inheriting it, since Google has not published v5p's own spmem size. Bank widths and port counts are not published, so no decoder or mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the Fetch Unit's outstanding-read queue)** — Storage — a flop array or a small SRAM — plus write and read pointer counters, D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers (about 28 transistors per mirror-cell full adder), plus full/empty comparators: XNOR gates per pointer bit (about 10-12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree. The queue of in-flight reads is what hides HBM latency while the scVPU works the previous batch. The number of outstanding reads per tile, the queue depth and the entry width are not published, so no storage total is claimed: a queue's transistor count needs a depth and an entry width, and neither is published for the Fetch Unit. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the Flush Unit's writeback staging)** — The same FIFO form: storage plus write and read pointer counters with full-adder incrementers, plus full/empty comparators built from XNOR gates per pointer bit feeding an AND tree. Its writeback path stages completed embedding updates before they leave the tile, so the scVPU is not stalled on HBM write latency. Queue depth, entry width and the write-combining policy are not published, so no storage total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (the scVPU — 8-wide SIMD per tile)** — Each of the 8 lanes bottoms out in a gate-level multiplier: AND gates forming the partial products from the operand bits, a compressor tree of full adders (about 28-transistor mirror cells, primer bottom layer) collapsing them, and one final carry-propagate adder finishing the sum; the lane ALU's adder/subtractor is the same full-adder chain, and the 8 lanes' results are selected by transmission-gate mux trees.
