Arithmetic from the published geometry: 16 tiles x 8 lanes = 128 SIMD lanes per SparseCore, 512 lanes per chip. Per-lane operand widths, the multiplier radix, the compressor-tree depth and the ALU pipeline depth are not published, so no per-lane gate total is claimed. The ISCA paper notes the scVPU reuses the TensorCore VPU's ALUs; that reuse is at the block level and no gate-level sharing figure is published. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (the cross-channel fabric across the 16 spmem banks)** — Five consumers, sixteen bank ports: each consumer selects among the 16 banks with a 16:1 mux tree per bit — 15 2:1 transmission-gate muxes (about 4 transistors each, about 60 transistors per bit per consumer), with the selects decoded by AND trees from the bank address — so the full fabric is 75 2:1 muxes per bit across the five consumers, arithmetic from the published 5x16 counts. Where two cross-channel units want the same bank in the same cycle, the fabric needs an arbiter (a priority-encoder tree plus grant flops, the standard arbiter form); the arbitration policy is not published, so the arbiter's size is not claimed either, and whether the fabric is a full crossbar or a narrower shared bus is not published. The bank port widths are not published, so no fabric total is claimed beyond the per-bit mux count. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (deduplication — ID equality)** — One XNOR gate per ID bit (about 10-12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree: the AND output is high exactly when two col_ids are identical, which is the gate-level content of deduplication — repeated IDs collapse to one row before the reduction runs. The ID width, the number of comparators and whether dedup is done by sorted compare, hashing or a content-addressed structure are not published, so no comparator total is claimed. If dedup were CAM-based it would be the primer's CAM cell form (SRAM cell plus XOR match logic feeding a matchline), but the paper does not say that, so only the candidate forms are named, conditionally, and neither is asserted. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (the cross-channel reduction)** — Sixteen banks narrow to one pooled vector per sample through a vector adder tree whose nodes are the primer's full adder (about 28 transistors per mirror cell): 15 adds per vector element in 4 levels (log2 16), with the adds running element-wise across the 8-wide SIMD shape. The tree depth follows from the published bank count; the adder width and the reduction order are not published beyond the 8-wide SIMD shape, so no transistor total is claimed for the tree. Standard construction.
- **Counter (per-partition limit counters and the index walk)** — A binary counter is D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each, primer bottom layer) plus a full-adder incrementer (about 28 transistors per mirror-cell full adder), with a terminal-count comparator — XNOR gates per count bit feeding an AND tree — where the walk must stop. One such counter walks each partition's ID list as the Fetch Unit gathers it; the compiled limits (max_ids_per_partition, max_unique_ids_per_partition) are the bounds it walks against, but they are per-model compile-time constants in XLA, not chip registers — the gate-level content is the walker, not the limit value. Counter widths are not published, and the limit values are not chip parameters, so no per-counter transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (tile-to-HBM-channel select and spmem bank select)** — The select muxes are trees of 2:1 muxes; each 2:1 mux is two transmission gates (one NMOS plus one PMOS per leg, 4 transistors) or an equivalent NAND-gate cell, with selects decoded by AND trees from the tile and bank addresses. Arithmetic from the published bank count: the bank select is a 16-way select, 15 2:1 muxes per bit. Each tile's reads go to its own HBM channel, so a channel-select mux steers each tile's Fetch Unit to its channel — but the HBM channel count per chip, the mux radix on the HBM side and the bank-select timing are not published, so no mux-tree total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Google publishes the SparseCore's tile geometry and none of its circuits: 16 tiles per SparseCore, an 8-wide scVPU per tile, 2.5 MiB spmem in 16 banks (v4 geometry), five cross-channel units, one sequencer orchestrating all 16 tiles in lockstep, and the per-partition compile-time limits. Every gate and transistor figure above is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer, and every total is arithmetic from a published geometry, labelled as such. The new derived figures here are the spmem 6T cell totals — 125,829,120 cell transistors per SparseCore, 7,864,320 per bank, 503,316,480 per chip — arithmetic from the v4 2.5 MiB geometry v5p inherits (v5p's own spmem size is unpublished, so these totals are conditional on that inheritance); the 15 adds in 4 levels of the 16-bank reduction tree; the 15 2:1 muxes per bit of a 16-way bank select; and the 75 2:1 muxes per bit across the five-consumer cross-channel fabric. The synchronizer question has a negative answer carried over from Level-3: the 16 tiles run in lockstep under one sequencer in a single clock domain, and the SparseCore-to-TensorCore handoff goes through HBM under XLA's pipeline schedule, so there is no two-flop synchronizer inside the SparseCore to decompose. Fetch and Flush queue depths and entry widths, scVPU operand widths, multiplier radix and pipeline depth, cross-channel arbitration, spmem bank widths and port counts, and v5p's spmem size are not published, and this decomposition invents none of them.

#### Down to the gates: The pod-scale interconnect — ICI 3D torus and the optical circuit switch

Google publishes no gate-level structure for the pod interconnect — the Google Cloud docs describe the pod geometry (8,960 chips, 140 cubes, 6,144-chip largest slice, 1,200 GB/s bidirectional ICI, the 3D torus, the twisted-torus gains, ICI resiliency) and the ISCA 2023 paper describes the Palomar geometry (136x136, 128 ports plus 8 spares), and both stop there. What follows takes each of the ten Level-3 primitives one level further, into the gates it is built from and the transistors those gates are built from, using the primer's bottom layer (universal NAND/NOR gates, latch and master-slave D flip-flop, 6T SRAM cell, CAM cell, full adder). Every gate structure below is the generic textbook construction of the named primitive, labelled standard construction; it is never a claim about Google's actual netlist. Two primitives in this block are not transistors at all — the Palomar switching fabric and the circulator are optical and mechanical — and their gate-level content is stated as that absence. The only pod-specific numbers are the published geometries already recorded at Levels 2-3 and the arithmetic derived transparently from them.

- **FIFO / queue (the ICI port input queue)** — Storage — a flop array or a small SRAM — plus write and read pointer counters, D flip-flops with full-adder incrementers (about 28 transistors per mirror-cell full adder), plus full/empty comparators: XNOR gates per pointer bit (about 10-12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree, with Gray-coded pointers where the queue crosses clock domains at the ICI port's receive side. The queue is what lets a chip hold an arriving packet while its router arbitrates the next hop, so the hop-by-hop neighbour exchanges of the Level-2 trace never stall the link. Queue depth, entry width and the number of queues per port are not published, so no storage total is claimed: a queue's transistor count needs a depth and an entry width, and neither is published for the ICI ports. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (the on-chip ICI router switch)** — Each output port selects among the seven inputs with a 7:1 mux tree per bit — 6 2:1 transmission-gate muxes (about 4 transistors each, about 24 transistors per bit per output), with the selects decoded by AND trees from the routing decision — so the whole router is 42 2:1 muxes per bit across its seven outputs, arithmetic from the published 3D-torus topology (six neighbours plus local injection). The twist of a twisted torus changes which node the wrap-around edges connect to, not the degree, so the crossbar stays 7-port and the twist lives in the OCS routing tables. Crossbar radix beyond the 7-port count, arbitration and port widths are not published, so no router total is claimed beyond the per-bit mux count. Standard construction.
- **Switch arbiter (the router's port arbitrator)** — A priority-encoder tree of AND/OR gates over the request bits, a grant register of D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each, primer bottom layer) holding the winner, and grant muxes — transmission-gate 2:1 muxes, about 4 transistors each — steering the granted input toward the output port while the losers wait in their input queues. The arbitration policy — round-robin, oldest-first, or dimension-priority — and the arbiter's structure are not published, so the encoder's size is not claimed: the policy decides the tree's shape, and Google publishes no policy. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (the routing decision — coordinate compare)** — Each hop's routing decision is a coordinate compare built the standard way: one XNOR gate per coordinate bit (about 10-12 transistors each) feeding an AND tree for the equality form — is this packet addressed to my coordinates? — or a subtractor, XOR gates forming the difference bits with a full-adder borrow chain, for the magnitude form that picks the next dimension and direction. The docs confirm the effect, not the mechanism: twisting gives shorter packet routes. The coordinate widths are not published, so no comparator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar — optical (the Palomar OCS MEMS-mirror array)** — Zero transistors in the switching fabric itself. The OCS is a crossbar built from mirrors instead of transistors: 136 x 136 = 18,496 MEMS mirrors (arithmetic from the published geometry), each mirror electrostatically tilted to reflect one input fibre to one output fibre. Switching is mechanical — a mirror moving, not a transistor switching — and there is no store-and-forward and no packet buffer anywhere in the light path. What is electronics is the mirror drive: the OCS controller's per-mirror drive electrodes and their driver circuits, which set each mirror's angle from the routing table (decomposed in the next two items), plus the 8 spare ports' test and repair paths. Mirror switching time is in milliseconds (Level-2, verified fact records). The v5p OCS count is not published. Standard construction — with the distinction stated plainly: the mirrors are MEMS devices, not CMOS gates.
- **Mux / demux (the circulator — splitting both directions off one fibre)** — Zero transistors. The circulator is a passive optical device — in the standard circulator form a Faraday rotator plus polarizing beam splitters — that routes outgoing light to the fibre and incoming light to the receiver. It is a mux/demux in function, not in gates: there is no transistor, no select line and no switching event in the light path, only the non-reciprocal rotation of the light's polarization. The circulator's insertion loss, isolation and port count beyond the published 128-plus-8 geometry are not published. Standard construction, in its optical form.
- **SRAM bank / table (the OCS routing table)** — Rows of 6T SRAM cells (primer, bottom layer) behind a row decoder — a tree of NAND gates selecting one wordline — transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers, holding one entry per OCS port: the mirror setting for the job's torus, regular or twisted. Arithmetic bound from the published geometry: 136 entries, one per port of the 136x136 switch. The entry width — the mirror-setting bits per port — is not published, so no cell total is claimed: the total is 6 x 136 x W cell transistors for an unpublished W, and this decomposition asserts no value for W. The table lives in the OCS controller, not on the TPU chip. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the OCS topology controller and ICI resiliency)** — State bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each, primer bottom layer); next-state and output logic are NAND/NOR networks stepping the controller through its sequence — the OCS controller sets the mirror array to the job's topology, and the ICI resiliency logic reroutes ICI connections around failed OCSes and optical links at the cost of temporary ICI degradation. The controller's state count, the reroute latency and the failover policy are not published, so no flop count is claimed: a controller's gate total needs a state count Google never gives. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (the electrical-to-optical clock-domain crossing)** — The cube-edge conversion crosses clock domains — the chip's ICI clock to the optical link's serial clock — and the standard construction is a SerDes clock-data-recovery block with an elastic buffer absorbing the phase difference between the two domains: the elastic buffer is a small FIFO (storage plus pointer counters plus full/empty comparators, the FIFO form), and where a single-bit control crosses domains it is a two-flop synchronizer (about 40-56 transistors per bit, primer). Elastic-buffer depth, SerDes rate and the CDR loop structure are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue — none in the optical path** — Zero gates. The one place a queue looks necessary is inside the OCS, and there is none: the OCS is a circuit switch, not a packet switch — light is reflected by a mirror, never stored — so no FIFO or queue exists in the optical path. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence: all queueing in this block lives at the chip's ICI ports, decomposed in the first item. Standard construction.

Honesty: Google publishes the pod geometry and none of its circuits: the 3D torus topology, the 8,960-chip pod, the 6,144-chip largest slice, 1,200 GB/s bidirectional ICI, the twisted-torus gains, ICI resiliency, and the Palomar 136x136 geometry. Every gate and transistor figure above is standard construction from the primer's bottom layer, and every total is arithmetic from a published geometry, labelled as such. The new derived figures here are the router crossbar's 6 2:1 muxes per bit per output port — 42 2:1 muxes per bit across the 7-port router — arithmetic from the published 3D-torus topology; the 136-entry bound on the OCS routing table, arithmetic from the published 136-port geometry (the entry width is unpublished, so no cell total is claimed); and the two zero-gate primitives — the Palomar switching fabric is 18,496 MEMS mirrors, not transistors, and the circulator is a passive optical device, not a gate network. ICI port queue depths and entry widths, router port widths and arbitration policy, coordinate widths, SerDes rates, elastic-buffer depth, OCS controller internals and the v5p OCS count are not published, and this decomposition invents none of them.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [unverifiable] **Google TPU v5p** — Level-4 decomposition scope boundary: Google publishes no gate-level structure for the SparseCore or the pod interconnect; the Level-4 text therefore decomposes every primitive as the generic textbook construction of that primitive, labelled standard construction, using only Google's published per-block geometry plus figures explicitly labelled as arithmetic derived from that geometry (spmem 6T cell totals 125,829,120 per SparseCore / 7,864,320 per bank / 503,316,480 per chip, arithmetic from the v4 2.5 MiB geometry v5p inherits; 15 adds in 4 levels for the 16-bank reduction; 15 2:1 muxes per bit for 16-way bank select; 75 2:1 muxes per bit across the five-consumer cross-channel fabric; 6 2:1 muxes per bit per router output, 42 per bit across the 7-port router; 136-entry OCS routing-table bound; 18,496 MEMS mirrors). The Palomar switching fabric and the circulator decompose to zero transistors — they are MEMS and optical devices, not gates — and the FIFO/queue primitive decomposes to zero gates in the optical path because the OCS is a circuit switch. Source: Google Cloud, "TPU v5p" docs; OpenXLA, "A deep dive into SparseCore for Large Embedding Models (LEM)"; Jouppi et al., ISCA 2023.

### Graphcore GC200 IPU

#### Down to the gates: The IPU tile — a barrel-threaded core with 624 KiB of its own SRAM and an AMP

Graphcore publishes no gate-level structure for the GC200 — the Hot Chips 33 deck and the Frontiers supplement describe the tile's contract (1,472 tiles, 624 KiB SRAM per tile, 7 contexts on 6 slots, the MAIN/AUX split, the 16x16 AMP, the RNG, the sparse load/store) and stop there. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about Graphcore's circuits.

- **FSM / controller (the barrel-threaded slot scheduler — Supervisor and Worker dispatch)** — The scheduler is a small state machine, built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 6 round-robin slots need a 3-bit rotation counter — 3 flip-flops, about 60–84 transistors, plus a 3-bit incrementer of about 3 full adders, about 84 transistors — and 7 contexts need 3-bit context IDs, so the 6 slot-to-context assignments are 6 x 3 = 18 flip-flops, about 360–504 transistors. The RUN/EXIT decode is part of the tile's 32-bit instruction decoder, whose structure Graphcore does not publish, so no decoder gate count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Register file (per-thread architectural state)** — A register file is an array of multi-ported bit cells: each bit cell is a storage latch plus one access transistor per read port and one per write port, so a 2-read/1-write cell is about 10–12 transistors in the standard construction, and a 32-bit register is 32 of them, about 320–384 transistors. The quad-register load moves 128 bits at once — four 32-bit registers read in parallel — so the read path is four 32-bit register reads, not one wide one. The register count per thread, the port counts and the bypass network are not published, so no total is claimed: a register-file gate total needs a register count Graphcore never gives. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the tile's 624 KiB private scratchpad)** — The scratchpad is a 6T SRAM array: one 6-transistor cell per bit, plus a row decoder (a NAND/NOR tree that turns the address into one wordline), column muxes (transmission gates, 2 transistors per 2:1 mux per bit) and sense amplifiers (about 6–8 transistors per bitline) — the primer bottom layer's 6T cell. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 624 KiB per tile is 5,111,808 bits, so 5,111,808 6T cells, 30,670,848 cell transistors per tile; across 1,472 tiles that is 7,524,581,376 bits, 45,147,488,256 cell transistors for the tile SRAM arrays alone — and the bit total checks exactly against the deck's own structural table at 897 MiB. How the 624 KiB is organised into banks, the bank widths and port counts are not published, so the decoder radix, the column-mux radix and the sense-amplifier count are not claimed; there is no tag array, no replacement logic and no coherence hardware, because the memory is a compiler-managed scratchpad, not a cache. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (MAIN/AUX operand select and the multi-load/store path)** — Operand steering is muxes: a 2:1 mux is 2 transistors per bit in the transmission-gate form (primer bottom layer) or 4 gates, about 16 transistors per bit, in the NAND/NOR-tree form. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the 128-bit quad-register load path steered between MAIN and AUX is one 128-bit 2:1 mux, 256 transistors in the transmission-gate form or about 2,048 in the NAND/NOR form, per steered path. The mux radix, the operand-select timing and the bypass paths between MAIN and AUX are not published, so no total across the tile's steering is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (the AMP — 16x16 FP16xFP16 with FP32 accumulation)** — A floating-point multiplier is a mantissa multiplier plus exponent logic: the mantissa multiply is an AND-gate partial-product array feeding a carry-save adder tree, and the accumulator is a full adder per mantissa bit (about 28 transistors each, primer bottom layer). Arithmetic from the published geometry: an FP16 mantissa is 11 bits (10 explicit plus the implicit leading 1), so one FP16 multiplier is an 11x11 array, 121 partial-product AND gates; the AMP's 16x16 array is 256 multipliers per tile, 30,976 partial-product AND gates per tile, 45,596,672 across all 1,472 tiles. The AMP's pipeline depth, the multiplier array's internal tiling and the accumulator register widths are not published, so no full gate total for the AMP is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (AMP FP32 accumulation and the scalar FMA)** — An FP32 adder is a 24-bit mantissa adder (23 explicit bits plus the implicit leading 1) built from 24 full adders — about 672 transistors in ripple-carry form, fewer levels in carry-lookahead form — plus exponent compare and alignment logic. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the AMP accumulates 16 products per output element, so the accumulation tree is 4 levels deep (log2 16 = 4), and the scalar path is one FMA per cycle per tile, about 4 TFLOPS across the chip (Level-2). The tree depth, the adder widths and the accumulation order are not published, so the 4-level depth is the shape the published 16-wide accumulation forces, not a claimed circuit. Standard construction.
- **Counter (the sparse-gather pointer walk — cumulative-delta offsets)** — The gather walk is a counter plus an adder: the running base is a register, and each 4-bit delta is added onto it. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the 16-bit absolute offsets give a 16-bit base register — 16 flip-flops, about 320–448 transistors — and the running add is a 16-bit adder, 16 full adders, about 448 transistors; the 4-bit delta add is 4 full adders, about 112 transistors. The pointer-list depth, the number of parallel gather lanes and the address-generation pipeline depth are not published, so no total across the gather unit is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter and XOR/shift network (the enhanced xoroshiro128+ PRNG)** — The generator is a 128-bit state register plus an XOR/shift network and a 64-bit addition: the state is 128 flip-flops, about 2,560–3,584 transistors; the xoroshiro128+ update is shifts and XORs across two 64-bit words, about 128 XOR2 gates, about 1,280–1,536 transistors; the '+' is a 64-bit adder, 64 full adders, about 1,792 transistors. The 6th-order Irwin-Hall Gaussian shaper sums 6 uniform samples, so it is 5 adders over the sample width — but the sample width is not published, so no transistor total is claimed for the shaper. The state storage, the shaper's adder widths and the per-thread seeding are not published. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (stochastic-rounding compare)** — A magnitude comparator is an XNOR per bit plus an AND tree: one XNOR2 gate (about 10–12 transistors) per compared bit, then a log2(N)-level AND tree to combine the per-bit results. The compare itself decides the rounding — the discarded fraction is compared against fresh random bits, and the result picks round-up or stay — so the rounding costs no extra cycles. The comparator width and the random-bit consumption per rounded value are not published, so no gate total is claimed; the compare-against-random-bits construction is the standard one for stochastic rounding, labelled as such. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (branch and conditional execution)** — A branch is a condition compare on a register value: a 32-bit equality compare is 32 XNOR2 gates, about 320–384 transistors, plus a 5-level AND tree of 31 AND2 gates, about 124–148 transistors, evaluated and acted on in the same cycle. There is no branch predictor and no speculation hardware to decompose — the platform has no speculative execution — so there are no predictor-table SRAM, no history-register and no recovery-mux gates at all: the comparator is the whole branch mechanism. The comparator width and the condition-code storage are not published, so the 32-bit figure is the standard form for the published 32-bit instruction width, not a claimed circuit. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (the 6-cycle instruction pipeline)** — Each pipeline stage is a register: a 32-bit instruction register is 32 master-slave D flip-flops, about 640–896 transistors per stage, so the instruction bits alone across 6 stages are about 3,840–5,376 transistors; a 128-bit quad-load data path where present is 128 flip-flops, about 2,560–3,584 transistors per stage. There is no interlock hardware and no hazard-detection logic to decompose: a long-running bundle blocks both pipelines and the compiler counts instructions to determine runtime, so the pipeline has no stall muxes, no scoreboard and no forwarding comparators — the absence is the design. The pipeline register count and widths are not published, so the totals above are per-stage, not a claimed tile total. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array / lookup table (the AUX transcendental unit)** — A transcendental unit is a lookup table plus a polynomial multiplier: the table is a ROM array (about 1 transistor per bit in the standard ROM form) or a small SRAM array (6 transistors per bit), and the polynomial is evaluated by a mantissa multiplier of the same form as the AMP's. The measured latencies — 3 cycles for div, exp2 and exp, 5 for sqrt and tanh, 6 for log — are the only published timing; the table sizes, the polynomial degree and the interpolation hardware are not published, so neither the table's bit count nor the multiplier's width is claimed, and both candidate table forms are named conditionally. Standard construction.

Honesty: Graphcore publishes the tile geometry and none of its circuits: 1,472 tiles, 624 KiB SRAM per tile, 7 contexts on 6 round-robin slots, 32-bit instructions, the MAIN/AUX split, the 16x16 AMP table, 128 random bits per cycle, the 16-bit/4-bit pointer lists and the 128-bit quad-register loads — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — SRAM bank organisation, register-file size and port counts, AMP pipeline depth, the PRNG's state storage, the transcendental unit's table sizes — Graphcore publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no cache and no speculation hardware anywhere in the tile, so there are no tag comparators, no replacement logic and no branch-predictor gates to decompose.

#### Down to the gates: The IPU-Exchange and BSP synchronisation — a stateless all-to-all fabric

Graphcore publishes no gate-level structure for the IPU-Exchange — the Hot Chips 33 deck and the Frontiers supplement describe the fabric's contract (the 1600 x 36-bit spine, one 36-bit pipelined send channel per tile, one 1600-way receive mux per tile, 32 bits per cycle per tile, no queues, no arbiters, no packet overheads, mesochronous clocking with 3 cycles of drift, the ~150-cycle sync, 15 ns per hop) and stop there. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about Graphcore's circuits. Two primitives decompose to zero gates, and that absence is the design.

- **Comparator (the hardware global barrier — AND-reduction over all tiles)** — The barrier is an AND-reduction: every tile's done signal feeds an AND tree, and the tree's output is the barrier firing. Arithmetic from the published geometry: an AND-reduction over 1,472 done signals is 1,471 AND2 gates — about 5,884 transistors at 4 per gate — in 11 levels (log2 1,472 is about 10.5, rounded up). The reduction-tree depth, fan-in and the per-tile completion-signal width are not published, so the 1,471-gate figure is the shape the published tile count forces in the standard tree construction, not a claimed circuit; the inter-chip leg costs 15 ns per hop over the IPU-Links. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (Poplar's cycle-exact transmit, receive and select schedule)** — The per-tile sequencer is a cycle counter plus select state: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network. An N-bit counter is N flip-flops plus an N-bit incrementer of N full adders, about 28 transistors each — but the schedule length, and therefore the counter width, is not published, so no flop count is claimed. The select state that drives each tile's mux select lines each cycle is held per tile and advanced every clock cycle; Graphcore publishes neither its storage form nor its size, so both candidate forms are named conditionally — registers at about 20–28 transistors per bit, or SRAM at 6 transistors per bit — and neither is asserted. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (the 36-bit pipelined send channel and column transport)** — The send path is a pipeline of registers: one 36-bit stage register is 36 master-slave D flip-flops, about 720–1,008 transistors per stage, carrying 32 payload bits and 4 other bits per word — the 32-bits-per-cycle send and receive against the 36-bit channel is published geometry, while what the other 4 bits carry is not published. The number of pipeline stages in the channel and in the column transport is not published, so no total across the send path is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (the 1600 x 36-bit exchange spine)** — A textbook crossbar is built from muxes: one 1,600-input output is a 1,600:1 mux, 1,599 2:1 muxes, about 3,198 transistors per bit in the transmission-gate form — but that is a bound, not a claim about this chip. The spine is pipelined transport up and down the tile columns, not a monolithic mux crossbar: the selection lives in the per-tile receive muxes below, and the spine itself moves words to their destination column. The spine's column organisation and per-column wire counts are not published, so no crossbar gate total is claimed for the spine; the 1,600-input figure is the published spine geometry, and the 64 channels beyond the 1,536 physical tiles are arithmetic with the assumption stated (every physical tile holds a send channel; the IO-block count is not published). Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (the 1600-way receive mux per tile)** — The receive mux is a mux tree: a 1,600:1 mux per bit is 1,599 2:1 muxes in 11 levels of selection (ceil(log2 1,600) = 11 select bits, arithmetic from the published geometry). In the transmission-gate form that is 2 transistors per 2:1 mux per bit, 3,198 transistors per bit, 115,128 transistors for one tile's 36-bit receive mux; across all 1,472 tiles, 169,468,416 transistors for the receive muxes chip-wide. In the NAND/NOR-tree form each 2:1 mux is 4 gates, about 16 transistors per bit, roughly four times that. The mux's implementation, its select-line fan-out and its timing relative to the SRAM write are not published, so the totals are the standard-construction figures for the published 1,600-way geometry, not a claimed circuit. Standard construction.
- **Register file / table (the per-tile select state)** — The select state is a table, and a table is either registers or SRAM: as registers it is master-slave D flip-flops, about 20–28 transistors per bit; as SRAM it is 6T cells, 6 transistors per bit, plus a row decoder and sense amplifiers. Graphcore publishes neither the storage form nor the size of the per-tile select state, so no bit count and no transistor total is claimed — both candidate forms are named conditionally, and the state is advanced every clock cycle by the sequencer above. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue — none in the fabric** — Zero gates. The one place a queue looks necessary is in the fabric, and there is none: a word is never stored in flight — it leaves on its scheduled cycle and arrives on its scheduled cycle — so there is no store-and-forward, no head-of-line blocking and no queueing delay to decompose, and no credit counters either, because flow control is the static schedule, not credits. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence.
- **Switch arbiter — none in the fabric** — Zero gates. There is no switch arbiter in the fabric either: two tiles never contend for the same mux input in the same cycle because Poplar's schedule guarantees it in advance — the arbitration happens at compile time, in the scheduler, not in silicon at run time. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence, and that compile-time arbitration is exactly why exchange timing is deterministic.
- **Synchronizer (mesochronous clocking — 3 cycles of drift, no per-link synchronizer)** — Zero gates inside this block. The whole chip runs on one mesochronous clock with 3 cycles of global synchrony drift, so the exchange needs no per-link two-flop synchronizer: the 3-cycle drift is absorbed by the cycle-exact schedule, which knows all pipeline delays. The synchronizer-shaped question therefore has a negative answer inside this block; the only clock-domain crossing is at the chip edge, in the IPU-Link SerDes below, and the phase-alignment hardware that holds the 3-cycle bound is not published. There is nothing to decompose here: no synchronizer exists in the block.
- **SerDes (the IPU-Link — chip-to-chip escape)** — A SerDes is a serializer, a deserializer and clock recovery: the serializer is a shift register — one flip-flop per bit of the parallel word plus a mux tree to select the next bit out — so a 32:1 serializer is 32 flip-flops, about 640–896 transistors, plus 31 2:1 muxes per lane; the deserializer is the mirror image; the clock-data recovery loop is a phase detector (XOR gates), a loop filter (a counter) and a voltage-controlled oscillator, and the equalizer is a feed-forward adder tree plus a decision-feedback adder and comparator. The SerDes rate, lane count, encoding and per-link clocking are not published, so no per-link gate total is claimed: the 32 GB/s per link is arithmetic from the published 320 GB/s across 10 links, and the 15 ns per hop is the published inter-chip cost. Standard construction.

Honesty: Graphcore publishes the fabric geometry and none of its circuits: the 1600 x 36-bit spine, the 36-bit send channel, the 1600-way receive mux, 32 bits per cycle per tile, the ~150-cycle sync, 15 ns per hop, 3 cycles of drift, 10 IPU-Links at 320 GB/s — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — select-state storage and size, spine column organisation, SerDes rates and encoding, the IO-block count — Graphcore publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two primitives are deliberately absent, and that absence is the design: there is no FIFO/queue and no switch arbiter anywhere in the fabric, because addressing is by time and select state under a statically scheduled exchange.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [unverifiable] **Graphcore GC200 IPU** — Level-4 decomposition scope boundary: Graphcore publishes no gate-level structure for the GC200 tile or the IPU-Exchange; the Level-4 text therefore decomposes every primitive as the generic textbook construction of that primitive, labelled standard construction, using only Graphcore's published per-block geometry plus figures explicitly labelled as arithmetic derived from that geometry (624 KiB per tile = 5,111,808 bits = 30,670,848 6T cell transistors per tile; 7,524,581,376 bits = 45,147,488,256 cell transistors die-wide, checking exactly against the deck's 897 MiB; 121 partial-product AND gates per FP16 multiplier, 30,976 per tile, 45,596,672 chip-wide; 3,198 transistors per bit, 115,128 per tile mux, 169,468,416 chip-wide for the 1600-way receive mux; 1,471 AND2 gates, 5,884 transistors, for the barrier AND-reduction). Two primitives decompose to zero gates in the fabric (no FIFO/queue, no switch arbiter) and the synchronizer to zero gates in-block. Source: Knowles, "Graphcore Colossus Mk2 IPU", Hot Chips 33 (2021); Frontiers in High Performance Computing supplementary material §2.

### Tesla Dojo D1

#### Down to the gates: The D1 training node — an 8-wide, 4-way SMT core with 1.25 MB of ECC SRAM and an 8×8×4 matrix unit

Tesla publishes no gate-level structure for the D1 — the Hot Chips 34 deck and the IEEE Micro paper describe the node's contract (360 physical nodes in an 18x20 array with 354 available, 2 GHz, the 32-byte fetch window, the 8-wide decoder on two threads per cycle, the 4-wide 4-way SMT scalar scheduler, the 2-way SMT vector scheduler, the 64-byte SIMD unit and the four 8x8x4 matrix units, the five 64-byte SRAM ports, the 1.25 MB ECC SRAM, the FP32/BF16/CFP8/CFP16 formats) and stop there. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about Tesla's circuits. Two primitives decompose to zero gates, and that absence is the design.

- **FSM / controller (the branch predictor — BTB in the frontend)** — The branch predictor is a small state machine plus a lookup table: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each, primer bottom layer) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network, while the lookup itself is a tag compare — one XNOR2 gate (about 10–12 transistors) per tag bit plus a log2(N)-level AND tree — feeding a target-address mux. The BTB's size, its prediction scheme and its mispredict handling are not published, so no tag width, no table size and no gate total is claimed: a BTB gate total needs a table size Tesla never gives. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the small instruction cache — 32 bytes per cycle)** — The instruction cache is a 6T SRAM array: one 6-transistor cell per bit, plus a row decoder (a NAND/NOR tree that turns the address into one wordline), column muxes (transmission gates, 2 transistors per 2:1 mux per bit) and sense amplifiers (about 6–8 transistors per bitline) — the primer bottom layer's 6T cell. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the 32-byte fetch window is a 256-bit read port, so the fetch port's sense-amplifier array is 256 sense amplifiers, about 1,536–2,048 transistors. The cache's size, associativity and line width beyond the 32-byte fetch are not published, so no cell total is claimed for the cache itself. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the per-thread fetch buffers)** — A FIFO is a register array plus write and read pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is one flip-flop per bit (about 20–28 transistors each), each pointer is a counter of log2(depth) flip-flops plus an incrementer of the same number of full adders (about 28 transistors each), and full/empty is an equality compare of the two pointers. The buffer depth per thread and the fetch-buffer width are not published, so no pointer width and no total is claimed — a FIFO gate total needs a depth Tesla never gives. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the 8-wide decoder — two threads per cycle, frontend list parsing)** — A decoder is opcode comparators feeding control-signal generation: each instruction's opcode field is compared against the instruction patterns — one XNOR2 gate per compared bit plus an AND tree per pattern — and the matches drive the control lines for the scheduler, the list parser and the vector side. The frontend list parser that executes branches, predicated operations and immediate loads at decode is a comparator plus a small adder at the decode stage, of the same form as the primitives below. The decoder's internal staging, the list parser's table and the instruction width are not published, so no comparator count and no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (branch and predicated-operation evaluation in the frontend)** — A condition compare is an XNOR per bit plus an AND tree: one XNOR2 gate (about 10–12 transistors) per compared bit, then a log2(N)-level AND tree to combine the per-bit results, evaluated and acted on before the instruction enters the pipeline. The comparator width and the condition storage are not published, so no gate total is claimed; the compare-against-a-register form is the standard one for a frontend branch decision, labelled as such. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the 4-way SMT scalar scheduler)** — The scheduler is a state machine built the standard way: ready bits are flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each), issue selection is a priority encoder or round-robin arbiter (a comparator network plus an encoder tree), and the four threads' ready state is held per thread. The scheduler's queue depths and issue-selection policy are not published, so no ready-bit count, no encoder width and no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Register file (one per thread — scalar architectural state)** — A register file is an array of multi-ported bit cells: each bit cell is a storage latch plus one access transistor per read port and one per write port, so a 2-read/1-write cell is about 10–12 transistors in the standard construction, and a 32-bit register is 32 of them, about 320–384 transistors. There is one register file per thread, four in the node, but the register count per thread, the read/write port counts and the bypass network are not published, so no total is claimed: a register-file gate total needs a register count Tesla never gives. Standard construction.
- **Adder (the two integer ALUs and two address units)** — An integer ALU is an adder/subtractor plus a logic unit: a W-bit adder is W full adders, about 28 transistors each in the standard form (primer bottom layer), so a 32-bit adder would be about 896 transistors and a 64-bit adder about 1,792 — but the scalar datapath width is not published, so neither width is asserted and no ALU total is claimed. The two address units are adders of the same form, computing the tile's address stream. The ALU pipeline depth is not published. Standard construction.
- **Counter (the list parser and gather engine — address generation at 8- and 16-byte granularity)** — The gather walk is a counter plus address adders: the list parser walks the tile's index list — a pointer counter of log2(depth) flip-flops plus an incrementer — and each gather address is an adder over the running base, with the low 3 or 4 address bits fixed by the 8- or 16-byte granularity, so the counter advances in units of 8 or 16 bytes. The gather lane count, the list-parser's list depth and the address-generation pipeline depth are not published, so no pointer width, no lane count and no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the node's 1.25 MB ECC scratchpad — five 64-byte ports)** — The scratchpad is a 6T SRAM array: one 6-transistor cell per bit, plus a row decoder (a NAND/NOR tree that turns the address into one wordline), column muxes (transmission gates, 2 transistors per 2:1 mux per bit) and sense amplifiers (about 6–8 transistors per bitline) — the primer bottom layer's 6T cell. Arithmetic from the published geometry, reading Tesla's megabytes as decimal: 1.25 MB per node is 10,000,000 bits, so 10,000,000 6T cells, 60,000,000 cell transistors per node; across 354 available nodes that is 3,540,000,000 bits, 21,240,000,000 cell transistors — and the same arithmetic from the published 440 MB die total gives 3,520,000,000 bits, 21,120,000,000 cell transistors, the 0.6% gap being the 354 x 1.25 = 442.5 MB rounding against Tesla's 440 MB. The five 64-byte ports move 320 bytes per cycle on the SRAM side (Level-3 arithmetic), and each 512-bit port's sense-amplifier array is 512 sense amplifiers, about 3,072–4,096 transistors. ECC adds check bits per word — the standard form is an XOR-tree encoder per write and a syndrome comparator per read — but the ECC granularity is not published, so no check-bit total is claimed. How the 1.25 MB is organised into banks, the port arbitration between the five ports and the ECC granularity are not published. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (the five-port SRAM select)** — Port selection is muxes: a 5:1 mux per bit is four 2:1 muxes, 8 transistors per bit in the transmission-gate form (2 per 2:1 mux) or about 64 transistors per bit in the NAND/NOR-tree form (4 gates, about 16 transistors each, per 2:1 mux). Arithmetic from the published geometry: one 512-bit port selected 5-way is 512 x 8 = 4,096 transistors in the transmission-gate form, or 512 x 64 = 32,768 in the NAND/NOR form, per selected port. The mux radix, the arbitration policy between the five ports and the timing of a port's access are not published, so no total across the five ports is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the 2-way SMT vector scheduler)** — The vector scheduler is a state machine built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network, with a selection mux steering each vector instruction to the SIMD pipe or the matrix pipes. The scheduler's queue depth and its selection policy between the SIMD and matrix pipes are not published, so no queue depth and no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (the four 8×8×4 matrix units — 512 FLOPS/cycle)** — A floating-point multiplier is a mantissa multiplier plus exponent logic: the mantissa multiply is an AND-gate partial-product array feeding a carry-save adder tree, and the accumulator is a full adder per mantissa bit (about 28 transistors each, primer bottom layer). Arithmetic from the published geometry: a BF16 mantissa is 8 bits (7 explicit plus the implicit leading 1), so one BF16 multiplier is an 8x8 array, 64 partial-product AND gates; one 8x8x4 multiply is 256 multiply-accumulates, so 256 multipliers need 16,384 partial-product AND gates per 8x8x4 multiply per cycle. An FP32 mantissa is 24 bits, so an FP32 multiplier is a 24x24 array, 576 partial-product AND gates. The four named matrix units share the published 512 BF16 FLOPS per cycle — four units each doing a full 8x8x4 per cycle would be 2,048 FLOPS per cycle — so how the four units divide the one 8x8x4 multiply per cycle is unpublished, and no per-unit or per-node multiplier total is claimed beyond the per-multiply shape above. The multiplier array's internal tiling, the accumulator widths and the matrix pipeline depth are not published. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (FP32 accumulation and the 64-byte SIMD unit)** — The accumulation tree narrows the 256 products to 64 accumulators: each of the 64 outputs sums 4 products, so the tree is 3 FP32 adders per output in 2 levels, 192 FP32 adders per 8x8x4 multiply. Arithmetic from the published geometry: a 24-bit mantissa adder is 24 full adders, about 672 transistors in ripple-carry form, so the accumulation tree of one 8x8x4 multiply is 192 x 672 = 129,024 transistors in that form. The same add-then-accumulate shape is the 64-byte SIMD unit — 512 bits wide, 32 BF16 lanes by arithmetic (Level-3) — but the SIMD accumulate width and lane organisation are not published, so no SIMD adder total is claimed. As with the multiplier array, the four-unit division of the work is unpublished, so the 129,024-transistor figure is the shape of one 8x8x4 multiply per cycle, not a claimed per-node total. The adder-tree depth beyond the 2-level per-output shape, the accumulator register widths and the SIMD lane organisation are not published. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (the scalar-ahead-of-vector pipeline)** — Each pipeline stage is a register: a W-bit stage is W master-slave D flip-flops, about 20–28 transistors each. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the 32-byte fetch window is a 256-bit stage register, 256 flip-flops, about 5,120–7,168 transistors per fetch stage; a 512-bit vector operand stage is 512 flip-flops, about 10,240–14,336 transistors per stage. The number of pipeline stages and the vector/matrix pipeline depths are not published, so no total across the pipeline is claimed. No interlock or hazard-detection structure is published for the node — the published behaviour is that the scalar side runs ahead of the vector side until a scheduler fills — so no scoreboard or forwarding-comparator gates are claimed. Standard construction.
- **Data cache / tag array — none in the node** — Zero gates. There is no data cache anywhere in the node: the 1.25 MB SRAM is a software-managed scratchpad, not a cache, so there is no tag array, no replacement logic and no coherence hardware to decompose — the SRAM's five-port contract is the whole memory system. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence.
- **TLB / page-walk hardware — none in the node** — Zero gates. There is no virtual memory support and therefore no TLB and no page-walk hardware, no in-order retirement logic and no precise exceptions outside debug mode. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence, and that absence is the deal Dojo makes for a compiler-scheduled training node.

Honesty: Tesla publishes the node geometry and none of its circuits: 360 physical nodes in an 18x20 array with 354 available, 2 GHz, 32 bytes fetched per cycle, 8-wide decode on two threads, a 4-wide 4-way SMT scalar scheduler with two integer ALUs and two address units, one register file per thread, a 2-way SMT vector scheduler, a 64-byte SIMD unit, four 8x8x4 matrix units at 512 BF16 FLOPS per cycle, 1.25 MB of ECC SRAM with five 64-byte ports, two 512-bit loads per cycle, FP32/BF16/CFP8/CFP16 formats with up to 16 usable simultaneously — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. The SRAM cell totals read Tesla's "1.25 MB" and "440 MB" as decimal megabytes (1 MB = 10^6 bytes); the MiB reading would give 62,914,560 6T cells per node instead of 60,000,000, a 4.9% difference, and neither reading is asserted as Tesla's own unit. Below that level — SRAM bank organisation, BTB size, register-file size and port counts, vector/matrix pipeline depths, gather-engine lane count — Tesla publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no data cache, no TLB and no virtual memory anywhere in the node, and there is no in-order retirement logic or precise-exception hardware outside debug mode.

#### Down to the gates: The 2D mesh NoC and die-edge SerDes — a seamless mesh from node to ExaPOD

Tesla publishes no gate-level structure for the mesh or the SerDes — the Hot Chips 34 deck and the IEEE Micro paper describe the fabric's contract (one packet in and one packet out in all four directions per node per cycle, one 64-byte mesh-stop read and write per cycle, 64 bytes per cycle per direction, 256 GB/s bidirectional on every row and column, 10 TB/s on-chip, 576 SerDes lanes at 112 Gb/s, about 100 ns die-to-die, no end-to-end ordering with packet counting at the destination, TTPoE at 50 GB/s per link with 30 hops against 4) and stop there. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about Tesla's circuits. One primitive decomposes to zero gates, and that absence is the design.

- **SRAM bank (the mesh stop's 64-byte read and write ports)** — The mesh-stop ports are two of the five SRAM ports decomposed in the node block above: the same 6T cell array, row decoder, column muxes and sense amplifiers. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the mesh stop's 64-byte read port is a 512-bit read path, so its sense-amplifier array is 512 sense amplifiers, about 3,072–4,096 transistors, and the 64-byte write port is the mirror image on the write side. One 64-byte mesh-stop read per cycle at 2 GHz is 128 GB/s into the router, and one 64-byte write per cycle is 128 GB/s out of it (Level-3 arithmetic). The mesh-stop port arbitration against the load/store ports is not published. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (router input buffering — depth unpublished)** — A router input FIFO is a register array plus write and read pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is one flip-flop per bit (about 20–28 transistors each), each pointer is a counter of log2(depth) flip-flops plus an incrementer of the same number of full adders (about 28 transistors each), and full/empty is an equality compare of the two pointers. At minimum each direction needs a one-packet holding register between its arrival cycle and its departure cycle, but the packet format and size are not published, so no bit count, no depth and no total is claimed — a router-buffer gate total needs a packet size Tesla never gives. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (the router's four-direction switch)** — A router crossbar is muxes: one output selecting among five inputs is a 5:1 mux per bit, four 2:1 muxes, 8 transistors per bit in the transmission-gate form (2 per 2:1 mux) or about 64 transistors per bit in the NAND/NOR-tree form, with 3 select bits per output (Level-3 arithmetic) — 15 select bits across the five outputs. The packet width is not published, so no per-output bit count and no crossbar gate total is claimed: the 5x5 form is the standard construction for a router of this port count, labelled as such. The crossbar's implementation and the per-direction wire counts are not published. Standard construction.
- **Switch arbiter (output arbitration — scheme unpublished)** — An arbiter is a priority encoder or a round-robin selector: a fixed-priority arbiter is a comparator network plus an encoder tree, a round-robin arbiter adds a rotating priority register of log2(N) flip-flops. Up to five inputs can want the same output in one cycle, so the router must arbitrate — but Tesla publishes no arbitration scheme, no priority rule and no fairness guarantee for the D1 router, so neither standard form is asserted and no gate total is claimed. Any arbitration policy named here would be invention, so none is. Standard construction, conditionally.
- **FSM / controller (route and direction select)** — Route selection is a state machine built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network, driven by the packet's destination against the router's own coordinates. The compiler knows the topology, including which of the 360 nodes are unavailable, and places work accordingly, so routing is at least partly a compile-time decision; the router's own routing algorithm, its direction-select logic and any deadlock-avoidance scheme are not published, so no state count and no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (the one-cycle-per-hop forwarding path)** — Each hop is a pipeline stage: a packet-width register of one flip-flop per bit (about 20–28 transistors each) between the input and the output. The one-cycle-per-hop figure is unverifiable in this run — the only textual statement is a secondary blog, and the deck's network-interface slide was read only as a reproduced image (Level-2) — and the packet size is not published, so no register width and no gate total is claimed. The pipeline register count and widths follow the unpublished packet size. Standard construction.
- **SerDes (the 576-lane die edge)** — A SerDes is a serializer, a deserializer and clock recovery: the serializer is a shift register — one flip-flop per bit of the parallel word plus a mux tree to select the next bit out — so an N-bit parallel word is N flip-flops, about 20–28 transistors each, plus N-1 2:1 muxes per lane; the deserializer is the mirror image; the clock-data recovery loop is a phase detector (XOR gates), a loop filter (a counter) and a voltage-controlled oscillator, and the equalizer is a feed-forward adder tree plus a decision-feedback adder and comparator. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 576 lanes at 112 Gb/s is 64,512 Gb/s, 8,064 GB/s across all four die edges, about 2 TB/s per edge with 144 lanes per edge — the lane-to-edge split is arithmetic, not published. The parallel word width, the encoding, the lane-to-edge assignment and the per-lane clocking are not published, so no per-lane gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (the die-edge clock-domain crossing)** — Two dies are two clock domains, so the die edge is a clock-domain crossing by construction: the standard form is a two-flop synchronizer per bit, two master-slave D flip-flops, about 40–56 transistors per bit. The ~100 ns die-to-die latency is about 200 cycles at the 2 GHz node clock (Level-3 arithmetic), two orders of magnitude above a single-cycle on-die hop — but the synchronizer's construction, the SerDes' internal pipeline depth and the latency's split between serialisation and retiming are not published, and the bit width crossing the edge is unpublished, so no synchronizer total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (packet counting at the destination — the synchronisation mechanism)** — Packet counting is a counter plus a comparator: an N-bit counter is N flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) plus an N-bit incrementer of N full adders (about 28 transistors each), and the compare against the expected count is N XNOR2 gates (about 10–12 transistors each) plus a log2(N)-level AND tree. The counter width, the expected-count storage and the compare are not published — the expected count is a property of the compiler-defined synchronisation tree, not of the hardware — and there is no hardware barrier network to decompose instead. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (TTPoE — the Z-plane transport)** — The TTPoE engine is a state machine built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network, sequencing transmit and receive over the 50 GB/s link. The TTPoE engine's internal primitives — its packet buffers, its transmit/receive sequencing, its DMA into the tile — are not published, so no buffer depth, no state count and no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **SerDes (the DIP escape — 400 Gb/s NIC and 32 GB HBM per card)** — The DIP's SerDes is the same standard construction as the die-edge SerDes above — serializer shift register, deserializer, clock-data recovery and equalizer — but the DIP sits outside the D1 die, and its internal primitives — the HBM interface, the NIC's SerDes, the PCIe path — are not published. The per-DIP rate is disputed, 900 GB/s against 800 GB/s (Level-2), so no per-link rate and no gate total is claimed. Standard construction, conditionally.
- **Credit counter — no hardware flow control published** — Zero gates. There is no published hardware flow control in the mesh: no credit counters, no backpressure scheme and no published buffer accounting between routers. Flow control, as far as the published material goes, is the compiler's placement — it knows the topology and the traffic pattern in advance — plus packet counting at the destination. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence.

Honesty: Tesla publishes the fabric geometry and none of its circuits: one packet in and out in all four directions per node per cycle, one 64-byte mesh-stop read and write per cycle, 64 bytes per cycle per direction, 256 GB/s bidirectional on every row and column, 10 TB/s on-chip, 576 SerDes lanes at 112 Gb/s, about 100 ns die-to-die latency, 50 GB/s TTPoE links over 400 Gb/s Ethernet, 30 mesh hops against 4 Z-plane hops — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — router buffer depths, arbitration, packet format and size, SerDes lane-to-edge assignment — Tesla publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no hardware ordering guarantee and no hardware barrier network — synchronisation is packet counting under a compiler-defined tree — and there is no hardware flow control in the mesh, so there is no credit counter to decompose.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [unverifiable] **Tesla Dojo D1** — Level-4 decomposition scope boundary: Tesla publishes no gate-level structure for the D1 node or the mesh at Level-4 depth; the Level-4 text therefore decomposes every primitive as the generic textbook construction of that primitive, labelled standard construction, using only Tesla's published per-block geometry plus figures explicitly labelled as arithmetic derived from that geometry (1.25 MB SRAM per node = 10,000,000 bits = 60,000,000 6T cell transistors per node; 3,540,000,000 bits = 21,240,000,000 cell transistors across 354 nodes, checking against the published 440 MB die total at 21,120,000,000; 16,384 partial-product AND gates per 8x8x4 multiply; 192 FP32 adders, 129,024 transistors, for the accumulation tree of one 8x8x4 multiply; 576 SerDes lanes at 112 Gb/s = 8,064 GB/s). Two primitives decompose to zero gates in the node (no data cache/tag array, no TLB/page-walk hardware) and one in the fabric (no hardware flow control / credit counter). Source: Talpes, "DOJO: The Microarchitecture of Tesla's Exa-Scale Computer", Hot Chips 34 (2022); Talpes et al., IEEE Micro 43(3):31–39, 2023.

### AWS Inferentia2 & Trainium

#### Down to the gates: The Tensor Engine and its two SRAMs — a 128x128 systolic array fed by a 24 MiB SBUF and drained into a 2 MiB PSUM

AWS publishes no gate-level structure for Inferentia2 or Trainium — the NKI architecture guide describes the Tensor Engine's contract (a 128x128 systolic array, 92 TFLOPS maximum for BF16/FP16/TF32/cFP8, 24 MiB of SBUF in 128 partitions of 192 KiB, 2 MiB of PSUM in 128 partitions of 16 KiB, tile limits M at most 128, K at most 128 and N at most 512, a MultiplyMoving initiation interval of roughly max(N, 64) Tensor Engine cycles, about 60 cycles of tensor-access overhead, 128 elements per cycle at 1.4 GHz on each SBUF/PSUM interface, four engine sequencers with private 32-bit scalar registers, atomic semaphores in hardware, and the compiler-enforced shared-port rules) and stops there. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about AWS's circuits. Two primitives decompose to zero gates, and that absence is the design.

- **SRAM bank (SBUF — 128 partitions of 192 KiB)** — The SBUF and PSUM are 6T SRAM arrays: one 6-transistor cell per bit, plus a row decoder (a NAND/NOR tree that turns the address into one wordline), column muxes (transmission gates, 2 transistors per 2:1 mux per bit) and sense amplifiers (about 6–8 transistors per bitline) — the primer bottom layer's 6T cell. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the 24 MiB SBUF is 201,326,592 bits, so 201,326,592 6T cells, 1,207,959,552 cell transistors; one 192 KiB SBUF partition is 1,572,864 bits, 9,437,184 cell transistors. The 2 MiB PSUM is 16,777,216 bits, 100,663,296 cell transistors; one 16 KiB PSUM partition is 131,072 bits, 786,432 cell transistors; one PSUM bank of 512 FP32 values is 16,384 bits, 98,304 cell transistors. A 128-element read at FP32 width is a 4,096-bit read port, so its sense-amplifier array is 4,096 sense amplifiers, about 24,576–32,768 transistors — arithmetic at FP32 width, since the element width depends on the data type. How a 192 KiB partition is organised into banks, its line width and its port count beyond the 128-element interface are not published. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (the 128x128 systolic MAC array)** — Each processing element is one multiplier plus one adder: the mantissa multiply is an AND-gate partial-product array feeding a carry-save adder tree of full adders, and the accumulate is a full adder per mantissa bit — the primer bottom layer's full-adder cell, about 28 transistors each. Arithmetic from the published geometry: a BF16 mantissa is 8 bits (7 explicit plus the implicit leading 1), so one BF16 multiplier is an 8x8 array, 64 partial-product AND gates; across the 128x128 array that is 16,384 multipliers, 1,048,576 partial-product AND gates per cycle. An FP32 mantissa is 24 bits, so an FP32 multiplier is a 24x24 array, 576 partial-product AND gates. The 16,384 MACs at 2 FLOPs per MAC per cycle and 2.8 GHz give 91.75 TFLOPS, the guide's 92 TFLOPS maximum. The array's internal tiling, the per-PE multiplier width beyond the published data types and the accumulator register widths are not published. Standard construction.
- **Register file (the stationary storage — one weight per processing element)** — The stationary storage is a register file: one weight per processing element, 16,384 weights parked for a full [128,128] tile. At gate level a register file is an array of storage cells behind wordline decoders and column muxes. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 16,384 BF16 weights at 16 bits each are 262,144 bits, 32 KiB of stationary storage per array. The storage form is not published, so both candidate standard forms are stated conditionally and neither is asserted: as a 6T SRAM array that is 262,144 cells, 1,572,864 cell transistors; as flip-flops it is 262,144 D flip-flops at about 20–28 transistors each, 5,242,880–7,340,032 transistors. Its read/write port count is not published. Standard construction, conditionally.
- **Adder (FP32 accumulation — the column add chain and PSUM read-accumulate-write)** — The FP32 accumulation is adders in two places: inside the array, each processing element adds its product into the partial sum arriving from the element above — a column-wise add chain of one FP32 adder per processing element — and at the array's foot, PSUM's near-memory accumulation does a read-accumulate-write on every 4-byte element, one FP32 adder per bank. At gate level an FP32 adder is an exponent compare and subtractor, a 24-bit mantissa adder of 24 full adders, and normalize-and-round logic. Arithmetic from the published geometry: a 24-bit mantissa adder is 24 full adders, about 672 transistors in ripple-carry form, so the 16,384 processing elements' mantissa adders are 11,010,048 transistors, and the PSUM side is 8 banks per partition across 128 partitions, 1,024 bank adders, 688,128 transistors of mantissa adder — both figures are the mantissa-adder shape only, since the exponent and normalization logic around each add is unpublished. The adder widths beyond the published 32-bit element and the pipeline depth of the accumulation path are not published. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (SBUF partition select and PSUM bank select)** — Partition and bank selection is mux trees: a 128:1 select is a 7-bit index driving a binary tree of 127 2:1 muxes per data bit in 7 levels, and an 8:1 bank select is a 3-bit index driving 7 2:1 muxes per data bit in 3 levels. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one data bit's 128:1 select is 127 2:1 muxes, 254 transistors in the transmission-gate form (2 per 2:1 mux) or about 2,032 in the NAND/NOR-tree form (about 16 transistors per 2:1 mux); one data bit's 8:1 bank select is 7 2:1 muxes, 14 transistors in the transmission-gate form or about 112 in the NAND/NOR form. The mux radix, the select encoding and the timing of a partition access are not published, so no total across the interface width is claimed — the interface moves 128 elements per cycle but the element width depends on the data type. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (VectorE Reshape banks to 32 partitions; GpSimd to 16 partitions)** — The companion-engine crossbars are muxes: each Reshape bank output selects among its 32 partitions, a 32:1 mux per data bit — 31 2:1 muxes, 62 transistors in the transmission-gate form — under a 5-bit select, so one Reshape bank's 32 outputs are 992 2:1 muxes per data bit. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 4 Reshape banks x 32 partitions = 128 partitions and 8 GpSimd processors x 16 partitions = 128 partitions — the two crossbars tile the whole SBUF between them. The GpSimd connection is fixed partition groups (processor 0 to partitions 0–15, and so on), so its gate content is wiring plus the per-processor read/write port muxes, whose radix is not published. The crossbar radix, the per-output arbitration and the wire counts are not published. Standard construction.
- **Shuffle / permutation network (the Reshape bank's 32x32 transpose and 32-partition shuffle)** — The Reshape bank's 32x32 transpose and 32-partition shuffle are a mux network: each of the 32 outputs selects among 32 inputs, a 32:1 mux per data bit — 31 2:1 muxes, 62 transistors in the transmission-gate form — the same shape as the Reshape crossbar above, with a 32x32-element staging buffer behind it. Arithmetic from the published geometry, conditioned on element width: at FP32 width the 32x32 staging buffer is 32,768 flip-flops, about 655,360–917,504 transistors; the element width is not published, so no buffer total is asserted. The permutation network's stage count, mux radix and the transpose's buffering are not published. No barrel shifter is published anywhere in this block. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the four engine sequencers and the Sync Engine)** — Each sequencer is a state machine built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network, with instruction fetch, decode and issue driven by opcode comparators — one XNOR2 gate (about 10–12 transistors) per compared opcode bit plus an AND tree per instruction pattern. Arithmetic from the published geometry: each sequencer's private 32-bit scalar registers are 32 flip-flops each, about 640–896 transistors per register; there are four engine sequencers plus the Sync Engine, five in a core. The sequencers' queue depths, issue widths and hazard handling are not published. Standard construction.
- **Counter (initiation-interval, accumulation-group and tensor-access counters)** — The block's timing is counting, and a counter is flip-flops plus an incrementer: an N-bit counter is N master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) plus an N-bit incrementer of N full adders (about 28 transistors each). Arithmetic from the published bounds: N is at most 512, so the initiation-interval counter is 9 bits, about 432–504 transistors; eight outstanding accumulation groups need a 3-bit group index, about 144–168 transistors; the 60-cycle tensor-access overhead is a 6-bit count, about 288–336 transistors. The counters' actual widths are arithmetic, not published figures. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (hardware semaphores and partition-alignment checks)** — A semaphore test and an alignment check are both compares: a compare of an N-bit value against zero or against a legal boundary is one XNOR2 gate (about 10–12 transistors) per compared bit plus a log2(N)-level AND tree to combine the per-bit results. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the partition-alignment check compares a 7-bit partition index against the legal set, so 7 XNOR2 gates plus a 3-level AND tree per check. The semaphore count and widths, and the alignment-check implementation, are not published. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline registers (the deeply pipelined TensorE and VectorE datapaths)** — Each pipeline stage is a register: a W-bit stage is W master-slave D flip-flops, about 20–28 transistors each. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the SBUF/PSUM interface moves 128 elements per cycle, so one interface stage at FP32 width is 4,096 flip-flops, about 81,920–114,688 transistors — arithmetic at FP32 width, since the element width depends on the data type. The pipeline stage count, the stage latch widths beyond the published 128-element interfaces and the bypass/forwarding network are not published. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (engine instruction streams and sequencer fetch queues)** — A FIFO is a register array plus write and read pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the storage is one flip-flop per bit (about 20–28 transistors each), each pointer is a counter of log2(depth) flip-flops plus an incrementer of the same number of full adders (about 28 transistors each), and full/empty is an equality compare of the two pointers. The queue depths, the fetch widths and the semaphore-wait queueing are not published, so no pointer width and no total is claimed — a FIFO gate total needs a depth AWS never gives. The published contract is the rate — 128 elements per cycle at 1.4 GHz per interface — not the buffering. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (clock-domain crossings — 2.8, 1.4 and 1.12 GHz)** — The block spans three clock domains by construction: Tensor Engine at 2.8 GHz, Vector Engine at 1.12 GHz, Scalar and GpSimd Engines at 1.4 GHz, with the SBUF/PSUM interface at 1.4 GHz. The standard form for a crossing is a two-flop synchronizer per bit — two master-slave D flip-flops, about 40–56 transistors per bit — but AWS publishes no synchronizer structure, no crossing scheme and no latency for the crossings, and this decomposition invents none of them: no synchronizer total is claimed, since the bit width crossing each domain boundary is unpublished. Standard construction, conditionally.
- **Switch arbiter — absent by design (compiler-enforced serialisation)** — Zero gates. There is no hardware arbiter for the shared SRAM ports, because the serialisation is done by the compiler: VectorE and GpSimdE cannot access SBUF in parallel, and VectorE and ScalarE cannot access PSUM in parallel, and this is enforced by Neuron Compiler during NKI kernel compilation. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence.
- **CAM / TCAM — none in the block** — Zero gates. There is no associative lookup anywhere in this block: SBUF and PSUM are directly addressed by partition plus free-dimension offset, the stationary weights are indexed by their processing element, and the PSUM banks are indexed by accumulation group. No content-addressable structure is published for the Tensor Engine or its SRAMs, so there is no CAM cell — no SRAM cell plus XOR match logic, no matchline — to decompose. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence.

Honesty: AWS publishes the Tensor Engine geometry and none of its circuits: 128 rows and 128 columns of processing elements; 92 TFLOPS maximum for BF16/FP16/TF32/cFP8 and 23 TFLOPS for FP32; accumulation always FP32; SBUF 24 MiB in 128 partitions of 192 KiB and PSUM 2 MiB in 128 partitions of 16 KiB; each PSUM partition in 8 banks of 512 32-bit values; tile limits M at most 128, K at most 128, N at most 512; MultiplyMoving initiation interval roughly max(N, 64) Tensor Engine cycles; tensor access overhead about 60 cycles; SBUF/PSUM peak 128 elements per cycle at 1.4 GHz; Vector Engine 128 lanes at 1.12 GHz with four Reshape banks of 32 partitions and four Compute banks of 32 lanes; Scalar Engine 128 lanes at 1.4 GHz; GpSimd eight 512-bit processors at 1.4 GHz with 64 KiB TCM at 3-cycle latency and 16 SBUF partitions per processor; each engine with its own sequencer and private 32-bit scalar registers; the Sync Engine triggering DMA; atomic semaphores in hardware; the shared-port rules enforced by the compiler — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Two Tensor Engines at 92 TFLOPS each multiply to 184 TFLOPS against the chip's rated 190 FP16/BF16 TFLOPS; the guide does not explain the 6 TFLOPS gap, and this section claims no resolution. Below that level — SRAM bank organisation within a partition, per-PE circuit detail, sequencer queue depths, synchronizer construction, semaphore widths — AWS publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no cache anywhere in the core, so there is no tag array and no coherence to decompose; and there is no hardware arbiter for the shared SRAM ports, because the compiler serialises the conflicting accesses.

#### Down to the gates: DMA, the CC cores and NeuronLink-v2 — the movement fabric that keeps two cores and sixteen chips fed

AWS publishes no gate-level structure for the movement fabric — the NKI guide describes the fabric's contract (16 DMA engines per NeuronCore, 32 per device, each processing one transfer at a time at a peak of 27 GiB/s; the 128x512 FP32 load example as 16 transfers of 8 DMA buffers each; the 4 KiB free-dimension and ideally-128 partition-dimension rule; 2 HBM stacks with 32 GiB and 820 GB/s; 1 TB/s DMA bandwidth with inline compression/decompression; 6 CC cores; 2 NeuronLink-v2 links on Inferentia2 and 4 on Trainium; 16 Trainium chips per Trn1 instance) and stops there. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about AWS's circuits. Two primitives decompose to zero gates, and that absence is the design.

- **FSM / controller (the Sync Engine and the DMA engine controllers)** — The Sync Engine and each DMA engine controller are state machines built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network, sequencing descriptor fetch, scatter-gather list walk and issue. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 16 DMA engines per core run in parallel, 32 per device, each processing one transfer at a time. The DMA engine's internal state machine — descriptor fetch, scatter-gather list walk, issue sequencing — is not published, so no state count and no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (DMA scatter-gather buffer lists)** — A transfer's scatter-gather list is a descriptor queue: a FIFO of register storage plus write and read pointer counters plus full/empty comparators — the storage one flip-flop per bit (about 20–28 transistors each), each pointer a counter of log2(depth) flip-flops plus an incrementer of the same number of full adders (about 28 transistors each). Arithmetic from the published geometry: the published tiling example is 16 transfers of 8 DMA buffers each, so the per-transfer list index is 3 bits, the transfer index per core is 4 bits, and a full-width tile's buffer count is 7 bits. The list depth per transfer beyond the published 8-buffer example, the descriptor width and any per-engine buffer queue are not published, so no FIFO total is claimed. Standard construction.
