- **Counter (DMA buffer and transfer counting)** — The fabric counts in buffers and transfers, and a counter is flip-flops plus an incrementer: an N-bit counter is N master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) plus an N-bit incrementer of N full adders (about 28 transistors each). Arithmetic from the published geometry: 16 transfers need a 4-bit transfer index per core, about 192–224 transistors; 8 buffers per transfer a 3-bit buffer index, about 144–168 transistors; 128 buffers for a full-width tile a 7-bit buffer count, about 336–392 transistors. The counters' actual widths are arithmetic, not published figures. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (DMA engine to SBUF partition routing)** — Sixteen DMA engines per core share one 128-partition SBUF, so each transfer's buffers are routed to their partitions through mux trees: routing one buffer stream to one of 128 partitions is a 128:1 select, a 7-bit index driving a binary tree of 127 2:1 muxes per data bit in 7 levels. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one data bit's 128:1 select is 127 2:1 muxes, 254 transistors in the transmission-gate form (2 per 2:1 mux) or about 2,032 in the NAND/NOR-tree form (about 16 transistors per 2:1 mux); one engine's buffer stream fans out to eight different partitions per transfer, and sixteen engines' streams interleave across all 128 partitions. The mux radix, the select encoding and the per-cycle routing rate beyond the published 27 GiB/s per engine are not published. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (the DMA-to-SBUF interconnect)** — The interconnect between the 16 DMA engines and the 128 SBUF partitions is architecturally a crossbar — any engine to any partition, one buffer at a time — and a crossbar is muxes: each output selecting among 16 engines is a 16:1 mux per data bit, 15 2:1 muxes, 30 transistors in the transmission-gate form, under a 4-bit select. The published contract is the per-engine rate and the buffer geometry, not the switch: the crossbar's radix, port count, arbitration and wire counts are not published, so no total across the 128 outputs is claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (SBUF as the DMA landing zone; the two HBM stacks)** — The DMA engines' destination is the SBUF — the 6T SRAM array decomposed in the first block: 24 MiB is 201,326,592 bits, 1,207,959,552 cell transistors, and one 192 KiB partition is 1,572,864 bits, 9,437,184 cell transistors. Their source is the HBM, which is DRAM, not SRAM: its leaf cell is one transistor plus one capacitor (1T1C) per bit, not a 6T cell. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 32 GiB is 274,877,906,944 bits, so the two HBM stacks hold 274,877,906,944 1T1C cells, one transistor each. The HBM's internal organisation — channel count, bank count, bank-group structure — is not published by AWS, and the two stacks' split of the 820 GB/s is not published either. Standard construction for the SBUF side; the HBM side is the DRAM cell form, not the SRAM form.
- **Comparator (DMA buffer contiguity and partition-boundary checks)** — A DMA buffer must be contiguous in the address map, and a tensor's partitions must start at a legal boundary — both are compares: the buffer's start and length against the partition boundary, and the tensor's start partition against the legal set. At gate level a compare is one XNOR2 gate (about 10–12 transistors) per compared bit plus a log2(N)-level AND tree — the same form as the semaphore and alignment compares in the first block. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the start-partition check compares a 7-bit partition index, so 7 XNOR2 gates plus a 3-level AND tree per check. The compare implementation, the boundary-check widths and any error signalling are not published. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the six CC cores)** — The six CC cores are named here as controllers with unpublished internals, and nothing inside them is decomposed: AWS publishes no CC-core internals — no queue depths, no arbitration, no reduction datapath — so no gate form, no transistor count and no internal primitive is asserted for them. The collective layer is documented at the level of counts and purpose — six CC cores for collective communication — and this section does not invent the rest.
- **SerDes (NeuronLink-v2 links)** — A SerDes is a serializer, a deserializer and clock recovery: the serializer is a shift register — one flip-flop per bit of the parallel word plus a mux tree to select the next bit out — so an N-bit parallel word is N flip-flops, about 20–28 transistors each, plus N-1 2:1 muxes per lane; the deserializer is the mirror image; the clock-data recovery loop is a phase detector (XOR gates), a loop filter (a counter) and a voltage-controlled oscillator, and the equalizer is a feed-forward adder tree plus a decision-feedback adder and comparator. The per-link rate is not published by AWS — secondary estimates range from 192 GiB/s to about 800 GB/s per chip — so no per-link total is claimed. The SerDes lane count per link, the encoding, the signalling rate and the per-link clocking are not published. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (the chip-to-chip clock-domain crossing)** — Two chips are two clock domains, so the NeuronLink-v2 link is a clock-domain crossing by construction, and the standard form is a two-flop synchronizer per bit — two master-slave D flip-flops, about 40–56 transistors per bit. AWS publishes no synchronizer structure, no retiming scheme and no link latency, and this decomposition invents none of them: no synchronizer total is claimed, since the bit width crossing the link is unpublished. Standard construction, conditionally.
- **Credit counter — no published flow control** — Zero gates. There is no published hardware flow control for NeuronLink-v2: no credit counters, no backpressure scheme and no published buffer accounting between chips. Flow control, as far as the published material goes, is the compiler's scheduling — the collectives are scheduled to overlap compute rather than serialise behind it. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence.
- **Compression engine (inline compression/decompression on the DMA path)** — The device DMA bandwidth is rated at 1 TB/s with inline memory compression/decompression, so there is a compression engine on the DMA path, between the HBM and the SBUF — but its algorithm, its compression ratio, its datapath width and whether it sits per DMA engine or shared across the device are not published. No gate form is asserted for it: a compressor's gates depend entirely on the unpublished algorithm, so the engine is named for its published function only.
- **Adder tree — none in the fabric** — Zero gates. There is no adder tree anywhere in the movement fabric: the all-reduce's adds are done by the receiving core's own engines — the same Vector Engine that does layer norms does the all-reduce's adds — not by the fabric. The fabric moves gradients and activations; the engines add them. The Vector Engine's adder tree is decomposed in the first block. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence.
- **Pipeline registers (DMA data-path staging)** — A DMA transfer stages data between two memories at different rates — 27 GiB/s per engine against 820 GB/s of shared HBM — so the data path must be latched as it crosses the HBM interface, the compression engine and the SBUF interface. At gate level each stage is a register of one master-slave D flip-flop per bit (about 20–28 transistors each). The stage count, the latch widths and the staging depth are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Switch arbiter (HBM arbitration among 32 DMA engines — scheme unpublished)** — Thirty-two DMA engines share one 820 GiB/s HBM pool, so the HBM interface must arbitrate among engines that want the same stack in the same cycle. An arbiter is a priority encoder or a round-robin selector: a fixed-priority arbiter is a comparator network plus an encoder tree, a round-robin arbiter adds a rotating priority register of log2(N) flip-flops. AWS publishes no arbitration scheme, no priority rule, no fairness guarantee and no per-engine queue depth for the DMA engines, so neither standard form is asserted and no gate total is claimed. Any arbitration policy named here would be invention, so none is. Standard construction, conditionally.

Honesty: AWS publishes the fabric geometry and none of its circuits: 16 DMA engines per NeuronCore, each processing one transfer at a time at a peak of 27 GiB/s; the 128x512 FP32 load example as 16 transfers of 8 DMA buffers each; the 4 KiB free-dimension and ideally-128 partition-dimension rule; 2 HBM stacks with 32 GiB and 820 GB/s; 1 TB/s DMA bandwidth with inline memory compression/decompression; 6 CC cores; 2 NeuronLink-v2 links on Inferentia2 and 4 on Trainium; 16 Trainium chips per Trn1 instance — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — DMA engine internals, scatter-gather list depths, CC-core internals, NeuronLink lane counts and signalling rate, HBM arbitration, the compression engine's algorithm — AWS publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no hardware flow control published for NeuronLink-v2, and there is no adder tree anywhere in the fabric, because the all-reduce's adds are done by the receiving core's Vector Engine, not by the movement fabric.

### Groq LPU

#### Inside the signature block: The TSP streaming datapath — MXM, VXM and SXM chained as one spatial pipeline

**Inside it.** The chip is organised as vertical functional slices — MEM, MXM, VXM, SXM and ICU — each slice a stack of 20 tiles, each tile one 16-lane superlane, so a full slice is a 320-lane SIMD unit and the smallest vector is 16 elements. Instructions flow northward up a slice one tile per cycle while data flows east and west on stream registers, so an instruction and its operands meet at a precise time and place the compiler chose in advance. There are no arbiters, no caches, no branch predictors and no general-purpose register file: streams are the only operand transport, and each stream element is 1 byte, with wider types built from several streams. The MXM is four independent 320x320 multiply-accumulate planes — 409,600 MACCs — each plane built from twenty 16x16 supercells that produce a partial sum each cycle and pass it to the adjacent tile. Weights are installed into the planes from streams with Load Weights and Install Weights instructions; with weights in place, every cycle each plane produces a new 320-element dot product from streaming activations, accumulated in int32 or fp32 with a single rounding step at the end, and fp16 uses two byte-planes in tandem. The VXM is 5,120 vector ALUs — 16 per lane arranged as a 4x4 mesh per superlane — doing pointwise arithmetic, requantisation and activations such as ReLU, TanH, Exp and RSqrt, with saturating and modulo variants instead of condition codes; two or more ALUs in a lane can be chained so intermediate results never touch memory. The SXM is the reshaping fabric: paired north and south lane shifters with a select, a permuter applying a programmed bijection over the 320 lanes, a distributor remapping the 16 lanes inside a superlane including zero-fill for padding, a 16x16 transposer, rotate for 3x3 and 4x4 blocks, and deskew. A layer is a chain — MEM reads activations onto streams, the MXM multiplies, the VXM requantises and activates, the SXM reshapes, MEM writes the result — and the ICU, under 3 percent of the die, keeps the 144 independent instruction queues fed with 640-byte Ifetch fills while Sync and Notify provide the one chip-wide barrier at program start. Groq publishes no MXM supercell internals beyond the 16x16 geometry, no VXM ALU bit-widths beyond the published data types, and no SXM permuter or distributor table sizes, so this is the datapath's contract, not its circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one 320x320 int8 matmul tile through the streaming datapath.**
1. **Weights are staged in MEM, laid out toward the middle of the chip.** The compiler has placed the layer's weight tile in the 88 MEM slices, choosing slices close to the MXM so the transit from memory slice to matrix plane is short — the paper's roofline discussion says the measured results come from weights laid out toward the middle of the chip for exactly this reason. The weights sit in SRAM as 16-byte words, one byte per lane, waiting to be streamed.
2. **Load Weights and Install Weights park all 409,600 weights in under 40 cycles.** The MXM's sequencer issues LW and IW: 16 streams of 16 bytes install 256 8-bit weights into each supercell every cycle, and with all 32 streams in each direction feeding both MXM hemispheres at once, all four 320x320 planes are loaded in 20 cycles by arithmetic — inside the paper's under-40-cycles bound including SRAM and network transit delay. The weights now sit in the planes, one per MACC, and will not move again until the next tile.
3. **Activations stream in from MEM and meet the instruction in flight.** A MEM Read puts the activation vector onto a stream, 320 bytes wide, flowing east or west toward the MXM. Because instructions propagate northward one tile per cycle while the stream flows horizontally, successive 16-element superlanes of the vector lag by one cycle each — the spatial stagger — so the activation superlane and the MXM instruction arrive at each tile in the same cycle, exactly as the compiler scheduled.
4. **The MXM produces a new 320-element dot product every cycle.** Each of the four planes multiplies its installed 320x320 weight tile by the arriving activation vector and accumulates the partial sums down its supercell columns, producing one 320-element int32 or fp32 result vector per cycle with a single rounding step at the end. If the contraction is deeper than one tile, the ACC instruction accumulates the plane's output across passes; the result never leaves the streaming datapath.
5. **The result chains straight into the VXM — no MEM round-trip.** The MXM's output stream flows on to the VXM, whose 16 ALUs per lane requantise the int32 result back to int8 and apply the activation function — ReLU, say — in one chained pass, with the ALUs' saturating variants handling overflow instead of flags. Nothing is written to SRAM between the matmul and the activation: the chain is the whole point of the spatial pipeline.
6. **The result is written back, and the next tile is already installing.** The finished activation vector is written back to MEM by a Write instruction, or reshaped through the SXM — transposed, permuted or shifted — on its way to the next layer's MXM. While the VXM drains this tile, the next tile's weights are already installing into the MXM planes, so the array never waits for its operands; the only idle time is the pipeline fill and drain at the start and end of a layer, which the compiler shrinks by interleaving banks so a new pipeline can start before the old one has finished writing.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves two walls at once: the weight re-fetch wall — weights are installed once into the MXM planes and then every cycle each plane produces a new 320-element dot product from activations streaming past, so no operand is ever fetched per multiply; and the intermediate round-trip wall — chaining slices means an MXM result flows straight into the VXM for requantisation and activation without a write to SRAM and a read back. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the 320-wide tile ceiling — a matmul must fill a 320x320 plane, so channel depths that are not multiples of 320 under-use the array, and the paper's own ResNet50 work shows 256-deep channels split across passes with idle MACCs; the stagger wall — the compiler must solve a two-dimensional schedule in time and space, with every stream arriving at the exact cycle its instruction reaches the right tile, so a scheduling mistake is a wrong result rather than a stall; and the VXM depth wall — when the vector-operation chain after a matmul is too deep, the VXM ALUs cannot stream at full bandwidth and the MXM waits, a throughput delay the paper says is short but real.

**Governing numbers.** Four independent 320x320 MACC planes = 409,600 MACCs; 320x320 = 102,400 MACCs per plane; 820 TeraOps/s peak at 1 GHz (409,600 x 2 ops x 1 GHz = 819.2 TeraOps/s by arithmetic); Groq quotes 750 INT8 TOPS and 188 FP16 TFLOPS at 900 MHz (vendor figures — the INT8 figure is 1.7 percent above the 737 TOPS the published MACC count and clock multiply to, and the FP16 figure matches one-op-per-MAC counting, 184 TFLOPS, rather than two, 369 TFLOPS); 5,120 vector ALUs = 320 lanes x 16 ALUs per lane; 20-stage vector pipeline per slice, 16 lanes per tile (one superlane), 320-lane maximum vector, 16-lane minimum vector; 144 independent instruction queues, one or more instructions issued per cycle each; ICU under 3 percent of die area; chip-wide barrier 35 cycles; Ifetch fills a queue with 640 bytes; 64 logical streams per lane, 32 Eastward and 32 Westward; one stream element is 1 byte, int16 takes 2 streams, int32 and fp32 take 4; all 409,600 weights install into the MXM planes in under 40 cycles (20 cycles by arithmetic: 4 planes x 20 supercells x 256 weights per cycle); MXM accumulates in int32 or fp32 with a single rounding step at the end; SXM does at most four simultaneous 16x16 transposes (two instances, two transpose instructions each); ResNet50 batch-1: 20.4K images per second, 49 us per image (1/20,400 s = 49.02 us); die 25x29 mm, 14 nm, 900 MHz nominal, 26.8B transistors, 30K deep learning ops per second per transistor.

**Primary source.** Abts et al., Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, ISCA 2020 — functional slicing, slice pipelines and superlanes, instruction queues and streams, MXM planes and supercells, weight install, VXM ALU mesh and chaining, SXM transpose/permute/distributor, ICU area and barrier, staggered execution, ResNet50 results, die and transistor numbers (read live, full paper); Groq, Groq Language Processing Unit (LPU) Architecture, ALCF AI Testbed workshop deck, June 2024 — 750 INT8 TOPS, 188 FP16 TFLOPS, 5,120 vector ALUs, 320x320 fused dot product, MXM numeric modes.

#### Inside the signature block: The SRAM-only memory system and the deterministic chip-to-chip fabric — 220 MiB of flat SRAM and software-scheduled RealScale links

**Inside it.** There is no DRAM and no HBM anywhere in the design: the whole memory system is 220 MiB of on-chip SRAM in 88 MEM slices, 44 per hemisphere, each slice 20 tiles of 8,192 16-byte words — 2.5 MiB per slice — with each byte of a word mapped to one lane. Each MEM slice is a pseudo-dual-port SRAM with two banks, so the compiler can read operands from one bank and write results to the other in the same cycle, and the bank bit is exposed in the ISA so the compiler manages the banks explicitly: 176-way memory concurrency in total. The address space is a flat, partitioned global address space laid out uniformly across the 88 slices, with direct addressing in the Read and Write instructions and stream-indirect addressing for gather and scatter, where the address map itself arrives on a stream. A read from a MEM slice creates a 320-byte stream and a write terminates one, and the compiler places each tensor's concurrent stream operands in separate slices so streams pick up operands as they propagate toward the compute slices. Off-chip, the same determinism extends across chips through sixteen x4 C2C links: a Send instruction pushes a whole 320-byte vector onto a link as one flit, and a Receive emplaces it directly into the destination chip's MEM at a compiler-chosen address — no packet headers, no routing tables, no queues, no virtual channels and no backpressure, with 97.5 percent encoding efficiency. Each TSP is both endpoint and router, and the compiler schedules every vector onto a specific link at a specific cycle, using the chip's own SRAM as the intermediate buffer at each hop so tensors are pushed to the chip that will consume them and the request leg of a remote transaction disappears. Synchrony across independent chip clocks is maintained by hardware aligned counters — an 8-bit counter with a sub-256-cycle epoch, exchanged continuously between peers so each link's latency can be measured — plus DESKEW instructions that align execution to epoch boundaries and RUNTIME_DESKEW instructions that re-align clock drift mid-program; measured intra-node link latency is about 216 to 217 cycles. The topology is a software-scheduled Dragonfly: 7 local links fully connect the 8 TSPs of a 4U node, 4 global links per TSP build 32-port virtual routers, 264 TSPs hold 56 GiB of global SRAM, a rack holds 72 TSPs, and the largest configuration is 10,440 TSPs with a 5-hop diameter and more than 2 TB of global memory reachable in under 3 microseconds. Groq publishes no SRAM bank organisation beyond the slice, tile and bank counts, no C2C SerDes internals beyond the signalling rate and cabling, and no per-slice queue depths, so this is the fabric's contract, not its circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one 320-byte activation vector from a source chip's MEM to a destination chip's MEM.**
1. **The compiler schedules the Send at a known cycle.** The model has been partitioned across chips, so this layer's activation vector lives on chip A and the next layer runs on chip B. The compiler knows the exact cycle the vector will be ready and the exact cycle chip B must consume it, and it writes a Send instruction into chip A's C2C queue and a matching Receive into chip B's — no runtime discovery, no handshake, no request leg.
2. **Source MEM reads the 320-byte vector onto a stream.** At the scheduled cycle, a MEM Read on chip A pulls the vector out of its slice — one 320-byte stream, one byte per lane — and it flows east or west across the chip toward the C2C module at the chip edge, one stream-register hop per cycle, exactly like any other operand on its way to a compute slice.
3. **Send pushes the vector onto a C2C link as one flit.** The C2C module takes the 320-byte vector and transmits it whole on one of the sixteen x4 links — the vector is the flow-control unit, so there is no packetisation, no header and no routing lookup; the link is simply reserved for that vector at that cycle. At 30 Gbps per lane the four lanes carry 120 Gbps, and the link normally operates at 25 Gbps per lane for 100 Gbps.
4. **The vector crosses the link; the clocks do not match.** The two chips have independent clocks — the links are plesiochronous — so the vector arrives at chip B with a latency the compiler already measured and booked: about 216 to 217 cycles inside a node, characterised over 100,000 iterations. The SXM's deskew instruction exists for exactly this: aligning data that arrives across plesiochronous links.
5. **Receive emplaces the vector straight into destination MEM.** Chip B's C2C module receives the vector and writes it directly into chip B's SRAM at the address the compiler chose when it scheduled the transfer — the vector never passes through a queue, a buffer pool or a cache, because there is none. It is now an ordinary tensor in chip B's flat address space, indistinguishable from one computed locally.
6. **Chip B consumes it at the exact scheduled cycle, in lock-step.** Because both chips aligned to the same hardware-aligned-counter epoch with DESKEW at program start, and re-align drift with RUNTIME_DESKEW during execution, chip B's next layer reads the vector at the cycle the compiler promised. If the vector must travel further, the intermediate TSP forwards it hop by hop, buffering it in its own SRAM at each stop — virtual cut-through with the SRAM as the buffer — for at most 5 hops across the whole 10,440-chip system, and the compiler knew every hop in advance.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves two walls at once: the DRAM wall — there is no DRAM or HBM anywhere in the design, so weights live in SRAM next to the compute and a token's forward pass never waits on an off-chip memory access; and the network non-determinism wall — with no arbiters, no queues, no virtual channels and no backpressure anywhere in the fabric, the arrival cycle of every vector is a compile-time number, so multi-chip latency is a value in a contract rather than a distribution. Creates three new bottlenecks instead: the capacity wall — a model must fit in 220 MiB per chip, so growing a model means adding chips and the per-chip SRAM is the hard ceiling on what one chip can hold; the global-bandwidth cliff — the Dragonfly gives about 50 GB/s of global bandwidth per TSP up to several hundred chips but only about 14 GB/s per TSP once the system grows beyond 264 TSPs, so the fabric, not the MXM, sets the scale-out ceiling; and the static-shape wall — software-scheduled networking only works because the traffic pattern is known at compile time from the static computation graph, so data-dependent communication and dynamic shapes cannot be scheduled and the compiler must know the whole conversation in advance.

**Governing numbers.** 220 MiB on-chip SRAM = 88 MEM slices x 2.5 MiB, 44 slices per hemisphere, 20 tiles per slice, 8,192 16-byte words per tile, 13-bit physical addressing; 220 MiB = 230,686,720 bytes, about 230 MB decimal; each MEM slice is pseudo-dual-port with 2 banks, 88 x 2 = 176-way memory concurrency; a read from one MEM slice creates a 320-byte stream and a write terminates one; SRAM bandwidth 55 TiB/s at 1 GHz per the paper's equation 2 (direct multiplication of its factors gives 56,320 bytes per cycle, 56.32 TB/s); stream-register bandwidth 20 TiB/s at 1 GHz per the paper's equation 1 (20,480 bytes per cycle, 20.48 TB/s); Groq quotes 80 TB/s on-die memory bandwidth (vendor figure — it does not reproduce from either paper equation, which give 56.32 TB/s SRAM and 20.48 TB/s stream bandwidth); C2C: 16 links x 4 lanes at 30 Gbps = 3.84 Tb/s = 480 GB/s total, 240 GB/s per direction; standard operating rate 25 Gbps per lane, 100 Gbps per link, 400 GB/s total; one 320-byte vector is the flow-control unit (flit), 97.5 percent encoding efficiency (320/328 bytes); hardware aligned counter (HAC) epoch under 256 cycles (252 cycles); measured intra-node C2C link latency mean about 216-217 cycles over 100K iterations (min 209, max 228, standard deviation about 2.6-2.9); at 900 MHz, 217 cycles is about 241 ns; 7 local links and 4 global links per TSP; node is 8 TSPs in a 4U chassis; 264 TSPs hold 56 GiB of global SRAM (264 x 220 MiB = 56.7 GiB); rack is 72 TSPs; largest configuration 10,440 TSPs, 5-hop diameter, more than 2 TB of global memory reachable in under 3 us end-to-end latency; global bandwidth about 50 GB/s per TSP up to several hundred TSPs, about 14 GB/s per TSP beyond 264; host interface PCIe Gen4 x16.

**Primary source.** Abts et al., Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, ISCA 2020 — MEM slice geometry and pseudo-dual-port SRAM, bandwidth equations, C2C links and PCIe host interface, ECC (read live, full paper); Abts et al., A Software-defined Tensor Streaming Multiprocessor for Large-scale Machine Learning, ISCA 2022 — Dragonfly topology and packaging hierarchy, C2C operating rate and cabling, software-scheduled networking, HAC and DESKEW synchronisation, measured link latency, bandwidth profile, global-memory latency (read live, full paper); Groq, Groq Language Processing Unit (LPU) Architecture, ALCF AI Testbed workshop deck, June 2024 — 230 MB SRAM, 80 TB/s on-die bandwidth, 480 GB/s networking, 88 MEM slices with 8192 addresses, software-scheduled network and dragonfly slides.

#### Down to the gates: The TSP streaming datapath — MXM, VXM and SXM chained as one spatial pipeline

Groq publishes no gate-level structure for the TSP — the ISCA 2020 and ISCA 2022 papers and the ALCF deck describe the datapath's contract (four 320x320 MXM planes of 16x16 supercells, 5,120 vector ALUs, the SXM's shifters, permuter, distributor and transposer, the 144 instruction queues and the 640-byte Ifetch fill, the 35-cycle barrier, the 16-bit NOP repeat count) and stop there. The one chip-level transistor figure the papers do publish frames this whole section: "yields a peak performance of 820 TeraOps/sec from 26.8B transistors on-chip — 30K deep learning Ops/sec/transistor." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §VII), spent on "(1) fixed or floating-point ALUs for arithmetic, and (2) storage and communicating data among the available ALUs." What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about Groq's circuits.

- **Multiplier array (the MXM supercell MACCs)** — A multiply-accumulate unit is a multiplier plus an accumulator adder: the multiplier is an AND-gate partial-product array feeding a full-adder compressor tree and one final carry-propagate adder, and the accumulator is a full-adder chain over the partial sum. Arithmetic from the published geometry, in the standard int8 array-multiplier form: one 8x8 multiplier is 64 AND2 gates (64 x 6 = 384 transistors) plus 56 full adders in the array (56 x 28 = 1,568 transistors) plus a 16-bit final adder (16 x 28 = 448 transistors), about 2,400 transistors per multiplier; across the four planes that is 409,600 x 2,400 = 983,040,000 transistors for the multipliers alone, and the int32 accumulate adder adds 32 full adders per MACC (32 x 28 = 896 transistors), 409,600 x 896 = 367,001,600 transistors. The fp16 case is a different multiplier — an 11-bit mantissa multiplier plus exponent adder and normalisation logic — and no count is claimed for it. The multiplier count and layout inside one 16x16 supercell are not published, so the per-MACC shape above is the standard construction, not Groq's netlist. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree (MXM partial-sum accumulation)** — The accumulation tree narrows each output element's 320 products to one dot product: a binary tree of adders, one per pair merged, log2(320) = 9 levels deep for 320 inputs. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one output element's tree is 319 int32 adders, 319 x 32 full adders = 10,208 full adders, about 285,824 transistors in ripple-carry form, with a single rounding step at the end — "with only a single rounding step at the end to convert to int32 or fp32 results." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.D). How the 320 output elements' trees are shared across the plane's 20 supercells is not published, so no plane total is claimed: a plane total needs the sharing Groq never gives. The adder-tree depth, the accumulation order and the accumulator register widths beyond the int32/fp32 result types are not published. Standard construction.
- **Register file (the installed MXM weights)** — Each installed weight is one stored bit pattern held in place until the next tile: the two candidate storage forms are flip-flops or SRAM cells, and the paper does not say which. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 409,600 weights x 8 bits = 3,276,800 bits; as flip-flops that is 3,276,800 x 20-28 = 65,536,000-91,750,400 transistors; as 6T SRAM cells that is 3,276,800 x 6 = 19,660,800 cell transistors, plus the row decoder and sense amplifiers of the primer's SRAM bank form. The install path is streams: "It requires 16 streams each with 16 bytes to install 256 8-bit weights (IW) in each supercell on every cycle." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.D). The weight registers' circuit form — SRAM cells or flip-flops — is not published, so neither form is asserted. Standard construction.
- **Accumulator registers (the MXM output accumulators)** — Each accumulator is a register plus its adder: the int32 or fp32 output stream's accumulator holds the running sum in flip-flops and adds each new plane output into it with a full-adder chain. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 4 planes x 320 output elements = 1,280 accumulator registers, each 32 bits, so 1,280 x 32 = 40,960 register bits; as D flip-flops that is 40,960 x 20-28 = 819,200-1,146,880 transistors, plus one 32-bit adder per accumulator (32 full adders, about 896 transistors each). The accumulator register implementation and the ACC instruction's accumulation timing are not published. Standard construction.
- **Stream registers (the chip-wide streaming register file)** — A stream register is one 8-bit pipeline register: 8 master-slave D flip-flops, about 160-224 transistors, holding one byte of a stream for one cycle — one hop. Arithmetic from the published counts, as logical-stream arithmetic: 64 streams per lane x 320 lanes = 20,480 logical stream registers, 20,480 x 8 = 163,840 bits, as flip-flops 163,840 x 20-28 = 3,276,800-4,587,520 transistors. The physical register count and how the file is banked are not published, so the 20,480 figure is the logical stream count, not a claimed netlist total. The transit delay is "the distance (in cycles) between SRj and SRi" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III) — one register, one cycle, one hop. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the 144 instruction queues)** — An instruction queue is a FIFO: storage (one flip-flop per bit), a write pointer counter and a read pointer counter (each log2(depth) flip-flops plus an incrementer of the same number of full adders), and full/empty comparators (an equality compare of the two pointers). Arithmetic from the published geometry, as a minimum: each queue holds at least one 640-byte Ifetch fill, so 144 queues x 640 bytes = 92,160 bytes = 737,280 bits minimum, as flip-flops 737,280 x 20-28 = 14,745,600-20,643,840 transistors minimum. The queue depth beyond the 640-byte fill and the per-queue issue width are not published, so the pointer width and the true depth have no claimed total — a FIFO gate total needs a depth Groq never gives. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the ICU dispatch and staggered execution)** — The ICU is a state machine built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network, sequencing one instruction per queue per cycle and staggering it northward one tile per cycle across the slice's 20 tiles. Each instruction carries temporal parameters — "dfunc functional delay" and "dskew instruction-operand skew" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III) — so the stagger is a 20-stage pipeline of instruction registers: one instruction register per tile, one flip-flop per instruction bit per stage. The instruction width is not published, so no per-stage bit count and no sequencer total is claimed. The sequencer's state count and decode depth are not published. The ICU's smallness is published: the instruction control unit accounts for "less the 3% of the area." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §II). Standard construction.
- **Comparator (the Sync/Notify barrier)** — The barrier is an AND-reduction over the parked queues' Sync state plus the notifier's Notify: one AND gate per pair of inputs merged, log2(143) = 8 levels deep for 143 parked queues. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 143 inputs need 142 AND2 gates, 142 x 6 = 852 transistors for the reduction tree, plus one Sync-state flip-flop per queue (144 x 20-28 = 2,880-4,032 transistors). The barrier completes in 35 cycles: "A chip-wide barrier synchronization can be accomplished in 35 clock cycles, from the time the Notify is issued to the time the Sync is satisfied and retired to allow subsequent instructions to flow." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.A). The AND-reduction construction is the standard one for a barrier, labelled as such; the reduction-tree depth and fan-in are not published. Standard construction.
- **Counter (the NOP repeat count and logical time)** — A NOP wait is a 16-bit down-counter: 16 D flip-flops holding the count plus a 16-bit decrementer of 16 full adders, with a zero-detect comparator (16 XNOR gates feeding an AND tree) ending the wait. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one counter is 16 x 20-28 = 320-448 transistors of flip-flops plus 16 x 28 = 448 transistors of incrementer, 768-896 transistors; across the 144 instruction queues that is 144 x 768-896 = 110,592-129,024 transistors. "A NOP has a repeat count 16-bit field which allows 1 NOP to wait from 1 ns up to 65 us for a 1GHz clock." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.A). The counter's implementation and the clock-gating granularity are not published — the NOP "is implemented in the ICU's tile and common to all functional slices" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.A), and the slice can "turn off the clock enables when NOP-ing for anything longer than a few cycles" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.A). Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (the VXM 4x4 ALU mesh)** — Each vector ALU is an adder plus a multiplier plus logic: a 32-bit adder is 32 full adders, and a 32-bit fixed-point multiplier is an AND-gate partial-product array feeding a full-adder compressor tree and one final adder. Arithmetic from the published geometry, in the standard fixed-point array form: one 32x32 multiplier is 1,024 AND2 gates (1,024 x 6 = 6,144 transistors) plus 992 full adders in the array (992 x 28 = 27,776 transistors); across the mesh that is 5,120 x 1,024 = 5,242,880 AND gates, 31,457,280 transistors of partial products, and 5,120 x 27,776 = 142,213,120 transistors of adder array. The 32-bit adder adds 32 x 28 = 896 transistors per ALU, 5,120 x 896 = 4,587,520 transistors across the mesh. The fp32 case is a different multiplier — a 24-bit mantissa multiplier plus exponent adder and normalisation — and no count is claimed for it. The ALUs "do not produce condition codes or status flags" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.C); the saturating and modulo variants are a compare plus a select mux on the adder's output, of the standard form below. The ALU bit-widths beyond the published data types and the mesh's internal routing are not published. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (VXM ALU chaining)** — Chaining is a mux per ALU input: a 2:1 transmission-gate mux, 2 transistors per input leg, 4 transistors per mux per bit, selecting between the stream register and the previous ALU's output. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one 32-bit chained input is 32 muxes, 32 x 4 = 128 transistors. "The TSP supports chaining together two or more vector ALUs within each lane, allowing multiple ALU operations to be performed without committing the intermediate results to main memory, saving a write and subsequent read of each intermediate result." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.C). The chaining mux radix, the bypass timing and the number of chainable stages are not published, so no per-lane mux total is claimed — a chaining total needs the stage count Groq never gives. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (the SXM lane-shifter select)** — The lane-shifter select is a 3-way mux per lane: north-shifted, south-shifted, or unshifted, built as two 2:1 transmission-gate muxes per bit, 8 transistors per bit. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one byte-wide lane select is 8 bits x 8 = 64 transistors; across the 320 lanes that is 320 x 64 = 20,480 transistors for the select muxes. "The lane-shifters are usually allocated in pairs since we typically shift a vector up or down and select which elements we want from either (i) North-shifted, (ii) South-shifted, or (iii) unshifted data elements" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.E). The shift amounts, the shifter implementation and the select timing are not published. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (the SXM permuter)** — A permuter is a crossbar: one mux tree per output lane, each tree selecting among all 320 input lanes. Arithmetic from the published geometry, in the standard full-crossbar form: one 320:1 mux tree is 319 2:1 muxes, so 320 outputs need 320 x 319 = 102,080 2:1 muxes per bit; byte-wide that is 102,080 x 8 = 816,640 muxes, 816,640 x 4 = 3,266,560 transistors in the transmission-gate form. The programmed bijection is held in a select table: 320 outputs x 9 select bits (log2 320 = 8.32, so 9 bits) = 2,880 bits, as flip-flops 2,880 x 20-28 = 57,600-80,640 transistors. "the SXM provides a permute instruction which employs a programmed bijection to remap the 320 lanes on a set of similarly indexed streams, one per superlane." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.E). A multistage (Benes-style) realisation would use fewer muxes than the full crossbar, so the 3,266,560-transistor figure is the full-crossbar standard form, not Groq's implementation; the permutation table's size, storage form and select-line fan-out are not published. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (the SXM distributor)** — The distributor is a mux tree per output element plus a zero-fill gate: each of the 16 outputs selects among the 16 lanes of its superlane, and any output can be forced to zero. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one 16:1 mux tree is 15 2:1 muxes, so one distributor is 16 outputs x 15 = 240 muxes per bit, byte-wide 240 x 8 = 1,920 muxes; across the 8 distributors (4 per hemisphere x 2 hemispheres) that is 8 x 1,920 = 15,360 muxes, 15,360 x 4 = 61,440 transistors in the transmission-gate form. Zero-fill is one AND gate per bit: 8 distributors x 16 outputs x 8 bits = 1,024 AND2 gates, 1,024 x 6 = 6,144 transistors. The mapping table is 16 outputs x 4 select bits = 64 bits per distributor, 8 x 64 = 512 bits, as flip-flops 512 x 20-28 = 10,240-14,336 transistors. "The distributor slice within the SXM is used to arbitrarily remap the 16 lanes within each superlane. As streams pass through the distributor, they can be remapped at full bandwidth, or zero-fill any or all of the 16 elements." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.E). The mapping table's size and storage form are not published. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (the SXM transposer)** — A transposer is storage plus a read-pattern change: 16 streams of 16 elements are written in row order and read in column order, so the exchange is the addressing, not gates. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one 16x16 transpose holds 256 bytes = 2,048 bits; as flip-flops that is 2,048 x 20-28 = 40,960-57,344 transistors per transposer, as 6T SRAM cells 2,048 x 6 = 12,288 cell transistors; across the 4 transposers (2 per hemisphere x 2 hemispheres, "yielding a maximum of four (4) simultaneous transpose 16x16 operations." — verified, Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.E) that is 8,192 bits, 163,840-229,376 transistors as flip-flops or 49,152 cell transistors as SRAM. "A transpose operation takes 16 incoming streams and produces 16 output streams with the rows and columns exchanged." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.E). The transposer's internal storage — registers or SRAM — is not published, so neither form is asserted. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (the SXM rotate)** — A barrel shifter is log2(n) stages of 2:1 muxes, each stage shifting by a power of two, so all rotations of the block appear at once. Arithmetic from the published geometry: for n=4, 2 stages x 4 muxes per bit = 8 2:1 muxes per bit; byte-wide 8 x 8 = 64 muxes, 64 x 4 = 256 transistors per rotate unit in the transmission-gate form. Rotate generates every rotation of a small block at once: the ISA table defines Rotate as rotating n x n input data to generate n-squared output streams with all possible rotations, for n=3 or n=4 (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III, instruction table). The number of rotate units and the rotate latency are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: Groq publishes the datapath geometry and none of its circuits: four 320x320 MXM planes, twenty 16x16 supercells per plane, 256 weights installed per supercell per cycle, 5,120 vector ALUs, 64 streams per lane, 144 instruction queues, the 640-byte Ifetch fill, the 35-cycle barrier, the 16-bit NOP repeat count, the four simultaneous 16x16 transposes, the 4 distributors and 2 transposers per hemisphere, 820 TeraOps/sec from 26.8B transistors at 1 GHz in 14nm — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — supercell multiplier layout, VXM ALU bit-widths, permuter and distributor table sizes, instruction-queue depths, the shifter select timing — Groq publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no general-purpose register file and no arbiter anywhere in the datapath, because streams are the only operand transport and the compiler schedules every interception.

#### Down to the gates: The SRAM-only memory system and the deterministic chip-to-chip fabric — 220 MiB of flat SRAM and software-scheduled RealScale links

Groq publishes no gate-level structure for the memory system or the fabric either — the two ISCA papers describe the contract (88 slices of 2.5 MiB, 8,192 addresses per slice, 16 x4 links at 30 Gbps, the 320-byte flit at 97.5 percent encoding efficiency, the 252-cycle HAC epoch, the DESKEW instructions, the measured 216-217-cycle link latency) and stop there. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about Groq's circuits. Three primitives decompose to zero gates, and that absence is the design.

- **SRAM bank (the MEM slice pseudo-dual-port SRAM)** — A MEM slice is a 6T SRAM array: one 6-transistor cell per bit, plus a row decoder (a NAND/NOR tree that turns the address into one wordline), column muxes (transmission gates, 2 transistors per 2:1 mux per bit) and sense amplifiers (about 6-8 transistors per bitline) — the primer bottom layer's 6T cell. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 220 MiB is 230,686,720 bytes = 1,845,493,760 bits, so 1,845,493,760 6T cells, 11,072,962,560 cell transistors across the chip; one 2.5 MiB slice is 20,971,520 bits, 125,829,120 cell transistors, and 88 slices x 125,829,120 = 11,072,962,560, consistent. "Each MEM slice contains pseudo-dual-port SRAMs that are capable of servicing a pair of read and write requests simultaneously assuming they are not targeting the same bank." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.B), with "up to 176-way memory concurrency — 88 slices each with 2 banks" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.B). How each bank is organised into rows, columns and sense amplifiers, and the bank line widths, are not published. Standard construction.
- **Address decoder (MEM slice row decode)** — The slice address is decoded by a pre-decoded NAND tree: the 13 address bits are pre-decoded into true and complement lines, and one NAND tree per wordline combines one line from each bit group to raise exactly one of the 8,192 wordlines. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 8,192 addresses per slice is a 13-bit address (2^13 = 8,192), so the slice has 8,192 wordlines. Reads and writes use direct addressing, "since the address is fully specified in the instruction itself" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.B), while gather and scatter use stream-indirect addressing, where "the physical address comes from the stream value, providing a layer of indirection in the memory referencing." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III.B) — the indirect path adds a 13-bit 2:1 mux selecting between the instruction address and the stream value, 13 x 4 = 52 transistors per slice in the transmission-gate form. The decoder's structure — row decoder, column muxes, pre-decode — is not published, so no decoder gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (the bank select)** — The bank select is a 2:1 mux per data bit steering the vector to one bank or the other: a transmission-gate mux, 2 transistors per input leg, 4 transistors per mux per bit. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one 320-byte vector is 2,560 bits, so a full-width bank-select mux is 2,560 x 4 = 10,240 transistors per slice; across the 88 slices that is 88 x 10,240 = 901,120 transistors. The transpose path uses exactly this: "we take advantage the pseudo-dual-ported SRAM for dual read/write access per slice with a read of inputs from one bank and a write of the results to the opposite bank of the SRAM." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §IV.A). The bank-select mux's radix, timing and conflict handling when both accesses target the same bank are not published. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the instruction-dispatch slices)** — An instruction-dispatch slice is the same 6T SRAM array as the data slices above: one 6-transistor cell per bit, plus a row decoder, column muxes and sense amplifiers — the primer bottom layer's 6T cell. "the compiler reserves several MEM slices to serve as 'instruction dispatch' slices where the machine-coded instructions are stored and supplied on streams to service Ifetch instructions on different functional slices where the instructions will eventually be executed." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §IV). How many slices are reserved for dispatch, and how the compiler lays program text across them, are not published, so no cell total is claimed for the dispatch slices — a dispatch total needs a slice count Groq never gives. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue — none in the memory system or fabric** — Zero gates. There is no queue anywhere on the data path: a read from a MEM slice creates a 320-byte stream and a write terminates one, and a vector in flight is held in stream registers, not in a buffer. The 2022 paper's flow-control section states the network has no packet headers, no routing tables, no queues, no virtual channels and no backpressure (Level-2 — verified, fact records). A vector is never stored in flight in a queue, so there is no store-and-forward, no head-of-line blocking and no queueing delay to decompose. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence.
- **Switch arbiter — none in the fabric** — Zero gates. There is no switch arbiter in the fabric: the compiler schedules every vector onto a specific link at a specific cycle, and "the hardware is disallowed from asserting back pressure which would disrupt deterministic operation of the network." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §2.3). Two vectors never contend for the same link in the same cycle because the compiler's schedule guarantees it in advance — the arbitration happens at compile time, in the scheduler, not in silicon at run time — and that absence is why multi-chip latency is a contract value rather than a distribution. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence.
- **Crossbar (the X-dimension stream mesh between slices)** — The mesh is muxes at every slice: a stream passing a slice either continues east or west, turns around, or exits into the slice, and each choice is a mux per bit on the stream's path. Arithmetic from the published geometry: a turn-around is a 2:1 transmission-gate mux per bit, 4 transistors per mux per bit, so one byte-wide stream's turn-around is 8 x 4 = 32 transistors. "the on-chip network is implemented as X-dim mesh and Y-dim mesh of tiles with X-Y dimension order routing. Each instruction specifies the first hop direction (East or West), so memory instruction semantics have both an address and a dataflow direction" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §I.B), and streams "can be logically 'turned around' (ie. reverse their direction of flow from East-to-West, or vice versa) at any slice." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §II.E). The mesh's per-tile switching radix and port counts are not published beyond this routing contract, so no per-slice mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **SerDes (the C2C links)** — A SerDes is a serializer, a deserializer and clock recovery: the serializer is a shift register — one flip-flop per bit of the parallel word plus a mux tree to select the next bit out — the deserializer is the mirror image, and the clock-data recovery loop is a phase detector (XOR gates), a loop filter (a counter) and a voltage-controlled oscillator. The parallel word is one flip-flop per bit, about 20-28 transistors each, so the serializer's gate form is one D flip-flop per parallel bit plus the output mux tree. "The first TSP implementation (Figure 5) has a total of sixteen (16) x4 links operating at 30 Gbps each for a total off-chip bandwidth of 16 x4 x30Gb/s x2 directions = 3.84 Tb/s of off-chip pin bandwidth" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §II), normally operated at 25 Gbps per lane, "with a combined bandwidth of 100 Gbps across the four lanes in a link." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §2.3). The parallel word width, the encoding, the equalisation, the clocking and the lane-bonding are not published, so no per-lane gate total is claimed; the clock-data recovery oscillator is analog and sits below the primer's digital floor. Standard construction.
- **Encoder (the flit encoding)** — The flit encoder is a small framing block: it appends the 8 overhead bytes to the 320-byte vector and presents the 328-byte flit to the link, in the standard form a counter sequencing the vector bytes plus a mux inserting the overhead bytes at their positions. Arithmetic from the published figures: "an encoding efficiency of 97.5% (320/328 bytes)" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, Fig. 11), so 328 - 320 = 8 bytes of overhead per flit. There are no packet headers to encode, because the flit carries no header at all — "a vector is the flow control unit (flit)." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §2.3). The encoder's logic and the 8 overhead bytes' contents are not published, so no encoder gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (the hardware aligned counter, HAC)** — The HAC is an 8-bit free-running counter: 8 D flip-flops holding the count plus an 8-bit incrementer of 8 full adders, with four of the 256 values reserved for special control codes. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one HAC is 8 x 20-28 = 160-224 transistors of flip-flops plus 8 x 28 = 224 transistors of incrementer, 384-448 transistors. "Each TSP maintains a free-running internal hardware aligned counter (HAC) with a low (< 256 cycle) overflow period." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §3.1), and "the period is the epoch length or 252 clock cycles. The HAC is an 8-bit counter, but 4 values are reserved for special control codes." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §3.1). The counters are "continuously (every 256 cycles) exchanged to maintain a global consensus time" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §3.1). The counter's exchange mechanism and the latency-measurement registers are not published. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (DESKEW and RUNTIME_DESKEW)** — DESKEW is a state machine built the standard way: state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network, pausing issue until the next epoch boundary. The boundary detect is an 8-bit equality comparator on the HAC: 8 XNOR gates (8 x 10-12 = 80-96 transistors) feeding a 7-gate AND tree (7 x 6 = 42 transistors), 122-138 transistors in the standard form. "When a functional unit executes a DESKEW, it will pause issuing subsequent instructions on that functional unit until the next time the HAC overflows or the epoch boundary." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §3.2). RUNTIME_DESKEW adds a stall counter loaded from its single delay parameter: "To reconcile the local vs global time, a RUNTIME_DESKEW instruction is provided in the ISA. The instruction takes a single parameter" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §3.3). The DESKEW controller's state and the stall counter's width are not published, so no controller total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (plesiochronous link alignment)** — Zero synchronizer gates. The chips do not share a clock — the links are plesiochronous — and the papers describe no two-flop synchronizer or phase aligner at any link: alignment is done by the HAC epoch and the DESKEW instructions, not by per-link synchronizer hardware. The ISA table gives "Deskew: Manage skew across plesiochronous links" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §III, instruction table), and the measured intra-node link latency of about 216-217 cycles is a booked compile-time value, not a synchronizer delay. The deskew logic's implementation is not published, so no deskew gate form is claimed either. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence.
- **Credit counter — none in the fabric** — Zero gates. There is no credit-based flow control in the fabric: "the hardware is disallowed from asserting back pressure which would disrupt deterministic operation of the network." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §2.3). The compiler schedules every vector onto a specific link at a specific cycle, so the transmitter never overflows and the receiver never underflows by construction — the schedule is the flow control, and there is no credit counter, no buffer-occupancy tracking and no throttle signal to decompose. The gate-level content of this primitive is its absence.
- **Pipeline registers (virtual cut-through staging in SRAM)** — No additional gates. A vector travelling more than one hop is staged in the intermediate chip's own SRAM — "a vector is the flow control unit (flit). Since the network path is fully deterministic, a tensor consisting of one or more vector flits can be scheduled using virtual cut through flow control since the receiving TSP can immediately begin sending vectors to the next-hop of the tensor's path." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §2.3) — so the staging is the MEM banks themselves, already decomposed as the SRAM bank above, and the in-flight vector is held in the stream registers decomposed in the datapath block. At the destination, a Receive emplaces the vector directly into the destination chip's MEM at the address the compiler chose, so the vector never passes through a queue or a buffer pool, because there is none. There are no separate pipeline registers to count here, and none are claimed — counting the SRAM and stream registers again would double-count.
- **XOR tree / ECC check (SECDED over SRAM and stream registers)** — The SECDED check is an XOR tree: each of the 9 check bits is the parity (XOR) of a subset of the 128 data bits, and the check side recomputes the same parities and compares them against the stored check bits. Arithmetic from the published geometry: one check bit is the XOR of about 64 data bits, about 63 XOR2 gates in a tree 6 levels deep (log2 64 = 6), so one encoder is about 9 x 63 = 567 XOR2 gates, 567 x 10-12 = 5,670-6,804 transistors; the check bits are generated only at the producer — "we take advantage of the producer-consumer nature of the stream programming model and generate ECC check bits only at the producer" (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §II.D) — which avoids replicating the XOR tree across the wide word. The check bits are stored alongside the words: "they are stored alongside the 128-bit memory word as 9-bit ECC, 137-bits in total. The ECC scheme implements SECDED (single-error correction with double-error detection) to allow us to tolerate a single-bit error in the memory word or anywhere along the streaming data path." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2020, §II.D). Stored ECC arithmetic: 230,686,720 bytes / 16 bytes per word = 14,417,920 words, x 9 check bits = 129,761,280 ECC bits, x 6 = 778,567,680 cell transistors; with the data cells the SRAM totals 11,851,530,240 cell transistors. Per slice: 20 tiles x 8,192 words = 163,840 words, x 9 = 1,474,560 ECC bits, 8,847,360 cell transistors. Corrected errors are recorded in a control and status register, whose width is not published. The XOR tree's depth and the check-bit generation timing are not published. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (source-based Dragonfly routing)** — Routing is a state machine built the standard way — state bits are master-slave D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each) and next-state logic is a NAND/NOR network — but the state it sequences is the program itself: there is no routing table in silicon, because the compiler writes each vector's link and cycle into the program and the chip executes the schedule. "The TSP acts as both a processing element (endpoint) and network switch for moving tensors across the communication links." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §1), and "The pin-bandwidth from each TSP is partitioned into 7 local links and 4 global links." (verified — Abts et al., ISCA 2022, §2.2), with the 7 local links fully connecting the 8 TSPs of a node and the 4 global links building 32-port virtual routers. The per-link send/receive sequencing is a few state flops plus next-state logic per link, but the link count in the Dragonfly is 11 of the 16 physical links and the sequencing state is not published, so no controller total is claimed. The routing controller's state — the schedule itself, held in the instruction-dispatch slices — is the program text, already decomposed above. Standard construction.

Honesty: Groq publishes the fabric geometry and none of its circuits: 88 MEM slices, 2 banks per slice, 8,192 addresses per slice, 2.5 MiB per slice, 16 x4 C2C links at 30 Gbps per lane (25 Gbps operating), the 320-byte flit, 97.5 percent encoding efficiency, the 8-bit HAC with a 252-cycle epoch, the 216-217-cycle measured link latency, the 7 local and 4 global links per TSP — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — SRAM bank organisation, address-decoder structure, SerDes equalisation and clocking, encoder logic, per-slice queue depths — Groq publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Three things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no FIFO/queue, no switch arbiter and no credit counter anywhere in the fabric, because flow control is the compiler's static schedule, not hardware.

Source: Abts et al., Think Fast: A Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) for Accelerating Deep Learning Workloads, ISCA 2020, §VII. The paper's "30K" is its own rounding: 820e12 / 26.8e9 = 30,597 Ops/sec/transistor. Distinct from the disputed marketed 750 INT8 TOPS figure (Level-2): 820 is the paper's peak at 1 GHz across all four MXM planes plus the VXM; no reconciliation is attempted between the two figures.

Sync/Notify barrier 142 AND2 gates, 852 transistors, plus 144 Sync-state flip-flops 2,880-4,032 transistors; 16-bit NOP counter 768-896 transistors each, 110,592-129,024 across 144 queues; 5,120 VXM ALUs, 32x32 multiplier 1,024 AND2 per ALU, 5,242,880 AND gates, 31,457,280 transistors of partial products, 992 full adders per ALU, 142,213,120 transistors of adder array, 32-bit adder 896 transistors per ALU, 4,587,520 total; ### SambaNova SN40L

#### Down to the gates: The PCU/PMU tile pair and the three-fabric RDN — the reconfigurable spatial fabric

SambaNova publishes no gate-level structure for the PCU, the PMU or the RDN — the arXiv paper (§IV-A–C) and the Hot Chips 2024 deck describe the tile’s contract (1,040 PCUs and 1,040 PMUs per socket, the header/body/tail PCU datapath, the broadcast buffer, the cross-lane reduction tree, the 4-addresses-per-cycle PMU address pipeline, the data-alignment crossbars, the three RDN fabrics, the flow-ID and sequence-ID mechanisms, the credit-based flow control) and stop there. The one chip-level transistor figure the deck does publish frames this whole section: 102B transistors on TSMC 5nm for the socket, against 638 BF16 TFLOPS — about 6,255 BF16 FLOPS per second per transistor by arithmetic. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about SambaNova’s circuits.

- **Pipeline registers and stage muxes (the PCU header, body and tail)** — A pipeline stage boundary is a register: one D flip-flop per bit of the vector operand, about 20-28 transistors each, clocked once per stage. The header, body and tail are three sections of one datapath, so a vector operand crossing from header to body to tail passes through two stage registers at minimum, and each body stage adds one more. The body’s configuration — systolic array or SIMD core — is selected by stage muxes set at compile time: a 2:1 mux is 4 transistors per bit in transmission-gate form, so selecting between two datapath configurations costs 4 transistors per operand bit per select point, and the select bits themselves are configuration flip-flops loaded from the compiled schedule. The PCU stage count is not published, so no register count and no mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Broadcast buffer (the systolic input staging)** — The broadcast buffer stages each input element once and fans it out across the systolic lanes: at the primitive level that is a register holding the element plus a fan-out of wires and, where the same element feeds several lanes at different times, a mux per lane selecting staged or fresh data. One staged element is one register of one flip-flop per bit (about 20-28 transistors each); the fan-out itself is wires, not gates, and a per-lane 2:1 staging mux adds 4 transistors per bit per lane. Whether the buffer is built from registers or SRAM, and its depth and width, are not published, so no buffer total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (the systolic MACCs)** — A multiply-accumulate unit is a multiplier plus an accumulator adder: the multiplier is an AND-gate partial-product array feeding a full-adder compressor tree and one final carry-propagate adder, and the accumulator is a full-adder chain over the partial sum. Arithmetic from the published geometry, in the standard array-multiplier form: one 8x8 multiplier (the INT8 and BF16-mantissa case) is 64 AND2 gates (64 x 6 = 384 transistors) plus 56 full adders in the array (56 x 28 = 1,568 transistors) plus a 16-bit final adder (16 x 28 = 448 transistors), about 2,400 transistors per multiplier; one 32x32 INT32 multiplier is 1,024 AND2 gates (6,144 transistors) plus 992 full adders (27,776 transistors) plus a 64-bit final adder (1,792 transistors), about 35,712 transistors; one FP32 multiplier is a 24x24 mantissa array (576 AND2, 3,456 transistors; 552 full adders, 15,456 transistors; 48-bit final adder, 1,344 transistors — about 20,256 transistors) plus an 8-bit exponent adder (8 full adders, 224 transistors) and normalisation logic, for which no count is claimed. The socket-level rate bounds the array without revealing it: 638 BF16 TFLOPS at a clock published only as under 2 GHz is at least 319,000 BF16 FLOPS per cycle across the socket, about 307 per PCU per cycle — arithmetic, not a per-PCU multiplier count, because the paper publishes no lane count (the deck says only M lanes) and no utilisation, so no MACC total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Accumulator registers (the output-stationary partial sums)** — Each stationary sum is an accumulator register, one per systolic element, holding the running total until the tile is finished: one D flip-flop per bit of the sum (about 20-28 transistors each) plus the full-adder chain that adds each new product into it — a 32-bit accumulate adder is 32 full adders, about 896 transistors. Arithmetic from the published data types only: one FP32 accumulator is 32 register bits, 640-896 transistors of flip-flops plus 896 transistors of adder; one BF16 accumulator is 16 register bits, 320-448 transistors plus a 16-bit adder of 448 transistors. The accumulator count is the systolic array’s element count, which is the unpublished lane count M times the unpublished array depth, so no socket total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree and muxes (the cross-lane reduction network)** — A cross-lane reduction is a binary adder tree: for M lanes, M-1 adders in log2(M) levels, each adder a full-adder chain over the lane width — a 32-bit adder is 32 full adders, about 896 transistors — with muxes selecting which lanes feed the tree, 4 transistors per bit per 2:1 mux. The paper calls it an optional cross-lane reduction network and the deck calls it a reduction tree along the vectorized dimension, but the tree depth, fan-in and lane count are not published, so no tree total is claimed: the form is M-1 adders and the count needs the M SambaNova never gives. Lane-wise reductions in pure SIMD fashion are the same tree with the muxes selecting a subset of lanes. Standard construction.
- **Counter and FSM (the PCU loop counters and loop-done control events)** — A loop counter is a register plus an incrementer: an N-bit counter is N D flip-flops (N x 20-28 transistors) plus an N-bit incrementer of N full adders (N x 28 transistors), so a 16-bit counter is 768-896 transistors, and the done event is a comparator — one XOR per bit plus an AND tree — against the programmed maximum. The event itself is a single bit carried on the control fabric to the next unit: the fabric is circuit-switched single-bit wires, so the token is one flip-flop at the consuming unit and wires in between, not gates. The counter width and the event-generation FSM’s state count are not published, so no counter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Function units (the PCU tail — transcendental, RNG, stochastic rounding, format conversion)** — The tail’s functions are the one place where the standard constructions are only candidates: a transcendental function is built in the standard way as a lookup table (an SRAM bank plus a row decoder) or as an iterative datapath (multiplier plus adder plus a small FSM), a random number generator as a linear-feedback shift register (one flip-flop per state bit plus one XOR per feedback tap), stochastic rounding as a comparator fed by the RNG output against the discarded low bits, and format conversion as a shifter plus an exponent adder (an 8-bit adder is 8 full adders, 224 transistors) with a rounding mux. How SambaNova implements any of these four is not published — no table size, no iteration count, no RNG width — so none of these forms is asserted for the SN40L and no transistor total is claimed for the tail. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (the PMU scratchpad SRAM instances)** — The PMU scratchpad is an array of 6T SRAM cells: each stored bit is 6 transistors (two cross-coupled inverters, 4 transistors, plus two access transistors), plus the per-bank row decoder, column muxes and sense amplifiers of the primer’s SRAM bank form. Arithmetic from the published geometry: 520 MiB of PMU SRAM across 1,040 PMUs is 0.5 MiB per PMU by arithmetic from the published totals — 4,194,304 bits per PMU, 25,165,824 6T cell transistors per PMU; across the socket 4,362,076,160 bits, 26,172,456,960 cell transistors; per die (520 PMUs) 2,181,038,080 bits, 13,086,228,480 cell transistors. Against the deck’s 102B transistors for the socket, the PMU cells alone are 25.7 percent by arithmetic. The deck’s round ‘520 MB’ reading would give 24,960,000,000 cell transistors, 4.6 percent lower — the MiB reading from the paper’s Table II is used here. The PMU bank count and organisation are not published, so the decoder, mux and sense-amplifier totals — which need the bank count — are not claimed. Standard construction.
- **Address decoder and comparator (PMU bank-bit decode and address predication)** — Each generated address is decoded to a bank by its programmable bank bits: a decoder is a NAND/NOR tree, one AND gate per bank-select line fed by the bank-bit inverters — a 4-transistor NAND2 per select term in the standard form — and the address is checked by a range comparator (one XOR per address bit plus an AND tree over the bits, an XOR2 is 10-12 transistors) and a predicate bit (one flip-flop per generated address, 20-28 transistors). The paper publishes the mechanism — programmable bank-bit locations and a programmable valid range or predicate bit per address — but not the bank count, the comparator width or the predicate storage, so no decoder or comparator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Integer ALU array (the PMU scalar ALU pipeline)** — The PMU address pipeline is a chain of integer ALUs, one per stage: each stage’s adder is a full-adder chain (a 32-bit adder is 32 full adders, about 896 transistors), its bitfield extraction is a mux tree (a 32-bit extract is 32 2:1 muxes per select level, 4 transistors per mux), and its shift-and-set is a barrel shifter (a 32-bit shifter is 5 levels of 32 muxes, 160 muxes, 640 transistors). The deck publishes the rate — 4 addresses per cycle — so four address computations leave the pipeline per cycle, but the stage count is software-configured and not published as a number, so no ALU count is claimed: four addresses per cycle is a rate, not a stage count. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar (the PMU data-alignment crossbars)** — A data-alignment crossbar is a mux tree per output: for R inputs, R-1 2:1 muxes per output bit (4 transistors per mux), so a 32-bit output selecting among R sources is 32 x (R-1) muxes, and the select bits are configuration flip-flops loaded from the compiled schedule. The diagonally striped transpose format is a placement rule, not gates: tensors are written striped across banks so the same crossbar reads them transposed at full bandwidth. The crossbar radix and the lookup-table sizes are not published, so no crossbar total is claimed — the form is R-1 muxes per bit and the count needs the R SambaNova never gives. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the RDN input and output FIFOs at every unit)** — A FIFO is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: as registers, N entries of W bits is N x W D flip-flops (N x W x 20-28 transistors); the write and read pointers are counters (an N-bit pointer counter is N flip-flops plus N full adders); full and empty are comparators of the two pointers (one XOR per pointer bit plus an AND tree). The out-of-order peek added in SN40L is a mux per peek port selecting among the FIFO’s entries — one N:1 mux per peeked bit, N-1 2:1 muxes in a binary tree of log2(N) levels. FIFO depths are not published, so no FIFO total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar and switch arbiter (the RDN mesh switches)** — Each mesh switch is a crossbar under an arbiter: the crossbar is a mux tree per output port (for R input ports, R-1 2:1 muxes per output bit, 4 transistors per mux), and the arbiter is a priority encoder (one AND gate per requester in the standard form, fed by the request bits) plus a grant flip-flop per output port (20-28 transistors each) holding the winner until the packet clears. The paper calls the switches non-blocking, which is a statement about the switch behaviour, not a published circuit — a non-blocking switch still needs the same muxes and arbiter, sized by a radix SambaNova does not publish. The switch radix and port counts are not published, so no switch total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator / decoder (flow-ID decode and rewrite at every switch port)** — Flow-ID handling is a lookup plus a rewrite: the flow ID carried with the packet is decoded at every switch port — a decoder, one AND gate per table entry fed by the flow-ID bits — and reassigned from the switch’s flow table before forwarding. The flow table itself is a small SRAM or register array indexed by the incoming flow ID: one entry per flow, one flip-flop or 6T cell per stored bit, plus the rewrite mux selecting the new ID (a 2:1 mux per rewritten bit, 4 transistors). Flow-table sizes and depths are not published, so no table total is claimed; the SN40L change to an MPLS-like label-swapping scheme changes what the table holds (a sequence of IDs per flow), not the gate form. Standard construction.
- **Comparator / address logic (the sequence-ID reorder logic)** — Reordering by sequence ID is a comparator plus an address computation: the sequence ID in each vector packet is compared against the expected ID (one XOR per ID bit plus an AND tree) and fed as an operand into the PMU’s address logic, which computes the write address that places the packet in order — the same full-adder chains as the PMU address pipeline, one 32-bit adder being 32 full adders, about 896 transistors. The sequence-ID width and the reorder logic’s implementation are not published, so no comparator or address-logic total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (RDN credit-based flow control)** — A credit counter is a counter like the PCU’s loop counter: an N-bit up/down counter (N flip-flops, N full adders and a 2:1 mux per bit selecting increment or decrement, 4 transistors per mux), so a 16-bit credit counter is 832-960 transistors, decremented on send and incremented on credit return, with a zero comparator (one NOR per bit plus an AND tree) gating the next send. The paper publishes the scheme — credit-based flow control at every hop, plus coarse-grained software tokens end to end — but no counter width and no FIFO depth, so no credit-counter total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: SambaNova publishes the tile geometry and none of its circuits: 1,040 PCUs and 1,040 PMUs per socket, 520 MiB of PMU SRAM, the header/body/tail datapath, the broadcast buffer, the cross-lane reduction tree, the 4-addresses-per-cycle PMU address pipeline, the data-alignment crossbars, the three RDN fabrics, the flow-ID and sequence-ID mechanisms, the credit-based flow control — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — PCU lane and stage counts, PMU bank count and organisation, RDN switch radix and port counts, input/output FIFO depths, crossbar radices, flow-table sizes, sequence-ID widths, credit-counter widths — SambaNova publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no dynamic scheduler anywhere in the tile, because the compiler’s place-and-route fixes every route, flow ID, sequence ID and credit arrangement at compile time; and there is no cache tag array anywhere on the tile, because the PMU scratchpads are software-managed and there is no cache to tag.

#### Down to the gates: The three-tier memory system and the AGCU at the fabric edge — DDR → HBM → PMU SRAM promotion

SambaNova publishes no gate-level structure for the AGCU, the TLN or the die-to-die and host interfaces either — the paper (§IV, §IV-D) and the Hot Chips 2024 deck describe the memory system’s contract (520 MiB of PMU SRAM, 64 GiB of HBM at 1.8 TB/s per socket, up to 1.5 TiB of DDR at over 200 GB/s per socket, 1,600 GB/s switching bandwidth, the AGCU’s scalar address-generation pipeline and counters, the Segment Lookaside Buffer, the four TLN networks, Y-X dimension-order routing, end-to-end credits, the die-to-die interface and PCIe DMA) and stop there. The same framing figure applies: the deck’s 102B transistors for the socket, of which the PMU SRAM cells alone account for about a quarter by arithmetic (26,172,456,960 cell transistors, 25.7 percent). What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors on the same terms as the tile block: published geometry stays published, arithmetic is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction, labelled as such.
