- **Integer ALU array (the AGCU scalar address-generation pipeline)** — The AGCU address pipeline is the PMU’s address logic without the SRAM: the same integer ALU stages — a 32-bit adder is 32 full adders, about 896 transistors per stage — with the same bitfield-extract mux trees and barrel shifters, producing the DDR and HBM read and write addresses instead of scratchpad addresses. The paper publishes the similarity and nothing else about the AGCU pipeline: its stage count and addresses-per-cycle are not published, and the 4-addresses-per-cycle figure belongs to the PMU pipeline, not the AGCU, so no ALU count is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (the AGCU counters)** — The AGCU counters are the same counter form as the PCU’s loop counters: an N-bit counter is N D flip-flops (N x 20-28 transistors) plus an N-bit incrementer of N full adders (N x 28 transistors), so a 16-bit counter is 768-896 transistors, sequencing the request streams for each promotion and each kernel launch. Counter widths and counts are not published, so no counter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **CAM / TCAM (the Segment Lookaside Buffer)** — A lookaside buffer is a CAM: each entry is a CAM cell — a 6T SRAM cell (6 transistors) plus an XOR match circuit (4 transistors in the standard form), 10 transistors per stored bit — with all match lines feeding a priority encoder that selects the matching entry. The deck names the structure a Segment Lookaside Buffer for virtual-physical address translation, but SambaNova publishes no SLB entry count, key width or internal organisation, so no entry total and no cell total is claimed, and the CAM form is the standard construction for a translation lookaside buffer, not a published fact about the SN40L. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the AGCU request-coalescing buffers)** — The coalescing buffers are FIFOs in the same standard form as the RDN’s: N entries of W bits as D flip-flops (N x W x 20-28 transistors), a write and a read pointer counter each, and full/empty comparators — plus, for coalescing, a comparator per buffered request checking whether an incoming reply matches an outstanding request (one XOR per address bit plus an AND tree). The coalescing window and the buffer depths are not published, so no buffer total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the TLN Data, Request and Response network FIFOs)** — Each of the TLN’s three data-bearing networks queues its packets in FIFOs at the routers — requests out, data and acknowledgements back — in the same standard FIFO form: N x W flip-flops plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators. The Response network’s write acknowledgements and interrupts are one-bit payloads in the same FIFO form, one flip-flop per queued acknowledgement. FIFO depths and packet widths are not published, so no TLN FIFO total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (the TLN Credit network)** — The TLN’s fourth network carries nothing but credits, and each sender holds a credit counter per destination in the same up/down counter form as the RDN’s: N flip-flops, N full adders and a 2:1 mux per bit selecting increment or decrement, so a 16-bit counter is 832-960 transistors, with a zero comparator gating the next send. Counter widths are not published, so no credit-counter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar and FSM (the TLN router — Y-X dimension-order routing)** — Each TLN router is a crossbar under a Y-X routing FSM: the crossbar is a mux tree per output port (for R ports, R-1 2:1 muxes per output bit, 4 transistors per mux), and the routing FSM is a state machine built the standard way — state bits in master-slave D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each) and next-state logic as a NAND/NOR network, driven by a comparator on the packet’s destination coordinates against the router’s own (one XOR per coordinate bit plus an AND tree). Router radix, port counts and link rates are not published, so no router total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer and FIFO (the die-to-die interface)** — The die-to-die interface crosses between two clock domains, so each crossing bit passes through a two-flip-flop synchronizer — two D flip-flops in series (40-56 transistors per bit) — and the staged data sits in a FIFO in the same standard form as the RDN’s (N x W flip-flops plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators). The two dies stream directly without going through off-chip memory, but the die-to-die bandwidth is not published, so no synchronizer width and no FIFO total is claimed, and the two-flip-flop form is the standard construction, not a published fact about the interface. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the PCIe DMA engine queues)** — The DMA engine’s queues are FIFOs in the same standard form: N entries of W bits as D flip-flops (N x W x 20-28 transistors) plus write/read pointer counters plus full/empty comparators, one queue per direction — host-to-device and device-to-host — with the direct host-to-tile path bypassing device memory through its own queue. Queue depths and the DMA channel count are not published, so no DMA queue total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the HBM and DDR controller request queues)** — Each memory controller queues the AGCUs’ requests in FIFOs in the same standard form: N entries of W bits as D flip-flops plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators, with a scheduler FSM selecting the next request (state flip-flops plus NAND/NOR next-state logic). The tier gap is the reason the queues exist at all: HBM at 1.8 TB/s against DDR at over 200 GB/s is a 9x gap by arithmetic from the published figures, so the controller queues absorb the bursts the slower tier cannot take. Controller queue depths and the controller count are not published, so no controller queue total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the P2P protocol engine)** — The P2P protocol engine is a protocol FSM in the AGCU: state bits in master-slave D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each) with next-state logic as a NAND/NOR network, opening a direct tile-to-tile stream across the TLN and the inter-socket links and holding the stream’s state — source, destination, outstanding count — in its registers until the collective completes. Link rates and the engine’s state count are not published, so no engine total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (the AGCU tile-side RDN port selection)** — The AGCU multiplexes its three RDN ports onto the tile fabric on one side and the TLN on the other: a mux per port bit (4 transistors per 2:1 mux) selecting vector data, scalar addresses or control tokens onto the fabric, and a demux per port bit on the return path. Port widths are not published, so no mux total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the hardware-orchestrated kernel-launch schedule)** — The kernel-launch schedule is a three-command FSM held in dedicated AGCU hardware: Program Load, Argument Load, Kernel Execute — three states in the standard form (two state flip-flops, 40-56 transistors, plus NAND/NOR next-state logic), with the schedule’s arguments held in registers loaded by the Argument Load command. The schedule itself is the FSM’s state, held in dedicated hardware, and its size is not published, so no schedule total is claimed; the measured effect is already recorded at Level-2 — hardware orchestration speeds autoregressive decoding 1.4x to 8x over software orchestration. Standard construction.

Honesty: SambaNova publishes the memory geometry and none of its circuits: 520 MiB PMU SRAM, 64 GiB HBM at 1.8 TB/s per socket, up to 1.5 TiB DDR at over 200 GB/s per socket, 1,600 GB/s switching bandwidth with a Llama 3.1 8B switch under 0.01 s, the AGCU’s scalar address-generation pipeline and counters, the Segment Lookaside Buffer, the four TLN networks, Y-X dimension-order routing, end-to-end credits, the die-to-die interface and PCIe DMA — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — AGCU queue depths and coalescing window, SLB entry count and organisation, TLN link rates, die-to-die bandwidth, DMA and memory-controller queue depths — SambaNova publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. One thing is absent by design and is stated as such: there is no hardware cache anywhere in the three tiers, because the compiler manages every symbol’s tier, lifetime and spill order explicitly.
**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [unverifiable] **SambaNova SN40L** — Level-4 decomposition scope boundary: SambaNova publishes no gate-level structure for the SN40L; the Level-4 text therefore decomposes every primitive as the generic textbook construction of that primitive, labelled standard construction, using only SambaNova's published per-block geometry plus figures explicitly labelled as arithmetic derived from that geometry (PMU SRAM 520 MiB = 4,362,076,160 bits = 26,172,456,960 6T cell transistors per socket; 0.5 MiB per PMU = 4,194,304 bits = 25,165,824 cell transistors; per die 260 MiB = 2,181,038,080 bits = 13,086,228,480 cell transistors; PMU cells 25.7 percent of the deck's 102B transistors; 638 BF16 TFLOPS at a clock published only as under 2 GHz is at least 319,000 FLOPS per cycle per socket, about 307 per PCU per cycle; 638 TFLOPS from 102B transistors is about 6,255 BF16 FLOPS per second per transistor; 8x8 multiplier about 2,400 transistors; 32x32 INT32 multiplier about 35,712 transistors; FP32 mantissa multiplier about 20,256 transistors plus a 224-transistor exponent adder; 16-bit counter 768-896 transistors; 16-bit up/down counter 832-960 transistors; CAM cell 10 transistors; HBM/DDR 9x bandwidth gap). The tail's transcendental, RNG, stochastic-rounding and format-conversion functions are named only as candidate standard constructions, none asserted for the SN40L. No primitive decomposes to zero gates; two things are absent by design (no dynamic scheduler on the tile; no hardware cache in the three tiers). The deck's round '520 MB' reading would give 24,960,000,000 cell transistors, 4.6 percent lower than the MiB reading used. Source: SambaNova SN40L: Scaling the AI Memory Wall with Dataflow and Composition of Experts; SambaNova SN40L RDU: Breaking the Barrier of Trillion+ Parameter Scale Gen AI Computing, Whole paper §§I–IX and Hot Chips 2024 deck (absence of gate-level structure across the documents; 'transistor', 'flip-flop' and '6T' do not occur in the arXiv text, checked live 2026-11-25).

### Apple Neural Engine (A17 / M-series)

**Added: 2026-11-22** (mirrored to the corpus 2026-11-26 with the Level-2 deepening; the corpus had no entry for it before this run)

**Specs (wiki card).** 16 cores · 35 TOPS (A17 Pro) · shared UMA

**What it is / why it matters.** Apple's fixed neural-network accelerator, present in every modern Apple SoC — from the first generation in the A11 (iPhone X, 2017) at 0.6 TFLOPS in FP16, through the fifth-generation 16-core A15 at 15.8 TFLOPS, to the A17 Pro at 35 TOPS and the M4 at 38 TOPS. It is the energy-efficient, high-throughput engine for ML inference on Apple silicon, in Apple's own words, and it is what makes on-device inference nearly free to invoke: it sits on the SoC fabric beside the ISP and GPU, its buffers live in the same unified-memory pool as everything else, and work arrives only as compiled Core ML graphs. A frame lands in unified memory once, the ISP writes it, the ANE works on it, and the result is already in shared memory for the next stage. Its power is placement, not peak TOPS.

**Building blocks.**
- **Neural Engine cores (16)** — Fixed-function convolution/MAC engines executing Core ML operators at 35 TOPS (A17 Pro). Apple does not publish the internal array topology — and it is not documented as a systolic array, so this breakdown does not claim one
- **Unified-memory access (no private interface)** — The ANE reads and writes the SoC's shared LPDDR pool directly. It has no memory controller and no dedicated DRAM of its own — the absence of a private memory interface is the design
- **Core ML graph interface** — Work arrives only as compiled Core ML graphs. Developers cannot program the ANE directly; the compiler and runtime are part of the block
- **SoC fabric port** — Sits on the same interconnect as the ISP and GPU, so camera frames flow ISP → ANE → GPU without leaving the SoC or being copied

**The piece that makes it special.** Placement over peak. On TOPS slides the ANE is mid-pack; in a phone it is unbeatable, because it sits one fabric hop from the camera pipeline and shares memory with everything. Its lesson generalises: for on-device inference, invocation cost and data copies matter more than the multiplier count.

#### Inside the signature block: The 16-core MAC array and the task-descriptor scheduler — a fixed datapath with no instruction set

**Inside it.** Sixteen compute cores sit around a central block of local memory — on the M1 die, seven cores down each side of the central L2 rectangle, two across the top, shared control logic along the bottom. Each core is a parallel array of multiply-accumulate lanes: 128 FP16 lanes per core, 256 in INT8, 2,048 FP16 lanes across the array. A lane is a 16-bit multiplier feeding a 32-bit accumulator held as Q16.16 fixed point and read out as FP16, saturating at 2^15, so a lane performs one scalar reduction over time — multiply, add into the running sum, repeat — and a dot product, a matrix row, or a convolution tap sequence are all the same operation with different operand scheduling; the core does not encode a CNN layer in hardware. Completed sums feed straight into a fused post-MAC activation block with no intermediate memory round-trip: identity, ReLU, or a 33-entry piecewise-linear lookup table for tanh, with the compiler folding constant scale and bias into the convolution weights first. There is no instruction set. Apple's compiler has already turned every neural operation into a chain of fixed-size task descriptors before execution begins, and the driver only stages that chain in memory, points the task manager at it with two registers, TM_ADDR and TM_INFO, and rings a doorbell, TM_PUSH; the hardware then owns the job until it raises a completion interrupt. The task manager schedules from eight task queues, each holding two ping-pong command-stream slots and a 32-entry base-address table that relocates the descriptor stream's relative addresses into IOMMU virtual addresses. A descriptor is a serialized register dump of the datapath, not code: for one 1x1 convolution it is 628 bytes split into Header, KernelDMASrc with 16 coefficient-DMA lanes, Common for tensor and convolution geometry, TileDMASrc for the activation-source DMA, L2 for local source and result configuration, PE, NE for MAC and post-processing, and TileDMADst for the result-destination DMA, each section a burst of register writes delivered by a ControlDMA engine. All of the deep numbers in this block are the M1 generation's, established by reverse engineering of the M1 ANE; Apple publishes no per-core lane count, accumulator width, or descriptor format for the A17 Pro — only 16 cores and 35 TOPS.

**Trace — one unit of work.**
1. **Core ML compiles the layer into task descriptors.**The layer leaves Core ML as a chain of fixed-size task descriptors: the 1x1 convolution becomes one 628-byte descriptor whose sections program the tensor geometry — 1 input group of 8 channels in, 3 out, 4 rows — the kernel and tile DMA sources, the L2 source and result, and the MAC and post-processing configuration. No CONV opcode is ever sent to the hardware.
2. **The driver stages the descriptor chain and rings the doorbell.**The driver writes the descriptor chain to memory, sets TM_ADDR to its address and TM_INFO to its descriptor count and size, and writes TM_PUSH; from that moment the ANE owns the job and the host does not direct a single arithmetic step.
3. **ControlDMA copies the descriptor into the configuration registers.**A ControlDMA engine burst-writes the descriptor's register values into the datapath's configuration registers — tensor dimensions, addresses, activation mode, dependencies — one section per register block.
4. **KernelDMA loads the weights into per-core kernel memory.**Sixteen coefficient lanes copy the 1x1 kernel weights from DRAM into each core's private 64 KiB kernel memory, where they will be reused across the whole output instead of being re-fetched per tap.
5. **TileDMA stages the activations into the shared L2.**TileDMASrc copies the input tile X from DRAM into the shared 2 MiB L2; the MAC cores then reduce one row of X against the resident weights, producing one row of Y, and repeat for all rows.
6. **Post-processing fuses in place and TileDMADst writes the result back.**The completed sums pass straight through the fused activation block and are stored in L2; TileDMADst then copies Y from L2 back to DRAM, and the task manager raises a completion interrupt. The whole pass touched DRAM twice — once to load, once to store — and never again in between.

**Bottleneck.** Relieves the dispatch wall and the kernel-reuse wall. The host never micromanages the arithmetic: it submits a descriptor chain, rings one doorbell, and gets an interrupt at completion, so the ANE's 2,048 MAC lanes run without host intervention; and the kernel is loaded once into per-core kernel memory and reused across the entire output, so a convolution's weights are fetched once per layer instead of once per tap. It creates two new bottlenecks instead. First, the fixed-datapath wall: there is no instruction set, so a workload the compiler cannot express as task descriptors does not run at all — new operators need a compiler path, not a kernel, and the ANE cannot be reprogrammed around a workload it was not built for. Second, the serial-DMA wall: the kernel and tile DMA engines are sent serially, one at a time, so their times add — measured on M3, a combined kernel-plus-tile transfer costs the sum of the two isolated transfers, and neither engine alone reaches the GPU's DRAM read rate.

**Numbers.** 16 compute cores (M1 generation, reverse-engineered); 128 FP16 MAC lanes per core, 256 INT8; 2,048 FP16 lanes across the array; 4,096 operations per cycle at full occupancy by arithmetic (2,048 lanes x 2 operations); MAC accumulator 32-bit Q16.16 fixed point, saturates at 2^15, read out as FP16; fused activation modes: identity, ReLU, tanh as a 33-entry piecewise-linear lookup table over [0,4] with 1/8 knot spacing; task descriptor 628 bytes for a 1x1 convolution; 8 task queues, 2 ping-pong command-stream slots each, 32 base-address registers per queue; M1 11 TOPS; A15 15.8 TFLOPS; A17 Pro 35 TOPS (16 cores, up to 2x A16); M4 38 TOPS (60x the A11 first generation). A17 Pro per-core lane count, accumulator width and descriptor format are not published.

**Source.** Yoon, Retrospectively Reverse-Engineering Apple's Neural Engine, Aug 10, 2026 (eiln.github.io) — Asahi Linux reverse engineering of the M1 ANE: compute cores, MAC lanes and accumulator, fused activation and tanh lookup table, Task Manager and task queues, task-descriptor structure and the 1x1-convolution hexdump, the six-step execution sequence; Apple, Deploying Transformers on the Apple Neural Engine, Apple Machine Learning Research, 2022 — ANE as the energy-efficient high-throughput inference engine, Core ML hybrid execution plan; Apple Newsroom, Apple unveils iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max, Sept 12, 2023 — Neural Engine up to 2x faster; Apple Newsroom, Apple introduces M4 chip, May 7, 2024 — 38 TOPS, 60x the A11 first generation; Apple Newsroom, Apple unleashes M1, Nov 10, 2020 — 16-core architecture, 11 TOPS.

#### Inside the signature block: The memory system — a shared 2 MiB L2, per-core kernel memory, and three DMA engines

**Inside it.** Apple's unified memory means the ANE's buffers live in the same DRAM pool the CPU, GPU and ISP use — there is no private DRAM and no memory controller of the ANE's own — but the ANE does not stream straight out of that pool. Every byte passes through the ANE's own local memory first: a shared 2 MiB L2 that holds activation tiles, and per-core kernel memory of 64 KiB per core, 1 MiB across the sixteen cores, that holds weights. A third, per-core L1 staging area feeds the MAC inputs; its size is not published. Three DMA engines move data across that boundary: sixteen logical KernelDMASrc lanes copy weights from DRAM into the matching per-core kernel banks, load-only, since weights are never written back; TileDMASrc copies activation tiles from DRAM into L2; TileDMADst copies finished tiles from L2 back to DRAM, and because TileDMA is bidirectional and shared, an intermediate tile can feed the next operation without a DRAM round-trip. The split is the design's central commitment: kernels and tiles are different operand classes with different lifecycles, so they get different memories and different paths — and a kernel can only ever be loaded from DRAM, never from L2, so a tensor produced locally cannot become a kernel without going out to DRAM and back. On the M1 die the layout is literal: the ANE is built around the central L2 SRAM rectangle, seven cores down each side, two across the top, shared control logic along the bottom. The ANE's buffers also carry a layout rule from the compiler side: the last axis of an ANE buffer is not packed — it must be contiguous and aligned to 64 bytes — and a singleton last axis is padded to 64 bytes, costing 32 times the memory in FP16 and 64 times in INT8, which is what pushes buffers out of L2 residency and into DRAM. All of the sizes in this block are the M1 generation's; Apple publishes no L2, kernel-memory, or DMA figures for the A17 Pro.

**Trace — one unit of work.**
1. **The weights stream in from DRAM, and that stream sets the pace.**For a short-sequence transformer step the parameter tensors are fetched from memory and applied to too few inputs before the next parameter tensor is fetched, so fetching dominates latency: Apple's own measurement shows the optimized model's latency staying approximately constant across sequence lengths of 32, 64 and 128 at batch size 1 even though the computational load quadruples.
2. **KernelDMA loads the weights into per-core kernel memory.**The sixteen coefficient lanes copy the layer's weights from DRAM into each core's 64 KiB kernel bank, where they sit for the whole layer; the lanes make concurrent progress, but they share request generation, crossbar, cache and DRAM arbitration downstream.
3. **TileDMA stages the activations into the shared L2.**The input tile is copied from DRAM into the 2 MiB shared L2, and the MAC cores consume it from there — never from DRAM directly — with intermediate results held in L2 for the next operation instead of being written out.
4. **The MACs work from local memory only.**Each core reduces its rows against the weights resident in its kernel memory and the activations resident in L2; the roofline is the arithmetic: on M1, 11 TOPS against 68 GB/s of system DRAM bandwidth means each byte fetched from DRAM must support at least 162 operations, or DRAM — not the MAC array — sets the speed.
5. **Post-processing lands in L2, and TileDMADst writes the finished tile back.**The fused activation is applied as the sums complete and the result is stored in L2; only the finished tile goes back to DRAM through TileDMADst. On iPhone 13 the whole DistilBERT forward pass at sequence length 128, batch size 1, takes 3.47 ms at 0.454 W.
6. **The KV cache is where the split bites.**In autoregressive decoding each new token streams a substantial part of the model's parameters, and the KV cache — representations of earlier tokens, growing with the conversation — must be re-read through the same tile path; because kernels load only from DRAM and never from L2, a locally produced tensor cannot become a kernel without a DRAM round trip, so the cache's growth is paid in DRAM traffic, not in reuse.

**Bottleneck.** Relieves the copy wall at the system level: buffers live in the one shared pool, so the ISP can write a frame once and the ANE can work on it with no inter-engine copy and no staging buffer to manage — that is the ANE's placement advantage, and it is why Deep Fusion can run pixel-by-pixel processing on the Neural Engine straight off the camera pipeline. But the zero-copy is at the system level, not the hardware level: inside the ANE every tile is staged through the 2 MiB L2 and every kernel through per-core kernel memory, and that staging creates the memory wall. On M1 the roofline is 162 operations per byte of DRAM traffic — below that ratio, DRAM bandwidth, not the 2,048 MAC lanes, sets the speed — and short-sequence transformers live below it, bandwidth-bound with latency flat across sequence lengths. It creates a second bottleneck too: the split memory. Kernel and tile memories are separate, and kernels load only from DRAM, so a tensor the ANE itself produced cannot be reused as a kernel without a round trip through DRAM — the assumption that weights are fixed and activations flow one way, true for 2017 CNNs, is exactly what transformer KV caches violate.

**Numbers.** Shared L2 2 MiB (M1 generation); kernel memory 64 KiB per core, 1 MiB across 16 cores; per-core L1 MAC-input staging area, size not published; three DMA engines — 16 logical KernelDMASrc lanes (load-only), TileDMASrc, TileDMADst; M1 system DRAM bandwidth 68 GB/s; roofline ridge 162 operations per byte of DRAM traffic (M1, 11 TOPS / 68 GB/s, by arithmetic); ANE buffer last axis contiguous and aligned to 64 bytes; singleton last axis padded to 64 bytes costs 32x memory in FP16, 64x in INT8; DistilBERT on iPhone 13, sequence 128, batch 1: 3.47 ms at 0.454 W (9.44 ms at 0.072 W); M3 measured DRAM read throughput — KernelDMA 37.99 GB/s, TileDMA 59.08 GB/s, GPU 77.70 GB/s, M3 DRAM ceiling about 100 GB/s; kernel and tile DMA sent serially, runtimes additive. L2, kernel-memory and DMA figures for the A17 Pro are not published.

**Source.** Yoon, Retrospectively Reverse-Engineering Apple's Neural Engine, Aug 10, 2026 (eiln.github.io) — M1 memory hierarchy (shared 2 MiB L2, 64 KiB per-core KMem, per-core L1 staging), three DMA engines and their roles, the die layout around the central L2, the 162 OP/byte roofline, M3 DMA throughput measurements (KernelDMA 37.99 GB/s, TileDMA 59.08 GB/s, GPU 77.70 GB/s) and serial kernel/tile DMA; Apple, Deploying Transformers on the Apple Neural Engine, Apple Machine Learning Research, 2022 — 64-byte alignment, 32x/64x padding cost, L2 cache residency, bandwidth-bound short sequences, DistilBERT 3.47 ms at 0.454 W; Apple Newsroom, Apple introduces dual camera iPhone 11, Sept 10, 2019 — Deep Fusion enabled by the Neural Engine; Apple Newsroom, Apple unleashes M1, Nov 10, 2020 — unified memory architecture, 16-core Neural Engine at 11 TOPS.

#### Down to the primitives: The 16-core MAC array and the task-descriptor scheduler — a fixed datapath with no instruction set

Decomposed in trace order — a layer arrives as a chain of fixed-size task descriptors; the driver stages the chain and rings TM_PUSH; ControlDMA burst-writes the descriptor into the datapath's configuration registers; KernelDMA loads the weights into per-core kernel memory and TileDMA stages the activations into the shared L2; the 2,048 MAC lanes reduce row by row; completed sums pass straight through the fused activation into L2; TileDMADst writes the finished tile back and the Task Manager raises the completion interrupt. Yoon (2026) publishes the lane counts, the accumulator, the tanh lookup table, the task-queue register map, the descriptor layout and the six-step sequence, but nothing below that contract: no per-lane multiplier organisation, no adder carry structure, no Task Manager scheduling policy, no ControlDMA queue depth, no L1 staging size. Where a number below is computed from published geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **Register file (the datapath configuration registers)** — A task descriptor is a serialized register-file dump: "A TD is effectively a serialized register-file dump of the ANE's datapath registers." (verified — Yoon, 2026). Each descriptor section writes to one MMIO register block: "Since each section writes to one MMIO register block, TD divides cleanly into ANE's datapath sections:" — Common at 0x26bc00000, L2 at 0x26bc04000, PE at 0x26bc08000, NE/MAC at 0x26bc0c000, Tile DMA source at 0x26bc13000, Tile DMA destination at 0x26bc17000, Kernel at 0x26bc1f000, Task Manager at 0x26bc24000 and Task Queues at 0x26bc25000, each aperture 0x4000 bytes except the Task Manager and Task Queues at 0x1000. Three banks in the map are unidentified in the source (0x26bc10000, 0x26bc1b000, 0x26bc23000) — the article labels them Unknown, and this decomposition claims nothing about them.
- **DMA engine (ControlDMA — the descriptor burst-write)** — "ControlDMA is a flexible unidirectional DMA engine that copies N 32-bit words from IOMMU virtual DRAM into the ANE's physical register space." (verified — Yoon, 2026). "Each ControlDMA packet consists of a 32-bit transfer word followed by N consecutive 32-bit register values" — register count minus 1 in bits 31:26, first register base index in bits 25:2. The KernelDMASrc packet header decodes by arithmetic from that format: "count = (0xf401f800 >> 26) + 1 = 62 words" written to "register base = 0xf401f800 & 0x03fffffc = 0x1f800". ControlDMA's queue depth and request width are not published.
- **Counter (the TM_INFO descriptor counters)** — TM_INFO carries the launch size in two fields: "TM_INFO[31:16] = descriptor_dwords - 1" and "TM_INFO[15:0] = descriptor_count" (verified — Yoon, 2026). The article's RTL sketch maps the register onto two counters — a word counter that wraps at descriptor_dwords_minus_1 and increments a descriptor counter — and notes that encoding length − 1 is "an RTL-friendly way to terminate a zero-based counter out of the critical path." The sketch is the article's proposed implementation, not a published Apple circuit; the field split itself is the published fact.
- **FSM / controller (the Task Manager)** — "TM_ADDR and TM_INFO are global staging registers, and TM_PUSH atomically commits that staged launch state, given that nothing happens until TM_PUSH is written" (verified — Yoon, 2026). Once committed, "The hardware then owns the submission until completion, and raises an interrupt to the ARM64 core when it's done." The Task Manager's internal state machine, its scheduling policy across the eight queues and the contents of its priority table (TQ_PRTY_TABLE) are not published.
- **Register file (the task-queue register block)** — "There's 8 copies of the same register block (indexed by qid (0…7))" (verified — Yoon, 2026), one per queue, stepping 0x148 bytes per qid: STATUS, PRIORITY, VACANT and INFO, then the two command-stream slots — BAR1[0..31], NID1, SIZE2, ADDR2, BAR2[0..31], NID2, SIZE1 and ADDR1. The per-queue scheduling state (status, priority, vacancy) lives in the same block as the launch context it schedules.
- **FIFO / queue (the two ping-pong command-stream slots)** — Each task queue holds two command-stream descriptor sets: "The two slots are certainly a ping-pong staging scheme to let one slot execute, while software modifies the other slot." (verified — Yoon, 2026). The slot pair is the ANE's only command queueing — there is no ring buffer of descriptors; the driver stages one stream while the other runs. The descriptor count per stream is the TM_INFO count, not a queue depth, and no deeper queue exists to decompose.
- **Register file (the 32-entry BAR table)** — "The only thing important here is the 32-entry BAR table (base address register)." (verified — Yoon, 2026). The compiled command stream "only references virtual addresses by relative offsets, and BAR provides the base IOVA (IOMMU peripheral virtual address) relocation address." Each queue carries two BAR tables of 32 entries — BAR1 and BAR2, one per ping-pong slot — 64 entries per queue and 512 across the eight queues by arithmetic from the published layout. The entries are written as 32-bit words; the relocation arithmetic beyond base-plus-offset is not described.
- **Multiplier array (128 FP16 / 256 INT8 MAC lanes per core)** — "ANE has 16 parallel compute cores. Each compute core has 128 FP16 (or 256 INT8) parallel multiply-accumulate (MAC) lanes." (verified — Yoon, 2026). 2,048 FP16 lanes across the array by arithmetic. "The multiplier is 16-bit, accumulated in a 32-bit register as Q16.16, then read out as FP16 via sign-extend and etc." Whether one 16-bit multiplier serves two INT8 lanes or each INT8 lane has its own multiplier is not published.
- **Adder (the per-lane 32-bit accumulate adder)** — "Internally, the MAC datapath consists of a multiplier, adder, and a 32-bit accumulator register. Each cycle, the adder adds the fresh multiplier output with the previous sum, which then becomes the new running sum." (verified — Yoon, 2026). One adder per lane, 2,048 adders across the array by arithmetic from the published lane count. The adder's carry structure is not published.
- **Accumulator registers (the 32-bit Q16.16 running sums)** — "This feedback path keeps the partial sum in memory local to the MAC lane, so it does not need fetched from an external memory far away, between MAC cycles." (verified — Yoon, 2026). One 32-bit accumulator register per lane, 2,048 across the array by arithmetic. There is no cross-lane adder tree: reduction is over time inside each lane — "A MAC lane thus performs a scalar reduction over time." — so the ANE has no reduction network to decompose.
- **Comparator (accumulator saturation at 2^15)** — The accumulator clamps inside, not at FP16 readout: "Since 32768 is itself a valid FP16 word (0x7800), the ANE's 0x7c00 can't be FP16 output overflow, the clamp happens inside the accumulator, at 2^15. Thus the accumulator saturates at 2^15, exactly the range of a signed 32-bit fixed-point value with 16 fractional bits." (verified — Yoon, 2026). The saturation is a compare-and-clamp on the 32-bit sum; the comparator's implementation is not published.
- **Mux (activation-mode select: identity / ReLU / tanh LUT)** — The NE section's NonlinearMode field selects the post-MAC path: identity is mode 0, ReLU mode 1, tanh mode 2 with 33 FP16 words — "Thus, mode 2 selects a custom 33-entry lookup table." (verified — Yoon, 2026). Bias and post-scale modes (BiasMode, PostScaleMode) are further select fields in the same register block. The select logic's circuit form is not published.
- **Lookup table (the 33-entry piecewise-linear tanh table)** — "Those 33 FP16 words match 33 IEEE LE FP16 quantized samples of tanh(x)" (verified — Yoon, 2026): T_i = round_16(tanh(i/8)) for i = 0,…,32, knots at x_i = i/8 over [0,4] with 1/8 spacing. The input maps into the table as u = 2^R|x| with R = 3, and "⌊u⌋ and ⌈u⌉ select the adjacent entries, and α=u−⌊u⌋ gives the interpolation weight between them." The impulse test proves the interpolation: "Then sweep the input across the two cells around T_8. The measured output forms a triangle: magnitude rises linearly from 0 at |x|=7/8 to 1 at |x|=1, then falls linearly to 0 at |x|=9/8." The table is 33 FP16 words — 66 bytes by arithmetic — held in the compiled coefficient region at offset 0x4288; whether it lives in registers or a small SRAM, and the arithmetic that applies the interpolation weight, are not published.
- **Register file (fixed-point binary point — NE BinaryPoint=28)** — The decoded 1x1-convolution descriptor carries "NE: KernelFmt=2 BinaryPoint=28" (verified — Yoon, 2026, hexdump decode), the binary-point field that positions the fixed-point result of the NE section. The field's width and the scaling hardware it drives are not published beyond the decoded value.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the published M1 contract is 16 cores, 128 FP16 (256 INT8) MAC lanes per core, 2,048 lanes, a 16-bit multiplier with a 32-bit Q16.16 accumulator saturating at 2^15, a 33-entry tanh lookup table over [0,4], 8 task queues with two ping-pong slots and 32-entry BAR tables each, a 628-byte task descriptor, and the ControlDMA and TM_INFO field formats. Below that level — per-lane multiplier organisation in INT8, the adder's carry structure, the Task Manager's scheduling policy, ControlDMA queue depth, the lookup table's storage form and interpolation arithmetic — Apple publishes nothing and the reverse-engineering source describes no circuits, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no cross-lane adder tree, because each lane reduces over time in its own accumulator; and there is no instruction decoder, because the task descriptor is a register dump, not code.

#### Down to the primitives: The memory system — a shared 2 MiB L2, per-core kernel memory, and three DMA engines

Decomposed in trace order — DRAM feeds three DMA engines: KernelDMASrc's sixteen logical lanes copy weights into the sixteen per-core 64 KiB kernel banks, TileDMASrc copies activation tiles into the shared 2 MiB L2, the MAC cores reduce rows against resident weights and resident tiles, post-processing lands in L2, and TileDMADst copies the finished tile back to DRAM. The sixteen kernel lanes make concurrent progress but may merge into shared request generation, crossbar, cache and DRAM arbitration downstream, and the kernel and tile DMA engines are sent serially, so their times add. Yoon (2026) publishes the L2 and kernel-memory sizes, the three DMA engines, the lane count, the measured throughputs and the serial-DMA behaviour, but no SRAM bank organisation, no crossbar port counts, no DMA queue depths and no L1 staging size. Where a number below is computed from published geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **SRAM bank (the shared 2 MiB L2 tile memory)** — "shared ANE L2 memory, 2 MiB" (verified — Yoon, 2026), one bank shared across all sixteen cores, holding activation tiles and intermediate results so one operation's output can feed the next without a DRAM round-trip. The firmware's task-debug routine dumps it as a single 0x200000-byte region. The bank count, sub-banking and port count of the L2 are not published. On the die the layout is literal: the ANE is built around the central L2 SRAM rectangle, and "The 7+7 side cores take L2 ingress horizontally from the cyan vertical trunk; but the two top cores need the same horizontal wide interface rotated and escaped vertically, which likely produces that conspicuous vertical comb in the top ingress."
- **SRAM bank (per-core 64 KiB kernel memory, 16x = 1 MiB)** — "KMem: 16x per-core 64 KiB 'L1' SRAM for kernel. Total 1 MiB." (verified — Yoon, 2026). Each core's kernel bank is private and replicated — "Kernel memory is private per core (replicated 16x). They thought that weights would be reused many times per-core." The firmware dumps each 64 KiB bank separately (KMem #0 through #15). Kernel memory is load-only: "KernelDMA is unidirectional load-only. They thought that weights would not be written back." Whether each 64 KiB bank is one SRAM array or sub-banked is not published.
- **SRAM / staging (per-core L1 MAC-input staging area)** — "L1: 16x per-core MAC input 'L1' staging area." (verified — Yoon, 2026). The staging area feeds the MAC inputs from L2; its size is not published — the Level-2 boundary record already states this, and this run found nothing new on it.
- **DMA engine (KernelDMASrc — sixteen logical coefficient lanes)** — "KernelDMASrc[0..15]: sixteen logical coefficient lanes copy weights from DRAM into the matching per-core KMem banks." (verified — Yoon, 2026). "The sixteen KernelDMASrc register lanes do not by themselves prove sixteen physically independent DMA front ends." A lane-scaling experiment shows the logical lanes make concurrent progress, but "They may still merge into shared request-generation, crossbar, cache, and DRAM arbitration." The lane count is logical; the physical front-end count is not published.
- **DMA engine (TileDMASrc and TileDMADst)** — "TileDMASrc: copies tiles from DRAM to L2." and "TileDMADst: copies tiles from L2 to DRAM." (verified — Yoon, 2026). "TileDMA is bidirectional and shared. Intermediate tile outputs can be fed back without a round-trip to DRAM." The engines take source, destination and size and transfer that block of memory; their queue depths, request widths and address-counter widths are not published.
- **Crossbar and switch arbiter (shared request generation, crossbar, cache and DRAM arbitration)** — The sixteen kernel lanes "may still merge into shared request-generation, crossbar, cache, and DRAM arbitration." (verified — Yoon, 2026). The article's own words name the shared downstream fabric; its port counts, arbitration policy and per-agent bandwidth shares are not published. The serial kernel-plus-tile behaviour is measured at the DMA level, not in the fabric: "Thus, ANE's kernel and tile DMA requests are sent serially (one at a time)."
- **Address counters (TileSrc / TileDst geometry counters)** — The descriptor's TileSrc section programs base, row, plane, depth and group — "TileSrc: base=0 row=1 plane=4" and "TileSrc: depth=32 group=32" — and TileDst programs row, plane, depth and group — "TileDst: row=1 plane=4 depth=12 group=12" (verified — Yoon, 2026, hexdump decode). The DMA engines walk those geometries to generate strided addresses; the counter widths are not published.
- **Mux (the missing L2→KMem path — absent by design)** — There is no mux or path from L2 into kernel memory: "New kernels must be loaded from DRAM, and not L2." (verified — Yoon, 2026). The article argues the omission was a 2017 assumption, not a bandwidth decision: "I argue that a kernel path riding the same tile path is not that bad." and "Apple simply never expected L2-resident tensors to become kernels, which was a valid assumption in 2017." The absence is the primitive-level fact — a mux that does not exist — and it is what makes transformer KV caches pay a DRAM round trip for every kernel reload.
- **FIFO / queue (DMA staging — serial kernel-then-tile issue)** — The two DMA engines are not queued side by side: "Experiment shows that the kernel+tile combined runtime matched the sum of the isolated runtimes. If the requests overlapped at all, then the shorter path would contribute little or no additional time, but execution time (not throughput) is strictly monotonic." (verified — Yoon, 2026). The fitted model is T_AB = 0.001 + 0.939 T_A + 0.981 T_B. There is no published command queue or credit counter between the two engines; the serial issue is the observed behaviour.
- **Register file (L2 source/result configuration)** — The descriptor's L2 section programs the local source and result: "L2.Source: base=0 channel=1" and "L2.Result: base=0x20 channel=0 row=0" (verified — Yoon, 2026, hexdump decode). The L2 configuration registers select which tile region feeds the MACs and where the result lands; the register count beyond the decoded fields is not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the published M1 memory geometry is a shared 2 MiB L2, sixteen 64 KiB per-core kernel banks totalling 1 MiB, a per-core L1 staging area of unpublished size, sixteen logical KernelDMASrc lanes, TileDMASrc and TileDMADst, and measured M3 DRAM read throughputs of 37.99 GB/s (KernelDMA) and 59.08 GB/s (TileDMA) against a ~100 GB/s ceiling. Below that level — L2 bank organisation and port counts, kernel-memory sub-banking, the crossbar's port counts and arbitration policy, DMA queue depths and address-counter widths — Apple publishes nothing and the reverse-engineering source describes no circuits, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no L2→KMem path, because kernels load only from DRAM; and there is no parallel kernel-plus-tile DMA issue, because the two engines are sent serially and their runtimes add.

#### Down to the gates: The 16-core MAC array and the task-descriptor scheduler — a fixed datapath with no instruction set

Apple publishes no gate-level structure for the ANE — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the block. The deepest published description is Yoon's reverse engineering of the M1 ANE (2026), which maps the block at register and descriptor level: the 16-core MAC array, the 32-bit Q16.16 accumulator, the fused activation lookup table, the Task Manager and its eight task queues, and the 628-byte task descriptor. A gate-term search of that article this run found nothing: the words transistor, flip-flop, latch and NAND do not occur anywhere in its text. Its only circuit-adjacent material is a block diagram of one MAC lane — MULTIPLIER, 32-BIT ADDER, ACCUMULATOR — and an RTL sketch of the two TM_INFO counters, which the article itself presents as a proposed implementation, not a published Apple circuit. Apple's own publications describe the ANE's role and performance, never its circuits, and the only transistor figure anywhere in the published ANE material is the M4 SoC's 28-billion-transistor total, a chip count, not a circuit. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about Apple's circuits.

- **Register file (the datapath configuration registers)** — A task descriptor is a serialized register dump, so the configuration registers are the datapath's state: one D flip-flop per stored bit (about 20-28 transistors each, primer, bottom layer), with the descriptor's section writes landing through the ControlDMA data path. Arithmetic from the published geometry: the 628-byte descriptor for a 1x1 convolution is 157 32-bit words, so if every word lands in its own register field the configuration storage is at most 5,024 flip-flop bits, about 0.10-0.14M transistors — an upper bound, because the descriptor includes a header and the register count beyond the decoded fields is not published. The nine MMIO apertures are address space, not register counts: Common, L2, PE, NE/MAC, Tile DMA source and destination, Kernel, Task Manager and Task Queues occupy 0x4000-byte apertures (0x1000 for the Task Manager and Task Queues), and how many of those addresses are implemented registers is not published. Standard construction.
- **DMA engine (ControlDMA — the descriptor burst-write)** — ControlDMA at gate level is a small unidirectional DMA engine: a 32-bit address counter (32 D flip-flops plus a 32-bit incrementer of 32 full adders, about 1,536-1,792 transistors by the primer's counter form), a 32-bit data register holding the word in flight, a transfer-word decoder for the count-minus-1 and base-index fields, and an FSM sequencing the burst — state flip-flops plus NAND/NOR next-state logic. The transfer word itself is published: register count minus 1 in bits 31:26, first register base index in bits 25:2, and the decoded KernelDMASrc header 0xf401f800 is 62 words at register base 0x1f800 by arithmetic. ControlDMA's queue depth, request width and channel count are not published, so no engine total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (the TM_INFO descriptor counters)** — TM_INFO maps onto two counters in the article's own RTL sketch: a word counter that wraps at descriptor_dwords_minus_1 and increments a descriptor counter. The sketch is the article's proposed implementation, not a published Apple circuit — the published fact is the field split, descriptor_dwords minus 1 in bits [31:16] and descriptor_count in bits [15:0]. At gate level a counter is N flip-flops plus N full adders: both fields are 16 bits, so each counter is 16 flip-flops (320-448 transistors) plus a 16-bit incrementer (448 transistors), 768-896 transistors per counter, about 1,536-1,792 transistors for the pair — arithmetic from the published field widths, using the sketch's two-counter form. The terminal-count compare is one XOR per counter bit plus an AND tree, and encoding length minus 1 keeps the termination out of the critical path. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the Task Manager)** — The Task Manager at gate level is an FSM: state bits in master-slave D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each) with next-state and output logic as a NAND/NOR network, plus the TM_ADDR, TM_INFO and TM_PUSH staging registers it commits atomically on the doorbell write. The published contract is the launch behaviour — nothing happens until TM_PUSH is written, the hardware then owns the submission until it raises a completion interrupt — and the priority table TQ_PRTY_TABLE that the doorbell write carries. The state count, the scheduling policy across the eight queues and the priority table's contents are not published, so no FSM total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Register file (the task-queue register block)** — Each queue's register block is eight copies of the same storage, one per qid, stepping 0x148 bytes: STATUS, PRIORITY, VACANT and INFO, then the two command-stream slots with their BAR tables, NIDs, SIZEs and ADDRs. Arithmetic from the published layout: 0x148 bytes is 82 32-bit words per queue, and 64 of those words are the two 32-entry BAR tables, leaving 18 words per queue — 576 bits — of status, priority, vacancy and launch-context registers, 4,608 bits across the eight queues, about 0.09-0.13M transistors as flip-flops. The BAR storage itself is counted in its own primitive below, not here. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (the two ping-pong command-stream slots)** — The ping-pong slots are the ANE's only command queueing, and at gate level they are two register sets, not a FIFO: each slot holds one command stream's BAR table, NID, SIZE and ADDR, and a one-bit slot-select flip-flop chooses which slot executes while software modifies the other. There is no storage array, no write/read pointer counters and no full/empty comparators here, because there is no ring buffer of descriptors — the descriptor count per stream is the TM_INFO count, not a queue depth. The slot-select and the two BAR tables are the whole queueing mechanism, and the BAR transistor arithmetic is in the BAR primitive below. Standard construction.
- **Register file (the 32-entry BAR table)** — Each BAR table is 32 entries of 32-bit base addresses, two tables per queue (BAR1 and BAR2, one per ping-pong slot), 64 entries per queue and 512 across the eight queues by arithmetic from the published layout. As flip-flops that is 512 x 32 = 16,384 storage bits, about 0.33-0.46M transistors; as a small SRAM it would be 512 x 32 6T cells, 98,304 cell transistors plus the decoder and muxes — the storage form is not published, so neither total is claimed as the implementation, only the bit count is arithmetic from the published layout. The relocation itself is base-plus-offset addition, one small adder per address translation, of unpublished width. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (128 FP16 / 256 INT8 MAC lanes per core)** — Each MAC lane bottoms out in a 16-bit multiplier in the standard array form: AND gates form the partial products, a full-adder compressor tree collapses them, and one final carry-propagate adder finishes. Arithmetic from the published lane count, using the primer's cell costs (AND2 6 transistors, full adder about 28): one 16-bit multiplier is 256 AND gates (1,536 transistors) plus 240 full adders (6,720 transistors) plus a 32-bit final adder (896 transistors), about 9,152 transistors; across the 2,048 FP16 lanes that is about 18.7M transistors of multiplier. The FP16 path is the published one; the INT8 doubling to 256 lanes per core is not decomposed further, because whether one 16-bit multiplier serves two INT8 lanes or each INT8 lane has its own multiplier is not published — if the INT8 lanes are separate 8-bit multipliers, each is about 2,400 transistors by the same arithmetic (64 AND gates, 56 full adders, a 16-bit final adder) and 4,096 of them would be about 9.8M transistors, a conditional figure, not a claim. Standard construction.
- **Adder (the per-lane 32-bit accumulate adder)** — The per-lane adder is a 32-bit adder in the standard form: 32 full-adder cells (about 28 transistors each, primer, bottom layer), about 896 transistors per lane in ripple form, more with carry-lookahead prefix networks, which the article does not describe. Across the 2,048 lanes that is about 1.8M transistors of accumulate adder by arithmetic from the published lane count. The adder's carry structure — ripple, lookahead or prefix — is not published, so the ripple figure is the lower bound, not the implementation. Standard construction.
- **Accumulator registers (the 32-bit Q16.16 running sums)** — Each lane's running sum is a 32-bit register: 32 D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each), with the feedback path from the adder output back to the register input holding the partial sum local to the lane between MAC cycles — the article's own datapath diagram shows exactly this loop, MULTIPLIER, 32-BIT ADDER, ACCUMULATOR, with the sum fed back. Arithmetic from the published lane count: 2,048 lanes x 32 bits is 65,536 register bits, about 1.3-1.8M transistors of accumulator storage. There is no cross-lane adder tree to decompose, because each lane reduces over time in its own accumulator. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (accumulator saturation at 2^15)** — The saturation is a compare-and-clamp on the 32-bit sum: a comparator tree over the integer field of the Q16.16 sum — XOR gates per compared bit feeding an AND tree — testing whether the sum exceeds the signed 16-bit integer range, and a clamp mux selecting the saturated value when it does. The clamp mux is 32 2:1 muxes, 4 transistors per mux, 128 transistors per lane, about 0.26M transistors across the 2,048 lanes by arithmetic. The comparator's exact width and the clamp values' encoding are not published beyond the measured behaviour — the accumulator saturates at 2^15, proved by the 0x7c00 output for an input of 128 — so no comparator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux (activation-mode select: identity / ReLU / tanh LUT)** — The NonlinearMode field is a 2-bit select driving per-output muxes: identity passes the sum through, ReLU selects between the sum and zero, tanh selects the lookup-table output. At gate level that is a 3:1 mux per output bit — two 2:1 muxes in a tree, 8 transistors per bit — and the output is FP16, so 16 bits x 8 transistors is 128 transistors per lane, about 0.26M transistors across the 2,048 lanes by arithmetic. BiasMode and PostScaleMode are further select fields in the same register block, driving the same mux form at unpublished widths. The tanh interpolation hardware itself — the subtractor, multiplier and adder that apply the interpolation weight alpha — is not described in the source, so no interpolator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Lookup table (the 33-entry piecewise-linear tanh table)** — The table is 33 FP16 words, 528 bits of storage, held in the compiled coefficient region at offset 0x4288. As flip-flops that is 528 x 20-28 transistors, about 10.6-14.8K transistors; as a small ROM or SRAM it would be far fewer — 528 6T cells is 3,168 cell transistors plus a 5-bit row decoder — and the storage form is not published, so neither total is claimed as the implementation. The addressing is published in behaviour: u = 2^R|x| with R = 3 maps the input into table coordinates, floor and ceil select the adjacent entries through a 2:1 mux per bit, and alpha = u minus floor(u) is the interpolation weight between them — the impulse test proves the interpolation, a triangle rising from 0 at |x| = 7/8 to 1 at |x| = 1 and falling back to 0 at |x| = 9/8. Standard construction.
- **Register file (fixed-point binary point — NE BinaryPoint=28)** — The BinaryPoint field is a small register field in the NE section holding the value 28 in the decoded 1x1-convolution descriptor — the binary point that positions the fixed-point result. Its width is not published beyond the decoded value, which needs at least 5 bits to hold 28, so no register total is claimed. The scaling it drives is a shifter in the standard form — a barrel shifter is log2(W) stages of 2:1 muxes, 4 transistors per mux per bit — of unpublished width, and the field's only published content is the value itself. Standard construction.

Honesty: Apple publishes the ANE at block and register level only — 16 cores, 128 FP16 (256 INT8) MAC lanes per core, a 16-bit multiplier with a 32-bit Q16.16 accumulator saturating at 2^15, a 33-entry tanh lookup table over [0,4], 8 task queues with two ping-pong slots and 32-entry BAR tables each, a 628-byte task descriptor, and the ControlDMA and TM_INFO field formats (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the block appears in any Apple source or in the reverse-engineering writeup. Everything above is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about Apple's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable). Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no cross-lane adder tree, because each lane reduces over time in its own accumulator; and there is no instruction decoder, because the task descriptor is a register dump, not code.

#### Down to the gates: The memory system — a shared 2 MiB L2, per-core kernel memory, and three DMA engines

Apple publishes no gate-level structure for the ANE's memory system either — the published geometry is the M1 generation's: a shared 2 MiB L2, sixteen 64 KiB per-core kernel banks totalling 1 MiB, a per-core L1 staging area of unpublished size, sixteen logical KernelDMASrc lanes, TileDMASrc and TileDMADst, and measured M3 DRAM read throughputs of 37.99 GB/s for KernelDMA and 59.08 GB/s for TileDMA against a roughly 100 GB/s ceiling. The same gate-term search applies: the Yoon article's full text carries no transistor, flip-flop, latch or NAND content, and its die-layout description — the central L2 SRAM rectangle with seven cores down each side, two across the top and shared control logic along the bottom — is a floorplan observation, not a circuit. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors on the same terms as the MAC-array block: published geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about Apple's circuits.

- **SRAM bank (the shared 2 MiB L2 tile memory)** — The L2 is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. Arithmetic from the published size: 2 MiB is 16,777,216 bits, so the cell array alone is 100,663,296 transistors, about 100.7M — the cells, not the bank, because the bank count, sub-banking and port count are not published and the decoder, mux and sense-amplifier totals need them. The firmware dumps the L2 as a single 0x200000-byte region, and the die layout shows one central SRAM rectangle, but neither proves a single bank. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (per-core 64 KiB kernel memory, 16x = 1 MiB)** — Each core's kernel bank is the same 6T SRAM form: cell array, row decoder, column muxes and sense amplifiers, replicated sixteen times, load-only — weights are never written back. Arithmetic from the published size: 64 KiB per core is 524,288 bits, 3,145,728 cell transistors per bank; across the sixteen cores 1 MiB is 8,388,608 bits, 50,331,648 cell transistors, about 50.3M for the cell arrays alone. Whether each 64 KiB bank is one SRAM array or sub-banked is not published, so the decoder, mux and sense-amplifier totals are not claimed. Standard construction.
- **SRAM / staging (per-core L1 MAC-input staging area)** — The L1 staging area feeds the MAC inputs from L2, and its storage form is not published — it could be a register array of D flip-flops (about 20-28 transistors each per bit) or a small SRAM of 6T cells, and its size is not published either, so no transistor total is claimed at all. The gate form is therefore stated conditionally: as registers it would be one flip-flop per staged bit plus the muxes selecting staged or fresh operands, as SRAM it would be the primer's bank form at an unpublished capacity. This is the one primitive in the memory system with no published size to anchor any arithmetic to. Standard construction.
- **DMA engine (KernelDMASrc — sixteen logical coefficient lanes)** — Each logical lane at gate level is an address counter plus a data-path slice: a counter is N flip-flops plus N full adders, and the data path is registers plus muxes selecting the lane's weights into its kernel bank. The counter widths are not published — the addresses are IOMMU virtual addresses of unpublished width — so no lane total is claimed. The sixteen lanes make concurrent progress but may merge into shared request generation, crossbar, cache and DRAM arbitration downstream, so the sixteen logical lanes are not sixteen physically independent DMA front ends, and the physical front-end count is not published. Standard construction.
- **DMA engine (TileDMASrc and TileDMADst)** — TileDMASrc and TileDMADst are DMA engines in the same standard form as ControlDMA: address counters (N flip-flops plus N full adders each), data registers, transfer-size comparators and an FSM sequencing the block transfer — the engines take source, destination and size and transfer that block of memory. Their queue depths, request widths and address-counter widths are not published, so no engine total is claimed. TileDMA is bidirectional and shared, so one engine's data path serves both directions through direction-select muxes, and intermediate tile outputs can feed the next operation without a DRAM round-trip. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar and switch arbiter (shared request generation, crossbar, cache and DRAM arbitration)** — The shared downstream fabric is a crossbar under an arbiter in the standard form: per output bit a mux tree selecting among the input ports — an R:1 mux is R-1 2:1 muxes, 4 transistors per mux — and an arbiter that is a priority-encoder tree of AND/OR gates plus a grant register of D flip-flops holding the winner until the transfer clears. The article's own words name the shared fabric — the sixteen kernel lanes may merge into shared request generation, crossbar, cache and DRAM arbitration — but its port counts, arbitration policy and per-agent bandwidth shares are not published, so no crossbar or arbiter total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Address counters (TileSrc / TileDst geometry counters)** — The TileSrc and TileDst geometry fields — base, row, plane, depth, group — are address counters in the standard form: one counter per geometry dimension, each N flip-flops plus N full adders, with a terminal-count comparator (one XOR per bit plus an AND tree) stepping to the next row, plane or group. The decoded values are published — TileSrc base 0, row 1, plane 4, depth 32, group 32; TileDst row 1, plane 4, depth 12, group 12 — but the counter widths are not published, so no counter total is claimed. The counters generate the strided addresses the DMA engines walk; the stride arithmetic itself is the descriptor's geometry, not a separate circuit. Standard construction.
- **Mux (the missing L2→KMem path — absent by design)** — There is no mux to decompose here, and that is the primitive-level fact: no path runs from L2 into kernel memory, so there is no select network, no L2 read port feeding kernels and no gate count for this primitive — zero gates, by design, not by omission. A kernel path riding the tile path would have needed a mux per kernel-memory write bit selecting L2 or DRAM data, plus the L2 read port and address decode to feed it; Apple built none of it, because in 2017 it never expected L2-resident tensors to become kernels. The absence is what makes transformer KV caches pay a DRAM round trip for every kernel reload. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (DMA staging — serial kernel-then-tile issue)** — There is no FIFO or queue between the kernel and tile DMA engines to decompose: the two engines are sent serially, one at a time, so their runtimes add — the fitted model is T_AB = 0.001 + 0.939 T_A + 0.981 T_B — and no command queue or credit counter between them is published. At gate level the serial issue is the absence of queueing: no storage array, no pointer counters and no full/empty comparators sit between the two engines, because the issue order is fixed in the task descriptor chain, not arbitrated at run time. The queueing that does exist lives inside each engine's own request path, of unpublished depth. Standard construction.
- **Register file (L2 source/result configuration)** — The L2 source and result configuration is a small register file in the standard form: D flip-flops holding the decoded fields — L2.Source base 0, channel 1; L2.Result base 0x20, channel 0, row 0 — with the select logic routing the chosen tile region to the MACs and the result region to the write path. The register count beyond the decoded fields is not published, so no register total is claimed; the published content is the field values themselves, decoded from the 1x1-convolution descriptor. Standard construction.

Honesty: Apple publishes the M1 memory geometry and none of its circuits: a shared 2 MiB L2, sixteen 64 KiB per-core kernel banks totalling 1 MiB, a per-core L1 staging area of unpublished size, sixteen logical KernelDMASrc lanes, TileDMASrc and TileDMADst, and measured M3 DRAM read throughputs of 37.99 GB/s (KernelDMA) and 59.08 GB/s (TileDMA) against a roughly 100 GB/s ceiling (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and the arithmetic above is derived from those published sizes. Below that level — L2 bank organisation and port counts, kernel-memory sub-banking, the crossbar's port counts and arbitration policy, DMA queue depths and address-counter widths — Apple publishes nothing and the reverse-engineering source describes no circuits, and this decomposition invents nothing. Two things are absent by design and are stated as such: there is no L2-to-kernel-memory path, because kernels load only from DRAM; and there is no parallel kernel-plus-tile DMA issue, because the two engines are sent serially and their runtimes add.

**Key numbers.** A11 (2017) 0.6 TFLOPS FP16; A15 (2021) 15.8 TFLOPS, 26x the first generation; M1 11 TOPS at 68 GB/s system DRAM bandwidth; A17 Pro 35 TOPS, 16 cores, up to 2x the A16; M4 38 TOPS, 60x the A11 first generation, 28 billion transistors on second-generation 3 nm; 16 cores in every generation from A14/M1 onward.

**Signature ideas.**
1. **Placement over peak** — one fabric hop from the ISP and GPU, buffers in the shared pool: invocation cost and copies matter more than the multiplier count.
2. **Task descriptors instead of an instruction set** — the compiler turns a model into a chain of fixed-size register dumps; the driver rings one doorbell and the hardware owns the job to completion.
3. **The kernel/tile split** — weights live in private per-core kernel memory, activations in a shared L2, moved by three separate DMA engines; each operand class gets the lifecycle it needs.
4. **Fused post-MAC activation** — sums feed straight into identity, ReLU, or a 33-entry tanh lookup table with no intermediate memory round-trip.

**Limits & tradeoffs.** A closed box: operator coverage is fixed per silicon generation, the programming model is Apple's alone, and workloads that miss the supported op set fall back to GPU/CPU at a fraction of the efficiency. There is no instruction set, so a workload the compiler cannot express as task descriptors does not run. Short-sequence transformers are bandwidth-bound on the ANE — latency stays flat across sequence lengths 32 to 128 because fetching the weights dominates. And the split memory means a locally produced tensor cannot become a kernel without a DRAM round trip, which is exactly what transformer KV caches need.

**Lineage.** First generation in the A11 Bionic (iPhone X, 2017), built for dense CNNs — Face ID and Memoji. Eight cores from the A12, sixteen from the A14 and M1, which carried the ANE to the Mac and iPad. The fifth generation (A15) reached 15.8 TFLOPS; the A17 Pro doubled the A16 to 35 TOPS; the M4 reached 38 TOPS. It powers Face ID, Deep Fusion and the Photonic Engine, on-device Siri and autocorrect, Personal Voice, and Apple Intelligence. Its fixed-datapath bet — compile-time knowledge of the model in exchange for efficiency — is the ancestor every phone NPU since has copied, and the tension it created with transformer workloads is the reason later Apple silicon pairs the ANE with programmable GPU-side matrix hardware.

**One-line summary.** A fixed-function NPU that wins by placement, not peak: sixteen MAC cores around a shared L2, fed by compiled task descriptors and three DMA engines, sitting one fabric hop from the camera in a shared pool of memory.
