### NVIDIA NVENC / NVDEC (Ada)

**Added: 2026-11-22** (mirrored to the corpus 2026-11-26 with the Level-2 deepening; the corpus had no entry for it before this run)

**Specs (wiki card).** Dual NVENC in AD102 · AV1 encode · 8K60

**What it is / why it matters.** NVIDIA's fixed-function media engines: dual encoders with AV1 support, decoupled from CUDA cores so streaming never steals compute.

**Building blocks.**
- **Dual NVENC encode pipelines (8th gen)** — Two fully independent encoders — motion estimation, prediction, mode decision — running 8K60 or multiple concurrent streams without touching a single CUDA core
- **Multi-standard entropy engine** — CABAC for H.264/HEVC alongside AV1's multi-symbol arithmetic entropy coder. AV1 does not use CABAC, so Ada carries both entropy designs — breakdowns that list only 'CABAC' for an AV1 encoder are incomplete
- **Transform / quantisation + rate control** — The encode loop's back half: DCT/DST-class transforms, quantisation and per-frame rate control deciding where bits are spent
- **Optical Flow Accelerator** — A separate fixed-function block (shared with the DLSS pipeline) estimating dense inter-frame motion
- **NVDEC decode pipeline** — An independent decoder for AV1/HEVC/H.264/VP9 that runs concurrently with encode and with CUDA compute — three tenants, no interference

**The piece that makes it special.** Independence. NVENC's value is not raw encode quality — a slow software encoder still wins bits-per-quality — it is that encoding costs the GPU nothing. The streamer, the game and the recorder each get dedicated silicon, which is the heterogeneity argument in its purest form.

#### Inside the signature block: The dual NVENC encode pipelines — two 8th-generation encoders sharing one frame

**Inside it.** On the GeForce RTX 4090 and RTX 4080 the encode side of the media block is two complete 8th-generation NVENC engines; professional Ada parts with 12 GB of memory or more carry three. Each engine is a full end-to-end encoder in its own right — NVIDIA's application note defines the contract as motion estimation and mode decision, motion compensation and residual coding, and entropy coding, for H.264, HEVC 8- and 10-bit, and AV1 8- and 10-bit — so the second engine is not a helper that takes one stage off the first, it is a second whole encoder. Ada's new codec is AV1: the main profile at 8- and 10-bit, 4:2:0, up to 8192×8192, with up to seven reference frames and non-reference, reference and hierarchical B-frames — and because AV1 does not use CABAC, the entropy stage carries a second, multi-symbol arithmetic coder beside the CABAC path H.264 and HEVC use. The two engines are coordinated in two ways. For many sessions the driver load-balances encode jobs across them with no application code; for one big session, split-frame encoding (Video Codec SDK 12.0, HEVC and AV1 only) cuts a single frame in half and hands one half to each engine, which is the only way one session can exceed one engine's rate. A third mode exposes the motion estimator alone: ME-only mode returns macroblock-level motion vectors so an application can do depth estimation, frame interpolation, or hybrid encoding with NVENC doing the search and something else doing the rest. NVIDIA publishes no internal sub-block diagram for NVENC — no stage latencies, queue depths, reference-store sizes or buffer geometry — so this block describes the published pipeline stages and the API-visible contract, and invents no circuits inside them.

**Trace — one unit of work: one 8K60 AV1 frame through the dual encoders.**
1. **Frame arrives from VRAM.**A rendered or captured 8K frame is handed to the encode session from GPU memory; the graphics engine and CUDA cores are already free, because the frame's encode will not touch them.
2. **Split-frame decision.**For a single 8K60 session the application enables split-frame encoding, which cuts the frame between the two NVENC engines; for separate sessions the driver load-balances each engine's own stream instead. Without split-frame encoding a single session cannot exceed one engine's rate, however many engines the card has.
3. **Motion estimation and mode decision.**Each engine searches motion against up to seven AV1 reference frames and chooses intra or inter prediction per block — the most expensive stage of the pipeline, and the one ME-only mode exposes on its own.
4. **Compensation, transform, quantise.**Motion compensation forms the residual, which is transformed and quantised under the session's rate control — the preset and rate-control mode that decide the quality-versus-speed trade.
5. **Entropy coding.**The AV1 multi-symbol arithmetic coder packs the quantised residuals and mode data into the bitstream; H.264 and HEVC sessions take the CABAC path in the same engine instead.
6. **Bitstream out, halves rejoined.**Each engine emits its half's bitstream; the driver recombines the two halves into one 8K60 AV1 stream, while the third engine on professional parts encodes further 4K or 1080p streams in parallel.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the encode tax on the whole machine: before NVENC, streaming meant a second PC for capture or a slice of the gaming GPU's own compute; with the encode fully offloaded, the game renders, the stream encodes and the CPU stays out of both. Creates a fixed-function ceiling instead: the codec menu closes at tape-out — Ada has no VVC path — and a single session's speed is capped at one engine's rate unless split-frame encoding is switched on, so the second engine only helps a single stream when the application asks for it; NVIDIA positions 8K60 AV1 as a multiple-NVENC job in the SDK's own high-performance presets. The per-engine rate is also the unit of capacity: at 1080p one Ada engine encodes AV1 at 1,090 frames a second at the fastest preset, so the 8K60 headline is a two-engine achievement, not one engine with headroom to spare.

**Governing numbers.** 2 NVENC engines on GeForce RTX 4090/4080; 3 on Ada professional GPUs with 12 GB of memory or more; AV1 main profile, YUV 4:2:0, 8- and 10-bit, up to 8192×8192; up to 7 AV1 reference frames; per-engine 1080p encode rates on RTX 4090 at 2,415 MHz video clock (Video Codec SDK 13.0, indicative): AV1 1,090 fps (P1, CBR, low-latency), HEVC 1,055 fps (P1, CBR, low-latency), H.264 910 fps (P1, CBR, low-latency); dual NVENC: 8K60 or four 4K60; AV1 40% more efficient than the H.264 encoder in GeForce RTX 30 Series GPUs (NVIDIA); GeForce concurrent encode sessions: 12 per the October 2026 support matrix — the SDK 13.0 application note text still says 8 (see fact record). Internal stage latencies, queue depths and buffer sizes: not published.

**Primary source.** NVIDIA, 'NVIDIA Ada GPU Architecture' whitepaper V2.02 — 'NVIDIA Broadcast/Video' section and Conclusion; NVIDIA, 'NVIDIA Ada Lovelace Professional GPU Architecture' whitepaper v1.1 — NVENC section; NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.0, NVENC Application Note — §§1–4 and AV1/H.264/HEVC performance tables; NVIDIA Video Encode and Decode GPU Support Matrix (October 16, 2026).

#### Inside the signature block: The NVDEC decode pipeline — one 5th-generation decoder, independent of encode and compute

**Inside it.** Decode is a separate block from encode, and on GeForce it is a single one: every GeForce product carries one NVDEC, so the RTX 4090 pairs two encoders with one decoder, while select Quadro and Tesla parts carry two or three decoders per chip. The decoder is the 5th generation, first launched with Ampere: hardware decode of MPEG-2, VC-1, H.264, HEVC, VP8, VP9 and AV1, with 8192×8192 decode for HEVC, VP9 and AV1 and 8K60 decode fully supported. Its contract is independence: with decoding offloaded to NVDEC the graphics engine and CPU are free, and decode runs concurrently with encode and with CUDA post-processing — the transcoding triangle the Video Codec SDK is built around. NVDEC holds multiple hardware decoding contexts with what NVIDIA calls a negligible context-switching penalty, so many streams decode in parallel subject only to the engine's rate and available memory; the NVDECODE API also exposes post-processing on the decoded output — scaling, cropping, aspect-ratio conversion, deinterlacing and colour-space conversion — so the frame can leave NVDEC already in display form. NVIDIA publishes no internal sub-block diagram for NVDEC either — no entropy-decoder, inverse-transform or reference-store internals — so, as with NVENC, this block describes the published contract and the API-visible pipeline, not invented circuits.

**Trace — one unit of work: one AV1 frame through the decoder.**
1. **Bitstream arrives.**An AV1 bitstream is handed to a decode session; NVDEC selects that session's hardware context, a switch NVIDIA describes as carrying a negligible penalty.
2. **Entropy decode and reconstruction.**NVDEC parses the bitstream and reconstructs the frame against its reference frames — the inverse of the encode loop, carried out entirely in the fixed-function block with no CUDA involvement.
3. **Reference frames held in video memory.**Decoded frames stay available as references for the frames that follow them; the application never stages them through the CPU.
4. **Post-processing in the block.**The NVDECODE API's post-processing runs on the decoded output — scaling, cropping, aspect-ratio conversion, deinterlacing, colour-space conversion — so the frame can exit NVDEC already in its display or training format.
5. **Frame out, in parallel with everything else.**The decoded frame goes to the display engine or to a CUDA consumer, while NVENC encodes another stream and the SMs keep rendering — three tenants on one die, no interference.
6. **Next session, same engine.**A second stream's context is selected on the same single NVDEC; on GeForce the aggregate decode rate is one engine's rate, so a second stream shares the engine rather than getting a second one.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the decode tax the same way NVENC relieves encode: video playback and transcoding stop competing with the game or the training job for SMs and CPU cores, and the faster-than-real-time rate makes NVDEC a transcoding engine, not just a player. Creates a single-engine ceiling on GeForce: the RTX 4090's two encoders can outrun its one decoder, so a transcode farm that decodes as fast as it encodes wants the professional parts with two or three NVDECs, or more cards. And the codec menu is fixed like NVENC's: H.264 8K decode waits for Blackwell — Ada's NVDEC does not do 8192×8192 H.264.

**Governing numbers.** 1 NVDEC on all GeForce products (RTX 4090 included); 2–3 NVDEC engines on select Quadro/Tesla Ada parts; decode: MPEG-2, VC-1, H.264, HEVC, VP8, VP9, AV1; 8192×8192 decode for HEVC, VP9, AV1; 8K60 decode fully supported; per-engine 1080p decode rates on Ada at 2,160 MHz video clock (Video Codec SDK 13.0, indicative): AV1 1,018 fps, HEVC 1,641 fps, HEVC Main10 1,520 fps, VP9 1,290 fps, H.264 903 fps; multiple hardware decode contexts with negligible context-switching penalty; H.264 8192×8192 decode: not supported on Ada (Blackwell only). Internal stage breakdown: not published.

**Primary source.** NVIDIA, 'NVIDIA Ada GPU Architecture' whitepaper V2.02 — 'NVIDIA Broadcast/Video' section; NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.0, NVDEC Application Note — §§1–4 and decode performance table.

#### Down to the primitives: The dual NVENC encode pipelines — two 8th-generation encoders sharing one frame

The two NVENC engines run the published encode pipeline — motion estimation and mode decision, motion compensation and residual coding, entropy coding — and each stage is built from the primitives below. Numbers that come from a codec specification are spec facts about the algorithm, not published facts about Ada's silicon; where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **SRAM bank (reference frame store)** — The motion estimator searches against up to seven AV1 reference frames (verified — NVENC Application Note, SDK 13.0; already recorded at Level 2), so each engine must hold several decoded frames on chip while it searches them. That store is an SRAM bank — or a set of banks, one per reference — written by the reconstruction loop and read by the motion estimator and the motion compensator. Its capacity in frames, its banking and its port count are not published. Standard construction for the store itself; the seven-reference-frame figure is a published contract, not a bank size.
- **FIFO / queue (frame ingest and split-frame handoff)** — Frames arrive from VRAM and are queued to an encode session; in split-frame mode the frame is cut in half and one half is handed to each NVENC engine (verified — NVENC Application Note: split-frame encoding, SDK 12.0, HEVC and AV1 only; already recorded at Level 2). The ingest queue and the split-frame handoff are FIFOs decoupling the frame source from the two engines. Their depths and widths are not published.
- **Adder tree + comparator (motion-estimation SAD and best-match selection)** — Motion estimation scores each candidate displacement by a sum of absolute differences: per-pixel subtractors feeding an adder tree, with a comparator keeping the lowest-cost candidate as the search proceeds. The search is the most expensive stage of the pipeline, and the one ME-only mode exposes on its own (verified — NVENC Application Note; already recorded at Level 2). The candidate set, the search range, the block sizes the search covers and the SAD datapath width are not published. Standard construction for the SAD arithmetic.
- **Multiplier array (motion-compensation 8-tap interpolation)** — Sub-pixel motion compensation interpolates reference samples with the codec's filters, and AV1's are 8-tap: the spec names EIGHTTAP, EIGHTTAP_SMOOTH and EIGHTTAP_SHARP, and its inter-prediction process sums eight filter taps per sample (verified — AV1 Bitstream & Decoding Process Specification v1.0.0 with Errata 1, §7.11.3 inter prediction). Each tap is a multiply, so the interpolator is a multiplier array feeding an adder tree. This is a spec fact about the algorithm the silicon must implement, not a published fact about Ada's interpolator geometry — the array's width and tap parallelism are not published.
- **Adder tree + multiplier array (transform butterflies and quantisation)** — The residual is transformed and quantised. AV1's transform stage is four separable 1-D transforms — DCT, ADST, flipped ADST and identity — combinable into 16 2-D kernels, applied at 19 scales from 64x64 down to 4x4 (verified — libaom AV1 Encoder Guide: "AV1 implements the transform stage using 4 seperable 1-d transforms (DCT, ADST, FLIPADST and IDTX, where FLIPADST is the reversed version of ADST and IDTX is the identity transform) which can be combined to give 16 2-d combinations" and "These combinations can be applied at 19 different scales from 64x64 pixels down to 4x4 pixels"). A butterfly stage is an adder tree with coefficient multipliers; quantisation is a further multiply by the reciprocal step. Spec facts about the transform set; the butterfly depth, the multiplier count and the quantiser datapath are not published.
- **Register file (CDF probability tables and CABAC context models)** — The entropy stage keeps its probability state in tables. For AV1 the spec defines the CDF as "Cumulative distribution function representing the probability times 32768 that a symbol has value less than or equal to a given level" (verified — AV1 spec, §3 Terms and definitions), with the top entry equal to 1 << 15 (verified — AV1 spec, §8.3 Symbol decoding process), and the last CDF entry counting decoded symbols up to a maximum of 32 so the adaptation rate depends on it (verified — AV1 spec, §8.3). For H.264/HEVC the CABAC context models are a 127-state finite-state estimator per model, with probabilities in [0.01875, 0.98125] (verified — Fraunhofer HHI, CABAC: "Each probability model in CABAC can take one out of 127 different states with associated probability values p ranging in the interval [0.01875, 0,98125]"). The tables are a register file (or small SRAM) indexed by syntax element and context; the table count, entry count and banking are not published. Spec facts about the tables; nothing about Ada's table storage is published.
- **FSM / controller (the arithmetic coder state machine)** — AV1's entropy coder is an M-ary symbol arithmetic coder — "In contrast, AV1 uses an M-ary symbol arithmetic coder to compress the syntax elements, where integer M∈[2, 14]" (verified — libaom AV1 Encoder Guide) — and the spec's symbol decoding process is a range/value state machine with renormalisation after every symbol (verified — AV1 spec, §8.3). The coder's control is an FSM stepping through range subdivision, renormalisation and CDF update, while CABAC's binary M-coder runs the same shape of loop one bin at a time (verified — Fraunhofer HHI: "The design of CABAC involves the key elements of binarization, context modeling, and binary arithmetic coding"). The FSM's state count and the coder's symbol-per-clock rate are not published.
- **Barrel shifter (range renormalisation and bitstream packing)** — After each symbol the arithmetic coder renormalises: the spec sets bits = 15 − FloorLog2(SymbolRange) and shifts SymbolRange left by that amount (verified — AV1 spec, §8.3 Symbol decoding process), and the emitted bits are packed into the output stream. That variable shift is a barrel shifter, and the bitstream packer is a second one. The shift width and the packer's buffer depth are not published. Standard construction for the shifter; the renormalisation rule is a spec fact.
- **Comparator (mode decision — best prediction mode)** — Mode decision chooses intra or inter prediction per block — the stage the application note names alongside motion estimation (verified — NVENC Application Note; already recorded at Level 2) — by comparing the rate-distortion cost of the candidate modes and keeping the cheapest. AV1's mode space is large: 71 basic intra prediction modes and 56 single-frame inter prediction modes, plus compound modes (verified — libaom AV1 Encoder Guide: "AV1 also provides 71 basic intra prediction modes, 56 single frame inter prediction modes (7 reference frames x 4 modes x 2 for OBMC (overlapped block motion compensation)), 12768 compound inter prediction modes (that combine inter predictors from two reference frames) and 36708 compound inter / intra prediction modes"), over block partitions from 128x128 pixels down to 4x4 using a multi-layer recursive tree structure (verified — libaom AV1 Encoder Guide: "AV1 supports block partitions of various sizes from 128x128 pixels down to 4x4 pixels using a multi-layer recursive tree structure"). The cost comparison is a comparator tree; the cost metric, the candidate pruning and the comparator width are not published. Spec facts about the mode counts and partitions; the decision circuit is standard construction.
- **Priority encoder (transform-coefficient scan and end-of-block)** — Coefficient coding walks the block's coefficients in the spec's scan order and signals the end of block — the position of the last non-zero coefficient — before coding levels in reverse scan order (verified — libaom AV1 Encoder Guide: "The encoder will code transform block skip flag (txb_skip). If the skip flag is off, then the encoder will code the end of block position (eob) which is the scan index of the last non-zero coefficient plus one"). Finding the last non-zero coefficient in a coefficient vector is a priority-encoder operation. The scan tables are spec facts; the encoder's coefficient datapath width and the priority encoder's size are not published.
- **Counter (rate-control budget and CDF update count)** — Rate control — the preset and rate-control mode that decide the quality-versus-speed trade (verified — NVENC Application Note; already recorded at Level 2) — tracks bits spent against the frame budget with counters, and the CDF update count is itself a counter the spec bounds: "The last entry of the cdf array is used to keep a count of the number of times the symbol has been decoded (up to a maximum of 32). This allows the cdf adaption rate to depend on the number of times the symbol has been decoded." (verified — AV1 spec, §8.3). The 32 cap is a spec fact; the rate-control counters' widths and the budget arithmetic are not published.
- **Mux / demux (session load-balancing and split-frame routing)** — The driver load-balances encode sessions across the engines with no application code (verified — NVENC Application Note; already recorded at Level 2), and split-frame encoding routes one frame half to each engine. Both are mux/demux operations: sessions and frame halves steered to engine 0, 1 or 2, and the two half-bitstreams steered back to be recombined. The steering fabric's radix, widths and arbitration are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the published encode-pipeline facts are the SDK contract (motion estimation and mode decision, motion compensation and residual coding, entropy coding; up to 7 AV1 reference frames; split-frame encoding in SDK 12.0 for HEVC and AV1; ME-only mode) and the codec-spec facts (AV1 M-ary arithmetic coder with M in [2, 14]; CDF probability times 32768 with top entry 1 << 15 and update count capped at 32; 15-bit probability model with only the top 9 bits used by the encoder; 4 1-D transforms into 16 2-D kernels at 19 scales from 64x64 to 4x4; 71 intra and 56 single-frame inter modes over 128x128-to-4x4 partitions; 8-tap interpolation filters; CABAC binarization plus context modeling plus binary arithmetic coding with 127-state probability models). Below that level — reference-store capacity and banking, FIFO depths, SAD search range and datapath width, interpolator array width, butterfly depth and multiplier count, CDF/CABAC table counts and banking, coder FSM state count and symbol rate, renormalisation shift width, mode-decision cost metric, coefficient datapath width, rate-control counter widths, steering-fabric radix — NVIDIA publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing.

#### Down to the primitives: The NVDEC decode pipeline — one 5th-generation decoder, independent of encode and compute

Decode is the inverse of the encode loop, carried out entirely in the fixed-function block — entropy decode, reconstruction against reference frames, in-loop filtering, and the API's post-processing. As with NVENC, NVIDIA publishes no internals, so the primitives below are mapped from the published contract and the codec specifications.

- **SRAM bank (reference frame store and decoded-frame buffer)** — Decoded frames stay available as references for the frames that follow them (verified — NVDEC Application Note; already recorded at Level 2), and AV1 can reference up to seven of them (verified — AV1 spec, §3 constants: REFS_PER_FRAME 7, "Number of reference frames that can be used for inter prediction"; already recorded at Level 2). The store is an SRAM bank (or banks) written by the reconstruction loop and read by motion compensation and the in-loop filters. Its capacity, banking and port count are not published.
- **FIFO / queue (bitstream ingest and multi-context switching)** — NVDEC holds multiple hardware decoding contexts with what NVIDIA calls a negligible context-switching penalty (verified — NVDEC Application Note; already recorded at Level 2), so many streams decode in parallel on the one engine. The bitstream ingest path and the per-context state are queued and swapped through FIFOs and a context register file. Queue depths, context-store size and the switch mechanism are not published.
- **Register file (CDF tables and CABAC context state, per session)** — Each decode context carries its own probability state: AV1 CDF tables — probability times 32768, top entry 1 << 15, update count capped at 32 (verified — AV1 spec, §3 and §8.3) — and CABAC's 127-state context models (verified — Fraunhofer HHI: "Each probability model in CABAC can take one out of 127 different states with associated probability values p ranging in the interval [0.01875, 0,98125]"). The tables are a register file indexed by syntax element and context, one copy per active session. The table count and the per-context storage size are not published. Spec facts about the tables; nothing about Ada's storage is published.
- **FSM / controller (the symbol decoder state machine)** — The spec's symbol decoding process is a state machine: "The input to this process is an array cdf of length N + 1 which specifies the cumulative distribution for a symbol with N possible values. The output of this process is the variable symbol, containing a decoded syntax element. The process also modifies the input array cdf to adapt the probabilities to the content of the stream." (verified — AV1 spec, §8.3). The decoder's control FSM steps through range subdivision, renormalisation and CDF update for every symbol; CABAC's binary decoding loop is the same shape (verified — Fraunhofer HHI: "The design of CABAC involves the key elements of binarization, context modeling, and binary arithmetic coding"). The FSM's state count and symbols-per-clock rate are not published.
- **Barrel shifter (renormalisation and literal bit reads)** — The symbol decoder renormalises after every symbol — bits = 15 − FloorLog2(SymbolRange), SymbolRange shifted left by that amount (verified — AV1 spec, §8.3) — and literal/uncompressed header values are read straight from the bitstream. Both are barrel-shifter operations. The shift width and the bitstream reader's buffer depth are not published. Standard construction for the shifter; the renormalisation rule is a spec fact.
- **Adder tree + multiplier array (inverse-transform butterflies)** — Reconstruction inverts the encoder's transform: AV1's 16 separable 2-D kernels (DCT, ADST, flipped ADST, identity) at 19 scales from 64x64 to 4x4 (verified — libaom AV1 Encoder Guide), applied as two one-dimensional passes — the spec's inverse transform process is a 1-D row pass followed by a 1-D column pass with butterfly functions (verified — AV1 spec, §7.13 Inverse transform process: "1D transforms", "Butterfly functions", "2D inverse transform process"). A butterfly stage is an adder tree with coefficient multipliers. Spec facts about the transform set; the butterfly depth and multiplier count are not published.
- **Multiplier array (motion-compensation 8-tap interpolation)** — Inter prediction on decode interpolates reference samples with the same 8-tap filters as the encoder: EIGHTTAP, EIGHTTAP_SMOOTH and EIGHTTAP_SHARP, eight taps summed per sample (verified — AV1 Bitstream & Decoding Process Specification v1.0.0 with Errata 1, §7.11.3 inter prediction). Each tap is a multiply, so the interpolator is a multiplier array feeding an adder tree. Spec fact about the algorithm; the array's width and tap parallelism are not published.
- **Comparator (CDEF direction detection and deblocking edge decisions)** — The in-loop filters decide where and how strongly to filter. CDEF is the "Constrained Directional Enhancement Filter designed to adaptively filter blocks based on identifying the direction" (verified — AV1 spec, §3), so it must first detect the dominant direction by comparing directional gradients; the deblocking loop filter is "A filtering process applied to the reconstruction intended to reduce the visibility of block edges" (verified — AV1 spec, §3), so it compares samples across each block edge to set its strength. Both decisions are comparator operations. The direction-detection and edge-strength circuits are not published. Spec facts about what the filters do; the comparators are standard construction.
- **Adder tree + multiplier array (CDEF and loop-restoration filter taps)** — After deblocking, AV1 applies CDEF and then loop restoration: "AV1 supports three types of post encode in loop filtering to improve the quality of the reconstructed video" — deblocking, CDEF, and loop restoration (verified — libaom AV1 Encoder Guide), and the loop restoration filter "acts on units of either 64 x 64, 128 x 128, or 256 x 256 pixel blocks, refered to as loop restoration units. Each unit can independently select either to bypass filtering, use a Wiener filter, or use a self-guided filter." (verified — libaom AV1 Encoder Guide). CDEF applies a primary filter along the detected direction and a secondary filter at 45 degrees to it (verified — libaom AV1 Encoder Guide). Every filter tap is a multiply-accumulate, so the filter stages are multiplier arrays feeding adder trees. Spec facts about the filter structure; tap counts, coefficient widths and the filter datapath are not published.
- **Mux / demux (post-processing path select)** — The NVDECODE API's post-processing — scaling, cropping, aspect-ratio conversion, deinterlacing and colour-space conversion (verified — NVDEC Application Note; already recorded at Level 2) — runs on the decoded output inside the block, so the frame can exit already in display form. Each post-processing stage is selected in or out by muxes steering the frame through the chosen stages, and the scaling/cropping parameters select the active window. The mux radix, the scaler's tap structure and the stage order are not published.
- **Counter (tile and frame sequencing)** — Frames are decoded tile by tile — the spec caps a tile grid at 64 rows by 64 columns (verified — AV1 spec, §3 constants: MAX_TILE_ROWS 64, "Maximum number of tile rows"; MAX_TILE_COLS 64, "Maximum number of tile columns") — so the decoder sequences tiles and blocks with row/column counters, and counts decoded frames for reference-frame management. The 64×64 cap is a spec fact; the sequencer's counter widths and the tile-scheduling policy are not published.
- **Pipeline register (inter-stage latches)** — Work is latched between entropy decode, reconstruction, inverse transform, in-loop filtering and post-processing so the pipeline sustains its faster-than-real-time rate (verified — NVDEC Application Note: decode is much faster than real-time; already recorded at Level 2). The stage count, latch widths and stage latencies are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the published decode facts are the SDK contract (5th-generation NVDEC; MPEG-2, VC-1, H.264, HEVC, VP8, VP9 and AV1 decode; 8192x8192 decode for HEVC, VP9 and AV1; multiple hardware contexts with negligible switching penalty; post-processing of scale, crop, aspect ratio, deinterlace and colour-space conversion) and the codec-spec facts (AV1 CDF probability times 32768, top entry 1 << 15, update count capped at 32; symbol decoding as a range/value state machine with renormalisation bits = 15 − FloorLog2(SymbolRange); 16 2-D inverse-transform kernels at 19 scales; 8-tap interpolation filters; CDEF as a direction-adaptive filter and the loop filter as a block-edge filter; three in-loop filters with loop-restoration units of 64x64, 128x128 or 256x256, each bypass, Wiener or self-guided; tile grid capped at 64 rows by 64 columns). Below that level — reference-store capacity and banking, FIFO depths, context-store size, table counts and per-context storage, decoder FSM state count and symbol rate, bitstream-reader buffer depth, butterfly depth and multiplier count, interpolator width, direction-detection and edge-strength circuits, filter tap counts and coefficient widths, post-processing mux radix and scaler structure, sequencer counter widths, stage count and latch widths — NVIDIA publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing.

#### Down to the gates: The dual NVENC encode pipelines — two 8th-generation encoders sharing one frame

NVIDIA publishes no gate-level structure for NVENC or NVDEC — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for the Ada media engine. The deepest published description is the NVENC and NVDEC Application Notes (Video Codec SDK 13.0), which describe the pipeline stages, the API contract and the codec features at block level, and the codec specifications (AV1, HEVC, H.264), which define the algorithms the silicon must implement. What follows takes each Level-3 primitive down to gates and transistors: published spec geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about NVIDIA's circuits.

- **SRAM bank (reference frame store)** — The reference store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. The published contract is the frame count: up to seven AV1 reference frames must be held while the motion estimator searches them, so the store is seven frames deep at minimum — but a frame's bit count depends on the session's resolution and format, which are runtime parameters, not published silicon geometry, so no cell total is claimed. Whether the store is one bank or one bank per reference, and its port count, are not published. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (frame ingest and split-frame handoff)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each, incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The ingest queue and the split-frame handoff are FIFOs of this form, but their depths and widths are not published, so the pointer widths — and therefore the counter and comparator totals — are not claimed. The split itself is a demux steering one frame half to each of the two engines, counted in the mux primitive below. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree + comparator (motion-estimation SAD and best-match selection)** — A sum of absolute differences is subtractors, absolute-value logic and an adder tree: each per-pixel difference is a subtractor (one full adder per bit, about 28 transistors each, with the sign bit selecting the two's-complement negation through a mux), the absolute value is a conditional invert-and-increment, and the adder tree collapses the per-pixel differences pairwise — a tree of adders whose depth is log2 of the block size. The best-match selection is a comparator (one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree) holding the lowest cost so far, with a register holding the winning displacement. The candidate set, the search range, the block sizes searched and the SAD datapath width are not published, so no adder-tree or comparator total is claimed — only the form. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (motion-compensation 8-tap interpolation)** — Each filter tap is a multiply, so the interpolator is a multiplier array in the standard form: AND gates form the partial products, a full-adder compressor tree collapses them, and one final carry-propagate adder finishes. The published geometry is the tap count: eight taps per interpolated sample, so one interpolated sample costs eight multiplies in the standard form. The coefficient and sample widths are not published, so no multiplier total is claimed for Ada's interpolator; as an illustrative width only — not Ada's — a 16-bit by 16-bit array multiplier is 256 AND gates (1,536 transistors) plus 240 full adders (6,720 transistors) plus a 32-bit final adder (896 transistors), about 9,152 transistors per multiplier, and eight of them would be about 73K transistors per interpolated sample lane. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree + multiplier array (transform butterflies and quantisation)** — A butterfly stage is an adder tree with coefficient multipliers: each butterfly is a pair of adders (one sum, one difference) fed by multiplied inputs, and the stages cascade — a 1-D transform of N points is log2(N) butterfly stages in the standard form. The published geometry is the transform set: 16 separable 2-D kernels at 19 scales from 64x64 down to 4x4, so the largest butterfly stage spans 64 points. The coefficient widths, the multiplier count and the quantiser datapath are not published, so no butterfly or quantiser total is claimed. Quantisation itself is a multiply by the reciprocal step — one more multiplier in the standard array form per quantised coefficient — plus a rounding adder. Standard construction.
- **Register file (CDF probability tables and CABAC context models)** — The tables are a register file in the standard form: one D flip-flop per stored bit (about 20–28 transistors each), written by the CDF-update logic and read by the symbol coder, with a decoder selecting the entry by syntax element and context. Arithmetic from the published table geometry: an AV1 CDF entry holds a probability times 32768, with the top entry the constant 1 << 15, so each stored entry is a 15-bit value — 15 flip-flops, about 300–420 transistors per entry as register storage — and the update count, capped at 32, is a counter holding values 0–32, so 6 bits: 6 flip-flops (120–168 transistors) plus a 6-bit incrementer (168 transistors), 288–336 transistors. A CABAC context model holds one of 127 states, a 7-bit value, so each model is 7 flip-flops, about 140–196 transistors. The table count, the entry count and the banking are not published, so no register-file total is claimed — only the per-entry arithmetic. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the arithmetic coder state machine)** — The coder's control is an FSM in the standard form: state bits in master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) with next-state and output logic as a NAND/NOR network, plus the range and value staging registers the renormalisation loop steps through. The published contract is the loop itself: range subdivision, renormalisation after every symbol, and CDF update — the M-ary symbol coder with M in [2, 14] for AV1, and CABAC's binary M-coder running the same shape one bin at a time. The FSM's state count and the coder's symbol-per-clock rate are not published, so no FSM total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (range renormalisation and bitstream packing)** — A barrel shifter is log2(W) stages of 2:1 muxes (4 transistors per mux in transmission-gate form), one stage per shift-amount bit, shifting the whole word by a variable amount in one cycle. Arithmetic from the published renormalisation rule: bits = 15 − FloorLog2(SymbolRange), so the shift amount spans 0–15 — four shift-amount bits, four stages of 2:1 muxes per shifted bit. The range's bit width is not published, so no shifter total is claimed. The bitstream packer is a second barrel shifter of unpublished width, so no packer total is claimed either. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (mode decision — best prediction mode)** — Mode decision is a comparator tree in the standard form: each comparison is one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree, and a tournament tree over N candidates costs N−1 comparators. The published geometry is the mode space: 71 basic intra prediction modes and 56 single-frame inter prediction modes, plus compound modes, over partitions from 128x128 down to 4x4. The evaluated candidate set is pruned by an unpublished policy — the decision circuit does not compare all 127 single-frame modes every block — so no comparator total is claimed; the tree form and the per-comparison gate cost are the decomposition. Standard construction.
- **Priority encoder (transform-coefficient scan and end-of-block)** — Finding the last non-zero coefficient in a coefficient vector is a priority encoder in the standard form: an OR tree over the coefficient-nonzero flags to detect any set bit, and an AND/OR encoder tree producing the index of the highest set bit — log2(N) levels for an N-wide vector. The published geometry is the scan: coefficients are coded in the spec's scan order and the end-of-block position is the scan index of the last non-zero coefficient plus one, over transform blocks up to 64x64 (4,096 coefficients at the largest scale, by arithmetic from the published 19 scales). Whether the encoder processes coefficients in parallel or serially, and its datapath width, are not published, so no priority-encoder total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (rate-control budget and CDF update count)** — A counter is N flip-flops plus N full adders, with a terminal-count comparator (one XOR per bit plus an AND tree) raising the budget-exhausted or update-done flag. Arithmetic from the published bounds: the CDF update count is capped at 32, so its counter holds values 0–32 — 6 bits, 6 flip-flops (120–168 transistors) plus a 6-bit incrementer (168 transistors), 288–336 transistors. The rate-control budget counters' widths and the budget arithmetic are not published, so no rate-control total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (session load-balancing and split-frame routing)** — Session steering and split-frame routing are muxes in the standard form: a 2:1 transmission-gate mux is 4 transistors (2 per input leg), and an R:1 mux is R−1 2:1 muxes in a tree. The published geometry is the fan-out: two NVENC engines, so a session or frame half is steered to engine 0 or 1 through a 2:1 mux per routed bit, and the two half-bitstreams are steered back to be recombined through a second 2:1 mux per bit. The routed widths — how many bits of session state or frame data each mux carries — are not published, so no steering-fabric total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: NVIDIA publishes the NVENC pipeline at stage level only — two 8th-generation engines, split-frame encoding, a motion-estimation-only mode, up to seven AV1 reference frames, driver load-balancing across engines, presets and rate-control modes (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the block appears in any NVIDIA source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about NVIDIA's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable).

#### Down to the gates: The NVDEC decode pipeline — one 5th-generation decoder, independent of encode and compute

NVIDIA publishes no gate-level structure for NVDEC either — the published geometry is the API contract: a 5th-generation decoder, multiple hardware contexts with a negligible switching penalty, post-processing of scale, crop, aspect ratio, deinterlace and colour-space conversion, and decode much faster than real time. The same terms apply as for NVENC: published spec geometry stays published, arithmetic from that geometry is labelled as arithmetic, and every gate form is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive, labelled as such — never a claim about NVIDIA's circuits.

- **SRAM bank (reference frame store and decoded-frame buffer)** — The decoded-frame store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. The published contract is the frame count: up to seven AV1 reference frames (REFS_PER_FRAME 7) must stay available while later frames reference them, plus the decoded-frame buffer the post-processing stages read. A frame's bit count depends on the session's resolution and format, so no cell total is claimed; the capacity, banking and port count are not published. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (bitstream ingest and multi-context switching)** — A FIFO at gate level is a storage array plus two pointer counters plus full/empty comparators: the write pointer and read pointer are counters of N flip-flops plus N full adders each, incrementing on push and pop, and the full and empty flags are comparators over the pointer values — one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree. The bitstream ingest path and the per-context state are queued and swapped through FIFOs of this form, and each session's context — CDF tables, range/value state and tile position — is a context register file swapped on context switch. Queue depths, context-store size and the switch mechanism are not published, so no pointer widths or totals are claimed. Standard construction.
- **Register file (CDF tables and CABAC context state, per session)** — The tables are a register file in the standard form: one D flip-flop per stored bit (about 20–28 transistors each), with a decoder selecting the entry by syntax element and context — and on decode, one copy of the tables per active session. Arithmetic from the published table geometry: an AV1 CDF entry is a 15-bit value (probability times 32768, top entry the constant 1 << 15), so 15 flip-flops, about 300–420 transistors per entry, per context; a CABAC context model holds one of 127 states, a 7-bit value, so 7 flip-flops, about 140–196 transistors per model, per context. The table count per context and the number of simultaneously active contexts are not published, so no register-file total is claimed — only the per-entry, per-context arithmetic. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (the symbol decoder state machine)** — The decoder's control is an FSM in the standard form: state bits in master-slave D flip-flops (about 20–28 transistors each) with next-state and output logic as a NAND/NOR network, plus the range and value staging registers the symbol loop steps through. The published contract is the spec's symbol decoding process itself: an array cdf of length N+1 specifying the cumulative distribution for a symbol with N possible values, outputting the decoded symbol and adapting the cdf — a state machine stepping through range subdivision, renormalisation and CDF update for every symbol, with CABAC's binary decoding loop the same shape. The FSM's state count and symbols-per-clock rate are not published, so no FSM total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (renormalisation and literal bit reads)** — A barrel shifter is log2(W) stages of 2:1 muxes (4 transistors per mux in transmission-gate form), one stage per shift-amount bit, shifting the whole word by a variable amount in one cycle. Arithmetic from the published renormalisation rule: bits = 15 − FloorLog2(SymbolRange), so the shift amount spans 0–15 — four shift-amount bits, four stages of 2:1 muxes per shifted bit. The range's bit width is not published, so no renormalisation-shifter total is claimed. Literal and uncompressed header reads are a second barrel shifter pulling variable-length fields from the bitstream buffer, of unpublished width, so no reader total is claimed either. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree + multiplier array (inverse-transform butterflies)** — An inverse butterfly is the same adder-tree-with-multipliers form as the forward transform: pairs of adders fed by multiplied inputs, cascading through log2(N) stages for an N-point 1-D transform, applied as a row pass followed by a column pass. The published geometry is the transform set: 16 separable 2-D kernels (DCT, ADST, flipped ADST, identity) at 19 scales from 64x64 to 4x4, with the spec's 1-D row and column passes and butterfly functions. The butterfly depth, multiplier count and coefficient widths are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array (motion-compensation 8-tap interpolation)** — Each filter tap is a multiply, so the interpolator is a multiplier array in the standard form: AND gates form the partial products, a full-adder compressor tree collapses them, and one final carry-propagate adder finishes. The published geometry is the tap count: eight taps per interpolated sample, so one interpolated sample costs eight multiplies in the standard form. The coefficient and sample widths are not published, so no multiplier total is claimed for Ada's interpolator; as an illustrative width only — not Ada's — a 16-bit by 16-bit array multiplier is 256 AND gates (1,536 transistors) plus 240 full adders (6,720 transistors) plus a 32-bit final adder (896 transistors), about 9,152 transistors per multiplier, and eight of them would be about 73K transistors per interpolated sample lane. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (CDEF direction detection and deblocking edge decisions)** — Direction detection and edge-strength decisions are comparators in the standard form: one XOR per compared bit feeding an AND tree, comparing directional gradients to find the dominant direction for CDEF and comparing samples across each block edge to set the deblocking strength. The published contract is what the filters do — CDEF is the Constrained Directional Enhancement Filter that adaptively filters blocks based on identifying the direction, and the deblocking loop filter reduces the visibility of block edges — but the direction-detection and edge-strength circuits are not published, so no comparator total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree + multiplier array (CDEF and loop-restoration filter taps)** — Every filter tap is a multiply-accumulate: a multiplier in the standard array form feeding an adder tree that sums the tap products. The published geometry is the filter structure: three in-loop filters (deblocking, CDEF, loop restoration), CDEF applying a primary filter along the detected direction and a secondary filter at 45 degrees to it, and loop restoration acting on units of 64x64, 128x128 or 256x256 pixels, each unit independently selecting bypass, a Wiener filter or a self-guided filter. The tap counts, coefficient widths and filter datapath are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (post-processing path select)** — Each post-processing stage — scaling, cropping, aspect-ratio conversion, deinterlacing, colour-space conversion — is selected in or out by muxes in the standard form: a 2:1 transmission-gate mux is 4 transistors (2 per input leg), and an R:1 mux is R−1 2:1 muxes in a tree. The published contract is the stage list; the mux radix, the scaler's tap structure and the stage order are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (tile and frame sequencing)** — A counter is N flip-flops plus N full adders, with a terminal-count comparator (one XOR per bit plus an AND tree) stepping to the next tile or frame. Arithmetic from the published tile cap: the spec caps a tile grid at 64 rows by 64 columns, so the tile-row and tile-column indices run 0–63 — 6 bits each (2^6 = 64) — 6 flip-flops (120–168 transistors) plus a 6-bit incrementer (168 transistors), 288–336 transistors per counter, 576–672 transistors for the pair. The frame counter's width and the tile-scheduling policy are not published, so no sequencer total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline register (inter-stage latches)** — Inter-stage latches are D flip-flops in the standard form: one flip-flop per latched bit, about 20–28 transistors each, holding the entropy-decoder output for reconstruction, the reconstruction for the inverse transform, and the transform output for the in-loop filters and post-processing. The published contract is the pipeline behaviour — decode runs much faster than real time, so the stages sustain that rate — but the stage count, latch widths and stage latencies are not published, so no register total is claimed. Standard construction.

Honesty: NVIDIA publishes the NVDEC contract at API level only — 5th-generation decoder; MPEG-2, VC-1, H.264, HEVC, VP8, VP9 and AV1 decode; 8192x8192 decode for HEVC, VP9 and AV1; multiple hardware contexts with negligible switching penalty; post-processing stages (Level-2 and Level-3 fact records) — and no gate-level structure for any part of the block appears in any NVIDIA source. Everything below is the standard textbook construction of the named primitive, pointing at the primer's bottom layer; none of it is a claim about NVIDIA's actual netlist (new Level-4 fact record: unverifiable).

**How work flows.**
1. **Frames arrive from CUDA or capture.** Rendered or captured frames are queued to an encoder.
2. **Motion estimation + prediction.** The encoder finds inter-frame matches and forms residuals.
3. **Transform, quantise, entropy-code.** Residuals are compressed and packed by the codec's entropy engine into the outgoing bitstream.
4. **Decode proceeds in parallel.** NVDEC independently plays or analyses other streams on the same die.

**Key numbers.** 8th-generation NVENC, 5th-generation NVDEC; GeForce RTX 4090/4080: 2 NVENC engines, 1 NVDEC; Ada professional GPUs with 12 GB or more: 3 NVENC; AV1 encode 8/10-bit, 4:2:0, up to 8192×8192; 8K60 encode and decode; per-engine 1080p rates (RTX 4090, Video Codec SDK 13.0, indicative): AV1 encode 1,090 fps, HEVC encode 1,055 fps, H.264 encode 910 fps; per-engine 1080p decode rates (Ada, SDK 13.0, indicative): AV1 1,018 fps, HEVC 1,641 fps; GeForce concurrent encode sessions: 12 per the October 2026 support matrix (the SDK 13.0 application note text still says 8).

**Signature ideas.**
1. **Dual AV1 encoders** — Two complete 8th-generation encoders on the flagship GeForce parts, with split-frame encoding letting one 8K60 session use both at once.
2. **Optical flow accelerator for DLSS** — The same media die carries the OFA that feeds DLSS 3 frame generation (see the NVIDIA Ada Lovelace AD102 entry for its Level-2 treatment).
3. **Independent decode (NVDEC) pipeline** — A separate 5th-generation decoder that runs concurrently with encode and CUDA compute, so one die plays, records and renders at once.

**Limits & tradeoffs.** Frozen algorithms. Encode quality is whatever the fixed pipeline implements this generation, the codec menu closes at tape-out, and professionals still reach for software encoding when quality per bit is the metric.

**Lineage.** NVENC has shipped in NVIDIA GPUs since Kepler, one generation per architecture step; the 8th generation arrives with Ada and adds AV1 encoding, which Ampere could only decode. NVDEC's 5th generation first launched with Ampere and is carried over to Ada. The 9th-generation NVENC in Blackwell (Video Codec SDK 13.0) adds 4:2:2 and 10-bit H.264 encoding that Ada lacks.

**One-line summary.** Fixed-function media is the purest heterogeneity argument — a tiny block outperforms a giant GPU at its one job.
