### Apple Media Engine (M1 Pro/Max → M3)

**Added: 2026-11-22** (mirrored to the corpus 2026-11-26 with the Level-2 deepening; the corpus had no entry for it before this run)

**Specs (wiki card).** ProRes accelerators · H.264/HEVC/ProRes · AV1 decode (M3)

**What it is / why it matters.** Apple's fixed-function video block in the M-series Pro, Max and Ultra chips — the media engine that turned ProRes from a CPU codec into a laptop's native language. Introduced with M1 Pro and M1 Max in October 2021, carried through M2 Pro/Max and M3, it puts hardware H.264, HEVC, ProRes and ProRes RAW encode and decode beside the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine, reading and writing the same unified-memory pool, and adds hardware AV1 decode with the M3 generation. One engine set on Pro-class dies, two on Max, four on M3 Ultra — the media engine is the part of Apple silicon that scales by duplication.

**Building blocks.**
- **H.264 / HEVC encode + decode engines** — The conventional inter-frame codec path — motion estimation, prediction, transform, entropy — in fixed function. One encode engine on Pro-class dies, two on Max
- **ProRes accelerator** — Dedicated ProRes encode/decode. ProRes is an intra-frame codec: every frame is coded independently, so this block contains no motion estimation at all — its budget goes to very-high-bitrate DCT and entropy throughput, multiple 8K streams at once
- **AV1 decoder (M3 generation)** — Decode-only AV1 hardware added with M3. AV1 encode did not come with it — the engine's codec set is fixed per silicon generation
- **DMA into unified memory** — The engines read and write the SoC's shared memory pool directly; there is no dedicated video memory and no copy step

**The piece that makes it special.** ProRes in hardware. Apple turned its own codec into a platform moat by putting it in silicon across cameras, phones and laptops — and ProRes's intra-only design (no motion search, frames independent) is precisely what makes it cheap to accelerate and robust to edit. The special piece is a codec chosen for the hardware as much as hardware built for the codec.

#### Inside the signature block: The ProRes accelerator — an intra-frame codec turned into a stream-count machine

**Inside it.** ProRes is an intra-frame codec: every frame is encoded and decoded independently of every other frame, so there is no motion estimation, no reference-frame store and no group of pictures to rebuild when the playhead jumps — the white paper's own words make the consequence explicit, that this is what provides the greatest editing performance and flexibility. The accelerator's encode path is therefore the short pipeline: split the frame into blocks, DCT-transform, quantise, entropy-code — and the decode path is the exact inverse, with no temporal state carried between frames. ProRes is a variable bit rate codec, so the accelerator's rate control works per frame rather than per group of pictures. The same accelerator handles ProRes RAW, the sensor-data variant of the format, and Apple's tech specs list it as hardware-accelerated alongside conventional ProRes. The white paper also documents reduced-resolution decoding — half-size frames decode substantially faster than full-size ones — which is how a timeline scrubs at speed. Apple publishes no internal sub-block diagram for the media engine, no queue depths and no pipeline stage counts, so the stage order below is the codec-mandated pipeline and the API-visible contract, not a die photograph.

**Trace — one unit of work: one 4K ProRes 422 HQ frame through the decode path.**
1. **Decode job lands on the ProRes engine. **Final Cut Pro submits a frame decode to the media engine; the CPU and GPU never see the job, and the frame's bitstream already sits in unified memory.
2. **Bitstream read from unified memory. **The accelerator reads the frame's variable-bit-rate bitstream straight from the shared pool; there is no dedicated video memory and no copy step.
3. **Entropy decode unpacks the coefficients. **The variable-length codes are unpacked into quantised transform coefficients, in frame order — no reference frames to fetch, because no frame depends on any other.
4. **Inverse quantise and inverse DCT rebuild the blocks. **Coefficients are dequantised and inverse-transformed block by block into 10-bit 4:2:2 pixels; the 4444 flavours add full 4:4:4 chroma and the mathematically lossless alpha channel.
5. **Frame written back to unified memory. **The reconstructed frame lands in the shared pool, where the display engine or the compositor picks it up without another copy.
6. **Next stream starts on the second accelerator. **On Max-class silicon the second ProRes engine decodes the next stream in parallel; on Pro-class silicon the single engine moves to the next frame in the queue — the stream count, not the per-frame latency, is what the second engine buys.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the edit tax: before the accelerator, multistream ProRes playback was a CPU job — the white paper's own 2019 test shows a 16-inch MacBook Pro decoding 4 streams of 4K ProRes 422 HQ in Final Cut Pro, while M1 Pro plays 20 streams and M1 Max 30 — and the decode never touches the GPU, so grading and effects keep their compute. Creates a fixed-menu ceiling instead: the codec set is frozen at tape-out, so M1 and M2 owners got no AV1 decode no matter the software update, and the newest codec still waits for new silicon. The second new bottleneck is engine count, not memory: 30 streams of 4K ProRes 422 HQ at the white paper's 707 Mb/s target rate is about 2.7 GB/s of bitstream read by arithmetic — a small fraction of M1 Max's 400 GB/s of unified-memory bandwidth — so adding streams costs accelerators, not bandwidth.

**Governing numbers.** ProRes encode/decode engines: 1 on M1 Pro, M2 Pro and M3 Pro; 2 on M1 Max, M2 Max and M3 Max; 4 on M3 Ultra (2x the M3 Max media engine). Playback: M1 Pro up to 20 streams of 4K or 4 streams of 8K ProRes; M1 Max up to 30 streams of 4K or 7 streams of 8K ProRes; M3 Ultra up to 24 streams of 8K ProRes 422. M1 Max video encoding up to 2x faster than M1 Pro; M2 Max up to 2x faster than M2 Pro; M1 Max ProRes transcode in Compressor up to 10x faster than the previous-generation 16-inch MacBook Pro. ProRes 422 HQ target data rate approximately 220 Mb/s at 1920x1080 29.97 fps and 707 Mb/s at 3840x2160 24p; ProRes 4444 XQ approximately 500 Mb/s at 1920x1080 29.97 fps. 10-bit 4:2:2 for the 422 family; 4444 and 4444 XQ up to 12-bit with a mathematically lossless alpha channel up to 16 bits. Variable bit rate throughout.

**Primary source.** Apple, Apple ProRes White Paper (January 2020), read live — intra-frame definition, VBR, data-rate targets, multistream and half-size decoding; Apple Newsroom, Introducing M1 Pro and M1 Max (October 18, 2021) — two ProRes accelerators, 2x faster video encoding, 10x faster Compressor transcode; Apple Newsroom, Apple unveils M2 Pro and M2 Max (January 17, 2023) — two video encode and two ProRes engines, 2x faster encoding; Apple Newsroom, Apple reveals M3 Ultra (March 2025) — four ProRes encode and decode engines, up to 24 streams of 8K ProRes 422; Apple Support, MacBook Pro Tech Specs (Nov 2023) — M3 Pro/Max media engine lines; Wikipedia, Apple ProRes — DCT basis, citing the white paper p.19.

#### Inside the signature block: The H.264/HEVC encode and decode engines — the inter-frame path, doubled on Max

**Inside it.** The video encode and video decode engines are separate blocks from the ProRes accelerator — Apple's tech specs list them as separate lines — and they run the inter-frame codecs, H.264 and HEVC, where frames do depend on each other. The encode engine's job is the full long-GOP pipeline: motion estimation against reference frames, mode decision, transform and quantisation of the residual, and entropy coding; the decode engine runs the inverse, reconstructing each frame from its references and the in-loop filters. The decode engine is single on Pro- and Max-class silicon — only the encode engine doubles, to two on Max and four on M3 Ultra, and the decode engine doubles only at Ultra, to two. M3 adds hardware AV1 decode to the same engine set, on every M3 chip from the base M3 up; AV1 encode did not come with it, so AV1 encoding still falls back to software. The M2 generation carries the same structure — M2 Max has two video encode engines and two ProRes engines, up to 2x faster video encoding than M2 Pro. Apple publishes no internal sub-block diagram for these engines, no queue depths and no stage counts, so the stage order below is the codec-mandated pipeline and the API-visible contract, not a die photograph.

**Trace — one unit of work: one H.264/HEVC frame through the encode path.**
1. **Encode job lands on the video encode engine. **The driver submits the frame to the media engine's own queue; the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine never see it.
2. **Frame staged from unified memory. **The raw frame is read from the shared pool; reference frames for motion estimation sit beside it in the same memory.
3. **Motion estimation searches the references. **The engine searches reference frames for matching blocks and records motion vectors — the stage ProRes skips entirely, and the reason inter-frame encode costs more per frame than ProRes.
4. **Residual transformed, quantised and entropy-coded. **The prediction residual is transformed and quantised, then packed by the entropy coder into the bitstream.
5. **Reconstructed frame stored as a reference. **The encoded frame is decoded locally and written back to unified memory as a reference for the frames that follow.
6. **Bitstream out; second engine takes the next job. **The bitstream returns to unified memory for the app or storage; on Max-class silicon the second encode engine starts the next frame or the next stream in parallel, which is where the up-to-2x encoding speed comes from.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the encode tax that used to fall on the CPU or on shader time: a 4K transcode runs on fixed-function hardware while the GPU keeps rendering, and the same job can be split across two engines on Max. Creates a reference-frame traffic bill instead: every inter-frame encode reads and writes reference frames in unified memory, so the engine's throughput is bounded by memory traffic in a way the ProRes accelerator's is not. And the decode side is the lopsided half — Max doubles the encode engines but not the decode engine, so decode throughput is capped at one engine even on the biggest laptop chip, and AV1 decode-only means the newest codec still encodes in software.

**Governing numbers.** Video encode engines: 1 on M1 Pro, M2 Pro and M3 Pro; 2 on M1 Max, M2 Max and M3 Max; 4 on M3 Ultra. Video decode engines: 1 on M1 Pro through M3 Max; 2 on M3 Ultra. ProRes encode/decode engines: 1 on Pro-class, 2 on Max-class, 4 on M3 Ultra. AV1 decode: hardware-accelerated from the M3 generation on every M3 chip; AV1 encode: not in hardware. Codecs hardware-accelerated: H.264, HEVC, ProRes, ProRes RAW. M1 Max and M2 Max video encoding up to 2x faster than their Pro counterparts.

**Primary source.** Apple Support, MacBook Pro Tech Specs (14-inch and 16-inch, Nov 2023) — M3 Pro/Max media engine lines; Apple Newsroom, Apple reveals M3 Ultra (March 2025) — 2x the M3 Max media engine resources, four ProRes engines, up to 24 streams of 8K ProRes 422; Apple Mac Studio Tech Specs (as listed by Adorama) — M3 Ultra two video decode engines, four video encode engines, four ProRes engines; Apple Newsroom, Apple unveils M2 Pro and M2 Max (January 17, 2023) — two video encode engines and two ProRes engines, 2x faster encoding.

#### Down to the primitives: The ProRes accelerator — an intra-frame codec turned into a stream-count machine

The ProRes accelerator runs the published intra-frame pipeline — split the frame into blocks, DCT-transform, quantise, entropy-code on encode; the exact inverse on decode — and each stage is built from the primitives below. Numbers that come from a codec specification are spec facts about the algorithm, not published facts about Apple's silicon; where a primitive's geometry is not published, that is stated plainly.

- **FIFO / queue (frame bitstream ingest, decoded-frame output, stream queue across engines)** — Frames arrive as variable-bit-rate bitstreams from unified memory and decoded frames return the same way; on Max-class silicon the second ProRes engine decodes the next stream in parallel, and on M3 Ultra four engines share the work (verified — already recorded at Level 2: 1 engine on Pro-class, 2 on Max-class, 4 on M3 Ultra; up to 30 streams of 4K ProRes on M1 Max). The ingest queue, the output queue and the stream queue across the engines are FIFOs decoupling the frame source from the accelerators. Their depths and widths are not published.
- **SRAM bank (block store and line buffers — no reference-frame store)** — The frame is split into blocks before the transform, so the accelerator must hold blocks and their coefficients on chip while the pipeline works them — a block store built from SRAM banks or line buffers. What it does NOT hold is a reference frame: ProRes is intra-frame only, so there is no reference-frame store at all, and the Level-2 subs state that explicitly. The block store's capacity, banking and port count are not published. Standard construction for the store itself; the absence of a reference store is a published property of the codec.
- **Multiplier array + adder tree (DCT/IDCT butterflies and quantisation)** — ProRes is a DCT scalar codec — the white paper's definition, cited in the Apple ProRes entry (verified — Apple ProRes White Paper p.19; already recorded at Level 2) — and the decoding process applies an 8x8 two-dimensional inverse discrete cosine transform to each block of DCT coefficients (verified — SMPTE RDD 36:2022, section 7.4: "An inverse discrete cosine transform (IDCT) is applied to each of the color component DCT coefficient blocks to produce blocks of reconstructed color component values"; new fact record this run). A DCT/IDCT stage is a butterfly network: coefficient multipliers feeding adder trees, run as two one-dimensional passes. Quantisation is a further multiply by the quantiser step. Spec facts about the transform; the butterfly depth, the multiplier count and the quantiser datapath are not published.
- **Comparator (per-frame VBR rate-control quantiser selection)** — ProRes is a variable bit rate codec, so the rate control works per frame rather than per group of pictures (verified — Apple ProRes White Paper; already recorded at Level 2), choosing the quantiser for each frame against its bit budget. That choice is a comparator operation: the candidate quantiser's expected bit cost against the frame's remaining budget. The quantiser set, the cost metric and the comparator width are not published.
- **Barrel shifter (entropy-code bit packing and unpacking)** — The entropy stage packs quantised coefficients into variable-length codes on encode and unpacks them on decode — the last stage of the published pipeline (verified — already recorded at Level 2: the Level-2 subs name entropy coding as the final encode stage and entropy decoding as the first decode stage). Variable-length packing and unpacking is a barrel-shifter operation: bits shifted in and out of the stream by a code-dependent amount. The shift width and the bitstream buffer depth are not published. Standard construction for the shifter; the entropy-coding stage itself is a published pipeline fact.
- **FSM / controller (encode/decode pipeline sequencer and VBR rate-control loop)** — The accelerator sequences the codec-mandated stages — split, transform, quantise, entropy-code — and the per-frame VBR rate-control loop that re-selects the quantiser frame by frame. That sequencing and the rate-control loop are FSM/controller logic: one state machine stepping frames through the pipeline, one loop tracking bits spent against the frame budget. The state counts, the stage timing and the loop's arithmetic are not published.
- **Pipeline register (inter-stage latches)** — Work is latched between the split, transform, quantisation and entropy stages so the pipeline sustains the published multistream rates — up to 20 streams of 4K ProRes on M1 Pro and 30 on M1 Max (verified — already recorded at Level 2). The stage count, latch widths and stage latencies are not published.
- **Mux / demux (ProRes vs ProRes RAW, 422 vs 4444, half-size decode path select)** — The same accelerator handles ProRes RAW alongside conventional ProRes (verified — already recorded at Level 2), the 422 family at 10-bit 4:2:2 and the 4444 family at up to 12-bit 4:4:4 with the mathematically lossless alpha channel (verified — Apple ProRes White Paper; already recorded at Level 2), and half-size decoding that runs substantially faster for timeline scrubbing (verified — Apple ProRes White Paper; already recorded at Level 2). Each variant is a path select: muxes steering the frame through the RAW or conventional path, the 422 or 4444 chroma path, and the full-size or half-size decode path. The mux radix and the path-selection logic are not published.
- **Counter (frame and stream sequencing across engines)** — Frames are sequenced through the pipeline and streams are counted across the engines — the stream count, not the per-frame latency, is what the second engine buys (verified — already recorded at Level 2: the Level-2 trace). Frame counters track which frame of a stream is in flight; stream counters track which engine holds which stream. Their widths are not published.
- **Register file (per-stream frame parameters and quantiser state)** — Each stream in flight carries its own frame parameters — dimensions, flavour, chroma format, quantiser state — held in registers while the frame moves through the pipeline. With up to 30 streams of 4K ProRes on M1 Max (verified — already recorded at Level 2), the per-stream state is a register file indexed by stream. The entry count, entry width and banking are not published.
- **Crossbar / arbiter (stream dispatch across the 1/2/4 ProRes engines)** — Streams are dispatched to the available ProRes engines — one on Pro-class, two on Max-class, four on M3 Ultra (verified — already recorded at Level 2) — and the second engine on Max takes the next stream in parallel. That dispatch is a crossbar/arbiter operation: streams steered to engine 0, 1, 2 or 3, and decoded frames steered back to their callers. The arbiter's radix, widths and scheduling policy are not published.
- **Credit counter (unified-memory read/write flow control)** — The accelerator reads bitstreams and writes frames through unified memory with no dedicated video memory and no copy step (verified — already recorded at Level 2: the Level-2 trace). Flow control between the engine and the memory fabric is a credit counter in standard construction: reads and writes issued against outstanding credits, returned as they complete. The Level-2 bottleneck note puts 30 streams of 4K ProRes 422 HQ at about 2.7 GB/s of bitstream read against 400 GB/s of unified-memory bandwidth (verified — already recorded at Level 2), so the credit mechanism is not the bottleneck — but its depth, width and issue policy are not published. Standard construction for the credit mechanism; the bandwidth arithmetic is already recorded.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Apple publishes no internal sub-block diagram for the media engine — no stage latencies, queue depths, block-store sizes or buffer geometry — so the primitives above are mapped from the published pipeline stages and the codec specifications, not from a die diagram. Every number in this block that comes from a codec spec is a spec fact (the algorithm the silicon must implement); no parameter of the Apple media engine itself is claimed. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Down to the primitives: The H.264/HEVC encode and decode engines — the inter-frame path, doubled on Max

The video encode and decode engines run the published long-GOP pipeline — motion estimation against reference frames, mode decision, transform and quantisation of the residual, entropy coding — and the decode engine runs the inverse, reconstructing each frame from its references and the in-loop filters. As with ProRes, Apple publishes no internals, so the primitives below are mapped from the published contract and the codec specifications.

- **SRAM bank (reference frame store)** — Inter-frame encode reads and writes reference frames in unified memory, and the motion estimator searches against them — the long-GOP pipeline the Level-2 subs describe (verified — already recorded at Level 2). The frames the estimator searches must sit on chip while it works, so each engine holds several decoded frames in an SRAM bank — or a set of banks, one per reference — written by the reconstruction loop and read by the motion estimator and the motion compensator. Its capacity in frames, its banking and its port count are not published. Standard construction for the store itself; the reference-frame traffic bill is already recorded at Level 2.
- **FIFO / queue (bitstream ingest, reconstructed-frame output, job queue across the two encode engines)** — Raw frames arrive from unified memory, bitstreams return to it, and on Max-class silicon the second encode engine starts the next frame or the next stream in parallel (verified — already recorded at Level 2: the Level-2 trace; 2 encode engines on Max, 4 on M3 Ultra). The ingest queue, the output queue and the job queue across the two engines are FIFOs decoupling the frame source from the engines. Their depths and widths are not published.
- **Adder tree + comparator (motion-estimation SAD and best-match selection)** — Motion estimation scores each candidate displacement by a sum of absolute differences: per-pixel subtractors feeding an adder tree, with a comparator keeping the lowest-cost candidate as the search proceeds. The search is the stage ProRes skips entirely, and the reason inter-frame encode costs more per frame than ProRes (verified — already recorded at Level 2: the Level-2 trace). The candidate set, the search range, the block sizes the search covers and the SAD datapath width are not published. Standard construction for the SAD arithmetic.
- **Multiplier array + adder tree (transform and quantisation of the residual; inverse transform on decode)** — The prediction residual is transformed and quantised on encode, and the inverse transform rebuilds it on decode — the codec-mandated stages the Level-2 subs name (verified — already recorded at Level 2). A transform stage is a butterfly network: coefficient multipliers feeding adder trees, run as two one-dimensional passes; quantisation is a further multiply by the quantiser step. The transform set, the butterfly depth, the multiplier count and the quantiser datapath are not published. Standard construction for the butterfly; the stage order is a published pipeline fact.
- **Barrel shifter (entropy coding bit packing — CABAC/CAVLC)** — The entropy coder packs the quantised residual and the mode and motion-vector syntax into the bitstream — the last stage of the published encode pipeline (verified — already recorded at Level 2). H.264 and HEVC entropy-code with CABAC and CAVLC, both variable-length schemes, so the packing is a barrel-shifter operation: bits shifted into the stream by a code-dependent amount, and read back out by the same amount on decode. The shift width and the bitstream buffer depth are not published. Standard construction for the shifter; the entropy-coding stage is a published pipeline fact.
- **Register file (CABAC context models)** — The entropy stage keeps its probability state in tables. Each probability model in CABAC can take one out of 127 different states with associated probability values p ranging in the interval [0.01875, 0,98125] (verified — Fraunhofer HHI, CABAC: "Each probability model in CABAC can take one out of 127 different states with associated probability values p ranging in the interval [0.01875, 0,98125]"; new fact record this run), and the probability estimator is implemented as a simple finite-state machine with tabulated transition rules (verified — Fraunhofer HHI; new fact record this run). The tables are a register file (or small SRAM) indexed by syntax element and context. The table count, entry count and banking are not published. Spec facts about the tables; nothing about Apple's table storage is published.
- **FSM / controller (encode/decode pipeline sequencer and mode-decision state machine)** — The encode engine sequences motion estimation, mode decision, transform, quantisation and entropy coding, and the decode engine sequences the inverse — while the CABAC probability estimator itself steps through its 127 states as a finite-state machine (verified — Fraunhofer HHI; new fact record this run). The pipeline sequencer and the mode-decision state machine are FSM/controller logic. The state counts, the stage timing and the mode-decision cost metric are not published.
- **Mux / demux (H.264 vs HEVC vs AV1-decode path select; encode-engine 1 vs 2 dispatch on Max)** — The same engine set decodes H.264, HEVC and — from the M3 generation, on every M3 chip — AV1, while AV1 encode is not in hardware (verified — already recorded at Level 2: Apple Support tech specs and the M3 Ultra announcement). Each codec is a path select: muxes steering the frame through the H.264, HEVC or AV1-decode path, and on Max-class silicon the job dispatch steers the next frame to encode engine 1 or 2. The mux radix and the path-selection logic are not published.
- **Credit counter / arbiter (two encode engines sharing unified-memory bandwidth)** — Every inter-frame encode reads and writes reference frames in unified memory, so the engine's throughput is bounded by memory traffic in a way the ProRes accelerator's is not (verified — already recorded at Level 2: the Level-2 bottleneck note). On Max-class silicon two encode engines share that bandwidth, so their memory requests are arbitrated and flow-controlled — a credit counter and arbiter in standard construction, granting each engine its share of the fabric. The arbitration policy, the credit depth and any published rate are not published; no rate is claimed. Standard construction for the arbiter; the reference-frame traffic bill is already recorded.
- **Pipeline register (inter-stage latches)** — Work is latched between motion estimation, mode decision, transform, quantisation and entropy coding so the pipeline sustains the published encode rates — M1 Max and M2 Max video encoding up to 2x faster than their Pro counterparts (verified — already recorded at Level 2). The stage count, latch widths and stage latencies are not published.
- **Synchronizer (media-engine clock domain against the unified-memory / system fabric domain)** — Standard construction: wherever the media engine's clock meets the system fabric's clock, the crossing is a synchronizer — two flip-flop stages (or a FIFO-based crossing) that let a signal change domains without metastability. Apple publishes no clocking for the media engine, so whether the engine and the fabric share a clock, and where the synchronizers sit, is not a published fact; the primitive is named as the standard construction for the boundary, not as an Apple-published circuit.
- **Counter (frame and job sequencing; reference-frame management)** — Frames and jobs are sequenced through the engines, and the reconstructed frames written back as references must be tracked — which reference is current, which is oldest, which frame each new frame may predict from. Frame counters, job counters and reference-frame age counters do that bookkeeping. Their widths and the reference-management policy are not published.
- **Comparator (mode decision and in-loop filter edge decisions)** — Mode decision chooses intra or inter prediction per block — the stage the Level-2 subs name alongside motion estimation (verified — already recorded at Level 2) — by comparing the rate-distortion cost of the candidate modes and keeping the cheapest; and the decode engine's in-loop filters compare samples across each block edge to set their filtering strength (verified — already recorded at Level 2: the Level-2 subs name the in-loop filters as part of the decode path). Both decisions are comparator operations. The cost metric, the candidate pruning and the comparator widths are not published. The mode-decision and in-loop-filter stages are published pipeline facts; the comparators are standard construction.

**Parameter honesty.** Honesty: Apple publishes no internal sub-block diagram for the video encode and decode engines either — no stage latencies, queue depths, reference-store sizes or buffer geometry — so the primitives above are mapped from the published pipeline stages and the codec specifications, not from a die diagram. Every number that comes from a codec spec is a spec fact (the algorithm the silicon must implement); no parameter of the Apple media engine itself is claimed. Generic constructions are labelled standard construction.

#### Down to the gates: The ProRes accelerator — an intra-frame codec turned into a stream-count machine

Apple publishes no gate-level structure for the media engine — no netlist, no standard-cell description, no transistor count for any block. The deepest published description of the ProRes accelerator is the codec-mandated pipeline in the Apple ProRes White Paper and SMPTE RDD 36:2022: split the frame into blocks, apply an 8x8 two-dimensional inverse discrete cosine transform, quantise, entropy-code. The decomposition below maps each Level-3 primitive to its textbook gate-level construction, with arithmetic only from the published codec geometry.

- **FIFO / queue (frame bitstream ingest, decoded-frame output, stream queue across engines)** — A FIFO is a storage array plus two pointer counters and two comparators: a write pointer and a read pointer, each a binary counter of one D flip-flop per bit (20-28 transistors each, primer bottom layer) plus a one-bit incrementer of one full adder per bit (28 transistors each), and a full comparator and an empty comparator, each a per-bit XOR (12 transistors) feeding an OR tree (6 transistors per OR gate). The storage itself is either flip-flops (20-28 transistors per bit) or an SRAM array of 6T cells with a row decoder, column muxes and sense amplifiers. The ingest, output and stream queues have no published depths or widths, so no total is claimed; the per-bit costs above are the standard construction. Standard construction.
- **SRAM bank (block store and line buffers — no reference-frame store)** — The block store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree, 4 transistors per NAND2, selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. Arithmetic from the cell alone: every stored bit costs 6 transistors, so a block store of B bits is 6B transistors of cells before decoder, mux and sense-amplifier overhead. The store's capacity, banking and port count are not published, so B is not claimed. The absence is the other half of this prim: ProRes is intra-frame only, so there is no reference-frame store at all — zero gates, zero transistors, by published codec property rather than by unpublished geometry. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array + adder tree (DCT/IDCT butterflies and quantisation)** — The 8x8 IDCT is two one-dimensional passes of an 8-point DCT, and the standard Loeffler form of an 8-point DCT uses 11 multipliers and 29 adders per pass, so one 8x8 block needs 16 passes, 176 multipliers and 464 adders. Each multiplier in array form is N squared AND gates (6 transistors each) plus N times N minus 1 full adders (28 transistors each) plus a 32-bit final adder; a 16-bit array multiplier is 9,152 transistors by that arithmetic, so 176 of them would be 1,610,752 transistors, about 1.6M, and the 464 adders are 12,992 transistors, about 13K — conditional arithmetic, because the coefficient width of Apple's multipliers is not published and the DCT may be implemented in a distributed-arithmetic or ROM form instead of multipliers. Quantisation is a further multiply by the quantiser step, one multiplier per coefficient lane in the same form. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (per-frame VBR rate-control quantiser selection)** — The rate-control quantiser choice is a magnitude comparator: one XOR gate per compared bit (12 transistors each) feeding an OR tree (6 transistors per OR gate) that reports whether the candidate cost exceeds the frame budget, plus a register holding the best quantiser found so far. A 16-bit comparator in this form is 16 XOR gates and 15 OR gates, 192 plus 90, 282 transistors — an example of the form, not a published width, because the quantiser set, the cost metric and the comparator width are not published. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (entropy-code bit packing and unpacking)** — A barrel shifter is a logarithmic mux tree: for an N-bit shift, log2 N stages of N two-to-one transmission-gate muxes, 4 transistors per mux per bit. A 32-bit barrel shifter in this form is five stages of thirty-two muxes, 640 transistors; a 64-bit shifter is six stages of sixty-four muxes, 1,536 transistors. The shift amount comes from the entropy coder's code-length output, and the shifter's input and output registers are D flip-flops (20-28 transistors per bit). The shift width and the bitstream buffer depth are not published, so neither total is claimed as Apple's; the per-stage form is the standard construction. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (encode/decode pipeline sequencer and VBR rate-control loop)** — A pipeline sequencer is a finite-state machine: a state register of one D flip-flop per state bit (20-28 transistors each) whose next-state logic is a NAND/NOR gate network (4 transistors per NAND2 or NOR2) fed by the stage-done signals, and whose outputs drive the stage enables and the VBR rate-control loop's quantiser select. The rate-control loop adds a bit counter (one D flip-flop plus one full adder per bit) that tracks bits spent against the frame budget and feeds the quantiser comparator. The state count, the stage timing and the loop arithmetic are not published, so no state-register width or gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline register (inter-stage latches)** — An inter-stage latch is one D flip-flop per data bit: two cross-coupled latch stages, about 20-28 transistors per bit in a standard-cell library (primer, bottom layer). A pipeline stage W bits wide therefore costs W flip-flops, 20W to 28W transistors, plus the clock-tree buffering that distributes the clock to every latch — the clock network is itself inverter and buffer chains (2 transistors per inverter). The stage count, latch widths and stage latencies are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (ProRes vs ProRes RAW, 422 vs 4444, half-size decode path select)** — A path select is a transmission-gate mux: 2 transistors per input leg per bit, so a two-to-one mux costs 4 transistors per bit and a four-to-one mux 8 transistors per bit, with the select lines driven by the mode register. The ProRes versus ProRes RAW select, the 422 versus 4444 chroma select and the full-size versus half-size decode select are each muxes of this form steering whole pixel words between datapaths; a 12-bit pixel word through a two-to-one mux is 48 transistors as an example of the form. The mux radix and the path-selection logic are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (frame and stream sequencing across engines)** — A frame or stream counter is a binary counter: one D flip-flop per bit (20-28 transistors each) plus a one-bit incrementer of one full adder per bit (28 transistors each), so a 16-bit counter is 768-896 transistors by that arithmetic, and a terminal-count comparator (one XOR per bit plus an OR tree) for the wrap or the stream-end condition. Frame counters and stream counters are the same circuit in different widths; their widths are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Register file (per-stream frame parameters and quantiser state)** — A register file is an array of D flip-flops — 20-28 transistors per stored bit — with a write decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one entry) and a read mux per port (transmission-gate muxes, 2 transistors per input leg per bit). Per-stream frame parameters are one entry per stream, so the file's transistor count is the entry count times the entry width times 20-28, plus decoder and mux overhead — but the entry count, entry width and banking are not published, so no total is claimed; with up to 30 streams in flight the file is at most 30 entries wide in the published stream count, and nothing further. Standard construction.
- **Crossbar / arbiter (stream dispatch across the 1/2/4 ProRes engines)** — Stream dispatch is a crossbar of transmission-gate muxes: each output port takes a mux over the input streams, 2 transistors per input leg per bit, so a four-engine dispatch of a W-bit stream word costs 8W transistors of muxes, and the arbiter that grants the dispatch is a priority encoder (a NAND/NOR tree, 4 transistors per gate) plus a round-robin state register of one D flip-flop per grant bit. The arbiter's radix, widths and scheduling policy are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter (unified-memory read/write flow control)** — A credit counter is a binary up/down counter: one D flip-flop per bit (20-28 transistors each) plus a one-bit incrementer and a one-bit decrementer of one full adder per bit each (28 transistors each), with a zero comparator (one XOR per bit plus an OR tree) that stalls issue when the credit count reaches zero. A 16-bit credit counter in this form is 320-448 transistors of flip-flops plus 896 transistors of increment and decrement adders, 1,216-1,344 transistors before the comparator — an example of the form, because the credit depth, width and issue policy are not published. The Level-2 bandwidth arithmetic (about 2.7 GB/s of bitstream read against 400 GB/s of unified-memory bandwidth) is already recorded; it is reused here, not re-derived. Standard construction.

Honesty: Apple publishes no internal sub-block diagram for the media engine — no stage latencies, queue depths, block-store sizes or buffer geometry — so every gate and transistor figure below is textbook-standard construction, labelled as such, never a claim about Apple's circuits. Numbers that come from a codec specification are spec facts about the algorithm the silicon must implement; no parameter of the Apple media engine itself is claimed.

#### Down to the gates: The H.264/HEVC encode and decode engines — the inter-frame path, doubled on Max

Apple publishes no gate-level structure for the encode and decode engines either. The deepest published description is the codec-mandated long-GOP pipeline: motion estimation against reference frames, mode decision, transform and quantisation of the residual, entropy coding with CABAC/CAVLC, and the inverse on decode with in-loop filters. The decomposition below maps each Level-3 primitive to its textbook gate-level construction, with arithmetic only from the published codec geometry.

- **SRAM bank (reference frame store)** — The reference-frame store is an SRAM bank in the primer's form: rows of 6T SRAM cells — two cross-coupled inverters (4 transistors) plus two access transistors — behind a row decoder (a NAND-gate tree selecting one wordline), transmission-gate column muxes (2 transistors per leg) and latch-type differential sense amplifiers. Every stored bit costs 6 transistors of cells, so a store of B bits is 6B transistors before decoder, mux and sense-amplifier overhead. Its capacity in frames, its banking and its port count are not published, so B is not claimed; the reference-frame traffic bill is already recorded at Level 2 and is not re-derived here. Standard construction.
- **FIFO / queue (bitstream ingest, reconstructed-frame output, job queue across the two encode engines)** — A FIFO is a storage array plus two pointer counters and two comparators: a write pointer and a read pointer, each a binary counter of one D flip-flop per bit (20-28 transistors each) plus a one-bit incrementer of one full adder per bit (28 transistors each), and a full comparator and an empty comparator, each a per-bit XOR (12 transistors) feeding an OR tree (6 transistors per OR gate). The storage itself is either flip-flops (20-28 transistors per bit) or an SRAM array of 6T cells with a row decoder, column muxes and sense amplifiers. The ingest, output and job queues have no published depths or widths, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Adder tree + comparator (motion-estimation SAD and best-match selection)** — A sum of absolute differences for one 8x8 block of 8-bit samples is 64 absolute-difference units feeding a binary adder tree. Each absolute-difference unit is an 8-bit subtractor — 8 full adders, 224 transistors — plus the sign handling that takes the magnitude; 64 of them cost 14,336 transistors. The adder tree sums the 64 eight-bit differences in six levels: 32 nine-bit adders, 16 ten-bit, 8 eleven-bit, 4 twelve-bit, 2 thirteen-bit and 1 fourteen-bit adder, 624 full-adder bits in total, 17,472 transistors — so one 8x8 SAD unit is about 31,808 transistors, about 32K, before the sign handling. The best-match comparator is a magnitude comparator over the 14-bit SAD result (14 XOR gates plus a 13-gate OR tree, 246 transistors) and the best-value mux is a 14-bit two-to-one mux (56 transistors). All of this is conditional arithmetic for one 8x8 block: the candidate set, the search range and the block sizes the search covers are not published, so the number of SAD units in the motion estimator is not claimed. Standard construction.
- **Multiplier array + adder tree (transform and quantisation of the residual; inverse transform on decode)** — The transform stage is the same butterfly form as the ProRes IDCT: a two-dimensional transform run as two one-dimensional passes, each 8-point pass in the standard Loeffler form using 11 multipliers and 29 adders, so one 8x8 block needs 16 passes, 176 multipliers and 464 adders. Each multiplier in array form is N squared AND gates (6 transistors each) plus N times N minus 1 full adders (28 transistors each) plus a 32-bit final adder; a 16-bit array multiplier is 9,152 transistors by that arithmetic, so 176 of them would be 1,610,752 transistors, about 1.6M, and the 464 adders are 12,992 transistors, about 13K — conditional arithmetic, because the coefficient width of Apple's multipliers is not published and the transform set and butterfly depth are not published; the 8x8 block is one block size as an example of the form, since H.264 and HEVC also use 4x4 to 32x32 transforms. Quantisation is a further multiply by the quantiser step, one multiplier per coefficient lane in the same form; the inverse transform on decode is the same circuit run in reverse. Standard construction.
- **Barrel shifter (entropy coding bit packing — CABAC/CAVLC)** — A barrel shifter is a logarithmic mux tree: for an N-bit shift, log2 N stages of N two-to-one transmission-gate muxes, 4 transistors per mux per bit. A 32-bit barrel shifter in this form is five stages of thirty-two muxes, 640 transistors; a 64-bit shifter is six stages of sixty-four muxes, 1,536 transistors. CABAC and CAVLC both emit variable-length codes, so the shift amount comes from the entropy coder's code-length output, and the shifter's input and output registers are D flip-flops (20-28 transistors per bit). The shift width and the bitstream buffer depth are not published, so neither total is claimed as Apple's. Standard construction.
- **Register file (CABAC context models)** — The CABAC probability tables are a register file (or small SRAM): each probability model takes one of 127 states (Fraunhofer HHI, already recorded at Level 3), so the state register for one model is 7 D flip-flops (2 to the 7th is 128), 140-196 transistors, and the tabulated transition rules are a 127-entry table of 7-bit next states, 889 bits — 17,780-24,892 transistors as flip-flops, or 5,334 transistors as 6T cells. The table is indexed by syntax element and context through a decoder (a NAND-gate tree) and read through muxes (2 transistors per input leg per bit). The table count, entry count and banking are not published, so the number of models — and therefore the total — is not claimed; the per-model arithmetic above is the standard construction. Standard construction.
- **FSM / controller (encode/decode pipeline sequencer and mode-decision state machine)** — The encode sequencer and the decode sequencer are finite-state machines: a state register of one D flip-flop per state bit (20-28 transistors each) whose next-state logic is a NAND/NOR gate network (4 transistors per NAND2 or NOR2) fed by the stage-done signals, and whose outputs drive the stage enables, while the mode-decision state machine adds a cost register and a comparator that keeps the cheapest candidate. The CABAC probability estimator itself is a 127-state finite-state machine with tabulated transition rules (Fraunhofer HHI, already recorded at Level 3): a 7-bit state register, 140-196 transistors, stepping through the table above. The state counts, the stage timing and the mode-decision cost metric are not published, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Mux / demux (H.264 vs HEVC vs AV1-decode path select; encode-engine 1 vs 2 dispatch on Max)** — A codec path select is a transmission-gate mux: 2 transistors per input leg per bit, so a two-to-one mux costs 4 transistors per bit and a three-to-one mux 6 transistors per bit, with the select lines driven by the codec mode register. The H.264 versus HEVC versus AV1-decode select is a mux of this form steering whole pixel words between datapaths, and on Max-class silicon the job dispatch steers the next frame to encode engine 1 or 2 through the same form; a 12-bit pixel word through a two-to-one mux is 48 transistors as an example of the form. The mux radix and the path-selection logic are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Credit counter / arbiter (two encode engines sharing unified-memory bandwidth)** — Two encode engines sharing unified-memory bandwidth are arbitrated by a credit counter and arbiter: each engine's credit counter is a binary up/down counter — one D flip-flop per bit (20-28 transistors each) plus a one-bit incrementer and a one-bit decrementer of one full adder per bit each (28 transistors each) — and the arbiter that grants the fabric is a priority encoder (a NAND/NOR tree, 4 transistors per gate) plus a round-robin state register of one D flip-flop per grant bit. A 16-bit credit counter in this form is 320-448 transistors of flip-flops plus 896 transistors of increment and decrement adders, 1,216-1,344 transistors before the comparator — an example of the form, because the arbitration policy, the credit depth and any published rate are not published. Standard construction.
- **Pipeline register (inter-stage latches)** — An inter-stage latch is one D flip-flop per data bit: two cross-coupled latch stages, about 20-28 transistors per bit in a standard-cell library (primer, bottom layer). A pipeline stage W bits wide therefore costs W flip-flops, 20W to 28W transistors, plus the clock-tree buffering that distributes the clock to every latch — the clock network is itself inverter and buffer chains (2 transistors per inverter). The stage count, latch widths and stage latencies are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Synchronizer (media-engine clock domain against the unified-memory / system fabric domain)** — A clock-domain crossing is a synchronizer: two D flip-flops in series per signal bit (40-56 transistors per bit), the first sampling the incoming signal and the second re-sampling it a cycle later so a metastable first stage has a full cycle to resolve, or a FIFO-based crossing where the whole FIFO above is the synchronizer. The media engine's clock against the system fabric's clock is this boundary in standard construction: Apple publishes no clocking for the media engine, so whether the engine and the fabric share a clock, and where the synchronizers sit, is not a published fact, and no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Counter (frame and job sequencing; reference-frame management)** — A frame, job or reference-frame-age counter is a binary counter: one D flip-flop per bit (20-28 transistors each) plus a one-bit incrementer of one full adder per bit (28 transistors each), so a 16-bit counter is 768-896 transistors by that arithmetic, and a terminal-count comparator (one XOR per bit plus an OR tree) for the wrap or the reference-retirement condition. Frame counters, job counters and reference-frame age counters are the same circuit in different widths; their widths and the reference-management policy are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Comparator (mode decision and in-loop filter edge decisions)** — Mode decision is a magnitude comparator per candidate: one XOR gate per compared bit (12 transistors each) feeding an OR tree (6 transistors per OR gate) that reports which rate-distortion cost is lower, plus a register holding the best mode found so far; and the in-loop filters compare samples across each block edge to set their filtering strength, the same comparator form over sample differences. A 16-bit comparator in this form is 16 XOR gates and 15 OR gates, 192 plus 90, 282 transistors — an example of the form, not a published width, because the cost metric, the candidate pruning and the comparator widths are not published. Standard construction.

Honesty: Apple publishes no internal sub-block diagram for the video encode and decode engines either — no stage latencies, queue depths, reference-store sizes or buffer geometry — so every gate and transistor figure below is textbook-standard construction, labelled as such, never a claim about Apple's circuits. Numbers that come from a codec specification are spec facts about the algorithm the silicon must implement; no parameter of the Apple media engine itself is claimed.

**Key numbers.** M1 Pro/Max (October 2021) · M2 Pro/Max (January 2023) · M3 (November 2023) · M3 Ultra (March 2025); ProRes engines 1 (Pro) / 2 (Max) / 4 (M3 Ultra); video encode engines 1 / 2 / 4; video decode engines 1 / 1 / 2; playback up to 20 streams of 4K or 4 of 8K ProRes (M1 Pro), 30 of 4K or 7 of 8K (M1 Max), 24 of 8K (M3 Ultra); M1 Max and M2 Max video encoding up to 2x their Pro counterparts; unified memory bandwidth 200 GB/s (Pro) / 400 GB/s (Max) / 819 GB/s (M3 Ultra).

**Signature ideas.**
1. **ProRes in hardware** — Apple's own codec in silicon across cameras, phones and laptops; the intra-only design is what makes it cheap to accelerate and robust to edit.
2. **Scale by duplication** — the media engine grows by doubling engine counts (Pro → Max → Ultra) instead of redesigning the pipeline.
3. **The frozen menu** — each generation's codec set is fixed at tape-out; AV1 decode arrived only with M3, and AV1 encode still waits for a newer generation.
