### Scoreboarding (CDC 6600)

**Added: 2026-11-28** (added at the full Level-2/3/4 standard in a single run)

**What it is / why it matters.** The first dynamic instruction scheduling in hardware: a central scoreboard that tracks every functional unit and every register, issuing each instruction the moment its unit is free and its result register unreserved. Designed by James E. Thornton for the CDC 6600 (introduced September 1964) under Seymour Cray, it is the 1964 origin of out-of-order execution — the machine that first let hardware, not the compiler, decide when an instruction could run.

**Building blocks.** Six named pieces, and the connections between them are the design:
- **The scoreboard — Unit and Register Reservation Control** — the central table that issues every instruction and tracks every reservation: per-unit designators (function and mode Fm, result and operand registers Fi/Fj/Fk, producer identifiers Qj/Qk, Read Flags, busy bit) and per-register result reservations (Xi/Bi/Ai identifiers, one per operating register). It runs the two issue tests, places reservations in four steps, sends GO READ to start a unit and GO STORE to release its result.
- **Ten functional units** — Boolean, Shift, Fixed Add, Floating Add, Multiply (two units), Divide, Increment (two units) and Branch. Each unit is independent and non-pipelined: it takes an instruction at issue and stays busy for its whole latency — 3 minor cycles for fixed add, boolean, shift and increment, 4 for floating add, 10 for multiply, 29 for divide. Two identical units are provided for the Multiply and Increment functions, so two of those operations can run at once.
- **Twenty-four operating registers** — eight 60-bit X operand registers, eight 18-bit B index registers and eight 18-bit A address registers. Five memory trunks feed X1 through X5 (each with a partner address register A1 through A5) and two store registers X6 and X7 write back to storage. All data movement between storage and the units passes through these registers — the units never touch memory directly.
- **Instruction stack** — eight 60-bit words holding up to 32 fifteen-bit instructions, fed from central storage. The stack supplies the issue registers U1 and U2; a loop that fits in the stack runs without any storage reference for instructions. In straight-line code only the bottom two stack words are in use, refilled as fast as memory conflicts allow.
- **Operand and result trunks** — three operand trunks to and from each functional unit, and five memory trunks from storage into the central processor. Register entry and exit control gates every transfer with scoreboard tags — GO READ to move operands into a unit, GO STORE to move a result into its register — and seven trunks are controlled this way.
- **Release and GO STORE handshake** — a unit holds its result in a temporary result register and sends REQUEST RELEASE to the scoreboard, which checks that no earlier instruction still needs to read the result register (the All Clear condition) and that the result trunk is free, then answers GO STORE. The releasing unit's reservations clear, and every unit waiting on that result is signalled to read it.

**The piece that makes it special:** the reservation, not the execution. The scoreboard never computes anything — it only remembers: which unit is busy, which register is reserved for a result, and which operand is still owed by which unit. That bookkeeping is the whole trick: a snapshot of conditions taken at issue time, two tests to issue, and a release handshake to store. Every later scheduler — Tomasulo's reservation stations, the reorder buffer, the issue queue — is this same reservation idea, distributed or renamed, but the 6600 did it first with one central table.

**The architecture.** Thornton's own summary lists five ingredients for parallel execution of a single instruction stream: ten independent functional units, twenty-four registers, a control system with scoreboard, an instruction stack, and multiple paths to central storage. Around them the scoreboard runs four mechanisms:

- **Two tests to issue.** Instructions arrive in order from the stack through registers U1 and U2. The scoreboard issues from U2 only when the designated unit is not busy and the result register is not already reserved for a result by a previous instruction. With just those two restrictions on issuing, several independent chains of instructions may proceed concurrently, and instructions may issue every minor cycle in the absence of the two restraints. A 30-bit instruction needs two minor cycles to issue, with a SKIP cycle after it.
- **Reservations in four steps.** On a passing test the scoreboard sets the unit busy flag and enters the function mode (SET UNIT BUSY), copies the i, j and k fields into Fi, Fj and Fk (SET F), copies any previous result reservations on the operands into Qj and Qk (SET Q), and writes the unit number into the result register's X, B or A identifier (SET XBA). The conditions at the instant of issuance are set into the scoreboard — a snapshot, so to speak, of the pertinent conditions.
- **The three conflicts.** First order: the same unit or the same result register — resolved at issue by not issuing. Second order: an input operand not yet produced — resolved inside the unit, which waits while later instructions keep issuing. Third order: a result register that an earlier, unstarted instruction still needs as an input — resolved by holding the finished result in the unit until the reader has read. The scoreboard directs the functional unit in starting, obtaining its operands, and storing its result.
- **Issue–wait–execute–release lifecycle.** Issue is in order (from U2 into a unit); operand waiting happens inside the unit on its Read Flags; execution runs independently for 3 to 29 minor cycles; release is a handshake — REQUEST RELEASE from the unit, GO STORE from the scoreboard once All Clear holds. Loads and stores go through the registers only: writing an address register triggers the memory reference, and the data arrives in its partner X register through one of the five read channels.

**Key numbers.** CDC 6600, introduced September 1964; first machines delivered in 1965 to Livermore and Los Alamos; about 100 sold; up to about 3 MFLOPS, the world's fastest computer from 1964 to 1969. 10 MHz clock: a 100 ns minor cycle and a 1,000 ns major cycle. Central storage 131,072 60-bit words in 32 interleaved banks. Ten functional units; latencies in minor cycles: fixed add 3, boolean 3, shift 3, increment 3, floating add 4, floating multiply 10, floating divide 29, branch 8–14 by type. Issue at most one instruction per minor cycle; a unit is free one minor cycle after its result is placed. The whole machine held about 400,000 transistors.

**Signature ideas.**
1. **Centralized dynamic scheduling** — the scoreboard: the first hardware that let instructions execute out of order, by tracking reservations instead of program order.
2. **The three conflicts** — first, second and third order: the first taxonomy of hazards, still the vocabulary (structural, RAW, WAR) in every computer-architecture textbook.
3. **Reservation by designators** — Q identifiers naming the producing unit: the direct ancestor of Tomasulo's tags, which turned the unit number into a register name.
4. **Issue decoupled from execution** — one instruction per minor cycle into free units while earlier ones still run; the scoreboard keeps issuing while a divide works for 29 cycles.

**Limits & tradeoffs.** In-order issue is the hard limit: a first-order conflict stalls every later instruction, even one that is independent and aimed at a free unit — there is no issue queue to look past the stall. There is no register renaming, so a write-after-write conflict stalls issue and a write-after-read conflict holds a finished result inside its unit. The units are not pipelined, so a divide occupies its unit for 29 minor cycles. Out-of-order completion makes exceptions imprecise, and there is no speculation or recovery machinery. And the scoreboard itself is a single control bottleneck: at most one instruction can issue per minor cycle, and the translation networks that check every reservation grow with every unit and register added. The CDC 6400, the 6600's cheaper sibling, is the control case: same instruction set, one unified arithmetic unit, no overlap at all.

**Lineage.** Descended from nothing in particular — the scoreboard was the first dynamic scheduler; its immediate context was the 6600's ten independent functional units and 24 registers, the parallel hardware that made a reservation scheme practical. The CDC 6400 kept the instruction set but used a unified arithmetic unit and could not overlap instructions. Revived and generalized three years later by Tomasulo's algorithm (IBM System/360 Model 91, 1967), which distributed the scoreboard into reservation stations and added register renaming; the CDC 7600 (1969) kept scoreboarding with pipelined functional units. Hennessy and Patterson made the scoreboard the textbook scheme for dynamic scheduling, and every modern out-of-order core — issue queues, reservation stations, reorder buffers — descends from its reservation idea.

**One-line summary.** The scoreboard taught hardware to keep a running reservation file of every unit and register, so independent instructions could issue and finish out of order — the first dynamic scheduler, and the ancestor of every out-of-order core.

#### Inside the signature block: The scoreboard — the reservation table

**Inside it.** The scoreboard is two tables that meet at issue time. The unit side holds one set of designators per functional unit: the function and mode Fm, the result and operand register numbers Fi, Fj and Fk, the producer identifiers Qj and Qk naming the unit that will supply each operand, a Read Flag per operand, and a busy bit. The register side holds 24 XBA identifiers — one per operating register (8 X, 8 B, 8 A) — each holding the number of the unit that has reserved that register for a result. Unit numbers are octal: 00 Branch, 01 and 02 the two Increment units, 03 Shift, 04 Boolean, 05 Divide, 06 and 07 the two Multiply units, 11 through 15 the five Read Storage Channels, 16 Fixed Add and 17 the Add unit. At issue the scoreboard runs four sequential steps: SET UNIT BUSY, SET F, SET Q and SET XBA. After issue it directs the unit: GO READ when both Read Flags are set and the operand trunk is free, and GO STORE when the unit requests release and the All Clear condition holds. The Read Flag for an operand sets when the producing unit's Release signal arrives ANDed with the Q translation — the Q identifier can hold only one unit number, so only one Release signal is selected — or immediately at issue when Q is zero.

**Trace — one unit of work.**
1. **Two tests at U2.** The instruction stack delivers an instruction to register U2 — say a floating add X6 = X1 + X2. The scoreboard checks the Add unit's busy flag and the X6 result identifier. Both must be clear, or issue waits and every later instruction waits with it.
2. **Four reservation steps.** On a pass, the scoreboard sets the Add unit busy, copies i=6, j=1, k=2 into Fi, Fj, Fk, copies the current X1 and X2 identifiers into Qj and Qk (zero if no producer is pending), and writes unit number 17 into the X6 identifier. The Add unit now owns X6 until it releases.
3. **Wait on the Read Flags.** If X1 is owed by a multiply still running, Qj holds 06 and the j Read Flag stays clear. When the multiply requests release and the scoreboard answers GO STORE, its Release signal ANDs with the Qj translation and sets the flag. With both flags set and the operand trunk free, the scoreboard sends GO READ and X1 and X2 move into the Add unit.
4. **Execute for 4 minor cycles.** The Add unit computes for four minor cycles while the scoreboard issues later instructions into free units — a multiply, an increment, a shift — each placing its own reservations.
5. **Request release, GO STORE, clear.** Near the end of the add, the unit sends REQUEST RELEASE. The scoreboard checks All Clear — no earlier instruction still needs to read X6 — and the result trunk, then sends GO STORE. The result moves into X6, the X6 identifier clears, every unit waiting on X6 is signalled to read it, and the Add unit is free one minor cycle later.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the in-order stall: a slow divide no longer freezes the machine — independent adds, multiplies and increments flow around it, which is why Thornton's quadratic example runs in 46 minor cycles with the scoreboard against 78 counted sequentially. Creates two new ceilings: issue is strictly in order, so one first-order conflict stalls every later instruction even when its unit is free and its operands are ready — there is no queue to look past the stall — and with no renaming, a write-after-write conflict stalls issue while a write-after-read conflict holds a finished result inside its unit. The scoreboard's own translation networks are the hardware price, but Thornton's own accounting says they cost less than one functional unit.

**Governing numbers.** 10 functional units (Boolean, Shift, Fixed Add, Floating Add, Multiply x2, Divide, Increment x2, Branch); 24 operating registers (8 X 60-bit, 8 B 18-bit, 8 A 18-bit); 24 XBA result identifiers; Q identifiers 4-bit (unit numbers 00–17 octal); Fi/Fj/Fk 3-bit register numbers; 5 read storage channels (11–15) into X1–X5; 7 trunks under register entry/exit control; issue 1 instruction per minor cycle (100 ns); a unit is free 1 minor cycle after its result is placed; consecutive instruction words from storage need a minimum of 8 minor cycles.

**Primary source.** Thornton, "Design of a Computer: The Control Data 6600", Scott, Foresman, 1970, Ch. VI.C–D (esp. Fig. 75, reservation designators) and Ch. V; Thornton, "Parallel Operation in the Control Data 6600", Proc. AFIPS Fall Joint Computer Conference, 1964, pp. 33–40.

#### Inside the signature block: The three conflicts — first, second and third order

**Inside it.** Thornton names three conflicts, and the scoreboard resolves each in a different place. The first order conflict is a fight over the same functional unit or the same result register — two adds, or two instructions writing X6 — and it is resolved at issue by not issuing: the second instruction waits until the first completes. The second order conflict is an instruction that needs the result of a previous, uncompleted instruction as an input — X7 = X5 / X6 where X6 is still being computed — and it is resolved inside the unit: the instruction is issued but held in the Divide unit until result X6 is ready, while later instructions keep issuing. The third order conflict is an instruction ready to store its result in a register that an earlier, unstarted instruction still needs as an input — X4 = X0 + X6 finishing before the multiply that must read X4 has started — and it is resolved by holding the result in the functional unit: the fast add completes but cannot release X4 until the multiply's j Read Flag has been read. The three conflicts are the first taxonomy of hazards: first order is the structural plus write-after-write hazard, second order is read-after-write, third order is write-after-read.

**Trace — one unit of work.**
1. **Three instructions issue.** X3 = X1 / X2 issues to the Divide unit (29 minor cycles), X5 = X4 * X3 issues to a Multiply unit and waits on X3, and X4 = X0 + X6 issues to the Add unit — all on consecutive minor cycles, each placing its own reservations.
2. **The add runs first.** The Add unit needs only its operands X0 and X6, both ready, so it starts at once and finishes in 4 minor cycles — long before the divide (29 cycles) has produced X3 and the multiply has even started.
3. **The multiply waits on two flags.** The multiply's j Read Flag for X4 is set (X4 was ready at issue), but its k Read Flag for X3 is held by the second-order conflict on the divide. The multiply cannot start, so it has not yet read X4.
4. **The add requests release — and is refused.** The finished add sends REQUEST RELEASE for X4. The scoreboard computes All Clear for X4 and finds the multiply's j Read Flag still set — the multiply has not read X4 yet — so no GO STORE is sent. The add's result stays in its temporary result register.
5. **Release follows the read.** When the divide releases X3, the multiply's k flag sets, it reads X4 (clearing the j flag) and starts. Only then does All Clear hold for X4, the scoreboard sends GO STORE, and the add's result finally lands in X4 — the slow instruction's input was protected from the fast instruction's output.

**Bottleneck in / out.** Relieves the dependency stall: instructions no longer wait in program order for every earlier result — a divide's 29-cycle latency overlaps with independent work instead of serializing the machine. Creates the bottleneck that defines the scoreboard's limits: a held result ties up its functional unit, so a fast add that finishes early can sit occupied for dozens of cycles waiting for a slow consumer to read its input register — the unit cannot take new work until it releases. And because issue is in order, a first-order conflict anywhere stalls the whole issue stream behind it. The direct motivation for Tomasulo's distributed stations (which let a waiting instruction sit in a station instead of in a unit) and for register renaming (which removes the write-after-write stall at issue).

**Governing numbers.** Latencies in minor cycles (100 ns each): fixed add 3, boolean 3, shift 3, increment 3, floating add 4, floating multiply 10, floating divide 29, branch 8–14 by type; worked example (quadratic AX2 + BX + C = Y): 46 minor cycles with the scoreboard vs 78 counted sequentially; a unit is free 1 minor cycle after its result is placed in a register.

**Primary source.** Thornton, "Design of a Computer: The Control Data 6600", Scott, Foresman, 1970, Ch. VI.D–F (conflict definitions, worked third-order example, Example One timing).

#### Down to the primitives: The scoreboard — the reservation table

Decomposed in issue order — an instruction is tested, takes its reservations in four steps, waits on its Read Flags, fires on GO READ, and frees its unit on GO STORE. The book publishes the unit and register counts, the designator fields, the unit numbers 00–17 octal, the five read storage channels and the seven controlled trunks, but nothing below that contract: no translation-network fan-in, no scoreboard module count, no gate-level detail below the DCTL circuit level. Where a number below is computed from published geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **XBA result identifiers (24 x 4-bit)** — One identifier per operating register — 8 X, 8 B, 8 A — holding the number of the functional unit that has reserved that register for a result. The book is explicit that only two bits are necessary for the B and A identifiers (only three units produce B or A results) whereas four bits are needed for the X identifiers (up to ten units plus the five read channels produce X results). The identifier is set at issue (SET XBA) and cleared when the producing unit releases its result. Its storage cell form is not published.
- **Q identifiers (2 per unit, 4-bit)** — Qj and Qk in each functional unit name the unit that will produce the j and k operands — a 4-bit unit number, 00 through 17 octal. At issue, SET Q copies the current XBA identifier of each operand register into the unit's Q fields; a zero means no wait. The Q identifier can hold only one unit number, so only one Release signal is selected per operand — that single-producer rule is the whole dependency mechanism. The number of Q fields varies by unit (the k operand in the Increment units and the j operand in the Shift unit are noteworthy exceptions in the book), so no total bit count is claimed.
- **Read Flags (1-bit per operand)** — One flag per operand per unit, set when the operand is ready to be read. The flag sets when the Q-identified producer's Release signal arrives — the Release ANDs with the translation of the unit number held in Q — or immediately after issue when Q is zero. Both flags must be set before the unit may start, and a set flag is cleared when the unit starts, which is what makes the All Clear signal work. The flag's latch form is not published.
- **Unit-busy flags (1 per unit)** — One busy flag per functional unit, set at issue (SET UNIT BUSY) and cleared when the unit's result is placed in its register. The issue test reads this flag directly: a second instruction to the same unit is disallowed while it is set, and because two consecutive instructions to the same unit are one minor cycle apart, the set and the test must complete within one minor cycle. The flag's latch form is not published.
- **Fi/Fj/Fk register designators (3-bit each)** — The i, j and k fields of the instruction, copied into the unit at issue (SET F), each designating one of eight registers in the X, B or A group. Fi names the result register; Fj and Fk name the operand registers. The designators are translated to drive the All Clear network and the register entry/exit control. Their storage form is not published.
- **Q-translation decoders (AND networks)** — The network that turns a 4-bit Q value into the selection of one Release line: the Release signal from the Add unit, for example, is ANDed with the translation of the unit number held in Qk, so only the matching producer's release sets the flag. Release lines are fanned out to all Read Flag networks — the book's Figure 79 shows the Release for Read Storage Channel 5 going to the Q translation for unit number 15 on all nine units that take X operands. The decoder's gate count and fan-in are not published.
- **All-Clear network (per-register AND)** — For each of the 24 registers, an AND of the translated Fj/Fk designators with the associated Read Flags produces an All Clear signal: the register is all clear when no Read Flag is set for it. The 24 All Clear signals are combined with the translation of the result designator Fi to decide whether a requesting unit may release its result. The network's gate count is not published.
- **GO READ / GO STORE control tags + issue FSM** — The scoreboard's outputs are single-bit control tags: GO READ (Xi, Bj, Aj, Bk for the Increment trunk pair; Xi and Xk for the Multiply/Divide/Boolean pair; three tags for the Add/Fixed Add/Shift pair) gates operands onto the trunks, and GO STORE directs a requesting unit to transmit its result to the registers. The issue sequencer is a four-step FSM — SET UNIT BUSY, SET F, SET Q, SET XBA — executed in order at each issue. The FSM's state count and the tag drivers' circuit form are not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the book publishes the unit and register counts, the designator fields (Fm, Fi/Fj/Fk, Qj/Qk, Read Flags, XBA identifiers), the unit numbers 00–17 octal, the five read storage channels and the seven controlled trunks. Below that level — the internal fan-in of the translation networks, the number of modules the scoreboard occupies, any gate-level detail below the DCTL circuit level — the book publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. The machine was built from discrete-transistor DCTL modules, and no transistor count is claimed for the scoreboard itself.

#### Down to the primitives: The three conflicts — first, second and third order

Decomposed by conflict — the issue interlock stops the first order, the operand-wait interlock holds the second, the release interlock holds the third. The book publishes the conflict definitions, the worked third-order example and the timing rules, but no queue depths, module counts or gate-level detail for the interlocks. Where a number below is computed from published geometry it is labelled as arithmetic derived from the published geometry; everywhere else the primitive is named with its role and its parameters are stated plainly as not published.

- **First-order interlock (issue gate)** — Two AND conditions at issue: the designated unit's busy flag must be clear, and the result register's XBA identifier must be clear. Either one blocks the ISSUE command and stalls every later instruction — the scoreboard has no queue to look past the stall. The interlock is combinational: the two conditions are fairly simple to establish, which is why the issue decision is made quickly, within one minor cycle.
- **Second-order interlock (operand-wait)** — The Q identifiers plus Read Flags: an issued instruction waits inside its functional unit until both flags set, and the unit cannot start before that. The wait is per-unit, so a stalled divide does not block the issue of later instructions — this is the mechanism that lets independent chains proceed concurrently. No storage depth is involved: the wait state is two flag bits per unit.
- **Third-order interlock (release hold)** — The All Clear network plus the REQUEST RELEASE / GO STORE handshake: a finished unit holds its result in its temporary result register until All Clear holds for its result register. The hold is enforced by the scoreboard withholding GO STORE, not by any storage in the unit beyond its one result register. A held result occupies its unit for the whole wait — the cost of the third-order rule.
- **Temporary result registers (1 per unit, 60-bit)** — Each functional unit holds its result in a temporary result register until the scoreboard releases it. The register is 60 bits for X results and 18 bits for A/B results; the book's Figure 43 shows the temporary register between the unit and the result trunk. The register's cell form is not published.
- **Dependency crossbar (Release lines to Read Flag networks)** — Every unit's Release signal is fanned out to every other unit's Read Flag network, where it is ANDed with that unit's Q translation — the crossbar that makes a producer's release visible to exactly the waiters that named it. The book's Figure 79 draws the Release lines as they appear to the divisor input of the Divide unit and notes the same lines reach all nine units that take X operands. The fan-out and driver count are not published.
- **Data-trunk priority logic** — When several units become ready at once, they share operand trunks, so the data-trunk priority condition also controls which unit starts. The priority rule itself is not published in the book, and no priority-encoder width is claimed — the mechanism is named with its role, and its policy is stated as unpublished.
- **Register entry/exit control (7 trunks)** — The secondary control over data entering and leaving the registers: entry to the X, B or A registers is a direct result of the release mechanism, and exit control gates the operands onto the data trunks — seven trunks controlled in total, with the GO READ tags per trunk pair. The central storage entry trunk is also used by the exchange jump for initial loading. The trunk drivers' circuit form is not published.

**Parameter honesty.** Parameter honesty: the book publishes the conflict definitions, the worked third-order example and the timing rules (issue one per minor cycle, a unit free one minor cycle after its result is placed). Below that level — queue depths, module counts, any gate-level detail for the interlocks — the book publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. The dependency-matrix form of the Q/Release crossbar is described in the book's Figure 79, and its gate form is textbook-standard construction, not a 6600 netlist.

#### Down to the gates: The scoreboard — the reservation table

The 6600 was built from discrete silicon transistors in DCTL (Direct-Coupled Transistor Logic) modules on printed-circuit boards — not integrated standard cells — so there is no CMOS gate netlist to quote. What follows is the logical construction of each primitive in DCTL terms from Thornton's Chapter III, labelled standard construction throughout; the transistor counts are the book's own module counts, not a netlist. A gate-term search of the book this run found the DCTL circuit chapter, the flip-flop with clear/set input, the ground rules (five bases in-module, two by back-panel, six collectors for AND/OR) and the Boolean unit's module transistor counts.

- **XBA result identifiers (24 x 4-bit)** — Storage is DCTL flip-flops: the book's basic flip-flop (Fig. 18) has a clear/set network, up to five set inputs and five clear inputs, driven by a 25 ns clock pulse with a 5 ns inverter delay assumed. Arithmetic: 24 identifiers at 4 bits is 96 flip-flop bits of reservation storage, though the book's own note cuts it down — only two bits are necessary for the 8 B/A identifiers, so 16 X identifiers x 4 bits (64) plus 8 B/A identifiers x 2 bits (16) is 80 bits by arithmetic. The flip-flop's transistor count is not published, so no transistor total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **Q identifiers (2 per unit, 4-bit)** — Each Q is a 4-bit DCTL register — four flip-flops — written at issue by SET Q and read by the translation network. Arithmetic: ten units x 2 operands x 4 bits is up to 80 flip-flop bits, though the book notes not every unit uses both Q fields (the k operand in the Increment units and the j operand in the Shift unit are exceptions), so 80 is an upper bound, labelled arithmetic. Standard construction.
- **Read Flags (1-bit per operand)** — A Read Flag is a set/reset latch: set by the AND of the producer's Release signal with the Q translation, cleared when the unit starts. In DCTL the latch is two cross-coupled inverters with a clear/set network — the book's flip-flop with its clear/set input, driven by a 25 ns pulse. Arithmetic: ten units x 2 flags is 20 latch bits. Standard construction.
- **Unit-busy flags (1 per unit)** — One set/reset latch per unit — ten latches — set by the SET UNIT BUSY step and cleared when the unit's result is placed in its register. The set and the next issue's test must complete within one minor cycle (100 ns), which the book notes is convenient because the busy flag is used directly by the following instruction's issue test. Standard construction.
- **Fi/Fj/Fk register designators (3-bit each)** — Each designator is three DCTL flip-flops holding a 3-bit register number, written by SET F from the instruction's i, j and k fields. Arithmetic: ten units x 3 fields x 3 bits is 90 flip-flop bits. Their outputs feed the translation networks that drive the All Clear computation and the register entry/exit tags. Standard construction.
- **Q-translation decoders (AND networks)** — A 4-bit Q translation is a decoder: in DCTL, AND and OR are made by connecting collectors together — up to six collectors can be connected for OR and AND functions — and inversion is a single transistor. The decoder recognises one 4-bit unit number, so it is a 4-input AND (four collectors tied together) per value, plus the Release AND that gates the flag set. The book's own ground rules cap the fan-in at six collectors and the fan-out at five bases in a module (two by back-panel twisted pair), which bound how wide any one decoder can be. Standard construction.
- **All-Clear network (per-register AND)** — All Clear for one register is an AND over the translated Fj/Fk designators and the Read Flags — in DCTL, a wired-AND of collectors, up to six per node by the book's ground rules. Arithmetic: 24 registers need 24 such AND trees, each combining the flag states of the units that could be reading that register. The tree depth and gate count are not published, so no total is claimed. Standard construction.
- **GO READ / GO STORE control tags + issue FSM** — The control tags are single-bit DCTL outputs: GO READ and GO STORE are driven onto the trunk gates, and between chassis they travel on twisted-pair transmission lines — the book's driver sends 6.7 mA of a 10 mA total into a 130–150 ohm line, with a 4.3 ns per foot delay. The issue FSM is four sequential steps driven by the 25 ns clear/set clock pulse, its state held in DCTL flip-flops; the book does not publish the state count, so no gate total is claimed. Standard construction.

**Honesty.** Honesty: the book publishes the designator counts, the DCTL ground rules and the Boolean unit's module counts — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — any scoreboard schematic, module count or netlist — Thornton publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Every gate form above is the DCTL construction of that primitive from the book's Chapter III, never a claim about a 6600 netlist.

#### Down to the gates: The three conflicts — first, second and third order

The three interlocks at gate level are AND gates, latches and one register per unit, all in DCTL. As with the scoreboard block, the 1964 hardware was discrete-transistor DCTL, so all gate detail here is textbook-standard construction from the primer's bottom layer and the book's Chapter III, not a 6600 netlist. The book's own module counts anchor the scale: a Boolean-unit GA module holds 14 transistors per bit plus 5 for control (61 per 4-bit module) and a GB module 18 per bit plus 4 for control (58 per 3-bit module), with a nominal maximum of 64 transistors per module — and the whole 6600 held about 400,000 transistors in nearly 6,000 such modules.

- **First-order interlock (issue gate)** — Two AND conditions feeding the ISSUE command: unit-busy clear AND result-identifier clear. In DCTL each condition is a wired-AND of collectors (up to six per node), and the two combine in one more AND — a handful of transistors, since a DCTL inverter is a single transistor and an AND is a shared collector load. The issue decision must settle within one minor cycle (100 ns) against a 5 ns inverter delay, so the interlock is shallow by construction. Standard construction.
- **Second-order interlock (operand-wait)** — The wait is two latch bits per unit — the Read Flags — and one AND gate per flag (Release AND Q translation). No counter, no queue, no storage depth: the operand-wait state of the whole machine is 20 latch bits by arithmetic (ten units x 2 flags). When the producer releases, the AND fires and the flag sets within the 25 ns clear/set pulse. Standard construction.
- **Third-order interlock (release hold)** — The hold is the All Clear AND tree withholding GO STORE: the requesting unit's result register is a 60-bit DCTL register whose output gate stays shut until All Clear holds. The gate is one AND per result trunk, driven by the All Clear tree. The cost is visible at gate level too: the held result occupies the unit's register and the unit's busy latch for the whole wait, so the unit cannot accept new work. Standard construction.
- **Temporary result registers (1 per unit, 60-bit)** — Each unit's result register is 60 DCTL flip-flops for X results (18 for B/A results), written when the unit completes and read when GO STORE arrives. Arithmetic: the seven X-result units hold 420 flip-flop bits (7 x 60); the two Increment units write 18-bit A/B or 60-bit X results depending on the instruction, and the Branch unit writes no register, so no machine-wide total is claimed beyond the 420. The flip-flop transistor count is not published. Standard construction.
- **Dependency crossbar (Release lines to Read Flag networks)** — The crossbar is wiring plus one AND gate per (unit, operand) pair: each unit's Release line fans out to every other unit's Read Flag network, where the Q translation selects it. Arithmetic: up to 20 such AND gates (ten units x 2 operands), fewer in practice since not every unit uses both operand fields. The fan-out is bounded by the DCTL ground rule — a collector drives at most five bases in a module, two more by back-panel twisted pair — so a Release line that must reach nine units needs driver stages, which the book's transmission-line section provides. Standard construction.
- **Data-trunk priority logic** — Priority between simultaneously ready units is an arbiter: in DCTL terms a chain of AND gates that grants the highest-priority requester and blocks the rest. The book publishes the existence of the trunk-priority condition but not its policy or circuit, so the arbiter is named as standard construction with no width or gate count claimed. Standard construction.
- **Register entry/exit control (7 trunks)** — Each trunk's GO READ and GO STORE tags are single-bit DCTL outputs driving the trunk gates — transmission gates in modern terms, DCTL collector drivers in 1964 — with the twisted-pair drivers carrying the signals between chassis (6.7 mA into the line, 4.3 ns per foot). The register file itself is 24 registers of DCTL flip-flop storage: 8 x 60-bit X registers (480 bits) plus 8 x 18-bit B and 8 x 18-bit A (288 bits), 768 bits by arithmetic from the published register counts and widths. Standard construction.

**Honesty.** Honesty: the book publishes the DCTL ground rules, the Boolean unit's module transistor counts and the register widths — and the arithmetic below is derived from those published counts. Below that level — driver circuits, arbitration policy, any interlock schematic — Thornton publishes nothing, and this decomposition invents nothing. Every gate form above is the textbook-standard construction of that primitive from the primer's bottom layer and the book's Chapter III, never a claim about a 6600 netlist.

### Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons

**Added: 2026-11-28** (added at the full Level-2/3/4 standard in a single run)

**What it is / why it matters.** The art of guessing which way a branch goes before it is resolved — the speculation engine that keeps deep pipelines full. A conditional branch stalls the fetch stream until its condition is known; prediction lets the core fetch, decode and even issue down the guessed path instead of waiting. Smith's 1981 paper put it plainly: prediction exists so the machine can begin "fetching, decoding, and/or issuing subsequent instructions before the actual outcome is known." From a 2-bit counter per branch (1981) through two-level history (1991), gshare and tournament choosers (1993), the Alpha 21264's shipped tournament predictor (1998), perceptron predictors (2001) and TAGE (2006), the field's accuracy climbed from roughly 85–90% to 97–98% and beyond — and because a mispredict flushes the whole speculative pipeline, that climb is the difference between a fast core and a stalled one.

**Building blocks.** Eight named pieces, and the connections between them are the design:
- **The 2-bit saturating counter (bimodal)** — one tiny finite-state machine per branch: four states (strongly not-taken, weakly not-taken, weakly taken, strongly taken), incremented on taken and decremented on not-taken, saturating at 0 and 3. The prediction is the counter's high bit. The second bit is the whole idea: it adds hysteresis, so one anomalous outcome cannot flip the prediction. Smith (1981) found "a count of 2 bits often gives better accuracy than a count of one bit, but going to larger counters than 2 bits does not necessarily give better results."
- **History registers — global and per-branch** — shift registers that record the recent outcomes of branches, one bit per outcome (1 = taken, 0 = not-taken). A global history register (GHR) records the last outcomes of every branch in execution order; a per-branch history register records one branch's own last outcomes. Yeh & Patt (1991): "The history register is a shift register which shifts in bits representing the branch results of the most recent history information."
- **The pattern history table (PHT)** — the table the history indexes. Each entry holds the prediction state (a 2-bit counter in the classic design) for one history pattern; the history register's contents are the address. Yeh & Patt: the scheme "has two major data structures, the branch history register (HR) and the branch history pattern table (PT)." The same history pattern recurring means the same entry is consulted, so the table learns "what happened last time this pattern appeared."
- **The branch target buffer (BTB)** — a small cache that maps a branch's address to its target address (and, in Lee & Smith's design, to its prediction state). Direction prediction says taken or not; the BTB says where to. Without it, a correctly predicted taken branch still stalls while the target is computed. Lee & Smith (1984) built the BTB around "2-bit saturating up-down counters to collect history information which is then used to make predictions."
- **The return address stack (RAS)** — a tiny last-in-first-out stack that predicts the target of a return instruction from the address pushed by the matching call. Calls and returns pair up, so a stack predicts them almost perfectly where a BTB entry would alias. The Alpha 21264 shipped a 32-entry return address stack (per Microprocessor Report's coverage of the chip).
- **The chooser / meta-predictor** — a table of 2-bit counters that learns, per branch, which of two predictors to trust. McFarling (1993): the combining technique "uses a history mechanism to keep track of which predictor is most accurate for each branch so that the most accurate predictor can be used." The chooser is itself a saturating counter, nudged toward whichever sub-predictor was right last time.
- **TAGE tagged tables** — a base bimodal predictor backed by several tagged tables indexed by branch histories of geometrically increasing length. Each entry holds a signed 3-bit prediction counter, a partial tag and a 1-bit useful counter; the prediction comes from the tagged table with the longest matching history. Seznec's ISL-TAGE paper: "The TAGE predictor features a base predictor T_0 in charge of providing a basic prediction and a set of (partially) tagged predictor components Ti."
- **Perceptron weight tables** — rows of small signed weights, one row per branch, that vote on the outcome: the prediction is the sign of the weighted sum of the history bits. Jimenez & Lin (2001): "The source of our predictor's accuracy is its ability to use long history lengths, because the hardware resources for our method scale linearly, rather than exponentially, with the history length."

**The piece that makes it special:** the history-indexed table — prediction as a lookup keyed by the past. Nothing in a branch predictor computes anything about the program; it only remembers what happened last time the same situation arose, and looks it up. Every advance in forty years is a better index into that same table: a second bit of hysteresis (Smith), the history pattern as the address (Yeh & Patt), hashing the address into the history (McFarling's gshare), tags so different branches stop sharing entries (TAGE), and learned weights in place of counters (perceptron). The table is the computer; the index is the research.

**The architecture.** The predictor lives on the fetch side of the pipeline, in parallel with the instruction cache. At fetch, the PC is presented to the BTB and to the direction predictor at once: the BTB returns a target address if the branch has been seen before, the direction predictor returns taken/not-taken, and a next-PC mux picks the predicted target or the fall-through address — all in the fetch cycle, before the branch is even decoded. Calls push their return address onto the RAS; returns pop it. The prediction is carried along with the instruction as a tag; when the branch resolves in execute, the true outcome is compared with the prediction, and on a mismatch the pipeline flushes everything fetched down the wrong path and restarts at the correct target. Predictor tables are updated at retire, not at resolve, so wrong-path predictions never pollute the tables — but the delay means one table entry can mispredict several times in a row before its update lands, which is the problem Seznec's Immediate Update Mimicker exists to fix. Kessler's account of the Alpha 21264 adds one more fetch-side trick: line and way prediction, which predicts the I-cache line and way of the next fetch block so the branch predictor and tag comparison sit outside the critical fetch loop.

#### Inside the signature block: The two-level adaptive predictor — history picks the counter

Yeh & Patt's 1991 design has two structures and one rule. The **history register table (HRT)** is indexed by branch address and holds one shift register per branch; the **pattern history table (PT)** is a single global table of prediction state, indexed by the contents of a history register. The rule: predict from the pattern, then shift the outcome in.

**Sub-blocks.** (1) The per-branch history register table — an array of k-bit shift registers, one per tracked branch, indexed by low PC bits. (2) The global pattern table — 2^k entries of prediction state (the paper studies several finite-state automata for the entry, including the A2 saturating up-down counter). (3) The prediction function — a combinational read of the addressed entry's state, whose high bit is the prediction. (4) The update FSM — a Moore machine (the paper's words: "the finite-state machine is a Moore machine with the output z characterized by equation 1") that takes the old pattern-history bits and the branch outcome and produces the new bits. (5) The history shift logic — on resolution, the outcome shifts left into the history register's least-significant bit.

**Trace of one branch.** A conditional branch at PC 0x4000 is fetched. Its low PC bits index the HRT and read out its history register — say the last four outcomes were T-T-N-T, bits 1101. Those four bits address the pattern table; entry 1101 holds a 2-bit counter at value 3 (strongly taken), so the prediction is taken and fetch continues at the BTB's target. Three cycles later the branch resolves: it was in fact taken. The outcome 1 shifts into the history register (now 1011), and the counter in entry 1101 is incremented — it saturates at 3, so it stays. Had the branch been not-taken, the counter would have decremented to 2 (weakly taken) and the history would have become 1010 — and the next time pattern 1101 recurs, the same entry answers again, now one step closer to flipping.

**Bottleneck relieved, bottleneck created.** The two-level scheme relieves the ceiling of the single-level counter: a branch whose outcome depends on what other branches just did (a correlated branch) is now predicted from the pattern, not from its own past alone — 97% accuracy on nine of ten SPEC benchmarks against under 93% for the other schemes of the day, a 3% miss rate against a 7% best case. It creates three new bottlenecks. First, aliasing: two different branches (or two different history patterns) that hash to the same pattern-table entry share one counter and corrupt each other — the paper's tables have no tags, so there is no way to tell them apart. Second, exponential growth: a k-bit history needs 2^k pattern-table entries, so every extra history bit doubles the table; long histories are unaffordable in this form. Third, the update path: the pattern table is updated only when a branch resolves, so a hot branch can be mispredicted repeatedly while its update is still in flight.

**Governing numbers (published).** 97% accuracy / 3% miss rate on nine of ten SPEC benchmarks, versus under 93% / 7% best case for other schemes (Yeh & Patt 1991). Static prediction (predict all taken) achieves approximately 68% (Lee & Smith, as reported by Yeh & Patt). About 60% of conditional branches in the benchmarks are taken (Yeh & Patt 1991). History length k and table size are design parameters the paper explores across configurations; no single k is the paper's "the" answer, so none is quoted here as the design's number.

#### Inside the signature block: TAGE — tagged tables at geometric history lengths

Seznec and Michaud's TAGE (2006), in the form Seznec submitted to the Championship Branch Prediction contests, is the two-level idea with the aliasing problem attacked head-on: tag the entries, and give each table a different history length so short correlations and very long ones are both captured without one exponential table.

**Sub-blocks.** (1) The base predictor T0 — a simple PC-indexed 2-bit-counter bimodal table, with its hysteresis bit shared among several counters to save storage. (2) The tagged components T1…TM — independent tables, each indexed by the PC folded with a history of a different length; the lengths form a geometric series, so the longest tables see histories of up to 2,000 branches in the 512-Kbit ISL-TAGE submission. Each entry holds a 3-bit signed prediction counter, a partial tag and a 1-bit useful counter. (3) The tag comparators — one per table, comparing the computed tag against the stored tag to decide a hit. (4) The provider/alternate selection logic — the hitting component with the longest history provides the prediction; the next-longest hit (or the base prediction) is the alternate, used when the provider's counter is weak and the global USE_ALT_ON_NA 4-bit counter says the alternate has been better. (5) The allocation logic — on a misprediction by a component that is not the longest, new entries are allocated in longer-history components, choosing up to four entries whose useful bits are clear and never in consecutive tables. (6) The u-bit reset — a single 8-bit TICK counter watches allocation successes and failures and resets all useful bits when failures dominate. (7) The side predictors — a loop predictor, a statistical corrector, and the Immediate Update Mimicker (IUM), each addressing a failure class TAGE itself handles badly.

**Trace of one branch.** A conditional branch is fetched. In parallel, the base predictor and every tagged table are indexed by the PC folded with their history lengths; each table's tag comparator checks its stored tag. Suppose T3 and T7 hit. T7 uses the longer history, so it is the provider: its 3-bit counter's sign is the prediction, and T3's prediction is the alternate. If T7's counter is weak (confidence null) and the USE_ALT_ON_NA counter is negative, the alternate wins instead. Fetch proceeds down the predicted path. At retire, the provider's counter is updated; if the prediction was wrong and T7 is not the longest component, the allocator tries to place the branch in longer-history tables, picking entries with clear useful bits. The useful bit of the provider is set whenever the provider was right and the alternate was wrong. Meanwhile the loop predictor watches for the branch executing the same iteration count seven times in a row, and the statistical corrector sums its own tables' votes against the TAGE prediction, reverting it when the sum is large enough and disagrees.

**Bottleneck relieved, bottleneck created.** TAGE relieves the two-level scheme's exponential wall: geometric history lengths let one predictor capture correlations "even if the correlation is with very remote branches, e.g. on a 1000 bits branch history" (Seznec 2011) while tags stop unrelated branches from sharing entries. It creates new bottlenecks of its own: tag storage and comparison on every table every fetch; allocation pressure — a mispredicting branch must find a free useful-clear entry in a longer table or it is never learned; and the retire-time update delay, which lets one entry mispredict repeatedly before its correction lands (the IUM recovers about three-quarters of those). The side predictors add their own storage and a second decision to make.

**Governing numbers (published).** The ISL-TAGE submission (CBP-3, 2011) is a 16-component TAGE predictor — 15 tagged components plus the base bimodal predictor — at a 512-Kbit budget, with history lengths from 8 to 2,000. A tagged entry is a 3-bit prediction counter, a partial tag and a 1-bit useful counter. The loop predictor has 64 entries, 4-way skewed associative, 47 bits per entry (10-bit past iteration count, 10-bit speculative and 10-bit retire iteration counts, 10-bit partial tag, 3-bit confidence, 3-bit age, 1 direction bit) — 3,008 bits total — and provides its prediction once a loop has executed seven times with the same iteration count. The statistical corrector uses 5 logical tables at history lengths (0, 3, 8, 12, 17), sharing one interleaved 4K-entry table of 6-bit counters (3 KB); its prediction is the sign of the summed centered votes plus the TAGE output weighted ×8, reverted past a dynamic threshold. The IUM is a 64-entry fully-associative table of 20-bit entries (160 bytes) plus head/tail pointers. TAGE won the 2nd Championship Branch Prediction in 2006; TAGE-SC-L won the 4th (2014) and 5th (2016) contests in both the 32-Kbit and 256-Kbit categories.

#### Down to the primitives: The two-level adaptive predictor — history picks the counter

- **Shift register (global/per-branch history)** — a chain of D flip-flops, one per history bit, shifting the newest outcome into the least-significant position each time a branch resolves. Width equals the history length k; k is a design parameter the papers simulate across configurations, not a published constant of the design.
- **History register table (HRT)** — a small SRAM/register array indexed by low PC bits, one k-bit shift register per tracked branch. Depth and banking are not published for the paper's design; the table is a design parameter.
- **Pattern history table (PHT)** — an SRAM bank of 2-bit saturating counters, 2^k entries for a k-bit history, one counter per pattern. The entry width (2 bits) is published; the table depth follows from the chosen k and is not a fixed published number.
- **Saturating up/down counter (2-bit)** — the prediction state itself: increments on taken, decrements on not-taken, clamping at 0 and 3 instead of wrapping. The prediction is the counter's most-significant bit — a wire, not logic.
- **Index muxes** — the PC bits and history bits are muxed and concatenated into the PHT address; in gshare the two are XORed instead (see below).
- **Update FSM (Moore machine)** — combinational next-state logic taking the old pattern-history bits and the resolved outcome and producing the new bits; the prediction is a function of the state alone, which is what makes it a Moore machine in Yeh & Patt's terms.
- **gshare hash (McFarling's refinement)** — an XOR of the global history register with the low PC bits, forming a single PHT index so one table serves every history pattern and storage is shared instead of replicated per branch. The XOR width equals the index width; the specific history lengths McFarling simulated are not quoted here as the design's numbers.

#### Down to the primitives: TAGE — tagged tables at geometric history lengths

- **Tagged SRAM tables (T1…TM)** — one SRAM bank per component, each entry storing a partial tag, a 3-bit signed prediction counter and a 1-bit useful counter (ISL-TAGE). Table depths and tag widths vary by component and are design parameters; the 512-Kbit ISL-TAGE budget and 16-component count are published, per-component depths are not.
- **Tag comparators** — one comparator per tagged table: the computed tag is compared against the stored tag, bit by bit, to declare a hit or miss. A miss means that table abstains, however good its counter looks.
- **Hash/fold functions** — XOR trees that fold the PC together with the geometrically-long history into an index and a tag for each table. The fold widths follow the table sizes and are not published as fixed numbers.
- **Priority encoder (longest-match select)** — among the tables that hit, the one with the longest history wins; the encoder picks the highest-index hitting component and routes its counter's sign to the prediction mux, with the next-longest hit held as the alternate.
- **Base bimodal table (T0)** — a PC-indexed SRAM bank of 2-bit counters, with the hysteresis bit shared among several counters to save storage (ISL-TAGE). Depth is a design parameter.
- **Useful-bit counters + TICK** — one 1-bit useful counter per tagged entry, set when the provider is right and the alternate is wrong; a single 8-bit TICK counter monitors allocation success and failure and resets all useful bits when failures saturate it.
- **USE_ALT_ON_NA counter** — a single 4-bit counter tracking whether the alternate prediction beats the provider when the provider is weak; its sign decides whether the alternate is used.
- **Loop predictor tables** — a 64-entry, 4-way skewed-associative structure; each 47-bit entry holds iteration counts (10 bits past, 10 speculative, 10 retire), a 10-bit partial tag, 3-bit confidence, 3-bit age and 1 direction bit. Replacement is by age: an entry is replaceable only when its age counter is null, age starts at 7 on allocation and is reset to zero when the branch stops being a regular loop.
- **Statistical corrector tables** — 5 logical tables at history lengths (0, 3, 8, 12, 17) sharing one interleaved 4K-entry SRAM of 6-bit counters (3 KB); an adder tree sums the centered votes plus the TAGE output weighted ×8, and a dynamic-threshold comparator decides whether to revert the TAGE prediction.
- **IUM table** — a 64-entry fully-associative table (CAM) of 20-bit entries (160 bytes) plus head and tail pointers, remembering which TAGE entry predicted each in-flight branch so a re-fetch before retire can answer from the corrected outcome instead of the stale table.

#### Down to the gates: The two-level adaptive predictor — history picks the counter

- **History shift register** — k D flip-flops chained output-to-input, one per history bit. A D flip-flop is two cross-coupled latch stages, ≈20–28 transistors in a textbook standard-cell implementation; the shift itself is wires between stages, no gates. (Textbook-standard construction; the papers publish no flip-flop counts.)
- **2-bit saturating counter** — two D flip-flops holding the count, plus increment/decrement logic: a half-adder for the +1/−1 step and clamp logic (a small mux network) that holds the count at 0 and 3 instead of wrapping. The prediction is the high flip-flop's output — a wire. (Textbook-standard construction.)
- **Pattern history table SRAM** — a 6T-cell array (six transistors per stored bit) plus a row decoder, column muxes and sense amplifiers, in the primer's standard form. By arithmetic from the published geometry, the Alpha 21264's global predictor — 4,096 entries of 2-bit counters — is 8,192 data bits, or 49,152 cell transistors; its choice predictor, also 4,096 entries of 2-bit counters, is the same again; its local-history table — 1,024 entries of 10 bits — is 10,240 bits, or 61,440 cell transistors. (Arithmetic from Kessler's published table sizes; the 6T form is textbook-standard, not a claim about DEC's circuits.)
- **gshare XOR** — one XOR gate per index bit, XORing a history bit with a PC bit. Textbook construction: a 2-input XOR from four NAND2 gates, 16 transistors in the naive static-CMOS form. (Textbook-standard.)
- **Update FSM** — the Moore machine's next-state logic is a small combinational block of NAND/NOR gates driven by the old state bits and the resolved outcome; the state itself is the two flip-flops above. No gate count is published; the form is the textbook construction of a 2-bit FSM.

#### Down to the gates: TAGE — tagged tables at geometric history lengths

- **Tagged table SRAM** — each component is a 6T-cell array (tag bits + 3-bit counter + 1-bit useful bit per entry) with its own row decoder, column muxes and sense amplifiers, in the primer's standard form; the tables are bank-interleaved so adjacent history lengths share storage without a true multiported memory. Per-component depths are design parameters and are not published, so no per-table transistor total is claimed.
- **Tag comparator** — one XNOR gate per tag bit (textbook static-CMOS construction from NAND/NOR gates) feeding an AND-reduction tree that asserts hit only when every tag bit matches. A tag mismatch costs a whole table's vote in one gate delay of the tree.
- **Priority encoder (longest-match select)** — an OR-tree over the per-table hit signals feeding encoder logic that selects the highest-index hitting component; the prediction mux then steers that component's counter sign to the output. (Textbook-standard construction.)
- **Base bimodal table** — a 6T-cell SRAM bank of 2-bit counters, same standard form as the PHT above.
- **Useful-bit and TICK counters** — the 1-bit useful counter is a single D flip-flop with set/reset; the 8-bit TICK counter is eight flip-flops plus an incrementer (a ripple of half-adders, textbook-standard). The USE_ALT_ON_NA 4-bit counter is four flip-flops plus increment/decrement logic of the same form.
- **Loop predictor entry** — 47 D flip-flops of storage per entry (10 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 3 + 3 + 1 bits) plus a 10-bit tag comparator per way and age-comparison logic for replacement; the 4-way skewed-associative lookup is four parallel tag compares feeding a way-select mux. (Textbook-standard construction from the published 47-bit entry format.)
- **Statistical corrector adder tree** — the sum of the centered 6-bit votes is a tree of full adders; a full adder is two half adders (XOR/AND/OR gates), ≈28 transistors in the textbook static-CMOS mirror form, and the tree depth grows logarithmically with the number of tables summed. The dynamic-threshold compare is a magnitude comparator on the sum. (Textbook-standard construction.)
- **IUM CAM** — a fully-associative table: each 20-bit entry is a CAM cell (an SRAM cell plus XOR match logic feeding a matchline, in the primer's standard form) with a priority encoder selecting among matches, plus head/tail pointer counters (6-bit counters by arithmetic from 64 entries, textbook-standard incrementers).
- **Perceptron dot product** — the perceptron's vote is a sum of signed weights selected by the history bits: a row of weight registers feeding an adder tree of full adders, with the prediction taken from the sum's sign bit. The weights are small signed counters; their exact width is a design parameter and is not claimed here. (Textbook-standard construction of the summation; the linear-scaling claim is Jimenez & Lin's.)

**Honesty.** No vendor or paper in this entry publishes a netlist, schematic or gate count for a branch predictor as shipped — not for the Alpha 21264's tournament predictor, not for any TAGE implementation, not for a perceptron predictor. Every gate and transistor figure above is the textbook-standard construction of the named primitive from the primer's bottom layer, or arithmetic from a published table geometry (entry counts and widths) using the textbook 6T cell — never a claim about a specific chip's circuits. Where the papers publish a number, it is quoted with its source; where they do not, this entry says so.

**Key numbers.** Smith 1981 (ISCA 8, pp. 135–148): 2-bit counters beat 1-bit, larger counters do not necessarily help. Lee & Smith 1984: the branch target buffer. Yeh & Patt 1991: 97% accuracy, 3% miss rate on nine of ten SPEC benchmarks. McFarling 1993: 98.1% correct versus 97.1% for the best prior approach. Alpha 21264 (1998): 15 million transistors, 0.35 µm, 500–600 MHz; tournament predictor with 90–100% success on most simulated benchmarks; 7-cycle mispredict cost. Jimenez & Lin 2001: 4-KB perceptron, 1.94% misprediction rate on SPEC2000 integer, 53% better than gshare. TAGE (2006): CBP-2 winner; ISL-TAGE (2011): 16 components, 512 Kbits, histories 8–2,000; TAGE-SC-L: CBP-4 (2014) and CBP-5 (2016) winner in both size categories.

**Signature ideas.** (1) Hysteresis — one extra bit turns a last-outcome flip-flop into a predictor that survives a single anomaly. (2) History-indexed prediction — the pattern of recent branches, not the branch alone, picks the counter. (3) Hashing history with address — gshare lets one table serve every history pattern. (4) Tagged geometric histories — TAGE captures thousand-branch correlations without an exponential table. (5) Learned weights — the perceptron votes with a dot product, so cost grows linearly, not exponentially, with history length.

**Limits & tradeoffs.** Aliasing never goes away: any table without tags lets unrelated branches corrupt each other, and even TAGE's partial tags admit false matches. Tables start cold — the Alpha 21264 resets its predictor tables on a context switch, so every new context pays retraining; big tables warm slowly, small tables warm fast and forget fast. Latency fights accuracy: longer histories, more tables and wider adder trees all cost fetch-cycle time and power, which is why predictors are read in parallel with the I-cache and updated at retire. Deeper pipelines raise the stakes both ways: a correct prediction keeps more work flowing, a mispredict flushes more of it — the 21264's seven-cycle cost is the tax on every miss. Indirect branches need target prediction, not just direction, which is why TAGE grew an indirect sibling (ITTAGE, CBP-3 indirect champion 2011). And predictor state is observable timing state: the same tables that make speculation fast became a side channel (Spectre, 2018), so modern predictors also have to be partitioned or flushed on privilege changes — accuracy is no longer the only metric.

**Lineage.** Smith (1981, 2-bit counter) → Lee & Smith (1984, BTB and static training) → Yeh & Patt (1991 two-level adaptive; 1992, the GAg/GAp/PAg/PAp family naming) → McFarling (1993, gshare and the tournament chooser) → Alpha 21264 (1998, the first major shipped tournament predictor) → Jimenez & Lin (2001, perceptron) → Seznec & Michaud (2006, TAGE) → Seznec (2011, ISL-TAGE and TAGE-SC-L; CBP wins 2014 and 2016). The toolkit it built — counters with hysteresis, history-indexed tables, hashed indexes, tag-checked tables, choosers and learned weights — is the fetch-side vocabulary of every high-performance core since, and the Championship Branch Prediction contests still run on its terms.

**One-line summary.** A branch predictor is a small table of remembered pasts that guesses the future of control flow — and the whole history of the field is better ways to index that table.

**New fact records added in this run** (appended to `files/fact-records.json`; statuses per the fact standard):

- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — Prediction lets the machine fetch, decode and issue before the outcome is known. Source: Smith, "A Study of Branch Prediction Strategies", Proc. 8th ISCA, 1981, pp. 135–148.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — A 2-bit count often beats a 1-bit count, but larger counters do not necessarily help. Source: Smith 1981.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — The Branch Target Buffer uses 2-bit saturating up-down counters. Source: Lee & Smith, "Branch Prediction Strategies and Branch Target Buffer Design", IEEE Computer 17(1):6–22, Jan 1984 (as described in Yeh & Patt 1991).
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — Two-Level Adaptive Training achieves 97% accuracy on nine of ten SPEC benchmarks, vs under 93% for other schemes; 3% vs 7% miss rate. Source: Yeh & Patt, "Two-Level Adaptive Training Branch Prediction", Proc. 24th MICRO, 1991, pp. 51–61.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — The scheme's two major data structures are the branch history register and the branch history pattern table. Source: Yeh & Patt 1991.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — The history register is a shift register of the most recent branch results. Source: Yeh & Patt 1991.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — Static all-taken prediction achieves approximately 68% accuracy; about 60% of conditional branches are taken. Source: Yeh & Patt 1991 (citing Lee & Smith).
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — Combining predictors reaches 98.1% correct vs 97.1% for the best prior approach. Source: McFarling, "Combining Branch Predictors", DEC WRL TN-36, June 1993.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — McFarling's combining method tracks which predictor is most accurate per branch and uses that one. Source: McFarling 1993.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — Hashing branch history together with the branch address increases the usefulness of history. Source: McFarling 1993.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — The 21264 implements a sophisticated tournament branch prediction scheme choosing between local-history and global-history predictors. Source: Kessler, "The Alpha 21264 Microprocessor", IEEE Micro, Mar–Apr 1999.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — Local predictor: 10 bits of pattern history for up to 1,024 branches, picking from 1,024 prediction counters. Source: Kessler 1999.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — Global predictor: 4,096-entry table of 2-bit saturating counters indexed by the path history of the last 12 branches. Source: Kessler 1999.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — Choice predictor: 4,096-entry table of 2-bit counters indexed by the path history. Source: Kessler 1999.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — Tournament predictor: 90% to 100% success rate on most simulated applications/benchmarks. Source: Kessler 1999.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — Seven-cycle mispredict cost on the 21264. Source: Kessler 1999.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — 21264: 15 million transistors, 0.35-micron CMOS, 500–600 MHz. Source: Kessler 1999.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — TAGE is often considered state-of-the-art among conditional branch predictors proposed by academia. Source: Seznec, "A New Case for the TAGE Branch Predictor", Proc. 44th MICRO, 2011.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — TAGE features a base predictor T0 and a set of (partially) tagged predictor components Ti. Source: Seznec, "A 64 Kbytes ISL-TAGE branch predictor", JWAC-2/CBP-3, 2011.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — A tagged TAGE entry is a 3-bit signed counter, a partial tag and a 1-bit useful counter. Source: Seznec, ISL-TAGE, 2011.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — ISL-TAGE loop predictor: 64 entries, 4-way skewed associative, 47 bits per entry, 3,008 bits total. Source: Seznec, ISL-TAGE, 2011.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — Statistical corrector: 5 logical tables at history lengths (0,3,8,12,17), one interleaved 4K-entry table of 6-bit counters; prediction is the sign of the summed centered votes plus the TAGE output ×8. Source: Seznec, ISL-TAGE, 2011.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — IUM recovers about 3/4 of the mispredictions due to late update; 64×20 bits, 160 bytes. Source: Seznec, ISL-TAGE, 2011.
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — TAGE-SC-L won CBP-4 (2014) and CBP-5 (2016) in both 32-Kbit and 256-Kbit categories; (L-)TAGE won CBP-2 (2006). Source: Seznec, INRIA ALF branch-prediction research page (author's own championship record).
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — Perceptron predictor hardware scales linearly, not exponentially, with history length. Source: Jimenez & Lin, "Dynamic Branch Prediction with Perceptrons", Proc. 7th HPCA, 2001 (revised report).
- [verified] **Branch Prediction — From 2-Bit Counters to TAGE and Perceptrons** — At a 4-KB budget the global-history perceptron reaches a 1.94% misprediction rate on SPEC2000 integer, a 53% improvement over gshare. Source: Jimenez & Lin 2001.
